results.name: Uniform convergence theorem for slowly varying functions
aliases: uniform convergence theorem for regularly varying functions
results.statement: Let a > 0 and let L: [a, ∞) → (0, ∞) be a Lebesgue measurable function that is slowly varying, that is, L(λx)/L(x) → 1 as x → ∞ for every λ > 0. Then for every compact interval [c, d] ⊂ (0, ∞), sup_{c ≤ λ ≤ d} |L(λx)/L(x) − 1| → 0 as x → ∞. More generally, let f: [a, ∞) → (0, ∞) be measurable and regularly varying with index ρ ∈ ℝ, that is, f(λx)/f(x) → λ^ρ as x → ∞ for every λ > 0. Then sup_{c ≤ λ ≤ d} |f(λx)/f(x) − λ^ρ| → 0 as x → ∞.
hypotheses: The function L (or f) is Lebesgue measurable and positive on [a, ∞) for some a > 0.
For every λ > 0, L(λx)/L(x) → 1 as x → ∞ (or f(λx)/f(x) → λ^ρ for a fixed ρ ∈ ℝ).
The interval [c, d] is compact, with 0 < c ≤ d < ∞.

prerequisites.reason: Step s4 applies the reverse Fatou inequality of the Fatou–Lebesgue theorem to indicators of bad sets, which are bounded by the indicator of [−2K, 2K], and gets m(lim sup A_n) ≥ lim sup m(A_n).

definitions.name: slowly varying function
definitions.text: A positive measurable function L on [a, ∞) with L(λx)/L(x) → 1 as x → ∞ for every λ > 0. Examples are positive constants and log x.

definitions.name: regularly varying function
definitions.text: A positive measurable function f on [a, ∞) with f(λx)/f(x) → λ^ρ as x → ∞ for every λ > 0. The number ρ is the index. Equivalently f(x) = x^ρ L(x) with L slowly varying.

definitions.name: limit superior of sets
definitions.text: For sets A₁, A₂, …, lim sup A_n = ⋂_{k≥1} ⋃_{n≥k} A_n. It is the set of points that lie in infinitely many of the sets A_n.

source.excerpt: Theorem 1.2.4 (Uniform convergence theorem for regularly varying functions) … lim_{x→∞} f(tx)/f(x) = t^α, uniformly in t (a) on each [a, b] if α = 0, (b) on each (0, b] if α > 0, (c) on each [a, ∞) if α < 0.
source.attribution: © T. Mikosch. Quoted from the author's lecture notes for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The excerpt omits the source hypothesis that f is regularly varying with index α, and bounded on each interval (0, x] when α > 0. Each of the three source cases contains uniformity on every compact interval [c, d] ⊂ (0, ∞), which is the authored statement for every index, with no boundedness condition. The source states the theorem without proof. The authored proof follows the proof of Theorem 1.3 (uniform convergence theorem) in Geluk and de Haan, CWI Tract 40 (1987), pp. 4-5.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the proof of Theorem 1.3 in Geluk and de Haan, CWI Tract 40 (1987). No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement: the slowly varying case and the regularly varying case with any index ρ ∈ ℝ, on every compact interval [c, d] ⊂ (0, ∞).

steps.text: Reduce to the slowly varying case. If f is regularly varying with index ρ, then L(x) = x^(−ρ) f(x) is positive, measurable and slowly varying, and f(λx)/f(x) − λ^ρ = λ^ρ (L(λx)/L(x) − 1). For λ ∈ [c, d] the factor λ^ρ is at most max(c^ρ, d^ρ). So the general claim follows from the slowly varying case. Now let L be slowly varying. Put b = log a and h(u) = log L(e^u) for u ≥ b. Then h is measurable, and slow variation says that h(u + v) − h(u) → 0 as u → ∞ for every fixed v ∈ ℝ.

Reduce to a statement about h. Let K = max(|log c|, |log d|). Every λ ∈ [c, d] is λ = e^v with |v| ≤ K. With u = log x, |L(λx)/L(x) − 1| = |e^(h(u+v) − h(u)) − 1| ≤ e^(|h(u+v) − h(u)|) − 1. So it suffices to prove that S(u) = sup_{|v| ≤ K} |h(u + v) − h(u)| tends to 0 as u → ∞.

Suppose that S(u) does not tend to 0. Then there are ε > 0, points u_n → ∞ and shifts v_n ∈ [−K, K] with |h(u_n + v_n) − h(u_n)| ≥ ε for every n. Remove finitely many n so that u_n − 3K ≥ b. Let J = [−K, K], A_n = {y ∈ J : |h(u_n + y) − h(u_n)| ≥ ε/2} and B_n = {y ∈ J : |h(u_n + y) − h(u_n + v_n)| ≥ ε/2}. Both sets are measurable because h is measurable. If some y ∈ J were in neither set, the triangle inequality would give |h(u_n + v_n) − h(u_n)| < ε, which is false. So A_n ∪ B_n = J, and m(A_n) ≥ K or m(B_n) ≥ K, where m is Lebesgue measure.

Shift the second family. Let w_n = u_n + v_n, so w_n ≥ u_n − K → ∞, and let C_n = B_n − v_n. Then C_n ⊂ [−2K, 2K], m(C_n) = m(B_n) by translation invariance, and C_n is the set of z with |h(w_n + z) − h(w_n)| ≥ ε/2. Hence there is an infinite set N of indices with m(A_n) ≥ K for all n ∈ N, or with m(C_n) ≥ K for all n ∈ N. Consider the first case. The indicators of A_n, n ∈ N, are bounded by the integrable indicator of [−2K, 2K]. The reverse Fatou inequality gives m(lim sup_{n∈N} A_n) = ∫ lim sup 1_{A_n} dm ≥ lim sup ∫ 1_{A_n} dm ≥ K > 0. The second case gives m(lim sup_{n∈N} C_n) ≥ K in the same way.

Conclude. In the first case the limit superior set has positive measure, so it contains a point y*. This point lies in A_n for infinitely many n ∈ N, so |h(u_n + y*) − h(u_n)| ≥ ε/2 for infinitely many n, while u_n → ∞. This contradicts h(u + y*) − h(u) → 0 as u → ∞. In the second case a point z* in the limit superior of the C_n gives |h(w_n + z*) − h(w_n)| ≥ ε/2 for infinitely many n with w_n → ∞, which contradicts h(w + z*) − h(w) → 0. All points used lie in [b, ∞) because u_n − 3K ≥ b. Hence S(u) → 0, and steps s1 and s2 give both claims.

applications.title: Uniform Pareto approximation of excess probabilities for a loss
applications.inputs: A loss X with tail P(X > x) = F̄(x) = (x + 1)/(2x³) for x ≥ 1, ratios λ ∈ [1, 4] and a threshold x ≥ 1. The excess probability is P(X > λx | X > x) = F̄(λx)/F̄(x).
applications.hypotheses: F̄ is continuous, so measurable, and positive on [1, ∞). F̄(1) = 1, and F̄ decreases because its derivative is −x⁻⁴(2x + 3)/2 < 0. F̄(x) = x⁻² L(x) with L(x) = (1 + 1/x)/2 → 1/2, so L is slowly varying and F̄ is regularly varying with index −2. The interval [1, 4] is compact in (0, ∞).

steps.text: Compute the ratio: F̄(λx)/F̄(x) = λ⁻² (1 + 1/(λx))/(1 + 1/x) = λ⁻² (λx + 1)/(λ(x + 1)) = λ⁻² (1 − (1 − 1/λ)/(x + 1)). So the error of the Pareto value λ⁻² is e(λ, x) = (λ⁻² − λ⁻³)/(x + 1) ≥ 0 for λ ≥ 1.

Maximize g(λ) = λ⁻² − λ⁻³ on [1, 4]. Its derivative is λ⁻⁴(3 − 2λ), so the maximum is at λ = 3/2, with g(3/2) = 4/9 − 8/27 = 4/27. Hence sup_{1 ≤ λ ≤ 4} |F̄(λx)/F̄(x) − λ⁻²| = 4/(27(x + 1)), which tends to 0 as the theorem says.
The Pareto value is (2/3)² = 324/729, so the error at this point is 324/729 − 320/729 = 4/729. This equals the uniform bound 4/(27 · 27) at x = 26.

applications.conclusion: For every threshold x ≥ 1, the Pareto value λ⁻² approximates P(X > λx | X > x) with error at most 4/(27(x + 1)), uniformly for λ ∈ [1, 4]. At x = 26 the largest error is 4/729, at λ = 3/2.

limitations: The theorem gives uniformity only on compact subsets of (0, ∞). Uniformity on (0, d] for ρ > 0 or on [c, ∞) for ρ < 0 needs extra conditions and extra arguments.
The theorem gives no rate of convergence. A rate needs a second-order condition on L.

results.name: Karamata representation theorem for slowly varying functions
aliases: representation theorem for slowly varying functions
results.statement: Let a > 0 and let L: [a, ∞) → (0, ∞) be measurable. Then L is slowly varying if and only if L(x) = c(x) exp(∫_a^x ε(u)/u du) for all x ≥ a, where c and ε are measurable functions on [a, ∞), ε is bounded on bounded intervals, c(x) → c₀ ∈ (0, ∞) and ε(x) → 0 as x → ∞. Consequently, a measurable f: [a, ∞) → (0, ∞) is regularly varying with index ρ ∈ ℝ if and only if f(x) = c(x) exp(∫_a^x δ(u)/u du) for all x ≥ a, with c as above and δ measurable, bounded on bounded intervals and δ(u) → ρ as u → ∞.
hypotheses: The function L is measurable and positive on [a, ∞) for some a > 0.
For the direct part, L(λx)/L(x) → 1 as x → ∞ for every λ > 0.
For the converse, L has the stated form with measurable c and ε, ε bounded on bounded intervals, c(x) → c₀ ∈ (0, ∞) and ε(x) → 0.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 applies Karamata's integral theorem with index 0 to get local boundedness of L and the limit b(x) = x L(x)/F(x) → 1.
Step s2 uses the Lebesgue differentiation theorem to get F' = L almost everywhere for F(x) = ∫_X^x L(s) ds.
Step s2 uses the fundamental theorem of calculus for the absolutely continuous function log F to write log F(x) − log F(x₁) as an integral of b(s)/s.

definitions.name: Karamata ratio
definitions.text: For a positive locally integrable L and F(x) = ∫_X^x L(s) ds, the ratio b(x) = x L(x)/F(x). For slowly varying L it tends to 1.

source.excerpt: Theorem 1.2.1 (Representation theorem) A positive measurable function L on [x₀, ∞) is slowly varying if and only if it can be written in the form L(x) = c(x) exp{∫_{x₀}^x ε(y)/y dy} (1.2) where c(·) is a measurable non-negative function such that lim_{x→∞} c(x) = c₀ ∈ (0, ∞) and ε(x) → 0 as x → ∞.
source.attribution: © T. Mikosch. Quoted from the author's lecture notes for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states the theorem for slowly varying L, with the lower limit x₀ of the integral at the left end of the domain. The authored statement also requires ε to be measurable and bounded on bounded intervals, so that the integral exists, and adds the form for regularly varying functions that the source gives in Remark 1.2.2. The source gives no proof. The authored proof follows the proof of Theorem 1.5 (representation theorem) in Geluk and de Haan, CWI Tract 40 (1987), p. 8, which uses formula (1.14) from the proof of Karamata's theorem on p. 7.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the proof of Theorem 1.5 (representation theorem) in Geluk and de Haan, CWI Tract 40 (1987). No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement: both directions for slowly varying functions and both directions for regularly varying functions with any index ρ.

steps.text: Let L be slowly varying. Karamata's integral theorem with index 0 gives X ≥ a such that L is bounded on bounded subintervals of [X, ∞). With F(x) = ∫_X^x L(s) ds it also gives b(x) = x L(x)/F(x) → 1 as x → ∞. Fix x₁ > X. Then F(x) ≥ F(x₁) > 0 for x ≥ x₁, so b is measurable and bounded on bounded subintervals of [x₁, ∞).

Integrate the logarithmic derivative. F is absolutely continuous on bounded intervals because it is an indefinite integral, and the Lebesgue differentiation theorem gives F' = L almost everywhere. Since log is Lipschitz on [F(x₁), ∞), log F is absolutely continuous on each [x₁, y], with (log F)'(s) = L(s)/F(s) = b(s)/s almost everywhere. The fundamental theorem of calculus gives log F(x) = log F(x₁) + ∫_{x₁}^x b(s)/s ds for x ≥ x₁.

Write L in the required form. Since L(x) = b(x)F(x)/x and 1/x = (1/x₁) exp(−∫_{x₁}^x ds/s), step s2 gives L(x) = b(x)(F(x₁)/x₁) exp(∫_{x₁}^x (b(s) − 1)/s ds) for x ≥ x₁. Put c(x) = b(x)F(x₁)/x₁ and ε(s) = b(s) − 1 on [x₁, ∞), and put c(x) = L(x) and ε(s) = 0 on [a, x₁). Then L(x) = c(x) exp(∫_a^x ε(u)/u du) for all x ≥ a. Both functions are measurable, ε is bounded on bounded intervals, c(x) → c₀ = F(x₁)/x₁ ∈ (0, ∞) and ε(x) → 0.

Converse. Suppose that L has the representation and fix λ > 0. For x ≥ a·max(1, 1/λ), L(λx)/L(x) = (c(λx)/c(x)) exp(∫_x^{λx} ε(u)/u du), with an oriented integral. The first factor tends to c₀/c₀ = 1. The integral has absolute value at most sup{|ε(u)| : u ≥ min(x, λx)} · |log λ|, and this tends to 0 because ε(u) → 0. So L(λx)/L(x) → 1.

Regularly varying functions. If f is regularly varying with index ρ, then L(x) = x^(−ρ) f(x) is slowly varying. Its representation and x^ρ = a^ρ exp(∫_a^x ρ/u du) give f(x) = a^ρ c(x) exp(∫_a^x (ρ + ε(u))/u du). Here a^ρ c(x) → a^ρ c₀ ∈ (0, ∞), and δ = ρ + ε is measurable, bounded on bounded intervals and tends to ρ. Conversely, if f has such a form, then f(λx)/f(x) = (c(λx)/c(x)) λ^ρ exp(∫_x^{λx} (δ(u) − ρ)/u du), and the argument of step s4 with δ − ρ in place of ε gives f(λx)/f(x) → λ^ρ.

applications.title: Representation of the slowly varying factor of a Pareto-type loss tail
applications.inputs: A loss tail F̄(x) = (x + 1)/(2x³) = x⁻² L(x) on [1, ∞), with slowly varying factor L(x) = (x + 1)/(2x). The thresholds are y = 3 and x = 6.
applications.hypotheses: L is continuous and positive on [1, ∞), and L(λx)/L(x) = (λx + 1)/(λ(x + 1)) → 1 for every λ > 0. So L is measurable and slowly varying, and the theorem gives a representation of L.

steps.text: Find ε from the logarithmic derivative: log L(x) = log(x + 1) − log 2 − log x, so ε(x) = x (log L)'(x) = x/(x + 1) − 1 = −1/(x + 1). Then ε is continuous, bounded and ε(x) → 0.
Check the representation with a = 1 and c ≡ 1: ∫_1^x ε(u)/u du = −∫_1^x (1/u − 1/(u + 1)) du = log((x + 1)/(2x)) = log L(x). So L(x) = exp(∫_1^x ε(u)/u du), and c₀ = 1 = L(1).

Use the representation to bound ratios. For x ≥ y ≥ 1, L(x)/L(y) = exp(∫_y^x ε(u)/u du), and −1/(y + 1) ≤ ε(u) < 0 for u ≥ y. Hence (y/x)^(1/(y+1)) ≤ L(x)/L(y) < 1. For y = 3 and x = 6 the lower bound is (1/2)^(1/4).

Compute the ratio at y = 3 and x = 6: L(6)/L(3) = (7/12)/(4/6) = 7/8. Its fourth power is 2401/4096, which is larger than 1/2 = 2048/4096. So 7/8 lies above the lower bound (1/2)^(1/4), as step a3 says.
The tail ratio is F̄(6)/F̄(3) = (3/6)² · L(6)/L(3) = (1/4)(7/8) = 7/32. The representation bound puts it between (1/4)(1/2)^(1/4) and the Pareto value 1/4.

applications.conclusion: The factor L(x) = (x + 1)/(2x) has the Karamata representation with c ≡ 1 and ε(u) = −1/(u + 1). It gives (y/x)^(1/(y+1)) ≤ L(x)/L(y) < 1 for x ≥ y ≥ 1. At y = 3 and x = 6 the tail ratio is 7/32, just below the Pareto value 1/4.

limitations: The functions c and ε are not unique. In particular, c may carry all irregular behavior of L, and ε may be chosen continuous or smooth.
The representation does not give a rate. The size of ε controls the rate at which L(λx)/L(x) tends to 1.

results.name: Karamata characterization theorem for regularly varying functions
aliases: characterization theorem for regularly varying functions
results.statement: Let a > 0 and let f: [a, ∞) → (0, ∞) be Lebesgue measurable. Suppose that for every λ in a Lebesgue measurable set Λ ⊂ (0, ∞) of positive measure the limit g(λ) = lim_{t→∞} f(λt)/f(t) exists and lies in (0, ∞). Then there is ρ ∈ ℝ such that f(λt)/f(t) → λ^ρ as t → ∞ for every λ > 0. So f is regularly varying with index ρ, and g(λ) = λ^ρ for λ ∈ Λ.
hypotheses: The function f is Lebesgue measurable and positive on [a, ∞) for some a > 0.
The set Λ ⊂ (0, ∞) is Lebesgue measurable with positive measure.
For every λ ∈ Λ, f(λt)/f(t) has a finite positive limit as t → ∞.

prerequisites.reason: Steps s3 and s5 use Steinhaus' theorem: a measurable set A of positive measure has a difference set A − A that contains an interval around 0.
Step s1 uses the change of variables formula for the map λ ↦ log λ to show that log Λ has positive Lebesgue measure.

definitions.name: regularly varying function
definitions.text: A positive measurable function f on [a, ∞) with f(λx)/f(x) → λ^ρ as x → ∞ for every λ > 0. The number ρ is the index.

definitions.name: difference set
definitions.text: For a set A ⊂ ℝ, the difference set is A − A = {x − y : x, y ∈ A}. Steinhaus' theorem says that it contains an interval around 0 when A is measurable with positive measure.

definitions.name: additive function
definitions.text: A function φ: ℝ → ℝ with φ(v + w) = φ(v) + φ(w) for all real v and w. It is a group homomorphism of (ℝ, +).

source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: In the source, (1.6) is the limit lim_{t→∞} f(tx)/f(t), and f is defined on (0, ∞) and eventually positive. The authored statement takes f positive on [a, ∞) and asks the set of x to be measurable. The authored proof follows the source proof on pp. 3-4: it passes to F(t) = log f(e^t), uses Steinhaus' theorem to show that the limit exists for every x, and solves the additive equation (1.7). For the last step it uses Steinhaus' theorem a second time instead of Lusin's theorem.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the proof of Theorem 1.2 in Geluk and de Haan, CWI Tract 40 (1987), with a Steinhaus argument in place of the Lusin step. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement for every measurable set Λ of positive measure. The proof does not use the values of the limit g, only its existence.

steps.text: Pass to additive form. Put h(u) = log f(e^u) for u ≥ log a. Then h is measurable. Let K be the set of v ∈ ℝ for which φ(v) = lim_{u→∞} (h(u + v) − h(u)) exists in ℝ. Then K contains log Λ = {log λ : λ ∈ Λ}. Since Λ has positive measure, E = Λ ∩ [1/n, n] has positive measure for some n. The change of variables formula gives m(log E) = ∫_E λ⁻¹ dλ ≥ m(E)/n > 0. So log Λ has positive measure.

K is an additive subgroup and φ is additive on K. The point 0 lies in K with φ(0) = 0, because h(u) − h(u) = 0. If v, w ∈ K, then h(u + v + w) − h(u) = [h((u + w) + v) − h(u + w)] + [h(u + w) − h(u)], and both brackets converge as u → ∞ because u + w → ∞. So v + w ∈ K and φ(v + w) = φ(v) + φ(w). Also h(u − v) − h(u) = −[h((u − v) + v) − h(u − v)] → −φ(v), so −v ∈ K and φ(−v) = −φ(v).

K = ℝ. By Steinhaus' theorem, log Λ − log Λ contains an interval (−δ, δ) with δ > 0. This difference set lies in K because K is a group. Every real v equals N · (v/N) for an integer N with |v/N| < δ, so v is a sum of N elements of K and lies in K. Hence φ is defined on all of ℝ and φ(v + w) = φ(v) + φ(w) for all real v and w.

φ is measurable. For an integer n put φ_n(v) = h(n + v) − h(n) when n + v ≥ log a, and φ_n(v) = 0 otherwise. Each φ_n is measurable because h is measurable. For every fixed v, φ_n(v) → φ(v) as n → ∞ along the integers, because the limit over real u → ∞ exists. So φ is a pointwise limit of measurable functions and is measurable.

φ is linear. The sets E_N = {v ∈ [0, 1] : |φ(v)| ≤ N} are measurable and increase to [0, 1], so m(E_N) > 0 for some N. Steinhaus' theorem gives η > 0 with (−η, η) ⊂ E_N − E_N, so |φ(w)| ≤ 2N for |w| < η. Additivity gives φ(qy) = qφ(y) for integers q, so φ(r) = rφ(1) for rational r. For real x and an integer q ≥ 1, choose a rational r with |x − r| < η/q. Then |φ(x) − rφ(1)| = |φ(x − r)| = |φ(q(x − r))|/q ≤ 2N/q, and |rφ(1) − xφ(1)| ≤ |φ(1)|η/q. Let q → ∞ to get φ(x) = xφ(1).

Conclusion. Put ρ = φ(1). For λ > 0 and t ≥ max(a, a/λ), f(λt)/f(t) = exp(h(log t + log λ) − h(log t)). As t → ∞, the exponent tends to φ(log λ) = ρ log λ, so f(λt)/f(t) → λ^ρ. Hence f is regularly varying with index ρ, and g(λ) = λ^ρ for every λ ∈ Λ.

applications.title: Power-law scaling from ratio limits on an interval of scale factors
applications.inputs: A measurable positive tail F̄(t) = P(X > t), for example of a cluster size or a loss, for which F̄(λt)/F̄(t) → g(λ) ∈ (0, ∞) for every λ ∈ Λ = [1, 2], with g(2) = 1/8.
applications.hypotheses: F̄ is positive and measurable on [1, ∞) because it is monotone and positive. The set Λ = [1, 2] is measurable with measure 1 > 0, and the limit exists in (0, ∞) for every λ ∈ Λ by assumption.

steps.text: The theorem gives ρ with F̄(λt)/F̄(t) → λ^ρ for every λ > 0. At λ = 2 this says 2^ρ = g(2) = 1/8, so ρ = −3, and F̄ is regularly varying with index −3.
The limit at the scale factor λ = 3/2, inside Λ, must be g(3/2) = (3/2)⁻³ = 8/27. A measured limit different from 8/27 would contradict the hypothesis.
The theorem also predicts the limit outside Λ, where nothing was assumed. At λ = 10, P(X > 10t)/P(X > t) → 10⁻³ = 1/1000.

The positive measure of Λ matters. The function f(t) = 2^⌊log₂ t⌋ has f(2t)/f(t) = 2 for every t, so the limit exists on the null set {2^k : k ∈ ℤ}. But f(3t/2)/f(t) equals 1 at t = 2^n and 2 at t = 3 · 2^(n−1), so f is not regularly varying.

applications.conclusion: Ratio limits on the interval [1, 2] with g(2) = 1/8 force P(X > λt)/P(X > t) → λ⁻³ for every λ > 0. For example the limit is 8/27 at λ = 3/2 and 1/1000 at λ = 10. Ratio limits on a null set of scale factors do not give this conclusion.

limitations: The set Λ must have positive measure, or be large in another sense. Ratio limits on the null set {2^k} do not imply regular variation, as the function 2^⌊log₂ t⌋ shows.

The theorem needs f to be measurable. With the axiom of choice there is a non-linear additive φ: ℝ → ℝ, and f(t) = exp(φ(log t)) then has f(λt)/f(t) = exp(φ(log λ)) for all t, which is not a power of λ.

results.name: Karamata's integral theorem for regularly varying functions
results.statement: Let f: [a, ∞) → (0, ∞) be measurable and regularly varying with index α ∈ ℝ. Then there is X ≥ a such that f is bounded on every bounded subinterval of [X, ∞). Put F(x) = ∫_X^x f(s) ds for x ≥ X. (i) If α > −1, then F(x) → ∞ and x f(x)/F(x) → α + 1 as x → ∞. (ii) If α = −1, then x f(x)/F(x) → 0. If moreover ∫_X^∞ f(s) ds < ∞, then x f(x)/∫_x^∞ f(s) ds → 0. (iii) If α < −1, then ∫_x^∞ f(s) ds < ∞ for x ≥ X and x f(x)/∫_x^∞ f(s) ds → −α − 1. Conversely, let g: [a, ∞) → (0, ∞) be measurable and integrable on bounded intervals. If x g(x)/∫_a^x g(s) ds → c ∈ (0, ∞), then g is regularly varying with index c − 1. If ∫_a^∞ g(s) ds < ∞ and x g(x)/∫_x^∞ g(s) ds → c ∈ (0, ∞), then g is regularly varying with index −c − 1.
hypotheses: For the direct part, f is Lebesgue measurable and positive on [a, ∞), and f(λx)/f(x) → λ^α as x → ∞ for every λ > 0.
For the converse, g is positive, measurable and integrable on bounded subintervals of [a, ∞), and the ratio x g(x)/∫_a^x g (or x g(x)/∫_x^∞ g, with a finite tail integral) has a limit c ∈ (0, ∞).

prerequisites.reason: Steps s1, s2 and s7 use the uniform convergence theorem: s1 bounds f on dyadic blocks, and s2 and s7 pass the limit f(xu)/f(x) → u^α inside an integral over a compact u-interval.
Step s8 uses the Lebesgue differentiation theorem to get F' = g almost everywhere for the indefinite integral F of g.
Step s8 uses the fundamental theorem of calculus for absolutely continuous functions to write log F(λx) − log F(x) as the integral of (log F)'.

definitions.name: regularly varying function
definitions.text: A positive measurable function f on [a, ∞) with f(λx)/f(x) → λ^α as x → ∞ for every λ > 0. The number α is the index. Equivalently f(x) = x^α L(x) with L slowly varying.

definitions.name: asymptotic equivalence
definitions.text: Two positive functions u and v are asymptotically equivalent, u(x) ~ v(x), when u(x)/v(x) → 1 as x → ∞. So (i) says F(x) ~ x f(x)/(α + 1).

definitions.name: tail integral
definitions.text: For an integrable f on [x, ∞), the tail integral is ∫_x^∞ f(s) ds. It decreases to 0 as x → ∞.

source.citation: J. L. Geluk and L. de Haan, Regular Variation, Extensions and Tauberian Theorems, CWI Tract 40, Centrum voor Wiskunde en Informatica, Amsterdam, 1987.
source.revision: Scan of the 1987 printed edition (ISBN 90 6196 324 9) in the CWI repository.
source.module: Chapter I, Section I.1 Regularly varying functions
source.excerpt: Theorem 1.4 (Karamata's theorem) Suppose f ∈ RV_α. There exists t₀ > 0 such that f(t) is positive and locally bounded for t ≥ t₀. If α ≥ −1, then lim_{t→∞} t f(t)/∫_{t₀}^t f(s) ds = α + 1. If α < −1, or α = −1 and ∫_0^∞ f(s) ds < ∞, then lim_{t→∞} t f(t)/∫_t^∞ f(s) ds = −α − 1. Conversely: if (1.8) holds with −1 < α < ∞, then f ∈ RV_α; if (1.9) holds with −∞ < α < −1, then f ∈ RV_α.
source.attribution: © J. L. Geluk and L. de Haan. Quoted from CWI Tract 40 for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states the theorem for f ∈ RV_α with integrals from a point t₀ beyond which f is positive and locally bounded, and it gives the converse for −1 < α < ∞ and for α < −1. The authored statement writes the case α = −1 separately and writes the converse with the limit c = α + 1 or c = −α − 1. The authored proof follows the source proof on pp. 5-7: dyadic blocks, regular variation of the integral, the limit (1.11) from the uniform convergence theorem, and the converse through b(t) = t f(t)/F(t). For the converse it integrates (log F)' = b(t)/t directly instead of using formula (1.14).

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the proof of Theorem 1.4 (Karamata's theorem) in Geluk and de Haan, CWI Tract 40 (1987). No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement: local boundedness, the three cases α > −1, α = −1 and α < −1 of the direct part, and both forms of the converse.

steps.text: Local boundedness. The uniform convergence theorem on [1, 2] gives X ≥ a with f(λt)/f(t) ≤ M = 2^|α| + 1 for all t ≥ X and λ ∈ [1, 2]. Each s ∈ [2^n X, 2^(n+1) X] is s = λ 2^n X with λ ∈ [1, 2]. A chain of n + 1 such bounds along the points 2^k X gives f(s) ≤ M^(n+1) f(X). So f is bounded, and hence integrable, on every bounded subinterval of [X, ∞), and F is finite.

A limit for block integrals. Fix λ > 0. For x ≥ X/min(1, λ), the substitution s = xu gives F(λx) − F(x) = x f(x) ∫_1^λ (f(xu)/f(x)) du, with an oriented integral when λ < 1. By the uniform convergence theorem, f(xu)/f(x) → u^α uniformly for u between 1 and λ. Hence (F(λx) − F(x))/(x f(x)) → ∫_1^λ u^α du as x → ∞. Call this limit (∗).

Case α > −1, divergence of F. Since f(2s)/f(s) → 2^α > 1/2, there is s₀ ≥ X with f(2s) ≥ f(s)/2 for s ≥ s₀. Let I_n = ∫ f(s) ds over [2^n s₀, 2^(n+1) s₀]. The substitution s = 2u gives I_n = 2 ∫ f(2u) du over [2^(n−1) s₀, 2^n s₀], so I_n ≥ I_(n−1) for n ≥ 1. Hence F(2^(n+1) s₀) ≥ (n + 1) I₀ with I₀ > 0, and F(x) → ∞ because F is nondecreasing.

Case α > −1, regular variation of F. Fix λ > 0 and ε ∈ (0, 1). Pointwise regular variation gives t₁ ≥ max(X, X/λ) with (1 − ε)λ^α f(s) ≤ f(λs) ≤ (1 + ε)λ^α f(s) for s ≥ t₁. For x ≥ t₁, F(λx) = F(λt₁) + λ ∫_{t₁}^x f(λs) ds lies between F(λt₁) + (1 ∓ ε)λ^(α+1)(F(x) − F(t₁)). Divide by F(x) → ∞. Every limit point of F(λx)/F(x) lies in [(1 − ε)λ^(α+1), (1 + ε)λ^(α+1)], and ε → 0 gives F(λx)/F(x) → λ^(α+1).

Case α > −1, conclusion. Take λ = 2. By (∗), (F(2x) − F(x))/(x f(x)) → (2^(α+1) − 1)/(α + 1) > 0. By step s4, (F(2x) − F(x))/F(x) → 2^(α+1) − 1 > 0. The quotient of the second ratio by the first is x f(x)/F(x), so x f(x)/F(x) → α + 1.

Case α < −1. Choose η with 2^α < η < 1/2 and s₁ ≥ X with f(2s) ≤ η f(s) for s ≥ s₁. For the blocks J_n over [2^n s₁, 2^(n+1) s₁], the substitution s = 2u gives J_n ≤ 2η J_(n−1), so Σ J_n converges and G(x) = ∫_x^∞ f(s) ds is finite for x ≥ X. As in step s4, G(λx) = λ ∫_x^∞ f(λs) ds lies between (1 ∓ ε)λ^(α+1) G(x) for large x, so G(λx)/G(x) → λ^(α+1). Since G(x) − G(2x) = F(2x) − F(x), (∗) gives (G(x) − G(2x))/(x f(x)) → (1 − 2^(α+1))/(−α − 1) > 0, and (G(x) − G(2x))/G(x) → 1 − 2^(α+1) > 0. The quotient gives x f(x)/G(x) → −α − 1.

Case α = −1. Fix K > 1. For x ≥ KX, F(x) ≥ F(x) − F(x/K), and (∗) with λ = 1/K gives (F(x) − F(x/K))/(x f(x)) → ∫_{1/K}^1 u^(−1) du = log K. So lim sup x f(x)/F(x) ≤ 1/log K for every K > 1, and x f(x)/F(x) → 0. If ∫_X^∞ f(s) ds < ∞, then G(x) ≥ F(Kx) − F(x), and (∗) with λ = K gives (F(Kx) − F(x))/(x f(x)) → log K. So lim sup x f(x)/G(x) ≤ 1/log K for every K, and x f(x)/G(x) → 0.

Converse. Put F(x) = ∫_a^x g(s) ds and b(x) = x g(x)/F(x) → c. F is absolutely continuous on bounded intervals because it is an indefinite integral, and the Lebesgue differentiation theorem gives F' = g almost everywhere. On [x₁, y] with x₁ > a, F ≥ F(x₁) > 0 and log is Lipschitz on [F(x₁), ∞), so log F is absolutely continuous with (log F)' = b(s)/s almost everywhere. The fundamental theorem of calculus gives log F(λx) − log F(x) = ∫ b(s)/s ds over [x, λx], which tends to c log λ. So F(λx)/F(x) → λ^c, and g(λx)/g(x) = (b(λx)/b(x)) (F(λx)/F(x)) λ^(−1) → λ^(c−1). For the tail form, G(x) = ∫_x^∞ g has −(log G)' = b(s)/s almost everywhere with b(x) = x g(x)/G(x), so G(λx)/G(x) → λ^(−c), and g = bG/x is regularly varying with index −c − 1.

applications.title: Mean excess loss above a high threshold
applications.inputs: A loss X ≥ 1 with tail P(X > x) = F̄(x) = (x + 1)/(2x³) for x ≥ 1, and a threshold u = 9. The mean excess is e(u) = E[X − u | X > u] = ∫_u^∞ F̄(s) ds / F̄(u).
applications.hypotheses: F̄ is continuous and positive on [1, ∞). F̄(x) = x⁻² L(x) with L(x) = (1 + 1/x)/2 → 1/2, so F̄ is regularly varying with index α = −2 < −1. Case (iii) applies, and it predicts ∫_u^∞ F̄(s) ds ~ u F̄(u)/(−α − 1) = u F̄(u).

steps.text: Case (iii) of the theorem with α = −2 gives e(u) = ∫_u^∞ F̄(s) ds / F̄(u) ~ u/(−α − 1) = u as u → ∞. So the mean excess grows linearly, with slope 1.
Compute exactly: ∫_u^∞ (1/(2s²) + 1/(2s³)) ds = 1/(2u) + 1/(4u²) = (2u + 1)/(4u²). Division by F̄(u) = (u + 1)/(2u³) gives e(u) = u(2u + 1)/(2(u + 1)), so e(u)/u = (2u + 1)/(2u + 2) → 1.
The ratio of the exact mean excess to the prediction u = 9 is (171/20)/9 = 19/20. This equals (2u + 1)/(2u + 2) at u = 9.

applications.conclusion: The mean excess loss over a threshold u is asymptotically u, as Karamata's theorem predicts for tail index 2. At u = 9 the exact mean excess is 171/20 = 8.55, which is 5% below the prediction 9.

limitations: In the case α = −1 the theorem gives only x f(x) = o(F(x)). The integral F is then slowly varying, and its exact size depends on the slowly varying part of f.
The direct part gives no rate of convergence. A rate needs a second-order condition on f.

results.name: Potter bounds for regularly varying functions
aliases: Potter's theorem for regularly varying functions
results.statement: Let a > 0 and let f: [a, ∞) → (0, ∞) be measurable and regularly varying with index ρ ∈ ℝ. Then for every A > 1 and δ > 0 there is X ≥ a such that f(y)/f(x) ≤ A · max{(y/x)^(ρ+δ), (y/x)^(ρ−δ)} and f(y)/f(x) ≥ A⁻¹ · min{(y/x)^(ρ+δ), (y/x)^(ρ−δ)} for all x, y ≥ X. In particular, for every ε ∈ (0, 1) there is t₀ such that (1 − ε)λ^(ρ−ε) < f(λt)/f(t) < (1 + ε)λ^(ρ+ε) for all λ ≥ 1 and t ≥ t₀.
hypotheses: The function f is measurable and positive on [a, ∞) for some a > 0.
f(λx)/f(x) → λ^ρ as x → ∞ for every λ > 0.
The constants satisfy A > 1 and δ > 0 (or ε ∈ (0, 1) for the one-sided form).

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 writes f in the Karamata representation f(x) = c(x) exp(∫_a^x η(u)/u du) with c(x) → c₀ ∈ (0, ∞) and η(u) → ρ.

definitions.name: regularly varying function
definitions.text: A positive measurable function f on [a, ∞) with f(λx)/f(x) → λ^ρ as x → ∞ for every λ > 0. The number ρ is the index.

definitions.name: Karamata representation
definitions.text: A form f(x) = c(x) exp(∫_a^x η(u)/u du) with measurable c(x) → c₀ ∈ (0, ∞) and measurable η(u) → ρ, bounded on bounded intervals.

source.citation: R. S. Hazra, Essays on regular variations in classical and free setup: randomly weighted sums, products in CEVM and free subexponentiality, PhD thesis, Indian Statistical Institute, Kolkata, 2011.
source.revision: arXiv:1109.5880v1 (27 September 2011).
source.module: Chapter 1, Section 1.2 Regularly varying functions and random variables
source.excerpt: (Potter's bound, Resnick, 1987, Proposition 0.8). Suppose f ∈ RV_ρ, ρ ∈ ℝ. Take ε > 0. Then there exists t₀ such that for x ≥ 1, and t ≥ t₀, we have (1 − ε)x^{ρ−ε} < f(tx)/f(t) < (1 + ε)x^{ρ+ε}.
source.attribution: © R. S. Hazra. Quoted from the author's PhD thesis (arXiv:1109.5880) for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states the one-sided bound for x ≥ 1 and refers to Resnick (1987), Proposition 0.8, with no proof. The authored statement gives the two-sided form for all x, y ≥ X, with separate constants A and δ, and derives the source form from it. The authored proof derives both bounds from the Karamata representation theorem.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the standard derivation of Potter's bounds from the Karamata representation theorem. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement: the two-sided bounds for all x, y ≥ X and every A > 1 and δ > 0, and the one-sided form for ε ∈ (0, 1).

steps.text: Represent f. By the Karamata representation theorem, f(x) = c(x) exp(∫_a^x η(u)/u du) for all x ≥ a, where c and η are measurable, η is bounded on bounded intervals, c(x) → c₀ ∈ (0, ∞) and η(u) → ρ as u → ∞. For x, y ≥ a this gives f(y)/f(x) = (c(y)/c(x)) exp(∫_x^y η(u)/u du), with an oriented integral when y < x.
Choose X. Since c(x) → c₀ > 0 and η(u) → ρ, there is X ≥ a such that A^(−1/2) c₀ ≤ c(u) ≤ A^(1/2) c₀ and |η(u) − ρ| ≤ δ for all u ≥ X. Then A⁻¹ ≤ c(y)/c(x) ≤ A for all x, y ≥ X.

Bound the exponential factor. Let x, y ≥ X. If y ≥ x, then (ρ − δ)/u ≤ η(u)/u ≤ (ρ + δ)/u on [x, y], so (ρ − δ) log(y/x) ≤ ∫_x^y η(u)/u du ≤ (ρ + δ) log(y/x), and the exponential lies between (y/x)^(ρ−δ) and (y/x)^(ρ+δ). If y < x, then ∫_x^y η(u)/u du = −∫_y^x η(u)/u du lies between (ρ + δ) log(y/x) and (ρ − δ) log(y/x), and the exponential lies between (y/x)^(ρ+δ) and (y/x)^(ρ−δ). In both cases it lies between min{(y/x)^(ρ+δ), (y/x)^(ρ−δ)} and max{(y/x)^(ρ+δ), (y/x)^(ρ−δ)}.

Combine and read off the one-sided form. Multiplying the bounds of steps s2 and s3 gives both inequalities for all x, y ≥ X. For ε ∈ (0, 1), take A = 1 + ε/2 and δ = ε. Then A < 1 + ε and A⁻¹ ≥ 1 − ε/2 > 1 − ε. For t ≥ t₀ = X, λ ≥ 1, x = t and y = λt, the maximum is λ^(ρ+ε) and the minimum is λ^(ρ−ε). So (1 − ε)λ^(ρ−ε) < A⁻¹λ^(ρ−ε) ≤ f(λt)/f(t) ≤ Aλ^(ρ+ε) < (1 + ε)λ^(ρ+ε).

applications.title: Explicit Potter constants for a Pareto-type loss tail
applications.inputs: A loss tail F̄(x) = (x + 1)/(2x³) on [1, ∞), regularly varying with index ρ = −2, the constant A = 11/10 and the thresholds x = 10 and y = 20.
applications.hypotheses: F̄ is continuous and positive on [1, ∞), and F̄(λx)/F̄(x) = λ⁻²(λx + 1)/(λ(x + 1)) → λ⁻² for every λ > 0. So F̄ is measurable and regularly varying with index −2. A = 11/10 > 1, and δ > 0 is arbitrary.

steps.text: Write the ratio: F̄(y)/F̄(x) = (y/x)⁻² · (1 + 1/y)/(1 + 1/x). The second factor is the ratio L(y)/L(x) of the slowly varying part L(x) = (1 + 1/x)/2.

For x, y ≥ 10 both 1 + 1/x and 1 + 1/y lie in [1, 11/10], so L(y)/L(x) lies in [10/11, 11/10]. Hence A⁻¹(y/x)⁻² ≤ F̄(y)/F̄(x) ≤ A(y/x)⁻² with A = 11/10 and X = 10. Since (y/x)⁻² lies between the minimum and the maximum of (y/x)^(−2±δ), the Potter bounds hold with X = 10 for every δ > 0.
The Potter bounds at this point are A⁻¹/4 = 5/22 = 20/88 and A/4 = 11/40. The exact value 21/88 lies between them, since 21/88 < 11/40 = 24.2/88.

Use the bound for a risk estimate: for every threshold x ≥ 10, P(X > 10x)/P(X > x) ≤ (11/10) · 10⁻² = 11/1000. So a loss ten times above a high threshold is at most 11/1000 times as likely as the threshold excess.

applications.conclusion: For the tail (x + 1)/(2x³), the Potter bounds hold with A = 11/10 from X = 10 on, for every δ > 0. At x = 10 and y = 20 the exact ratio 21/88 lies between 5/22 and 11/40, and P(X > 10x) ≤ (11/1000) P(X > x) for all x ≥ 10.

limitations: The threshold X depends on A and δ and on the function f. The theorem gives no explicit value of X.
For a general slowly varying part the exponent margin δ > 0 is necessary. For example L(x) = log x grows faster than every constant, so the bounds fail with δ = 0.

results.name: Karamata's Tauberian theorem for Laplace-Stieltjes transforms
results.statement: Let U be a non-decreasing right-continuous function on ℝ with U(x) = 0 for x < 0, and let Û(s) = ∫_{[0,∞)} e^{−sx} dU(x) for s > 0, where the integral includes the jump U(0) at 0. Let L be slowly varying, that is, L is positive and measurable on some [x₀, ∞) and L(λx)/L(x) → 1 as x → ∞ for every λ > 0. Let c ≥ 0 and α ≥ 0. Then the following are equivalent. (a) U(x) ~ c x^α L(x)/Γ(1 + α) as x → ∞. (b) Û(s) is finite for every s > 0 and Û(s) ~ c s^(−α) L(1/s) as s ↓ 0. For c = 0 the relations mean U(x) = o(x^α L(x)) and Û(s) = o(s^(−α) L(1/s)). If c > 0, then each of (a) and (b) implies U(x) ~ Û(1/x)/Γ(1 + α).
hypotheses: U is non-decreasing and right-continuous on ℝ, and U(x) = 0 for x < 0.
L is slowly varying.
c ≥ 0 and α ≥ 0.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 uses Tonelli's form of Fubini's theorem to write the Laplace-Stieltjes transform Û(s) as s times the Laplace transform of U.
Steps s2 and s3 use Potter's bounds for the slowly varying function L to dominate the integrand and to bound L(1/s) from below.
Step s2 applies the dominated convergence theorem to the integral of e^(−t) s^α U(t/s)/L(1/s) over t.
Step s7 approximates two continuous functions on [0, 1] from below and from above by polynomials, uniformly within a given error.

definitions.name: Laplace-Stieltjes transform
definitions.text: For a non-decreasing right-continuous U with U(x) = 0 for x < 0, Û(s) = ∫_{[0,∞)} e^{−sx} dU(x), which is the Laplace transform of the measure μ with μ([0, x]) = U(x).

definitions.name: slowly varying function
definitions.text: A positive measurable function L on some [x₀, ∞) with L(λx)/L(x) → 1 as x → ∞ for every λ > 0.

source.citation: T. Mikosch, Regular Variation, Subexponentiality and Their Applications in Probability Theory, lecture notes, University of Groningen, EURANDOM Report 1999-013, Eindhoven, 1999.

source.module: Chapter 1, Section 1.2 Basic Properties
source.excerpt: (Karamata's Tauberian theorem) Let U be a non-decreasing, right-continuous function defined on [0, ∞). If L is slowly varying, c ≥ 0, α ≥ 0, then the following are equivalent: (a) U(x) ∼ c x^α L(x)/Γ(1 + α), x → ∞, (b) Û(s) = ∫_0^∞ e^{−sx} dU(x) ∼ c s^{−α} L(1/s), s ↓ 0. When c = 0, (a) is to be interpreted as U(x) = o(x^α L(x)) as x → ∞, similarly for (b).

source.alignment: The authored statement is Theorem 1.2.10 of the source with the convention U(x) = 0 for x < 0 written out, so that dU includes the jump U(0) at 0. It also states that Û is finite in (b), and it adds the relation U(x) ∼ Û(1/x)/Γ(1 + α) for c > 0, which the source gives as (c) after the theorem. The source states the theorem without proof and refers to Bingham, Goldie and Teugels. The authored proof uses Karamata's polynomial method for the Tauberian direction.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full equivalence for every c ≥ 0 and α ≥ 0, and the relation U(x) ~ Û(1/x)/Γ(1 + α) for c > 0.

steps.text: A formula for Û. Let μ be the measure on [0, ∞) with μ([0, x]) = U(x). For y ≥ 0, e^(−sy) = s ∫_y^∞ e^(−sx) dx. Tonelli's theorem for the non-negative integrand gives Û(s) = s ∫_0^∞ e^(−sx) U(x) dx = ∫_0^∞ e^(−t) U(t/s) dt for every s > 0, as an equality in [0, ∞].

From (a) to (b), main part. Put g_s(t) = s^α U(t/s)/L(1/s). For fixed t > 0, g_s(t) = [U(t/s)/((t/s)^α L(t/s))] · t^α · [L(t/s)/L(1/s)] → (c/Γ(1 + α)) t^α as s ↓ 0. By (a) and Potter's bounds with A = 2 and δ = 1/2, there are C and X ≥ x₀ such that U(x) ≤ C x^α L(x) for x ≥ X and L(y)/L(z) ≤ 2 max{(y/z)^(1/2), (y/z)^(−1/2)} for y, z ≥ X. For s ≤ 1/X and t ≥ sX this gives g_s(t) ≤ 2C(t^(α+1/2) + t^(α−1/2)). This bound is integrable against e^(−t) dt because α − 1/2 > −1. By dominated convergence, ∫_{sX}^∞ e^(−t) g_s(t) dt → (c/Γ(1 + α)) ∫_0^∞ e^(−t) t^α dt = c.

From (a) to (b), small t. For t < sX, U(t/s) ≤ U(X), so ∫_0^{sX} e^(−t) g_s(t) dt ≤ X U(X) s^(1+α)/L(1/s). The lower Potter bound with y = 1/s ≥ z = X gives L(1/s) ≥ (1/2) L(X) (sX)^(1/2). So this part is at most 2 X^(1/2) U(X) s^(α+1/2)/L(X), which tends to 0. With s1, Û(s)/(s^(−α) L(1/s)) = ∫_0^∞ e^(−t) g_s(t) dt → c. In particular Û(s) is finite for small s, so for all s > 0 because Û is non-increasing. This is (b), and for c = 0 it is the o-relation.
From (b) to (a) when c = 0. For x > 0, e^(−y/x) ≥ e^(−1) for y in [0, x]. So U(x) = μ([0, x]) ≤ e ∫_{[0,x]} e^(−y/x) μ(dy) ≤ e Û(1/x). If Û(s) = o(s^(−α) L(1/s)), then U(x) = o(x^α L(x)).

From (b) to (a) when c > 0, scaled measures. By (b), Û(s) > 0 for small s, so for large x the measure ν_x(B) = μ(xB)/Û(1/x) on [0, ∞) is defined. Its transform is ∫ e^(−ty) ν_x(dy) = Û(t/x)/Û(1/x), which tends to t^(−α) for every t > 0 by (b) and slow variation of L. Let ν_α(dy) = y^(α−1) dy/Γ(α) if α > 0, and let ν_0 be the unit mass at 0. Then ∫ e^(−ty) ν_α(dy) = t^(−α) by the definition of the Gamma function, ν_α([0, 1]) = 1/(αΓ(α)) = 1/Γ(1 + α), and ν_α has no atom at 1.

Polynomials and the target. For each k ≥ 0, ∫ e^(−y) (e^(−y))^k ν_x(dy) = ∫ e^(−(k+1)y) ν_x(dy) → (k + 1)^(−α) = ∫ e^(−y) (e^(−y))^k ν_α(dy). By linearity, ∫ e^(−y) P(e^(−y)) ν_x(dy) → ∫ e^(−y) P(e^(−y)) ν_α(dy) for every polynomial P. Let h(z) = 1/z for z in [1/e, 1] and h(z) = 0 for z in [0, 1/e). Then e^(−y) h(e^(−y)) is the indicator of y ≤ 1, so ∫ e^(−y) h(e^(−y)) ν_x(dy) = ν_x([0, 1]) = U(x)/Û(1/x).

The polynomial sandwich. Fix η > 0 and choose κ in (0, 1/10) with ν_α({y : |e^(−y) − 1/e| ≤ κ}) ≤ η/e, which is possible because ν_α has no atom at 1. Let g₂ be 0 on [0, 1/e − κ], linear from 0 to e on [1/e − κ, 1/e], and 1/z on [1/e, 1]. Let g₁ be 0 on [0, 1/e], linear from 0 to 1/(1/e + κ) on [1/e, 1/e + κ], and 1/z on [1/e + κ, 1]. Then g₁ and g₂ are continuous, g₁ ≤ h ≤ g₂, and 0 ≤ g₂ − g₁ ≤ e with g₂ = g₁ outside [1/e − κ, 1/e + κ]. By the Weierstrass theorem choose polynomials with |P₁ − (g₁ − η)| ≤ η and |P₂ − (g₂ + η)| ≤ η on [0, 1]. Then P₁ ≤ h ≤ P₂ and P₂ − P₁ ≤ 4η + (g₂ − g₁). Since e^(−y) ≤ 1 and ∫ e^(−y) ν_α(dy) = 1, ∫ e^(−y)(P₂ − P₁)(e^(−y)) ν_α(dy) ≤ 4η + e · η/e = 5η.

Conclusion. By s6 and s7, lim sup U(x)/Û(1/x) ≤ ∫ e^(−y) P₂(e^(−y)) ν_α(dy) ≤ ∫ e^(−y) P₁(e^(−y)) ν_α(dy) + 5η ≤ ν_α([0, 1]) + 5η. In the same way, lim inf U(x)/Û(1/x) ≥ ν_α([0, 1]) − 5η. Since η is arbitrary, U(x)/Û(1/x) → 1/Γ(1 + α). With (b) at s = 1/x this gives (a). For c > 0, (a) and (b) together give U(x) ~ Û(1/x)/Γ(1 + α).

applications.title: Number of states of a two-dimensional oscillator from its partition function
applications.inputs: A two-dimensional quantum harmonic oscillator in units with ħω = 1 has energy levels n = 0, 1, 2, … with degeneracy n + 1, after the zero-point energy is removed. N(E) is the number of states with energy at most E, and Z(β) = Σ (n + 1) e^(−βn) is the partition function at inverse temperature β.
applications.hypotheses: N is non-decreasing and right-continuous with N(E) = 0 for E < 0, and Z(β) = ∫ e^(−βE) dN(E) is its Laplace-Stieltjes transform.

steps.text: Sum the series: Z(β) = (1 − e^(−β))^(−2). As β ↓ 0, 1 − e^(−β) ~ β, so Z(β) ~ β^(−2). This is (b) with c = 1, α = 2 and L ≡ 1, the high-temperature limit.
Karamata's theorem gives N(E) ~ E²/Γ(3) = E²/2 as E → ∞, because Γ(3) = 2! = 2.
Check against the exact count. For an integer E, N(E) = 1 + 2 + ⋯ + (E + 1) = (E + 1)(E + 2)/2. At E = 100 this is 5151.
The ratio of the exact count to the prediction 100²/2 = 5000 is 5151/5000.
The relative error is 3/E + 2/E², which is 151/5000 at E = 100 and tends to 0 as E → ∞.

applications.conclusion: The high-temperature behaviour Z(β) ~ β^(−2) alone gives the state count N(E) ~ E²/2. At E = 100 the exact count 5151 differs from 5000 by about 3%.

limitations: The Tauberian direction needs a Tauberian condition such as the monotonicity of U. Without such a condition, (b) need not imply (a).
For c > 0 the theorem gives no rate of convergence. A rate needs further conditions on U and on L.

results.name: Breiman's lemma on products with a regularly varying factor
aliases: Breiman's theorem on products of random variables
results.statement: Let X and Y be independent non-negative random variables. Suppose that the tail P(X > x) is regularly varying with index −α for some α > 0, that is, P(X > λx)/P(X > x) → λ^(−α) as x → ∞ for every λ > 0. Suppose also that E(Y^(α+ε)) < ∞ for some ε > 0. Then P(XY > x)/P(X > x) → E(Y^α) as x → ∞. If moreover P(Y > 0) > 0, then P(XY > x) ~ E(Y^α) P(X > x), and the tail of XY is regularly varying with index −α.
hypotheses: X and Y are independent and non-negative.
P(X > x) > 0 for all x, and P(X > λx)/P(X > x) → λ^(−α) as x → ∞ for every λ > 0, with α > 0.
E(Y^(α+ε)) < ∞ for some ε > 0.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 uses Fubini's theorem for the product law of the independent pair (X, Y) to write P(XY > x) as an integral of P(X > x/y) against the law of Y.
Steps s2 and s3 use Potter's bounds for the tail of X: s2 for an integrable bound on P(X > x/y)/P(X > x), and s3 for the lower bound x^(α+ε) P(X > x) → ∞.
Step s2 applies the dominated convergence theorem to the integral over y ≤ x/x₀ with the bound 2(1 + y^(α+ε)).
Step s3 applies Markov's inequality to Y^(α+ε) to bound P(Y > x/x₀).

definitions.name: regularly varying tail
definitions.text: A random variable X ≥ 0 has a regularly varying tail with index −α when P(X > x) > 0 for all x and P(X > λx)/P(X > x) → λ^(−α) as x → ∞ for every λ > 0.

definitions.name: asymptotic equivalence
definitions.text: u(x) ~ v(x) means u(x)/v(x) → 1 as x → ∞.

source.citation: A. H. Jessen and T. Mikosch, Regularly varying functions, Publications de l'Institut Mathématique (Beograd), Nouvelle série 80(94) (2006), 171–192.
source.revision: Journal version, from the EMIS mirror of Publications de l'Institut Mathématique.
source.module: Section 4 Product-type functions, Subsection 4.1 One-dimensional results
source.excerpt: Lemma 4.2. Assume X1 and X2 are non-negative independent random variables and that X1 is regularly varying with index α > 0. (1) If there exists an ε > 0 such that E(X2^{α+ε}) < ∞, then (4.3) P(X1X2 > x) ∼ E(X2^α) P(X1 > x).
source.attribution: © A. H. Jessen and T. Mikosch. Quoted from Publications de l'Institut Mathématique for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states part (1) for a regularly varying X1 with index α > 0, which means a tail P(X1 > x) regularly varying with index −α. The authored statement writes the conclusion as a limit of the ratio, so that it also covers E(Y^α) = 0, and adds that XY is regularly varying when P(Y > 0) > 0. The source proves part (1) through decomposition (4.1) and a domination argument for large y. The authored proof splits at y = x/x₀ and dominates with Potter's bounds.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the decomposition and domination argument of Lemma 4.2(1) in Jessen and Mikosch (2006). No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement for every α > 0 and every ε > 0, including the case E(Y^α) = 0.

steps.text: Condition on Y. Write F̄(x) = P(X > x) and G for the law of Y. By independence and Fubini's theorem, P(XY > x) = ∫ P(Xy > x) G(dy). For x ≥ 0 the term y = 0 gives 0, so R(x) = P(XY > x)/F̄(x) = ∫_{(0,∞)} F̄(x/y)/F̄(x) G(dy). For each fixed y > 0, F̄(x/y)/F̄(x) → y^α as x → ∞, by regular variation with λ = 1/y.

The main part. Choose δ with 0 < δ < min(ε, α). Potter's bounds for F̄, with index −α, A = 2 and this δ, give x₀ > 0 such that F̄(u)/F̄(v) ≤ 2 max{(u/v)^(−α+δ), (u/v)^(−α−δ)} for u, v ≥ x₀. For x ≥ x₀ and 0 < y ≤ x/x₀, take u = x/y and v = x: F̄(x/y)/F̄(x) ≤ 2 max{y^(α−δ), y^(α+δ)} ≤ 2(1 + y^(α+ε)), because 0 < α − δ < α + δ < α + ε. The bound is G-integrable since E(Y^(α+ε)) < ∞. The integrands 1{y ≤ x/x₀} F̄(x/y)/F̄(x) tend to y^α pointwise, so dominated convergence gives I₁(x) = ∫_{(0, x/x₀]} F̄(x/y)/F̄(x) G(dy) → E(Y^α).

The remainder. Since F̄ ≤ 1, I₂(x) = ∫_{(x/x₀, ∞)} F̄(x/y)/F̄(x) G(dy) ≤ P(Y > x/x₀)/F̄(x). Markov's inequality gives P(Y > x/x₀) ≤ E(Y^(α+ε)) (x₀/x)^(α+ε). The lower Potter bound with u = x and v = x₀ gives F̄(x) ≥ (1/2)(x/x₀)^(−α−δ) F̄(x₀) for x ≥ x₀. Hence I₂(x) ≤ 2 E(Y^(α+ε)) x₀^(ε−δ) x^(δ−ε)/F̄(x₀), which tends to 0 because δ < ε.

Conclude. R(x) = I₁(x) + I₂(x) → E(Y^α). If P(Y > 0) > 0, then E(Y^α) > 0, so P(XY > x) ~ E(Y^α) F̄(x). For λ > 0, P(XY > λx)/P(XY > x) = (R(λx)/R(x)) · (F̄(λx)/F̄(x)) → λ^(−α). So the tail of XY is regularly varying with index −α.

applications.title: Return tail in a two-regime stochastic volatility model
applications.inputs: A return X = σZ with heavy-tailed noise Z, P(Z > x) = F̄(x) = (x + 1)/(2x³) for x ≥ 1, and an independent volatility σ that equals 1/2 or 2 with probability 1/2 each. The threshold is x = 99.
applications.hypotheses: Z and σ are independent and non-negative. F̄(x) = x⁻² L(x) with L(x) = (1 + 1/x)/2 → 1/2, so the tail of Z is regularly varying with index −2 and α = 2. σ is bounded, so E(σ^(2+ε)) < ∞ for every ε > 0.

steps.text: Breiman's lemma gives P(σZ > x)/P(Z > x) → E(σ²) = ((1/2)² + 2²)/2 = 17/8. Volatility switching raises the far tail of the return by the factor 17/8.

Compute exactly for x ≥ 2: P(σZ > x) = F̄(2x)/2 + F̄(x/2)/2. With F̄(2x)/F̄(x) = (2x + 1)/(8(x + 1)) and F̄(x/2)/F̄(x) = 4(x + 2)/(x + 1), the ratio is R(x) = (34x + 65)/(16(x + 1)), which tends to 34/16 = 17/8.
The error of the Breiman value at x = 99 is 3431/1600 − 17/8 = 31/1600, which is less than 1% of 17/8.

applications.conclusion: P(σZ > x) ~ (17/8) P(Z > x). At x = 99 the exact ratio is 3431/1600, within 31/1600 of the Breiman value 17/8.

limitations: The moment condition E(Y^(α+ε)) < ∞ cannot simply be dropped. If Y has a tail as heavy as the tail of X, the ratio can tend to infinity or have a different limit, as Lemma 4.1(2) and (3) of the source show for iid factors: there the ratio tends to infinity, or its only possible limit is 2E(X^α).
The lemma gives only first-order tail asymptotics. It gives no rate of convergence of the ratio.

results.name: Convolution tails and Kesten's bound for subexponential distributions
results.statement: Let F be a distribution function on [0, ∞) with F̄(x) = 1 − F(x) > 0 for all x. Write F^{n∗} for the n-fold convolution of F, the law of X₁ + ⋯ + Xₙ for independent Xᵢ with law F. Suppose that F is subexponential in the sense that F̄^{2∗}(x)/F̄(x) → 2 as x → ∞. Then the following hold. (a) F̄(x − y)/F̄(x) → 1 as x → ∞, uniformly for y in each bounded interval. (b) e^{εx} F̄(x) → ∞ as x → ∞ for every ε > 0. (c) F̄^{n∗}(x)/F̄(x) → n as x → ∞ for every n ≥ 2. (d) Kesten's bound: for every ε > 0 there is a finite constant K such that F̄^{n∗}(x) ≤ K(1 + ε)^n F̄(x) for all n ≥ 1 and all x ≥ 0.
hypotheses: F is a distribution function on [0, ∞) and F̄(x) > 0 for all x.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 uses Fubini's theorem for the product law of Sₙ and an independent X with law F to write F̄^{(n+1)∗}(x) as an expectation over X.

definitions.name: subexponential distribution
definitions.text: A distribution F on [0, ∞) with F̄(x) > 0 for all x is subexponential when F̄^{2∗}(x)/F̄(x) → 2 as x → ∞. Part (c) shows that then F̄^{n∗}(x)/F̄(x) → n for every n ≥ 2.

definitions.name: long-tailed distribution
definitions.text: F is long-tailed when F̄(x − y)/F̄(x) → 1 as x → ∞ for every real y.

source.citation: T. Mikosch, Regular Variation, Subexponentiality and Their Applications in Probability Theory, lecture notes, University of Groningen, EURANDOM Report 1999-013, Eindhoven, 1999.
source.revision: PDF of EURANDOM Report 1999-013 from the EURANDOM report archive.
source.module: Chapter 2, Section 2.2 Basic Properties
source.excerpt: Lemma 2.2.1 (Basic properties of subexponential distributions) (a) If F ∈ S, then uniformly on compact y-sets of (0, ∞), lim_{x→∞} F̄(x − y)/F̄(x) = 1. (2.2) (b) If (2.2) holds then, for all ε > 0, e^{εx} F̄(x) → ∞, x → ∞. (c) If F ∈ S then, given ε > 0, there exists a finite constant K so that for all n ≥ 2, F̄^{n∗}(x)/F̄(x) ≤ K(1 + ε)^n, x ≥ 0. (2.3)
source.attribution: © T. Mikosch. Quoted from the author's lecture notes for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: Parts (a), (b) and (d) of the authored statement are parts (a), (b) and (c) of the source. The source defines F ∈ S by F̄^{n∗}(x) ∼ n F̄(x) for all n ≥ 2 (Definition 2.1.1). The authored statement assumes this only for n = 2 and proves the case of general n as part (c), which the source attributes to Chistyakov in Remark 2.1.2 on p. 35. The authored proof of (a) and (b) uses monotonicity of F̄ in place of the uniform convergence and representation theorems that the source cites. The proof of (d) follows the source.

results.proof_status: authored proof. Parts (a), (b) and (c) use direct monotonicity and induction arguments. Part (d) follows the proof of Lemma 2.2.1(c) in the source. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement, parts (a) to (d).

steps.text: A convolution identity. Let X have law F and be independent of Sₙ = X₁ + ⋯ + Xₙ. Put G(z) = P(Sₙ > z), so G(z) = 1 for z < 0. By independence and Fubini's theorem, F̄^{(n+1)∗}(x) = E G(x − X) = F̄(x) + E[F̄^{n∗}(x − X); X ≤ x] for x ≥ 0. For n = 1 the hypothesis gives E[F̄(x − X); X ≤ x]/F̄(x) = F̄^{2∗}(x)/F̄(x) − 1 → 1. Call this relation (∗).

Part (a). Fix y ≥ 0 and let x > y. If X ≤ y, then F̄(x − X) ≥ F̄(x). If y < X ≤ x, then F̄(x − X) ≥ F̄(x − y). So E[F̄(x − X); X ≤ x] ≥ F̄(x) F(y) + F̄(x − y)(F(x) − F(y)). For large x, F(x) > F(y) because F(y) < 1. Hence 1 ≤ F̄(x − y)/F̄(x) ≤ (F̄^{2∗}(x)/F̄(x) − 1 − F(y))/(F(x) − F(y)). By (∗) the right side tends to (1 − F(y))/(1 − F(y)) = 1. For |y| ≤ Y, monotonicity of F̄ puts F̄(x − y)/F̄(x) between F̄(x + Y)/F̄(x) and F̄(x − Y)/F̄(x). Both bounds tend to 1, the first after the substitution x′ = x + Y. So the convergence is uniform on [−Y, Y].

Part (b). Fix ε > 0. By part (a) with y = 1, there is x₁ such that F̄(x) ≥ e^{−ε/2} F̄(x − 1) for all x ≥ x₁ + 1. Write x ≥ x₁ + 1 as x = x₁ + k + s with an integer k ≥ 1 and s in [0, 1). Apply the bound k times and use that F̄ is non-increasing: F̄(x) ≥ e^{−εk/2} F̄(x₁ + s) ≥ e^{−εk/2} F̄(x₁ + 1). Hence e^{εx} F̄(x) ≥ e^{εx₁} F̄(x₁ + 1) e^{εk/2}, which tends to ∞ as x → ∞.

Part (c), by induction on n. The case n = 2 is the hypothesis. Suppose F̄^{n∗}(z)/F̄(z) → n and let η > 0. Choose z₀ such that |F̄^{n∗}(z)/F̄(z) − n| ≤ η for z ≥ z₀. Split E[F̄^{n∗}(x − X); X ≤ x] at X = x − z₀. On {X ≤ x − z₀} the integrand is between (n − η) F̄(x − X) and (n + η) F̄(x − X). On {x − z₀ < X ≤ x} both F̄^{n∗}(x − X) and F̄(x − X) are at most 1, and P(x − z₀ < X ≤ x) = F̄(x − z₀) − F̄(x) = o(F̄(x)) by part (a). With (∗) this gives E[F̄(x − X); X ≤ x − z₀]/F̄(x) → 1, so the lim sup and lim inf of E[F̄^{n∗}(x − X); X ≤ x]/F̄(x) lie in [n − η, n + η]. Since η is arbitrary, s1 gives F̄^{(n+1)∗}(x)/F̄(x) → 1 + n.

Part (d). Fix ε > 0 and put αₙ = sup over x ≥ 0 of F̄^{n∗}(x)/F̄(x), so α₁ = 1. By (∗) choose T such that E[F̄(x − X); X ≤ x] ≤ (1 + ε) F̄(x) for x > T, and put A = 1/F̄(T). For x ≤ T the expectation in s1 is at most 1 ≤ A F̄(x). For x > T it is at most αₙ E[F̄(x − X); X ≤ x] ≤ αₙ(1 + ε) F̄(x). So αₙ₊₁ ≤ 1 + A + (1 + ε)αₙ, and each αₙ is finite. Put B = 1 + A. Induction gives αₙ ≤ (B/ε)((1 + ε)^n − 1): this holds for n = 1 because B ≥ 1, and the induction step is B + (1 + ε)(B/ε)((1 + ε)^n − 1) = (B/ε)((1 + ε)^{n+1} − 1). So K = (1 + A)/ε works.

applications.title: Aggregate claim tail with a geometric number of claims
applications.inputs: A portfolio has N claims, with P(N = n) = (1/4)(3/4)^n for n = 0, 1, 2, … Claim sizes X₁, X₂, … are independent of N and of each other, with Pareto tail F̄(x) = x⁻² for x ≥ 1. The aggregate claim is S_N = X₁ + ⋯ + X_N. Kesten's bound is used with ε = 1/4.
applications.hypotheses: The Pareto tail is regularly varying with index −2, so F is subexponential by the plan result that regularly varying tails are subexponential. E(1 + ε)^N is finite when (3/4)(1 + ε) < 1, which holds for ε = 1/4.

steps.text: The expected number of claims is E N = (3/4)/(1 − 3/4) = 3.

Condition on N: P(S_N > x)/F̄(x) = Σₙ P(N = n) F̄^{n∗}(x)/F̄(x). By part (c), the n-th term tends to n P(N = n). By part (d), it is at most K(5/4)^n P(N = n), and these bounds have the finite sum 4K. Dominated convergence for the series gives P(S_N > x)/F̄(x) → E N = 3.
So the aggregate tail at the level x = 100 is approximately 3 · 100⁻² = 3/10000, three times the tail of one claim.

applications.conclusion: P(S_N > x) ~ 3 x⁻² as x → ∞. Kesten's bound is the step that lets the limit pass through the random number of claims.

limitations: Kesten's bound gives only exponential growth in n. To use it for a random sum, the number of terms must have a finite moment E(1 + ε)^N for some ε > 0.
Part (c) is a first-order relation for fixed n. It does not hold uniformly in n.

results.name: Distributions with regularly varying tails are subexponential
results.statement: Let X, X₁, X₂, … be independent and identically distributed non-negative random variables with tail F̄(x) = P(X > x) > 0 for all x. Suppose that F̄ is regularly varying with index −α for some α ≥ 0, that is, F̄(λx)/F̄(x) → λ^(−α) as x → ∞ for every λ > 0. Write Sₙ = X₁ + ⋯ + Xₙ and Mₙ = max(X₁, …, Xₙ). Then for every n ≥ 2, P(Sₙ > x) ~ n F̄(x) ~ P(Mₙ > x) as x → ∞. So the distribution of X is subexponential.
hypotheses: X₁, X₂, … are independent copies of a non-negative random variable X.
F̄(x) = P(X > x) > 0 for all x.
F̄(λx)/F̄(x) → λ^(−α) as x → ∞ for every λ > 0, with α ≥ 0.

prerequisites.reason: Step s2 applies the union bound to the n events {Xᵢ > (1 − δ)x} and the n(n − 1)/2 events {Xᵢ > η, Xⱼ > η} that cover {Sₙ > x}.

definitions.name: regularly varying tail
definitions.text: A non-negative random variable X has a regularly varying tail with index −α when P(X > x) > 0 for all x and P(X > λx)/P(X > x) → λ^(−α) as x → ∞ for every λ > 0.

definitions.name: subexponential distribution
definitions.text: The distribution of a non-negative random variable X is subexponential when independent copies satisfy P(X₁ + ⋯ + Xₙ > x) ~ n P(X > x) ~ P(max(X₁, …, Xₙ) > x) as x → ∞ for n = 2, 3, …

source.module: Chapter 1, Section 1.3 Regularly Varying Random Variables, Subsection 1.3.1 Closure Properties
source.excerpt: Corollary 1.3.6 Let X, X1, ..., Xn be iid non-negative regularly varying random variables and Sn = X1 + ··· + Xn, n ≥ 1. Then P(X1 + ··· + Xn > x) ∼ n P(X > x) as x → ∞.
source.attribution: © T. Mikosch. Quoted from the author's lecture notes for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states relation (1.3), P(Sn > x) ∼ n P(X > x), for iid non-negative regularly varying X, and Definition 2.1.1 on p. 35 calls X subexponential when (1.3) and P(Mn > x) ∼ n P(X > x) hold. The authored statement combines the two and so says that a regularly varying tail is subexponential. The source derives the corollary from the two-summand Lemma 1.3.4 on p. 12. The authored proof runs the same argument for n summands at once and adds the bounds for the maximum.

results.proof_status: authored proof for n summands that follows the proof of Lemma 1.3.4 in the source. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement for every α ≥ 0 and every n ≥ 2, including the relation for the maximum.

steps.text: A covering of the event. Fix n ≥ 2 and δ with 0 < δ ≤ 1/2, and put η = δx/(n − 1). Suppose that no Xᵢ is larger than (1 − δ)x and that at most one Xᵢ is larger than η. Let k be that index, or any index if there is none. Then Xₖ ≤ (1 − δ)x, because η ≤ δx ≤ (1 − δ)x. The other n − 1 terms are at most η each. So Sₙ ≤ (1 − δ)x + (n − 1)η = x. Hence {Sₙ > x} is contained in the union of the events {Xᵢ > (1 − δ)x} and the events {Xᵢ > η, Xⱼ > η} with i < j.

The upper bound. The union bound and independence give P(Sₙ > x) ≤ n F̄((1 − δ)x) + (n(n − 1)/2) F̄(η)². Divide by n F̄(x). The first term tends to (1 − δ)^(−α) by regular variation with λ = 1 − δ. The second term is ((n − 1)/2) F̄(η) · F̄(η)/F̄(x). Here F̄(η)/F̄(x) → (δ/(n − 1))^(−α) and F̄(η) → 0, because η → ∞. So lim sup P(Sₙ > x)/(n F̄(x)) ≤ (1 − δ)^(−α). This is true for each δ in (0, 1/2], so the lim sup is at most 1.

The lower bound. Let Aᵢ = {Xᵢ > x}. If exactly k of these events occur, then the indicator of their union is at least k − k(k − 1)/2. This is true for k = 0, for k = 1 and k = 2 with equality, and for k ≥ 3 because then k(3 − k)/2 ≤ 0. Take expectations and use independence: P(A₁ ∪ ⋯ ∪ Aₙ) ≥ n F̄(x) − (n(n − 1)/2) F̄(x)². All Xⱼ are non-negative, so each Aᵢ is contained in {Sₙ > x}. Hence P(Sₙ > x)/(n F̄(x)) ≥ 1 − ((n − 1)/2) F̄(x), which tends to 1.

Conclude. Steps s2 and s3 give P(Sₙ > x) ~ n F̄(x). The event {Mₙ > x} is exactly A₁ ∪ ⋯ ∪ Aₙ, so the union bound and step s3 give n F̄(x) − (n(n − 1)/2) F̄(x)² ≤ P(Mₙ > x) ≤ n F̄(x). Since F̄(x) → 0, P(Mₙ > x) ~ n F̄(x). Both relations hold for every n ≥ 2, so the distribution of X is subexponential.

applications.title: Total of five Pareto insurance claims
applications.inputs: Five independent claims with Pareto tail F̄(x) = x⁻² for x ≥ 1, in units of the smallest possible claim. The threshold is x = 10⁴. The upper bound uses δ = 1/10, so η = δx/4 = 250.
applications.hypotheses: The claims are independent, identically distributed and non-negative. F̄(λx)/F̄(x) = λ⁻² for x ≥ max(1, 1/λ), so the tail is regularly varying with α = 2.

steps.text: The theorem gives the approximation P(S₅ > 10⁴) ≈ 5 F̄(10⁴) = 5 · 10⁻⁸ = 1/20000000. The same value approximates P(M₅ > 10⁴), the chance that one claim alone exceeds the threshold.
The lower bound of step s3 gives P(S₅ > x)/(5 F̄(x)) ≥ 1 − 2 F̄(x) = 49999999/50000000 at x = 10⁴.

The upper bound of step s2 with δ = 1/10 is (5 F̄(9000) + 10 F̄(250)²)/(5 F̄(10⁴)) = 100/81 + 32/625 = 65092/50625, about 1.286. The term 100/81 comes from the shrunk threshold (1 − δ)x, and 32/625 comes from two large claims at once.

So the exact tail P(S₅ > 10⁴) is between 0.99999998 and 1.286 times 5 · 10⁻⁸. A smaller δ makes the first term closer to 1 but makes the second term larger at this x. The theorem says that both errors go to 0 as x → ∞.

applications.conclusion: The chance that the total of five claims exceeds 10⁴ is about 5 · 10⁻⁸, the chance that the largest claim alone exceeds 10⁴. The explicit bounds put the ratio between 49999999/50000000 and 65092/50625.

limitations: The result is first order. The bounds in the proof converge slowly, and the ratio P(Sₙ > x)/(n F̄(x)) can stay far from 1 at moderate x.
Subexponential distributions form a larger class. For example, Weibull-type tails exp(−x^τ) with 0 < τ < 1 are subexponential but not regularly varying.

results.name: Weak consistency of the Hill estimator
aliases: Mason's theorem on the Hill estimator
results.statement: Let X₁, X₂, … be independent random variables with common distribution function F such that F̄(x) = 1 − F(x) = x^(−α) L(x) for x > 0, where α > 0 and L is slowly varying. Let X_{1,n} ≥ X_{2,n} ≥ ⋯ ≥ X_{n,n} be the order statistics of X₁, …, Xₙ in decreasing order, and let k = k(n) satisfy k → ∞ and k/n → 0 as n → ∞. Put H_{k,n} = (1/k) Σ_{j=1}^{k} (ln X_{j,n} − ln X_{k+1,n}) on the event X_{k+1,n} > 0, whose probability tends to 1, and give H_{k,n} any value outside it. Then H_{k,n} → 1/α in probability, and the Hill estimator α̂_n = 1/H_{k,n} (defined when H_{k,n} > 0) converges to α in probability. The same holds for the variant (1/k) Σ_{j=1}^{k} (ln X_{j,n} − ln X_{k,n}), which uses the k-th largest value as the threshold.
hypotheses: X₁, X₂, … are independent with common distribution function F.
F̄(x) = x^(−α) L(x) for x > 0, with α > 0 and L slowly varying.
k = k(n) → ∞ and k(n)/n → 0 as n → ∞.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 uses the Rényi representation: the order statistics of F are the quantile function U applied to exponentials of exponential order statistics, whose normalized spacings are independent standard exponentials.
Step s1 applies the weak law of large numbers to the mean S_k/k of k independent standard exponential variables.
Step s3 applies Markov's inequality to the squared deviation of a binomial count to show that the (k + 1)-th largest exponential tends to infinity.
Step s4 applies Potter's bounds to the regularly varying quantile function U to compare ln U(y) − ln U(z) with (1/α) ln(y/z).
Step s5 uses the continuous mapping theorem with h ↦ 1/h, which is continuous at 1/α > 0, to pass from H_{k,n} to the Hill estimator.

definitions.name: Hill estimator
definitions.text: For decreasing order statistics X_{1,n} ≥ ⋯ ≥ X_{n,n}, H_{k,n} = (1/k) Σ_{j=1}^{k} (ln X_{j,n} − ln X_{k+1,n}) estimates 1/α, and α̂_n = 1/H_{k,n} estimates the tail index α.

definitions.name: quantile function
definitions.text: U(y) = inf{x : F(x) ≥ 1 − 1/y} for y > 1. If Y has P(Y > y) = 1/y for y ≥ 1, then U(Y) has distribution function F.

source.citation: T. Mikosch, Regular Variation, Subexponentiality and Their Applications in Probability Theory, lecture notes, University of Groningen, EURANDOM Report 1999-013, Eindhoven, 1999.

source.module: Chapter 1, Section 1.4 Applications, Subsection 1.4.4 Estimation of a Regularly Varying Tail
source.excerpt: (Properties of the Hill estimator) Suppose (Xn) is strictly stationary with marginal distribution F satisfying for some α > 0 and slowly varying L, F̄(x) = P(X > x) = x^{−α}L(x), x > 0. Let α̂^{(H)} = α̂^{(H)}_{k,n} be the Hill estimator (1.31). (a) (Weak consistency) Assume that one of the following conditions is satisfied: (Xn) is iid, (Xn) is weakly dependent, (Xn) is a linear process. If k → ∞, k/n → 0 for n → ∞, then α̂^{(H)} →P α.
source.attribution: © T. Mikosch. Quoted from the author's lecture notes for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The authored statement is the iid case of part (a) of Theorem 1.4.44. The source estimator (1.31) uses the k-th largest value X_{k,n} as the threshold. The authored statement uses X_{k+1,n} and covers the source form as a variant. It also says what happens on the event X_{k+1,n} ≤ 0. The source gives no proof. The authored proof follows the proof of weak consistency in Dekkers, Einmahl and de Haan (1989): quantile representation, Potter bounds for the quantile function and a law of large numbers.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the proof of weak consistency in Dekkers, Einmahl and de Haan (1989), specialized to a positive index. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement for iid data, every α > 0 and every sequence k(n) with k → ∞ and k/n → 0, including the variant with threshold X_{k,n}.

steps.text: Representation. Let U(y) = inf{x : F̄(x) ≤ 1/y} for y > 1. Let E_(1) ≥ ⋯ ≥ E_(n) be the decreasing order statistics of n independent standard exponential variables. By the Rényi representation, (X_{1,n}, …, X_{n,n}) has the same law as (U(e^{E_(1)}), …, U(e^{E_(n)})), and the variables i(E_(i) − E_(i+1)), i = 1, …, n − 1, are independent standard exponentials. So S_k = Σ_{j=1}^{k} (E_(j) − E_(k+1)) = Σ_{i=1}^{k} i(E_(i) − E_(i+1)) is a sum of k independent standard exponentials. By the weak law of large numbers, S_k/k → 1 in probability as k → ∞. From now on, work with this representation.

U is regularly varying with index γ = 1/α. Since F̄ is right-continuous and positive, F̄(U(y)) ≤ 1/y, F̄(x) > 1/y for x < U(y), and u = U(y) → ∞ as y → ∞. For η in (0, 1), y F̄((1 − η)u) > 1, so y F̄(u) > F̄(u)/F̄((1 − η)u) → (1 − η)^α. With y F̄(u) ≤ 1 this gives y F̄(U(y)) → 1. Now fix λ > 0 and put c = λ^(1/α). Then λy F̄((1 ± η)cu) = λ · y F̄(u) · F̄((1 ± η)cu)/F̄(u) → (1 ± η)^(−α). For large y, λy F̄((1 + η)cu) < 1 gives U(λy) ≤ (1 + η)cu, and λy F̄((1 − η)cu) > 1 gives U(λy) ≥ (1 − η)cu. Since η is arbitrary, U(λy)/U(y) → λ^(1/α).

The threshold tends to infinity. Fix M > 0 and put p = e^(−M). The event E_(k+1) ≤ M means that at most k of the n exponentials exceed M. Their number B is binomial with parameters n and p. Since k/n → 0, k ≤ np/2 for large n. Markov's inequality for (B − np)² gives P(B ≤ k) ≤ P(|B − np| ≥ np/2) ≤ 4np(1 − p)/(np)² ≤ 4/(np) → 0. So E_(k+1) → ∞ in probability.

The Potter comparison. Fix δ in (0, 1). Potter's bounds for U with A = e^δ give X such that U > 0 on [X, ∞) and e^(−δ)(y/z)^(γ−δ) ≤ U(y)/U(z) ≤ e^δ (y/z)^(γ+δ) for y ≥ z ≥ X. Hence |ln U(y) − ln U(z) − γ ln(y/z)| ≤ δ ln(y/z) + δ. On the event G = {e^{E_(k+1)} ≥ X}, take z = e^{E_(k+1)} and y = e^{E_(j)} for j ≤ k, and average over j. This gives X_{k+1,n} > 0 and |H_{k,n} − γ S_k/k| ≤ δ(S_k/k + 1) on G.

Conclusion. On G and on {|S_k/k − 1| ≤ 1}, step s4 gives |H_{k,n} − γ| ≤ 3δ + γ|S_k/k − 1|. Given η in (0, 1), take δ = η/6. Then |H_{k,n} − γ| > η implies that G fails or |S_k/k − 1| > min(1, η/(2γ)). Both probabilities tend to 0 by s1 and s3. So H_{k,n} → γ = 1/α in probability, and P(H_{k,n} > 0) → 1. The map h ↦ 1/h is continuous at γ > 0, so α̂_n → α in probability by the continuous mapping theorem. For the variant with threshold X_{k,n}, the j = k term is 0, so the variant equals ((k − 1)/k) H_{k−1,n}. Since k − 1 → ∞ and (k − 1)/n → 0, it also tends to 1/α in probability.

applications.title: Precision of the Hill estimate for exact Pareto losses
applications.inputs: Losses are iid with exact Pareto tail F̄(x) = x⁻² for x ≥ 1, so α = 2 and γ = 1/2. The sample size n is at least 401, and the estimate uses the k = 400 largest losses.
applications.hypotheses: The tail is x^(−α) L(x) with L ≡ 1 on [1, ∞), which is slowly varying. The quantile function is exactly U(y) = y^(1/2).

steps.text: For exact Pareto data, U(y)/U(z) = (y/z)^(1/2), so step s4 holds with δ = 0 and H_{k,n} = (1/2) S_k/k exactly. S_k is a sum of 400 independent standard exponentials, so E H = 1/2 and Var H = (1/2)²/400 = 1/1600.
Chebyshev's inequality gives P(|H − 1/2| ≥ 1/20) ≤ (1/1600)/(1/20)² = 1/4.
In the same case α̂ is smaller than 1/(1/2 − 1/20) = 20/9.
For a tail x^(−2) L(x) with a non-constant L, step s4 adds the Potter error δ. This error is small only when the threshold X_{k+1,n} is large, which is why the theorem needs k/n → 0.

applications.conclusion: With the 400 largest of at least 401 exact Pareto losses with α = 2, the Hill estimate lies between 20/11 ≈ 1.82 and 20/9 ≈ 2.22 with probability at least 3/4.

limitations: Consistency gives no rate. The rate and the choice of k depend on second-order behaviour of L, which the theorem does not control.
The proof is for iid data. The source also states consistency for weakly dependent data and linear processes, which need other arguments.

results.name: Gnedenko's characterization of the Fréchet domain of attraction
aliases: Fréchet maximum domain of attraction criterion
Gnedenko's theorem on the Fréchet domain
results.statement: Let F be a distribution function, let F̄ = 1 − F and x_F = sup{x : F(x) < 1}, and let α > 0. Let Φ_α(x) = 0 for x ≤ 0 and Φ_α(x) = exp(−x^(−α)) for x > 0. Then F belongs to the domain of attraction of Φ_α, that is, there are constants a_n > 0 and b_n ∈ ℝ with F^n(a_n x + b_n) → Φ_α(x) for every real x, if and only if x_F = ∞ and F̄(tx)/F̄(t) → x^(−α) as t → ∞ for every x > 0. In that case one can take b_n = 0 and a_n = U(n), where U(t) = inf{x : F̄(x) ≤ 1/t}.
hypotheses: F is a distribution function on ℝ, and F^n is the distribution function of the maximum of n independent variables with law F.
α > 0 is fixed, and Φ_α is the Fréchet distribution function with index α.

prerequisites.reason: Steps s2 and s3 translate F^n(u_n) → e^(−τ) into n(1 − F(u_n)) → τ and back, in both directions of the proof.
Step s5 passes to the limit in a dyadic telescoping sum whose number of terms grows, with a geometric summable bound.
Steps s2 and s3 trap n(1 − F(a_n)) and (U(ty) − b(t))/a(t) between two sequences with the same limit.

concepts: domain of attraction of an extreme value law

definitions.name: tail quantile function
definitions.text: U(t) = inf{x : 1 − F(x) ≤ 1/t} for t > 1. It is non-decreasing, and by right continuity of F, U(t) ≤ x holds if and only if 1 − F(x) ≤ 1/t.

definitions.name: regularly varying function with index ρ
definitions.text: A positive measurable function g on (c, ∞) with g(tx)/g(t) → x^ρ as t → ∞ for every x > 0.

source.citation: A. Bovier, Gaussian Processes on Trees: From Spin Glasses to Branching Brownian Motion, Cambridge Studies in Advanced Mathematics 163, Cambridge University Press, 2017.
source.revision: Author's version of the book, preface dated Bonn, May 2016, distributed from the author's home page.
source.module: Chapter 1 Extreme Value Theory for iid Sequences, Section 1.2 Extremal Distributions
source.excerpt: Theorem 1.14 The following conditions are necessary and sufficient for a distribution function, F, to belong to the domain of attraction … (i) Fréchet: x_F = +∞, lim_{t↑∞} (1 − F(tx))/(1 − F(t)) = x^(−α), ∀x > 0, α > 0.
source.attribution: © A. Bovier. Quoted from the author's version of Gaussian Processes on Trees for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The authored statement is part (i) of the source theorem, with the norming a_n = U(n), b_n = 0 added. The source gives no proof and refers to Resnick (1987). The proof of sufficiency follows de Haan, Mathematical Centre Tract 32 (1970), Theorem 2.3.1, part a). The proof of necessity replaces de Haan's convergence-of-types argument by an inversion of the tail through U.

results.proof_status: authored proof. Sufficiency follows de Haan (1970), Theorem 2.3.1. Necessity uses an inversion of the tail quantile function. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Both directions of the equivalence for every α > 0, and the choice a_n = U(n), b_n = 0 of the norming constants.

steps.text: Inversion. For t > 1 the set {x : F̄(x) ≤ 1/t} is not empty and is bounded below, so U(t) is a real number, and U is non-decreasing. If F̄(x) ≤ 1/t, then U(t) ≤ x. Conversely, if U(t) ≤ x, there are points y_k ↓ U(t) of the set, so right continuity gives F̄(U(t)) ≤ 1/t and F̄(x) ≤ 1/t. Thus U(t) ≤ x if and only if F̄(x) ≤ 1/t, and U(t) > x if and only if F̄(x) > 1/t. If x_F < ∞, then F̄(x_F) = 0 and U(t) ≤ x_F for all t.

Sufficiency. Assume x_F = ∞ and F̄(tx)/F̄(t) → x^(−α). Put a_n = U(n). Since F̄(x) > 0 for every x, step s1 gives U(n) > x as soon as 1/n < F̄(x), so a_n → ∞. Fix ε ∈ (0, 1). By step s1, F̄(a_n) ≤ 1/n < F̄((1 − ε)a_n). So 1 ≥ nF̄(a_n) > F̄(a_n)/F̄((1 − ε)a_n), and the right side tends to (1 − ε)^α by regular variation at t = (1 − ε)a_n. As ε is arbitrary, nF̄(a_n) → 1. For x > 0, nF̄(a_n x) = nF̄(a_n) · F̄(a_n x)/F̄(a_n) → x^(−α). The Poisson criterion with u_n = a_n x and τ = x^(−α) gives F^n(a_n x) → exp(−x^(−α)). For x ≤ 0 and every y > 0, F^n(a_n x) ≤ F^n(a_n y) → exp(−y^(−α)), and y ↓ 0 gives F^n(a_n x) → 0 = Φ_α(x).

Necessity, inversion of the limit. Assume F^n(a_n x + b_n) → Φ_α(x) for every x, and put γ = 1/α. For x > 0 the Poisson criterion gives nF̄(a_n x + b_n) → x^(−α). Fix y > 0 and 0 < ε < y^γ, and put x₊ = y^γ + ε and x₋ = y^γ − ε. Then x₊^(−α) < 1/y < x₋^(−α), so for large n, F̄(a_n x₊ + b_n) < 1/(ny) < F̄(a_n x₋ + b_n). By step s1, a_n x₋ + b_n < U(ny) ≤ a_n x₊ + b_n. Hence (U(ny) − b_n)/a_n → y^γ for every y > 0. Put a(t) = a_⌊t⌋ and b(t) = b_⌊t⌋ for real t ≥ 2. For n = ⌊t⌋ and δ > 0, ny ≤ ty ≤ n(1 + δ)y when t is large, so (U(ny) − b_n)/a_n ≤ (U(ty) − b(t))/a(t) ≤ (U(n(1 + δ)y) − b_n)/a_n. Let t → ∞ and then δ → 0: (U(ty) − b(t))/a(t) → y^γ for every y > 0.

Ratio of the scales. Fix y > 0. Apply step s3 at t with the arguments y and 2y, and at ty with the arguments 1 and 2. This gives U(2ty) − U(ty) = a(t)((2^γ − 1)y^γ + o(1)) and U(2ty) − U(ty) = a(ty)(2^γ − 1 + o(1)) as t → ∞. Since 2^γ − 1 > 0, a(ty)/a(t) → y^γ. In particular a(2s)/a(s) → 2^γ and (U(2s) − U(s))/a(s) → 2^γ − 1 as s → ∞.

Centring. Fix ρ with 1 < ρ < 2^γ, and s₀ ≥ 2 such that a(2s) ≥ ρa(s) and 0 ≤ (U(2s) − U(s))/a(s) ≤ 2^γ for all s ≥ s₀. For t ≥ 2s₀ let K = K(t) be the integer with s₀ ≤ 2^(−K)t < 2s₀. Then a(t) ≥ ρ^K a(2^(−K)t) ≥ ρ^K m, where m > 0 is the least of the finitely many values a_k with s₀ − 1 < k < 2s₀. So a(t) → ∞. Telescope: (U(t) − U(2^(−K)t))/a(t) = Σ_{j=1}^{K} c_j(t) with c_j(t) = (U(2s) − U(s))/a(s) · a(s)/a(t) at s = 2^(−j)t. Here 0 ≤ c_j(t) ≤ 2^γ ρ^(−j), and c_j(t) → (2^γ − 1)2^(−jγ) for each fixed j by step s4. Tannery's theorem gives the limit Σ_{j≥1} (2^γ − 1)2^(−jγ) = 1. The value U(2^(−K)t) lies between U(s₀) and U(2s₀), so U(t)/a(t) → 1. Then b(t)/a(t) → 0 by step s3 at y = 1, and U(t) → ∞, so x_F = ∞ by step s1. Finally U(ty)/U(t) = (U(ty)/a(ty)) · (a(ty)/a(t)) · (a(t)/U(t)) → y^γ for every y > 0.

Regular variation of the tail. For large x put t = 1/F̄(x), which is finite because x_F = ∞ and tends to ∞ as x → ∞. By step s1, U(t) ≤ x < U(t(1 + δ)) for every δ > 0. Fix λ > 0. If 0 < c < λ^α, then U(tc)/U(t) → c^γ < λ, so U(tc) < λU(t) ≤ λx for large x, and step s1 gives F̄(λx)/F̄(x) = tF̄(λx) ≤ 1/c. If c > (1 + δ)λ^α, then U(tc)/U(t(1 + δ)) → (c/(1 + δ))^γ > λ, so U(tc) > λx for large x, and tF̄(λx) > 1/c. Letting c tend to λ^α and δ to 0 gives F̄(λx)/F̄(x) → λ^(−α).

applications.title: Largest of 10001 log-logistic losses
applications.inputs: Losses X₁, …, X_n are independent with the log-logistic (Fisk) law F(x) = x²/(1 + x²) for x ≥ 0, so F̄(x) = 1/(1 + x²). The sample size is n = 10001, and the level of interest is 300.
applications.hypotheses: x_F = ∞ and F̄(tx)/F̄(t) = (1 + t²)/(1 + t²x²) → x^(−2), so the tail is regularly varying with index −2 and α = 2.

steps.text: The norming constant is a_n = U(n), the solution of 1/(1 + x²) = 1/n, so a_n = √(n − 1) = √10000 = 100. The level 300 is a_n x with x = 3.
The theorem gives P(M_n ≤ 300) ≈ Φ₂(3) = exp(−3^(−2)) = exp(−1/9) ≈ 0.89484.
The exact mean number of exceedances is nF̄(300) = 10001/(1 + 300²) = 10001/90001 ≈ 0.111121, close to 3^(−2) = 1/9.
The exact probability is (1 − 1/90001)^10001 ≈ 0.89483, which differs from exp(−1/9) by about 10^(−5).

applications.conclusion: The largest of the 10001 losses stays below 300 with probability about 0.895, and the Fréchet approximation with a_n = 100 is accurate to about 10^(−5) here.

limitations: The theorem gives the limit law and the norming constants, but no rate of convergence. A slowly varying factor in the tail, such as log x, can make the convergence very slow.
Regular variation is a property of the far tail only. A finite sample cannot verify it, and the index α must be estimated, for example with the Hill estimator.
