results.name: Gnedenko's characterization of the Weibull domain of attraction
aliases: Weibull maximum domain of attraction criterion
Gnedenko's theorem on the Weibull domain
results.statement: Let F be a distribution function, let F̄ = 1 − F and x_F = sup{x : F(x) < 1}, and let α > 0. Let Ψ_α(x) = exp(−(−x)^α) for x < 0 and Ψ_α(x) = 1 for x ≥ 0. Then F belongs to the domain of attraction of Ψ_α, that is, there are constants a_n > 0 and b_n ∈ ℝ with F^n(a_n x + b_n) → Ψ_α(x) for every real x, if and only if x_F < ∞ and F̄(x_F − xh)/F̄(x_F − h) → x^α as h ↓ 0 for every x > 0. In that case one can take b_n = x_F and a_n = x_F − U(n), where U(t) = inf{x : F̄(x) ≤ 1/t}.
hypotheses: F is a distribution function on ℝ, and F^n is the distribution function of the maximum of n independent variables with law F.
α > 0 is fixed, and Ψ_α is the Weibull extreme value distribution function with index α.

prerequisites.reason: Steps s2 and s5 apply the Fréchet criterion to the transformed distribution function F*(y) = F(x_F − 1/y).
Step s3 turns the Weibull limit of F^n(a_n x + b_n) into limits of the mean numbers of exceedances n(1 − F(a_n x + b_n)).
Step s4 passes to the limit in the infinite dyadic sum of increments of U, with a geometric summable bound.
Steps s3 and s5 trap a monotone expression between two bounds with the same limit.

concepts: domain of attraction of an extreme value law
regular variation at a finite endpoint

definitions.name: tail quantile function
definitions.text: U(t) = inf{x : 1 − F(x) ≤ 1/t} for t > 1. It is non-decreasing, and U(t) ≤ x holds if and only if 1 − F(x) ≤ 1/t.

definitions.name: transformed distribution function
definitions.text: For x_F < ∞, F*(y) = F(x_F − 1/y) for y > 0 and F*(y) = 0 for y ≤ 0. It maps the behaviour of F near x_F to the behaviour of F* near +∞.

source.citation: A. Bovier, Gaussian Processes on Trees: From Spin Glasses to Branching Brownian Motion, Cambridge Studies in Advanced Mathematics 163, Cambridge University Press, 2017.
source.revision: Author's version of the book, preface dated Bonn, May 2016, distributed from the author's home page.
source.module: Chapter 1 Extreme Value Theory for iid Sequences, Section 1.2 Extremal Distributions
source.excerpt: Theorem 1.14 The following conditions are necessary and sufficient for a distribution function, F, to belong to the domain of attraction … (ii) Weibull: x_F < +∞, lim_{h↓0} (1 − F(x_F − xh))/(1 − F(x_F − h)) = x^α, ∀x > 0, α > 0.
source.attribution: © A. Bovier. Quoted from the author's version of Gaussian Processes on Trees for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The authored statement is part (ii) of the source theorem, with the norming a_n = x_F − U(n), b_n = x_F added. The source prints "x_F =< +∞" and "h↓∞", and the excerpt corrects these misprints to x_F < +∞ and h↓0. The source gives no proof. The authored proof follows de Haan, Mathematical Centre Tract 32 (1970), Theorem 2.3.2, which reduces the Weibull case to the Fréchet case through F(x_F − 1/y), with a dyadic sum in place of de Haan's Lemma 2.3.1 b).

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows de Haan (1970), Theorem 2.3.2, through the Fréchet criterion. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Both directions of the equivalence for every α > 0, and the choice a_n = x_F − U(n), b_n = x_F of the norming constants.

steps.text: Transformation. Let x_F < ∞. If F has an atom p = F(x_F) − F(x_F−) > 0, then F̄(x_F − h) → p as h ↓ 0, so the ratio in the tail condition tends to 1 and not to x^α for x ≠ 1. If F has no atom at x_F, then F*(y) = F(x_F − 1/y) for y > 0 and F*(y) = 0 for y ≤ 0 is a distribution function, since y ↦ x_F − 1/y is continuous and increasing from (0, ∞) onto (−∞, x_F). Its tail F̄*(y) = F̄(x_F − 1/y) is positive for all y because F(x) < 1 for x < x_F, so x_{F*} = ∞. With h = 1/t and x = 1/y, F̄*(ty)/F̄*(t) = F̄(x_F − xh)/F̄(x_F − h). So the tail condition of the theorem holds if and only if F̄* is regularly varying with index −α. Also F*^n(y) = F^n(x_F − 1/y) for y > 0.

Sufficiency. Assume x_F < ∞ and the tail condition. By step s1, F has no atom at x_F, and F* is in the domain of attraction of Φ_α with c_n = U*(n) = inf{y : F̄*(y) ≤ 1/n} and centring 0. Since F̄(x) → 0 as x ↑ x_F, U(n) < x_F, and the increasing substitution x = x_F − 1/y gives c_n = 1/(x_F − U(n)). For x < 0, F^n(x_F + x/c_n) = F*^n(c_n · (−1/x)) → Φ_α(−1/x) = exp(−(−x)^α). For x ≥ 0, x_F + x/c_n ≥ x_F and F^n(x_F + x/c_n) = 1. So F^n(a_n x + b_n) → Ψ_α(x) with a_n = x_F − U(n) and b_n = x_F.

Necessity, inversion of the limit. Assume F^n(a_n x + b_n) → Ψ_α(x) for every x, and put γ = 1/α. The Poisson criterion gives nF̄(a_n x + b_n) → (−x)^α for x < 0 and → 0 for x ≥ 0. Fix y > 0 and ε > 0, and put x₊ = −y^(−γ) + ε and x₋ = −y^(−γ) − ε. The limits at x₊ and x₋ are below and above 1/y, so for large n, F̄(a_n x₊ + b_n) < 1/(ny) < F̄(a_n x₋ + b_n). Since U(s) ≤ x if and only if F̄(x) ≤ 1/s, this gives a_n x₋ + b_n < U(ny) ≤ a_n x₊ + b_n. So (U(ny) − b_n)/a_n → −y^(−γ). Put a(t) = a_⌊t⌋ and b(t) = b_⌊t⌋. Monotonicity of U between ny and n(1 + δ)y, with n = ⌊t⌋, gives (U(ty) − b(t))/a(t) → −y^(−γ) as t → ∞ for every y > 0.

Finite endpoint. Apply step s3 at t with the arguments y and 2y, and at ty with the arguments 1 and 2: U(2ty) − U(ty) = a(t)((1 − 2^(−γ))y^(−γ) + o(1)) = a(ty)(1 − 2^(−γ) + o(1)). So a(ty)/a(t) → y^(−γ), and (U(2s) − U(s))/a(s) → 1 − 2^(−γ). Fix ρ with 2^(−γ) < ρ < 1 and s₀ ≥ 2 with a(2s) ≤ ρa(s) and 0 ≤ U(2s) − U(s) ≤ a(s) for s ≥ s₀. For t ≥ s₀, the increments U(2^(j+1)t) − U(2^j t) are at most ρ^j a(t), so U is bounded and has a limit U(∞). Every x < x_F has F̄(x) > 0 and so x < U(t) for large t, and U(t) ≤ x_F if x_F < ∞. Hence x_F = U(∞) < ∞. Dividing the telescoping series x_F − U(t) = Σ_{j≥0} (U(2^(j+1)t) − U(2^j t)) by a(t), each term tends to (1 − 2^(−γ))2^(−jγ) and is at most ρ^j. Tannery's theorem gives (x_F − U(t))/a(t) → 1. With step s3 at y = 1, (x_F − b_n)/a_n → 1 − 1 = 0.

Necessity, reduction to the Fréchet case. F has no atom at x_F. Otherwise F^n(x) ≤ (1 − p)^n → 0 for every x < x_F, and the limit e^(−1) at x = −1 forces b_n − a_n ≥ x_F for large n. Then F^n(b_n − a_n) = 1, which contradicts the limit e^(−1). So F* is a distribution function. For y > 0, x_F − a_n/y = a_n(−1/y + ε_n) + b_n with ε_n = (x_F − b_n)/a_n → 0. For each η > 0 and large n, monotonicity gives F^n(a_n(−1/y − η) + b_n) ≤ F*^n(y/a_n) ≤ F^n(a_n(−1/y + η) + b_n). Continuity of Ψ_α then gives F*^n(y/a_n) → Ψ_α(−1/y) = exp(−y^(−α)) = Φ_α(y). For y ≤ 0, F*^n(y/a_n) = 0 = Φ_α(y). The Fréchet criterion now says that F̄* is regularly varying with index −α, and step s1 turns this into the tail condition.

applications.title: Largest total of two uniform delays among 200 packets
applications.inputs: Each of n = 200 packets has a total delay X = D₁ + D₂, where D₁ and D₂ are independent and uniform on [0, 1] seconds. The delays of different packets are independent. The level of interest is 1.85 seconds.
applications.hypotheses: X has the triangular law on [0, 2], so x_F = 2 and F̄(2 − h) = h²/2 for 0 ≤ h ≤ 1. Then F̄(2 − xh)/F̄(2 − h) = x² for small h, and α = 2.

steps.text: U(n) solves h²/2 = 1/n with h = 2 − U(n), so a_n = 2 − U(n) = √(2/n) = √(1/100) = 0.1 and b_n = 2. The level 1.85 is b_n + a_n x with x = −1.5.
The theorem gives P(M_n ≤ 1.85) ≈ Ψ₂(−1.5) = exp(−1.5²) = exp(−2.25) ≈ 0.1054.
The exact mean number of exceedances is nF̄(1.85) = 200 · (0.15)²/2 = 2.25, which equals (−x)^α = 1.5² exactly.
The exact probability is (1 − 0.01125)^200 ≈ 0.1041, so the Weibull approximation is off by about 0.0014.

applications.conclusion: With probability about 0.10, all 200 total delays stay below 1.85 seconds. The largest delay is thus typically within a few multiples of a_n = 0.1 s of the endpoint 2 s.

limitations: The criterion needs the exact endpoint x_F. In statistical use x_F is unknown and must be estimated together with α.
The theorem gives no rate of convergence. In the worked example the error at n = 200 is about 0.0014, and slowly varying factors near x_F can make it much larger.

results.name: De Haan's characterization of the Gumbel domain of attraction
aliases: Gnedenko–de Haan characterization of the Gumbel domain
Gumbel maximum domain of attraction criterion
results.statement: Let F be a distribution function with right endpoint x_F = sup{x : F(x) < 1} ≤ ∞, let F̄ = 1 − F, and let Λ(x) = exp(−e^(−x)). Then F belongs to the domain of attraction of Λ, that is, there are constants a_n > 0 and b_n ∈ ℝ with F^n(a_n x + b_n) → Λ(x) for every real x, if and only if there is a positive function g on (−∞, x_F) with F̄(t + xg(t))/F̄(t) → e^(−x) as t ↑ x_F for every real x. In that case ∫_t^{x_F} F̄(s) ds < ∞ for every t < x_F, the mean excess function f(t) = ∫_t^{x_F} F̄(s) ds / F̄(t) can be taken as g, and one can take b_n = U(n) = inf{x : F̄(x) ≤ 1/n} and a_n = f(b_n).
hypotheses: F is a distribution function on ℝ, and F^n is the distribution function of the maximum of n independent variables with law F.
Λ(x) = exp(−e^(−x)) is the Gumbel distribution function.

prerequisites.reason: Steps s1 and s7 turn n(1 − F(a_n x + b_n)) → e^(−x) into the Gumbel limit F^n(a_n x + b_n) → Λ(x), and step s2 uses the converse.
Step s5 computes the integral of the quantile function as the tail integral of G by exchanging the order of integration.

concepts: domain of attraction of an extreme value law

definitions.name: mean excess function
definitions.text: f(t) = ∫_t^{x_F} (1 − F(s)) ds / (1 − F(t)) for t < x_F. If X has law F and E X⁺ < ∞, then f(t) = E[X − t | X > t].

definitions.name: auxiliary function
definitions.text: A positive function g on (−∞, x_F) with (1 − F(t + xg(t)))/(1 − F(t)) → e^(−x) as t ↑ x_F for all real x. Two auxiliary functions g₁ and g₂ satisfy g₁(t)/g₂(t) → 1.

source.citation: A. Bovier, Gaussian Processes on Trees: From Spin Glasses to Branching Brownian Motion, Cambridge Studies in Advanced Mathematics 163, Cambridge University Press, 2017.
source.revision: Author's version of the book, preface dated Bonn, May 2016, distributed from the author's home page.
source.module: Chapter 1 Extreme Value Theory for iid Sequences, Section 1.2 Extremal Distributions
source.excerpt: Theorem 1.14 The following conditions are necessary and sufficient for a distribution function, F, to belong to the domain of attraction … (iii) Gumbel: ∃g(t) > 0, lim_{t↑x_F} (1 − F(t + xg(t)))/(1 − F(t)) = e^(−x), ∀x ∈ ℝ.
source.attribution: © A. Bovier. Quoted from the author's version of Gaussian Processes on Trees for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The authored statement is part (iii) of the source theorem. It adds de Haan's choice of the auxiliary function as the mean excess function and the norming constants of de Haan (1970), Corollary 2.5.1. The source gives no proof. The outline follows de Haan, Mathematical Centre Tract 32 (1970), Theorem 2.5.1 and its proof, pp. 87-89, with the results of Section 2.4 that this proof uses.

results.proof_status: outline of the cited published proof. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of Theorem 2.5.1 in de Haan (1970), pp. 87-89, and of Corollary 2.5.1, pp. 89-90. Steps s2, s3 and s4 take Theorem 2.4.1 (Mejzler), Theorem 2.4.2 (Gnedenko), Lemma 2.4.3 and Theorem 1.4.3 from the source without their proofs. Here V(p) = inf{y : F̄(y) ≤ p} for 0 < p < 1, which is the function U of the source, so that U(n) = V(1/n).

steps.text: Sufficiency (Theorem 2.4.2 b) of the source). Suppose that g is an auxiliary function. The limit excludes an atom of F at a finite x_F, because then the ratio tends to 1 or is 0. Put b(s) = V(1/s) < x_F. For every ε > 0, F̄(b(s)) ≤ 1/s ≤ F̄(b(s)−) ≤ F̄(b(s) − εg(b(s))), and the limit gives e^(−ε) ≤ liminf sF̄(b(s)) ≤ 1. So nF̄(b_n) → 1 and nF̄(g(b_n)x + b_n) → e^(−x) for every x. The Poisson criterion gives F^n(a_n x + b_n) → Λ(x) with b_n = V(1/n) and a_n = g(b_n).

Necessity, first form (Corollary 2.4.1 and Theorem 2.4.1 of the source). If F is in the domain of attraction of Λ, the Poisson criterion and convergence of types give s F̄(a(s)x + b(s)) → e^(−x) as s → ∞ for every x, with b(s) = V(1/s) and a(s) = V(1/(se)) − V(1/s). Mejzler's theorem (Theorem 2.4.1) also gives (V(tx) − V(t))/(V(ty) − V(t)) → log x / log y as t ↓ 0, for all x, y > 0 with y ≠ 1. Substituting s = 1/F̄(t) gives some auxiliary function (Theorem 2.4.2 a)), so the condition of the theorem is necessary.

Smoothing (Lemma 2.4.3 of the source). There is a distribution function G that is continuous, strictly increasing on (−∞, x_F) and has the same endpoint, with F̄(x)/Ḡ(x) → 1 as x ↑ x_F (2.5.3). The source builds G by linear interpolation across the jumps and the flat parts of F, and uses that the limit in step s2 is uniform for x in compact sets. The auxiliary function of F is then also one for G, so G is in the domain of attraction of Λ by Theorem 2.4.2.

Integral auxiliary function (Theorem 1.4.3 and (2.5.6) of the source). Let V_G(p) = inf{y : Ḡ(y) ≤ p}, which is continuous and strictly monotone. Step s2 for G gives the logarithmic ratio limit of V_G at 0, and Theorem 1.4.3 turns it into (V_G(t/e) − V_G(t)) / ((1/t)∫_0^t V_G(p) dp − V_G(t)) → 1 as t ↓ 0, with a finite integral. Convergence of types for families (Lemma 2.4.1) then gives s Ḡ(a(s)x + b(s)) → e^(−x) with b(s) = V_G(1/s) and a(s) = s∫_0^{1/s} V_G(p) dp − V_G(1/s).

Mean excess form for G ((2.5.4) and (2.5.5) of the source). Put s = 1/Ḡ(t) for t < x_F. Then b(s) = V_G(Ḡ(t)) = t because G is continuous and strictly increasing. Since V_G(p) > y holds exactly when p < Ḡ(y), Tonelli's theorem gives ∫_0^{Ḡ(t)} (V_G(p) − t) dp = ∫_t^{x_F} Ḡ(y) dy. So a(s) = g(t) = ∫_t^{x_F} Ḡ(y) dy / Ḡ(t), and step s4 becomes Ḡ(t + xg(t))/Ḡ(t) → e^(−x) as t ↑ x_F.

Transfer to F. Lemma 1.2.1 b) of the source says that tail integrals of two functions with ratio tending to 1 also have ratio tending to 1. With (2.5.3) this gives ∫_t^{x_F} F̄ / ∫_t^{x_F} Ḡ → 1, so the integral for F is finite and f(t)/g(t) → 1. By (2.5.3) and step s5, F̄(t + xg(t))/F̄(t) → e^(−x). Lemma 2.4.2 of the source lets an auxiliary function be replaced by an asymptotically equal one, which gives F̄(t + xf(t))/F̄(t) → e^(−x) for all x. This is (2.5.1) with the mean excess function (2.5.2).

Norming (Corollary 2.5.1 of the source). Take b_n = inf{x : F̄(x) ≤ 1/n} = U(n). Step s1 with g = f gives nF̄(b_n) → 1, hence n F̄(f(b_n)x + b_n) = nF̄(b_n) · F̄(b_n + xf(b_n))/F̄(b_n) → e^(−x). The Poisson criterion gives F^n(a_n x + b_n) → exp(−e^(−x)) with a_n = f(b_n).

source.ref: L. de Haan, On Regular Variation and Its Application to the Weak Convergence of Sample Extremes, Mathematical Centre Tracts 32, Mathematisch Centrum, Amsterdam, 1970, Theorem 2.5.1 and Corollary 2.5.1 with their proofs, pp. 87-90, and Theorems 2.4.1, 2.4.2 and Lemma 2.4.3, pp. 76-87.

applications.title: Longest of 10000 Erlang-2 calls
applications.inputs: A call centre has n = 10000 independent calls. Each call has two independent exponential phases with mean 1 minute, so its duration has the Erlang-2 law with F̄(x) = (1 + x)e^(−x) for x ≥ 0. The level of interest is 15 minutes.
applications.hypotheses: x_F = ∞. The tail integral is ∫_t^∞ (1 + s)e^(−s) ds = (2 + t)e^(−t), so the mean excess function is f(t) = (2 + t)/(1 + t). Then F̄(t + xf(t))/F̄(t) = (1 + t + xf(t))/(1 + t) · e^(−xf(t)) → e^(−x), because f(t) → 1.

steps.text: b_n = U(n) solves (1 + b)e^(−b) = 10^(−4). The iteration b = log 10^4 + log(1 + b) converges to b_n ≈ 11.756 minutes.
a_n = f(b_n) = (2 + 11.756)/(1 + 11.756) ≈ 1.0784 minutes. For comparison, at t = 12 the mean excess is f(12) = 14/13 ≈ 1.077 minutes.
The exact value is (1 − 16e^(−15))^10000 ≈ exp(−0.04894) ≈ 0.9522, so the Gumbel approximation is off by about 0.0004.

applications.conclusion: With probability about 0.95, no call of the 10000 lasts more than 15 minutes. The longest call is about 11.76 minutes plus a Gumbel variable on the scale of the mean excess, about 1.08 minutes.

limitations: This record is an outline. Steps s2 to s4 use Mejzler's theorem, Gnedenko's theorem, the smoothing Lemma 2.4.3 and Theorem 1.4.3 of the source without proof.
The theorem gives no rate of convergence. For Gaussian tails the error decreases only like 1/log n, so the Gumbel approximation can be poor for moderate n.
In applications the mean excess function must be estimated from data, and its estimate is unstable at high levels.

results.name: Von Mises condition for the Gumbel domain of attraction
aliases: von Mises' sufficient condition for the Gumbel domain
von Mises criterion for the double exponential limit
results.statement: Let F be a distribution function with a density f and right endpoint x_F = sup{x : F(x) < 1} ≤ ∞, and let F̄ = 1 − F. Suppose that f is positive and differentiable on an interval (z₀, x_F), and that the function h = F̄/f satisfies h'(x) → 0 as x ↑ x_F. Then F̄(t + xh(t))/F̄(t) → e^(−x) as t ↑ x_F for every real x, and F belongs to the domain of attraction of Λ(x) = exp(−e^(−x)): with b_n = U(n) = inf{x : F̄(x) ≤ 1/n} and a_n = h(b_n), F^n(a_n x + b_n) → Λ(x) for every real x.
hypotheses: F has a density f, and f is positive and differentiable on an interval (z₀, x_F) below the right endpoint x_F ≤ ∞.
The function h = (1 − F)/f satisfies h'(x) → 0 as x ↑ x_F (von Mises' condition).

prerequisites.reason: Steps s1 and s2 integrate the derivatives of log(1 − F) and of h to get the representation of the tail and the size of h.
Step s3 bounds h(s) − h(t) by sup|h'| times |s − t| on the short interval between t and t + xh(t).
Step s4 substitutes s = t + uh(t) in the integral of 1/h over the interval from t to t + xh(t).
Step s5 turns n(1 − F(a_n x + b_n)) → e^(−x) into the Gumbel limit F^n(a_n x + b_n) → exp(−e^(−x)).

concepts: domain of attraction of an extreme value law

definitions.name: von Mises function
definitions.text: A distribution function F whose density f is positive and differentiable near the right endpoint x_F, with d/dx((1 − F(x))/f(x)) → 0 as x ↑ x_F. The function h = (1 − F)/f is the reciprocal of the hazard rate.

source.citation: A. A. Balkema and L. de Haan, On R. von Mises' condition for the domain of attraction of exp(−e^(−x)), Annals of Mathematical Statistics 43 (1972), 1352–1354. Circulated as Report SW 10/71, Afdeling Mathematische Statistiek, Mathematisch Centrum, Amsterdam, 1971.
source.revision: Report SW 10/71 of the Mathematisch Centrum (June 1971), scanned copy in the CWI repository.
source.module: Introduction, Theorem 1 and equation (2)
source.excerpt: Theorem 1. Suppose F(x) is a distribution function with a density f(x) which is positive and differentiable on a left neighbourhood of x₀. If (2) lim_{x↑x₀} d/dx ((1 − F(x))/f(x)) = 0, then F ∈ D(Λ).
source.attribution: © A. A. Balkema and L. de Haan. Quoted from the authors' report for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The authored statement is the source theorem with x₀ written x_F, the auxiliary function h = (1 − F)/f made explicit and the norming constants b_n = U(n), a_n = h(b_n) added. The source attributes the theorem to von Mises (1936) and gives no proof. The authored proof is the standard argument through the representation 1 − F(x) = (1 − F(z)) exp(−∫_z^x ds/h(s)).

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the standard representation argument for von Mises functions. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The auxiliary limit and the Gumbel limit with b_n = U(n), a_n = h(b_n), for finite and for infinite endpoints.

steps.text: Representation. On (z₀, x_F) the tail F̄ is positive, because F(x) < 1 for x < x_F, and differentiable with F̄' = −f. So log F̄ has the derivative −f/F̄ = −1/h, which is continuous because h is differentiable. Fix z ∈ (z₀, x_F). By the fundamental theorem of calculus, F̄(x) = F̄(z) exp(−∫_z^x ds/h(s)) for z ≤ x < x_F. Since F has a density, F̄(x) → 0 as x ↑ x_F also when x_F < ∞, so ∫_z^{x_F} ds/h(s) = ∞.

Size of h. Let ε > 0 and choose z_ε < x_F with |h'| ≤ ε on (z_ε, x_F). If x_F = ∞, then h(t) = h(z_ε) + ∫_{z_ε}^t h' ≤ h(z_ε) + ε(t − z_ε) for t > z_ε, so limsup h(t)/t ≤ ε and h(t)/t → 0. If x_F < ∞, then h is Lipschitz near x_F and has a limit L ≥ 0 at x_F. If L > 0, the integral of 1/h near x_F would be finite, against step s1. So L = 0, and h(t) = −∫_t^{x_F} h'(s) ds ≤ ε(x_F − t) for t > z_ε, so h(t)/(x_F − t) → 0. In both cases, for each fixed x, the interval between t and t + xh(t) lies in (z_ε, x_F) for t close to x_F, and t + xh(t) → x_F.

h is almost constant on the scale h(t). Fix x and let I_t be the closed interval between t and t + xh(t). By step s2, I_t ⊂ (z_ε, x_F) for t close to x_F. The mean value theorem gives |h(s) − h(t)| ≤ ε|s − t| ≤ ε|x|h(t) for s ∈ I_t. Since ε is arbitrary, sup_{s ∈ I_t} |h(s)/h(t) − 1| → 0 as t ↑ x_F.

Auxiliary limit. By step s1, F̄(t + xh(t))/F̄(t) = exp(−∫_t^{t+xh(t)} ds/h(s)). The substitution s = t + uh(t) gives ∫_t^{t+xh(t)} ds/h(s) = ∫_0^x h(t)/h(t + uh(t)) du. By step s3 the integrand tends to 1 uniformly for u between 0 and x, so the integral tends to x. Hence F̄(t + xh(t))/F̄(t) → e^(−x) as t ↑ x_F, for every real x.

Gumbel limit. F̄ is continuous and strictly decreasing on (z₀, x_F) and tends to 0 at x_F. So for large n, b_n = U(n) lies in (z₀, x_F) and F̄(b_n) = 1/n by the intermediate value property, and b_n ↑ x_F. With a_n = h(b_n) > 0, step s4 at t = b_n gives nF̄(a_n x + b_n) = F̄(b_n + xh(b_n))/F̄(b_n) → e^(−x). The Poisson criterion with τ = e^(−x) gives F^n(a_n x + b_n) → exp(−e^(−x)) for every real x.

applications.title: Highest of 1000 Rayleigh waves in a storm
applications.inputs: In a narrow-band sea with significant wave height H_s = 4 m, individual wave heights follow the Rayleigh law P(H > y) = exp(−2y²/H_s²) = exp(−y²/8) for y ≥ 0. A storm has n = 1000 waves, taken as independent. The level of interest is 9 m.
applications.hypotheses: The density is f(y) = (y/4) exp(−y²/8), positive and differentiable on (0, ∞), and x_F = ∞. Then h(y) = F̄(y)/f(y) = 4/y and h'(y) = −4/y² → 0, so von Mises' condition holds.

steps.text: The level 9 m is b_n + a_n x with x = (9 − 7.434)/0.538 ≈ 2.911. The theorem gives P(max ≤ 9) ≈ exp(−e^(−2.911)) = exp(−0.0544) ≈ 0.947.
The exact tail at 9 m is F̄(9) = exp(−9²/8) = exp(−81/8) ≈ 4.007 · 10^(−5), so the exact value is (1 − F̄(9))^1000 ≈ exp(−0.0401) ≈ 0.961.
Here F̄(b_n + xa_n)/F̄(b_n) = exp(−x − x²/(4 log n)) exactly, because a_n b_n = 4. The correction x²/(4 log n) ≈ 8.47/27.63 ≈ 0.307 explains the gap between 0.0544 and 0.0401.

applications.conclusion: The highest of the 1000 waves exceeds 9 m with probability about 0.04, and the Gumbel limit gives 0.053. The theorem gives the right location 7.4 m and scale 0.54 m, but for Gaussian-type tails the error decreases only like 1/log n.

limitations: The condition is sufficient, not necessary. A distribution function with atoms or without a density can be in the Gumbel domain, and Balkema and de Haan show that every such law is tail equivalent to a von Mises function.
The theorem gives no rate. For tails like exp(−x²) the error in the Gumbel approximation is of order 1/log n.

results.name: Poisson criterion for the maxima of independent variables at high levels
results.statement: Let X₁, X₂, … be independent random variables with a common distribution function F, and let M_n = max(X₁, …, X_n). Let (u_n) be a sequence of real numbers and let τ ∈ [0, ∞]. Then P(M_n ≤ u_n) → e^(−τ) as n → ∞ if and only if n(1 − F(u_n)) → τ. Here e^(−∞) = 0.
hypotheses: The variables X₁, X₂, … are independent, and each has the distribution function F.
The levels u_n are real numbers, and the target value τ lies in the extended half-line [0, ∞].

prerequisites.reason: Step s2 compares log(1 − p) with −p through the Taylor series of the logarithm at 1, with an explicit bound on the remainder.
Step s5 extracts a subsequence along which n(1 − F(u_n)) converges in the compact set [0, ∞], by the Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem.

definitions.name: sample maximum
definitions.text: M_n = max(X₁, …, X_n). For independent X_i with distribution function F, P(M_n ≤ u) = F(u)^n for every real u.

definitions.name: exceedance
definitions.text: An index i ≤ n with X_i > u_n. The number of exceedances has the binomial law with parameters n and 1 − F(u_n), and {M_n ≤ u_n} is the event that no exceedance occurs.

source.citation: M. R. Leadbetter and H. Rootzén, Extremal theory for stochastic processes, Annals of Probability 16 (1988), 431–478. Circulated as Preprint 1987 No. 5, Institute of Mathematical Statistics, University of Copenhagen.
source.revision: Preprint 1987 No. 5 of the Institute of Mathematical Statistics, University of Copenhagen (August 1987), scanned copy in the institute's preprint archive.
source.module: Section 1, Subsection 1.2 Classical extreme value theory
source.excerpt: Lemma 1.2.2. Let {u_n, n ≥ 1} be constants and 0 ≤ τ ≤ ∞. If ξ₁, ξ₂, … are i.i.d. with d.f. F then (1.2.2) P{M_n ≤ u_n} → e^(−τ) if and only if (1.2.3) n(1 − F(u_n)) → τ.
source.attribution: © M. R. Leadbetter and H. Rootzén. Quoted from the authors' preprint for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The authored statement is the source lemma with the notation M_n and the convention e^(−∞) = 0 made explicit. The source calls the lemma almost trivially proved and gives no proof. The authored proof writes P(M_n ≤ u_n) = (1 − F(u_n))^n, compares log(1 − p) with −p, and proves the converse with subsequences.

results.proof_status: authored proof of the cited lemma by the product formula and a subsequence argument. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Both directions of the criterion, for every τ in [0, ∞], including τ = 0 and τ = ∞.

steps.text: Set p_n = 1 − F(u_n), a number in [0, 1]. The event {M_n ≤ u_n} is the event that X_i ≤ u_n for every i ≤ n. By independence, P(M_n ≤ u_n) = ∏_{i=1}^n P(X_i ≤ u_n) = (1 − p_n)^n. So the claim is that (1 − p_n)^n → e^(−τ) if and only if n p_n → τ.

Two elementary bounds. First, 1 − p ≤ e^(−p) for every real p, because the convex function e^(−p) lies above its tangent line 1 − p at 0. Hence (1 − p)^n ≤ e^(−np) for p ∈ [0, 1]. Second, for p ∈ [0, 1/2] the Taylor series log(1 − p) = −Σ_{k≥1} p^k/k gives −p − p² ≤ log(1 − p) ≤ −p, because Σ_{k≥2} p^k/k ≤ (p²/2) Σ_{j≥0} p^j = p²/(2(1 − p)) ≤ p².

Let (n_k) be a strictly increasing sequence of positive integers with n_k p_{n_k} → σ for some finite σ ≥ 0. Then p_{n_k} ≤ (σ + 1)/n_k for large k, so p_{n_k} → 0 and p_{n_k} ≤ 1/2 for large k. Step s2 gives |n_k log(1 − p_{n_k}) + n_k p_{n_k}| ≤ n_k p_{n_k}² = (n_k p_{n_k}) p_{n_k}, and the right side tends to σ · 0 = 0. So n_k log(1 − p_{n_k}) → −σ, and (1 − p_{n_k})^{n_k} → e^(−σ) by continuity of the exponential function.

Let (n_k) be a strictly increasing sequence with n_k p_{n_k} → ∞. Step s2 gives 0 ≤ (1 − p_{n_k})^{n_k} ≤ exp(−n_k p_{n_k}) → 0 = e^(−∞). With n_k = k, steps s3 and s4 prove sufficiency: if n p_n → τ ∈ [0, ∞], then P(M_n ≤ u_n) = (1 − p_n)^n → e^(−τ).

Necessity. Suppose that (1 − p_n)^n → e^(−τ) but n p_n does not tend to τ in [0, ∞]. Then there are a neighbourhood V of τ in [0, ∞] and a strictly increasing sequence (m_j) with m_j p_{m_j} ∉ V for every j. The extended half-line [0, ∞] is sequentially compact: a bounded sequence has a convergent subsequence by the Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem, and an unbounded one has a subsequence that tends to ∞. So a subsequence (n_k) of (m_j) has n_k p_{n_k} → σ for some σ ∈ [0, ∞] outside V, and σ ≠ τ. Steps s3 and s4 give (1 − p_{n_k})^{n_k} → e^(−σ). This limit must equal e^(−τ), and x ↦ e^(−x) is injective on [0, ∞]. So σ = τ, which is a contradiction. Hence n p_n → τ.

applications.title: Largest claim in a portfolio of Pareto insurance claims
applications.inputs: n = 10,000 independent insurance claims with the Pareto tail 1 − F(x) = x^(−2) for x ≥ 1, and F(x) = 0 for x < 1. The claims are in units of the smallest possible claim. The level of interest is u = 200.
applications.hypotheses: The claims are independent with the common distribution function F. Along the sequence of levels u_n = 2√n, the mean number of exceedances is n(1 − F(u_n)) = n/(4n) = 1/4 for every n, so the criterion applies with τ = 1/4. The instance n = 10,000 has u_n = 200.

steps.text: The mean number of claims above the level is n(1 − F(u)) = n u^(−2). For n = 10,000 and u = 200 this is 10000 · (1/200)² = 1/4.
The criterion with τ = 1/4 gives P(M_n ≤ 2√n) → e^(−1/4) ≈ 0.7788. So in a large portfolio the largest claim stays below 2√n with probability about 0.78.
Step s2 of the proof also bounds the error in the instance. With p = 1/40000 and n = 10,000, the error term n p² is 10000 · (1/40000)² = 1/160000.

So n log(1 − p) lies between −1/4 − 1/160000 and −1/4. The exact value P(M_n ≤ 200) = (1 − 1/40000)^10000 lies between e^(−1/4 − 1/160000) and e^(−1/4), and the ratio of the two bounds is e^(−1/160000) > 1 − 10^(−5).

applications.conclusion: For 10,000 independent Pareto claims with tail x^(−2), the probability that no claim exceeds 200 is e^(−1/4) ≈ 0.7788, with a relative error less than 10^(−5).

limitations: The criterion is for independent variables. For a stationary dependent sequence the limit of P(M_n ≤ u_n) can be e^(−θτ), where θ ∈ [0, 1] is the extremal index.

A sequence u_n with n(1 − F(u_n)) → τ ∈ (0, ∞) need not exist. It exists if and only if (1 − F(x))/(1 − F(x−)) → 1 as x increases to the right endpoint of F, and the Poisson and geometric laws fail this condition.

results.name: Poisson limit of the point process of exceedances
results.statement: Let X₁, X₂, … be independent random variables with a common distribution function F. Let τ ∈ (0, ∞), and let u_n be real numbers with n(1 − F(u_n)) → τ. Let N_n be the point process on [0, ∞) with a point at i/n for each index i ≥ 1 with X_i > u_n, so N_n(B) = #{i ≥ 1 : i/n ∈ B, X_i > u_n}. Then N_n converges to the homogeneous Poisson process N on [0, ∞) with intensity τ in the following sense. (a) For every continuous function f ≥ 0 on [0, ∞) with compact support, E exp(−Σ_{i≥1} f(i/n) 1{X_i > u_n}) → exp(−τ ∫₀^∞ (1 − e^(−f(x))) dx), which is the Laplace functional E exp(−∫ f dN). (b) For disjoint bounded intervals I₁, …, I_k in [0, ∞), the vector (N_n(I₁), …, N_n(I_k)) converges in distribution to a vector of independent Poisson variables with means τ|I₁|, …, τ|I_k|. In particular P(N_n(I) = 0) → e^(−τ|I|).
hypotheses: The variables X₁, X₂, … are independent, and each has the distribution function F.
The levels u_n satisfy n(1 − F(u_n)) → τ for a fixed τ ∈ (0, ∞).

prerequisites.reason: Step s2 writes the Laplace functional of N_n as a product of the expectations of independent factors.
Step s3 compares log(1 − y) with −y through the Taylor series of the logarithm, with a remainder of at most y² for y ≤ 1/2.
Step s5 is the Poisson limit theorem for the binomial counts N_n(I_j), whose means tend to τ|I_j|.

definitions.name: homogeneous Poisson process with intensity τ
definitions.text: A random counting measure N on [0, ∞) such that N(I₁), …, N(I_k) are independent Poisson variables with means τ|I₁|, …, τ|I_k| for disjoint bounded intervals. Its Laplace functional is E exp(−∫ f dN) = exp(−τ ∫ (1 − e^(−f(x))) dx) for measurable f ≥ 0.

definitions.name: weak convergence of point processes
definitions.text: Convergence in distribution of random counting measures in the vague topology. It is equivalent to the convergence of the Laplace functionals E exp(−∫ f dN_n) for every continuous f ≥ 0 with compact support, so part (a) is the weak convergence N_n ⇒ N.

source.citation: Anton Bovier, Gaussian Processes on Trees: From Spin Glasses to Branching Brownian Motion, Cambridge Studies in Advanced Mathematics 163, Cambridge University Press, 2017.
source.revision: Author's version with preface dated Bonn, May 2016, linked from the author's lecture notes page at the University of Bonn.
source.module: Chapter 2 Extremal Processes, Section 2.5 Point Processes of Extremes
source.excerpt: Theorem 2.27 Let (X_i)_{i∈ℕ} be iid random variables with marginal distribution function F. Let τ > 0 and assume that there is u_n ≡ u_n(τ) such that lim_{n↑∞} n(1 − F(u_n(τ))) = τ. Then the point process Ñ_n ≡ Σ_{i=−∞}^{∞} δ_{i/n} 1_{X_i > u_n(τ)} (2.64) converges weakly to the Poisson point process Ñ on ℝ with intensity measure τ dx.
source.attribution: © Anton Bovier. Quoted from the author's version of the book for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source prints t for τ in the hypothesis and sums over all integers i although the sequence is indexed by ℕ. The authored statement uses the indices i ≥ 1 and the half-line [0, ∞), and it states the convergence through Laplace functionals and joint counts. The source proves weak convergence with Kallenberg's theorem from the mean counts and the probabilities of empty sets. The authored proof computes the Laplace functionals and the joint counts directly.

results.proof_status: authored proof that computes the Laplace functionals and the joint counts, in place of the Kallenberg criterion of the cited proof. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Parts (a) and (b) of the statement. The equivalence of part (a) with weak convergence in the vague topology is the standard Laplace functional criterion and is not proved here.

steps.text: Set p_n = 1 − F(u_n) and B_i = 1{X_i > u_n}. For fixed n, the B_i, i ≥ 1, are independent Bernoulli variables with mean p_n. Since n p_n → τ < ∞, p_n → 0 and n p_n² = (n p_n) p_n → 0. Choose n₀ with p_n ≤ 1/2 for n ≥ n₀.

Part (a). Let f ≥ 0 be continuous with support in [0, L], and let g = 1 − e^(−f). Then g is continuous with values in [0, 1) and support in [0, L]. Only the indices i ≤ nL have f(i/n) ≠ 0. By independence, E exp(−Σ_i f(i/n) B_i) = ∏_{i ≤ nL} E exp(−f(i/n) B_i) = ∏_{i ≤ nL} (1 − p_n g(i/n)), because exp(−f(i/n) B_i) equals e^(−f(i/n)) with probability p_n and 1 otherwise.

For y ∈ [0, 1/2] the Taylor series of the logarithm gives |log(1 − y) + y| ≤ y². With y_i = p_n g(i/n) ≤ 1/2 for n ≥ n₀, the logarithm of the product in step s2 differs from −p_n Σ_{i≥1} g(i/n) by at most p_n² (nL + 1), which tends to 0. Also p_n Σ_{i≥1} g(i/n) = (n p_n) · (1/n) Σ_{i≥1} g(i/n). The factor (1/n) Σ_{i≥1} g(i/n) is a Riemann sum of the continuous compactly supported function g, so it tends to ∫₀^∞ g(x) dx. Hence the logarithm tends to −τ ∫₀^∞ (1 − e^(−f(x))) dx, and part (a) follows by continuity of the exponential function.

Part (b). For a bounded interval I of length ℓ, the set A_n(I) = {i ≥ 1 : i/n ∈ I} has m_n(I) elements with |m_n(I) − nℓ| ≤ 1, because consecutive points of the grid (1/n)ℤ are 1/n apart. So m_n(I)/n → ℓ and m_n(I) p_n → τℓ. The count N_n(I) = Σ_{i ∈ A_n(I)} B_i has the binomial law with parameters m_n(I) and p_n. For disjoint intervals I₁, …, I_k the index sets A_n(I_j) are disjoint, so the counts N_n(I_j) are functions of disjoint families of the independent B_i and are independent.

Fix j and write m = m_n(I_j) and λ = τ|I_j|. If λ = 0, then m ≤ 1 and P(N_n(I_j) ≥ 1) ≤ p_n → 0, which is the Poisson law with mean 0. If λ > 0, then m → ∞, and for fixed s, P(N_n(I_j) = s) = ∏_{r<s}(1 − r/m) · (m p_n)^s/s! · (1 − p_n)^m (1 − p_n)^(−s). Here m log(1 − p_n) → −λ by the bound of step s3, so the probability tends to e^(−λ) λ^s/s!. This is the Poisson limit theorem. By the independence of step s4, the joint probability mass function of (N_n(I₁), …, N_n(I_k)) is the product of the marginal ones. It converges at every point of ℕ^k to the product of the Poisson mass functions, which gives convergence in distribution. The case s = 0 gives P(N_n(I) = 0) → e^(−τ|I|).

applications.title: Exceedances of the one-year rainfall level in a decade of daily data
applications.inputs: An idealized record of n = 3650 daily rainfall maxima over ten years, modelled as independent with a common distribution function F. The threshold u is the one-year level, with daily exceedance probability 1 − F(u) = 1/365. The time axis is scaled so that the decade is the interval [0, 1].
applications.hypotheses: The daily values are independent with law F. Along levels u_n with n(1 − F(u_n)) = 10, the theorem applies with τ = 10. The instance n = 3650 has 1 − F(u_n) = 1/365.

steps.text: The mean number of exceedances in the decade is τ = n(1 − F(u)) = 3650 · (1/365) = 10.
One year is an interval I of length 1/10, so N_n(I) is approximately Poisson with mean τ|I| = 10 · (1/10) = 1. The probability of a year with no exceedance is about e^(−1) ≈ 0.368.

The two halves of the decade are disjoint intervals of length 1/2, so their counts are asymptotically independent Poisson variables with mean 5. The probability of exactly 5 exceedances in each half is about (e^(−5) 5⁵/5!)², and 5⁵/5! = 625/24.
Numerically e^(−5) · 625/24 ≈ 0.1755, so the probability of 5 exceedances in each half is about 0.1755² ≈ 0.0308, and the probability of 10 exceedances in total is e^(−10) 10^10/10! ≈ 0.1251.

applications.conclusion: In the idealized model, a decade of daily data has about 10 exceedances of the one-year level, the yearly counts are approximately independent Poisson variables with mean 1, and about 37 percent of the years have no exceedance.

limitations: The proof gives Laplace functionals for continuous test functions and joint counts on intervals. Weak convergence in the vague topology then follows from the standard Laplace functional criterion, which this record does not prove.
For stationary dependent sequences, exceedances can form clusters, and the limit is a compound Poisson process when the extremal index is less than 1.

results.name: Limit law of the k-th largest order statistic
results.statement: Let X₁, X₂, … be independent random variables with a common distribution function F. For n ≥ k let M_n^(k) be the k-th largest of X₁, …, X_n, and let S_n(u) = #{i ≤ n : X_i > u}. Let (u_n) be real numbers and fix k ≥ 1. (a) If n(1 − F(u_n)) → τ ∈ [0, ∞), then P(M_n^(k) ≤ u_n) = P(S_n(u_n) < k) → e^(−τ) Σ_{s=0}^{k−1} τ^s/s!. (b) Conversely, if P(M_n^(k) ≤ u_n) → e^(−τ) Σ_{s=0}^{k−1} τ^s/s! for some τ ∈ [0, ∞], with value 0 for τ = ∞, then n(1 − F(u_n)) → τ. (c) If a_n > 0, b_n are real and P(a_n(M_n − b_n) ≤ x) → G(x) at a point x, then P(a_n(M_n^(k) − b_n) ≤ x) → G(x) Σ_{s=0}^{k−1} (−log G(x))^s/s!, with value 0 when G(x) = 0.
hypotheses: The variables X₁, X₂, … are independent, and each has the distribution function F.
The integer k ≥ 1 is fixed, and u_n are real levels. In part (c), a_n > 0 and b_n are real normalizing constants, and the maximum M_n = M_n^(1) satisfies P(a_n(M_n − b_n) ≤ x) → G(x) at the point x.

prerequisites.reason: Step s2 uses the criterion to get (1 − p_n)^n → e^(−τ), and step s5 uses it to turn the limit G(x) of the maximum into n(1 − F(u_n)) → −log G(x).
Step s2 is the Poisson limit theorem for the binomial number of exceedances, which the step computes term by term.
Step s3 bounds P(S_n < k) by Chebyshev's inequality when the mean number n p_n of exceedances tends to infinity.
Step s4 extracts a subsequence along which n(1 − F(u_n)) converges in [0, ∞], by the Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem.

definitions.name: k-th largest order statistic
definitions.text: For n ≥ k, M_n^(k) is the k-th value when X₁, …, X_n are listed in decreasing order, so M_n^(1) = M_n is the maximum and M_n^(1) ≥ M_n^(2) ≥ … ≥ M_n^(n).

definitions.name: number of exceedances
definitions.text: S_n(u) = #{i ≤ n : X_i > u}. For independent X_i with distribution function F it has the binomial law with parameters n and 1 − F(u).

source.citation: Anton Bovier, Gaussian Processes on Trees: From Spin Glasses to Branching Brownian Motion, Cambridge Studies in Advanced Mathematics 163, Cambridge University Press, 2017.
source.revision: Author's version with preface dated Bonn, May 2016, linked from the author's lecture notes page at the University of Bonn.
source.module: Chapter 1 Extreme Value Theory for iid Sequences, Section 1.3 Level-Crossings and kth Maxima
source.excerpt: Theorem 1.16 Let X_i be iid random variables with common distribution F. If u_n is a sequence such that lim_{n↑∞} n(1 − F(u_n)) = τ, 0 < τ < ∞, (1.67) then lim_{n↑∞} P(M^k_n ≤ u_n) = lim_{n↑∞} P(S_n(u_n) < k) = e^(−τ) Σ_{s=0}^{k−1} τ^s/s!. (1.68)
source.attribution: © Anton Bovier. Quoted from the author's version of the book for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: Part (a) is the source theorem extended to τ = 0. Parts (b) and (c) add the converse and the form with normalizing constants, which the source discusses only for the maximum. The proof of part (a) follows the source proof, which expands the binomial probabilities of S_n(u_n). Parts (b) and (c) use the monotonicity of the Poisson distribution function in τ and the Poisson criterion for the maximum.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the binomial computation in the proof of Theorem 1.16 of the cited source. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Parts (a), (b) and (c) for every fixed k ≥ 1, with τ ∈ [0, ∞) in part (a) and τ ∈ [0, ∞] in part (b).

steps.text: Event identity. If at least k of X₁, …, X_n exceed u, then the k-th largest value exceeds u. If at most k − 1 of them exceed u, then the k-th largest value is at most u. So {M_n^(k) ≤ u} = {S_n(u) < k}. Set p_n = 1 − F(u_n). The indicators 1{X_i > u_n}, i ≤ n, are independent Bernoulli variables with mean p_n, so S_n(u_n) has the binomial law with parameters n and p_n.

Part (a). Let n p_n → τ < ∞. Then p_n → 0, so p_n < 1 for large n. For fixed s ≥ 0 and n ≥ s, P(S_n(u_n) = s) = C(n, s) p_n^s (1 − p_n)^(n−s) = [∏_{j=0}^{s−1} (1 − j/n)] · (n p_n)^s/s! · (1 − p_n)^n · (1 − p_n)^(−s). As n → ∞ the product tends to 1, (n p_n)^s → τ^s, (1 − p_n)^(−s) → 1, and (1 − p_n)^n = P(M_n ≤ u_n) → e^(−τ) by the Poisson criterion for maxima. So P(S_n(u_n) = s) → e^(−τ) τ^s/s!, which is the Poisson limit theorem. Summation over s = 0, …, k − 1 and step s1 give P(M_n^(k) ≤ u_n) → Q_k(τ), where Q_k(τ) = e^(−τ) Σ_{s<k} τ^s/s!.

The case n p_n → ∞. The binomial law has mean E S_n = n p_n and variance n p_n(1 − p_n) ≤ n p_n. When n p_n > k, the event {S_n < k} implies |S_n − n p_n| > n p_n − k. Chebyshev's inequality gives P(S_n(u_n) < k) ≤ n p_n/(n p_n − k)², which tends to 0. So P(M_n^(k) ≤ u_n) → 0 = Q_k(∞), with Q_k(∞) = 0 by convention.

Part (b). The function Q_k is the probability that a Poisson variable with mean τ is less than k. Its derivative is Q_k'(τ) = e^(−τ)[Σ_{s=1}^{k−1} τ^(s−1)/(s−1)! − Σ_{s=0}^{k−1} τ^s/s!] = −e^(−τ) τ^(k−1)/(k−1)!, which is negative for τ > 0. So Q_k is strictly decreasing on [0, ∞), with Q_k(τ) > 0 for finite τ and Q_k(τ) → 0 = Q_k(∞) as τ → ∞. Hence Q_k is injective on [0, ∞]. Suppose P(M_n^(k) ≤ u_n) → Q_k(τ) but n p_n does not tend to τ. By the Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem in the compact set [0, ∞], a subsequence has n p_n → σ ∈ [0, ∞] with σ ≠ τ. Steps s2 and s3, applied along the subsequence, give the limit Q_k(σ) ≠ Q_k(τ). This is a contradiction, so n p_n → τ.

Part (c). Fix x with P(a_n(M_n − b_n) ≤ x) → G(x), and set u_n = b_n + x/a_n and τ = −log G(x) ∈ [0, ∞], with τ = ∞ when G(x) = 0. Then P(M_n ≤ u_n) → e^(−τ). Part (b) with k = 1, which is the Poisson criterion for maxima, gives n(1 − F(u_n)) → τ. If τ < ∞, part (a) gives P(a_n(M_n^(k) − b_n) ≤ x) = P(M_n^(k) ≤ u_n) → e^(−τ) Σ_{s<k} τ^s/s! = G(x) Σ_{s<k} (−log G(x))^s/s!. If τ = ∞, step s3 gives the limit 0.

applications.title: A reinsurance layer that responds to the third-largest claim
applications.inputs: n = 10,000 independent insurance claims with the Pareto tail 1 − F(x) = x^(−2) for x ≥ 1. A reinsurance layer pays only when the third-largest claim exceeds the level 200, so k = 3 and u = 200.
applications.hypotheses: The claims are independent with the common distribution function F. Along the levels u_n = 2√n the mean number of exceedances is n(1 − F(u_n)) = 1/4 for every n, so part (a) applies with τ = 1/4. The instance n = 10,000 has u_n = 200.

steps.text: The mean number of claims above 200 is τ = 10000 · (1/200)² = 1/4.
The third-largest claim is at most 200 exactly when fewer than 3 claims exceed 200. Part (a) gives the limit e^(−1/4)(1 + 1/4 + (1/4)²/2), and the bracket equals 41/32.

With e^(−1/4) ≈ 0.778801, the case k = 3 gives (41/32) · 0.778801 ≈ 0.99784. So the layer is used with probability about 0.0022, while a cover on the largest claim at the same level is used with probability about 0.22.

applications.conclusion: For 10,000 independent Pareto claims with tail x^(−2), the third-largest claim exceeds 200 with probability about 1 − (41/32)e^(−1/4) ≈ 0.0022, one hundredth of the probability for the largest claim.

limitations: The theorem is for independent variables. For stationary sequences with clusters of exceedances, the number of exceedances has a compound Poisson limit, and the limit of P(M_n^(k) ≤ u_n) depends on the cluster size distribution.
The theorem gives the law of one order statistic at a time. Joint laws of several top order statistics need the counts above several levels, or the point process of exceedances.

results.name: Rényi representation of exponential order statistics
results.statement: Let Y₁, …, Y_n be independent standard exponential random variables with order statistics Y_(1) ≥ Y_(2) ≥ … ≥ Y_(n), and let E₁, …, E_n be independent standard exponential random variables. Then the vector (Y_(1), …, Y_(n)) has the same law as (Σ_{k=1}^n E_k/k, Σ_{k=2}^n E_k/k, …, E_n/n). Equivalently, with Y_(n+1) = 0, the normalized spacings k(Y_(k) − Y_(k+1)), k = 1, …, n, are independent standard exponential variables. Moreover, let F be any distribution function, U(t) = inf{x : F(x) ≥ 1 − 1/t} for t > 1, and X_(1) ≥ … ≥ X_(n) the order statistics of n independent variables with law F. Then (X_(1), …, X_(n)) has the same law as (U(e^(Y_(1))), …, U(e^(Y_(n)))).
hypotheses: Y₁, …, Y_n are independent, each with the standard exponential law P(Y_j > y) = e^(−y) for y ≥ 0.
For the last part, X₁, …, X_n are independent with an arbitrary common distribution function F, and U is the tail quantile function of F.

prerequisites.reason: Step s2 transforms the joint density of the ordered exponential sample to the normalized spacings with a linear map of Jacobian determinant n!.

definitions.name: order statistics
definitions.text: For real numbers y₁, …, y_n, the values y_(1) ≥ y_(2) ≥ … ≥ y_(n) are the same numbers listed in decreasing order, with repetitions.

definitions.name: normalized spacings
definitions.text: For an exponential sample, the variables k(Y_(k) − Y_(k+1)), k = 1, …, n, with the convention Y_(n+1) = 0.

definitions.name: tail quantile function
definitions.text: U(t) = inf{x : F(x) ≥ 1 − 1/t} for t > 1. It is the generalized inverse of 1/(1 − F), and U(t) ≤ x holds exactly when F(x) ≥ 1 − 1/t.

source.citation: Stéphane Boucheron and Maud Thomas, Concentration inequalities for order statistics, Electronic Communications in Probability 17 (2012), paper no. 51, 1–12.
source.module: Section 2 Order statistics and spacings
source.excerpt: Theorem 2.5. (Rényi's representation) Let X_(1) ≥ … ≥ X_(n) be the order statistics of a sample from distribution F, let U = (1/(1 − F))^←, let Y_(1) ≥ Y_(2) ≥ … ≥ Y_(n) be the order statistics of an independent sample of the exponential distribution, then (Y_(n), …, Y_(i), …, Y_(1)) ∼ (E_n/n, …, Σ_{k=i}^n E_k/k, …, Σ_{k=1}^n E_k/k) …
source.attribution: © Stéphane Boucheron and Maud Thomas. Quoted from the authors' arXiv preprint for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The authored statement is the source theorem with the spacing form added and with U written out as in the source's Definition 2.4. The source states the theorem without proof and refers to the literature. The authored proof uses the joint density of the ordered exponential sample, a linear change of variables to the spacings, and the quantile transform.

results.proof_status: authored proof of the cited theorem by the joint density of order statistics and the quantile transform. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement, for every n ≥ 1 and every distribution function F.

steps.text: Let Z₁ < Z₂ < … < Z_n be the exponential sample in increasing order, so Z_m = Y_(n−m+1). Ties have probability 0 because the law has a density. For a Borel set A in the region R = {0 < z₁ < … < z_n}, the event {Z ∈ A} is the disjoint union over the n! permutations π of {(Y_π(1), …, Y_π(n)) ∈ A}, up to a null set. Each of these events has probability ∫_A ∏ e^(−z_j) dz. So Z has the density n! exp(−Σ_j z_j) on R.

Define w_j = (n − j + 1)(z_j − z_{j−1}) for j = 1, …, n, with z₀ = 0. This linear map sends R one to one onto (0, ∞)^n. Its matrix is lower triangular with diagonal entries n, n − 1, …, 1, so its Jacobian determinant is n!. Each z_m is the sum of the increments z_j − z_{j−1} for j ≤ m, so Σ_m z_m = Σ_j (n − j + 1)(z_j − z_{j−1}) = Σ_j w_j. The change of variables formula gives W the density n! e^(−Σ w_j)/n! = ∏_j e^(−w_j) on (0, ∞)^n. So W₁, …, W_n are independent standard exponential variables.

Invert the map: Z_m = Σ_{j=1}^m W_j/(n − j + 1). Put E_k = W_{n−k+1}, which is again an independent standard exponential family. With k = n − j + 1, Y_(i) = Z_{n−i+1} = Σ_{j=1}^{n−i+1} W_j/(n − j + 1) = Σ_{k=i}^n E_k/k for every i. This is the first claim. It also gives k(Y_(k) − Y_(k+1)) = E_k for k = 1, …, n, which is the spacing form.

Quantile transform. For t > 1 the set S_t = {x : F(x) ≥ 1 − 1/t} is nonempty, bounded below, closed under increase, and closed from the right because F is right-continuous. So S_t = [U(t), ∞), and U(t) ≤ x if and only if F(x) ≥ 1 − 1/t. For a standard exponential Y, e^Y > 1 almost surely, and P(U(e^Y) ≤ x) = P(e^(−Y) ≥ 1 − F(x)). If F(x) < 1 this is P(Y ≤ −log(1 − F(x))) = F(x), and if F(x) = 1 it is 1 = F(x). So U(e^(Y₁)), …, U(e^(Y_n)) are independent with law F.

The map g = U ∘ exp is non-decreasing. If g(y_j) > g(y_(i)), then y_j > y_(i), so at most i − 1 of the values g(y_j) exceed g(y_(i)). At least i of them are at least g(y_(i)), namely those with y_j ≥ y_(i). Hence g(y_(i)) is the i-th largest of the values g(y_j). Since the vector of order statistics is a fixed measurable function of the sample, step s4 gives (X_(1), …, X_(n)) the same law as (g(Y_(1)), …, g(Y_(n))) = (U(e^(Y_(1))), …, U(e^(Y_(n)))).

applications.title: Exact law of the Hill estimator for a Pareto sample
applications.inputs: An independent sample of size n > k from the Pareto law F(x) = 1 − x^(−α) for x ≥ 1, with tail index α = 2. The Hill estimator built on the k = 50 largest values is H_k = (1/k) Σ_{i=1}^k log(X_(i)/X_(k+1)).
applications.hypotheses: The sample is independent with distribution function F. For t > 1, U(t) = inf{x ≥ 1 : x^(−α) ≤ 1/t} = t^(1/α), so the representation gives log X_(i) = Y_(i)/α jointly in i, in law.

steps.text: By the representation, log(X_(i)/X_(k+1)) = (Y_(i) − Y_(k+1))/α = (1/α) Σ_{j=i}^k E_j/j in law, jointly for i = 1, …, k.
Sum over i = 1, …, k. The term E_j/j appears for the j indices i ≤ j, so Σ_{i=1}^k (Y_(i) − Y_(k+1)) = Σ_{j=1}^k E_j. Hence kαH_k has the Gamma law with shape k and scale 1.
So E H_k = 1/α = 1/2 exactly, and Var H_k = 1/(kα²) = 1/(50 · 2²) = 1/200 for every sample size n > 50.
The standard deviation is (1/200)^(1/2) ≈ 0.0707. So the Hill estimate of 1/α = 0.5 from the top 50 values has a relative standard error of about 14 percent, independent of n.

applications.conclusion: For an exact Pareto sample with α = 2, the Hill estimator on the top 50 values is unbiased for 1/α = 0.5 and has variance exactly 1/200, because kαH_k has the Gamma(50, 1) law.

limitations: The independent spacings are a property of the exponential law. For another law F the representation holds through the transform U ∘ exp, which is not affine in general, so the spacings of the X sample are dependent in general.
The representation does not give the dependence between the order statistics of two different samples, nor the order statistics of dependent variables.

results.name: Gumbel limit for maxima of independent standard Gaussian variables
results.statement: Let X₁, X₂, … be independent random variables with the standard normal law N(0, 1), and let M_n = max(X₁, …, X_n). For n ≥ 3 put a_n = √(2 log n) and b_n = √(2 log n) − (log log n + log(4π))/(2√(2 log n)). Then P(a_n(M_n − b_n) ≤ x) → exp(−e^(−x)) as n → ∞, for every real x.
hypotheses: The variables X₁, X₂, … are independent, and each has the standard normal law N(0, 1).
The normalizing constants are a_n = √(2 log n) and b_n = √(2 log n) − (log log n + log(4π))/(2√(2 log n)), for n ≥ 3.

prerequisites.reason: Step s4 turns the limit n(1 − Φ(u_n)) → e^(−x) of the mean number of exceedances into the limit of P(M_n ≤ u_n).
Step s1 proves the lower Mills bound by integrating the exact derivative of φ(t)(1/t − 1/t³) from u to infinity.

definitions.name: standard normal tail
definitions.text: 1 − Φ(u) = ∫_u^∞ φ(t) dt with φ(t) = (2π)^(−1/2) e^(−t²/2). Its ratio to φ(u)/u tends to 1 as u → ∞ (Mills ratio).

definitions.name: Gumbel distribution
definitions.text: The distribution function Λ(x) = exp(−e^(−x)), x ∈ ℝ. It is the extreme value law of type I.

source.citation: Anton Bovier, Gaussian Processes on Trees: From Spin Glasses to Branching Brownian Motion, Cambridge Studies in Advanced Mathematics 163, Cambridge University Press, 2017.
source.revision: Author's version with preface dated Bonn, May 2016, linked from the author's lecture notes page at the University of Bonn.
source.module: Chapter 1 Extreme Value Theory for iid Sequences, Section 1.2 Extremal Distributions
source.excerpt: Theorem 1.2 Let X_i, i ∈ ℕ be iid normal random variables. Let b_n ≡ √(2 ln n) − (ln ln n + ln(4π))/(2√(2 ln n)), (1.18) and a_n = √(2 ln n). (1.19) Then, for any x ∈ ℝ, lim_{n↑∞} P(a_n(M_n − b_n) ≤ x) = e^(−e^(−x)). (1.20)
source.attribution: © Anton Bovier. Quoted from the author's version of the book for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source says normal for standard normal and writes ln for the natural logarithm. The authored statement makes the law N(0, 1) and the condition n ≥ 3 explicit. The source derives the constants from the Mills bounds (Lemma 1.1, p. 3) and the Poisson limit of the binomial law. The authored proof follows that computation and proves the Mills bounds.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the computation before Theorem 1.2 of the cited source. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement for every real x.

steps.text: Mills bounds. Let φ(t) = (2π)^(−1/2) e^(−t²/2), so φ'(t) = −tφ(t). For u > 0, 1 − Φ(u) = ∫_u^∞ φ(t) dt ≤ ∫_u^∞ (t/u) φ(t) dt = φ(u)/u. The derivative of φ(t)(1/t − 1/t³) is −φ(t)(1 − 3/t⁴), and φ(t)(1/t − 1/t³) → 0 as t → ∞. The fundamental theorem of calculus gives φ(u)(1/u − 1/u³) = ∫_u^∞ φ(t)(1 − 3/t⁴) dt ≤ 1 − Φ(u). Hence 1 − u^(−2) ≤ (1 − Φ(u)) u/φ(u) ≤ 1 for u > 0.

Fix x and put u_n = b_n + x/a_n. Write L = log n, a = a_n = √(2L) and c = c_n = (log L + log 4π)/(2a), so b_n = a − c. Then c → 0 and c/a = (log L + log 4π)/(4L) → 0, so u_n/a_n = 1 − c/a + x/a² → 1 and u_n → ∞. Expand u_n² = (a − c)² + 2x(a − c)/a + x²/a² = 2L − (log L + log 4π) + c² + 2x − 2xc/a + x²/a². Since c², c/a and 1/a² tend to 0, u_n²/2 = L − (1/2)log L − (1/2)log 4π + x + o(1).

Compute log(n φ(u_n)/u_n) = L − u_n²/2 − (1/2)log 2π − log u_n. Here log u_n = log a_n + log(u_n/a_n) = (1/2)log 2 + (1/2)log L + o(1). Step s2 gives log(n φ(u_n)/u_n) = (1/2)log L + (1/2)log 4π − x − (1/2)log 2π − (1/2)log 2 − (1/2)log L + o(1) = −x + (1/2)log(4π/(2π · 2)) + o(1) = −x + o(1). So n φ(u_n)/u_n → e^(−x). Since u_n → ∞, step s1 gives n(1 − Φ(u_n)) = (n φ(u_n)/u_n)(1 + O(u_n^(−2))) → e^(−x).

The event {a_n(M_n − b_n) ≤ x} equals {M_n ≤ u_n} because a_n > 0. The Poisson criterion for maxima of independent variables, with τ = e^(−x) ∈ (0, ∞), turns n(1 − Φ(u_n)) → e^(−x) into P(M_n ≤ u_n) → exp(−e^(−x)). This holds for every real x.

applications.title: Ground-state energy of the random energy model with 20 spins
applications.inputs: Derrida's random energy model with N = 20 Ising spins and coupling J = 1. Each of the n = 2^N configurations σ has the energy E_σ = −√(N/2) X_σ, where the X_σ are independent standard normal variables. The ground-state energy is E_min = −√(N/2) M_n with M_n = max_σ X_σ.
applications.hypotheses: The X_σ are independent with law N(0, 1) by the definition of the model, and n = 2^20 ≥ 3. So the theorem applies to M_n with the constants a_n and b_n of the statement.

steps.text: The number of configurations is n = 2^20 = 1,048,576, so log n = 20 log 2 ≈ 13.8629.

The theorem gives M_n ≈ b_n + G/a_n with G Gumbel distributed. The median of G is −log log 2 ≈ 0.3665, so the median of M_n is about 4.7755 + 0.3665/5.2655 ≈ 4.8451. The exact median, the root u of Φ(u)^n = 1/2, is about 4.8364.

The median ground-state energy is about −√10 · 4.8451 ≈ −15.32, or −0.766 per spin. The limit per spin as N → ∞ is −√(log 2) ≈ −0.833. The correction −(log log n + log 4π)/(2a_n) in b_n explains most of the gap.

applications.conclusion: For the random energy model with 20 spins, the ground-state energy has median about −15.3, or −0.766 per spin, with Gumbel fluctuations of order √10/a_n ≈ 0.6. The Gumbel prediction for the median of M_n is within 0.01 of the exact value.

limitations: The convergence is slow. The error in the distribution function is of order (log log n)²/log n, so the second-order term in b_n matters for moderate n.
The theorem is for independent variables. For stationary Gaussian sequences, Berman's condition r_n log n → 0 on the covariances keeps the same limit, and stronger correlations can change it.

results.name: Extremal types theorem for stationary sequences
aliases: Extremal types theorem under condition D(u_n)
results.statement: Let ξ₁, ξ₂, … be a strictly stationary sequence of random variables and let M_n = max(ξ₁, …, ξ_n). Suppose that there are constants a_n > 0 and b_n such that P(a_n(M_n − b_n) ≤ x) → G(x) at every continuity point x of a non-degenerate distribution function G. Suppose that for every real x the condition D(u_n) holds for the levels u_n = x/a_n + b_n. Then G is max-stable: for every integer k ≥ 1 there are α_k > 0 and β_k with G^k(α_k x + β_k) = G(x) for all x. Hence G is of the same type as one of the three extreme value distributions: the Gumbel law exp(−e^(−x)), the Fréchet law exp(−x^(−α)) for x > 0, or the Weibull law exp(−(−x)^α) for x ≤ 0, with α > 0.
hypotheses: The sequence ξ₁, ξ₂, … is strictly stationary.
There are constants a_n > 0 and b_n such that a_n(M_n − b_n) converges in distribution to a non-degenerate distribution function G.
For every real x, Leadbetter's condition D(u_n) holds for the level sequence u_n = x/a_n + b_n.

prerequisites.reason: Step s5 uses the analytic half of the proof of the Fisher–Tippett–Gnedenko theorem: every non-degenerate max-stable distribution function is of extreme value type.

definitions.name: condition D(u_n)
definitions.text: For levels u_n, let α_{n,l} be the largest value of |P(ξ_i ≤ u_n for all i ∈ I ∪ J) − P(ξ_i ≤ u_n for all i ∈ I) P(ξ_j ≤ u_n for all j ∈ J)| over all index sets I = {i_1 < … < i_p} and J = {j_1 < … < j_q} in {1, …, n} with j_1 − i_p ≥ l. D(u_n) holds if α_{n,l_n} → 0 for some sequence l_n = o(n).

definitions.name: max-stable distribution
definitions.text: A distribution function G such that for every n ≥ 1 there are constants α_n > 0 and β_n with G^n(α_n x + β_n) = G(x) for all x. So the maximum of n i.i.d. copies with law G has a law of the same type as G.

definitions.name: same type
definitions.text: Two distribution functions G and H are of the same type if H(x) = G(αx + β) for all x, for some constants α > 0 and β.

source.citation: M. R. Leadbetter and Holger Rootzén, Extremal theory for stochastic processes, Preprint 1987 No. 5, Institute of Mathematical Statistics, University of Copenhagen; published in Annals of Probability 16 (1988), 431-478.
source.revision: University of Copenhagen preprint, 1987 No. 5 (scanned typescript).
source.module: Section 2.1 The Extremal Types Theorem for stationary sequences
source.excerpt: Theorem 2.1.2. (Extremal Types Theorem for Stationary Sequences) Let {ξ_n} be a stationary sequence such that M_n = max(ξ_1, ξ_2, …, ξ_n) has a non-degenerate limiting distribution G as in (1.2.1). Suppose that D(u_n) holds for each u_n of the form u_n = x/a_n + b_n, for x with 0 < G(x) < 1. Then G is one of the three classical extremal types.
source.attribution: © M. R. Leadbetter and Holger Rootzén. Quoted from the University of Copenhagen preprint for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source asks for D(u_n) only at the levels with 0 < G(x) < 1. The authored statement asks for D(u_n) at every real x, which is a stronger hypothesis. With it, step s3 gives convergence at every continuity point of G without an extra argument at the levels where G(x) = 0. The outline follows the proof that the source indicates: Lemma 2.1.1, max-stability of G as in [66, Theorem 3.3.3], and the classification of max-stable laws.

results.proof_status: outline of the cited published proof. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof that Leadbetter and Rootzén (1987), Section 2.1, indicate for Theorem 2.1.2, with the max-stability argument of [66, Theorem 3.3.3] (Leadbetter, Lindgren and Rootzén, 1983). Step s1 takes the block approximation of Lemma 2.1.1 from the source, step s4 cites the convergence of types theorem, and step s5 cites the classification of max-stable laws.

steps.text: Block approximation (Lemma 2.1.1 of the source). Let D(u_n) hold with α_{n,l_n} → 0 and l_n = o(n). Let k_n ≥ 1 be integers with k_n = o(n), k_n l_n = o(n) and k_n α_{n,l_n} → 0. Lemma 2.1.1 of the source proves that P(M_n ≤ u_n) − P^{k_n}(M_{r_n} ≤ u_n) → 0 as n → ∞, with r_n = [n/k_n]. The source describes the proof. Cut {1, …, n} into k_n intervals of length r_n and remove a subinterval of length l_n at the right end of each. The maxima over the k_n remaining intervals are separated by at least l_n, so D(u_n) makes their joint probability differ from the product of the marginal probabilities by at most k_n α_{n,l_n}. The lemma also controls the removed subintervals, whose total length k_n l_n is o(n).

A fixed number of blocks. Fix an integer k ≥ 1 and a real x, and put u_m = x/a_m + b_m. By hypothesis D(u_m) holds with some l_m = o(m) and α_{m,l_m} → 0. The constant sequence k_m = k satisfies k = o(m), k l_m = o(m) and k α_{m,l_m} → 0. So step s1 gives P(M_m ≤ u_m) − P^k(M_{[m/k]} ≤ u_m) → 0 as m → ∞. Along the subsequence m = nk we have [m/k] = n, so P(M_{nk} ≤ u_{nk}) − P^k(M_n ≤ u_{nk}) → 0 as n → ∞.

A second normalization of M_n. Let x be a continuity point of G. The sequence (nk) is a subsequence of (n), so P(M_{nk} ≤ u_{nk}) = P(a_{nk}(M_{nk} − b_{nk}) ≤ x) → G(x). Step s2 then gives P^k(M_n ≤ u_{nk}) → G(x). The map t ↦ t^{1/k} is continuous on [0, 1], so P(a_{nk}(M_n − b_{nk}) ≤ x) → G(x)^{1/k}. The function G^{1/k} is a non-degenerate distribution function with the same continuity points as G. So a_{nk}(M_n − b_{nk}) converges in distribution to G^{1/k}, while a_n(M_n − b_n) converges in distribution to G.

Max-stability by convergence of types. In step s3 the same random variables M_n have two affine normalizations with non-degenerate limits. Khintchine's convergence of types theorem gives a_n/a_{nk} → α_k > 0 and a_n(b_{nk} − b_n) → β_k, and G^{1/k}(x) = G(α_k x + β_k) for all x. Raise both sides to the power k: G^k(α_k x + β_k) = G(x) for all x. This holds for every k ≥ 1, so G is max-stable in the sense of Section 1.2 of the source. The source takes this step from [66, Theorem 3.3.3].

Classification of max-stable laws. A non-degenerate max-stable distribution function is of the same type as a Gumbel, Fréchet or Weibull law. This is the analytic second half of the proof of the extremal types theorem for i.i.d. sequences (Theorem 1.2.1 of the source). The source notes that this half uses no probability and applies verbatim in the dependent case, and it refers to de Haan's inverse function proof in [66]. With step s4 this gives the conclusion.

source.ref: M. R. Leadbetter and H. Rootzén, Extremal theory for stochastic processes, University of Copenhagen Preprint 1987 No. 5 (Ann. Probab. 16 (1988) 431-478), Lemma 2.1.1 and Theorem 2.1.2, pp. 10-11.

applications.title: Maxima of two-day losses with Pareto daily losses
applications.inputs: Daily losses η₁, η₂, … are i.i.d. with the Pareto tail P(η > y) = y^(−2) for y ≥ 1. The two-day loss on day j is ξ_j = max(η_j, η_{j+1}). We study M_n = max(ξ₁, …, ξ_n) with a_n = n^(−1/2) and b_n = 0.
applications.hypotheses: The sequence (ξ_j) is a function of a shifted i.i.d. sequence, so it is strictly stationary. It is 1-dependent, which gives D(u_n) at every level (step a1). Step a2 shows that n^(−1/2) M_n has a non-degenerate limit.

steps.text: Condition D(u_n). If j_1 − i_p ≥ 2, the variables ξ_i for i ∈ I use only η_1, …, η_{i_p + 1}, and the variables ξ_j for j ∈ J use only η_{j_1}, η_{j_1 + 1}, …. These sets of η's are disjoint, so the two events are independent and α_{n,2} = 0. So D(u_n) holds with l_n = 2 for every level sequence.

The limit law. M_n = max(η_1, …, η_{n+1}), so for x > 0 and n x² ≥ 1 we get P(M_n ≤ √n x) = (1 − 1/(n x²))^(n+1) → exp(−x^(−2)). For x ≤ 0 the probability is 0. So G(x) = exp(−x^(−2)) for x > 0, which is non-degenerate.

Max-stability, as step s4 predicts. With k = 4 the constants are α_4 = lim a_n/a_{4n} = √4 = 2 and β_4 = 0. Then G^4(2x) = exp(−4 · (2x)^(−2)) = exp(−x^(−2)) = G(x), because the exponent factor 4 · (1/2)² equals 1.
A finite-n value. For n = 4 and x = 1 the exact probability is P(M_4 ≤ 2) = (1 − 1/4)^5 = 243/1024 ≈ 0.237. The limit value is G(1) = e^(−1) ≈ 0.368, so the convergence is slow for small n.

applications.conclusion: The limit of n^(−1/2) max(ξ₁, …, ξ_n) is the Fréchet law exp(−x^(−2)) with α = 2. This is one of the three extreme value types, as the theorem predicts for this dependent sequence.

limitations: The theorem does not say that a limit exists. It only restricts the possible non-degenerate limits. Existence depends on the tail of the marginal law and on the dependence.
The theorem does not identify the type or the constants. Under D(u_n) the type is that of the associated i.i.d. sequence when the extremal index is positive, but the limit can change by a power G^θ.
Some restriction on the dependence is necessary. For example, if all ξ_i are equal, M_n has the law of ξ_1, so every distribution function can appear as the limit.

results.name: Extremal index theorem for stationary sequences
aliases: Power relation between dependent and independent maxima
results.statement: Let ξ₁, ξ₂, … be a strictly stationary sequence with marginal distribution function F and maxima M_n = max(ξ₁, …, ξ_n). Let ξ̂₁, ξ̂₂, … be i.i.d. with distribution function F and M̂_n = max(ξ̂₁, …, ξ̂_n). Suppose that (ξ_n) has extremal index θ: for each τ > 0 there are levels u_n(τ) with n(1 − F(u_n(τ))) → τ and P(M_n ≤ u_n(τ)) → e^(−θτ). Then 0 ≤ θ ≤ 1. If θ > 0, then for every sequence of constants v_n and every ρ ∈ [0, 1], P(M̂_n ≤ v_n) → ρ if and only if P(M_n ≤ v_n) → ρ^θ. In particular, for constants a_n > 0 and b_n and a distribution function G, P(a_n(M̂_n − b_n) ≤ x) → G(x) at every continuity point x of G if and only if P(a_n(M_n − b_n) ≤ x) → G(x)^θ at every continuity point x of G.
hypotheses: The sequence ξ₁, ξ₂, … is strictly stationary with marginal distribution function F, and ξ̂₁, ξ̂₂, … is i.i.d. with distribution function F.
The sequence (ξ_n) has an extremal index θ: for each τ > 0 there are levels u_n(τ) with n(1 − F(u_n(τ))) → τ and P(M_n ≤ u_n(τ)) → e^(−θτ).
For the power relation: θ > 0.

prerequisites.reason: Steps s3, s4 and s5 use the i.i.d. criterion: F(v_n)^n → e^(−τ) if and only if n(1 − F(v_n)) → τ, for 0 ≤ τ ≤ ∞.

definitions.name: extremal index
definitions.text: A number θ such that for each τ > 0 there are levels u_n(τ) with n(1 − F(u_n(τ))) → τ and P(M_n ≤ u_n(τ)) → e^(−θτ). For an i.i.d. sequence θ = 1. A value θ < 1 means that high exceedances occur in clusters of mean size about 1/θ.

definitions.name: associated independent sequence
definitions.text: The i.i.d. sequence ξ̂₁, ξ̂₂, … with the same marginal distribution function F as the stationary sequence (ξ_n). Its maxima are written M̂_n.

source.citation: M. R. Leadbetter and Holger Rootzén, Extremal theory for stochastic processes, Preprint 1987 No. 5, Institute of Mathematical Statistics, University of Copenhagen; published in Annals of Probability 16 (1988), 431-478.
source.revision: University of Copenhagen preprint, 1987 No. 5 (scanned typescript).
source.module: Section 2.2 The Extremal Index
source.excerpt: Theorem 2.2.1 Let the stationary sequence {ξ_n} have extremal index θ > 0. If P{a_n(M̂_n − b_n) ≤ x} → G(x) then P{a_n(M_n − b_n) ≤ x} → G^θ(x) and conversely. That is M_n has an asymptotic distribution if and only if M̂_n does, with the power relation between the limits and the same normalizing constants.
source.attribution: © M. R. Leadbetter and Holger Rootzén. Quoted from the University of Copenhagen preprint for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The authored statement adds the bound 0 ≤ θ ≤ 1, which the source proves on p. 12, and the level form of the equivalence, which the source states on p. 13 just before Theorem 2.2.1. The source says that the level form follows by obvious arguments from [64] (Leadbetter, 1983). The steps write out these arguments and then take v_n = x/a_n + b_n, as the source does.

results.proof_status: outline of the cited published proof. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow Leadbetter and Rootzén (1987), Section 2.2, pp. 12-13: the union bound argument for θ ≤ 1 and the level equivalence that the source attributes to [64] (Leadbetter, 1983), followed by Theorem 2.2.1. Step s3 takes Lemma 1.2.2 of the source. The steps give each inference, so the outline covers the full statement.

steps.text: Range of θ. The limit e^(−θτ) of probabilities is at most 1, so θ ≥ 0. By the union bound and stationarity, P(M_n > u_n(τ)) ≤ n(1 − F(u_n(τ))) → τ. So e^(−θτ) ≥ 1 − τ for every τ > 0, that is (1 − e^(−θτ))/τ ≤ 1. The left side tends to θ as τ ↓ 0, so θ ≤ 1. This is the argument of the source on p. 12.

The limit depends only on n(1 − F(v_n)). For levels v ≤ w, the event {M_n ≤ w} \ {M_n ≤ v} implies that some ξ_i lies in (v, w]. The union bound and stationarity give 0 ≤ P(M_n ≤ w) − P(M_n ≤ v) ≤ n(F(w) − F(v)). So |P(M_n ≤ v_n) − P(M_n ≤ u_n(τ))| ≤ |n(1 − F(u_n(τ))) − n(1 − F(v_n))|. If n(1 − F(v_n)) → τ ∈ (0, ∞), the right side tends to 0 and P(M_n ≤ v_n) → e^(−θτ). The same argument holds along any subsequence of n.

The i.i.d. side. P(M̂_n ≤ v_n) = F(v_n)^n. Lemma 1.2.2 of the source states that, for 0 ≤ τ ≤ ∞, F(v_n)^n → e^(−τ) if and only if n(1 − F(v_n)) → τ. The proof compares n log F(v_n) with −n(1 − F(v_n)), term by term in n, so the criterion also holds along any subsequence of n.

From ρ to ρ^θ. Let θ > 0 and P(M̂_n ≤ v_n) → ρ, and put τ = −log ρ ∈ [0, ∞]. Step s3 gives n(1 − F(v_n)) → τ. If 0 < τ < ∞, step s2 gives P(M_n ≤ v_n) → e^(−θτ) = ρ^θ. If τ = 0, the union bound gives P(M_n ≤ v_n) ≥ 1 − n(1 − F(v_n)) → 1 = ρ^θ. If τ = ∞, fix σ > 0. Eventually n(1 − F(v_n)) > n(1 − F(u_n(σ))), so F(v_n) < F(u_n(σ)) and v_n < u_n(σ). Then P(M_n ≤ v_n) ≤ P(M_n ≤ u_n(σ)) → e^(−θσ). This holds for every σ > 0 and θ > 0, so P(M_n ≤ v_n) → 0 = ρ^θ. All three cases also hold along subsequences.

From ρ^θ back to ρ. Let θ > 0 and P(M_n ≤ v_n) → ρ^θ. Every subsequence of n has a further subsequence along which n(1 − F(v_n)) → τ′ for some τ′ ∈ [0, ∞], because [0, ∞] is compact. Along it, step s3 gives P(M̂_n ≤ v_n) → e^(−τ′), and step s4 gives P(M_n ≤ v_n) → e^(−θτ′). So e^(−θτ′) = ρ^θ. For θ > 0 the map τ ↦ e^(−θτ) is injective on [0, ∞], so e^(−τ′) = ρ. Every subsequence has a further subsequence along which P(M̂_n ≤ v_n) → ρ, so P(M̂_n ≤ v_n) → ρ.

Normalized maxima (Theorem 2.2.1 of the source). Fix a continuity point x of G and apply steps s4 and s5 with v_n = x/a_n + b_n and ρ = G(x). This gives P(a_n(M̂_n − b_n) ≤ x) → G(x) if and only if P(a_n(M_n − b_n) ≤ x) → G(x)^θ. For θ > 0 the map t ↦ t^θ is a homeomorphism of [0, 1], so G and G^θ have the same continuity points. Hence the two convergence statements in distribution are equivalent.

source.ref: M. R. Leadbetter and H. Rootzén, Extremal theory for stochastic processes, University of Copenhagen Preprint 1987 No. 5 (Ann. Probab. 16 (1988) 431-478), Section 2.2 and Theorem 2.2.1, pp. 11-13.

applications.title: Clustered extremes in a max-autoregressive loss process
applications.inputs: Fix a = 3/4. Let Z₂, Z₃, … be i.i.d. unit Fréchet, P(Z ≤ z) = exp(−1/z) for z > 0, and let ξ₁ be unit Fréchet and independent of them. Define ξ_j = max(a ξ_{j−1}, (1 − a) Z_j) for j ≥ 2. We study the yearly maximum M_365.
applications.hypotheses: If ξ_{j−1} is unit Fréchet, then P(ξ_j ≤ x) = exp(−a/x) exp(−(1 − a)/x) = exp(−1/x). So the Markov chain (ξ_j) starts in its stationary law and is strictly stationary with F(x) = exp(−1/x). Step a1 shows that the extremal index exists and equals 1 − a = 1/4 > 0.

steps.text: Extremal index. For u > 0, M_n ≤ u holds if and only if ξ₁ ≤ u and (1 − a) Z_j ≤ u for j = 2, …, n, because ξ_{j−1} ≤ u implies a ξ_{j−1} ≤ u. So P(M_n ≤ u) = exp(−1/u) exp(−(n − 1)(1 − a)/u). With u_n(τ) = n/τ we have n(1 − F(u_n(τ))) = n(1 − e^(−τ/n)) → τ and P(M_n ≤ u_n(τ)) → e^(−(1 − a)τ). So θ = 1 − a = 1/4.
The independent comparison. For the associated i.i.d. sequence, P(M̂_n ≤ n x) = exp(−1/(n x))^n = exp(−1/x) = G(x) for every n. So the theorem gives P(M_n ≤ n x) → G(x)^θ = exp(−1/(4x)).

Exact value for a year. With n = 365 and the level 365 x, the formula of step a1 gives P(M_365 ≤ 365 x) = exp(−(1 + 364 · (1/4))/(365 x)) = exp(−(92/365)/x). The limit exponent is θ/x = (91.25/365)/x, which is very close.

Interpretation. At x = 1 the dependent sequence gives P(M_365 ≤ 365) ≈ e^(−0.252) ≈ 0.777, while the i.i.d. sequence gives e^(−1) ≈ 0.368. High values come in clusters of mean size 1/θ = 4 days, so there are fewer independent chances to exceed the level.

applications.conclusion: The max-autoregressive process with a = 3/4 has extremal index θ = 1/4. Its normalized yearly maximum M_n/n has the limit exp(−1/(4x)) = G(x)^(1/4), the power of the i.i.d. Fréchet limit that the theorem predicts.

limitations: The theorem assumes that the extremal index exists. Under D(u_n(τ)) for each τ > 0, the source states (p. 12) that the lim sup and lim inf of P(M_n ≤ u_n(τ)) have the forms e^(−θτ) and e^(−θ′τ), so θ exists as soon as one of these limits exists.
For θ = 0 the power relation fails. Examples with θ = 0, or with no extremal index, exist but are rare in applications.
The theorem does not compute θ. For θ = 1 a sufficient condition is D′(u_n) (relation (2.2.1) of the source). Other cases need direct estimates of the cluster sizes.
