results.name: Elementary renewal theorem
results.statement: Let ξ₁, ξ₂, … be independent and identically distributed random variables with P(ξ₁ > 0) = 1 and mean µ = E ξ₁ ∈ (0, ∞]. Set T₀ = 0, T_k = ξ₁ + ⋯ + ξ_k, N(t) = #{k ≥ 1 : T_k ≤ t} and m(t) = E N(t). Then m(t) < ∞ for every t ≥ 0, and m(t)/t → 1/µ as t → ∞, with the convention 1/∞ = 0.
hypotheses: The interarrival times ξ₁, ξ₂, … are independent and identically distributed.
Each ξ_i is strictly positive almost surely. The mean µ = E ξ₁ lies in (0, ∞] and can be infinite.

prerequisites.reason: Steps s2 and s3 apply Wald's equation E T_ν = µ E ν to the first passage index ν = ν_t, which is a stopping time with finite mean.
Step s5 uses the monotone convergence theorem to show that E min(ξ₁, c) increases to µ as c → ∞.
Step s1 sums the geometric bound (1 − ε^K)^m over m to show that the first passage index has finite mean.

definitions.name: renewal process
definitions.text: The sequence T₀ = 0, T_k = ξ₁ + ⋯ + ξ_k of partial sums of independent, identically distributed and positive interarrival times ξ_i. Each T_k is a renewal epoch.

definitions.name: renewal function
definitions.text: m(t) = E N(t), where N(t) = #{k ≥ 1 : T_k ≤ t} is the number of renewals in the interval (0, t].

definitions.name: stopping time
definitions.text: A random index ν with values in {1, 2, …} such that, for each k, the event {ν = k} is determined by ξ₁, …, ξ_k.

source.module: Chapter 4, Section 4.6.2 The elementary renewal theorem
source.excerpt: Theorem 4.6.1 (The elementary renewal theorem). Let {N(t); t > 0} be a renewal counting process with mean inter-renewal interval X̄. Then lim_{t→∞} E[N(t)]/t = 1/X̄.
source.attribution: © Robert G. Gallager. Quoted from the MIT OpenCourseWare notes Discrete Stochastic Processes, Chapter 4, for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states the limit for a renewal counting process with mean interval X̄ and remarks after the proof that the limit is 0 when the mean is infinite. The authored statement includes the infinite mean case and the finiteness of m(t). The authored proof follows the source proof: Wald's equation at the first renewal after t for the lower bound, and truncation of the intervals for the upper bound. Step s1 adds the block argument for E N(t) < ∞, which the source leaves to an exercise.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the Wald equation and truncation proof of the cited source. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement, for every law of ξ₁ on (0, ∞), including the case µ = ∞. No condition on the arithmetic type of the law is needed.

steps.text: Let ν_t = inf{k ≥ 1 : T_k > t}. Because T_k is strictly increasing, ν_t = 1 + N(t). Since P(ξ₁ > 1/n) increases to P(ξ₁ > 0) = 1, there is δ > 0 with ε = P(ξ₁ > δ) > 0. Fix t ≥ 0 and an integer K ≥ 1 with Kδ ≥ t. If all K variables of a block ξ_{(j−1)K+1}, …, ξ_{jK} exceed δ, then T_{jK} > Kδ ≥ t. The event {ν_t > mK} equals {T_{mK} ≤ t}, so no block j ≤ m has this property. The blocks are independent, hence P(ν_t > mK) ≤ (1 − ε^K)^m. Therefore E ν_t = Σ_{n≥0} P(ν_t > n) ≤ K Σ_{m≥0} (1 − ε^K)^m = K ε^(−K) < ∞, and m(t) < ∞.

Lower bound. The event {ν_t = k} = {T_{k−1} ≤ t < T_k} is determined by ξ₁, …, ξ_k, so ν_t is a stopping time, and E ν_t < ∞ by step s1. If µ < ∞, Wald's equation gives E T_{ν_t} = µ E ν_t. Since T_{ν_t} > t, this gives µ(1 + m(t)) > t, so lim inf m(t)/t ≥ lim inf (1/µ − 1/t) = 1/µ. If µ = ∞, the bound lim inf m(t)/t ≥ 0 = 1/µ holds trivially.

Bounded intervals. Suppose that P(ξ₁ ≤ c) = 1 for a constant c > 0. Then T_{ν_t} = T_{ν_t − 1} + ξ_{ν_t} ≤ t + c, because T_{ν_t − 1} ≤ t by the definition of ν_t. Wald's equation gives µ E ν_t = E T_{ν_t} ≤ t + c, so 1 + m(t) ≤ (t + c)/µ in this case.

Truncation. Fix c > 0 and let ξ̄_i = min(ξ_i, c). These variables are independent, identically distributed, positive and bounded by c, with mean µ_c = E min(ξ₁, c) ∈ (0, c]. Their partial sums satisfy T̄_k ≤ T_k, so T_k ≤ t implies T̄_k ≤ t, and the first passage index ν̄_t of the truncated sums satisfies ν̄_t ≥ ν_t. Step s3 applied to ξ̄ gives 1 + m(t) = E ν_t ≤ E ν̄_t ≤ (t + c)/µ_c. Hence lim sup m(t)/t ≤ 1/µ_c for every c > 0.

As c increases to ∞, min(ξ₁, c) increases to ξ₁, so the monotone convergence theorem gives µ_c ↑ µ, also when µ = ∞. Letting c → ∞ in step s4 gives lim sup m(t)/t ≤ 1/µ. Together with step s2, lim m(t)/t = 1/µ.

applications.title: Expected number of insurance claims with Erlang waiting times
applications.inputs: Claims arrive at the epochs of a renewal process. Each waiting time ξ_i has the Erlang law with shape 2 and rate λ = 3 per day, so ξ_i is the sum of two independent exponential times of mean 1/3 day. The horizon is t = 100 days.
applications.hypotheses: The waiting times are independent, identically distributed and strictly positive. Their mean is µ = 2/λ = 2/3 day, so 1/µ = 3/2 claims per day.

steps.text: The elementary renewal theorem gives m(t)/t → 1/µ = λ/2 = 3/2 claims per day. To first order, m(100) is about 150 claims.
Exact count: each ξ_i is the sum of two exponential gaps, so T_k is the (2k)-th point of a Poisson process P of rate λ. Hence N(t) = ⌊P(t)/2⌋ and m(t) = (E P(t) − P(P(t) is odd))/2.
The Poisson law gives P(P(t) is odd) = e^(−λt) sinh(λt) = (1 − e^(−2λt))/2. So m(t) = λt/2 − 1/4 + e^(−2λt)/4, and m(t)/t − λ/2 = (e^(−2λt) − 1)/(4t) → 0, as the theorem states.
At λ = 3 and t = 100, the main terms give λt/2 − 1/4 = 599/4 = 149.75 claims. The remaining term e^(−600)/4 is negligible.

applications.conclusion: m(100) = 599/4 + e^(−600)/4, and m(t)/t tends to 3/2 claims per day. The constant −1/4 equals E ξ²/(2µ²) − 1 = 3/4 − 1. The elementary renewal theorem does not give this second-order constant.

limitations: The theorem gives only the average rate 1/µ over [0, t]. The local statement m(t + h) − m(t) → h/µ needs a nonarithmetic law and is the Blackwell renewal theorem.
For a nonarithmetic law with E ξ₁² < ∞, m(t) = t/µ + E ξ₁²/(2µ²) − 1 + o(1). This second-order term needs the key renewal theorem.

results.name: Blackwell's renewal theorem
results.statement: Let ξ₁, ξ₂, … be i.i.d. nonnegative random variables with P(ξ₁ = 0) < 1, whose distribution F is nonarithmetic: it is not concentrated on {0, δ, 2δ, …} for any δ > 0. Let µ = E ξ₁ ∈ (0, ∞], T₀ = 0, T_n = ξ₁ + ⋯ + ξ_n, and let U(A) = Σ_(n≥0) P(T_n ∈ A) be the renewal measure. Then for every h > 0, U([t, t + h]) → h/µ as t → ∞, with 1/∞ = 0. The same limit holds for the intervals (t, t + h], [t, t + h) and (t, t + h).
hypotheses: The steps ξ_i are i.i.d. and nonnegative, and P(ξ₁ = 0) < 1. The mean µ can be infinite.
The step distribution is nonarithmetic: it is not concentrated on a lattice {0, δ, 2δ, …} with δ > 0.

prerequisites.reason: Steps s1 and s5 exchange sums and integrals of nonnegative terms with Tonelli's theorem, for the tail identity and for the smoothed tail identity.
Step s2 takes a locally uniform limit of the bounded equicontinuous translates of the smoothed renewal function with the Arzelà–Ascoli theorem.
Steps s2, s3 and s5 pass limits through integrals with bounded integrands by dominated convergence.
Step s3 uses Doob's martingale convergence theorem for the bounded martingale g(x − T_n).
Step s3 uses the Hewitt–Savage zero-one law to show that the limit of the martingale g(x − T_n) is almost surely constant.
Step s5 uses Fatou's lemma to show that the limit constant is 0 when the mean is infinite.

source.module: Section 2, Blackwell's Renewal Theorem
source.excerpt: Theorem 1 (Blackwell’s Renewal Theorem) For any fixed h > 0 the renewal function fulfills V(a) − V(a − h) → h/EX₁ (a → ∞), where 1/EX₁ := 0 in the case EX₁ = ∞.
source.attribution: © Jürgen Dippon and Harro Walk. Quoted from the preprint Simplified Analytical Proof of Blackwell's Renewal Theorem (Stuttgarter Mathematische Berichte 2004/013) for identification of the cited result.

source.alignment: The source assumes on p. 3 a nonnegative X₁ with F(0) < 1 and a nonarithmetic law, and states the limit of V(a) − V(a − h) = U((a − h, a]). The authored statement has the same hypotheses and gives the limit for closed, open and half-open windows. The authored proof follows the 1st, 3rd and 4th steps of the source proof (smoothing by a trapezoid, the Arzelà–Ascoli limit and the identification of the constant). It replaces the Fourier analytic 2nd step of the source by the martingale proof of the Choquet–Deny theorem, so that no moment condition is needed.

steps.text: Basic bounds and identities. Choose δ > 0 with p = P(ξ₁ > δ) > 0, and K ≥ a/δ. If K consecutive steps all exceed δ, the walk passes a, so the number N_a of n ≥ 0 with T_n ≤ a satisfies P(N_a > mK) ≤ (1 − p^K)^m, and V(a) = U[0, a] = E N_a < ∞. For an interval I of length a with left end s, let σ = inf{n : T_n ≥ s}. On {σ = k} the walk T_(k+j) − T_k, j ≥ 0, is independent of {σ = k} and has the law of (T_j), and each renewal in I is a T_(σ+j) with T_(σ+j) − T_σ ≤ a. Summing over k gives U(I) ≤ V(a). Conditioning on ξ₁ gives the renewal equation U = δ₀ + F ∗ U. For s ≥ 0, N_s < ∞ almost surely, so exactly one n has T_n ≤ s < T_(n+1). Independence of ξ_(n+1) and T_n and Tonelli's theorem give the tail identity ∫_[0,s] (1 − F(s − y)) U(dy) = 1. Tonelli also gives µ = ∫₀^∞ (1 − F(t)) dt.

Smoothing and selection. Fix a function z ≥ 0 with support in [−b, b] and Lipschitz constant L, and let w(x) = ∫ z(x − y) U(dy). By step s1, 0 ≤ w ≤ sup z · V(2b), and |w(x) − w(x′)| ≤ L |x − x′| V(2b + 1) for |x − x′| ≤ 1. The renewal equation convolved with z gives w(x) = z(x) + ∫ w(x − t) F(dt). Take any sequence τ_k → ∞. The functions w(· + τ_k) are uniformly bounded and equicontinuous, so the Arzelà–Ascoli theorem and a diagonal argument give a subsequence that converges uniformly on compact sets to a bounded continuous function g. In w(x + τ_k) = z(x + τ_k) + ∫ w(x + τ_k − t) F(dt) the first term is 0 for large k, and dominated convergence gives g(x) = ∫ g(x − t) F(dt) for every x ∈ ℝ.

Martingale argument. Fix x, let M_n = g(x − T_n) and F_n = σ(ξ₁, …, ξ_n). Since ξ_(n+1) is independent of F_n, E[M_(n+1) | F_n] = ∫ g(x − T_n − t) F(dt) = M_n, so (M_n) is a bounded martingale. Doob's convergence theorem gives M_n → M_∞ almost surely. A permutation of ξ₁, …, ξ_m changes no T_n with n ≥ m, so M_∞ = lim sup M_n is invariant under finite permutations, and the Hewitt–Savage zero-one law makes it almost surely constant. For A ∈ F₁ and n ≥ 1, E[M_n 1_A] = E[M₁ 1_A], and bounded convergence gives E[M_∞ 1_A] = E[M₁ 1_A] and E M_∞ = g(x). So M₁ = E[M_∞ | F₁] = g(x), that is, g(x − ξ₁) = g(x) almost surely. The open set {t : g(x − t) ≠ g(x)} has F-measure 0, so it does not meet the support S of F.

The limit is constant. By step s3, g(x + p) = g(x) for all x ∈ ℝ and p ∈ S. The set P of periods of g is a subgroup of ℝ, closed because g is continuous, and S ⊂ P. A closed subgroup of ℝ is {0}, δℤ for some δ > 0, or ℝ. P = {0} is impossible because P(ξ₁ = 0) < 1 puts a positive point in S. If P = δℤ, then F is concentrated on S ⊂ δℤ ∩ [0, ∞) = {0, δ, 2δ, …}, so F is arithmetic. Hence P = ℝ, and g is a constant κ.

Identification of the constant. For x ∈ ℝ, the substitution s = t + y, Tonelli's theorem and the tail identity of step s1 give ∫₀^∞ w(x − t)(1 − F(t)) dt = ∫₀^∞ z(x − s) [∫_[0,s] (1 − F(s − y)) U(dy)] ds = ∫_(−∞)^x z(r) dr. Put x = τ_k along the subsequence of step s2. The right side tends to ∫ z, and w(τ_k − t) → κ for every t. If µ < ∞, w is bounded and ∫₀^∞ (1 − F) = µ, so dominated convergence gives κµ = ∫ z. If µ = ∞, Fatou's lemma gives κ · ∞ ≤ ∫ z, so κ = 0. In both cases w(τ_k) → (∫ z)/µ. Every sequence τ_k → ∞ has such a subsequence, so w(τ) → (∫ z)/µ as τ → ∞.

Sandwich. Fix h > 0 and 0 < c < h/2. Let z₊ be the trapezoid that is 1 on [0, h], 0 outside (−c, h + c) and linear between, and z₋ the trapezoid that is 1 on [c, h − c], 0 outside (0, h) and linear between. Both are Lipschitz, ∫ z₊ = h + c and ∫ z₋ = h − c. For an interval I with (t, t + h) ⊂ I ⊂ [t, t + h], z₋(t + h − y) ≤ 1_I(y) ≤ z₊(t + h − y), so ∫ z₋(t + h − y) U(dy) ≤ U(I) ≤ ∫ z₊(t + h − y) U(dy). Step s5 gives (h − c)/µ ≤ lim inf U(I) ≤ lim sup U(I) ≤ (h + c)/µ as t → ∞, and c → 0 gives U(I) → h/µ.

applications.title: Counts of a scale-of-two particle counter
applications.inputs: Particles reach a detector as a Poisson stream of rate λ = 4 per second. A scale-of-two counter records every second particle. T_n is the time of the n-th recorded count, and the window has length h = 1/2 second.
applications.hypotheses: The gaps between recorded counts are sums of two independent exponential times of rate 4, so they are i.i.d. with the Gamma(2, 4) law and mean µ = 2/λ = 1/2. This law has a density, so it is not concentrated on a lattice and is nonarithmetic.

steps.text: Blackwell's theorem gives U((t, t + h]) → h/µ. The expected number of recorded counts in a half-second window far from time 0 tends to (1/2)/(1/2) = 1.
Here the limit can be checked exactly. The renewal density is u(t) = Σ_n λ^(2n) t^(2n−1) e^(−λt)/(2n − 1)! = λ e^(−λt) sinh(λt) = (λ/2)(1 − e^(−2λt)).
Integration gives U((t, t + h]) = λh/2 − (e^(−2λt) − e^(−2λ(t+h)))/4. At t = 1 and h = 1/2 this is 1 − (e^(−8) − e^(−12))/4 ≈ 0.99992, already close to the limit 1.

The nonarithmetic condition is necessary. If each gap were 1 or 2 seconds with probability 1/2, the Erdős–Feller–Pollard theorem gives U([n − 1/4, n + 1/4]) → 2/3 for integers n, while U([n + 1/4, n + 3/4]) = 0, so no limit h/µ = 1/3 exists.

applications.conclusion: Far from time 0 the scale-of-two counter records on average one count per half-second window, and the error decays like e^(−8t).

limitations: The theorem gives no rate of convergence. Rates need extra conditions, for example a density and moments of the step law.
For an arithmetic law on the lattice δℤ the limit holds only along the lattice: U({nδ}) → δ/µ, which is the Erdős–Feller–Pollard theorem.
The extension from windows to integrals of directly Riemann integrable functions is the key renewal theorem.

results.name: Key renewal theorem
aliases: Renewal theorem for directly Riemann integrable functions
results.statement: Let ξ₁, ξ₂, … be i.i.d. nonnegative random variables with P(ξ₁ = 0) < 1 and a nonarithmetic distribution F (not concentrated on {0, δ, 2δ, …} for any δ > 0). Let µ = E ξ₁ ∈ (0, ∞], T_n = ξ₁ + ⋯ + ξ_n with T₀ = 0, and U(A) = Σ_(n≥0) P(T_n ∈ A). Let h : [0, ∞) → ℝ be Borel measurable and directly Riemann integrable: for every δ > 0 the suprema M_k(δ) and infima m_k(δ) of h on [kδ, (k + 1)δ), k ≥ 0, satisfy Σ_k (|M_k(δ)| + |m_k(δ)|) < ∞, and δ Σ_k (M_k(δ) − m_k(δ)) → 0 as δ → 0. Then H(t) = ∫_[0,t] h(t − s) U(ds) is finite for every t ≥ 0, and H(t) → (1/µ) ∫₀^∞ h(s) ds as t → ∞, with 1/∞ = 0. The same limit holds for ∫_(0,t] h(t − s) U(ds).
hypotheses: The steps are i.i.d. and nonnegative with P(ξ₁ = 0) < 1, and the mean µ can be infinite.
The step distribution F is nonarithmetic.
The function h is Borel measurable and directly Riemann integrable on [0, ∞).

prerequisites.reason: Step s2 uses Blackwell's renewal theorem for the windows (t − (k + 1)δ, t − kδ] of a step function.

definitions.text: U(A) = Σ_(n≥0) P(T_n ∈ A), the expected number of renewal times T_n, including T₀ = 0, in the set A.

definitions.name: directly Riemann integrable function
definitions.text: A function on [0, ∞) whose upper and lower Riemann sums over the whole half line, for cells of length δ, converge absolutely and have the same limit as δ → 0.

source.excerpt: Theorem 4.7.3 (Key renewal theorem). Let r(x) ≥ 0 be a directly Riemann integrable function, and let m(t) = E[N(t)] for a non-arithmetic renewal process. Then lim_{t→∞} ∫_{τ=0}^t r(t − τ) dm(τ) = (1/X̄) ∫_0^∞ r(x) dx.

source.alignment: The source states the theorem for r ≥ 0 and the renewal function m(t) = E[N(t)], which does not count the renewal at time 0, and gives no proof. The authored statement allows signed h, defines direct Riemann integrability explicitly, and covers both U and U − δ₀. The authored proof follows the proof of Theorem 2.6.12 in Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th edition, pp. 101-102: step functions by Blackwell's theorem, then upper and lower sums.

proof.scope: The full statement, for finite and infinite mean.

steps.text: Local bound and finiteness. Choose η > 0 with p = P(ξ₁ > η) > 0 and K ≥ δ/η. If K consecutive steps all exceed η, the walk passes δ, so the number N of n with T_n ≤ δ satisfies P(N > mK) ≤ (1 − p^K)^m, and C_δ = U[0, δ] = E N < ∞. For an interval I of length δ with left end s, let σ be the first n with T_n ≥ s. The walk T_(σ+j) − T_σ, j ≥ 0, has the law of (T_j), and every renewal in I is a T_(σ+j) with T_(σ+j) − T_σ ≤ δ, so U(I) ≤ C_δ. For s ∈ [0, t], t − s lies in the cell [kδ, (k + 1)δ) exactly when s ∈ J_k(t) = (t − (k + 1)δ, t − kδ]. Hence ∫_[0,t] |h(t − s)| U(ds) ≤ C_δ Σ_k (|M_k(δ)| + |m_k(δ)|) < ∞. The terms of the convergent series tend to 0, so h(x) → 0 as x → ∞. Thus the integrals over [0, t] and (0, t] differ by h(t) U({0}) → 0, and it suffices to treat H.

Step functions. Let g = Σ_k a_k 1_[kδ,(k+1)δ) with Σ_k |a_k| < ∞. Then ∫_[0,t] g(t − s) U(ds) = Σ_k a_k U(J_k(t)). For each fixed k, J_k(t) is a window of length δ whose left end t − (k + 1)δ tends to ∞, so Blackwell's renewal theorem gives U(J_k(t)) → δ/µ. Given ε > 0, choose K with C_δ Σ_(k≥K) |a_k| ≤ ε and (δ/µ) Σ_(k≥K) |a_k| ≤ ε. By step s1 the terms with k ≥ K contribute at most ε for every t, and the finitely many terms with k < K converge. Hence lim sup_t |∫_[0,t] g(t − s) U(ds) − (δ/µ) Σ_k a_k| ≤ 2ε, and ∫_[0,t] g(t − s) U(ds) → (δ/µ) Σ_k a_k = (1/µ) ∫₀^∞ g(s) ds.

Upper and lower sums. For δ > 0 let g₊ = Σ_k M_k(δ) 1_[kδ,(k+1)δ) and g₋ = Σ_k m_k(δ) 1_[kδ,(k+1)δ). Both have absolutely summable coefficients, and g₋ ≤ h ≤ g₊ on [0, ∞). Since U ≥ 0, ∫_[0,t] g₋(t − s) U(ds) ≤ H(t) ≤ ∫_[0,t] g₊(t − s) U(ds). Step s2 gives I_δ/µ ≤ lim inf H(t) ≤ lim sup H(t) ≤ Ī_δ/µ, where Ī_δ = δ Σ_k M_k(δ) and I_δ = δ Σ_k m_k(δ). The step functions are integrable and h is measurable, so h is Lebesgue integrable and I_δ ≤ ∫₀^∞ h(s) ds ≤ Ī_δ.

Conclusion. By hypothesis Ī_δ − I_δ = δ Σ_k (M_k(δ) − m_k(δ)) → 0 as δ → 0, so both sums tend to ∫₀^∞ h(s) ds by step s3. The bounds of step s3 then give lim H(t) = (1/µ) ∫₀^∞ h(s) ds. If µ = ∞, both bounds are 0 for every δ and H(t) → 0.

applications.title: Waiting time for the next bus and the inspection paradox
applications.inputs: Buses leave a stop with i.i.d. gaps ξ_i uniform on [0, 20] minutes, so µ = 10. A passenger arrives at a large time t. B_t is the time from t until the next bus, and x = 5 minutes.
applications.hypotheses: The gaps are i.i.d., nonnegative and not all 0. The uniform law has a density, so it is nonarithmetic. The function h_x(u) = P(ξ₁ > u + x) is shown to be directly Riemann integrable in step a2.

steps.text: B_t > x exactly when some T_n ≤ t has T_(n+1) > t + x. Independence of ξ_(n+1) and T_n gives P(B_t > x) = Σ_n ∫_[0,t] P(ξ > t + x − s) P(T_n ∈ ds) = ∫_[0,t] h_x(t − s) U(ds).

h_x is nonincreasing, nonnegative and integrable. So M_k = h_x(kδ) and m_k ≥ h_x((k + 1)δ), the sum δ Σ_k (M_k − m_k) telescopes to at most δ h_x(0) → 0, and δ Σ_k M_k ≤ δ + ∫ h_x < ∞. Hence h_x is directly Riemann integrable.
The theorem gives P(B_t > x) → (1/µ) ∫_x^20 (1 − y/20) dy = (20 − x)²/400. For x = 5 the limit is 225/400 = 9/16.

With h(u) = E(ξ − u)⁺, also nonincreasing with integral E ξ²/2 = 200/3, Tonelli's theorem gives E B_t = ∫_[0,t] h(t − s) U(ds). The theorem gives E B_t → E ξ²/(2µ) = 20/3 minutes, more than half of the mean gap, 5 minutes.

applications.conclusion: A passenger who arrives at a large time waits more than 5 minutes with probability 9/16 and waits 20/3 minutes on average, because long gaps are more likely to contain the arrival time.

limitations: Lebesgue integrability of a bounded h is not enough. For steps in {1, √2} and h the indicator of the countable set {m + n√2 : m, n ∈ ℤ} ∩ [0, ∞), ∫ h = 0, but H(t) = U[0, t] → ∞ along the renewal times t = m + n√2 with m, n ≥ 0.
For an arithmetic step law the limit holds only along the lattice, with a sum over lattice points in place of the integral.
The theorem gives no rate of convergence. Rates need extra conditions on the step law, such as a density or exponential moments.

results.name: Renewal-reward theorem
aliases: Strong law of large numbers for renewal-reward processes
results.statement: Let (r₁, t₁), (r₂, t₂), … be independent and identically distributed pairs of random variables with t_i ≥ 0, 0 < µ = E t₁ < ∞ and E|r₁| < ∞. Let T_n = t₁ + ⋯ + t_n, N(t) = max{n ≥ 0 : T_n ≤ t} and R(t) = Σ_(i=1)^(N(t)) r_i, the total reward of the cycles that end by time t. Then R(t)/t → E r₁ / E t₁ almost surely as t → ∞.
hypotheses: The cycle pairs (r_i, t_i) are independent and identically distributed. The reward r_i can depend on the length t_i of its own cycle.
The cycle lengths are nonnegative with finite positive mean 0 < E t₁ < ∞.
The reward of a cycle is integrable: E|r₁| < ∞.

prerequisites.reason: Steps s1 and s3 apply the strong law of large numbers to the cycle lengths t_i and to the rewards r_i.

definitions.name: renewal-reward process
definitions.text: R(t) = Σ_(i=1)^(N(t)) r_i, where the reward r_i is earned at the end of cycle i and the pairs (r_i, t_i) are i.i.d.

The authored statement adds the integrability conditions that the source leaves implicit. The authored proof follows the source proof of Theorems 3.1 and 3.3, and adds the details that make N(t) finite and let the strong law pass along the random index N(t).

proof.scope: The full statement.

steps.text: The cycle lengths t_i are i.i.d. and nonnegative with mean µ ∈ (0, ∞), so the strong law of large numbers gives T_n/n → µ almost surely. On this event T_n → ∞, so for every t the set {n : T_n ≤ t} is finite and N(t) is finite. Each T_n is finite, so N(t) ≥ n for t ≥ T_n. Hence N(t) is nondecreasing and N(t) → ∞ as t → ∞.

For t with N(t) ≥ 1 the definition of N(t) gives T_(N(t)) ≤ t < T_(N(t)+1). Division by N(t) gives T_(N(t))/N(t) ≤ t/N(t) < (T_(N(t)+1)/(N(t)+1)) · ((N(t)+1)/N(t)). If a_n → a and N(t) → ∞ through the integers, then a_(N(t)) → a: for ε > 0 take n₀ with |a_n − a| < ε for n ≥ n₀, and then t₀ with N(t) ≥ n₀ for t ≥ t₀. So both bounds tend to µ, and N(t)/t → 1/µ almost surely.

The rewards r_i are i.i.d. with E|r₁| < ∞, so the strong law of large numbers gives (1/n) Σ_(i=1)^n r_i → E r₁ almost surely. The rule of step s2 for limits along N(t) gives R(t)/N(t) = (1/N(t)) Σ_(i=1)^(N(t)) r_i → E r₁ almost surely as t → ∞.

The events of steps s1, s2 and s3 each have probability one, so their intersection has probability one. On it, for all large t, N(t) ≥ 1 and R(t)/t = (R(t)/N(t)) · (N(t)/t). The product of the two limits gives R(t)/t → E r₁ · (1/µ) = E r₁ / E t₁.

applications.title: Long-run cost of an age replacement policy
applications.inputs: A component has a lifetime L that is uniform on [0, 10] years. It is replaced at failure or at age 5, whichever comes first. A planned replacement costs 1 unit and a replacement after failure costs 3 units. Each new component is independent of the earlier ones.
applications.hypotheses: Cycle i ends at a replacement, so t_i = min(L_i, 5) and r_i = 3 if L_i < 5, else r_i = 1. The pairs (r_i, t_i) are i.i.d., 0 < E t₁ ≤ 5 and |r_i| ≤ 3, so the theorem applies.

steps.text: The mean cycle length is E min(L, 5) = ∫₀⁵ P(L > x) dx = ∫₀⁵ (1 − x/10) dx = 5 − 25/20 = 15/4 years.
A failure comes before age 5 with probability 1/2, so the mean cost per cycle is E r₁ = 1 · 1/2 + 3 · 1/2 = 2 units.
The theorem gives the long-run cost per year R(t)/t → E r₁ / E t₁ = 2/(15/4) = 8/15 almost surely.
Without planned replacements, each cycle is a full lifetime with mean 5 years and cost 3, so the long-run cost per year is 3/5 = 9/15. The age 5 policy saves 1/15 unit per year.

applications.conclusion: Replacement at failure or at age 5 costs 8/15 unit per year in the long run, which is less than the 3/5 unit per year of replacement at failure only.

limitations: The theorem counts the reward of a cycle at its end. For rewards that accumulate during a cycle, a separate argument must show that the partial reward of the current cycle is small compared with t, for example a bound by an integrable variable Y_(N(t)+1).
The almost sure limit does not by itself give E R(t)/t → E r₁/E t₁. That version needs Wald's equation, the elementary renewal theorem and control of the last cycle.
If E t₁ = ∞, then N(t)/t → 0 and R(t)/t → 0 almost surely, which this statement does not include.

results.name: Erdős–Feller–Pollard renewal theorem
results.statement: Let f₁, f₂, … be nonnegative numbers with Σ_k f_k = 1, such that the greatest common divisor of {k ≥ 1 : f_k > 0} is 1, and let µ = Σ_k k f_k ∈ [1, ∞]. Define u₀ = 1 and u_n = Σ_(k=1)^n f_k u_(n−k) for n ≥ 1. Then u_n → 1/µ as n → ∞, with 1/∞ = 0. In terms of a random walk S_m = X₁ + ⋯ + X_m with independent steps of law P(X_i = k) = f_k, u_n is the probability that S_m = n for some m ≥ 0.
hypotheses: The numbers f_k, k ≥ 1, are nonnegative with sum 1. Their mean µ = Σ_k k f_k can be infinite.
The greatest common divisor of the support {k : f_k > 0} is 1.
The sequence u solves the renewal equation u₀ = 1 and u_n = Σ_(k=1)^n f_k u_(n−k) for n ≥ 1.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 exchanges the order of the nonnegative double sum Σ_k Σ_(j>k) f_j = Σ_j j f_j with Tonelli's theorem to get Σ_k r_k = µ.
Step s3 uses Bézout's identity Σ c_i a_i = 1 for finitely many support points to write every large integer as a nonnegative combination of them.

definitions.name: renewal sequence
definitions.text: The solution u of u₀ = 1 and u_n = Σ_(k=1)^n f_k u_(n−k). It equals the probability that the random walk with step law f visits the integer n.

definitions.name: aperiodic step law
definitions.text: A law f on {1, 2, …} whose support {k : f_k > 0} has greatest common divisor 1.

definitions.name: tail sum
definitions.text: r_k = Σ_(j>k) f_j = P(X₁ > k) for k ≥ 0. The tail sums add up to the mean: Σ_(k≥0) r_k = µ.

source.citation: Steven P. Lalley, Renewal Theory, lecture notes, University of Chicago.
source.revision: PDF of the notes on the author's course page (13 pages, PDF created 2018-05-10).
source.module: Section 2, The Feller-Erdös-Pollard renewal theorem
source.excerpt: Theorem 1. (Feller-Erdös-Pollard) Let (Sn)n≥0 be an ordinary arithmetic renewal process whose inter-occurrence time distribution fk = P{Xi = k} has finite mean 0 < µ < ∞ and is not supported by any proper additive subgroup of the integers (i.e., there is no m ≥ 2 such that P{Xi ∈ mZ} = 1). Let u be the associated renewal measure. Then lim_{k→∞} u(k) = lim_{k→∞} P{Sn = k for some n ≥ 0} = 1/µ.
source.attribution: © Steven P. Lalley. Quoted from the author's lecture notes Renewal Theory for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states the theorem for a finite mean and proves it with a Markov chain and with a coupling. The authored statement works with the renewal equation (the source's Proposition 1) and includes the infinite mean case with limit 0, as in the original paper of Erdős, Feller and Pollard (Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. 55 (1949), 201-204). The authored proof follows the elementary proof of that paper on pp. 203-204, with an explicit Bézout bound for the representation of large integers.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the elementary proof of Erdős, Feller and Pollard (1949). No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement, for finite and infinite mean. Step s5 is needed only when µ < ∞.

steps.text: Bounds and tail identity. By strong induction, 0 ≤ u_n ≤ Σ_(k=1)^n f_k ≤ 1. Let r_k = Σ_(j>k) f_j for k ≥ 0, so r₀ = 1 and r_(k−1) − r_k = f_k. Let D_n = Σ_(k=0)^n r_k u_(n−k). Then D₀ = 1, and for n ≥ 1, D_n − D_(n−1) = u_n + Σ_(k=1)^n (r_k − r_(k−1)) u_(n−k) = u_n − Σ_(k=1)^n f_k u_(n−k) = 0. Hence Σ_(k=0)^n r_k u_(n−k) = 1 for every n ≥ 0. Tonelli's theorem for the nonnegative double sum gives Σ_(k≥0) r_k = Σ_j j f_j = µ.

Shifts along a lim sup sequence. Let λ = lim sup u_n and choose n_v → ∞ with u_(n_v) → λ. Let f_j > 0 and λ′ = lim inf_v u_(n_v − j), and suppose λ′ < λ. Fix ε > 0 and N ≥ j with Σ_(k>N) f_k < ε. For all large v, u_(n_v − k) ≤ λ + ε for k ≤ N, and u ≤ 1, so u_(n_v) ≤ (1 − f_j)(λ + ε) + f_j u_(n_v − j) + ε. Along a subsequence with u_(n_v − j) → λ′, this gives λ ≤ (1 − f_j)(λ + ε) + f_j λ′ + ε. As ε → 0, f_j λ ≤ f_j λ′, so λ ≤ λ′, a contradiction. Hence u_(n_v − j) → λ. The sequence n_v − j has the same property as n_v, so by induction u_(n_v − s) → λ for every finite sum s of points of A = {k : f_k > 0}.

Large integers are sums of support points. The greatest common divisor of A ∩ [1, n] is a nonincreasing positive integer for n ≥ min A, so it is eventually constant, equal to some g. Every point of A lies in some A ∩ [1, n], so g divides every point of A and g = 1. Hence finitely many points a₁, …, a_t of A have greatest common divisor 1, and Bézout's identity gives integers c_i with Σ c_i a_i = 1. Let N₀ = (a₁ − 1) Σ_i |c_i| a_i. For n ≥ N₀ write n − N₀ = q a₁ + ρ with q ≥ 0 and 0 ≤ ρ < a₁. Then n = q a₁ + Σ_i (ρ c_i + (a₁ − 1)|c_i|) a_i, and each coefficient is at least (a₁ − 1 − ρ)|c_i| ≥ 0. By step s2, u_(n_v − s) → λ for every fixed s ≥ N₀.

Upper bound. Fix M. For large v, the tail identity at index n_v − N₀ and the positivity of all terms give 1 ≥ Σ_(k=0)^M r_k u_(n_v − N₀ − k). By step s3 each term tends to r_k λ as v → ∞, so λ Σ_(k=0)^M r_k ≤ 1. Letting M → ∞ gives λµ ≤ 1. If µ = ∞, then λ = 0, and u_n → 0 = 1/µ because u_n ≥ 0.

Lower bound when µ < ∞. Let λ_* = lim inf u_n and choose n′_v with u_(n′_v) → λ_*. If f_j > 0 and λ″ = lim sup_v u_(n′_v − j) > λ_*, fix ε > 0 and N as in step s2, and let ℓ = max(λ_* − ε, 0). For large v, u_(n′_v − k) ≥ ℓ for k ≤ N, so u_(n′_v) ≥ (1 − f_j − ε)ℓ + f_j u_(n′_v − j). Along a subsequence, λ_* ≥ (1 − f_j − ε)ℓ + f_j λ″, and ε → 0 gives λ_* ≥ λ″, a contradiction. With step s3, u_(n′_v − s) → λ_* for every s ≥ N₀. Since u ≤ 1, the tail identity at n′_v − N₀ gives 1 ≤ Σ_(k=0)^M r_k u_(n′_v − N₀ − k) + Σ_(k>M) r_k, so 1 ≤ λ_* Σ_(k≤M) r_k + Σ_(k>M) r_k. As M → ∞, with Σ_k r_k = µ < ∞, λ_* µ ≥ 1. With step s4, u_n → 1/µ.

applications.title: Density of tile boundaries in a random monomer–dimer tiling
applications.inputs: Tiles of length 1 (monomers) and length 2 (dimers) are laid on the sites of a line from site 0 to the right. Each tile is independently a monomer or a dimer with probability 1/2. u_n is the probability that a tile boundary falls at site n.
applications.hypotheses: The step law is f₁ = f₂ = 1/2, so the support {1, 2} has greatest common divisor 1 and µ = 1 · 1/2 + 2 · 1/2 = 3/2. The last tile before a boundary at n has length 1 or 2, so u solves the renewal equation.

steps.text: The theorem gives u_n → 1/µ = 2/3. Far from the origin, two sites in three carry a tile boundary.
The renewal equation is u_n = u_(n−1)/2 + u_(n−2)/2 with u₀ = 1 and u₁ = 1/2. Its characteristic roots are 1 and −1/2, and the initial values give u_n = 2/3 + (1/3)(−1/2)^n.
For example, the recursion gives u₂ = 3/4, u₃ = 5/8 and u₄ = (5/8 + 3/4)/2 = 11/16, and the closed form gives u₄ = 2/3 + (1/3)(1/16) = 11/16.
The error |u_n − 2/3| = (1/3) 2^(−n) decays geometrically. With dimers only (f₂ = 1) the greatest common divisor is 2, and u_n alternates between 1 and 0, so the gcd condition cannot be dropped.

applications.conclusion: The density of tile boundaries converges to 1/µ = 2/3, the inverse of the mean tile length, at the geometric rate 2^(−n).

limitations: The gcd condition is necessary. If the support lies in dℤ with d ≥ 2, then u_n = 0 for n ∉ dℤ, and u_(nd) → d/µ instead.
The theorem gives no rate of convergence. A geometric rate needs more, for example an exponential moment of the step law.
The analogue for nonarithmetic step laws on the real line is the Blackwell renewal theorem.

results.name: Wald's fundamental identity of sequential analysis
results.statement: Let X₁, X₂, … be independent and identically distributed real random variables with P(X₁ ≠ 0) > 0, and let S_n = X₁ + ⋯ + X_n. Fix α > 0 > β and let J = min{n ≥ 1 : S_n ≥ α or S_n ≤ β}. Then J < ∞ almost surely, and there are m ≥ 1 and q < 1 with P(J > km) ≤ q^k for all k ≥ 1. Moreover, for every real r with E e^(rX₁) < ∞, set γ(r) = ln E e^(rX₁). Then E[exp(rS_J − Jγ(r))] = 1.
hypotheses: The steps X₁, X₂, … are independent and identically distributed, and P(X₁ ≠ 0) > 0.
The thresholds satisfy β < 0 < α, and J is the first index n ≥ 1 with S_n ∉ (β, α).
For the identity, the real number r satisfies E e^(rX₁) < ∞.

prerequisites.reason: Step s3 uses Tonelli's theorem to show that the product of the tilted laws has density exp(r s_n − nγ(r)) with respect to the product of the original laws.
Step s4 uses the monotone convergence theorem to exchange the expectation with the sum over n of nonnegative terms.

definitions.name: semi-invariant moment generating function
definitions.text: γ(r) = ln E e^(rX₁), the logarithm of the moment generating function of one step. It is also called the cumulant generating function.

definitions.name: exit index
definitions.text: J = min{n ≥ 1 : S_n ≥ α or S_n ≤ β}, the first index at which the random walk leaves the open interval (β, α).

definitions.name: exponentially tilted law
definitions.text: For r with E e^(rX₁) < ∞, the probability measure F_r(dx) = e^(rx − γ(r)) F(dx), where F is the law of X₁.

source.citation: Robert G. Gallager, Discrete Stochastic Processes, Chapter 7: Random Walks, Large Deviations, and Martingales, course notes for MIT 6.262, Spring 2011, MIT OpenCourseWare. A revised version appeared as Stochastic Processes: Theory for Applications, Cambridge University Press, 2013.
source.revision: MIT OpenCourseWare PDF of Chapter 7 of the Spring 2011 course notes (PDF created 2011-07-20).
source.module: Chapter 7, Section 7.5.1 Wald's identity for two thresholds
source.excerpt: Theorem 7.5.1 (Wald's identity). Let {Xi; i ≥ 1} be IID and let γ(r) = ln{E[e^{rX}]} be the semi-invariant MGF of each Xi. Assume γ(r) is finite in the open interval (r−, r+) with r− < 0 < r+. For each n ≥ 1, let Sn = X1 + · · · + Xn. Let α > 0 and β < 0 be arbitrary real numbers, and let J be the smallest n for which either Sn ≥ α or Sn ≤ β. Then for all r ∈ (r−, r+), E[exp(rSJ − Jγ(r))] = 1.
source.attribution: © Robert G. Gallager. Quoted from the MIT OpenCourseWare notes Discrete Stochastic Processes, Chapter 7, for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source assumes that γ is finite on an open interval around 0 and takes r in that interval. Its proof treats discrete steps and uses Lemma 7.5.1 (p. 335) for the finiteness of J, which needs steps that are not identically 0. The authored statement makes this condition explicit, includes the geometric tail bound of Lemma 7.5.1, and allows every r with E e^(rX₁) < ∞. The authored proof follows the tilting proof of the source for a general step law with product measures.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the exponential tilting proof of the cited source. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement for every step law with P(X₁ ≠ 0) > 0 and every real r with a finite moment generating function, including discrete, continuous and mixed laws.

steps.text: Finiteness of J. Suppose that P(X₁ > 0) > 0. The case P(X₁ < 0) > 0 is the mirror image. Since P(X₁ > 1/k) increases to P(X₁ > 0), there is δ > 0 with p = P(X₁ > δ) > 0. Choose an integer m ≥ 1 with mδ ≥ α − β. Let G_k be the event that X_i > δ for every i with (k − 1)m < i ≤ km. On {J > (k − 1)m}, S_((k−1)m) > β (also for k = 1, as S₀ = 0). If G_k also occurs, then S_(km) > β + mδ ≥ α, so J ≤ km. Hence {J > km} lies in the intersection of the complements of G₁, …, G_k. These events are independent, so P(J > km) ≤ (1 − p^m)^k with q = 1 − p^m < 1, and J < ∞ almost surely.

Tilting. Fix r with E e^(rX₁) < ∞ and let F be the law of X₁. Then F_r(dx) = e^(rx − γ(r)) F(dx) is a probability measure, because its total mass is E e^(rX₁) e^(−γ(r)) = 1. Its density e^(rx − γ(r)) is strictly positive, so F_r and F have the same null sets. In particular F_r({0}) = 1 if and only if F({0}) = 1, so F_r is not the point mass at 0.

Let A_n be the set of x ∈ ℝⁿ with β < x₁ + ⋯ + x_i < α for i < n, and x₁ + ⋯ + x_n ≥ α or x₁ + ⋯ + x_n ≤ β. It is a Borel set, and {J = n} = {(X₁, …, X_n) ∈ A_n}. By Tonelli's theorem, the product measure F_rⁿ has density Π_i e^(rx_i − γ(r)) = exp(r s_n − nγ(r)) with respect to Fⁿ, where s_n = x₁ + ⋯ + x_n. Let Y₁, Y₂, … be independent with law F_r and let J^Y be their exit index. Then P(J^Y = n) = F_rⁿ(A_n) = E[exp(rS_n − nγ(r)); J = n] for every n ≥ 1.

By step s2 the walk with steps Y_i satisfies the hypothesis of step s1, so Σ_n P(J^Y = n) = P(J^Y < ∞) = 1. Step s1 for the original steps gives J < ∞ almost surely. The monotone convergence theorem, applied to the nonnegative terms exp(rS_n − nγ(r)) 1{J = n}, gives E[exp(rS_J − Jγ(r))] = Σ_n E[exp(rS_n − nγ(r)); J = n] = Σ_n P(J^Y = n) = 1.

applications.title: Error probability and mean length of a sequential test for a biased coin
applications.inputs: A coin shows heads with probability 1/3 under H₀ and 2/3 under H₁. A sequential probability ratio test adds the log-likelihood ratio X = ln 2 for each head and X = −ln 2 for each tail. It accepts H₁ when S_n ≥ 2 ln 2 and accepts H₀ when S_n ≤ −2 ln 2.
applications.hypotheses: Under H₀ the tosses are independent, and X = ±ln 2 is not 0, with E e^(rX) < ∞ for every r. The thresholds are α = 2 ln 2 > 0 > β = −2 ln 2.

steps.text: The steps are ±ln 2, so the walk S_n hits the thresholds exactly: S_J = 2 ln 2 or S_J = −2 ln 2, with no overshoot.
Under H₀, E e^X = (1/3) · 2 + (2/3) · (1/2) = 1, so γ(1) = 0. The identity at r = 1 gives 1 = E e^(S_J) = 4P(accept H₁) + (1/4)(1 − P(accept H₁)).
Solve for the type I error: P(accept H₁ | H₀) = (1 − 1/4)/(4 − 1/4) = 1/5.
Wald's equation E S_J = E J · E X gives the mean sample size. In units of ln 2, E S_J = (1/5) · 2 − (4/5) · 2 = −6/5 and E X = 1/3 − 2/3 = −1/3, so E J = 18/5 tosses.

applications.conclusion: Under H₀ the test accepts H₁ with probability 1/5 and stops after 18/5 = 3.6 tosses on average. When the steps overshoot the thresholds, the same identity at γ(r) = 0 gives only Wald's approximations to the error probabilities.

limitations: The identity holds only at r with E e^(rX₁) < ∞. For a heavy-tailed step law this can be r = 0 alone, where the identity is trivial.
In general S_J overshoots the thresholds. Exact error probabilities then need the law of the overshoot, and the identity alone gives bounds such as Wald's approximations.
If the moment generating function is finite near 0, differentiation at r = 0 gives Wald's equation E S_J = E J · E X₁ and the second identity E(S_J − J E X₁)² = Var X₁ · E J.

results.name: Pollaczek–Khinchine mean value formula
aliases: Pollaczek–Khintchine formula for the M/G/1 queue
Pollaczek–Khinchine transform of the M/G/1 waiting time
results.statement: Consider the first-come first-served M/G/1 queue: customers arrive at the points of a Poisson process of rate λ > 0, the service times S₀, S₁, … are i.i.d. nonnegative random variables independent of the arrivals, with mean E S, and ρ = λ E S < 1. Customer 0 arrives at an empty system. Let W_n be the waiting time of customer n before its service, and let X_n be the number of arrivals during the sojourn time W_n + S_n of customer n (the number of customers that customer n leaves behind when S > 0 a.s.). Then W_n converges in distribution to a random variable W with E e^(−θW) = (1 − ρ)θ/(θ − λ(1 − E e^(−θS))) for every θ > 0, and E W = λ E S²/(2(1 − ρ)). Also X_n converges in distribution to X∞, and E X∞ = ρ + λ² E S²/(2(1 − ρ)). Both means are infinite exactly when E S² = ∞.
hypotheses: Arrivals form a Poisson process of rate λ > 0, so the interarrival times T₀, T₁, … are i.i.d. exponential with mean 1/λ.
The service times S₀, S₁, … are i.i.d., nonnegative, independent of the arrivals, and ρ = λ E S < 1.
The discipline is first-come first-served with one server, and customer 0 arrives at an empty system.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 uses the Lindley representation W_n =D max_{k≤n} S_k of the waiting times and its limit sup_k S_k for a random walk with negative drift.
Step s2 integrates the conditional transform over the law of W + S with Fubini's theorem, because T is independent of W + S.
Steps s3 and s5 pass limits through bounded expectations with the dominated convergence theorem: φ(θ) → 1 as θ ↓ 0, and continuity of the Poisson mixture probabilities.
Steps s3 and s4 identify the limits of increasing difference quotients, (1 − E e^(−θS))/θ and (1 − E e^(−θW))/θ, with the monotone convergence theorem.

definitions.name: M/G/1 queue
definitions.text: A single-server queue with Poisson arrivals (M), i.i.d. service times with a general law (G) and unlimited waiting space.

definitions.name: traffic intensity
definitions.text: ρ = λ E S, the mean amount of work that arrives per unit time. The queue is stable when ρ < 1.

definitions.name: Laplace transform of a nonnegative random variable
definitions.text: E e^(−θY) for θ ≥ 0. It determines the law of Y, and its difference quotients at θ = 0 give the moments of Y.

source.citation: Ward Whitt, The M/G/1 Queue, lecture notes for IEOR 6711: Stochastic Models I, Columbia University, 2012.
source.revision: Lecture notes of Thursday, November 1, 2012, 3 pages.
source.module: The M/G/1 Queue, A Markov chain and the main results
source.excerpt: Theorem 0.1 (Pollaczek-Khintchine formulas for the M/G/1 queue) The stochastic process {Xn : n ≥ 0} is an irreducible aperiodic DTMC. If ρ ≡ λE[S] < 1, then the DTMC is positive recurrent and Xn ⇒ X∞ as n → ∞ … This limiting distribution has the relatively simple Pollaczek-Khintchine formula for its mean; i.e., E[X∞] = ρ + ρ²(c²s + 1)/(2(1 − ρ)).
source.attribution: © Ward Whitt. Quoted from the author's IEOR 6711 lecture notes on the M/G/1 queue for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states the mean of the number left behind at departures, with c_s² = Var S/(E S)², which equals the authored formula because ρ²(c_s² + 1) = λ² E S². The authored statement adds the transform and the mean of the stationary waiting time, and it states the case E S² = ∞. The source proves the theorem with the embedded Markov chain, generating functions and L'Hôpital's rule. The authored proof instead solves Lindley's equation with Laplace transforms and then mixes a Poisson count over the sojourn time.

source_references.citation: Rick Durrett, Essentials of Stochastic Processes, 2nd edition, Springer, 2012.
source_references.revision: Almost Final Version of the 2nd Edition, December 2011, 226 pages.
source_references.excerpt: Example 3.7. Workload in the M/G/1 queue. … PASTA implies that arriving customers see the long run average behavior so the workload they see Z = WQ, so we have WQ = λ(E sᵢ)WQ + λE(sᵢ²/2). Solving for WQ now gives WQ = λE(sᵢ²/2)/(1 − λE sᵢ) (3.7) the so-called Pollaczek-Khintchine formula.
source_references.attribution: © Rick Durrett. Quoted from the author's online version of Essentials of Stochastic Processes for identification of the cited result.
source_references.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source_references.alignment: The textbook gives the waiting-time form W_Q = λ E S²/(2(1 − ρ)) of the formula with a cost-equation argument and PASTA. The authored record states the same mean for the limit law of the waiting times and proves it from Lindley's equation.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the Lindley-equation transform method, not the embedded Markov chain proof of the cited source. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement, including the case E S² = ∞ in which both means are infinite.

steps.text: Set ξ_n = S_n − T_n, where T_n is the time between the arrivals of customers n and n + 1. The ξ_n are i.i.d. with mean E S − 1/λ = −(1 − ρ)/λ < 0, and W_{n+1} = (W_n + ξ_n)⁺ with W₀ = 0. The Lindley representation gives W_n =D M_n = max_{k≤n} (ξ₀ + … + ξ_{k−1}), and M_n increases to M = sup_k (ξ₀ + … + ξ_{k−1}), which is finite a.s. So W_n converges in distribution to W := M. Also M = max(0, ξ₀ + M′) with M′ = sup_{k≥0} (ξ₁ + … + ξ_k), and M′ has the law of M and is independent of ξ₀. Hence W =D (W + S − T)⁺, where W, S and T are independent, S has the service law and T is exponential with rate λ.

Fix θ > 0 with θ ≠ λ, and let φ(θ) = E e^(−θW) and σ(θ) = E e^(−θS). For a constant v ≥ 0, E e^(−θ(v−T)⁺) = P(T > v) + ∫₀^v λe^(−λt) e^(−θ(v−t)) dt = e^(−λv) + λ(e^(−λv) − e^(−θv))/(θ − λ) = (θe^(−λv) − λe^(−θv))/(θ − λ). Put v = W + S, which is independent of T, and integrate with Fubini's theorem. Since W and S are independent, E e^(−θ(W+S)) = φ(θ)σ(θ). Step s1 gives φ(θ)(θ − λ) = cθ − λφ(θ)σ(θ), where c = E e^(−λ(W+S)) is a constant.

Let D(θ) = θ − λ(1 − σ(θ)). Since 1 − e^(−x) ≤ x for x ≥ 0, 1 − σ(θ) ≤ θ E S, so D(θ) ≥ (1 − ρ)θ > 0. Step s2 gives φ(θ) = cθ/D(θ) for θ ≠ λ. As θ ↓ 0, φ(θ) → 1 by dominated convergence, because W is finite a.s. Also (1 − e^(−θs))/θ increases to s as θ ↓ 0, so (1 − σ(θ))/θ → E S by monotone convergence, and D(θ)/θ → 1 − ρ. Hence c = 1 − ρ and φ(θ) = (1 − ρ)θ/(θ − λ(1 − σ(θ))) for θ ≠ λ. Both sides are continuous in θ > 0, so the formula holds also at θ = λ.

The quotient (1 − e^(−θw))/θ increases to w as θ ↓ 0, so E W = lim_{θ↓0} (1 − φ(θ))/θ in [0, ∞] by monotone convergence. From step s3, 1 − φ(θ) = (ρθ − λ(1 − σ(θ)))/D(θ) = λ(σ(θ) − 1 + θ E S)/D(θ). Taylor's formula with integral remainder gives e^(−x) − 1 + x = x² ∫₀¹ (1 − u)e^(−ux) du, and the integral decreases in x with value 1/2 at x = 0. So (e^(−θs) − 1 + θs)/θ² increases to s²/2 as θ ↓ 0, and monotone convergence gives (σ(θ) − 1 + θ E S)/θ² → E S²/2 in [0, ∞]. With D(θ)/θ → 1 − ρ this gives E W = λ E S²/(2(1 − ρ)), and both sides are infinite exactly when E S² = ∞.

W_n is a function of T₀, …, T_{n−1} and S₀, …, S_{n−1}, and the arrivals after the arrival of customer n form a Poisson process of rate λ that is independent of (W_n, S_n). So, given W_n + S_n = x, X_n has the Poisson law with mean λx. Then P(X_n = k) = E f_k(W_n), where f_k(w) = E[e^(−λ(w+S))(λ(w+S))^k/k!] is bounded and continuous by dominated convergence. Since W_n converges in distribution to W, P(X_n = k) → E f_k(W) for each k. So X_n converges in distribution to the mixed Poisson variable X∞ with random mean λ(W + S), where W and S are independent. Hence E X∞ = λ(E W + E S) = ρ + λ² E S²/(2(1 − ρ)). Since λ² E S² = ρ²(Var S/(E S)² + 1), this is the formula of the source.

applications.title: Regular service halves the mean delay of a single-server queue
applications.inputs: A single-server queue with Poisson arrivals of rate λ = 4/5 per minute. Case A: every service takes exactly 1 minute (M/D/1). Case B: service times are exponential with mean 1 minute (M/M/1). The queue serves customers in order of arrival.
applications.hypotheses: Arrivals are Poisson and service times are i.i.d. and independent of the arrivals. In both cases E S = 1, so ρ = 4/5 < 1. E S² = 1 in case A and E S² = 2 in case B.

steps.text: Case A: E S² = 1, so the mean stationary wait is E W = λ E S²/(2(1 − ρ)) = (4/5) · 1/(2 · (1/5)) = 2 minutes.

Case B: E S² = 2 for an exponential law with mean 1, so E W = (4/5) · 2/(2 · (1/5)) = 4 minutes. The transform is φ(θ) = (1/5)θ/(θ − (4/5)θ/(1 + θ)) = (1/5)(1 + θ)/(θ + 1/5), and −φ′(0) = 4 confirms the mean.
The number left behind at a departure has mean E X∞ = ρ + λ² E S²/(2(1 − ρ)). In case A this is 4/5 + (16/25)/(2/5) = 12/5 customers.
In case B the same formula gives 4/5 + (16/25) · 2/(2/5) = 4 customers. This equals ρ/(1 − ρ), the mean of the geometric stationary law of the M/M/1 queue, which is a check of the formula.

applications.conclusion: At the same load ρ = 4/5, constant service times give a mean wait of 2 minutes and exponential service times give 4 minutes. The mean wait depends on the service law only through E S², so less variable service halves the delay.

limitations: The formula needs Poisson arrivals. For general renewal arrivals the mean wait is not a function of the first two moments, and Kingman's bound gives only an upper bound.

The formula gives the mean only. The full law of W follows from the transform, for example as the geometric sum of i.i.d. equilibrium service times (the Pollaczek–Khinchine representation), which this record does not derive.
The number X∞ is the number left behind at departures. Its law equals the time-stationary law of the number in system by PASTA and a level-crossing argument, which this record does not prove.

results.name: Little's law
results.statement: Let 0 ≤ t₁ ≤ t₂ ≤ … be real numbers with t_n → ∞ (the arrival times of customers to a system), and let W₁, W₂, … ≥ 0 (their sojourn times, so customer n departs at t_n + W_n). Let N(t) = #{n : t_n ≤ t} and L(t) = #{n : t_n ≤ t < t_n + W_n}. Suppose that the limits λ = lim_{t→∞} N(t)/t and w = lim_{n→∞} (1/n) ∑_{j=1}^n W_j exist and are finite. Then the limit l = lim_{t→∞} (1/t) ∫₀^t L(s) ds exists, and l = λw.
hypotheses: The arrival times satisfy 0 ≤ t₁ ≤ t₂ ≤ … and t_n → ∞. The arrival rate λ = lim N(t)/t exists and is finite.
The sojourn times satisfy W_n ≥ 0. Their running average converges to a finite limit w.

prerequisites.reason: Step s6 squeezes the time average of L between the lower bound λw/(1 + ε) and the upper bound λw.

definitions.name: arrival counting process
definitions.text: N(t) = #{n : t_n ≤ t}, the number of arrivals in [0, t]. It is finite for every t because t_n → ∞.

definitions.name: number in system
definitions.text: L(t) = #{n : t_n ≤ t < t_n + W_n}, the number of customers that have arrived and not yet departed at time t.

definitions.name: sample-path averages
definitions.text: The arrival rate λ = lim N(t)/t, the average sojourn time w = lim (1/n) ∑_{j≤n} W_j, and the time-average number in system l = lim (1/t) ∫₀^t L(s) ds, all along one fixed sequence.

source.citation: Karl Sigman, Notes on Little's Law (l = λw), lecture notes, Columbia University, 2009.
source.revision: Notes with copyright 2009 by Karl Sigman, 5 pages.
source.module: Section 1.1 Little's Law
source.excerpt: Theorem 1.1 (l = λw) If both λ and w exist and are finite, then l exists and l = λw.
source.attribution: © Karl Sigman. Quoted from the author's lecture notes on Little's law for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source defines λ, w and l in equations (4) to (6) as limits along one sample path, and it allows departures in any order. The authored statement writes these definitions into the theorem and allows equal arrival times (batch arrivals), which the source treats in Lemma 1.1. The authored proof follows the source proof, which is Stidham's sample-path argument: the area bounds (7), Lemma 1.1 and the comparison with arrivals before t/(1 + ε).

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the sample-path proof of Theorem 1.1 in Sigman's notes. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement, including the case λ = 0 and arrival times that are equal (batch arrivals).

steps.text: Because t_n → ∞, N(t) is finite for every t, and N(t) → ∞ as t → ∞. Customer j is in the system exactly on the interval [t_j, t_j + W_j), so L(s) = ∑_{j : t_j ≤ s} 1{s < t_j + W_j}. On [0, t] only the N(t) customers with t_j ≤ t contribute, so L is a finite sum of indicator functions of intervals there. Integrate term by term: ∫₀^t L(s) ds = ∑_{j : t_j ≤ t} min(W_j, t − t_j).

Bound the area. Each term min(W_j, t − t_j) is at most W_j, so ∫₀^t L(s) ds ≤ A(t) := ∑_{j=1}^{N(t)} W_j. A customer with t_j + W_j ≤ t contributes exactly W_j, and every other term is nonnegative. A customer that has departed by time t has also arrived by time t. So ∫₀^t L(s) ds ≥ B(t) := ∑_{j : t_j + W_j ≤ t} W_j.

Limit of the upper bound. Let a_n = (1/n) ∑_{j=1}^n W_j, so a_n → w. For N(t) ≥ 1, A(t)/t = (N(t)/t) · a_{N(t)}. Since N(t) is an integer that tends to ∞, a_{N(t)} → w. Hence A(t)/t → λw. The same holds along any function s(t) → ∞ in place of t.

Single sojourn times are negligible. First, W_n/n = a_n − ((n − 1)/n) a_{n−1} → w − w = 0. Next, every j ≤ n has t_j ≤ t_n, so N(t_n) ≥ n, and for t_n > 0 we get n/t_n ≤ N(t_n)/t_n. The right side tends to λ because t_n → ∞, so n/t_n is bounded for large n. Hence W_n/t_n = (W_n/n)(n/t_n) → 0. This holds also when λ = 0.

Limit of the lower bound. Fix ε > 0. By step s4 there is n₀ such that t_j > 0 and W_j ≤ ε t_j for all j ≥ n₀. If j ≥ n₀ and t_j ≤ t/(1 + ε), then t_j + W_j ≤ (1 + ε) t_j ≤ t, so customer j has departed by time t. Hence B(t) ≥ ∑_{j=n₀}^{N(t/(1+ε))} W_j ≥ A(t/(1 + ε)) − ∑_{j<n₀} W_j. The last sum is a constant. Divide by t and use step s3 with s(t) = t/(1 + ε): lim inf_{t→∞} B(t)/t ≥ λw/(1 + ε).

Combine steps s2, s3 and s5: λw/(1 + ε) ≤ lim inf (1/t) ∫₀^t L(s) ds ≤ lim sup (1/t) ∫₀^t L(s) ds ≤ lim A(t)/t = λw. This holds for every ε > 0. Let ε → 0. The lim inf and the lim sup are both equal to λw, so the limit l exists and l = λw by the squeeze theorem.

applications.title: Queue length and server utilization of a single-server queue
applications.inputs: One long sample path of a single-server queue. Customers arrive at the long-run rate λ = 3/4 per minute. Customer n waits D_n ≥ 0 minutes before service and is served for S_n minutes. The running averages of the delays and of the service times converge to wq = 3 minutes and s̄ = 1 minute. Each customer leaves at the end of service, so the sojourn time is W_n = D_n + S_n.
applications.hypotheses: The arrival times are the same for the whole system and for the waiting room, and λ = 3/4 is finite. The sojourn times W_n and D_n are nonnegative, and their running averages converge to w = wq + s̄ = 4 and to wq = 3. No assumption on the laws of the arrival or service times is needed.

steps.text: The running average of W_j = D_j + S_j is the sum of the two running averages, so w = wq + s̄ = 3 + 1 = 4 minutes. Little's law for the whole system gives l = λw = (3/4) · 4 = 3 customers.
Take the waiting room as the system. Customer n enters it at t_n and stays D_n. Little's law gives the time-average queue length lq = λ wq = (3/4) · 3 = 9/4 customers.
The number of customers in service at time t is L(t) − Lq(t). Its time average is l − lq = λ(w − wq) = λ s̄ = (3/4) · (3 + 1) − (3/4) · 3 = 3/4.

With one server, the number in service is 1 when the server is busy and 0 when it is idle. So the time average 3/4 is the long-run fraction of time that the server is busy, and the server is idle for the fraction 1/4.

applications.conclusion: The time-average number in the system is 3, the time-average queue length is 9/4, and the server utilization is ρ = λ s̄ = 3/4. These are the M/M/1 values for ρ = 3/4, but the derivation uses no assumption on the laws of the arrival and service times.

limitations: The law relates three long-run averages on one sample path. It does not compute λ or w: they must come from another argument, such as a renewal or ergodic theorem.
If the average sojourn time w does not exist or is infinite, the law gives no conclusion about the time-average number in the system.
The stationary version E L = λ E W for expectations (L under the stationary law, W under the Palm law of arrivals) needs a separate argument.

results.name: Kingman's bound for the mean waiting time of the GI/G/1 queue
aliases: Kingman's upper bound for the GI/G/1 queue
results.statement: Let the interarrival times t₀, t₁, … and the service times s₀, s₁, … be two independent sequences of i.i.d. nonnegative random variables, with means a = E t₀ ∈ (0, ∞) and b = E s₀, finite variances σ_a² = Var t₀ and σ_s² = Var s₀, arrival rate λ = 1/a and traffic intensity ρ = λb < 1. Let W₀ = 0 and W_{n+1} = (W_n + s_n − t_n)⁺. Then W_n converges in distribution to the stationary waiting time W, and for every n ≥ 0, E W_n ≤ E W ≤ λ(σ_a² + σ_s²)/(2(1 − ρ)).
hypotheses: The sequences (t_n) and (s_n) are independent, and each consists of i.i.d. nonnegative random variables.
The means satisfy 0 < a < ∞ and ρ = b/a < 1, and the variances σ_a² and σ_s² are finite.
The queue starts empty: W₀ = 0, and W_{n+1} = (W_n + s_n − t_n)⁺ (Lindley's recursion).

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 uses the Lindley representation W_n =D max_{k≤n} S_k and the stationary law W =D sup_k S_k for a random walk with negative drift.
Step s2 bounds (∑_{k<n} |ξ_k|)² by n ∑_{k<n} ξ_k² with the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, which shows that E W_n² is finite.
Step s4 uses Jensen's inequality E I_n² ≥ (E I_n)² for the idle time I_n.
Step s5 passes from the bound on E max_{k≤n} S_k to the bound on E sup_k S_k with the monotone convergence theorem.

definitions.name: Lindley recursion
definitions.text: The waiting time of customer n + 1 in a first-come first-served single-server queue is W_{n+1} = (W_n + s_n − t_n)⁺, where x⁺ = max(x, 0).

definitions.name: traffic intensity
definitions.text: ρ = λb = b/a, the mean work that arrives per unit time. The queue is stable when ρ < 1.

definitions.name: stationary waiting time
definitions.text: A random variable W with the limit law of W_n. For ρ < 1 it has the law of sup_{k≥0} S_k, where S_k = ∑_{i<k} (s_i − t_i).

source.citation: Sergey Foss, The G/G/1 queue, in Wiley Encyclopedia of Operations Research and Management Science, Wiley, 2011.
source.revision: Author's manuscript, PDF created 2010-03-29, 7 pages.
source.module: Section 1.2 Moments of the stationary waiting time
source.excerpt: Proposition 1.4. Assume ρ < 1. Let W be the stationary waiting time. … EW ≤ λ(Var t₁ + Var s₁)/(2(1 − ρ)). … ξ =D ξ₁ are assumed to be independent.
source.attribution: © Sergey Foss. Quoted from the author's manuscript of the encyclopedia article The G/G/1 queue for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states the upper bound as the right side of inequality (9), together with a lower bound and the moment identities (7) and (8). The authored statement keeps only the upper bound, makes the moment conditions explicit, and adds the bound for every W_n of the queue that starts empty. The source derives (9) from the identity (8) for the idle period. The authored proof gives the same estimate directly from the Lindley recursion: it squares the decomposition W_n + ξ_n = W_{n+1} − I_n and uses the monotonicity of E W_n.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the second-moment argument behind inequality (9) of Proposition 1.4 in Foss's article. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement, for every n and for the stationary waiting time.

steps.text: Set ξ_n = s_n − t_n. The ξ_n are i.i.d. with mean μ = b − a = −(1 − ρ)/λ < 0 and variance Var ξ = σ_a² + σ_s², because s_n and t_n are independent. Let S₀ = 0, S_k = ξ₀ + … + ξ_{k−1} and M_n = max_{0≤k≤n} S_k. The Lindley representation gives W_n =D M_n when W₀ = 0. Since μ < 0, M = sup_k S_k is finite a.s., M_n ↑ M, and W_n converges in distribution to W =D M. Because M_n is nondecreasing in n, E W_n = E M_n and E W_n² = E M_n² are nondecreasing in n.

The second moments are finite. By induction, W_{n+1} ≤ W_n + |ξ_n|, so W_n ≤ ∑_{k<n} |ξ_k|. The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives W_n² ≤ n ∑_{k<n} ξ_k², so E W_n² ≤ n² E ξ₀² < ∞. Also W_n is a function of ξ₀, …, ξ_{n−1} only, so W_n is independent of ξ_n.

Let I_n = (W_n + ξ_n)⁻ = max(0, −(W_n + ξ_n)), the idle time of the server before customer n + 1 arrives. Since x = x⁺ − x⁻ and x⁺x⁻ = 0, we get W_n + ξ_n = W_{n+1} − I_n and W_{n+1} I_n = 0. Square the first identity: (W_n + ξ_n)² = W_{n+1}² + I_n². Take expectations and use the independence of W_n and ξ_n: E W_{n+1}² + E I_n² = E W_n² + 2μ E W_n + E ξ₀². The first identity in expectation gives E I_n = E W_{n+1} − E W_n − μ.

By step s1, E W_{n+1}² ≥ E W_n², so the identity of step s3 gives 2|μ| E W_n = −2μ E W_n ≤ E ξ₀² − E I_n². Also by step s1, E W_{n+1} ≥ E W_n, so E I_n ≥ −μ = |μ| > 0. Jensen's inequality gives E I_n² ≥ (E I_n)² ≥ μ². Hence 2|μ| E W_n ≤ E ξ₀² − μ² = Var ξ₀ = σ_a² + σ_s², for every n ≥ 0.

Since M_n ↑ M and M_n ≥ 0, the monotone convergence theorem gives E W = E M = lim_n E M_n = lim_n E W_n ≤ (σ_a² + σ_s²)/(2|μ|). Also E W_n = E M_n ≤ E M = E W. Finally |μ| = a − b = (1 − ρ)/λ, so (σ_a² + σ_s²)/(2|μ|) = λ(σ_a² + σ_s²)/(2(1 − ρ)). This proves E W_n ≤ E W ≤ λ(σ_a² + σ_s²)/(2(1 − ρ)).

applications.title: Mean delay bound for a buffer with uniform interarrival and service times
applications.inputs: A single-server buffer. Interarrival times are i.i.d. uniform on [0, 2] microseconds. Service (transmission) times are i.i.d. uniform on [0, 1.8] microseconds, independent of the arrivals. The buffer starts empty.
applications.hypotheses: Both sequences are i.i.d., nonnegative and independent of each other. The means are a = 1 and b = 9/10, so ρ = 9/10 < 1. Uniform laws have finite variances. The waiting times follow Lindley's recursion with W₀ = 0.

steps.text: A uniform law on [0, c] has mean c/2 and variance c²/12. So a = 1, λ = 1, σ_a² = 2²/12 = 1/3, b = 9/10 and σ_s² = (9/5)²/12 = 27/100. The traffic intensity is ρ = λb = 9/10.
Kingman's bound gives E W ≤ λ(σ_a² + σ_s²)/(2(1 − ρ)) = (1/3 + 27/100)/(2 · (1 − 9/10)) = 181/60 microseconds, which is about 3.02 microseconds.
The same bound holds for the mean waiting time E W_n of every packet n, because the buffer starts empty and E W_n ≤ E W.

If the transmission time were constant 0.9 microseconds, then σ_s² = 0 and the bound becomes (1/3)/(2 · (1 − 9/10)) = 5/3 microseconds. The variance of the service time adds 181/60 − 5/3 = 27/20 microseconds to the bound.

applications.conclusion: The mean waiting time in the buffer is at most 181/60 microseconds for every packet and in steady state. The bound uses only the first two moments of the interarrival and service times.

limitations: The bound uses only means and variances. It is not sharp for fixed ρ: for the M/M/1 queue with λ = 4/5 and mean service time 1, the bound is 41/8 while E W = 4.
The bound is asymptotically sharp in heavy traffic: (1 − ρ) E W tends to λ(σ_a² + σ_s²)/2 as ρ ↑ 1 under suitable uniform integrability conditions. That limit is a separate theorem.
The source also gives the lower bound E W ≥ (ρ² + λ²σ_s² − 2ρ)/(2λ(1 − ρ)), which this record does not prove.

results.name: Erlang loss formula
results.statement: Consider the M/M/c/c loss system: c ≥ 1 servers and no waiting room, arrivals at the points of a Poisson process of rate λ > 0, and i.i.d. exponential service times with rate μ > 0, independent of the arrivals. An arrival that finds all c servers busy is blocked and lost. Let a = λ/μ. Then the number of busy servers X(t) has the unique stationary distribution π_k = (a^k/k!)/∑_{j=0}^c a^j/j!, k = 0, …, c. If X(0) has law π, then for every t > 0 the expected number of blocked arrivals in [0, t] is λtπ_c, so the blocking probability is B(c, a) = π_c = (a^c/c!)/∑_{j=0}^c a^j/j!. It satisfies B(0, a) = 1 and B(c, a) = aB(c − 1, a)/(c + aB(c − 1, a)).
hypotheses: Arrivals form a Poisson process of rate λ > 0.
Service times are i.i.d. exponential with rate μ > 0 and independent of the arrival process.
There are c ≥ 1 servers and no waiting room. An arrival that finds all servers busy is lost.

prerequisites.reason: Step s4 passes to the limit h → 0 in the Riemann sums for the number of blocked arrivals with the dominated convergence theorem, with dominating variable N(t).

definitions.name: offered load
definitions.text: a = λ/μ, the mean number of arrivals during one mean service time, measured in erlangs.

definitions.name: blocking probability
definitions.text: The ratio of the expected number of blocked arrivals in [0, t] to the expected number λt of all arrivals in [0, t], for the system in its stationary state.

definitions.name: birth–death chain on {0, …, c}
definitions.text: A continuous-time Markov chain that jumps only from k to k + 1 (rate λ_k) or from k to k − 1 (rate μ_k). Here λ_k = λ for k < c and μ_k = kμ.

source.citation: Ivo Adan and Jacques Resing, Queueing Systems, lecture notes, Department of Mathematics and Computing Science, Eindhoven University of Technology, 2015.
source.revision: Version of March 26, 2015, 182 pages.
source.module: Chapter 11, Section 11.2 M/G/c/c queue, and Section 11.3 Stable recursion for B(c, ρ)
source.excerpt: Example 11.2.1 (M/M/c/c) In this model the service times are exponentially distributed with mean 1/µ. … From figure 11.1 we immediately obtain that pn−1 λ = pn nµ, n = 1, 2, . . . , c. Hence, it is readily verified that pn = ((λ/µ)^n/n!)/Σ_{n=0}^c (λ/µ)^n/n!, n = 0, 1, . . . , c … Hence, the so-called blocking probability B(c, ρ) is given by B(c, ρ) = pc = (ρ^c/c!)/Σ_{n=0}^c ρ^n/n!. (11.2) The name given to this formula is Erlang’s loss formula.
source.attribution: © Ivo Adan and Jacques Resing. Quoted from the authors' lecture notes Queueing Systems for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states the M/M/c/c case in Example 11.2.1, obtains the stationary law from the balance equations p_{n−1}λ = p_n nµ, and identifies the blocking probability with p_c by the PASTA property. It also states insensitivity to the service law without proof, and it derives the recursion (11.3) in Section 11.3 on p. 116. The authored statement keeps the exponential case, defines the blocking probability through expected counts, and includes the recursion. The authored proof follows the same balance argument and proves the needed case of PASTA with Riemann sums.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the balance-equation and PASTA argument of Example 11.2.1 in the notes of Adan and Resing. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement for the stationary system: the stationary law, the blocking probability and the recursion.

steps.text: The number of busy servers X(t) is a continuous-time Markov chain on {0, …, c}. In state k the next event is either an arrival, after an exponential time of rate λ, or one of the k service completions, each after an exponential time of rate μ. By the memoryless property and independence, these clocks restart at every event. So the chain jumps from k to k + 1 at rate λ when k < c, and from k to k − 1 at rate kμ. Arrivals in state c do not change X.

Let Q be the generator of this chain. A probability vector π satisfies πQ = 0 if and only if it is stationary, because P(t) = e^(tQ) on a finite state space, so πP(t) = π for all t exactly when πQ = 0. Sum the equations (πQ)_j = 0 over j = 0, …, k. All flows inside {0, …, k} cancel, and only the flows across the cut between k and k + 1 remain: π_k λ = π_{k+1}(k + 1)μ for 0 ≤ k < c. This is detailed balance. It gives π_k = π_0 a^k/k!, and normalization gives π_k = (a^k/k!)/∑_{j=0}^c a^j/j!. So the stationary distribution exists and is unique.

Let N be the arrival process and start X(0) with law π, so P(X(s) = c) = π_c for all s. The number of blocked arrivals in [0, t] is K(t) = ∑_i 1{τ_i ≤ t, X(τ_i−) = c}, where τ_i are the arrival times. Fix h = t/n and set K_h = ∑_{k<n} 1{X(kh) = c}(N((k + 1)h) − N(kh)). The state X(kh) depends only on X(0), the arrivals before kh and the service times. The Poisson increment N((k + 1)h) − N(kh) is independent of all of these, with mean λh. So E K_h = ∑_{k<n} λh π_c = λtπ_c.

Almost surely the chain and the arrival process have finitely many event times in [0, t], all distinct and none at a grid point kh for any rational h. Take h smaller than the smallest gap between these event times. Then each interval (kh, (k + 1)h] holds at most one event, and an arrival τ_i in it has no other event in [kh, τ_i), so X(kh) = X(τ_i−). Hence K_h → K(t) a.s. as n → ∞. Since 0 ≤ K_h ≤ N(t) and E N(t) = λt < ∞, dominated convergence gives E K(t) = lim E K_h = λtπ_c. The expected number of all arrivals is λt, so the blocking probability is π_c = B(c, a).

For the recursion, write S_c = ∑_{j=0}^c a^j/j!, so B(c, a) = (a^c/c!)/S_c and B(0, a) = 1. Since S_c = S_{c−1} + a^c/c!, we get 1/B(c, a) = c! S_{c−1}/a^c + 1 = (c/a) · (c − 1)! S_{c−1}/a^(c−1) + 1 = (c/a)/B(c − 1, a) + 1. Solving gives B(c, a) = aB(c − 1, a)/(c + aB(c − 1, a)).

applications.title: Dimensioning a group of telephone lines
applications.inputs: Calls arrive at a group of c lines as a Poisson process of rate λ = 2 per minute. Call durations are exponential with mean 1 minute (μ = 1). A call that finds all lines busy is lost. First take c = 3 lines.
applications.hypotheses: Arrivals are Poisson, durations are i.i.d. exponential and independent of the arrivals, and there is no waiting room. The offered load is a = λ/μ = 2 erlangs.

steps.text: The unnormalized weights a^k/k! for k = 0, 1, 2, 3 are 1, 2, 2 and 8/6 = 4/3. Their sum is 19/3.
The blocking probability is B(3, 2) = (4/3)/(19/3) = 4/19, which is about 0.21. So about one call in five is lost.
The mean number of busy lines is ∑ kπ_k = (0 + 2 + 4 + 4)/(19/3) = 30/19. This equals a(1 − B) = 2 · 15/19, the carried load that Little's law gives for the accepted calls.

Continue the recursion: B(4, 2) = 2/21, B(5, 2) = 4/109, B(6, 2) = 4/331 and B(7, 2) = (8/331)/(7 + 8/331) = 8/2325, which is about 0.0034. Six lines lose 1.2% of the calls and seven lines lose 0.34%.

applications.conclusion: With 2 erlangs of offered load, 3 lines lose 4/19 of the calls. At least 7 lines are necessary to keep the loss below 1%.

limitations: The formula is insensitive: it holds for any service-time law with mean 1/μ. The source states this fact without proof, and this record proves the formula only for exponential service times.

The record proves the blocking probability for the stationary system. For another initial state, the long-run fraction of blocked arrivals tends to π_c by the ergodic theorem for finite Markov chains, which is a separate result.
Blocked arrivals must leave the system. If they retry, or if they wait in a queue (Erlang C), the formula does not apply.

results.name: Dufresne's identity for exponential functionals of Brownian motion
aliases: law of the perpetuity of Brownian motion with drift
results.statement: Let B be a standard Brownian motion, let µ > 0, and put A_∞ = ∫_0^∞ exp(2(B_s − µs)) ds. Then A_∞ < ∞ a.s., and A_∞ has the same law as 1/(2γ_µ), where γ_µ has the gamma density x^{µ−1} e^{−x}/Γ(µ) on (0, ∞). Equivalently, A_∞ has the density a^{−µ−1} e^{−1/(2a)}/(2^µ Γ(µ)) on (0, ∞).
hypotheses: B is a standard one-dimensional Brownian motion that starts at 0.
The drift parameter µ is strictly positive.

prerequisites.reason: Step s4 applies Itô's formula to e^{−λA_t} ψ(λ e^{2X_t}) to show that this bounded process is a local martingale.
Step s1 uses the strong law of large numbers for the increments of B to show B_t/t → 0, so that A_∞ is finite.
Step s1 controls the oscillation of B between integer times with the Borel-Cantelli lemma.
Steps s2 and s5 use dominated convergence, to differentiate the gamma integral under the integral sign and to let t → ∞.
Step s6 uses Weierstrass approximation, the special case on [0, 1], to show that the moments of e^{−A_∞} determine its law.

definitions.name: exponential functional
definitions.text: The integral A_∞ = ∫_0^∞ exp(2(B_s − µs)) ds of geometric Brownian motion with negative drift over the whole time axis.

definitions.name: gamma distribution with parameter µ
definitions.text: The law on (0, ∞) with density x^{µ−1} e^{−x}/Γ(µ).

source.citation: Hiroyuki Matsumoto and Marc Yor, Exponential functionals of Brownian motion, I: Probability laws at fixed time, Probability Surveys 2 (2005), 312–347.
source.revision: arXiv math/0511517v1 (21 November 2005), which carries the journal pagination of Probability Surveys 2 (2005).
source.module: Section 6, Perpetual functionals
source.excerpt: Theorem 6.2. Let µ > 0. Then, A∞^{(−µ)} is distributed as (2γµ)^{−1}, where γµ denotes a gamma random variable with parameter µ.
source.attribution: © Hiroyuki Matsumoto and Marc Yor. Quoted from the survey Exponential functionals of Brownian motion, I: Probability laws at fixed time for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source writes A∞^{(−µ)} = ∫_0^∞ exp(2B_s^{(−µ)}) ds with B_s^{(−µ)} = B_s − µs, and attributes the theorem to Dufresne (1990). The authored statement adds finiteness and the density. The source gives an analytic proof through hitting-time transforms and the Bessel function K_µ. The authored proof instead checks the Laplace transform of 1/(2γ_µ) directly: it solves the generator equation and builds a bounded martingale with Itô's formula.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the Laplace-transform characterization behind Theorem 6.2 of Matsumoto and Yor, by a bounded martingale built from the gamma integral. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement for every µ > 0.

steps.text: A_∞ is finite. Put X_s = B_s − µs. The strong law of large numbers for the i.i.d. increments B_n − B_{n−1} gives B_n/n → 0 a.s. The variables M_n = max_{n≤t≤n+1} |B_t − B_n| are i.i.d., and E M_0² ≤ 4 by Doob's L² maximal inequality, so ∑_n P(M_n > εn) < ∞ for every ε > 0, and M_n/n → 0 a.s. by the Borel-Cantelli lemma. Hence B_t/t → 0 a.s. So X_t → −∞, and e^{2X_s} ≤ e^{−µs} for all large s, which gives A_∞ < ∞ a.s.

The candidate transform. For c ≥ 0 put w_c(x) = e^{−x − c/(2x)} and ψ(c) = E exp(−c/(2γ_µ)) = Γ(µ)^{−1} ∫_0^∞ x^{µ−1} w_c(x) dx. Then 0 < ψ ≤ 1, and ψ is continuous on [0, ∞) with ψ(0) = 1 by dominated convergence. For c ≥ c_0 > 0 the k-th derivative in c of the integrand is (−1/(2x))^k x^{µ−1} w_c(x), which is bounded by (2x)^{−k} x^{µ−1} e^{−x − c_0/(2x)}, an integrable function. So ψ ∈ C²(0, ∞), with ψ'(c) = −Γ(µ)^{−1} ∫ (1/2) x^{µ−2} w_c dx and ψ''(c) = Γ(µ)^{−1} ∫ (1/4) x^{µ−3} w_c dx.

The generator equation. For c > 0, 2cψ''(c) + 2(1 − µ)ψ'(c) − ψ(c) = Γ(µ)^{−1} ∫_0^∞ [(c/2) x^{µ−3} + (µ − 1) x^{µ−2} − x^{µ−1}] w_c(x) dx. The bracket times w_c(x) is the derivative of x^{µ−1} w_c(x), because w_c'(x) = (−1 + c/(2x²)) w_c(x). Since x^{µ−1} w_c(x) → 0 as x ↓ 0 and as x → ∞, the integral is 0. So 2cψ'' + 2(1 − µ)ψ' − ψ = 0 on (0, ∞).

A bounded martingale. Fix λ > 0, put Y_t = λ e^{2X_t} > 0, A_t = ∫_0^t e^{2X_s} ds and N_t = e^{−λA_t} ψ(Y_t). Itô's formula gives dY_t = Y_t (2 dB_t + 2(1 − µ) dt) and d⟨Y⟩_t = 4Y_t² dt, and dA_t = Y_t dt/λ. Itô's formula for F(a, y) = e^{−λa} ψ(y), which is C² on R × (0, ∞), gives dN_t = e^{−λA_t} Y_t [2Y_t ψ''(Y_t) + 2(1 − µ) ψ'(Y_t) − ψ(Y_t)] dt + 2 e^{−λA_t} Y_t ψ'(Y_t) dB_t. The dt term is 0 by s3. So N is a continuous local martingale with |N_t| ≤ 1, hence a martingale, and E N_t = N_0 = ψ(λ) for every t.

Letting t → ∞. By s1, X_t → −∞, so Y_t → 0 and ψ(Y_t) → ψ(0) = 1 by continuity, and A_t increases to A_∞ < ∞. So N_t → e^{−λA_∞} a.s. Since |N_t| ≤ 1, dominated convergence gives E e^{−λA_∞} = ψ(λ) = E e^{−λ/(2γ_µ)} for every λ > 0.

Identification of the law. Take λ = k for k = 1, 2, …. The variables U = e^{−A_∞} and V = e^{−1/(2γ_µ)} take values in [0, 1] and satisfy E U^k = E V^k for every k ≥ 0. By the Weierstrass approximation theorem, E g(U) = E g(V) for every continuous g on [0, 1], so U and V have the same law. Hence A_∞ = −log U has the law of 1/(2γ_µ). The density follows from the change of variables a = 1/(2x) in the gamma density.

applications.title: Present value of a perpetuity with Brownian discounting
applications.inputs: A perpetuity pays 1 per unit time forever. Money is discounted with the random factor exp(−δt − σW_t), where W is a standard Brownian motion, δ = 1/20 and σ = 1/5. The present value is P = ∫_0^∞ exp(−δt − σW_t) dt.
applications.hypotheses: The process B_s = −(σ/2) W_{4s/σ²} is a standard Brownian motion. The substitution t = 4s/σ² gives P = (4/σ²) ∫_0^∞ exp(2(B_s − µs)) ds with µ = 2δ/σ² > 0, so the identity applies.

steps.text: The drift parameter is µ = 2δ/σ² = 2 · (1/20)/(1/25) = 5/2.
By the identity, P has the law of (4/σ²)/(2γ_µ) = 50/γ_{5/2}.
For µ > 1, E(1/γ_µ) = Γ(µ − 1)/Γ(µ) = 1/(µ − 1). So E P = 50/(3/2) = 100/3, which agrees with 1/(δ − σ²/2) from E e^{−σW_t} = e^{σ²t/2}.

applications.conclusion: The present value P has the law of 50/γ_{5/2}, with mean 100/3 ≈ 33.3 and variance 20000/9, so its standard deviation is about 47.1.

limitations: The identity needs a strictly negative drift in the exponent. If µ ≤ 0, the integral ∫_0^∞ exp(2(B_s − µs)) ds is infinite almost surely.
The identity concerns the integral over the whole time axis. The law of the integral up to a fixed time t is much more complicated and involves the Hartman-Watson distributions.
