results.name: Optimality of a barrier strategy for dividends in the Brownian risk model
aliases: de Finetti's dividend problem for Brownian motion with drift
optimal dividend barrier for the diffusion risk model
results.statement: Let B be a standard Brownian motion for a filtration that satisfies the usual conditions, and let X_t = x + µt + σB_t with x ≥ 0, µ ∈ ℝ and σ > 0. A dividend strategy is an adapted, nondecreasing, right-continuous process L with L_{0−} = 0. Its reserve is U_t = X_t − L_t, its ruin time is τ = inf{t ≥ 0 : U_t < 0}, and it is admissible if every lump satisfies ΔL_t ≤ X_t − L_{t−} for t ≤ τ. For a discount rate q > 0 put v_L(x) = E ∫_{[0, τ]} e^{−qt} dL_t and v*(x) = sup_L v_L(x) over admissible L. Let θ+ > 0 > θ− be the roots of (σ²/2)θ² + µθ − q = 0, and let g(y) = e^{θ+ y} − e^{θ− y}. (a) If µ > 0, put c* = 2 log(−θ−/θ+)/(θ+ − θ−) > 0. Then v*(x) = g(x)/g'(c*) for 0 ≤ x ≤ c*, v*(x) = x − c* + µ/q for x ≥ c*, and g(c*)/g'(c*) = µ/q. The barrier strategy L*_t = max{0, sup_{s≤t} X_s − c*} is optimal. (b) If µ ≤ 0, then v*(x) = x, and the payment of the whole reserve x at time 0 is optimal.
hypotheses: The uncontrolled reserve is a Brownian motion with drift µ ∈ ℝ, volatility σ > 0 and initial value x ≥ 0.
The discount rate q is strictly positive.
Dividend strategies are adapted, nondecreasing and right-continuous, and a lump payment never exceeds the current reserve.

prerequisites.reason: Step s3 expands e^{−qt}V(U_t) with Itô's formula. The jump terms of the dividend process are added to the continuous formula.
Steps s4 and s6 use that a stochastic integral with a bounded integrand is a martingale with mean 0.
Steps s4 and s6 let the time horizon t tend to infinity in the discounted dividend integral by monotone convergence.

definitions.name: barrier strategy at level c
definitions.text: The dividend strategy L_t = max{0, sup_{s≤t} X_s − c}. It pays out every part of the reserve above c and nothing else, so the reserve X − L stays at or below c.

definitions.name: admissible dividend strategy
definitions.text: An adapted, nondecreasing, right-continuous process L with L_{0−} = 0 whose lump payments never exceed the reserve just before the payment.

source.citation: Florin Avram, Zbigniew Palmowski and Martijn R. Pistorius, On the optimal dividend problem for a spectrally negative Lévy process, The Annals of Applied Probability 17 (2007), no. 1, 156–180.
source.revision: arXiv math/0702893v1 (28 February 2007). The file carries the journal text in the IMS arXiv format with its own page numbers 1 to 27.
source.module: Section 6.1, Small claims: Brownian motion (the application of Theorem 2 of Section 5.1)
source.excerpt: … so that W (q) (c∗ )/W (q)′ (c∗ ) = µ/q, as Gerber and Shiu [12] have found before, and the optimal level c∗ is explicitly given by c∗ = log((δ + ω)/(δ − ω))^{1/δ}. Since (σ²/2) vc′′∗ (x) + µvc′∗ (x) − qvc∗ (x) < 0 for x > c∗ , it follows by Theorem 2 that πc∗ is the optimal strategy as shown before by Jeanblanc and Shiryaev [15].
source.attribution: © Institute of Mathematical Statistics, 2007. Quoted from the arXiv copy of the article by Avram, Palmowski and Pistorius for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: Theorem 2 (p. 14) treats spectrally negative Lévy processes. Section 6.1 (p. 23) applies it to X_t = σB_t + µt. There the scale function is W^(q)(x) = (e^{(δ−ω)x} − e^{−(δ+ω)x})/(σ²δ) with δ = σ^{−2}(µ² + 2qσ²)^{1/2} and ω = µ/σ². So θ+ = δ − ω, θ− = −(δ + ω), and the source's c* equals the authored c*. The section also states that for µ ≤ 0 it is optimal to pay out all dividends at once. The source uses left-continuous strategies and a strict bound on lump payments. The authored statement uses right-continuous strategies and allows a lump equal to the reserve. The authored proof is a direct verification argument for the Brownian case and does not use scale functions.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the verification argument behind Theorem 2 of Avram, Palmowski and Pistorius, specialized to Brownian motion with drift. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement, for both signs of the drift.

steps.text: The function g. Since θ+θ− = −2q/σ² < 0, the roots satisfy θ+ > 0 > θ−, and θ+ + θ− = −2µ/σ². Both exponentials solve (σ²/2)f'' + µf' − qf = 0, so g does too, and g(0) = 0. Also g'(y) = θ+e^{θ+y} − θ−e^{θ−y} > 0 and g'''(y) = θ+³e^{θ+y} − θ−³e^{θ−y} > 0. So g'' is strictly increasing, and g''(y) = 0 exactly when e^{(θ+−θ−)y} = (θ−/θ+)². If µ > 0, then −θ− > θ+, so this zero is c* > 0. Thus g'' < 0 on (−∞, c*), g''(c*) = 0 and g'' > 0 on (c*, ∞). Hence g' decreases on [0, c*], and g'(y) ≥ g'(c*) > 0 for all y ≥ 0.

The candidate value function. If µ > 0, put V(y) = g(y)/g'(c*) for y ≤ c* and V(y) = y − c* + g(c*)/g'(c*) for y ≥ c*. If µ ≤ 0, put V(y) = y for all real y. In the first case the values, the first derivatives (both 1) and the second derivatives (g''(c*)/g'(c*) = 0 and 0) agree at c*, so V ∈ C²(ℝ) in both cases. By s1, V(0) = 0, and 1 ≤ V' ≤ K on [0, ∞) with K = g'(0)/g'(c*) (or K = 1 if µ ≤ 0). So V ≥ 0 on [0, ∞). Put GV = (σ²/2)V'' + µV' − qV. If µ > 0, then GV = 0 on (−∞, c*] by s1. At c* this gives µ = qV(c*), so g(c*)/g'(c*) = µ/q. For y > c*, GV(y) = µ − qV(y) < µ − qV(c*) = 0. If µ ≤ 0, then GV(y) = µ − qy ≤ 0 for y ≥ 0. So GV ≤ 0 on [0, ∞) in both cases.

Itô expansion. Fix an admissible L with ruin time τ, and write L^c for the continuous part of L. The reserve U = X − L is a semimartingale with continuous martingale part σB, and its jumps are −ΔL. Itô's formula for semimartingales, which adds the jump terms of the finite-variation part to the continuous formula, gives with U_{0−} = x: e^{−q(t∧τ)}V(U_{t∧τ}) = V(x) + ∫_0^{t∧τ} e^{−qs}GV(U_s) ds + σ∫_0^{t∧τ} e^{−qs}V'(U_s) dB_s − ∫_0^{t∧τ} e^{−qs}V'(U_{s−}) dL^c_s + Σ_{0≤s≤t∧τ} e^{−qs}[V(U_s) − V(U_{s−})]. Here U_t ≥ 0 for t < τ. At a finite τ admissibility gives U_τ ≥ 0, and right-continuity gives U_τ ≤ 0, so U_τ = 0. Thus U_s and U_{s−} lie in [0, ∞) for all s ≤ τ.

Upper bound. In s3, GV(U_s) ≤ 0 and V'(U_{s−}) ≥ 1 for s ≤ τ by s2. For each jump, V(U_s) − V(U_{s−}) = −∫_{U_s}^{U_{s−}} V'(y) dy ≤ −ΔL_s, because both end points lie in [0, ∞). Hence e^{−q(t∧τ)}V(U_{t∧τ}) ≤ V(x) − ∫_{[0, t∧τ]} e^{−qs} dL_s + M_t, where M_t = σ∫_0^{t∧τ} e^{−qs}V'(U_s) dB_s. The integrand of M is bounded by σK, so M is a martingale with E M_t = 0. Since V(U_{t∧τ}) ≥ 0, we get E∫_{[0, t∧τ]} e^{−qs} dL_s ≤ V(x). Monotone convergence as t → ∞ gives v_L(x) ≤ V(x). So v* ≤ V.

The reflected reserve. Let µ > 0, M_t = sup_{s≤t} X_s and L*_t = (M_t − c*)^+. Then L* is adapted, nondecreasing and continuous on [0, ∞), and its only lump is L*_0 = (x − c*)^+ ≤ x at time 0, so L* is admissible. The reserve U* = X − L* is continuous and satisfies U* ≤ c*, because X ≤ M ≤ L* + c*. Suppose U*_{t0} < c* at some t0 > 0. If M_{t0} > c*, then X_{t0} < M_{t0}, so X < M_{t0} on an open interval around t0, and M and L* are constant there. If M_{t0} ≤ c*, then X_{t0} = U*_{t0} < c*, so X < c* near t0 and L* = 0 there. Hence L* increases on (0, ∞) only at times with U* = c*.

The barrier strategy attains V when µ > 0. Apply s3 to L*, with ruin time τ*. For s ≤ τ*, U*_s ∈ [0, c*], so GV(U*_s) = 0. By s5, dL* charges on (0, ∞) only the times with U* = c*, where V' = 1. At time 0, V(U*_0) − V(x) = V(min{x, c*}) − V(x) = −(x − c*)^+ because V' = 1 on [c*, ∞). So s3 holds with equality: e^{−q(t∧τ*)}V(U*_{t∧τ*}) = V(x) − ∫_{[0, t∧τ*]} e^{−qs} dL*_s + M*_t, and E M*_t = 0 as in s4. On {τ* ≤ t} we have U*_{τ*} = 0 and V(0) = 0, and on {τ* > t} the term is at most e^{−qt}V(c*). So E∫_{[0, t∧τ*]} e^{−qs} dL*_s ≥ V(x) − e^{−qt}V(c*). Monotone convergence gives v_{L*}(x) ≥ V(x), and s4 gives v* = V = v_{L*}. The formulas of part (a) follow from s2.

Zero or negative drift. Let µ ≤ 0, so V(y) = y. The strategy L_t = x for all t ≥ 0 pays the whole reserve at time 0. It is admissible because ΔL_0 = x = X_0 − L_{0−}. Its only payment occurs at time 0 ≤ τ, so v_L(x) = x = V(x). With s4 this gives v*(x) = x, and this strategy is optimal. This proves part (b).

applications.title: Optimal dividend barrier for a company with drift one half
applications.inputs: The reserve of a company is X_t = x + t/2 + B_t, so µ = 1/2 and σ = 1. Shareholders discount dividends at the rate q = 3/8. The company pays dividends until the reserve becomes negative.
applications.hypotheses: The drift µ = 1/2 is positive, σ = 1 > 0 and q = 3/8 > 0, so part (a) of the theorem applies.

steps.text: The equation (1/2)θ² + (1/2)θ − 3/8 = 0 has the root θ+ = 1/2, as this substitution shows.
The same substitution shows that the other root is θ− = −3/2.
The barrier satisfies e^{(θ+−θ−)c*} = (θ−/θ+)² = 9. Since θ+ − θ− = 2, we get e^{c*} = 3, so c* = log 3 ≈ 1.099.
With w = e^{c*/2}, so w⁴ = 9, the value at the barrier is g(c*)/g'(c*) = (w⁴ − 1)/((1/2)w⁴ + 3/2). It equals µ/q = (1/2)/(3/8) = 4/3.

For the initial reserve x = c* + 2 ≈ 3.10, the optimal strategy pays the lump 2 at once and then reflects the reserve at c*. Its value is v*(x) = 2 + 4/3 = 10/3 ≈ 3.33. This is more than the value x ≈ 3.10 of an immediate payment of the whole reserve.

applications.conclusion: The company should keep a reserve of at most log 3 ≈ 1.10 and pay out every excess at once. The expected discounted dividends are 4/3 when the reserve starts at the barrier.

limitations: The theorem uses a Brownian motion with constant drift and volatility. For reserve processes with jumps, such as the Cramér-Lundberg model, a barrier strategy is optimal only under extra conditions on the claim sizes, and band strategies can be optimal.
The theorem allows dividend payments without an upper bound on the rate. If the dividend rate is bounded, the optimal strategy is a threshold strategy that pays at the maximal rate above a level.
The objective ignores the cost of ruin. Models with capital injections, transaction costs or a penalty at ruin have different optimal strategies.

results.name: Snell envelope theorem for finite-horizon optimal stopping
aliases: Snell envelope solves finite-horizon optimal stopping
results.statement: Let (Ω, F, (F_n)_{0≤n≤N}, P) be a filtered probability space with N < ∞, and let (G_n)_{0≤n≤N} be adapted with E max_{0≤n≤N} |G_n| < ∞. Define S_N = G_N and S_n = max(G_n, E(S_{n+1} | F_n)) for n = N − 1, …, 0, and τ_n = min{k : n ≤ k ≤ N, S_k = G_k}. For 0 ≤ n ≤ N let M_n be the set of stopping times τ with n ≤ τ ≤ N, and V_n = sup_{τ∈M_n} E G_τ. Then the following hold for every n. (a) S_n ≥ E(G_τ | F_n) a.s. for every τ ∈ M_n, and S_n = E(G_{τ_n} | F_n) a.s. (b) V_n = E S_n = E G_{τ_n}, so τ_n is optimal. (c) Every optimal τ* ∈ M_n satisfies τ_n ≤ τ* a.s. (d) (S_k)_{n≤k≤N} is the smallest supermartingale that dominates (G_k)_{n≤k≤N}. (e) The stopped process (S_{k∧τ_n})_{n≤k≤N} is a martingale.
hypotheses: The horizon N is finite, and (F_n)_{0≤n≤N} is a filtration on a probability space.
The gain process (G_n)_{0≤n≤N} is adapted, and E max_{0≤n≤N} |G_n| < ∞.

prerequisites.reason: Steps s2 and s3 condition first on F_k and then on F_{k−1} with the tower property of conditional expectation.
Step s6 uses optional sampling for the supermartingale S and the bounded stopping times n ≤ τ* ≤ N to get E S_{τ*} ≤ E S_n.

definitions.name: stopping time
definitions.text: A random variable τ with values in {0, 1, …, N} such that {τ ≤ k} ∈ F_k for every k. The decision to stop at time k uses only the information F_k.

definitions.name: Snell envelope
definitions.text: The process S defined by S_N = G_N and S_n = max(G_n, E(S_{n+1} | F_n)), the value at time n of the best continuation of the stopping problem.

definitions.name: supermartingale
definitions.text: An adapted integrable process (X_k) with E(X_{k+1} | F_k) ≤ X_k a.s. for every k.

source.excerpt: (Finite horizon) I. For all 0 ≤ n ≤ N we have: (a) S_n^N ≥ E(G_τ | F_n), ∀τ ∈ M_n^N; (b) S_n^N = E(G_{τ_n^N} | F_n). II. Moreover, if 0 ≤ n ≤ N is given and fixed, then we have: (c) τ_n^N is optimal in V_n^N = sup_{n≤τ≤N} EG_τ; (d) if τ* is also optimal then τ_n^N ≤ τ*; (e) the sequence (S_k^N)_{n≤k≤N} is the smallest supermartingale which dominates (G_k)_{n≤k≤N} (Snell’s envelope); (f) the stopped sequence (S^N_{k∧τ_n^N})_{n≤k≤N} is a martingale.

The authored statement merges parts (b) and (c) of the source into the value identity V_n = E S_n = E G_{τ_n}. The authored proof follows the proof of the source on pp. 45-54: backward induction for (a), the same computation with equalities for the identity S_n = E(G_{τ_n} | F_n), and the same arguments for minimality, the smallest supermartingale and the stopped martingale.

proof.scope: The full statement, all five parts, for every 0 ≤ n ≤ N.

steps.text: The objects are well defined. Backward induction shows that S_n is F_n-measurable and integrable, because |S_n| ≤ |G_n| + E(|S_{n+1}| | F_n). For τ ∈ M_n, G_τ = ∑_{k=n}^N 1{τ = k} G_k is integrable since |G_τ| ≤ max_k |G_k|. The time τ_n is a stopping time in M_n, since {τ_n ≤ k} = ∪_{j=n}^k {S_j = G_j} ∈ F_k and S_N = G_N gives τ_n ≤ N.

Proof of the inequality in (a) by backward induction on n. For n = N, M_N = {N} and S_N = G_N. Assume the inequality for n = k, and let τ ∈ M_{k−1}. Then τ̄ = max(τ, k) ∈ M_k, the event {τ ≥ k} = {τ ≤ k − 1}ᶜ is in F_{k−1}, and G_τ = G_τ̄ on {τ ≥ k}. The tower property gives E(G_τ | F_{k−1}) = 1{τ = k − 1} G_{k−1} + 1{τ ≥ k} E(E(G_τ̄ | F_k) | F_{k−1}). The induction hypothesis gives E(G_τ̄ | F_k) ≤ S_k. Hence E(G_τ | F_{k−1}) ≤ 1{τ = k − 1} G_{k−1} + 1{τ ≥ k} E(S_k | F_{k−1}) ≤ S_{k−1}, because S_{k−1} is at least G_{k−1} and at least E(S_k | F_{k−1}).

Proof of S_n = E(G_{τ_n} | F_n) by the same induction. For n = N it is S_N = G_N. Assume it for n = k. The event {τ_{k−1} ≥ k} = {S_{k−1} > G_{k−1}} is in F_{k−1}. On this event, τ_{k−1} = τ_k, and S_{k−1} = E(S_k | F_{k−1}) because the maximum is not attained by G_{k−1}. On the complement, τ_{k−1} = k − 1 and S_{k−1} = G_{k−1}. The tower property and the induction hypothesis give E(G_{τ_{k−1}} | F_{k−1}) = 1{τ_{k−1} = k − 1} G_{k−1} + 1{τ_{k−1} ≥ k} E(E(G_{τ_k} | F_k) | F_{k−1}) = 1{τ_{k−1} = k − 1} S_{k−1} + 1{τ_{k−1} ≥ k} E(S_k | F_{k−1}) = S_{k−1}.
Proof of (b). Take expectations in (a): E S_n ≥ E G_τ for every τ ∈ M_n, so E S_n ≥ V_n. Also E S_n = E G_{τ_n} ≤ V_n because τ_n ∈ M_n. Hence V_n = E S_n = E G_{τ_n}, and τ_n is optimal.

Proof of (d). By definition S_k ≥ G_k and S_k ≥ E(S_{k+1} | F_k), so (S_k) is a supermartingale that dominates (G_k). Let (S̃_k)_{n≤k≤N} be another supermartingale with S̃_k ≥ G_k. Then S̃_N ≥ G_N = S_N. If S̃_l ≥ S_l for some l > n, then S_{l−1} = max(G_{l−1}, E(S_l | F_{l−1})) ≤ max(S̃_{l−1}, E(S̃_l | F_{l−1})) = S̃_{l−1}. Backward induction gives S̃_k ≥ S_k for all n ≤ k ≤ N.

Proof of (e) and (c). For n ≤ k < N, the event {τ_n ≥ k + 1} is in F_k and lies in {S_k > G_k}, where S_k = E(S_{k+1} | F_k). So E(S_{(k+1)∧τ_n} | F_k) = 1{τ_n ≤ k} S_{k∧τ_n} + 1{τ_n ≥ k + 1} E(S_{k+1} | F_k) = S_{k∧τ_n}, which is (e). For (c), let τ* ∈ M_n be optimal. Since S ≥ G, S_{τ*} ≥ G_{τ*}. Optional sampling for the supermartingale S gives E S_{τ*} ≤ E S_n = V_n. If P(S_{τ*} > G_{τ*}) > 0, then E G_{τ*} < E S_{τ*} ≤ V_n, which contradicts optimality. So S_{τ*} = G_{τ*} a.s., and τ_n ≤ τ* a.s. because τ_n is the first k ≥ n with S_k = G_k.

applications.title: American put option in a two-period binomial model
applications.inputs: A stock with the price P₀ = 4 moves up by the factor 2 or down by the factor 1/2 in each of two periods. The interest rate per period is r = 1/4, so the risk-neutral probability of an up move is p = (1 + r − 1/2)/(2 − 1/2) = 1/2. An American put with strike 5 pays (5 − P_n)⁺ if it is exercised at time n ∈ {0, 1, 2}. The discounted gain is G_n = (4/5)^n (5 − P_n)⁺.
applications.hypotheses: The horizon N = 2 is finite. The filtration is generated by the two coin tosses, and G_n depends only on the first n tosses. The sample space is finite, so E max |G_n| < ∞. The theorem applies under the risk-neutral measure, where the moves are independent with probability 1/2 each.

steps.text: At time 2 the stock is 16, 4 or 1, and the undiscounted payoffs (5 − P₂)⁺ are 0, 1 and 4. In undiscounted units at time 1, the continuation value is (4/5) times the average of the two next payoffs.

After an up move (P₁ = 8): exercise pays 0 and continuation is (4/5) · (1/2) · (0 + 1) = 2/5, so the envelope is 2/5 and the holder continues. After a down move (P₁ = 2): exercise pays 3 and continuation is (4/5) · (1/2) · (1 + 4) = 2, so the envelope is 3 and the holder exercises.
At time 0: exercise pays 1 and continuation is (4/5) · (1/2) · (2/5 + 3) = 34/25 = 1.36. So S₀ = max(1, 34/25) = 34/25 and the holder does not exercise at time 0.

The optimal time τ₀ is the first time with S_k = G_k: exercise at time 1 after a down move, and otherwise wait to time 2. Under the risk-neutral measure, V₀ = E G_{τ₀} = (1/2) · (4/5) · 3 + (1/4) · (16/25) · 1 + (1/4) · (16/25) · 0 = 34/25.

applications.conclusion: The value of the optimal stopping problem, which is the no-arbitrage price of the American put, is 34/25 = 1.36. The optimal rule exercises at time 1 after a down move and otherwise waits to maturity.

limitations: Backward induction needs a finite horizon. For an infinite horizon the envelope is defined by an essential supremum, and an optimal stopping time can fail to exist.

The theorem characterizes the solution but does not make it computable when F_n is large. In a Markov setting the envelope is a function of the current state, which reduces the recursion to a dynamic-programming equation.

essential supremum solution of optimal stopping
results.statement: Let (Ω, F, (F_n)_{n≥0}, P) be a filtered probability space, and let (G_n)_{n≥0} be an adapted process with E sup_{k≥0} |G_k| < ∞. For n ≥ 0 let M_n be the set of finite stopping times τ with τ ≥ n, let V_n = sup_{τ∈M_n} E G_τ, let S_n = ess sup_{τ∈M_n} E(G_τ | F_n), and let τ_n = inf{k ≥ n : S_k = G_k} with inf ∅ = ∞. A time τ* ∈ M_n is optimal if E G_{τ*} = V_n. Then the following hold for every n ≥ 0. (a) S_n = max(G_n, E(S_{n+1} | F_n)) a.s., S_n ≥ E(G_τ | F_n) a.s. for every τ ∈ M_n, and V_n = E S_n. (b) (S_k)_{k≥n} is the smallest supermartingale that dominates (G_k)_{k≥n}, and the stopped process (S_{k∧τ_n})_{k≥n} is a martingale. (c) Every optimal τ* ∈ M_n satisfies τ_n ≤ τ* a.s. (d) If P(τ_n < ∞) = 1, then S_n = E(G_{τ_n} | F_n) a.s. and τ_n is optimal. If P(τ_n = ∞) > 0, then no optimal stopping time exists in M_n.
hypotheses: (F_n)_{n≥0} is a filtration on a probability space, and the gain process (G_n)_{n≥0} is adapted to it.
The gain process satisfies E sup_{k≥0} |G_k| < ∞.

prerequisites.reason: The infinite-horizon theorem extends the finite-horizon backward induction, and steps s4 and s5 repeat its one-step arguments.
Steps s3 and s4 condition first on F_{n+1} and then on F_n with the tower property.
Step s3 uses the monotone convergence theorem, in its plain and conditional forms, for an increasing sequence of conditional gains.
Step s5 uses dominated convergence with the integrable bound G* to show that stopped values converge in L¹.
Step s6 uses the conditional form of Fatou's lemma, with the integrable lower bound −G*, to pass from bounded to finite stopping times.
Step s6 uses optional sampling for a supermartingale and the bounded stopping times τ ∧ m.

definitions.name: essential supremum
definitions.text: For a family {Z_α} of random variables, the a.s. smallest random variable Z* with Z_α ≤ Z* a.s. for every α. It exists and is the supremum of a countable subfamily.

definitions.name: Snell envelope
definitions.text: The process S_n = ess sup_{τ∈M_n} E(G_τ | F_n), the best conditional gain at time n over all finite stopping times τ ≥ n.

definitions.name: supermartingale
definitions.text: An adapted integrable process (X_k) with E(X_{k+1} | F_k) ≤ X_k a.s. for every k.

It states minimality of τ_n and the smallest-supermartingale property without the assumption P(τ_n < ∞) = 1. The authored proof follows the proof of the source on slides 59-75: the essential supremum lemma, upward directedness, conditional monotone convergence for the recurrence, the stopped martingale and the limit to τ_n. For the smallest supermartingale it uses conditional Fatou with the bound −G*, which the source mentions on slide 72, in place of part II.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the essential-supremum proof of Theorem 2 in Shiryaev's lecture slides, with a Fatou argument for the smallest supermartingale. No local formal verification.

proof.scope: The full statement, parts (a) to (d), for every n ≥ 0.

steps.text: Essential supremum lemma. Let {Z_α : α ∈ A} be any family of random variables. Let a be the supremum of E arctan(sup_{α∈C} Z_α) over countable C ⊂ A, choose countable C_j with values that tend to a, and put J = ∪_j C_j and Z* = sup_{α∈J} Z_α, so E arctan Z* = a. If P(Z_α > Z*) > 0 for some α, then E arctan(Z* ∨ Z_α) > a with J ∪ {α} countable, which is impossible. So Z_α ≤ Z* a.s. for every α, and every Z̃ with Z_α ≤ Z̃ a.s. for all α satisfies Z* ≤ Z̃ a.s., because J is countable. If the family is upward directed (for α, β there is γ with Z_γ ≥ Z_α ∨ Z_β a.s.), enumerate J = {α_1, α_2, …}, put β_1 = α_1 and choose β_{j+1} with Z_{β_{j+1}} ≥ Z_{β_j} ∨ Z_{α_{j+1}}. Then Z_{β_j} increases a.s. to Z*.

Basic bounds. Put G* = sup_k |G_k|, which is integrable. For τ ∈ M_n, |G_τ| ≤ G*, so |E(G_τ | F_n)| ≤ E(G* | F_n). By s1, S_n is a countable supremum of F_n-measurable variables, so S_n is F_n-measurable. The constant time n gives S_n ≥ G_n ≥ −E(G* | F_n), and the second property of s1 gives S_n ≤ E(G* | F_n). So |S_n| ≤ E(G* | F_n), and S_n is integrable. The time τ_n is a stopping time, because {τ_n ≤ k} = ∪_{j=n}^k {S_j = G_j} ∈ F_k.

Upward directedness and the value. Fix m. For σ_1, σ_2 ∈ M_m let A = {E(G_{σ_1} | F_m) ≥ E(G_{σ_2} | F_m)} ∈ F_m and σ_3 = σ_1 on A and σ_3 = σ_2 on Aᶜ. Since A ∈ F_m and σ_1, σ_2 ≥ m, σ_3 ∈ M_m, and E(G_{σ_3} | F_m) = E(G_{σ_1} | F_m) ∨ E(G_{σ_2} | F_m). By s1 there are ρ_j ∈ M_m with E(G_{ρ_j} | F_m) increasing a.s. to S_m. This sequence is bounded below by the integrable E(G_{ρ_1} | F_m), so monotone convergence gives E S_m = lim_j E G_{ρ_j} ≤ V_m. Also E S_m ≥ E G_τ for every τ ∈ M_m, so V_m = E S_m.

The recurrence. Take m = n + 1 in s3. Conditional monotone convergence and the tower property give E(S_{n+1} | F_n) = lim_j E(G_{ρ_j} | F_n) ≤ S_n, since ρ_j ∈ M_{n+1} ⊂ M_n. With S_n ≥ G_n this gives S_n ≥ max(G_n, E(S_{n+1} | F_n)). Conversely, let τ ∈ M_n and τ̄ = τ ∨ (n + 1) ∈ M_{n+1}. Since {τ ≥ n + 1} ∈ F_n, E(G_τ | F_n) = 1{τ = n} G_n + 1{τ ≥ n + 1} E(E(G_τ̄ | F_{n+1}) | F_n) ≤ 1{τ = n} G_n + 1{τ ≥ n + 1} E(S_{n+1} | F_n) ≤ max(G_n, E(S_{n+1} | F_n)). The second property of s1 gives S_n ≤ max(G_n, E(S_{n+1} | F_n)). So (a) holds, and S is a supermartingale that dominates G.

The stopped martingale and a limit. For k ≥ n the event {τ_n > k} is in F_k, and on it S_k > G_k, so S_k = E(S_{k+1} | F_k) by s4. Hence E(S_{(k+1)∧τ_n} | F_k) = 1{τ_n ≤ k} S_{k∧τ_n} + 1{τ_n > k} E(S_{k+1} | F_k) = S_{k∧τ_n}, which is the martingale claim of (b). Next let σ ≥ n be an a.s. finite stopping time. Since {σ > m} ∈ F_m and |S_j| ≤ E(G* | F_j), E(1{σ > m} |S_m|) ≤ E(1{σ > m} G*) and E(1{σ > m} |S_σ|) = ∑_{j>m} E(1{σ = j} |S_j|) ≤ E(1{σ > m} G*). So E|S_{σ∧m} − S_σ| ≤ 2 E(1{σ > m} G*), which tends to 0 by dominated convergence.

The smallest supermartingale. Let (S̃_k)_{k≥n} be a supermartingale with S̃_k ≥ G_k for k ≥ n. Fix k ≥ n and τ ∈ M_k. For m ≥ k, optional sampling for bounded stopping times gives E(S̃_{τ∧m} | F_k) ≤ S̃_k. As m → ∞, S̃_{τ∧m} → S̃_τ a.s., and S̃_{τ∧m} ≥ G_{τ∧m} ≥ −G*. The conditional Fatou lemma gives E(S̃_τ | F_k) ≤ lim inf_m E(S̃_{τ∧m} | F_k) ≤ S̃_k. Hence E(G_τ | F_k) ≤ E(S̃_τ | F_k) ≤ S̃_k for every τ ∈ M_k, and the second property of s1 gives S_k ≤ S̃_k. With s4 this proves (b). The same argument with S̃ = S gives E S_τ ≤ E S_n for every τ ∈ M_n.

Optimal times. For (c), let τ* ∈ M_n be optimal. Since S ≥ G, s6 and s3 give E G_{τ*} ≤ E S_{τ*} ≤ E S_n = V_n = E G_{τ*}. So E(S_{τ*} − G_{τ*}) = 0 with S_{τ*} − G_{τ*} ≥ 0, hence S_{τ*} = G_{τ*} a.s., and τ_n ≤ τ* a.s. by the definition of τ_n. For (d), assume P(τ_n < ∞) = 1. The martingale of s5 gives S_n = E(S_{τ_n∧m} | F_n) for every m ≥ n, and the L¹ limit of s5 with σ = τ_n gives S_n = E(S_{τ_n} | F_n) = E(G_{τ_n} | F_n), because S_{τ_n} = G_{τ_n}. Then E G_{τ_n} = E S_n = V_n, so τ_n is optimal. If P(τ_n = ∞) > 0, an optimal τ* would satisfy τ_n ≤ τ* < ∞ a.s. by (c), which is impossible.

applications.title: Selling an asset with discounted random offers
applications.inputs: Offers X_0, X_1, … arrive one per period and are independent and uniform on [0, 1]. An offer must be accepted at once or it is lost. Money received at time k is discounted by the factor (4/5)^k, so the gain is G_k = (4/5)^k X_k and F_n is generated by X_0, …, X_n.
applications.hypotheses: The gain G_k depends only on X_0, …, X_k, so it is adapted. Also 0 ≤ G_k ≤ 1, so E sup_k |G_k| ≤ 1 < ∞, and the theorem applies.

steps.text: Put Ŝ_k = (4/5)^k max(X_k, 1/2). By independence, E(Ŝ_{k+1} | F_k) = (4/5)^{k+1} · 5/8 = (4/5)^k · 1/2. So Ŝ_k = max(G_k, E(Ŝ_{k+1} | F_k)), and Ŝ is a supermartingale that dominates G. Part (b) gives S_k ≤ Ŝ_k.

Let ρ_k be the first j ≥ k with X_j ≥ 1/2, which is finite a.s. On {X_k < 1/2}, E(G_{ρ_k} | F_k) = (4/5)^k w, where w = (4/5) · ((1/2) · (3/4) + (1/2) · w) because E(X 1{X ≥ 1/2}) = 3/8. So w = 1/2, and E(G_{ρ_k} | F_k) = Ŝ_k on both {X_k < 1/2} and {X_k ≥ 1/2}. Part (a) gives S_k ≥ Ŝ_k, so S = Ŝ.

S_k = G_k exactly when X_k ≥ 1/2, so τ_0 = ρ_0 is finite a.s. and is optimal by part (d). The value is V_0 = E S_0 = 5/8. As a check, E G_{τ_0} = ∑_{k≥0} (1/2)^k (4/5)^k (3/8) = (3/8)/(1 − 2/5) = 5/8.

applications.conclusion: The optimal rule accepts the first offer that is at least 1/2, and the optimal expected discounted gain is V_0 = 5/8.

limitations: The condition E sup_k |G_k| < ∞ is essential. Without it the limits of the finite-horizon envelopes and values can be strictly smaller than S_n and V_n, as the source notes on slide 74.

The recurrence S_n = max(G_n, E(S_{n+1} | F_n)) alone does not determine S in infinite horizon. For G = 0, every constant c ≥ 0 satisfies it. To compute S one needs the smallest-supermartingale property or the limit of finite horizons.
An optimal stopping time can fail to exist. Part (d) shows that this happens exactly when P(τ_n = ∞) > 0.

results.name: Optimal stopping rule for the secretary problem
results.statement: Let n ≥ 2 applicants, ranked without ties, arrive in a uniformly random order, so that all n! orders are equally likely. After the interview of applicant k, the employer knows only the relative ranks of the first k applicants and must accept applicant k at once or reject the applicant forever. The aim is to maximize the probability of accepting the best applicant. Let s_n be the largest s ∈ {2, …, n} with ∑_{j=s−1}^{n−1} 1/j ≥ 1. Then the rule that rejects the first s_n − 1 applicants and accepts the first later applicant who is better than all earlier ones is optimal among all rules that use only relative ranks. Its success probability is V_n = ((s_n − 1)/n) ∑_{j=s_n−1}^{n−1} 1/j. Moreover s_n/n → 1/e and V_n → 1/e as n → ∞.
hypotheses: All n! orders of the n applicants are equally likely, and the applicants have a strict ranking.
Each decision uses only the relative ranks of the applicants seen so far, and a rejected applicant cannot be recalled.

prerequisites.reason: Steps s3 and s4 apply the odds theorem to the indicators of relatively best applicants, with odds r_k = 1/(k − 1).
Step s5 compares the harmonic sums with integrals of 1/x to locate s_n and V_n.
Step s5 obtains the limits of s_n/n and V_n by squeezing them between bounds that tend to 1/e.

definitions.name: relative rank
definitions.text: The rank X_k ∈ {1, …, k} of applicant k among the first k applicants, with rank 1 for the best.

definitions.name: candidate
definitions.text: An applicant who is better than all earlier applicants, that is, an applicant with relative rank 1.

source.citation: Rémi Dendievel, New developments of the odds theorem, arXiv:1212.1391 [math.PR], 2012.
source.revision: arXiv v1, 6 December 2012.
source.module: Section 1, The Original Odds Theorem, Examples of applications, 1) Classical Secretary Problem
source.excerpt: 1) Classical Secretary Problem. … An observation at time k is a record if and only if his relative rank among the first k variables is 1. It is known that pk = 1/k. … The s index in the odds theorem can be computed and gives the optimal strategy. It is the largest s such that ∑_{j=s}^n (j − 1)^{−1} ≥ 1. Therefore V(n) = ((s − 1)/n) ∑_{j=s−1}^{n−1} j^{−1}. Note that s = s(n) ∼ n/e and thus V(n) → 1/e.
source.attribution: © Rémi Dendievel. Quoted from the arXiv preprint New developments of the odds theorem for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source derives the secretary rule as the first application of its Theorem 1, the odds theorem of Bruss, in the paragraph that follows the theorem. It gives the threshold s and the value V(n), and states s(n) ∼ n/e and V(n) → 1/e without proof. The authored statement makes the model explicit, and the authored proof adds the independence of the relative ranks, the reduction to the odds theorem and the integral bounds for the limits.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the reduction to the odds theorem in Dendievel's survey, with an added proof of the independence of relative ranks and of the limits. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement: optimality of the threshold rule, the exact value, and both limits.

steps.text: Independence of relative ranks. Let X_k ∈ {1, …, k} be the relative rank of applicant k among the first k. The map from orders to (X_1, …, X_n) is injective, because X_n gives the overall rank of the last applicant, and the remaining relative ranks give the order of the first n − 1 applicants by induction. The target set {1} × {1, 2} × … × {1, …, n} also has n! elements, so the map is a bijection. A uniform order therefore gives a uniform point of the product set, so X_1, …, X_n are independent and X_k is uniform on {1, …, k}.

Reduction to stopping on the last success. Let F_k be generated by X_1, …, X_k and I_k = 1{X_k = 1}. By s1 the I_k are independent with p_k = 1/k, each I_k is F_k-measurable, and (I_{k+1}, …, I_n) depends only on X_{k+1}, …, X_n, so it is independent of F_k. Applicant τ is the best of all applicants exactly when I_τ = 1 and I_j = 0 for all j > τ: the overall best is a candidate, and no later applicant can then be a candidate. A rule that uses only relative ranks is a stopping time of (F_k).

Application of the odds theorem. Here p_1 = 1, so r_1 = ∞, and r_k = (1/k)/(1 − 1/k) = 1/(k − 1) for k ≥ 2. So R_l = ∑_{k=l}^n 1/(k − 1) = ∑_{j=l−1}^{n−1} 1/j for l ≥ 2. Since R_2 = ∑_{j=1}^{n−1} 1/j ≥ 1, the threshold of the odds theorem is the largest l ≥ 2 with R_l ≥ 1, which is s_n. The odds theorem, with the filtration (F_k), shows that the rule that waits until s_n and then accepts the first candidate is optimal.

The value. Since s_n ≥ 2, every p_j with j ≥ s_n is less than 1, so the odds theorem gives V_n = (∏_{j=s_n}^n q_j) R_{s_n}. The product telescopes: ∏_{j=s}^n (j − 1)/j = (s − 1)/n. Hence V_n = ((s_n − 1)/n) ∑_{j=s_n−1}^{n−1} 1/j.

The limits. Write H(a, b) = ∑_{j=a}^b 1/j. Comparison with ∫ dx/x gives log((b + 1)/a) ≤ H(a, b) for 1 ≤ a ≤ b, and H(a, b) ≤ log(b/(a − 1)) for 2 ≤ a ≤ b. Let s = s_n. If s < n, the maximality of s gives H(s, n − 1) < 1, so log(n/s) < 1 and s > n/e, which also holds if s = n. Since H(s − 1, n − 1) ≥ 1, either s = 2 or log((n − 1)/(s − 2)) ≥ 1, and in both cases s ≤ (n − 1)/e + 2. So s_n/n → 1/e by squeezing. Finally 1 ≤ H(s − 1, n − 1) ≤ 1 + 1/(s − 1), because H(s, n − 1) < 1 or s = n, so (s − 1)/n ≤ V_n ≤ (s − 1)/n + 1/n, and V_n → 1/e.

applications.title: Optimal rule and success probability for ten applicants
applications.inputs: There are n = 10 applicants in a uniformly random order, and the employer sees only relative ranks.
applications.hypotheses: The model satisfies both hypotheses, so the threshold s_10 and the value V_10 follow from the theorem.

steps.text: The tail sum from 4 is H(4, 9) = 1/4 + 1/5 + … + 1/9 = 2509/2520 < 1, so s = 5 does not satisfy the condition.
The tail sum from 3 is H(3, 9) = 3349/2520 ≥ 1, so s_10 = 4. The rule rejects the first 3 applicants and accepts the next candidate.
As a check, the rule that rejects 4 applicants succeeds with probability (4/10) · H(4, 9) = 2509/6300 ≈ 0.3983, which is slightly smaller.

applications.conclusion: With 10 applicants the optimal rule rejects the first 3 and then accepts the first candidate. It selects the best applicant with probability 3349/8400 ≈ 0.399, a little above 1/e ≈ 0.368.

limitations: The result holds only for the zero-one payoff: win if the best applicant is chosen. For other payoffs, such as the expected rank, the optimal rule is different and is not a single threshold.
The number n of applicants must be known, and the order must be uniformly random. If the employer sees the values of the applicants and knows their distribution, a better rule exists.

results.name: Bruss odds theorem
aliases: sum the odds to one and stop
results.statement: Let I_1, …, I_n be independent indicator random variables with p_j = P(I_j = 1), q_j = 1 − p_j and odds r_j = p_j/q_j ∈ [0, ∞], where r_j = ∞ if p_j = 1. Let (F_k)_{1≤k≤n} be a filtration such that, for every k, I_k is F_k-measurable and (I_{k+1}, …, I_n) is independent of F_k. A stopping time τ with values in {1, …, n} wins if I_τ = 1 and I_j = 0 for all j > τ. Put R_l = ∑_{j=l}^n r_j and s = max({1} ∪ {l : R_l ≥ 1}). Let τ_s be the first k ≥ s with I_k = 1, and τ_s = n if there is no such k. Then τ_s maximizes the probability of a win over all such stopping times. The maximal probability is the probability of exactly one success among I_s, …, I_n, V = ∑_{k=s}^n p_k ∏_{s≤j≤n, j≠k} q_j. If p_j < 1 for all j ≥ s, then V = (∏_{j=s}^n q_j)(∑_{j=s}^n r_j).
hypotheses: The indicators I_1, …, I_n are independent, and their success probabilities p_j are known.
For every k, I_k is F_k-measurable and (I_{k+1}, …, I_n) is independent of F_k.

prerequisites.reason: Steps s2 and s6 use the finite-horizon Snell envelope theorem: the value of the stopping problem is E S_1 for the backward recursion S_k = max(G_k, E(S_{k+1} | F_k)).

definitions.name: odds
definitions.text: For an event with probability p < 1, the ratio r = p/(1 − p) of the probability of success to the probability of failure.

definitions.name: threshold rule
definitions.text: A stopping rule that ignores all indices before a fixed index s and then stops at the first success.

source.citation: A. M. Kabaeva, A. V. Logachov and A. A. Yambartsev, Bounds for the Success Probability in the Odds Theorem, arXiv:2511.21370 [math.PR], 2025. The theorem is due to F. T. Bruss, Sum the Odds to One and Stop, Ann. Probab. 28(3) (2000), 1384–1391.
source.revision: arXiv v1, 26 November 2025.
source.module: Section 1, Introduction and main results
source.excerpt: Theorem 1 ([3], Bruss’ odds theorem of optimal stopping) An optimal stopping rule τ ∈ L is to stop at the first index k ≥ s (if such exists) with Ik = 1, where s = max{1, max{l : ∑_{j=l}^n rj ≥ 1}}, with the convention max{∅} = −∞. The corresponding probability of “winning” is Vn := P(Iτ = 1, Iτ+1 = 0, . . . , In = 0) = ∏_{j=s}^n qj ∑_{l=s}^n rl.
source.attribution: © A. M. Kabaeva, A. V. Logachov and A. A. Yambartsev. Quoted from the arXiv preprint Bounds for the Success Probability in the Odds Theorem for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source restates Bruss's theorem (its reference [3]) with the filtration generated by I_1, …, I_k. The authored statement allows any filtration that makes the future indicators independent of the past, which the secretary problem needs. It also writes the value as the probability of exactly one success, which stays correct when some p_j = 1. The authored proof computes the Snell envelope by backward induction, not by Bruss's original argument.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the backward induction of the finite-horizon Snell envelope theorem for the gain I_k ∏_{j>k} q_j. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement: optimality of τ_s and the value formula, including indices with p_j = 1.

steps.text: Reduction to a gain process. Put Q_m = ∏_{j=m}^n q_j for 1 ≤ m ≤ n + 1, with Q_{n+1} = 1, and G_k = I_k Q_{k+1}. For a stopping time τ with values in {1, …, n}, the event {τ = k, I_k = 1} is in F_k, and (I_{k+1}, …, I_n) is independent of F_k. Hence P(τ wins) = ∑_k P(τ = k, I_k = 1) P(I_{k+1} = … = I_n = 0) = ∑_k E(1{τ = k} I_k) Q_{k+1} = E G_τ. So the problem is the finite-horizon optimal stopping problem for the bounded adapted gain G.

Form of the Snell envelope. Let S_n = G_n and S_k = max(G_k, E(S_{k+1} | F_k)). Backward induction shows S_k = max(I_k Q_{k+1}, c_k) with numbers c_k ≥ 0 given by c_n = 0 and c_{k−1} = p_k max(Q_{k+1}, c_k) + q_k c_k. Indeed S_n = I_n = max(I_n Q_{n+1}, 0). If S_k = max(I_k Q_{k+1}, c_k) with a number c_k ≥ 0, then S_k is a function of I_k, and I_k is independent of F_{k−1}. So E(S_k | F_{k−1}) = E S_k = p_k max(Q_{k+1}, c_k) + q_k max(0, c_k) = c_{k−1} ≥ 0, and S_{k−1} = max(I_{k−1} Q_k, c_{k−1}).

Exactly one success. Let f(m) be the probability of exactly one success among I_m, …, I_n, with f(n + 1) = 0. Conditioning on I_m gives f(m) = p_m Q_{m+1} + q_m f(m + 1). For l > s, R_l < 1 by the definition of s, so r_j < ∞ and q_j > 0 for every j > s. Hence for s < l ≤ n, f(l) = ∑_{k=l}^n p_k ∏_{j≠k} q_j = Q_l R_l < Q_l, and also f(n + 1) = 0 < 1 = Q_{n+1}.

The envelope from s on. Backward induction gives c_k = f(k + 1) for s − 1 ≤ k ≤ n, where c_0 is defined by the same recursion when s = 1. The claim holds for k = n. If c_k = f(k + 1) for some k ≥ s, then c_k ≤ Q_{k+1} by s3, so c_{k−1} = p_k Q_{k+1} + q_k f(k + 1) = f(k). So for k ≥ s, S_k = I_k Q_{k+1} + (1 − I_k) f(k + 1), and the envelope equals the gain at every success at or after s.

The envelope before s. If s ≥ 2, then R_s ≥ 1, so Q_s ≤ f(s): this is clear if Q_s = 0, and otherwise f(s) = Q_s R_s. For k ≤ s − 1 also Q_{k+1} ≤ Q_s ≤ f(s). Since c_{s−1} = f(s) by s4, S_{s−1} = max(I_{s−1} Q_s, f(s)) = f(s), so c_{s−2} = f(s), and backward induction gives S_k = f(s) for 1 ≤ k ≤ s − 1. Hence E S_1 = f(s). If s = 1, s4 gives E S_1 = p_1 Q_2 + q_1 f(2) = f(1). So E S_1 = f(s) in both cases.

Optimality of τ_s. By the finite-horizon Snell envelope theorem and s1, the largest win probability over stopping times with values in {1, …, n} is E S_1 = f(s). The time τ_s is a stopping time, since {τ_s ≤ k} = ∪_{j=s}^k {I_j = 1} ∈ F_k for k < n. It wins exactly when I_s, …, I_n contain exactly one success: with no success it stops at n with I_n = 0, and with two or more successes a success follows τ_s. So P(τ_s wins) = f(s) and τ_s is optimal. If p_j < 1 for all j ≥ s, then f(s) = Q_s R_s, which is the product formula.

applications.title: Betting on the last six in ten throws of a die
applications.inputs: A fair die is thrown 10 times. After each throw the player may stop and name that throw. The player wins if the named throw shows 6 and no later throw shows 6. Let I_k = 1 if throw k shows 6, so p_k = 1/6 for every k.
applications.hypotheses: The throws are independent with the known probability 1/6, and F_k is generated by the first k throws, so the theorem applies.

steps.text: Every throw has odds r_k = (1/6)/(5/6) = 1/5.
The tail sums are R_l = (11 − l)/5. So R_6 = 1 and R_7 = 4/5 < 1, and the threshold is s = 6. The rule ignores throws 1 to 5 and names the first 6 from throw 6 on.
No p_k equals 1, so the win probability is V = (5/6)^5 · R_6 = (5/6)^5 = 3125/7776 ≈ 0.402.
As a check, the threshold 7 gives (5/6)^4 · 4/5 = 125/324 ≈ 0.386, which is smaller. The threshold 5 gives (5/6)^6 · 6/5 = 3125/7776, the same value, because R_6 = 1 exactly.

applications.conclusion: The optimal rule names the first 6 among the last five throws, and it wins with probability 3125/7776 ≈ 0.402.

limitations: The theorem needs independent indicators with known success probabilities. If the probabilities are unknown, a rule that inserts estimated odds is not covered by the theorem.
The objective is to stop on the last success. Other objectives, such as stopping on one of the last m successes, need different thresholds.

results.name: Dynkin's characterization of the optimal stopping value
aliases: value of optimal stopping is the smallest excessive majorant
results.statement: Let X = (X_n)_{n≥0} be a time-homogeneous Markov chain with state space (E, B), defined on (Ω, F, (F_n), P_x) with X₀ = x under P_x, such that x ↦ P_x(A) is measurable and E_x[f(X_n, X_{n+1}, …) | F_n] = E_{X_n}[f(X₀, X₁, …)] for every n and every measurable f ≥ 0. Write TF(x) = E_x F(X₁) and QF = max(G, TF). Let G: E → ℝ be measurable with E_x sup_{n≥0} |G(X_n)| < ∞ for every x. Let V(x) = sup_τ E_x G(X_τ), where τ runs over the (F_n)-stopping times with P_x(τ < ∞) = 1. Then (a) QⁿG increases to V as n → ∞. (b) V satisfies the Wald–Bellman equation V = max(G, TV), so TV ≤ V. (c) V is the smallest excessive majorant of G: every measurable F: E → ℝ with F ≥ G and TF ≤ F satisfies F ≥ V.
hypotheses: X is a time-homogeneous Markov chain with respect to the filtration (F_n): conditionally on F_n, the future (X_n, X_{n+1}, …) has the law P_{X_n}, and x ↦ P_x(A) is measurable for every event A.
The gain function G: E → ℝ is measurable, and E_x sup_{n≥0} |G(X_n)| < ∞ for every x in E.
The admissible stopping times τ are (F_n)-stopping times with P_x(τ < ∞) = 1.

prerequisites.reason: Step s2 uses the monotone convergence theorem to pass to the limit in T QⁿG, because QⁿG increases and is bounded below by an integrable function.
Step s4 applies the optional stopping theorem to the supermartingale U(X_n) at the bounded stopping time τ ∧ k.
Step s4 uses the dominated convergence theorem with the integrable bound sup_n |G(X_n)| to let k → ∞ in E_x G(X_{τ∧k}).

definitions.name: excessive function
definitions.text: A measurable function F on E with TF ≤ F, where TF(x) = E_x F(X₁). The process F(X_n) is then a supermartingale under every P_x. Shiryaev calls such functions superharmonic.

definitions.name: excessive majorant
definitions.text: An excessive function F with F ≥ G on E.

definitions.name: Wald–Bellman operator
definitions.text: QF = max(G, TF). QⁿG(x) is the best expected gain from x with at most n steps of observation.

source.citation: Albert N. Shiryaev, Five lectures on the general theory of optimal stopping, lecture slides, Manchester, January 17–20, 2006.
source.revision: Slides of the Manchester lectures of January 2006 (PDF created 2006-01-21), 140 pages, hosted on the home page of G. Peskir.
source.module: Lectures 2–3, B. Markovian approach, Optimal stopping for infinite horizon
source.excerpt: Assume Ex supn≥0 |G(Xn)| < ∞, x ∈ E. … IV. The value function V is the smallest superharmonic function (Dynkin’s characterization) (T V ≤ V) which dominates the gain function G on E, or, equivalently, (V(Xn))n≥0 is the smallest supermartingale (under Px, x ∈ E) which dominates (G(Xn))n≥0.
source.attribution: © Albert N. Shiryaev. Quoted from the slides of his Manchester lectures on optimal stopping for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states Theorem 6 for a chain on ℝ^d in six parts, and gives the iterative method V = lim QⁿG as the next corollary. The authored statement keeps part I (Wald–Bellman equation), part IV (Dynkin's characterization) and the corollary, for a general measurable state space. The authored proof follows the iterative method: it builds the smallest excessive majorant as the limit of QⁿG and identifies it with V by supermartingale and martingale arguments.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the iterative method of the cited lectures. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Parts (a), (b) and (c) of the statement under all listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Bounds. Let Z = sup_n |G(X_n)| and H(x) = E_x Z < ∞. The Markov property gives E_x[sup_{j≥k} |G(X_j)| | F_k] = H(X_k), so E_x H(X_k) ≤ E_x Z < ∞ for every k. The operator Q is monotone: F₁ ≤ F₂ implies TF₁ ≤ TF₂ and QF₁ ≤ QF₂. Since QG ≥ G, induction gives Q^{n+1}G ≥ QⁿG. Induction also gives |QⁿG| ≤ H: if |QⁿG| ≤ H, then TQⁿG(x) ≤ E_x H(X₁) = E_x sup_{j≥1} |G(X_j)| ≤ H(x), and Q^{n+1}G ≥ G ≥ −H. So QⁿG increases to a measurable limit U with G ≤ U ≤ H.

U is an excessive majorant. Under P_x the functions QⁿG(X₁) increase to U(X₁) and are bounded below by −H(X₁), which is integrable by step s1. Monotone convergence gives TQⁿG(x) → TU(x). Let n → ∞ in Q^{n+1}G = max(G, TQⁿG) to get U = max(G, TU). So U ≥ G and TU ≤ U.

U is the smallest excessive majorant. Let F: E → ℝ be measurable with F ≥ G and TF ≤ F. Here TF(x) is well defined in (−∞, ∞] because F(X₁)⁻ ≤ |G(X₁)| ≤ Z. Then QF = max(G, TF) ≤ F. If QⁿG ≤ F, monotonicity gives Q^{n+1}G ≤ QF ≤ F. By induction QⁿG ≤ F for every n, and so U ≤ F.

V ≤ U. Fix x. Each U(X_n) is integrable because |U| ≤ H, and the Markov property gives E_x[U(X_{n+1}) | F_n] = TU(X_n) ≤ U(X_n). So (U(X_n)) is a supermartingale under P_x. Let τ be a stopping time with P_x(τ < ∞) = 1. The optional stopping theorem at the bounded time τ ∧ k gives E_x G(X_{τ∧k}) ≤ E_x U(X_{τ∧k}) ≤ U(x). As k → ∞, G(X_{τ∧k}) → G(X_τ) almost surely, with |G(X_{τ∧k})| ≤ Z. Dominated convergence gives E_x G(X_τ) ≤ U(x). The supremum over τ gives V(x) ≤ U(x).

V ≥ U. Fix n and set Y_k = Q^{n−k}G(X_k) for 0 ≤ k ≤ n. Let τ_n = min{k ≤ n : Y_k = G(X_k)}, which is at most n because Y_n = G(X_n). On the event {τ_n > k}, which is in F_k, Y_k > G(X_k), so Y_k = TQ^{n−k−1}G(X_k) = E_x[Y_{k+1} | F_k] by the Markov property. Hence E_x[Y_{(k+1)∧τ_n} − Y_{k∧τ_n} | F_k] = 1{τ_n > k}(E_x[Y_{k+1} | F_k] − Y_k) = 0. Summation over k < n gives E_x G(X_{τ_n}) = E_x Y_{τ_n} = Y₀ = QⁿG(x). Since τ_n ≤ n is admissible, V(x) ≥ QⁿG(x) for every n, and so V ≥ U.
Steps s4 and s5 give V = U = lim QⁿG, which is part (a). Step s2 gives V = max(G, TV), which is part (b). Step s3 gives F ≥ U = V for every measurable F with F ≥ G and TF ≤ F, which is part (c).

applications.title: Stopping a fair random walk with a table of rewards
applications.inputs: A player moves on E = {0, 1, 2, 3, 4} by a fair random walk: from 1, 2 or 3 the chain moves one step left or right with probability 1/2 each, and the states 0 and 4 are absorbing. Stopping at state x pays G(x), with G = (0, 2, 1, 3, 0).
applications.hypotheses: X is a time-homogeneous Markov chain on a finite set, and G is bounded by 3, so E_x sup_n |G(X_n)| ≤ 3. An excessive function F satisfies (F(x − 1) + F(x + 1))/2 ≤ F(x) at x = 1, 2, 3, which means that F is concave on {0, …, 4}.

steps.text: Compute QG = max(G, TG). Here TG(1) = (0 + 1)/2 = 1/2, TG(2) = (2 + 3)/2 = 5/2 and TG(3) = (1 + 0)/2 = 1/2, and TG = G at the absorbing states. So QG = (0, 2, 5/2, 3, 0).

Compute Q²G = max(G, T QG). At x = 2, T QG(2) = (2 + 3)/2 = 5/2 again. At x = 1, T QG(1) = (0 + 5/2)/2 = 5/4 < 2. At x = 3, T QG(3) = (5/2 + 0)/2 = 5/4 < 3. So Q²G = QG, and the iteration has stopped: V = (0, 2, 5/2, 3, 0).

V is the smallest concave function on {0, …, 4} above G: it joins the points (0, 0), (1, 2), (3, 3) and (4, 0) by straight lines, with slopes 2, 1/2, 1/2 and −3. Any concave majorant must lie above the chord from (1, 2) to (3, 3) at x = 2, so it is at least 5/2 there.
The stopping set is D = {x : V(x) = G(x)} = {0, 1, 3, 4}. From x = 2 the player takes one step and then stops, and gains 2 or 3 with probability 1/2 each, which is 5/2 = V(2).

applications.conclusion: The value is V = (0, 2, 5/2, 3, 0), the concave hull of the rewards. The player continues only at state 2 and stops everywhere else.

limitations: The theorem identifies the value but does not by itself give an optimal rule. The first entry time into {V = G} is optimal when it is finite almost surely, which is part II of the source theorem.

The integrability condition E_x sup_n |G(X_n)| < ∞ cannot be dropped. For the simple symmetric random walk on ℤ with G(x) = x, QⁿG = G for every n, but the hitting time of x + N gives V(x) ≥ x + N for every N, so V = ∞.

results.name: Verification theorem with smooth fit for optimal stopping of diffusions
results.statement: Let (Ω, ℱ, {ℱ_t}, P) carry an ℱ_t-Wiener process W. Let I ⊂ ℝ be an open interval, let b, σ : I → ℝ be continuous, and let X be a continuous adapted process with X_t ∈ I for all t ≥ 0 and X_t = X₀ + ∫₀ᵗ b(X_s) ds + ∫₀ᵗ σ(X_s) dW_s. Let λ ≥ 0 and let w, z : I → ℝ be continuous. For a stopping time τ with τ < ∞ a.s. put J[τ] = E[∫₀^τ e^(−λs) w(X_s) ds + e^(−λτ) z(X_τ)] when this expectation is defined. Let F ⊂ I be a finite set with σ(a) ≠ 0 for every a ∈ F. Let V : I → ℝ be C¹ on I and C² on I ∖ F, with V'' bounded near each point of F, and put 𝓛V = bV' + ½σ²V'' on I ∖ F. Suppose that min{𝓛V(x) − λV(x) + w(x), z(x) − V(x)} = 0 for every x ∈ I ∖ F and that E|V(X₀)| < ∞. Let D = {x ∈ I : V(x) < z(x)} and τ* = inf{t ≥ 0 : X_t ∉ D}. Let 𝒦 be the class of stopping times τ with τ < ∞ a.s. for which M_τ = ∫₀^τ e^(−λs) V'(X_s) σ(X_s) dW_s is integrable with E M_τ = 0. If τ* ∈ 𝒦, then J[τ] is defined in (−∞, ∞] for every τ ∈ 𝒦, J[τ*] = E V(X₀), and J[τ*] ≤ J[τ] for every τ ∈ 𝒦.
hypotheses: X is a continuous solution of dX_t = b(X_t) dt + σ(X_t) dW_t that stays in the open interval I, with b and σ continuous on I.
The running cost w and the stopping cost z are continuous on I, and λ ≥ 0.
V is C¹ on I and C² on I ∖ F for a finite set F, V'' is bounded near each point of F, and σ(a) ≠ 0 for a ∈ F.
V solves min{𝓛V − λV + w, z − V} = 0 on I ∖ F, and E|V(X₀)| < ∞.
The exit time τ* of X from D = {V < z} belongs to the class 𝒦.

prerequisites.reason: Steps s1 and s3 apply Itô's formula to C² functions of the stopped diffusion: to F_ε in step s1 and to e^(−λt)V_n(x) in step s3.
Steps s1 and s3 bound the second moments of stochastic integrals with small integrands by the Itô isometry, so these integrals tend to 0 in L².
Step s2 writes V' − V'(x₀) as the integral of the piecewise continuous second derivative h, which needs the fundamental theorem of calculus on each piece.
Step s3 passes to the limit in the time integral of h_n(X_s)σ(X_s)², which converges for almost every s and is bounded.

definitions.name: variational inequality
definitions.text: The equation min{𝓛V − λV + w, z − V} = 0. It says that V ≤ z everywhere, that λV − 𝓛V ≤ w everywhere, and that at each point one of the two holds with equality.

definitions.name: continuation region
definitions.text: The set D = {x : V(x) < z(x)} where continuing is cheaper than stopping. The candidate optimal rule stops at the first exit time of X from D.

definitions.name: smooth fit
definitions.text: The condition that V is C¹ also across the boundary of D, where V meets the stopping cost z. In general V is not C² there.

source.citation: Ramon van Handel, Stochastic Calculus, Filtering, and Stochastic Control, lecture notes for ACM 217, California Institute of Technology, 2007.

source.module: Chapter 8 Optimal stopping and impulse control, Section 8.1 Optimal stopping and variational inequalities
source.excerpt: Proposition 8.1.3. Let K ⊂ Rn be a set such that Xt ∈ K for all t. Suppose there is a function V : K → R, which is sufficiently smooth to apply Itô's rule, such that min{L V (x) − λV (x) + w(x), z(x) − V (x)} = 0, and |E(V (X0 ))| < ∞. Define the set D = {x ∈ K : V (x) < z(x)}, and denote by K the class of admissible stopping rules τ such that τ < ∞ a.s. and … Suppose that τ∗ = inf{t : Xt ∉ D} is in K. Then J[τ∗] ≤ J[τ] for any τ ∈ K, and the optimal cost can be expressed as E(V (X0 )) = J[τ∗].
source.attribution: © Ramon van Handel. Quoted from the author's lecture notes for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: Proposition 8.1.3 on p. 210 is the verification theorem in ℝⁿ for any V that is smooth enough for Itô's rule, and Proposition 8.1.5 gives such a rule in one dimension for C¹ functions with a measurable second derivative, with a proof cited to Rogers and Williams. The authored statement is one-dimensional and allows finitely many points where V is only C¹, which is the smooth fit case. It also shows that J[τ] is defined for τ ∈ 𝒦 instead of assuming it. Steps s4 and s5 follow the proof of Proposition 8.1.3, and steps s1 to s3 prove the needed Itô rule directly.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the proof of Proposition 8.1.3 in van Handel's ACM 217 notes, with an authored proof of the needed Itô rule. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full theorem as stated. The proof of the Itô rule for V uses a localization: choose compact intervals [α_k, β_k] that increase to I and let T_k = k ∧ inf{t ≥ 0 : X_t ∉ (α_k, β_k)}. Every path is continuous and stays in I, so T_k ↑ ∞, and on [0, T_k] the process X stays in [α_k, β_k], where |b|, |σ| ≤ C_k.

steps.text: Zero time at a point. Fix a ∈ I, t ≥ 0 and k. For small ε > 0 let g_ε : ℝ → [0, 1] be continuous, equal to 1 on [a − ε, a + ε] and to 0 outside (a − 2ε, a + 2ε), and let F_ε(x) = ∫_a^x ∫_a^y g_ε(u) du dy. Then F_ε is C², F_ε'' = g_ε, |F_ε'| ≤ 4ε and |F_ε(x)| ≤ 4ε|x − a|. Itô's formula for the process stopped at T_k gives ½∫₀^(t∧T_k) g_ε(X_s)σ(X_s)² ds = F_ε(X_(t∧T_k)) − F_ε(X₀) − ∫₀^(t∧T_k) F_ε'(X_s)b(X_s) ds − ∫₀^(t∧T_k) F_ε'(X_s)σ(X_s) dW_s. As ε ↓ 0 the first two terms on the right tend to 0 pointwise, the third is at most 4εC_k t, and the last has second moment at most 16ε²C_k²t by the Itô isometry. So the left side tends to 0 in probability. The left side is at least ½σ(a)²·Leb{s ≤ t ∧ T_k : X_s = a}, which does not depend on ε. So this quantity is 0 a.s., and k → ∞ gives σ(a)²·Leb{s ≤ t : X_s = a} = 0 a.s. Since F is finite and σ ≠ 0 on F, the set {s ≥ 0 : X_s ∈ F} has Lebesgue measure 0 a.s.

Approximation of V. Let h = V'' on I ∖ F and h = 0 on F. Then h is bounded on each compact subset of I. V' is continuous on I and C¹ on each component of I ∖ F with a derivative that is bounded near the end points, so the fundamental theorem of calculus gives V'(y) = V'(x₀) + ∫_(x₀)^y h(u) du for a fixed x₀ ∈ I. For large n the intervals [a − 1/n, a + 1/n], a ∈ F, are disjoint and lie in I. Let h_n = h outside their union and let h_n be linear on each of them, between the values h(a − 1/n) and h(a + 1/n). Then h_n is continuous, |h_n| is bounded on each compact subset of I uniformly in n, and h_n → h on I ∖ F. Put V_n(x) = V(x₀) + V'(x₀)(x − x₀) + ∫_(x₀)^x ∫_(x₀)^y h_n(u) du dy. Then V_n is C² with V_n'' = h_n. Let G ⊂ I be a compact interval that contains x₀ and the intervals [a − 1/n, a + 1/n]. On G, h_n = h except on a set of length at most 2|F|/n, and |h_n − h| ≤ 2 sup_G |h|. So |V_n' − V'| ≤ ∫_G |h_n − h| ≤ 4|F| sup_G |h| / n on G. Since V_n(x₀) = V(x₀), V_n' → V' and V_n → V uniformly on G.

Itô's rule for V. Multiply V_n by a smooth cutoff that equals 1 on [α_k, β_k] and vanishes outside a compact subset of I. Itô's formula for e^(−λt) times this C² function, at the time t ∧ T_k, gives e^(−λ(t∧T_k))V_n(X_(t∧T_k)) = V_n(X₀) + ∫₀^(t∧T_k) e^(−λs)(bV_n' + ½σ²h_n − λV_n)(X_s) ds + ∫₀^(t∧T_k) e^(−λs)V_n'(X_s)σ(X_s) dW_s. Let n → ∞. The terms with V_n and V_n' converge because of the uniform convergence on [α_k, β_k] in step s2. The stochastic integrals converge in L² by the Itô isometry, because sup over [α_k, β_k] of |V_n' − V'| tends to 0 and |σ| ≤ C_k. The term with h_n converges by dominated convergence: h_n(X_s) → h(X_s) for every s with X_s ∉ F, which is almost every s by step s1, and |h_n σ²| is bounded on [α_k, β_k]. Put 𝓛V = bV' + ½σ²h on all of I. Its values on F do not matter, by step s1. The limit gives e^(−λt)V(X_t) = V(X₀) + ∫₀ᵗ e^(−λs)(𝓛V − λV)(X_s) ds + M_t at t ∧ T_k, and k → ∞ gives it at each fixed t a.s. Both sides are continuous in t, so the identity holds for all t at once, and so at every finite random time τ.

Lower bound for every τ ∈ 𝒦. The variational inequality gives λV − 𝓛V ≤ w and V ≤ z on I ∖ F. Since V and z are continuous and I ∖ F is dense in I, also V ≤ z on I. Let Y_τ = e^(−λτ)V(X_τ) + ∫₀^τ e^(−λs)(λV − 𝓛V)(X_s) ds and Z_τ = ∫₀^τ e^(−λs)w(X_s) ds + e^(−λτ)z(X_τ). The time integrals are finite because τ < ∞ a.s. and the path on [0, τ] lies in a compact subset of I. By step s3, Y_τ = V(X₀) + M_τ, so Y_τ is integrable and E Y_τ = E V(X₀). By step s1 the times s with X_s ∈ F form a Lebesgue null set, so Y_τ ≤ Z_τ a.s. Then the negative part of Z_τ is at most the negative part of Y_τ, which is integrable. So J[τ] = E Z_τ is defined in (−∞, ∞] and J[τ] ≥ E V(X₀).

Equality for τ*. D is open in I because V and z are continuous, so I ∖ D = {V = z} is closed in I. For s < τ* the point X_s lies in D, where z − V > 0, so the variational inequality forces 𝓛V − λV + w = 0 at X_s whenever X_s ∉ F. Since τ* < ∞ a.s., the definition of τ* gives times t_j ≥ τ* with t_j → τ* and X_(t_j) ∈ I ∖ D. By continuity of X and closedness of I ∖ D in I, X_(τ*) ∈ I ∖ D, so V(X_(τ*)) = z(X_(τ*)). With step s1, Y_(τ*) = Z_(τ*) a.s. Since τ* ∈ 𝒦, step s4 gives J[τ*] = E Y_(τ*) = E V(X₀) ≤ J[τ] for every τ ∈ 𝒦.

applications.title: When to close a facility whose running cost follows a geometric Brownian motion
applications.inputs: The running cost rate of a facility is X_t, with dX_t = ½X_t dt + X_t dW_t and X₀ = 12, so X_t = 12e^(W_t). Closing costs K = 10 once, and costs are discounted at rate λ = 2. The owner minimizes J[τ] = E[∫₀^τ e^(−2s)X_s ds + 10e^(−2τ)] over the closing time τ. The candidate is V(x) = 2x/3 − x²/90 for 0 < x ≤ 30 and V(x) = 10 for x ≥ 30, with I = (0, ∞) and F = {30}.
applications.hypotheses: Here b(x) = x/2 and σ(x) = x are continuous, and X stays in (0, ∞). The costs w(x) = x and z(x) = 10 are continuous. V is C² off F = {30}, V'' is bounded, and σ(30) = 30 ≠ 0. Steps a2 and a3 check C¹ at 30 and the variational inequality. X₀ is constant, so E|V(X₀)| < ∞. Step a4 shows that τ* ∈ 𝒦.

steps.text: In the continuation region V solves 𝓛V − 2V + x = 0 with 𝓛V = (x/2)V' + (x²/2)V''. The particular solution is x/(λ − 1/2) = 2x/3. A power x^γ solves the homogeneous equation when ½γ(γ − 1) + ½γ − 2 = 0, that is γ² = 4, and γ = 2 keeps V bounded near 0.

Value matching and smooth fit for V = 2x/3 + Ax² at a level ℓ: V'(ℓ) = 2/3 + 2Aℓ = 0 gives A = −1/(3ℓ), and then V(ℓ) = 2ℓ/3 − ℓ/3 = ℓ/3 = 10 gives ℓ = 30 and A = −1/90. The check below is V'(30) = 0.

Variational inequality. On (0, 30), 𝓛V − 2V + x = (x/3 − x²/90) − x²/90 − (4x/3 − x²/45) + x = 0, and z − V = (x − 30)²/90 > 0. On (30, ∞), 𝓛V − 2V + x = x − 20 > 0 and z − V = 0. So D = (0, 30). Value matching holds: V(30) = 20 − 10 = 10.

τ* = inf{t : X_t ≥ 30} is the first time W_t reaches log(5/2), so τ* < ∞ a.s. For x ≤ 30, |xV'(x)| = x(2/3 − x/45) ≤ 5, with the maximum at x = 15, and xV'(x) = 0 for x ≥ 30. So the integrand of M is at most 5e^(−2s), M is a martingale bounded in L², and E M_τ = 0 for every stopping time τ. So τ* ∈ 𝒦, and 𝒦 contains every a.s. finite stopping time.
The optimal cost from X₀ = 12 is V(12) = 8 − 144/90 = 32/5. Closing at once costs 10. Keeping the facility open forever costs E∫₀^∞ e^(−2s)X_s ds = 12/(3/2) = 8.

applications.conclusion: The owner closes the facility when the running cost rate first reaches 30, three times the closing cost. From X₀ = 12 the expected discounted cost is 32/5, and no a.s. finite closing time gives a lower cost.

limitations: The theorem is a sufficient condition. It does not say that such a V exists, and it does not prove the smooth fit principle, which states that under conditions the value function is C¹ across the boundary of D.

The optimality holds only in the class 𝒦 of a.s. finite stopping times with E M_τ = 0. The source states the theorem in ℝⁿ for any V that is smooth enough for Itô's rule, and the authored statement covers only one dimension with finitely many points where V is not C².

Remark 8.1.6 of the source notes that the variational inequality often has many solutions, and that often only one of them is continuously differentiable. The C¹ condition selects that solution, because without it Itô's rule for V gains a local time term at the boundary.

results.name: McKean's formula for the perpetual American put
aliases: price of the perpetual American put option
results.statement: Let r > 0, σ > 0 and K > 0. Under the risk-neutral measure P*, let (B_t)_{t≥0} be a standard Brownian motion with respect to a filtration (F_t) that satisfies the usual conditions, and let S_t = x exp(σB_t + (r − σ²/2)t) with x > 0. Let γ = 2r/σ² and L* = 2rK/(2r + σ²). For a stopping time τ with values in [0, ∞], read e^{−rτ}(K − S_τ)⁺ as 0 on {τ = ∞}. Then for every x > 0, sup_τ E*[e^{−rτ}(K − S_τ)⁺] = V(x), where V(x) = K − x for 0 < x ≤ L* and V(x) = (K − L*)(x/L*)^{−γ} = (Kσ²/(2r + σ²))((2r + σ²)x/(2rK))^{−2r/σ²} for x ≥ L*. The supremum is over all (F_t)-stopping times, and the first hitting time τ* = inf{t ≥ 0 : S_t ≤ L*} attains it.
hypotheses: The interest rate r, the volatility σ and the strike K are strictly positive constants.
Under P*, the asset price is the geometric Brownian motion S_t = x exp(σB_t + (r − σ²/2)t), where B is a standard Brownian motion for a filtration that satisfies the usual conditions.
Exercise at a stopping time τ pays (K − S_τ)⁺ at time τ, and no exercise (τ = ∞) pays 0.

prerequisites.reason: Step s2 applies Itô's formula to e^{−rt} g_ε(X_t) for the smooth mollified candidate g_ε and the semimartingale X_t = log S_t.
Step s2 uses the Itô isometry: the stochastic integral of the bounded integrand e^{−rs}σ g_ε′(X_s) is a square-integrable martingale on each [0, T].
Step s3 applies the optional stopping theorem to the bounded supermartingale e^{−rt}V(S_t), and step s4 applies it to the exponential martingale Z at the bounded times t ∧ τ*.
Steps s3 and s4 let t → ∞ in expectations of processes that are bounded by the constants K and L*^{−γ}, with the dominated convergence theorem.

definitions.name: perpetual American put
definitions.text: A contract that pays (K − S_τ)⁺ at a time τ chosen by the holder, with no expiry date. Its price is the supremum of the discounted expected payoff over all stopping times.

definitions.name: exercise boundary
definitions.text: The level L*: the optimal rule exercises the first time the price falls to L* or below. On (0, L*] the value equals the payoff K − x.

source.excerpt: Proposition 15.4. Assume that r > 0. The price of the perpetual American put option is given for all t ⩾ 0 by fL∗(St) = Sup_{τ⩾t, τ Stopping time} E∗[e^{−(τ−t)r}(K − Sτ)^+ | St] = E∗[e^{−(τL∗−t)r}(K − SτL∗)^+ | St] = K − St, 0 < St ⩽ L∗; (K − L∗)(St/L∗)^{−2r/σ²} = (Kσ²/(2r + σ²))((2r + σ²)St/(2rK))^{−2r/σ²}, St ⩾ L∗.

source.alignment: Proposition 15.4 on p. 545 states the formula at a general time t with the conditional expectation given S_t. The authored statement takes t = 0, which is the same result because the problem is time-homogeneous. The source proves the upper bound with Itô's formula and the inequality (15.16b), and the lower bound from Proposition 15.2 and Lemma 15.1 on pp. 538-539. The authored proof follows the same two parts. It adds a mollification in log coordinates because the candidate value is only C¹ at L*, and it proves the lower bound with the exponential martingale of Lemma 15.1.

proof.scope: The value formula for every initial price x > 0 and the optimality of τ*, for r > 0.

steps.text: The candidate. Here K − L* = K/(1 + γ) and L* = γK/(1 + γ). Both branches of V equal K − L* at L*. The left derivative at L* is −1, and the right derivative is −γ(K − L*)/L* = −1, so V is C¹ on (0, ∞). V′ is −1 on (0, L*] and −γ(K − L*)L*^γ x^{−γ−1}, which increases from −1 to 0, on [L*, ∞). So V is convex and lies above its tangent line at L*, which is x ↦ K − x. Since also V > 0, V ≥ (K − x)⁺. Let 𝓛V(x) = ½σ²x²V″(x) + rxV′(x) − rV(x) for x ≠ L*. On (0, L*), 𝓛V = −rx − r(K − x) = −rK < 0. On (L*, ∞), V = c x^{−γ} and 𝓛V = c x^{−γ}(½σ²γ(γ + 1) − rγ − r) = 0, because ½σ²γ = r.

Supermartingale. Let X_t = log S_t = log x + σB_t + μt with μ = r − σ²/2, and g(z) = V(e^z). Then 0 < g < K, g is C¹, and |g′| ≤ L*: g′(z) = −e^z for z < log L*, and |g′| = γg ≤ γ(K − L*) = L* for z > log L*. Also g″ is bounded off log L*, so g′ is Lipschitz, and Ag = ½σ²g″ + μg′ − rg equals (𝓛V)(e^z) ≤ 0 almost everywhere. Let ρ_ε ≥ 0 be a smooth mollifier supported in [−ε, ε] and g_ε = g ∗ ρ_ε. Then g_ε is smooth, |g_ε′| ≤ L*, |g_ε − g| ≤ εL*, and Ag_ε = (Ag) ∗ ρ_ε ≤ 0. Itô's formula gives e^{−rt}g_ε(X_t) = g_ε(X₀) + ∫₀^t e^{−rs}Ag_ε(X_s) ds + ∫₀^t e^{−rs}σg_ε′(X_s) dB_s. The ds integral is nonincreasing in t. The dB integral has a bounded integrand, so by the Itô isometry it is a martingale. Hence e^{−rt}g_ε(X_t) is a supermartingale. Since |g_ε − g| ≤ εL*, letting ε → 0 in E*[e^{−rt}g_ε(X_t) | F_s] ≤ e^{−rs}g_ε(X_s) shows that M_t = e^{−rt}V(S_t) is a supermartingale, with 0 < M_t < K.

Upper bound. Let τ be a stopping time and t ≥ 0. The optional stopping theorem for the bounded supermartingale M at the bounded times 0 ≤ τ ∧ t gives E*[e^{−r(τ∧t)}V(S_{τ∧t})] ≤ V(x). As t → ∞, the integrand tends to e^{−rτ}V(S_τ) on {τ < ∞}, and it is at most Ke^{−rt} → 0 on {τ = ∞}. Dominated convergence with the bound K gives E*[e^{−rτ}V(S_τ)1{τ < ∞}] ≤ V(x). Since V ≥ (K − x)⁺ by step s1, E*[e^{−rτ}(K − S_τ)⁺] ≤ V(x) for every stopping time τ.

Attainment. If x ≤ L*, then τ* = 0 and the payoff is K − x = V(x). Let x > L*. The process Z_t = e^{−rt}S_t^{−γ} = x^{−γ}exp(−γσB_t − ½γ²σ²t) is a martingale, because −γμ − r = −½γ²σ² follows from ½σ²γ = r, and for a = −γσ the increment B_{t+h} − B_t ~ N(0, h) is independent of F_t with E exp(a(B_{t+h} − B_t) − a²h/2) = 1. By continuity S_t ≥ L* for t ≤ τ*, so 0 < Z_{t∧τ*} ≤ L*^{−γ}. Optional stopping gives E* Z_{t∧τ*} = x^{−γ}. As t → ∞, Z_{t∧τ*} tends to e^{−rτ*}L*^{−γ} on {τ* < ∞}, because S_{τ*} = L*, and to 0 on {τ* = ∞}. Dominated convergence gives E*[e^{−rτ*}1{τ* < ∞}] = (x/L*)^{−γ}. So E*[e^{−rτ*}(K − S_{τ*})⁺] = (K − L*)(x/L*)^{−γ} = V(x).
Conclusion. Steps s3 and s4 give sup_τ E*[e^{−rτ}(K − S_τ)⁺] = V(x), and τ* attains the supremum. The second form of V follows from K − L* = Kσ²/(2r + σ²) and x/L* = (2r + σ²)x/(2rK).

applications.title: Price and exercise level of a perpetual put
applications.inputs: Interest rate r = 4% per year, volatility σ = 20% per year and strike K = 90. The current price of the asset is S₀ = 90 (at the money) or S₀ = 120.
applications.hypotheses: r = 0.04 > 0, σ = 0.2 > 0 and K = 90 > 0. The asset follows the Black–Scholes model, which is a geometric Brownian motion with drift r under P*.

steps.text: γ = 2r/σ² = 0.08/0.04 = 2, and L* = γK/(1 + γ) = 2 · 90/3 = 60. The holder exercises the first time the price falls to 60.
At L* the two branches meet with slope −γ(K − L*)/L* = −2 · 30/60 = −1, which is the slope of the payoff K − x. This is the smooth fit condition.
At S₀ = 90 > L*, V(90) = (K − L*)(L*/90)² = 30 · (60/90)² = 40/3, about 13.33. Immediate exercise pays (90 − 90)⁺ = 0, so the option is worth much more than its exercise value.
At S₀ = 120, V(120) = 30 · (60/120)² = 15/2. At S₀ = 50 ≤ L*, the holder exercises at once and receives V(50) = 90 − 50 = 40.

applications.conclusion: With r = 4%, σ = 20% and K = 90, the perpetual put is worth 40/3 at the money and 15/2 at S₀ = 120. The optimal rule exercises when the price first reaches 60.

limitations: The formula needs r > 0. For r = 0 the price S_t tends to 0 almost surely, the supremum equals K, and no stopping time attains it.
There is no closed formula for an American put with a finite maturity. Its exercise boundary depends on the time to maturity and solves a free-boundary problem.
The proof verifies the given candidate V. It does not by itself explain how to find L*: in the source, smooth fit at L* selects L* among the values f_L of the rules that exercise at a fixed level L.

results.name: Wald–Wolfowitz optimality of the sequential probability ratio test
results.statement: Let P ≠ Q be probability measures on a measurable space (𝒳, ℬ). Let ν = P + Q and let f = (dQ/dν)/(dP/dν), with values in [0, ∞], be the likelihood ratio of Q to P. Under either law μ ∈ {P, Q} the observations X₁, X₂, … are i.i.d. with law μ. Put r₀ = 1 and r_n = f(X₁)⋯f(X_n), a product that is defined with probability 1 under P and under Q. A sequential test φ decides after each n ≥ 0 observations, as a measurable function of X₁, …, X_n and of a randomization that is independent of the observations, to stop and accept P, to stop and accept Q, or to continue. Its sample size N_φ ∈ {0, 1, 2, …, ∞} is the time at which it stops. Its error probabilities are α_P(φ) = P(φ accepts Q) and α_Q(φ) = Q(φ accepts P). For 0 < A < 1 < B < ∞ the sequential probability ratio test ψ = SPRT(A, B) stops at N_ψ = min{n ≥ 1 : r_n ≤ A or r_n ≥ B}, and accepts P if r_N ≤ A and Q if r_N ≥ B. Then E_P N_ψ < ∞ and E_Q N_ψ < ∞. Moreover, every sequential test φ with α_P(φ) ≤ α_P(ψ), α_Q(φ) ≤ α_Q(ψ), E_P N_φ < ∞ and E_Q N_φ < ∞ satisfies E_P N_ψ ≤ E_P N_φ and E_Q N_ψ ≤ E_Q N_φ.
hypotheses: P and Q are distinct probability measures on the same measurable space.
Under either law the observations X₁, X₂, … are independent and identically distributed.
The thresholds of the SPRT satisfy 0 < A < 1 < B < ∞.
The competing sequential test φ, which may be randomized, has α_P(φ) ≤ α_P(ψ), α_Q(φ) ≤ α_Q(ψ), E_P N_φ < ∞ and E_Q N_φ < ∞.

prerequisites.reason: Step s2: Lemma 1.7.1 splits the Bayes risk of a test over the first observation and the later observations with the Tonelli–Fubini theorem.
Step s3: Lemma 1.7.4 covers the compact interval [0, 1] of priors by finitely many intervals on which one test is ε-optimal.
Steps s3 and s5: the thresholds p_L and p_U are roots of continuous functions, and Lemma 1.7.10 solves j(c) = A/B by the intermediate value theorem.
Step s4: the risk of the SPRT on the paths that have not stopped by time n tends to 0 by dominated convergence with the geometric tail bound.

definitions.name: sequential test
definitions.text: A rule that, after each number n ≥ 0 of observations, uses X₁, …, X_n and an independent randomization to stop and accept P, to stop and accept Q, or to take one more observation. Its sample size N is the stopping time at which it decides.

definitions.name: error probabilities
definitions.text: α_P(φ) = P(φ accepts Q) is the probability of rejecting P when P is true, and α_Q(φ) = Q(φ accepts P) is the probability of rejecting Q when Q is true. A test that never stops rejects nothing.

definitions.name: sequential probability ratio test
definitions.text: SPRT(A, B) observes until the likelihood ratio r_n = f(X₁)⋯f(X_n) leaves the interval (A, B), and then accepts P if r_n ≤ A and Q if r_n ≥ B.

source.excerpt: … if ψ is a sequential probability ratio test with α(P, ψ) = α and α(Q, ψ) = γ, then in the class of all sequential tests φ with α(P, φ) ≤ α and α(Q, φ) ≤ γ, the SPRT ψ minimizes EP,φ N, and it minimizes EQ,φ N.

The excerpt is the restatement of the theorem that directly follows it. The authored statement adds the hypothesis that φ has finite mean sample sizes under P and Q, writes out the likelihood ratio and the class of randomized tests, and makes P ≠ Q explicit, as Lemmas 1.5.2 and 1.7.10 of the notes do. The outline follows the Bayes argument of Section 1.7 of the notes and Case I of its proof of Theorem 1.5.1.

source_references.alignment: Section 1.7 proves Theorem 1.5.1 for randomized tests. Lemmas 1.7.1 to 1.7.10 set up the Bayes problem and show that the SPRT is Bayes, and the proof on pp. 7-8 compares a test with the SPRT in three cases. The authored outline follows the lemmas and Case I, which is the case of finite mean sample sizes.

results.proof_status: outline of the cited published proof. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of Theorem 1.5.1 in Dudley's 18.466 lecture notes, Lemma 1.5.2 of Section 1.5 and Section 1.7, pp. 1-7, in the case of finite mean sample sizes (Case I of the source). Step s1 takes the geometric tail bound from Lemma 1.5.2. Steps s2 and s3 take Lemma 1.7.1, Lemma 1.7.4 and Proposition 1.7.6 from the source. Step s4 takes Theorem 1.7.7 and Lemma 1.7.8, and step s5 takes Lemmas 1.7.9 and 1.7.10.

steps.text: Finite mean sample size of the SPRT. Lemma 1.5.2 of the source proves that there are δ ∈ (0, 1) and C < ∞ with μ(N_ψ > n) ≤ C(1 − δ)^n for μ = P and μ = Q. Put Z_i = log f(X_i) and S_n = Z₁ + ⋯ + Z_n, so N_ψ > n exactly when log A < S_j < log B for j = 1, …, n. Since P ≠ Q, the law of Z₁ is not the point mass at 0 under μ, so there is b > 0 with p = μ(|Z₁| ≥ b)/2 > 0. Then μ(Z₁ ≥ b) ≥ p or μ(Z₁ ≤ −b) ≥ p, and for m with mb > log(B/A) the event D_i = {|S_{im} − S_{(i−1)m}| > log(B/A)} has probability at least p^m. The events D_i are independent, and on D_i the walk leaves (log A, log B) by time im. So μ(N_ψ > im) ≤ (1 − p^m)^i, and E_P N_ψ and E_Q N_ψ are finite.

Bayes risk and its first-step form. Fix a cost c > 0 per observation, a loss v ∈ (0, 1) for accepting Q under P, the loss w = 1 − v for accepting P under Q, and a prior p = π(P), q = 1 − p. The risk of a test is r(p, φ) = pvα_P(φ) + qwα_Q(φ) + pcE_P N_φ + qcE_Q N_φ, which is affine in p. Let r(p) be the infimum of r(p, φ) over the tests that take at least one observation. As an infimum of affine functions r is concave, so it is continuous on (0, 1). The bounds c ≤ r(p) ≤ min(c + pv, c + (1 − p)w) give continuity at 0 and 1. A test without observations has risk pv or (1 − p)w, so the Bayes risk is R(p) = min(pv, r(p), (1 − p)w), which is (1.7.5). Lemma 1.7.1 of the source uses the Tonelli–Fubini theorem to show that a test with φ₀ ≡ 0 has risk c + ∫ r(p_x, φ^(x)) d(pP + qQ)(x), where p_x = p/(p + qf(x)) is the posterior probability of P and φ^(x) is the test that the first observation x leaves.

Thresholds and the Bellman equation. If r(w) ≤ vw, the concave function r(p) − pv is positive at p = 0 and at most 0 at p = w, so it has a unique root p_L ∈ (0, w]. In the same way r(p) − (1 − p)w has a unique root p_U ∈ [w, 1). If r(w) > vw, the source puts p_L = p_U = w. Then R(p) = pv for p ≤ p_L, R(p) = (1 − p)w for p ≥ p_U, and R(p) = r(p) between them. Proposition 1.7.6 of the source proves R(p) = c + ∫ R(p_x) d(pP + qQ)(x) for p_L < p < p_U. The lower bound follows from Lemma 1.7.1. For the upper bound, Lemma 1.7.4 covers [0, 1] by finitely many intervals and chooses on each one a test whose risk is within ε of R, so the test that applies the choice for p_x after the first observation is measurable and has risk at most c + ε + ∫ R(p_x) d(pP + qQ)(x).

The SPRT is Bayes. Put A(p) = p(1 − p_U)/(qp_U) and B(p) = p(1 − p_L)/(qp_L). After n observations the posterior probability of P is p/(p + qr_n). It is at least p_U exactly when r_n ≤ A(p), and at most p_L exactly when r_n ≥ B(p). Theorem 1.7.7 of the source proves that SPRT(A(p), B(p)) has risk R(p). If p ≥ p_U or p ≤ p_L, the test decides at once with risk R(p). If p_L < p < p_U, Lemma 1.7.8 shows by induction on n, with the Bellman equation of step s3, that R(p) is at least the part T_n(p) of the risk of the SPRT on the paths that stop by time n. On the paths that stop at time n the loss is at most nc + max(v, w). With the geometric tail of step s1 the sum of (a + nc)(1 − δ)^n converges, so the remaining risk tends to 0 by dominated convergence, and the risk of the SPRT is at most R(p).

A prior near 0 or near 1 that makes the given SPRT Bayes. Lemma 1.7.10 of the source proves that for each ε > 0 there are c > 0, v ∈ (0, 1) and p ∈ (0, ε) with A(p) = A and B(p) = B, and also such a p ∈ (1 − ε, 1). Fix v ∈ (1 − ε/B, 1). Lemma 1.7.9 shows that p_L and p_U are continuous in c > 0, because r(p) is nondecreasing and locally Lipschitz in c. So j(c) = p_L(1 − p_U)/(p_U(1 − p_L)) is continuous. It equals 1 when c > vw, since then r(w) ≥ c > vw. It tends to 0 as c → 0, since fixed-sample tests with small error probabilities give sup_p r(p) → 0, so p_L → 0 and p_U → 1. The intermediate value theorem gives c with j(c) = A/B. For p = p_LB/(1 − p_L + p_LB), one has p/q = p_LB/(1 − p_L) = p_UA/(1 − p_U), so A(p) = A, B(p) = B and p ≤ p_LB ≤ wB < ε. With v ∈ (0, Aε) instead, the same construction gives q ≤ (1 − p_U)/A ≤ v/A < ε.

Comparison with a competing test (Case I of the source). Let φ satisfy the hypotheses, and put d_P = E_P N_φ − E_P N_ψ and d_Q = E_Q N_φ − E_Q N_ψ, which are finite by step s1 and the hypothesis. Take the problem of step s5 with p < ε. Since ψ is Bayes and r(p, φ) is finite, 0 ≤ r(p, φ) − r(p, ψ) = pv(α_P(φ) − α_P(ψ)) + qw(α_Q(φ) − α_Q(ψ)) + c(pd_P + qd_Q). The two error terms are at most 0, so pd_P + qd_Q ≥ 0 after division by c > 0. Hence d_Q ≥ −(p/q)|d_P| ≥ −ε|d_P|/(1 − ε) for each ε ∈ (0, 1), and so d_Q ≥ 0. The problem of step s5 with q < ε gives d_P ≥ −ε|d_Q|/(1 − ε) in the same way, so d_P ≥ 0.
