applications.title: Acceptance sampling that decides between an old and an improved process
applications.inputs: Each tested unit passes with probability 1/3 under the old process P and with probability 2/3 under the improved process Q. The inspector uses ψ = SPRT(1/4, 4). For comparison, a fixed-sample plan tests 7 units and accepts Q when at least 4 of them pass.
applications.hypotheses: P ≠ Q because the pass probabilities differ. The units are independent with the same pass probability, so the observations are i.i.d. under each law. The thresholds satisfy 0 < 1/4 < 1 < 4 < ∞. The fixed-sample plan is a sequential test with N = 7 under both laws, so its mean sample sizes are finite.

steps.text: The likelihood ratio is f(pass) = (2/3)/(1/3) = 2 and f(fail) = (1/3)/(2/3) = 1/2. So r_n = 2^(S_n), where S_n is the number of passes minus the number of failures. The SPRT stops when S_n = −2 and accepts P, or when S_n = 2 and accepts Q. Because S_n moves by ±1, r_N is exactly 1/4 or 4.

Under P, E_P f(X₁) = 1, so r_n is a martingale. The stopped values r_{min(n, N)} stay in [1/4, 4] and N_ψ < ∞ almost surely, so optional stopping gives 1 = E_P r_N = 4α_P(ψ) + (1/4)(1 − α_P(ψ)). Hence α_P(ψ) = (1 − 1/4)/(4 − 1/4) = 1/5.

Under Q, 1/r_n is a martingale, and 1 = E_Q(1/r_N) = 4α_Q(ψ) + (1/4)(1 − α_Q(ψ)). Hence α_Q(ψ) = (4 − 1)(1/4)/(4 − 1/4) = 1/5, which is the formula α₁ = (B − 1)A/(B − A) of the source's example after Proposition 1.5.3.

Under P a step of S_n has mean 1/3 − 2/3 = −1/3, and E_P S_N = 2 · (1/5) − 2 · (4/5) = −6/5. Wald's equation gives E_P N_ψ = (−6/5)/(−1/3) = 18/5. The problem is symmetric under the exchange of P and Q, so E_Q N_ψ = 18/5 as well.

For the fixed-sample plan, α_P = P(at least 4 of 7 pass) = (35 · 2³ + 21 · 2² + 7 · 2 + 1)/3⁷ = 379/2187, which is less than 1/5. By symmetry α_Q = 379/2187 as well. So the plan satisfies the hypotheses of the theorem, and its sample size 7 is at least 18/5, as the theorem requires.

applications.conclusion: The SPRT has both error probabilities equal to 1/5 and uses 18/5 = 3.6 units on average under each process. By the theorem, no sampling plan with both error probabilities at most 1/5 and finite mean sample sizes uses fewer units on average under the old process or under the improved process. The fixed plan with 7 units meets the error bound but uses almost twice as many units.

limitations: The authored statement assumes finite mean sample sizes E_P N_φ and E_Q N_φ for the competing test. Theorem 1.5.1 of the source states the result without this assumption and treats an infinite mean in Cases II and III of its proof, which this outline does not follow.

The theorem compares mean sample sizes only under P and under Q. Under a third law, for example an intermediate parameter value, the SPRT need not be optimal. The Kiefer–Weiss problem studies tests that minimize the largest mean sample size over a family of laws.

The theorem does not give the error probabilities of ψ in closed form. Proposition 1.5.3 of the source gives α_P(ψ) ≤ (1 − α_Q(ψ))/B ≤ 1/B and α_Q(ψ) ≤ (1 − α_P(ψ))A ≤ A, with equality in the first and third bounds when r_N is always A or B.

results.name: Prophet inequality of Krengel, Sucheston and Garling
results.statement: Let X₁, …, X_n be independent, nonnegative and integrable random variables, and let M_n = max_{1≤j≤n} X_j. Let m be a median of M_n, so that P(M_n < m) ≤ 1/2 and P(M_n > m) ≤ 1/2, and set β = Σ_{i=1}^{n} E(X_i − m)⁺. Let s(m) be the first j ≤ n with X_j > m, and let t(m) be the first j ≤ n with X_j ≥ m, with the value n if there is no such j. If m ≤ β, then E M_n ≤ 2 E X_{s(m)}. If m ≥ β, then E M_n ≤ 2 E X_{t(m)}. Hence E M_n ≤ 2 sup_N E X_N, where N runs over the stopping times of X₁, …, X_n with values in {1, …, n}. For an infinite sequence X₁, X₂, … of independent nonnegative random variables, E sup_n X_n ≤ 2 sup_N E X_N, where N runs over the stopping times that are finite almost surely.
hypotheses: The random variables X₁, X₂, … are independent and nonnegative.
In the finite statement, each X_i is integrable.
The stopping times are adapted to the observations: the event {N = j} depends only on X₁, …, X_j.

prerequisites.reason: Step s5 uses the monotone convergence theorem to show that E M_n increases to E sup_n X_n for an infinite sequence.

definitions.name: median
definitions.text: A number m with P(Y < m) ≤ 1/2 and P(Y > m) ≤ 1/2. Every real random variable Y has at least one median.

definitions.name: threshold stopping rule
definitions.text: A rule that stops at the first observation above a fixed level c, and at the last time n if no observation is above c. Here s(c) uses X_j > c and t(c) uses X_j ≥ c.

definitions.name: prophet value and stopping value
definitions.text: The prophet value E max_j X_j is what a player who sees all values in advance obtains. The stopping value sup_N E X_N is what a player who must decide at each time from past values can obtain.

source.citation: Thomas S. Ferguson, Optimal Stopping and Applications, online book, Mathematics Department, University of California, Los Angeles.
source.revision: Author's online version, Chapter 3 file sr3.pdf (PDF created 2008-07-20), 13 pages.
source.module: Chapter 3 The existence of optimal stopping rules, Section 3.4 Prophet Inequalities
source.excerpt: Then one of the two stopping rules, s(m) or t(m), will achieve at least half of EMn. More precisely, Theorem 5. If m ≤ β, then E(Mn) ≤ 2E(Xs(m)). If m ≥ β, then E(Mn) ≤ 2E(Xt(m)).
source.attribution: © Thomas S. Ferguson. Quoted from the author's online book Optimal Stopping and Applications for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states the threshold form of the prophet inequality as Theorem 5 and derives M* ≤ 2V* (its inequalities (19) and (21), PDF page 9) from it. The authored statement makes the integrability condition explicit and includes the infinite sequence. The proof follows the Samuel-Cahn argument of the source for s(m), and it writes out the case t(m), which the source calls analogous.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the Samuel-Cahn threshold proof of the cited source. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement: both threshold cases for finite n, the bound by the stopping value, and the infinite sequence.

steps.text: The median m is nonnegative, because M_n ≥ 0 and P(M_n > m) ≤ 1/2. Write p = P(M_n > m) ≤ 1/2 and q = P(M_n < m) ≤ 1/2. Since (M_n − m)⁺ = max_i (X_i − m)⁺ ≤ Σ_i (X_i − m)⁺, we get E M_n ≤ m + E(M_n − m)⁺ ≤ m + β. This is the only bound on the prophet value that the proof needs.

Let τ be s(m) or t(m). Both are stopping times with values in {1, …, n}. If τ ≥ i and X_i > m, then no earlier X_j met the threshold and X_i meets it, so τ = i. Therefore (X_τ − m)⁺ = Σ_i (X_i − m)⁺ 1{τ = i} = Σ_i (X_i − m)⁺ 1{τ ≥ i}. The event {τ ≥ i} depends only on X₁, …, X_{i−1}, so it is independent of X_i. Hence E(X_τ − m)⁺ = Σ_i E(X_i − m)⁺ P(τ ≥ i).

Case m ≤ β with τ = s(m). The event {M_n ≤ m} is contained in {s(m) ≥ i} for every i, so P(s(m) ≥ i) ≥ 1 − p and step s2 gives E(X_{s(m)} − m)⁺ ≥ β(1 − p). If M_n > m, then X_{s(m)} > m. If M_n ≤ m, then X_{s(m)} = X_n ≤ m. So P(X_{s(m)} > m) = p. Since X_n ≥ 0, E X_{s(m)} ≥ E[X_{s(m)} 1{X_{s(m)} > m}] = E(X_{s(m)} − m)⁺ + m p ≥ β(1 − p) + m p = β − (β − m)p. With β − m ≥ 0 and p ≤ 1/2, this is at least (m + β)/2, which is at least E M_n / 2 by step s1.

Case m ≥ β with τ = t(m). The event {M_n < m} is contained in {t(m) ≥ i} for every i, so step s2 gives E(X_{t(m)} − m)⁺ ≥ β q. If M_n ≥ m, then X_{t(m)} ≥ m. If M_n < m, then X_{t(m)} = X_n < m. So P(X_{t(m)} ≥ m) = 1 − q. Since X_n ≥ 0, E X_{t(m)} ≥ E[X_{t(m)} 1{X_{t(m)} ≥ m}] = E(X_{t(m)} − m)⁺ + m(1 − q) ≥ β q + m(1 − q) = m − (m − β)q. With m − β ≥ 0 and q ≤ 1/2, this is at least (m + β)/2 ≥ E M_n / 2. Steps s3 and s4 together give E M_n ≤ 2 sup_N E X_N.

Infinite sequence. If E X_i = ∞ for some i, the rule N = i gives sup_N E X_N = ∞ and there is nothing to prove. Otherwise every X_i is integrable. The maxima M_n increase to sup_n X_n, so monotone convergence gives E M_n → E sup_n X_n. A stopping time with values in {1, …, n} is finite, so sup_N E X_N ≥ E M_n / 2 for every n by step s4. Let n → ∞ to get E sup_n X_n ≤ 2 sup_N E X_N.

applications.title: Selling an asset to two sequential bidders
applications.inputs: A seller receives two offers in turn and must accept or reject each offer at once. The first offer is X₁ = 2. The second offer X₂ is 10 with probability 1/5 and 0 with probability 4/5, independent of X₁.
applications.hypotheses: The offers are independent, nonnegative and bounded, so they are integrable. A selling rule may use only the offers seen so far, so it is a stopping time of X₁, X₂.

steps.text: The prophet value is E max(X₁, X₂). The maximum is 10 with probability 1/5 and 2 with probability 4/5.
The value m = 2 is a median of M₂, because P(M₂ < 2) = 0 and P(M₂ > 2) = 1/5. Then β = E(X₁ − 2)⁺ + E(X₂ − 2)⁺ = 0 + 8 · (1/5).

Since m = 2 ≥ β = 8/5, the theorem uses the rule t(2), which accepts the first offer of at least 2. It accepts X₁ = 2, so E X_{t(2)} = 2. The theorem gives 18/5 ≤ 2 · 2 = 4, and the proof gives the finer bound E X_{t(2)} ≥ (m + β)/2 = 9/5.
No rule does better than 2 here: accepting X₁ gives 2 and waiting gives E X₂ = 2. So the prophet's advantage is the factor (18/5)/2 = 9/5, which is below the universal factor 2.

applications.conclusion: The simple rule 'accept the first offer of at least the median of the maximum' earns 2, while a prophet earns 18/5. The ratio 9/5 respects the prophet bound 2.

limitations: The constant 2 is sharp. For X₁ = 1 and X₂ = B with probability 1/B and 0 otherwise, the prophet value is 2 − 1/B and the stopping value is 1.
Nonnegativity matters. With X₁ = 1 and X₂ = ±B with probability 1/2 each, the prophet value is (B + 1)/2 and the stopping value is 1.
For independent variables in [0, 1], Hill and Kertz proved the sharper bound E sup X_n ≤ V* + 1/4, where V* is the stopping value.

results.name: Gittins index theorem
aliases: optimality of the Gittins index policy
results.statement: Let k ≥ 1 and α ∈ (0, 1). For each arm i = 1, …, k let E_i be a countable set, P_i a transition matrix on E_i, r_i: E_i → ℝ a bounded reward function and x_i ∈ E_i an initial state. On a probability space let Y¹, …, Y^k be independent Markov chains, where Y^i = (Y^i_u)_{u≥0} has Y^i_0 = x_i and transition matrix P_i, and let U be uniform on [0, 1] and independent of the chains. At each time t = 1, 2, … a policy π chooses an arm A_t. With n_l(t − 1) = #{s < t : A_s = l}, the state of arm l at time t is S_l(t) = Y^l_{n_l(t−1)}, so only the chosen arm moves. A_t must be a measurable function of U, of A_1, …, A_{t−1} and of the states S_l(s) for l ≤ k and s ≤ t. The value of π is V(π) = E Σ_{t≥1} α^{t−1} r_{A_t}(S_{A_t}(t)). The Gittins index of a state x ∈ E_i is g_i(x) = sup_τ E_x[Σ_{u=0}^{τ−1} α^u r_i(Y_u)] / E_x[Σ_{u=0}^{τ−1} α^u], where Y is a Markov chain with transition matrix P_i and Y₀ = x, and τ runs over the stopping times of its natural filtration with 1 ≤ τ ≤ ∞. A Gittins index policy is a policy with g_{A_t}(S_{A_t}(t)) = max_l g_l(S_l(t)) for every t. Then every Gittins index policy π* satisfies V(π*) = sup_π V(π), where the supremum is over all policies.
hypotheses: The arms are independent Markov chains on countable state spaces, and an arm changes its state only when it is played.
Each reward function r_i is bounded, and the rewards are discounted geometrically with a factor α ∈ (0, 1).
A policy chooses each arm from the past and present states, the past actions and an independent randomization U.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 obtains the calibration function v_γ as the unique bounded fixed point of the contraction f ↦ max(0, r − γ + αPf).
Step s1 applies the optional stopping theorem to the supermartingale N at the bounded times 1 ≤ σ ∧ n and to the stopped martingale N_{t∧κ}.
Steps s1 and s4 pass to the limit in discounted sums with bounded rewards by the dominated convergence theorem, with the bound Σ_t α^{t−1}(C + |γ|).

definitions.name: Gittins index
definitions.text: g_i(x) is the largest discounted reward rate that arm i can earn from state x, over all rules that play the arm at least once and then stop at a stopping time. It is also the retirement charge per play at which a player is indifferent between playing and not playing.

definitions.name: prevailing charge
definitions.text: G_i(t) is the minimum of the Gittins indices of the states that arm i has visited up to time t. It does not increase in time.

definitions.name: policy
definitions.text: A rule that chooses at each time t an arm A_t from the information observed so far and an independent random variable U, so that randomized rules are allowed.

source.citation: Thomas S. Ferguson, Optimal Stopping and Applications, online book, Mathematics Department, University of California, Los Angeles.
source.revision: Author's online version, Chapter 7 file sr7.pdf (PDF created 2008-07-20), 13 pages.
source.module: Chapter 7 Bandit problems, Section 7.3 The Gittins Index Theorem
source.excerpt: Theorem 4. For a k -armed bandit problem with independent arms and geometric discount, any Gittins index rule is optimal.
source.attribution: © Thomas S. Ferguson. Quoted from the author's online book Optimal Stopping and Applications for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: Ferguson states Theorem 4 for k independent arms with general reward sequences X(j, t) and sup E|X(j, t)| < ∞, and with the index defined by the same ratio of discounted sums. The authored statement is the Markov case with countable state spaces and bounded rewards, which makes the index a function of the current state. Ferguson proves the theorem with the interchange argument of Varaiya, Walrand and Buyukkoc. The authored proof instead follows the prevailing charge proof of Weber in the form of Theorem 35.9 of Lattimore and Szepesvári, and it proves the calibration facts of their Lemma 35.7 and the interleaving Lemma 35.10, which the book leaves as exercises.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the prevailing charge proof of Theorem 35.9 in Lattimore and Szepesvári, Bandit Algorithms. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The whole statement, for countable state spaces, bounded rewards and randomized policies.

steps.text: Calibration of one arm. Fix an arm i, write r = r_i, P = P_i and C = sup|r|, and fix γ ∈ ℝ. The map f ↦ max(0, r − γ + αPf) is a contraction with constant α for the sup norm on bounded functions on E_i, because |max(0, a) − max(0, b)| ≤ |a − b|. By the Banach fixed-point theorem it has a unique bounded fixed point v_γ ≥ 0. Let c_γ = r − γ + αPv_γ, so v_γ = max(0, c_γ). For the chain Y from x, N_t = Σ_{u<t} α^u(r(Y_u) − γ) + α^t v_γ(Y_t) satisfies E[N_{t+1} − N_t | F_t] = α^t(c_γ(Y_t) − v_γ(Y_t)) ≤ 0, so N is a supermartingale. For a stopping time σ ≥ 1, optional stopping at the bounded times 1 ≤ σ ∧ n gives E_x N_{σ∧n} ≤ E_x N_1 = c_γ(x). Since v_γ ≥ 0, dominated convergence as n → ∞ gives E_x Σ_{u<σ} α^u(r(Y_u) − γ) ≤ c_γ(x). For κ = min{u ≥ 1 : v_γ(Y_u) = 0}, the process N_{t∧κ}, t ≥ 1, is a martingale, because v_γ = c_γ where v_γ > 0. As t → ∞, α^{t∧κ}v_γ(Y_{t∧κ}) → 0, because v_γ(Y_κ) = 0 on {κ < ∞}. Dominated convergence gives E_x Σ_{u<κ} α^u(r(Y_u) − γ) = c_γ(x).

Index and calibration. For a stopping time σ ≥ 1 let D_σ = E_x Σ_{u<σ} α^u, which lies in [1, 1/(1 − α)], and let R_σ be the ratio in the definition of g_i(x). Then E_x Σ_{u<σ} α^u(r(Y_u) − γ) = D_σ(R_σ − γ), and step s1 gives c_γ(x) = max_{σ≥1} D_σ(R_σ − γ), attained at κ. Hence c_γ(x) ≤ 0 if and only if R_σ ≤ γ for every σ, that is g_i(x) ≤ γ. If g_i(x) ≥ γ, then for every ε > 0 some σ has R_σ > γ − ε, so c_γ(x) > −ε/(1 − α), and c_γ(x) ≥ 0. Two facts follow. (a) v_γ(x) = 0 if and only if g_i(x) ≤ γ. (b) If g_i(x) ≥ γ, then v_γ(x) = r(x) − γ + αPv_γ(x).

Prevailing charges. Fix a policy and an arm i. Let G_i(t) = min_{u≤n_i(t−1)} g_i(Y^i_u), the smallest index of the states of arm i up to time t. G_i does not increase in t. Let τ_1 be the first time with A_t = i, and τ_{j+1} = min{t > τ_j : A_t = i and g_i(S_i(t)) ≤ G_i(τ_j)}, with min ∅ = ∞. On {τ_j < ∞} let γ_j = G_i(τ_j) and T_j = {t : A_t = i, τ_j ≤ t < τ_{j+1}}. Induction on j gives g_i(S_i(τ_j)) = γ_j. At τ_1 arm i has visited only x_i. For the step from j to j + 1, the states of arm i up to τ_{j+1} are those up to τ_j, the states at the plays in T_j after τ_j, which have index > γ_j, and S_i(τ_{j+1}), which has index ≤ γ_j. So G_i(t) = γ_j and g_i(S_i(t)) ≥ γ_j for every t ∈ T_j. The sets T_j partition the times at which arm i is played, and γ_j takes values in the countable set g_i(E_i).

Bound by the prevailing charge. Let F_t be generated by U, the history up to time t and A_t. Every event of F_t, intersected with {A_t = i, n_i(t − 1) = m}, is determined by U, the other chains and Y^i_0, …, Y^i_m. By independence and the Markov property, E[f(Y^i_{m+1}) | F_t] = P_if(S_i(t)) on this event for bounded f. Let S⁺_i(t) = Y^i_{n_i(t−1)+1} be the state after a play at t, and v = v_{γ_j} for arm i. For t ∈ T_j, fact (b) gives r_i(S_i(t)) − γ_j = v(S_i(t)) − αP_iv(S_i(t)). Summation over t and over the values of γ_j, with dominated convergence, gives E Σ_{t∈T_j} α^{t−1}(r_i(S_i(t)) − γ_j) = E Σ_{t∈T_j} α^{t−1}(v(S_i(t)) − αv(S⁺_i(t))). Let t_1 < t_2 < … be the elements of T_j. Arm i does not move between plays, so S⁺_i(t_l) = S_i(t_{l+1}), and the sum is α^{t_1−1}v(S_i(τ_j)) − Σ_l (α^{t_l} − α^{t_{l+1}−1})v(S_i(t_{l+1})) − ρ, where ρ = α^{t_L}v(S⁺_i(t_L)) ≥ 0 if T_j ends at t_L, and ρ = 0 if T_j is infinite. Fact (a) gives v(S_i(τ_j)) = 0, and the other terms are ≤ 0 because t_{l+1} − 1 ≥ t_l and v ≥ 0. Summation over j and i, with G_i(t) = γ_j on T_j, gives V(π) ≤ E Σ_t α^{t−1}G_{A_t}(t).

Equality for a Gittins index policy π*. At τ_j, π* chose arm i, so γ_j = g_i(S_i(τ_j)) ≥ g_l(S_l(τ_j)) for every l. The other arms do not move while arm i is played. So after a run of plays of arm i from τ_j, if g_i(S_i(t)) > γ_j, arm i has the strictly largest index and π* plays it again. Hence T_j = {τ_j, τ_j + 1, …, κ_j − 1} with κ_j = min{t > τ_j : g_i(S_i(t)) ≤ γ_j}. In the sum of step s4 the middle terms are 0, and ρ = α^{κ_j−1}v(S_i(κ_j)) = 0 by fact (a), or ρ = 0 if κ_j = ∞. So V(π*) = E Σ_t α^{t−1}G_{A_t}(t) under π*.

π* is greedy in the prevailing charges. Let H_{l,m} = min_{u≤m} g_l(Y^l_u). For each arm l this sequence does not increase in m, it depends only on the chain Y^l, and G_l(t) = H_{l,n_l(t−1)}. Under π*, let a = A_t, m = n_a(t − 1) and u ≤ m with H_{a,m} = g_a(Y^a_u). Arm a was played in state Y^a_u at some time s ≤ t, and π* chose it then, so g_a(Y^a_u) ≥ g_l(S_l(s)) ≥ G_l(s) ≥ G_l(t) for every l. Hence G_{A_t}(t) = max_l H_{l,n_l(t−1)}: at every time π* takes the largest current term among the sequences H_l.

Interleaving lemma. Let h_1, …, h_k be nonincreasing sequences bounded by C. An action sequence a interleaves them with terms I_t(a) = h_{a_t, n_{a_t}(t−1)}, and a greedy sequence a* takes a largest current term at each step. For m ≥ 1 let c_l be the number of terms that the first m steps take from h_l, and F(c) = Σ_l Σ_{u<c_l} h_{l,u}. Let c* be the counts of a*. If c ≠ c*, choose l with c_l > c*_l and l′ with c_{l′} < c*_{l′}. When a* took its last term h_{l′,c*_{l′}−1}, the current term of h_l was h_{l,p} with p ≤ c*_l, so h_{l′,c_{l′}} ≥ h_{l′,c*_{l′}−1} ≥ h_{l,p} ≥ h_{l,c_l−1}. Moving one term from l to l′ does not decrease F and brings c closer to c*. By induction F(c) ≤ F(c*). With α^{t−1} = (1 − α)Σ_{m≥t} α^{m−1}, Σ_t α^{t−1}I_t(a) = (1 − α)Σ_m α^{m−1} Σ_{t≤m} I_t(a) ≤ (1 − α)Σ_m α^{m−1} F(c*(m)) = Σ_t α^{t−1}I_t(a*). The right side is the same for every greedy a*, because F(c*(m)) is the maximum of F over the counts with sum m.

Conclusion. Let W(H) be the greedy value of step s7 for the sequences H_l. It depends only on the chains, not on the policy. For any policy π, step s4 and step s7 with I_t(A) = H_{A_t,n_{A_t}(t−1)} = G_{A_t}(t) give V(π) ≤ E Σ_t α^{t−1}G_{A_t}(t) ≤ E W(H). For π*, steps s5 and s6 give V(π*) = E Σ_t α^{t−1}G_{A_t}(t) = E W(H). Hence V(π*) ≥ V(π) for every policy π, and V(π*) = sup_π V(π).

applications.title: A standard treatment against a new treatment of unknown quality
applications.inputs: Discount factor α = 1/2. Arm 1 is a standard treatment with a known reward 1/4 at every play. Arm 2 is a new treatment in state u (untested). A play in state u gives reward 0 and reveals the quality: the arm moves to state G with probability 1/2 and to state B with probability 1/2. G and B are absorbing, with rewards 1 and 0 per play.
applications.hypotheses: Each arm is a Markov chain on a finite state space: {s} for arm 1 and {u, G, B} for arm 2. The rewards are bounded by 1, and α = 1/2 lies in (0, 1). The arms are independent, and arm 1 does not move when arm 2 is played.

steps.text: A state with a constant reward c from then on has index c, because every ratio in the definition equals c. So g_1(s) = 1/4, g_2(G) = 1 and g_2(B) = 0.

Index of u. The rule that plays u and then continues in G and stops in B earns (1/2) Σ_{t≥1} (1/2)^t = 1/2 discounted reward over a discounted time 1 + (1/2)·1 = 3/2. Its rate is 1/3. With a charge γ = 1/3, every rule has a profit at most −1/3 + (1/2)(2/3)·1 = 0, because in G each play earns 2/3 net and in B each play loses 1/3. So g_2(u) = 1/3.

The Gittins index policy plays arm 2 first, because 1/3 > 1/4. If the treatment is good, its index 1 stays above 1/4 and the policy uses it forever, which gives Σ_{t≥2} (1/2)^{t−1} = 1. If it is bad, its index 0 is below 1/4 and the policy uses arm 1 forever, which gives Σ_{t≥2} (1/2)^{t−1}/4 = 1/4. The value is (1/2)·1 + (1/2)·(1/4) = 5/8.

For comparison, the policy that always uses the standard treatment has value (1/4)/(1 − 1/2) = 1/2 < 5/8. If the standard reward were c > 1/3, the index of arm 1 would exceed g_2(u), and the theorem would say that never testing is optimal. Indeed 2c > 1/2 + c/2 exactly when c > 1/3.

applications.conclusion: The new treatment is worth testing exactly when the standard reward is below its Gittins index 1/3. With a standard reward of 1/4, the index policy tests first and has the optimal value 5/8.

limitations: The theorem needs geometric discounting and arms that do not move when they are not played. For a finite horizon, or for restless arms whose states change at every time, index policies are in general not optimal.

The theorem shows optimality but does not compute the index. For finite state spaces the index can be computed by solving the calibration problem of step s1 for each state, for example by the largest-remaining-index algorithm.
The authored statement assumes countable state spaces and bounded rewards. The source states the result for independent reward sequences with uniformly bounded first moments.

results.name: Shiryaev's optimal rule for Bayesian quickest detection
results.statement: Let 0 < ρ < 1 and let the change point Γ satisfy P(Γ = n) = ρ(1 − ρ)^{n−1} for n ≥ 1. Conditionally on Γ, let X₁, X₂, … be independent, with density f₀ for n < Γ and density f₁ for n ≥ Γ with respect to a common σ-finite measure, where 0 < D(f₁‖f₀) < ∞. For a stopping time τ of the observations let ADD(τ) = E(τ − Γ)⁺ and PFA(τ) = P(τ < Γ). Let p_n = P(Γ ≤ n | X₁, …, X_n), with p₀ = 0. Fix α ∈ (0, 1). If a threshold A_α ∈ (0, 1) can be chosen such that the Shiryaev stopping time τ_S = inf{n ≥ 1 : p_n ≥ A_α} satisfies PFA(τ_S) = α, then τ_S minimizes ADD(τ) over all stopping times τ with PFA(τ) ≤ α.
hypotheses: The change point Γ is geometric on {1, 2, …} with parameter ρ ∈ (0, 1).
Conditionally on Γ, the observations are independent with density f₀ before Γ and density f₁ from Γ on, and 0 < D(f₁‖f₀) < ∞.
The threshold A_α ∈ (0, 1) gives the Shiryaev stopping time a false alarm probability exactly α.
results.empty_prerequisites_reason: The outline cites the source for the Lagrange multiplier, the dynamic programming equation and the concavity of the value function. No catalog result is used as a separate step.

definitions.name: average detection delay
definitions.text: ADD(τ) = E(τ − Γ)⁺, the mean number of observations between the change and the alarm, counted as 0 for a false alarm.

definitions.name: probability of false alarm
definitions.text: PFA(τ) = P(τ < Γ), the probability that the alarm comes before the change.

definitions.name: Shiryaev statistic
definitions.text: The posterior probability p_n = P(Γ ≤ n | X₁, …, X_n) that the change has already happened at time n.

source.citation: Venugopal V. Veeravalli and Taposh Banerjee, Quickest Change Detection, arXiv:1210.5552 [math.ST], 2012.
source.revision: arXiv:1210.5552v1 (19 October 2012), 53 pages. The running header of the arXiv PDF shows its build date, November 27, 2024.
source.module: Section III Bayesian quickest change detection, Subsection A The Bayesian i.i.d. setting
source.excerpt: Theorem 3.1 ( [4], [5]): The optimal solution to Bayesian optimization problem of (10) is the Shiryaev algorithm/test, which is described by the stopping time: τS = inf {n ≥ 1 : pn ≥ Aα} (15) if Aα ∈ (0, 1) can be chosen such that PFA(τS) = α. (16)
source.attribution: © Venugopal V. Veeravalli and Taposh Banerjee. Quoted from the arXiv preprint for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: Theorem 3.1 on p. 11 states the optimality of the Shiryaev test for problem (10), which minimizes ADD over C_α = {τ : PFA(τ) ≤ α}, in the model (11) with a geometric change point and i.i.d. observations with densities f₀ and f₁. The authored statement writes the model and problem (10) out in full, and allows densities with respect to any common σ-finite measure, so that discrete observations are included. The source attributes the theorem to Shiryaev [4], [5] and gives a proof sketch on p. 12. The outline follows that sketch.

results.proof_status: outline of the cited published proof. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of Theorem 3.1 in Veeravalli and Banerjee (arXiv:1210.5552), pp. 11-12. Step s3 takes the existence of the Lagrange multiplier from Shiryaev [4], [5] as cited by the source, step s4 takes the dynamic programming equation from the source, and step s5 takes the concavity of the value function from the source.

steps.text: Posterior recursion. By Bayes' rule, p₀ = 0 and p_{n+1} = Φ(X_{n+1}, p_n) = p̃_nL(X_{n+1}) / (p̃_nL(X_{n+1}) + 1 − p̃_n), where p̃_n = p_n + (1 − p_n)ρ = P(Γ ≤ n + 1 | X₁, …, X_n) and L = f₁/f₀. This is (13)-(14) of the source. Given X₁, …, X_n, the next observation has density p̃_nf₁ + (1 − p̃_n)f₀, so (p_n) is a Markov chain for the observation filtration and is a sufficient statistic for the problem.

Costs in terms of the posterior. For a stopping time τ the event {n < τ} depends only on X₁, …, X_n. Since (τ − Γ)⁺ = Σ_{n≥0} 1{Γ ≤ n < τ}, the tower property gives ADD(τ) = E Σ_{n=0}^{τ−1} p_n. Similarly PFA(τ) = E[(1 − p_τ)1{τ < ∞}]. The source writes the same identities with the state Θ_n = 1{Γ ≤ n}: ADD(τ) = E Σ_{n<τ} 1{Θ_n = 1} and PFA(τ) = E 1{Θ_τ = 0}.

Lagrangian relaxation. For λ_f ≥ 0 the source considers J* = min_τ E[(τ − Γ)⁺ + λ_f 1{τ < Γ}], which is (17). If τ_λ solves (17) and PFA(τ_λ) = α, then every τ with PFA(τ) ≤ α satisfies ADD(τ) ≥ ADD(τ_λ) + λ_f(α − PFA(τ)) ≥ ADD(τ_λ), so τ_λ solves (10). The source cites Shiryaev [4], [5] for the fact that under (16) there is a λ_f for which the solution of (17) is the threshold rule with threshold A_α.

Bellman equation. With the posterior as state, (17) is an infinite-horizon dynamic programming problem with stopping cost λ_f(1 − p) and running cost p per step of continuation. The source states, with standard arguments [19], that its value J solves J(p) = min{λ_f(1 − p), p + A_J(p)} with A_J(p) = E[J(Φ(X, p))], where X has density p̃f₁ + (1 − p̃)f₀ and p̃ = p + (1 − p)ρ. This is (18), and the optimal rule stops exactly when λ_f(1 − p_n) ≤ p_n + A_J(p_n).

Concavity. The source states that an induction argument shows that J and A_J are nonnegative concave functions on [0, 1] with J(1) = A_J(1) = 0. The induction step works because p̃ is affine in p and, for concave J, the map q ↦ ∫ (qf₁ + (1 − q)f₀)(x) J(qf₁(x)/(qf₁(x) + (1 − q)f₀(x))) dx is a perspective of J and so is concave in q.

Threshold structure. The difference Δ(p) = p + A_J(p) − λ_f(1 − p) is concave and Δ(1) = 1 > 0. So the stopping set {p : Δ(p) ≥ 0} is an interval [A, 1], and the optimal rule for (17) is τ_S = inf{n ≥ 1 : p_n ≥ A}. For the multiplier of step s3 the threshold is A_α with PFA(τ_S) = α, and step s3 shows that τ_S minimizes ADD over all τ with PFA(τ) ≤ α.

source.ref: V. V. Veeravalli and T. Banerjee, Quickest Change Detection, arXiv:1210.5552, Theorem 3.1 and its proof, pp. 11-12.

applications.title: Detecting a fault on a production line from defect indicators
applications.inputs: Each item is defective with probability 1/4 before a fault and 3/4 after it, so f₀(1) = 1/4, f₀(0) = 3/4, f₁(1) = 3/4 and f₁(0) = 1/4 for the defect indicator X_n. The fault time Γ is geometric with ρ = 1/10. The monitor uses the Shiryaev rule with threshold A = 4/5, and the first three items are defective.
applications.hypotheses: Γ is geometric with ρ = 1/10. Given Γ, the indicators are independent with law f₀ before Γ and f₁ from Γ on, and D(f₁‖f₀) = (1/2) log 3 lies in (0, ∞). The false alarm level α is the value PFA(τ_S) of this rule, so the threshold A = 4/5 satisfies the hypothesis of the theorem.

steps.text: The likelihood ratios are L(1) = (3/4)/(1/4) = 3 and L(0) = 1/3. After the first defect, p̃₀ = 1/10 and p₁ = (1/10 · 3)/(1/10 · 3 + 9/10) = 1/4.
After the second defect, p̃₁ = 1/4 + (3/4)(1/10) = 13/40 and p₂ = (13/40 · 3)/(13/40 · 3 + 27/40) = 13/22, which is about 0.59 and below 4/5.
After the third defect, p̃₂ = 13/22 + (9/22)(1/10) = 139/220 and p₃ = (139/220 · 3)/(139/220 · 3 + 81/220) = 139/166, which is about 0.84. Since p₃ ≥ 4/5, the rule raises the alarm at n = 3.
At the alarm p_τ ≥ A, so PFA(τ_S) = E[1 − p_τ] ≤ 1 − 4/5 = 1/5. By the theorem, no monitoring rule with a false alarm probability at most α = PFA(τ_S) has a smaller mean detection delay.

applications.conclusion: The Shiryaev rule raises the alarm after three defective items in a row, when the posterior probability of a fault is 139/166. Its false alarm probability is at most 1/5, and it has the smallest mean delay among all rules with the same false alarm level.

limitations: The exact optimality needs the geometric prior and i.i.d. observations before and after the change. For non-i.i.d. models the Shiryaev rule is only asymptotically optimal as α → 0.
The theorem assumes that some threshold attains the false alarm level exactly. With discrete observations p_n takes discrete values, and an exact level may need a randomized rule.

The theorem does not give A_α in closed form. The choice A = 1 − α guarantees PFA(τ_S) ≤ α. If also 0 < D(f₀‖f₁) < ∞, the source shows in (35) that ADD(τ_S) ~ |log α|/(D(f₁‖f₀) + |log(1 − ρ)|) as α → 0.

results.name: Wald's equation and Wald's second identity
results.statement: Let X₁, X₂, … be independent and identically distributed random variables with E|X₁| < ∞ and mean μ = E X₁. Let (F_n)_{n≥0} be a filtration such that, for every n ≥ 1, X_n is F_n-measurable and independent of F_{n−1}. Set S₀ = 0 and S_n = X₁ + ⋯ + X_n. Let N be a stopping time for (F_n) with values in {0, 1, 2, …} and E N < ∞. Then (a) S_N is integrable and E S_N = μ E N (Wald's equation). (b) If also σ² = Var X₁ < ∞, then E(S_N − μN)² = σ² E N (Wald's second identity). In particular, E S_N² = σ² E N when μ = 0.
hypotheses: The random variables X₁, X₂, … are independent and identically distributed, with E|X₁| < ∞ and μ = E X₁.
For every n ≥ 1, X_n is F_n-measurable and independent of F_{n−1}.
N is a stopping time for (F_n) with values in {0, 1, 2, …} and E N < ∞.
For part (b) only: σ² = Var X₁ is finite.

prerequisites.reason: Steps s2 and s3 use Tonelli's theorem to take the expectation of a series of nonnegative terms term by term, and step s1 uses it for the tail sum formula E N = Σ P(N ≥ m).
Step s3 uses Fubini's theorem for the absolutely convergent series Σ X_m 1{N ≥ m} to take its expectation term by term.
Step s5 applies Fatou's lemma to the squared differences T_N − T_{N∧n} to show that T_{N∧n} converges to T_N in L².
Step s5 uses the monotone convergence theorem to show that E(N∧n) increases to E N.
Step s5 uses Minkowski's inequality in L² to pass from L² convergence of T_{N∧n} to convergence of the second moments.

concepts: independent and identically distributed random variables

definitions.name: stopping time
definitions.text: A random variable N with values in {0, 1, 2, …, ∞} such that the event {N = n} is in F_n for every n. The decision to stop at time n uses only the information available at time n.

definitions.name: filtration
definitions.text: An increasing sequence F₀ ⊂ F₁ ⊂ F₂ ⊂ ⋯ of σ-algebras. F_n holds the information that is available at time n.

source.citation: Thomas S. Ferguson, Optimal Stopping and Applications, online book, Mathematics Department, University of California, Los Angeles.
source.revision: Author's online version, Chapter 3 file sr3.pdf (PDF created 2008-07-20), 13 pages.
source.module: Chapter 3 The existence of optimal stopping rules, Section 3.3 The Wald Equation
source.excerpt: Theorem 4. Let X1, X2, . . . be a sequence of independent identically distributed random variables such that E|X1| < ∞, let µ = EX1, and let Sn = X1 + · · · + Xn. Let N be any stopping rule, adapted to X1, X2, . . . . Then, if EN < ∞, E(SN) = µE(N).
source.attribution: © Thomas S. Ferguson. Quoted from the author's online book Optimal Stopping and Applications for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states Wald's equation for stopping rules adapted to X₁, X₂, …. The authored statement allows any filtration for which X_n is independent of F_{n−1}, and it adds the second identity, which Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples (5th ed.), states as Exercise 4.8.4. Part (a) follows Proof #1 of the source, which exchanges two summations. Part (b) is authored with the same series, a direct L² computation and Fatou's lemma.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows Proof #1 of the cited source for part (a). No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Both parts of the statement, for every filtration with the stated independence property.

steps.text: Because N is a stopping time, {N ≥ m} = {N ≤ m − 1}ᶜ is in F_{m−1} for every m ≥ 1. By hypothesis X_m is independent of F_{m−1}, so X_m is independent of the event {N ≥ m}. The tail sum formula, which is Tonelli's theorem for the double sum Σ_m Σ_{k≥m} P(N = k), gives Σ_{m≥1} P(N ≥ m) = E N < ∞. In particular N < ∞ almost surely, and S_N = Σ_{m≥1} X_m 1{N ≥ m} pointwise, because only the terms with m ≤ N are nonzero.

Integrability. The terms |X_m| 1{N ≥ m} are nonnegative, so Tonelli's theorem gives E Σ_m |X_m| 1{N ≥ m} = Σ_m E|X_m| P(N ≥ m) = E|X₁| E N < ∞. Here the independence of step s1 splits each expectation into a product. Hence |S_N| ≤ Σ_m |X_m| 1{N ≥ m} is integrable.

Part (a). Step s2 shows that the series Σ_m X_m 1{N ≥ m} converges absolutely in L¹. Fubini's theorem therefore gives E S_N = Σ_m E[X_m 1{N ≥ m}]. Independence of X_m and {N ≥ m} gives E[X_m 1{N ≥ m}] = μ P(N ≥ m). Summation and step s1 give E S_N = μ Σ_m P(N ≥ m) = μ E N.

Part (b), stopped sums. Set Y_m = X_m − μ and T_n = S_n − nμ, so that E Y_m = 0 and E Y_m² = σ². For 0 ≤ k < n, T_{N∧n} − T_{N∧k} = Σ_{m=k+1}^{n} Y_m 1{N ≥ m}. Square and take expectations. For k < i < j ≤ n, the product Y_i 1{N ≥ i} 1{N ≥ j} = Y_i 1{N ≥ j} is F_{j−1}-measurable and square integrable, and Y_j is independent of F_{j−1} with mean 0. So every cross term E[Y_i Y_j 1{N ≥ j}] is 0. Each diagonal term is E[Y_m² 1{N ≥ m}] = σ² P(N ≥ m). Hence E(T_{N∧n} − T_{N∧k})² = σ² Σ_{m=k+1}^{n} P(N ≥ m) = σ² E(N∧n − N∧k). With k = 0 this gives E T_{N∧n}² = σ² E(N∧n).

Part (b), limit. Since N < ∞ almost surely, T_{N∧k} → T_N almost surely as k → ∞. Fatou's lemma and step s4 give E(T_N − T_{N∧n})² ≤ liminf_k E(T_{N∧k} − T_{N∧n})² = σ² Σ_{m>n} P(N ≥ m). The right side tends to 0 because Σ_m P(N ≥ m) = E N < ∞. So T_{N∧n} → T_N in L², and Minkowski's inequality gives E T_{N∧n}² → E T_N². Monotone convergence gives E(N∧n) ↑ E N. Step s4 then gives E(S_N − μN)² = E T_N² = σ² E N. For μ = 0 this reads E S_N² = σ² E N.

applications.title: Ruin probability and mean duration of a fair betting game
applications.inputs: A trader makes independent fair bets of one unit: each X_i is +1 or −1 with probability 1/2. The trader starts at S₀ = 0, stops at a loss limit of 3 units or at a profit target of 7 units, and N = min{n : S_n = −3 or S_n = 7}.
applications.hypotheses: The X_i are i.i.d. with μ = 0 and σ² = 1, and N is a stopping time for F_n = σ(X₁, …, X_n). From any position in (−3, 7), ten up-steps in a row end the game, so P(N > 10k) ≤ (1 − 2^(−10))^k. Hence E N = Σ_j P(N > j) ≤ 10 Σ_k (1 − 2^(−10))^k < ∞.

steps.text: Wald's equation with μ = 0 gives E S_N = 0. Since S_N is −3 or 7, write p = P(S_N = 7). Then −3(1 − p) + 7p = 0, so p = 3/10 and the probability of ruin is 7/10.
Wald's second identity with μ = 0 and σ² = 1 gives E N = E S_N². The second moment is 3² · (7/10) + 7² · (3/10).
So the mean number of bets is E N = 21 = 3 · 7. The same two identities give P(S_N = b) = a/(a + b) and E N = ab for a loss limit a and a profit target b.

applications.conclusion: The trader reaches the profit target with probability 3/10 and the game lasts 21 bets on average.

limitations: The condition E N < ∞ is necessary in general. For the simple symmetric walk and N = min{n : S_n = 1}, N is finite almost surely but E S_N = 1 ≠ 0 = μ E N.
Without identical distribution, part (a) needs extra conditions on the X_i, for example a uniform bound on E(|X_m| | F_{m−1}).

results.name: Kolmogorov–Chentsov continuity theorem
results.statement: Let (X_t)_{t∈[0,1]} be a stochastic process with values in ℝ^d, and let |·| be the Euclidean norm. Suppose that there are constants α > 0, β > 0 and K < ∞ such that E|X_t − X_s|^β ≤ K|t − s|^{1+α} for all s, t ∈ [0, 1]. Then X has a modification Y, that is a process with P(Y_t = X_t) = 1 for every t ∈ [0, 1], such that every path t ↦ Y_t is continuous and, for every γ ∈ (0, α/β), almost surely there is a finite random constant C with |Y_t − Y_s| ≤ C|t − s|^γ for all s, t ∈ [0, 1].
hypotheses: X = (X_t)_{t∈[0,1]} is a stochastic process with values in ℝ^d.
There are constants α > 0, β > 0 and K < ∞ with E|X_t − X_s|^β ≤ K|t − s|^{1+α} for all s, t ∈ [0, 1].

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 uses Markov's inequality for |X_t − X_s|^β to bound the probability of one large dyadic increment, and step s5 uses it to prove convergence in probability.
Step s1 applies the Borel–Cantelli lemma to the summable probabilities P(G_nᶜ), so almost surely all dyadic levels from some N(ω) on are good.

definitions.name: modification
definitions.text: A process Y is a modification of X if P(Y_t = X_t) = 1 for every t. The null set may depend on t, so a modification can have different path properties.

definitions.name: Hölder continuity
definitions.text: A function f on [0, 1] is Hölder continuous with exponent γ ∈ (0, 1] if |f(t) − f(s)| ≤ C|t − s|^γ for some constant C and all s, t.

source.citation: Andreas Eberle, Stochastic Analysis, lecture notes, University of Bonn, Winter Semester 2012/2013.
source.revision: Version of January 28, 2013, 229 pages.
source.module: Section 3.2 Stochastic flow and Markov property
source.excerpt: … then there exists a modification (ξu)u∈C of (Xu)u∈C such that E[sup_{u≠v} (||ξu − ξv||/|u − v|^α)^γ] < ∞ for any α ∈ [0, ε/γ). In particular, u ↦ ξu is almost surely α-Hölder continuous for any α < ε/γ.
source.attribution: © Andreas Eberle. Quoted from the author's lecture notes for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: Theorem 3.7 (Kolmogorov, Čentsov) on p. 127 treats a random field indexed by a product of n real intervals with values in a Banach space. Under E||X_u − X_v||^γ ≤ c|u − v|^{n+ε} it gives a modification with a finite moment of the Hölder norm of every exponent α < ε/γ. The authored statement is the case n = 1 with values in ℝ^d, with the source's (γ, ε, α) renamed (β, α, γ), and it keeps the almost sure Hölder continuity. The source gives no proof and cites Revuz and Yor. The authored proof follows the dyadic proof of Theorem 7.1.3 and Lemma 7.1.4 in Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th edition, pp. 357-358.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the dyadic chaining proof of Theorem 7.1.3 in Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The whole statement: existence of a continuous modification that is almost surely γ-Hölder for every γ < α/β, for an ℝ^d-valued process indexed by [0, 1].

steps.text: Good dyadic levels. Let D_n = {k2^{−n} : 0 ≤ k ≤ 2ⁿ} and D = ∪_n D_n. Fix γ ∈ (0, α/β) and let G_n be the event that |X(k2^{−n}) − X((k − 1)2^{−n})| ≤ 2^{−γn} for all 1 ≤ k ≤ 2ⁿ. Markov's inequality gives P(|X(k2^{−n}) − X((k − 1)2^{−n})| > 2^{−γn}) ≤ 2^{γβn} K 2^{−n(1+α)}. The union bound over the 2ⁿ values of k gives P(G_nᶜ) ≤ K 2^{−n(α−γβ)}, which is summable because α − γβ > 0. By the Borel–Cantelli lemma, the event Ω_γ = ∪_N ∩_{n≥N} G_n has probability 1. On Ω_γ let N(ω) be the least N with G_n for all n ≥ N.

Chaining for close dyadic points. Fix ω ∈ Ω_γ and q < r in D with r − q < 2^{−N}. Choose m ≥ N with 2^{−(m+1)} ≤ r − q < 2^{−m}. For n ≥ m let r_n = ⌊2ⁿr⌋2^{−n} and q_n = ⌈2ⁿq⌉2^{−n}. Then r_{n+1} − r_n and q_n − q_{n+1} are 0 or 2^{−(n+1)}, and r_n = r, q_n = q for large n. Since n + 1 > N, |X(r_{n+1}) − X(r_n)| ≤ 2^{−γ(n+1)}, so |X(r) − X(r_m)| ≤ Σ_{n>m} 2^{−γn} = 2^{−γ(m+1)}/(1 − 2^{−γ}), and the same bound holds for |X(q) − X(q_m)|. Also r_m ≤ r < q + 2^{−m} ≤ q_m + 2^{−m} and q_m − r_m < (q + 2^{−m}) − (r − 2^{−m}) < 2 · 2^{−m}. Both points lie in D_m, so q_m − r_m is 0 or 2^{−m}, and |X(q_m) − X(r_m)| ≤ 2^{−γm}. With 2^{−(m+1)} ≤ r − q this gives |X(r) − X(q)| ≤ C_γ(r − q)^γ, where C_γ = 2^γ + 2/(1 − 2^{−γ}).

All dyadic points. Let q < r in D with r − q ≥ 2^{−N}. The points of D_{N+1} in the open interval (q, r), together with q and r, cut [q, r] into at most 2^{N+1} pieces with dyadic end points and lengths in (0, 2^{−(N+1)}]. Step s2 bounds the increment over each piece by C_γ 2^{−γ(N+1)} ≤ C_γ(r − q)^γ. The triangle inequality gives |X(r) − X(q)| ≤ 2^{N+1}C_γ(r − q)^γ. With step s2, |X(r) − X(q)| ≤ C(ω)|r − q|^γ for all q, r ∈ D, where C(ω) = 2^{N(ω)+1}C_γ < ∞.

Extension. Choose γ_j ↑ α/β and let Ω* = ∩_j Ω_{γ_j}, an event of probability 1. On Ω* the map q ↦ X_q on the dense set D is uniformly continuous by step s3. So for each t ∈ [0, 1] and each sequence q_k → t in D, (X_{q_k}) is a Cauchy sequence in ℝ^d, and its limit does not depend on the sequence. Define Y_t as this limit on Ω* and Y_t = 0 off Ω*. Then Y_t is a random variable, Y = X on D for ω ∈ Ω*, and the limit of the bound of step s3 gives |Y_t − Y_s| ≤ C_j(ω)|t − s|^{γ_j} for all s, t and j. For γ < α/β choose γ_j ≥ γ. Since |t − s| ≤ 1, |Y_t − Y_s| ≤ C_j(ω)|t − s|^γ. Every path of Y is continuous.

Modification. Fix t ∈ [0, 1] and q_k → t in D. For η > 0, Markov's inequality gives P(|X_{q_k} − X_t| > η) ≤ η^{−β}K|q_k − t|^{1+α} → 0, so X_{q_k} → X_t in probability. Also X_{q_k} → Y_t on Ω*, so almost surely and therefore in probability. Limits in probability are almost surely equal, so P(Y_t = X_t) = 1. Hence Y is a modification of X with all the properties of the statement.

applications.title: Hölder paths of fractional Brownian motion in anomalous diffusion
applications.inputs: A tracer in a crowded medium is modelled by fractional Brownian motion X with Hurst index H = 3/4 on [0, 1]: a centred Gaussian process with E X_sX_t = (s^{2H} + t^{2H} − |t − s|^{2H})/2. Its mean square displacement E X_t² = t^{3/2} grows faster than linearly, so the motion is superdiffusive.
applications.hypotheses: X is a real stochastic process. The moment bound follows from the Gaussian law of the increments with the constants of steps a2 and a3.

steps.text: The increment X_t − X_s is centred Gaussian with variance t^{2H} + s^{2H} − 2 · (s^{2H} + t^{2H} − |t − s|^{2H})/2 = |t − s|^{2H}. So X_t − X_s has the law of |t − s|^H Z with Z ~ N(0, 1).
For β = 8 the Gaussian moment is E Z⁸ = 7 · 5 · 3 · 1 = 105. Hence E|X_t − X_s|⁸ = 105|t − s|^{8H} = 105|t − s|⁶.
The theorem applies with β = 8, K = 105 and 1 + α = 8H = 6, so α = 5. It gives a continuous modification that is almost surely γ-Hölder for every γ < α/β = (8 · 3/4 − 1)/8 = 5/8.

For β = 2p the same computation gives α/β = H − 1/(2p), which tends to H = 3/4 as p → ∞. Two continuous modifications agree almost surely on the countable set D, hence on [0, 1]. So one continuous version of X is almost surely γ-Hölder for every γ < 3/4.

applications.conclusion: The superdiffusive tracer with H = 3/4 has continuous paths that are almost surely Hölder continuous with every exponent γ < 3/4, which is rougher than a smooth path and smoother than a Brownian path.

limitations: The exponent 1 + α > 1 in the moment bound is necessary. A Poisson process N with rate λ satisfies E|N_t − N_s| = λ|t − s|, but it has no continuous modification, because a continuous integer-valued path is constant.

The theorem gives the Hölder exponents γ < α/β only. For Brownian motion the bound γ < 1/2 is sharp: almost surely the paths are not Hölder continuous with exponent 1/2, by Lévy's modulus of continuity.
On [0, ∞) the theorem applies on each interval [k, k + 1]. For a random field indexed by a box in ℝⁿ the exponent 1 + α becomes n + α, as in the cited source.

results.name: Law of the iterated logarithm for Brownian motion
aliases: Khinchin's law of the iterated logarithm for Brownian motion
results.statement: Let (B(t))_{t≥0} be a standard linear Brownian motion: B(0) = 0, the paths t ↦ B(t) are continuous, and for 0 ≤ t₀ < t₁ < … < t_k the increments B(t_i) − B(t_{i−1}) are independent with B(t_i) − B(t_{i−1}) ~ N(0, t_i − t_{i−1}). Let ψ(t) = √(2t log log t) for t > e. Then almost surely lim sup_{t→∞} B(t)/ψ(t) = 1 and lim inf_{t→∞} B(t)/ψ(t) = −1.
hypotheses: B is a standard linear Brownian motion: B(0) = 0, the paths are continuous, and the increments over disjoint time intervals are independent and centred normal with variance equal to the length of the interval.

prerequisites.reason: Step s2 uses the reflection principle P(max_{0≤s≤t} B(s) ≥ a) = P(|B(t)| ≥ a) to compute the probability of the event A_n.
Step s2 applies the Borel–Cantelli lemma to the summable probabilities P(A_n), so only finitely many A_n occur.
Step s4 applies the second Borel–Cantelli lemma to the independent events D_n with Σ P(D_n) = ∞, so infinitely many D_n occur.

definitions.name: envelope function ψ
definitions.text: ψ(t) = √(2t log log t) for t > e. It is increasing on (e, ∞), and ψ(t)/√t = √(2 log log t) tends to ∞ very slowly.

source.citation: Peter Mörters and Yuval Peres, Brownian Motion, Cambridge Series in Statistical and Probabilistic Mathematics 30, Cambridge University Press, 2010.
source.revision: Authors' version of the book (PDF created 2010-01-06), posted on the first author's home page.
source.module: Chapter 5, Section 5.1 The law of the iterated logarithm
source.excerpt: Theorem 5.1 (Law of the Iterated Logarithm for Brownian motion) Suppose {B(t) : t ⩾ 0} is a standard linear Brownian motion. Then, almost surely, lim sup_{t→∞} B(t)/√(2t log log(t)) = 1.
source.attribution: © Peter Mörters and Yuval Peres. Quoted from the authors' version of Brownian Motion for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states the lim sup and gives the lim inf in Remark 5.2. The authored statement contains both. The authored proof follows the proof of Theorem 5.1 on pp. 119-120: the upper bound along a geometric sequence with the reflection principle and the Borel–Cantelli lemma, and the lower bound with independent increments and the second Borel–Cantelli lemma. The source cites Lemma 12.9 for the Gaussian tail bounds. Step s1 proves them.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the proof of Theorem 5.1 in Mörters and Peres. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The lim sup and the lim inf of the statement, for a standard linear Brownian motion as t → ∞.

steps.text: Gaussian tails. Let Z ~ N(0, 1) with density φ(u) = e^{−u²/2}/√(2π). For x > 0, P(Z > x) = ∫_x^∞ φ(u) du ≤ ∫_x^∞ (u/x) φ(u) du = φ(x)/x. The function −φ(u)/u has derivative (1 + u^{−2})φ(u), so φ(x)/x = ∫_x^∞ (1 + u^{−2})φ(u) du ≤ (1 + x^{−2}) P(Z > x). Hence P(Z > x) ≥ xφ(x)/(1 + x²). For x ≥ 1 this gives φ(x)/(2x) ≤ P(Z > x) ≤ e^{−x²/2}. Also ψ is increasing on (e, ∞), because t log log t has derivative log log t + 1/log t > 0 there.

Upper bound along a geometric sequence. Fix ε > 0 and q > 1, and let A_n = {max_{0≤s≤qⁿ} B(s) ≥ (1 + ε)ψ(qⁿ)}. By the reflection principle, P(A_n) = P(|B(qⁿ)| ≥ (1 + ε)ψ(qⁿ)) = 2P(Z ≥ x_n), where x_n = (1 + ε)ψ(qⁿ)/√(qⁿ) = (1 + ε)√(2 log(n log q)). For large n, x_n ≥ 1, and step s1 gives P(A_n) ≤ 2e^{−x_n²/2} = 2(n log q)^{−(1+ε)²}. This is summable because (1 + ε)² > 1. By the Borel–Cantelli lemma, almost surely A_n occurs for only finitely many n.

Interpolation. Take ω outside A_n for all n ≥ n₀, with q^{n₀−1} > e. For t ≥ q^{n₀}, choose n > n₀ with q^{n−1} ≤ t < qⁿ. Then B(t) ≤ max_{s≤qⁿ} B(s) < (1 + ε)ψ(qⁿ). Since ψ is increasing, B(t)/ψ(t) < (1 + ε)ψ(qⁿ)/ψ(q^{n−1}) when B(t) ≥ 0, and this bound also holds when B(t) < 0. Now ψ(qⁿ)/ψ(q^{n−1}) = √q · √(log(n log q)/log((n − 1) log q)) → √q. So lim sup_{t→∞} B(t)/ψ(t) ≤ (1 + ε)√q almost surely. The choice ε = 1/k and q = 1 + 1/k for k = 1, 2, … excludes countably many null sets and gives lim sup B(t)/ψ(t) ≤ 1 almost surely.

Independent large increments. Fix an integer q ≥ 2 and let D_n = {B(qⁿ) − B(q^{n−1}) ≥ ψ(qⁿ − q^{n−1})}. The intervals (q^{n−1}, qⁿ] are disjoint, so the events D_n are independent. With y_n = √(2 log log(qⁿ − q^{n−1})), P(D_n) = P(Z ≥ y_n), and φ(y_n) = 1/(√(2π) log(qⁿ − q^{n−1})) ≥ 1/(√(2π) n log q). For large n, 1 ≤ y_n ≤ √(2 log(n log q)) ≤ 2√(log n), so step s1 gives P(D_n) ≥ φ(y_n)/(2y_n) ≥ c/(n√(log n)) with c = 1/(4√(2π) log q). The series Σ 1/(n√(log n)) diverges, by comparison with ∫ dx/(x√(log x)) = 2√(log x). By the second Borel–Cantelli lemma, almost surely D_n occurs for infinitely many n.

Lower bound. The process −B is also a standard Brownian motion, so step s3 applied to −B gives, almost surely, −B(t) ≤ 2ψ(t) for all large t. So almost surely, for infinitely many n, B(qⁿ) = B(q^{n−1}) + (B(qⁿ) − B(q^{n−1})) ≥ −2ψ(q^{n−1}) + ψ(qⁿ − q^{n−1}). Divide by ψ(qⁿ). Since log log q^{n−1} ≤ log log qⁿ, ψ(q^{n−1})/ψ(qⁿ) ≤ 1/√q. Also ψ(qⁿ − q^{n−1})/ψ(qⁿ) = √(1 − 1/q) · √(log log(qⁿ(1 − 1/q))/log log qⁿ) → √(1 − 1/q). Hence lim sup_{t→∞} B(t)/ψ(t) ≥ √(1 − 1/q) − 2/√q almost surely. Let q → ∞ through the integers to get lim sup B(t)/ψ(t) ≥ 1 almost surely.

Conclusion. Steps s3 and s5 give lim sup_{t→∞} B(t)/ψ(t) = 1 almost surely. The same result for the standard Brownian motion −B gives lim inf_{t→∞} B(t)/ψ(t) = −lim sup_{t→∞} (−B(t))/ψ(t) = −1 almost surely.

applications.title: Continuous monitoring of a z-test rejects a true null hypothesis
applications.inputs: Under a null hypothesis, a cumulative score S(t) is a standard Brownian motion, for example the continuous limit of a sum of centred observations with unit variance. An analyst computes the z-statistic Z(t) = S(t)/√t at every time t ≥ 1 and rejects the null hypothesis as soon as Z(t) ≥ 3. A test at one fixed time has level P(N(0, 1) ≥ 3), which is about 0.00135.
applications.hypotheses: Under the null hypothesis, S is a standard linear Brownian motion. This is the only hypothesis of the theorem.

steps.text: Fix ε = 1/4. The theorem gives lim sup S(t)/ψ(t) = 1 almost surely. So almost surely S(t) ≥ (3/4)ψ(t) = (3/4)√(2t log log t) at arbitrarily large times t.
At such a time, Z(t) = S(t)/√t ≥ (3/4)√(2 log log t). This is at least 3 when 2 log log t ≥ 9/(3/4)², that is when log log t ≥ 9/(2 · (3/4)²) = 8.

Hence almost surely there is a time t with log log t ≥ 8 and Z(t) ≥ 3. The analyst rejects the true null hypothesis with probability 1, although each fixed-time test has level about 0.00135. The time is very large (t ≥ e^{e⁸}), so in practice the effect builds up slowly.

The same argument works for every threshold c, because √(2 log log t) → ∞. By the upper bound of the theorem, a boundary (1 + ε)ψ(t) with ε > 0 is exceeded only up to a finite random time. So a boundary for continuous monitoring must grow at least at the rate ψ(t).

applications.conclusion: A fixed-level z-test that is repeated at all times rejects a true null hypothesis with probability 1. This is sampling to a foregone conclusion. The iterated logarithm gives the critical growth rate of a valid monitoring boundary.

limitations: The theorem concerns t → ∞. The local law lim sup_{t↓0} B(t)/√(2t log log(1/t)) = 1 follows by time inversion t B(1/t), which this record does not prove.
The integral test of Kolmogorov, Petrovsky and Erdős refines the theorem: it decides for each increasing function h whether B(t) ≥ √t h(t) at arbitrarily large times.

The law of the iterated logarithm of Hartman and Wintner for sums of independent identically distributed variables with finite variance needs an extra argument, for example Skorokhod embedding, which is not part of this record.

results.name: Itô's formula
results.statement: Let X = (X¹, …, X^d) be a d-dimensional process whose components are continuous semimartingales, and let F: ℝ^d → ℝ be twice continuously differentiable. Then almost surely, for all t ≥ 0, F(X_t) = F(X₀) + Σ_{i=1}^d ∫₀^t ∂_i F(X_s) dX^i_s + ½ Σ_{i,j=1}^d ∫₀^t ∂_i ∂_j F(X_s) d⟨X^i, X^j⟩_s. In particular, F(X) is a continuous semimartingale.
hypotheses: Each component X^i is a continuous semimartingale, that is, X^i = M^i + A^i with a continuous local martingale M^i and a continuous adapted process A^i of finite variation.
F is twice continuously differentiable on ℝ^d.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 expands each increment F(X_{t_{k+1}}) − F(X_{t_k}) with Taylor's theorem and the integral form of the remainder.
Step s2 uses the Itô isometry to show that left-point Riemann sums of a continuous integrand converge to the stochastic integral.
Step s2 passes to the limit in E ∫ (Hⁿ − H)² d⟨M⟩ with the dominated convergence theorem.
Steps s2 and s3 use the Heine–Cantor theorem: continuous functions on [0, t] and on compact subsets of ℝ^d are uniformly continuous.
Step s3 uses Slutsky's theorem: a product of a sequence that tends to 0 and a sequence that converges in probability tends to 0 in probability.
Step s4 writes products of increments as differences of squares with the polarization identity.
Step s4 extracts almost surely convergent subsequences from sequences that converge in probability with the Borel–Cantelli lemma.
Step s4 uses the Helly–Bray theorem: convergence of distribution functions on a dense set gives convergence of integrals of continuous functions.

definitions.name: continuous semimartingale
definitions.text: A process X = M + A, where M is a continuous local martingale and A is a continuous adapted process whose paths have finite variation on bounded intervals. The integral ∫ H dX is ∫ H dM + ∫ H dA.

definitions.name: quadratic covariation ⟨X^i, X^j⟩
definitions.text: The bracket of the local martingale parts of X^i and X^j. It is continuous, of finite variation, and for every t it is the limit in probability of Σ_k (X^i_{t_{k+1}} − X^i_{t_k})(X^j_{t_{k+1}} − X^j_{t_k}) over partitions of [0, t] whose mesh tends to 0.

definitions.name: stochastic integral of a continuous integrand
definitions.text: For a continuous adapted H and a continuous local martingale M, H·M is defined by stopping at times T_p that make M^{T_p} bounded in L² and H bounded, and by the Itô isometry on each stopped interval.

source.citation: Russell Lyons, Stochastic Calculus: lecture notes based on the book Brownian Motion, Martingales, and Stochastic Calculus by J.-F. Le Gall (Springer, 2016), Indiana University.

source.module: Chapter 5, Section 5.2 Itô's Formula
source.excerpt: Theorem 5.10 (Itô's Formula). Let X be a continuous semimartingale and F ∈ C²(ℝ) (i.e., twice continuously differentiable). Then ∀t ⩾ 0 F(X_t) = F(X_0) + ∫₀^t F′(X_s) dX_s + ½ ∫₀^t F″(X_s) d⟨X, X⟩_s.
source.attribution: © Russell Lyons. Quoted from the author's lecture notes for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The excerpt is the one-dimensional statement. The authored statement is the d-dimensional form that the source gives right after it on p. 69. The authored proof follows the proof of Theorem 5.10 on pp. 69-70: a Taylor expansion along a partition, left-point Riemann sums (Proposition 5.9), and weak convergence of the measures of squared increments along a subsequence (Lemma 5B). It writes the remainder in integral form and proves the Riemann sum step with the isometry.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the proof of Theorem 5.10 in the cited notes. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement in dimension d, for all t ≥ 0 simultaneously.

steps.text: Taylor expansion along a partition. Fix t > 0 and partitions 0 = t₀ⁿ < … < t_{pₙ}ⁿ = t with mesh tending to 0. Write ΔX_k = X_{t_{k+1}} − X_{t_k}. Taylor's theorem with integral remainder gives F(y) − F(x) = ∇F(x)·(y − x) + (y − x)ᵀ R(x, y)(y − x), where R(x, y) = ∫₀^1 (1 − u) ∇²F(x + u(y − x)) du is continuous and R(x, x) = ½∇²F(x). Telescoping over k gives F(X_t) − F(X₀) = S¹ₙ + S²ₙ, with S¹ₙ = Σ_k ∇F(X_{t_k})·ΔX_k and S²ₙ = Σ_k ΔX_kᵀ R(X_{t_k}, X_{t_{k+1}}) ΔX_k.

First-order sum. Let H be continuous and adapted, and X = M + A one component. The Riemann sum Σ_k H_{t_k} ΔX_k equals ∫₀^t Hⁿ dX for the step process Hⁿ = Σ_k H_{t_k} 1_(t_k, t_{k+1}]. Let T_p be the first time that |H| + |M| + ⟨M⟩ + (variation of A) reaches p, so T_p → ∞. On [0, t ∧ T_p], Hⁿ − H is bounded by 2p and tends to 0 uniformly, because the path of H is uniformly continuous on [0, t] by Heine–Cantor. The stopped martingale M^{T_p} is bounded in L², and the isometry gives E[(∫₀^{t∧T_p} (Hⁿ − H) dM)²] = E ∫₀^{t∧T_p} (Hⁿ − H)² d⟨M⟩ → 0 by dominated convergence. Also |∫₀^t (Hⁿ − H) dA| ≤ sup_{s≤t} |Hⁿ_s − H_s| · (variation of A on [0, t]) → 0. Since P(T_p < t) → 0, the sum converges in probability to ∫₀^t H dX. With H = ∂_i F(X), S¹ₙ → Σ_i ∫₀^t ∂_i F(X_s) dX^i_s in probability.

Freezing the remainder. The path X([0, t]) lies in a compact ball K(ω), and so do all segments between X_{t_k} and X_{t_{k+1}}. By Heine–Cantor, ∇²F is uniformly continuous on K(ω) and the path is uniformly continuous on [0, t], so max_k |ΔX_k| → 0 and εₙ = max_k ‖R(X_{t_k}, X_{t_{k+1}}) − ½∇²F(X_{t_k})‖ → 0 almost surely. The difference between S²ₙ and Qₙ = ½ Σ_k ΔX_kᵀ ∇²F(X_{t_k}) ΔX_k is at most εₙ Σ_k |ΔX_k|². The sum Σ_k |ΔX_k|² converges in probability to Σ_i ⟨X^i, X^i⟩_t by the definition of the bracket. Slutsky's theorem gives S²ₙ − Qₙ → 0 in probability.

Second-order sum. Fix i, j and let μₙ = Σ_k ΔX^i_k ΔX^j_k δ_{t_k}. Polarization gives μₙ = ¼(ν⁺ₙ − ν⁻ₙ) with the nonnegative measures ν^±ₙ = Σ_k (Δ(X^i ± X^j)_k)² δ_{t_k}. For each r ∈ [0, t], ν^±ₙ([0, r]) differs from the quadratic sum of X^i ± X^j over a partition of [0, r] by one boundary term that tends to 0 by continuity, so ν^±ₙ([0, r]) → ⟨X^i ± X^j⟩_r in probability. Take a countable dense set D ⊂ [0, t] with t ∈ D. Given any subsequence, Borel–Cantelli and a diagonal argument give a further subsequence along which this convergence holds almost surely for all r ∈ D. The limit functions are continuous, so Helly–Bray gives ∫ g dν^±ₙ → ∫₀^t g d⟨X^i ± X^j⟩ for every continuous g on [0, t]. With g = ∂_i∂_j F(X(ω)), polarization of the limit gives Σ_k ∂_i∂_j F(X_{t_k}) ΔX^i_k ΔX^j_k → ∫₀^t ∂_i∂_j F(X_s) d⟨X^i, X^j⟩_s almost surely along the subsequence. Every subsequence has such a further subsequence, so Qₙ → ½ Σ_{i,j} ∫₀^t ∂_i∂_j F(X_s) d⟨X^i, X^j⟩_s in probability.

Conclusion. For every n, F(X_t) − F(X₀) = S¹ₙ + (S²ₙ − Qₙ) + Qₙ. By steps s2 to s4 the right side converges in probability to Σ_i ∫₀^t ∂_i F(X_s) dX^i_s + ½ Σ_{i,j} ∫₀^t ∂_i∂_j F(X_s) d⟨X^i, X^j⟩_s, and limits in probability are almost surely unique. So the formula holds almost surely for each fixed t, hence for all rational t at once. Both sides have continuous paths in t, so the formula holds almost surely for all t ≥ 0. The right side is a continuous local martingale plus a continuous process of finite variation, so F(X) is a continuous semimartingale.

applications.title: Mean squared displacement and the non-Gaussian parameter of a diffusing particle
applications.inputs: A particle in d = 3 dimensions with diffusion coefficient D = 1/2 has position X_t = √(2D) B_t, where B is a standard 3-dimensional Brownian motion, so X₀ = 0. Observation time t = 4.
applications.hypotheses: Each X^i is a continuous martingale, hence a continuous semimartingale, with ⟨X^i, X^j⟩_t = 2D δ_ij t. The functions |x|² and |x|⁴ are twice continuously differentiable.

steps.text: With F(x) = |x|², ∂_i F = 2x_i and ∂_i∂_j F = 2δ_ij. Itô's formula gives |X_t|² = 2 Σ_i ∫₀^t X^i_s dX^i_s + 2dDt. The integrand satisfies E ∫₀^t (X^i_s)² 2D ds < ∞, so by the isometry the integral is a martingale with mean 0. Hence E|X_t|² = 2dDt = 2 · 3 · (1/2) · 4 = 12.

With F(x) = |x|⁴, ∂_i F = 4|x|² x_i and Σ_i ∂_i² F = 4(d + 2)|x|². Itô's formula gives |X_t|⁴ = martingale + 4D(d + 2) ∫₀^t |X_s|² ds, where the martingale has mean 0 because all moments of X_s are finite.
Taking expectations, E|X_t|⁴ = 4D(d + 2) ∫₀^t 2dDs ds = 4D² d(d + 2) t². For the data, E|X_4|⁴ = 4 · (1/2)² · 3 · 5 · 4² = 240.
The non-Gaussian parameter α₂ = d E|X|⁴ / ((d + 2)(E|X|²)²) − 1 measures deviations from Gaussian diffusion in experiments on colloids and glasses. Here α₂ = 3 · 240 / (5 · 12²) − 1 = 0.

applications.conclusion: Itô's formula gives E|X_t|² = 2dDt = 12 (the Einstein relation for the mean squared displacement) and E|X_t|⁴ = 4D²d(d + 2)t² = 240, so the non-Gaussian parameter of free Brownian diffusion is exactly 0.

limitations: The formula needs F ∈ C². For F(x) = |x − a| the second derivative is a point mass, and the correction term becomes local time (Tanaka's formula).
The formula is for continuous semimartingales. For semimartingales with jumps, a sum over the jumps of F(X_s) − F(X_{s−}) − ∇F(X_{s−})·ΔX_s must be added.

results.name: Lévy's characterization of Brownian motion
results.statement: Let (F_t) be a filtration and X = (X¹, …, X^d) a continuous process adapted to (F_t). The following are equivalent. (i) X is a d-dimensional (F_t)-Brownian motion: for all 0 ≤ s < t, X_t − X_s is independent of F_s and has the law N(0, (t − s)I). (ii) Each X^i is a continuous local martingale, and ⟨X^i, X^j⟩_t = δ_ij t for all i, j and all t ≥ 0.
hypotheses: X = (X¹, …, X^d) is a continuous process adapted to the filtration (F_t).
For the direction (ii) ⇒ (i): each X^i is a continuous local martingale and ⟨X^i, X^j⟩_t = δ_ij t.

prerequisites.reason: Step s2 applies Itô's formula to exp(iξ·X_t + |ξ|²t/2) to show that this process is a local martingale.
Step s3 uses the dominated convergence theorem for conditional expectations to show that a bounded local martingale is a true martingale.
Step s4 uses that a probability law on ℝ^m is determined by its characteristic function, a consequence of the Fourier inversion theorem.

definitions.name: continuous local martingale
definitions.text: A continuous adapted process M for which there are stopping times T_n ↑ ∞ such that each stopped process M^{T_n} − M₀ is a uniformly integrable martingale. The bracket ⟨M, N⟩ is the unique continuous finite-variation process with value 0 at time 0 such that (M − M₀)(N − N₀) − ⟨M, N⟩ is a continuous local martingale.

definitions.name: (F_t)-Brownian motion
definitions.text: A continuous adapted process X in ℝ^d such that for all s < t the increment X_t − X_s is independent of F_s and has the law N(0, (t − s)I).

source.citation: Russell Lyons, Stochastic Calculus: lecture notes based on the book Brownian Motion, Martingales, and Stochastic Calculus by J.-F. Le Gall (Springer, 2016), Indiana University.
source.revision: Author's online version dated August 23, 2026, 140 pages. The numbering follows Le Gall's book.
source.module: Chapter 5, Section 5.3.1 Lévy's Characterization of Brownian Motion
source.excerpt: Theorem 5.12 (Lévy). Let X = (X¹, . . . , X^d) be an adapted continuous process. The following are equivalent: (i) X is a d-dimensional (F_t)-Brownian motion. (ii) Each X^i is a continuous local martingale and ∀i, j, t ⟨X^i, X^j⟩_t = δ_ij t.
source.attribution: © Russell Lyons. Quoted from the author's lecture notes for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The authored statement is the same equivalence, with the definition of an (F_t)-Brownian motion written out through its increments. The source proves (ii) ⇒ (i) with the complex exponential martingale of Proposition 5.11 and refers to Chapter 4 for (i) ⇒ (ii). The authored proof follows the same route and also writes out (i) ⇒ (ii).

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the proof of Theorem 5.12 in the cited notes. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Both directions of the equivalence.

steps.text: (i) ⇒ (ii). Let Y = X − X₀. For s < t, Y_t − Y_s is independent of F_s, has mean 0 and covariance (t − s)I. So E[Y^i_t − Y^i_s | F_s] = 0, and Y^i is a martingale, hence X^i is a continuous local martingale. Expand Y^i_t Y^j_t − Y^i_s Y^j_s = (Y^i_t − Y^i_s)(Y^j_t − Y^j_s) + Y^i_s (Y^j_t − Y^j_s) + Y^j_s (Y^i_t − Y^i_s). Independence gives E[Y^i_t Y^j_t − Y^i_s Y^j_s | F_s] = δ_ij (t − s). So Y^i Y^j − δ_ij t is a continuous martingale. The bracket is unique, hence ⟨X^i, X^j⟩_t = δ_ij t.

(ii) ⇒ (i): an exponential local martingale. Fix ξ ∈ ℝ^d and set Z_t = exp(iξ·X_t + |ξ|²t/2). Apply Itô's formula to the real and imaginary parts of F(x, r) = exp(iξ·x + |ξ|²r/2), with the extra finite-variation component r = t. Since ⟨X^j, X^k⟩_t = δ_jk t and the bracket of t with anything is 0, Z_t = Z₀ + Σ_j ∫₀^t iξ_j Z_s dX^j_s + ∫₀^t (|ξ|²/2) Z_s ds − ½ Σ_{j,k} ξ_j ξ_k ∫₀^t Z_s δ_jk ds. The last two terms cancel. So Z − Z₀ is a stochastic integral against continuous local martingales, and Z is a complex continuous local martingale.

(ii) ⇒ (i): a true martingale. On [0, T], |Z_t| = e^(|ξ|²t/2) ≤ e^(|ξ|²T/2). Let T_n reduce Z − Z₀. For s < t ≤ T, E[Z_{t∧T_n} | F_s] = Z_{s∧T_n}. As n → ∞, Z_{t∧T_n} → Z_t and the terms are bounded by a constant, so dominated convergence for conditional expectations gives E[Z_t | F_s] = Z_s. Divide by Z_s, which has modulus at least 1 and is F_s-measurable: E[exp(iξ·(X_t − X_s)) | F_s] = exp(−|ξ|²(t − s)/2).

(ii) ⇒ (i): independence and the Gaussian law. Let W be any F_s-measurable random vector in ℝ^m and η ∈ ℝ^m. Multiply the identity of step s3 by exp(iη·W) and take expectations: E[exp(iη·W + iξ·(X_t − X_s))] = E[exp(iη·W)] exp(−|ξ|²(t − s)/2). The right side is the characteristic function of the product of the law of W and N(0, (t − s)I). A law on ℝ^(m+d) is determined by its characteristic function, so W and X_t − X_s are independent and X_t − X_s has the law N(0, (t − s)I). Since W is an arbitrary finite vector of F_s-measurable variables, X_t − X_s is independent of F_s. With continuity and adaptedness, X is a d-dimensional (F_t)-Brownian motion.

applications.title: Displacement of a rotating Brownian particle along its own axis
applications.inputs: A particle in the plane has translational noise B = (B¹, B²), a standard 2-dimensional Brownian motion. Its body axis has angle θ_t, a progressive process that may depend on the past of B, for example θ_t = B¹_t. The displacement along the body axis is W_t = ∫₀^t cos θ_s dB¹_s + ∫₀^t sin θ_s dB²_s. Time t = 2.
applications.hypotheses: The integrands are bounded and progressive, so W is a continuous martingale, hence a continuous local martingale. Its bracket is ⟨W⟩_t = ∫₀^t (cos²θ_s + sin²θ_s) ds = t, because ⟨B¹⟩_t = ⟨B²⟩_t = t and ⟨B¹, B²⟩ = 0.

steps.text: W is adapted, continuous, a continuous local martingale, and ⟨W⟩_t = t. By Lévy's characterization with d = 1, W is an (F_t)-Brownian motion, although the angle θ is random and depends on B.
So W_t has the law N(0, t) and its increments are independent. In particular E W_t² = t and E W_t⁴ = 3t², the moments of a centered Gaussian law.
For t = 2, E W_2⁴ = 3 · 2² = 12. Without Lévy's theorem this fourth moment is not obvious, because W is built from a path-dependent rotation.
The same argument for a fixed rotation gives the classical construction of correlated noises: W = (3/5)B¹ + (4/5)B² has ⟨W⟩_t = (9/25 + 16/25)t = t, so W is a Brownian motion with ⟨B¹, W⟩_t = (3/5)t.

applications.conclusion: The axial displacement W of the particle is a standard Brownian motion for every progressive orientation process θ, with E W_2⁴ = 12. In models of active particles this justifies treating the noise in the body frame as a Brownian motion.

limitations: Continuity is essential. The compensated Poisson process N_t − t is a martingale with the same predictable bracket t, but it is not a Brownian motion.
The theorem identifies Brownian motion only. For a general continuous local martingale, the Dambis–Dubins–Schwarz theorem gives a Brownian motion after a random time change by ⟨M⟩.

results.name: Burkholder–Davis–Gundy inequality
results.statement: For every p > 0 there are constants 0 < c_p ≤ C_p < ∞ such that, for every continuous local martingale M with M₀ = 0 and every stopping time T, c_p E[⟨M⟩_T^(p/2)] ≤ E[(M*_T)^p] ≤ C_p E[⟨M⟩_T^(p/2)], where M*_T = sup_{t≤T} |M_t| and ⟨M⟩ is the quadratic variation. One can take C_p = 2^(p(p+1)/2 + p + 1) and c_p = 2^(−p²/4 − 2p − 1). Both sides may be infinite.
hypotheses: M is a continuous local martingale with M₀ = 0.
T is a stopping time, possibly infinite, and p > 0.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 uses the martingale convergence theorem: the bounded stopped martingale M^{T_a ∧ T_{−b}} converges almost surely as t → ∞.
Step s1 passes E[M_{t ∧ T_a ∧ T_{−b}}] = 0 to the limit t → ∞ with the dominated convergence theorem.
Step s3 uses Doob's maximal inequality in L² to show that a continuous local martingale with zero bracket is identically zero.
Step s4 writes E[X^q] as ∫ q r^(q−1) P(X ≥ r) dr, an exchange of integrals justified by Fubini's theorem for nonnegative functions.
Step s5 removes the localization with the monotone convergence theorem.

definitions.name: quadratic variation ⟨M⟩
definitions.text: The unique continuous nondecreasing adapted process with ⟨M⟩₀ = 0 such that M² − ⟨M⟩ is a continuous local martingale. For each t it is the limit in probability of sums of squared increments of M over partitions of [0, t].

definitions.name: running maximum M*
definitions.text: M*_t = sup_{s≤t} |M_s|, and M*_∞ = sup_{s≥0} |M_s|.

definitions.name: hitting time T_x
definitions.text: T_x = inf{t ≥ 0 : M_t = x}, with inf ∅ = ∞. It is a stopping time because M is continuous and adapted.

proof.scope: Both inequalities for every p > 0 and every stopping time T, with the stated constants.

steps.text: Exit estimate. Let N be a continuous local martingale with N₀ = 0, a, b > 0, and A = {T_a < T_{−b}} for the hitting times of N. The stopped process N^{T_a ∧ T_{−b}} is a continuous local martingale bounded by max(a, b), so it is a bounded martingale with mean 0. By martingale convergence it has an almost sure limit L, and dominated convergence gives E L = 0. Now L = a on A, L ≥ −b off A, and L = 0 on {N*_∞ = 0}. So 0 = E L ≥ a P(A) − b P(A^c ∩ {N*_∞ > 0}) = (a + b) P(A) − b P(N*_∞ > 0), because A ⊂ {N*_∞ > 0}. Hence P(T_a < T_{−b}) ≤ b P(N*_∞ > 0)/(a + b).

Comparison of two processes. Let X, Y ≥ 0 be continuous adapted processes with X₀ = Y₀ = 0 such that X − Y is a continuous local martingale, and let 0 < β < α. On the event {sup X ≥ α, sup Y < β}, X − Y > −β at all times. Also X_t > α − (β − sup Y) at some time t, and there X_t − Y_t > α − β. So X − Y hits α − β and never hits −β. Step s1 with a = α − β and b = β gives P(sup X ≥ α, sup Y < β) ≤ (β/α) P((X − Y)*_∞ > 0).

Good-λ inequalities. Two facts about a continuous local martingale N with N₀ = 0 hold almost surely: N*_∞ = 0 implies ⟨N⟩_∞ = 0, because ⟨N⟩_t is a limit in probability of sums of squared increments, and ⟨N⟩_∞ = 0 implies N*_∞ = 0, because Doob's inequality for N stopped when ⟨N⟩ reaches ε gives E[(N*_∞)²; ⟨N⟩_∞ = 0] ≤ 4ε for every ε > 0. Fix r > 0. Upper case, 0 < b < 1: let S = inf{t : |M_t| ≥ √r} and N = M − M^S, so ⟨N⟩ = ⟨M⟩ − ⟨M⟩^S ≤ ⟨M⟩, N*_∞ ≥ M*_∞ − √r, and N*_∞ > 0 only if (M*_∞)² ≥ r. Step s2 with X = N², Y = ⟨N⟩, α = r, β = br gives P((M*_∞)² ≥ 4r, ⟨M⟩_∞ < br) ≤ P((N*_∞)² ≥ r, ⟨N⟩_∞ < br) ≤ b P((M*_∞)² ≥ r). Lower case, 0 < b < 1/4: let S = inf{t : ⟨M⟩_t ≥ r} and N = M − M^S, so ⟨N⟩_∞ = (⟨M⟩_∞ − r)⁺ and N*_∞ ≤ 2M*_∞. Step s2 with X = ⟨N⟩, Y = N², α = r, β = 4br gives P(⟨M⟩_∞ ≥ 2r, (M*_∞)² < br) ≤ P(⟨N⟩_∞ ≥ r, (N*_∞)² < 4br) ≤ 4b P(⟨N⟩_∞ > 0) ≤ 4b P(⟨M⟩_∞ ≥ r).

Integration of tails. For X ≥ 0, q > 0 and κ > 0, Fubini's theorem gives E X^q = κ^q ∫₀^∞ q r^(q−1) P(X ≥ κr) dr. Upper case: P((M*_∞)² ≥ 4r) ≤ P(⟨M⟩_∞ ≥ br) + b P((M*_∞)² ≥ r). Multiply by (p/2) r^(p/2−1) and integrate: 2^(−p) E(M*_∞)^p ≤ b^(−p/2) E⟨M⟩_∞^(p/2) + b E(M*_∞)^p. If E(M*_∞)^p < ∞, the choice b = 2^(−p−1) gives E(M*_∞)^p ≤ 2^(p(p+1)/2 + p + 1) E⟨M⟩_∞^(p/2). Lower case: P(⟨M⟩_∞ ≥ 2r) ≤ P((M*_∞)² ≥ br) + 4b P(⟨M⟩_∞ ≥ r), so 2^(−p/2) E⟨M⟩_∞^(p/2) ≤ b^(−p/2) E(M*_∞)^p + 4b E⟨M⟩_∞^(p/2). If E⟨M⟩_∞^(p/2) < ∞, the choice b = 2^(−p/2−3) < 1/4 gives E⟨M⟩_∞^(p/2) ≤ 2^(p²/4 + 2p + 1) E(M*_∞)^p.

Localization and general T. Let T_n = inf{t : |M_t| ≥ n}. The martingale M^{T_n} is bounded by n, so step s4 applies to it: E((M^{T_n})*_∞)^p ≤ C_p E⟨M⟩_{T_n}^(p/2) ≤ C_p E⟨M⟩_∞^(p/2). As n → ∞, (M^{T_n})*_∞ increases to M*_∞, and monotone convergence gives the upper bound. Let S_n = inf{t : ⟨M⟩_t ≥ n}. Then ⟨M^{S_n}⟩_∞ ≤ n, so step s4 gives c_p E⟨M⟩_{S_n}^(p/2) ≤ E((M^{S_n})*_∞)^p ≤ E(M*_∞)^p, and monotone convergence gives the lower bound. For a stopping time T, apply both bounds to M^T, using (M^T)*_∞ = M*_T and ⟨M^T⟩_∞ = ⟨M⟩_T.

applications.title: Hölder regularity of a diffusion with bounded noise amplitude
applications.inputs: A stochastic integral M_t = ∫₀^t σ_s dB_s with a standard Brownian motion B and a progressive volatility or noise amplitude σ with |σ_s| ≤ K = 2. Moment order p = 8 and time lag |t − s| = 1/4.
applications.hypotheses: For fixed s, N_u = M_{s+u} − M_s is a continuous local martingale with N₀ = 0 for the filtration (F_{s+u}), with ⟨N⟩_u = ∫_s^{s+u} σ_v² dv ≤ K² u. The deterministic time u = t − s is a stopping time.

steps.text: BDG for N at T = t − s gives E|M_t − M_s|^p ≤ E[(N*_T)^p] ≤ C_p E[⟨N⟩_T^(p/2)] ≤ C_p K^p |t − s|^(p/2).
For K = 2, p = 8 and |t − s| = 1/4, the factor K^p |t − s|^(p/2) equals 2⁸ · (1/4)⁴ = 1, so E|M_t − M_s|⁸ ≤ C_8.

The bound E|M_t − M_s|^p ≤ C |t − s|^(1 + β) with β = p/2 − 1 is the hypothesis of the Kolmogorov continuity theorem, which gives a version of M that is locally Hölder continuous of every order γ < β/p.
For p = 8 the Hölder exponent bound is β/p = (8/2 − 1)/8 = 3/8. Letting p → ∞ gives every order γ < 1/2, the same regularity as Brownian motion.

applications.conclusion: Every stochastic integral with a noise amplitude bounded by K has paths that are Hölder continuous of every order below 1/2, uniformly in the form of σ. The BDG inequality turns the bound on the bracket into the moment bound that Kolmogorov's theorem needs.

limitations: The constants from this proof grow like 2^(p²/2) and are far from optimal. The best constants are known only in some cases, for example C₂ = 4 from Doob's inequality.
For discontinuous martingales the inequality holds for p ≥ 1 with the square bracket [M] in place of ⟨M⟩, but it fails for p < 1 in general.

results.name: Novikov's criterion
results.statement: Let T > 0 and let M = (M_t)_{0≤t≤T} be a continuous local martingale with M₀ = 0. Suppose that K = E[exp(½⟨M⟩_T)] < ∞. Then the stochastic exponential E(M)_t = exp(M_t − ½⟨M⟩_t), 0 ≤ t ≤ T, is a martingale on [0, T], and E[E(M)_T] = 1. In particular, for an n-dimensional Brownian motion W and a progressive process F with E[exp(½∫₀^T ‖F_s‖² ds)] < ∞, the process exp(∫₀^t F_s·dW_s − ½∫₀^t ‖F_s‖² ds) is a martingale on [0, T].
hypotheses: M is a continuous local martingale on [0, T] with M₀ = 0.
E[exp(½⟨M⟩_T)] < ∞.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 uses Itô's formula to show that E(L) = 1 + ∫ E(L) dL, so the stochastic exponential of a continuous local martingale is a local martingale.
Step s1 applies Fatou's lemma for conditional expectations to show that a nonnegative local martingale is a supermartingale.
Step s2 bounds E exp(½M_σ) by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.
Step s3 uses the Vitali convergence theorem: a sequence bounded in L^u for some u > 1 that converges almost surely converges in L¹.
Steps s4 and s5 split E(√α M) into a power of E(M) and an exponential of M with Hölder's inequality.
Step s5 compares E exp(c M_T) with E exp(½ M_T) for c < ½ with Jensen's inequality for the convex function x ↦ x^(1/(2c)).

definitions.name: stochastic exponential E(M)
definitions.text: For a continuous local martingale M with M₀ = 0, E(M)_t = exp(M_t − ½⟨M⟩_t). It is the solution of dZ = Z dM with Z₀ = 1.

definitions.name: supermartingale
definitions.text: An adapted integrable process Z with E[Z_t | F_s] ≤ Z_s for all s ≤ t. A martingale is a supermartingale with equality.

definitions.name: quadratic variation ⟨M⟩
definitions.text: The unique continuous nondecreasing adapted process with ⟨M⟩₀ = 0 such that M² − ⟨M⟩ is a continuous local martingale. For M = ∫F·dW it equals ∫‖F_s‖² ds.
