results.name: Yamada–Watanabe criterion for pathwise uniqueness
results.statement: Let b, σ : [0, ∞) × ℝ → ℝ be Borel functions. Assume that there are constants γ > 0 and K ≥ 0 and a nondecreasing function ρ : [0, γ] → [0, ∞) with ρ(u) > 0 for 0 < u ≤ γ and ∫₀^γ ρ(u)⁻² du = ∞, such that |b(t, x) − b(t, y)| ≤ K|x − y| and |σ(t, x) − σ(t, y)| ≤ ρ(|x − y|) for all t ≥ 0 and all x, y ∈ ℝ with |x − y| ≤ γ. Let X and Y be two solutions of dX_t = b(t, X_t) dt + σ(t, X_t) dW_t on the same filtered probability space, with the same Brownian motion W and X₀ = Y₀ almost surely. Then X and Y are indistinguishable. So pathwise uniqueness holds for every initial distribution.
hypotheses: The drift b is Borel and Lipschitz in x with constant K for |x − y| ≤ γ, uniformly in t.
The diffusion coefficient σ is Borel and |σ(t, x) − σ(t, y)| ≤ ρ(|x − y|) for |x − y| ≤ γ, where ρ is nondecreasing, positive on (0, γ] and ∫₀^γ ρ(u)⁻² du = ∞.

X and Y are solutions on the same filtered probability space: continuous adapted processes with ∫₀ᵗ (|b(s, X_s)| + σ(s, X_s)²) ds < ∞ almost surely and X_t = X₀ + ∫₀ᵗ b(s, X_s) ds + ∫₀ᵗ σ(s, X_s) dW_s for all t, with the same Brownian motion W and X₀ = Y₀ almost surely.

prerequisites.reason: Step s3 applies Itô's formula to ψ_k(Z), where Z = X − Y and ψ_k is a C² approximation of |w|.
Step s3 shows that the stopped stochastic integral with a bounded integrand is a martingale with mean 0.
Step s4 exchanges expectation and time integral for the nonnegative bound K|Z_(s∧τ)| + 1/k.
Step s5 shows that u(t) = E|Z_(t∧τ)| is continuous, since |Z_(t∧τ)| ≤ γ and Z has continuous paths.
Step s5 concludes u ≡ 0 from u(t) ≤ K ∫₀ᵗ u(s) ds for the bounded continuous function u.

definitions.name: pathwise uniqueness
definitions.text: Any two solutions on the same filtered probability space, with the same Brownian motion and the same initial value, are indistinguishable.

definitions.name: indistinguishable
definitions.text: Two processes X and Y are indistinguishable if, almost surely, X_t = Y_t for all t ≥ 0 at once.

definitions.name: Osgood condition
definitions.text: The condition ∫₀^γ ρ(u)⁻² du = ∞ on the modulus ρ. For example ρ(u) = C√u satisfies it, because ∫₀^γ du/(C²u) = ∞.

source.citation: S. Altay and U. Schmock, Lecture notes on the Yamada–Watanabe condition for the pathwise uniqueness of solutions of certain stochastic differential equations, Vienna University of Technology, 2013 (last update 2016).
source.revision: Lecture notes dated April 25, 2013, last update March 14, 2016, posted on the second author's home page.
source.module: Section 2, Yamada–Watanabe condition for SDEs
source.excerpt: Theorem 2.1. Consider the stochastic differential equation (1.2). Assume that there exist a constant γ > 0 and functions κ, ϱ: [0, γ] → [0, ∞) satisfying κ(0) = 0, |b(t, x) − b(t, y)| ≤ κ(|x − y|), and ‖σ(t, x) − σ(t, y)‖_F ≤ ϱ(|x − y|) for all t ∈ [0, ∞) and x, y ∈ ℝⁿ with |x − y| ≤ γ. Furthermore, assume that ϱ is non-decreasing, ϱ(u) > 0 for all u ∈ (0, γ] and its square satisfies the Osgood condition … Then the pathwise uniqueness of solutions of (1.2) holds for every initial distribution µ.
source.attribution: © S. Altay and U. Schmock. Quoted from Lecture notes on the Yamada–Watanabe condition (Vienna University of Technology) for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source treats dimension n with an Osgood modulus κ for the drift and a concave majorant G. The authored statement is the one-dimensional case with κ(u) = Ku and G = κ, as in Remark 2.7, which contains Corollary 2.19 (σ Hölder of exponent 1/2). The authored proof follows the proof of Theorem 2.1 on pp. 6-9. Grönwall's lemma replaces Bihari's inequality, and the bounded stochastic integrand replaces the localizing stopping times.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the proof of Theorem 2.1 in Altay and Schmock's lecture notes. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full one-dimensional statement, for every initial distribution.

steps.text: Approximation of |w|. Since ρ is nondecreasing and positive on (0, γ], ρ⁻² is bounded on [a, γ] for each a > 0, while its integral over (0, γ] is infinite. So there are γ = a₀ > a₁ > a₂ > … with a_k → 0 and ∫ over (a_k, a_(k−1)) of ρ⁻² equal to k. The bound 2/(kρ²) is monotone and bounded there, with integral 2. So there is a continuous φ_k ≥ 0 with support in (a_k, a_(k−1)), φ_k ≤ 2/(kρ²) and ∫ φ_k = 1. Put ψ_k(w) = ∫₀^|w| ∫₀^v φ_k(u) du dv. Then ψ_k is C², ψ_k = 0 on [−a_k, a_k], |ψ_k′| ≤ 1, ψ_k″(w) = φ_k(|w|) and |w| − a_(k−1) ≤ ψ_k(w) ≤ |w|.

Difference process. Let Z = X − Y, β_s = b(s, X_s) − b(s, Y_s) and α_s = σ(s, X_s) − σ(s, Y_s). Then Z_t = ∫₀ᵗ β_s ds + ∫₀ᵗ α_s dW_s and Z₀ = 0. Let τ = inf{t ≥ 0 : |Z_t| ≥ γ}. It is a stopping time, because Z is continuous and adapted and the set {|z| ≥ γ} is closed. For s ≤ τ we have |Z_s| ≤ γ, so |β_s| ≤ K|Z_s| ≤ Kγ and |α_s| ≤ ρ(|Z_s|) ≤ ρ(γ).

Itô expansion. Itô's formula for ψ_k(Z), stopped at τ, gives ψ_k(Z_(t∧τ)) = ∫₀^(t∧τ) ψ_k′(Z_s)α_s dW_s + ∫₀^(t∧τ) [ψ_k′(Z_s)β_s + ½φ_k(|Z_s|)α_s²] ds. The stopped stochastic integral has the integrand 1{s ≤ τ}ψ_k′(Z_s)α_s, which is bounded by ρ(γ). By the Itô isometry it is a square-integrable martingale, so its expected value is 0.

Estimate. For s ≤ τ, |ψ_k′(Z_s)β_s| ≤ K|Z_s|. If φ_k(|Z_s|) ≠ 0, then a_k < |Z_s| < a_(k−1) and ρ(|Z_s|) > 0. So ½φ_k(|Z_s|)α_s² ≤ ½ · 2/(kρ(|Z_s|)²) · ρ(|Z_s|)² = 1/k. Take expected values in s3 and use Tonelli's theorem for the nonnegative bound: E ψ_k(Z_(t∧τ)) ≤ t/k + K ∫₀ᵗ E|Z_(s∧τ)| ds.

Grönwall step. Let u(t) = E|Z_(t∧τ)|. Then 0 ≤ u ≤ γ, and u is continuous by dominated convergence. Step s1 gives E ψ_k(Z_(t∧τ)) ≥ u(t) − a_(k−1). So u(t) ≤ a_(k−1) + t/k + K ∫₀ᵗ u(s) ds for every k. Let k → ∞: u(t) ≤ K ∫₀ᵗ u(s) ds for all t ≥ 0. Grönwall's lemma gives u ≡ 0.

Conclusion. For each t, Z_(t∧τ) = 0 almost surely. On {τ ≤ t}, continuity gives |Z_(t∧τ)| = |Z_τ| = γ > 0. So P(τ ≤ t) = 0 for every t, and Z_t = Z_(t∧τ) = 0 almost surely. Almost surely this holds for all rational t at once, and the continuity of Z gives Z_t = 0 for all t ≥ 0. So X and Y are indistinguishable.

applications.title: Squared distance of a diffusing particle from its start
applications.inputs: A particle performs a standard Brownian motion B = (B¹, B², B³) in ℝ³ from the origin. Its squared distance is R_t = |B_t|². Time t = 4.
applications.hypotheses: Itô's formula gives dR_t = 3 dt + 2 ∑ᵢ Bⁱ_t dBⁱ_t. Put β_t = ∫₀ᵗ ∑ᵢ (Bⁱ_s/|B_s|) dBⁱ_s, with the convention 0/0 = 1/√3 for each i. Then ⟨β⟩_t = t, so β is a Brownian motion by Lévy's characterization, and R solves dZ = 3 dt + 2√|Z| dβ with Z₀ = 0. The drift b ≡ 3 has K = 0. For σ(x) = 2√|x|, the inequalities |√a − √c| ≤ √|a − c| and ||x| − |y|| ≤ |x − y| give |σ(x) − σ(y)| ≤ ρ(|x − y|) with ρ(u) = 2√u.

steps.text: Osgood condition: ρ(u)² = 4u, so ∫₀¹ du/ρ(u)² = ∫₀¹ du/(4u) = ∞. The function ρ is nondecreasing and positive on (0, 1]. So every solution driven by β from 0 is indistinguishable from R. The Lipschitz theorem does not apply, because √ is not Lipschitz at 0.
Moments of the unique solution: d(Z²) = 2Z dZ + d⟨Z⟩ = 10Z dt + 4Z^(3/2) dβ, and R has all moments. So E Z_t = 3t and E Z_t² = 10 ∫₀ᵗ 3s ds = 15t². At t = 4, E Z₄ = 12 and E Z₄² = 240.
Variance: Var Z₄ = 240 − 12² = 96. This equals the variance of a sum of three independent squares of N(0, 4) variables, 3 · 2 · 4² = 96.

applications.conclusion: The square-root equation dZ = 3 dt + 2√|Z| dβ has exactly one solution for the given β, the squared distance R. At t = 4 its mean is 12 and its variance is 96.

limitations: The exponent 1/2 is sharp. For 0 < α < 1/2, the equation dX = |X|^α dW from 0 has the solution X ≡ 0 and also a solution that leaves 0, a time change of Brownian motion. So uniqueness fails.
The criterion is one-dimensional in this form. For dimension n ≥ 2 with zero drift, the proof in the source needs the stronger condition ∫₀^γ u ρ(u)⁻² du = ∞ (Remark 2.7).
Pathwise uniqueness gives no existence. Together with a weak solution, the Yamada–Watanabe theorem gives a unique strong solution.

Picard iteration for stochastic differential equations
results.statement: Let σ: ℝ₊ × ℝᵈ → ℝ^(d×m) and b: ℝ₊ × ℝᵈ → ℝᵈ be measurable. Suppose that there is K < ∞ with ‖σ(t, x) − σ(t, y)‖ ≤ K|x − y| and |b(t, x) − b(t, y)| ≤ K|x − y| for all t ≥ 0 and x, y ∈ ℝᵈ, where ‖·‖ is the Frobenius norm, and that ‖σ(t, 0)‖ and |b(t, 0)| are bounded on each interval [0, T]. Consider the equation dX_t = σ(t, X_t) dB_t + b(t, X_t) dt. (1) Pathwise uniqueness: on any filtered probability space with a complete filtration and an m-dimensional Brownian motion B, two continuous adapted solutions with X₀ = X₀′ almost surely are indistinguishable. (2) Strong existence: on every such space and for every x ∈ ℝᵈ there is a solution with X₀ = x that is adapted to the completed filtration of B, and E sup_{t≤T} |X_t|² < ∞ for every T.
hypotheses: σ and b are measurable and Lipschitz in the space variable with one constant K for all times.
‖σ(t, 0)‖ and |b(t, 0)| are bounded on every compact time interval [0, T].
B is an m-dimensional Brownian motion with respect to a complete filtration (F_t).

prerequisites.reason: Steps s1 and s3 bound the supremum of a stopped stochastic integral by Doob's L² maximal inequality.
Steps s1 and s6 compute the second moment of a stochastic integral with the Itô isometry.
Steps s1, s5 and s6 bound the square of a time integral and a first moment with the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.
Step s2 applies Grönwall's lemma to the localized mean square distance of two solutions and gets zero.
Step s5 sums the L² norms of the Picard increments with Minkowski's inequality to get convergence in L².

definitions.name: solution
definitions.text: A continuous (F_t)-adapted process X with X_t = X₀ + ∫₀ᵗ σ(s, X_s) dB_s + ∫₀ᵗ b(s, X_s) ds for all t ≥ 0, almost surely.

definitions.name: strong solution
definitions.text: A solution with a deterministic initial value x that is adapted to the completed filtration generated by the Brownian motion B.

definitions.name: pathwise uniqueness
definitions.text: Any two solutions on the same filtered space, driven by the same Brownian motion, with almost surely equal initial values, are indistinguishable.

source.citation: Russell Lyons, Stochastic Calculus: lecture notes based on the book Brownian Motion, Martingales, and Stochastic Calculus by J.-F. Le Gall (Springer, 2016), Indiana University.
source.revision: Author's online version dated August 23, 2026, 140 pages. The numbering follows Le Gall's book.
source.module: Chapter 8, Section 8.2 The Lipschitz Case
source.excerpt: Theorem 8.3. E(σ, b) has pathwise uniqueness and for every filtered probability space and associated Brownian motion, for all x ∈ ℝᵈ, Eₓ(σ, b) has a (unique) strong solution.
source.attribution: © Russell Lyons. Quoted from the author's lecture notes Stochastic Calculus for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source assumes that σ and b are continuous and Lipschitz in space uniformly in time. The authored statement only needs measurability and bounds on σ(t, 0) and b(t, 0) on compact time intervals, which is all that the proof uses. The authored proof follows the proof of Theorem 8.3 and Lemma 8A on pp. 106-108: localization and Grönwall's lemma for uniqueness, Picard iteration for existence. The source writes the proof for d = m = 1, and the authored proof uses norms in all dimensions.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the proof of Theorem 8.3 in Lyons's notes. No local formal verification.

proof.scope: The full statement in dimension d with an m-dimensional Brownian motion, for every deterministic initial value x.

steps.text: Key estimate. Let X and Y be continuous adapted processes, and let X̃_t = X̃₀ + ∫₀ᵗ σ(s, X_s) dB_s + ∫₀ᵗ b(s, X_s) ds, with Ỹ built from Y in the same way. For a stopping time τ and t ≥ 0, E sup_{s≤t} |X̃_{s∧τ} − Ỹ_{s∧τ}|² ≤ 3E|X̃₀ − Ỹ₀|² + 3(4 + t)K² ∫₀ᵗ E|X_{r∧τ} − Y_{r∧τ}|² dr. To prove it, use (a + b + c)² ≤ 3(a² + b² + c²). If the right side is finite, the stopped stochastic integral of σ(r, X_r) − σ(r, Y_r) is a square-integrable martingale. Doob's L² inequality and the Itô isometry bound its squared supremum in mean by 4E ∫₀^(t∧τ) ‖σ(r, X_r) − σ(r, Y_r)‖² dr ≤ 4K² ∫₀ᵗ E|X_{r∧τ} − Y_{r∧τ}|² dr, because X_r = X_{r∧τ} for r < τ. The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality bounds the squared drift difference by tK² ∫₀ᵗ |X_{r∧τ} − Y_{r∧τ}|² dr.

Uniqueness. Let X and X′ be solutions with the same B and X₀ = X₀′ a.s. Fix M > 0 and let τ = inf{t : |X_t| ≥ M or |X′_t| ≥ M}. On {τ = 0} both stopped processes equal X₀. Otherwise both stay in the closed ball of radius M up to τ. So g(t) = E sup_{s≤t} |X_{s∧τ} − X′_{s∧τ}|² ≤ 4M². A solution satisfies X̃ = X in step s1, so g(t) ≤ 3(4 + T)K² ∫₀ᵗ g(r) dr for t ≤ T. Grönwall's lemma gives g = 0 on [0, T]. As M → ∞, τ → ∞ because the paths are continuous. So X = X′ on [0, T] a.s. for every T.

Picard iterates. Fix x and set X⁰_t = x and X^(n+1)_t = x + ∫₀ᵗ σ(s, Xⁿ_s) dB_s + ∫₀ᵗ b(s, Xⁿ_s) ds. By induction each Xⁿ is continuous and adapted to the completed filtration of B. Let g_n(t) = E sup_{s≤t} |Xⁿ_s − X^(n−1)_s|². The integrands σ(s, x) and b(s, x) of X¹ − x are deterministic and bounded by a constant A_T on [0, T], by the Lipschitz bound and the bound at 0. Doob's inequality and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality give g₁(t) ≤ (8t + 2t²)A_T² ≤ C′_T for t ≤ T.

Factorial bound. Step s1 with τ = ∞, X̃ = X^(n+1), Ỹ = Xⁿ and equal initial values gives g_(n+1)(t) ≤ C_T ∫₀ᵗ g_n(r) dr for t ≤ T, with C_T = 3(4 + T)K², because E|Xⁿ_r − X^(n−1)_r|² ≤ g_n(r). The right side is finite by induction, so the step applies. Induction on n gives g_n(t) ≤ C′_T C_T^(n−1) t^(n−1)/(n − 1)! for t ≤ T.

Convergence. The bound of step s4 gives ∑_n g_n(T)^(1/2) < ∞. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, E sup_{t≤T} |X^(n+1)_t − Xⁿ_t| ≤ g_(n+1)(T)^(1/2). So ∑_n sup_{t≤T} |X^(n+1)_t − Xⁿ_t| has finite mean and is finite a.s. Hence Xⁿ converges uniformly on [0, T] a.s. to a continuous process X, adapted to the completed filtration of B. Minkowski's inequality gives (E sup_{t≤T} |Xⁿ_t − X_t|²)^(1/2) ≤ ∑_{k≥n} g_(k+1)(T)^(1/2) → 0. The limits for different T agree, so X is defined on ℝ₊ and E sup_{t≤T} |X_t|² < ∞.

The limit solves the equation. Fix t ≤ T. The Lipschitz bound and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality give E|∫₀ᵗ (b(s, Xⁿ_s) − b(s, X_s)) ds|² ≤ tK² ∫₀ᵗ E|Xⁿ_s − X_s|² ds → 0. The Itô isometry gives E|∫₀ᵗ (σ(s, Xⁿ_s) − σ(s, X_s)) dB_s|² ≤ K² ∫₀ᵗ E|Xⁿ_s − X_s|² ds → 0. So the right side of the recursion converges in L² to x + ∫₀ᵗ σ(s, X_s) dB_s + ∫₀ᵗ b(s, X_s) ds, and the left side X^(n+1)_t converges to X_t. The limits agree a.s. for each t, and both sides are continuous in t. So X is a strong solution with X₀ = x, and step s2 makes it unique.

applications.title: The Langevin equation for the velocity of a Brownian particle
applications.inputs: A particle of mass m in a fluid at temperature T_f has friction rate γ > 0. Put θ = k_B T_f/m. Its velocity solves dV_t = −γV_t dt + √(2γθ) dB_t with V₀ = v. Numbers: γ = 1 s⁻¹, θ = 1 m²/s², v = 2 m/s, and the time t = (ln 2)/γ.
applications.hypotheses: The equation is one-dimensional, with a one-dimensional Brownian motion, b(t, v) = −γv and σ(t, v) = √(2γθ). The drift is Lipschitz with K = γ, σ is constant, and b(t, 0) = 0. So both hypotheses hold, and the theorem gives exactly one solution, adapted to B.

steps.text: Candidate: V_t = e^(−γt) Y_t with Y_t = v + √(2γθ) ∫₀ᵗ e^(γs) dB_s. The product rule with the deterministic factor e^(−γt) gives dV_t = −γV_t dt + √(2γθ) dB_t. So the candidate is a continuous adapted solution, and by uniqueness it is the solution.
The stochastic integral has a deterministic integrand, so V_t is Gaussian. Its mean is e^(−γt) v. The Itô isometry gives Var V_t = 2γθ ∫₀ᵗ e^(−2γ(t−s)) ds = θ(1 − e^(−2γt)).
At t = (ln 2)/γ, e^(−γt) = 1/2. So E V_t = v/2 = 1 m/s and Var V_t = θ(1 − 1/4) = 3/4 m²/s². The mean square velocity is E V_t² = 1 + 3/4 = 7/4 m²/s².
As t → ∞, E V_t² → θ = k_B T_f/m. So the mean kinetic energy (1/2) m E V_t² tends to (1/2) k_B T_f, the equipartition value.

applications.conclusion: The Langevin equation has exactly one solution for each initial velocity. It is the Gaussian Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process with mean v e^(−γt) and variance (k_B T_f/m)(1 − e^(−2γt)). At t = (ln 2)/γ with the given numbers, E V_t² = 7/4 m²/s².

limitations: A global Lipschitz bound excludes drifts such as −x³. Locally Lipschitz coefficients give a unique solution only up to a possible explosion time.

Diffusion coefficients that are only Hölder continuous with exponent 1/2, as in the Feller or Cox–Ingersoll–Ross equation, are not covered. In dimension one the Yamada–Watanabe criterion gives pathwise uniqueness for them.
The theorem gives no information on the law of the solution beyond its moments. Laws and densities come from the Kolmogorov equations or from explicit formulas.

results.name: Stroock–Varadhan well-posedness of the martingale problem
aliases: well-posedness of the martingale problem for continuous nondegenerate diffusion coefficients
results.statement: Let a : [0, ∞) × ℝ^d → ℝ^(d×d) be continuous, with a(s, x) symmetric and positive definite for every (s, x), and let b : [0, ∞) × ℝ^d → ℝ^d be Borel. Assume |a_ij(s, x)| ≤ C(1 + |x|²) and |b_i(s, x)| ≤ C(1 + |x|) for a constant C. Put (L_s f)(x) = ½ ∑ a_ij(s, x) ∂_i∂_j f(x) + ∑ b_j(s, x) ∂_j f(x). Then for every s₀ ≥ 0 and x₀ ∈ ℝ^d there is exactly one probability measure P_(s₀,x₀) on the space of continuous paths x : [s₀, ∞) → ℝ^d such that x(s₀) = x₀ almost surely and f(x(t)) − f(x(s₀)) − ∫_(s₀)^t (L_s f)(x(s)) ds is a martingale for the natural filtration, for every f ∈ C_c^∞(ℝ^d). The family {P_(s,x)} is a Markov process with transition probability p(s, x, t, A) = P_(s,x)[x(t) ∈ A].
hypotheses: The diffusion matrix a(s, x) is continuous in (s, x), symmetric and positive definite for every (s, x), and |a_ij(s, x)| ≤ C(1 + |x|²).
The drift b(s, x) is Borel measurable and |b_i(s, x)| ≤ C(1 + |x|).

prerequisites.reason: Steps s2 and s6 apply Itô's formula to the Lyapunov function 1 + |x|² and to the solution u of the perturbed parabolic equation.
Step s3 removes the bounded drift b with Girsanov's theorem, which maps solutions for [a, 0] one-to-one onto solutions for [a, b].
Steps s4 and s6 use regular conditional distributions of a solution given F_τ, which are again solutions from (τ, x(τ)).

definitions.name: martingale problem
definitions.text: A probability measure P on continuous paths from (s₀, x₀) solves the martingale problem for L_s if f(x(t)) − f(x(s₀)) − ∫_(s₀)^t (L_s f)(x(s)) ds is a P-martingale for every smooth f with compact support.

definitions.name: well-posed
definitions.text: The martingale problem is well posed if it has exactly one solution from every starting point (s₀, x₀).

definitions.name: Green operator of the heat equation
definitions.text: (Gf)(s, x) = ∫_s^∞ ∫ f(t, y) p(s, x, t, y) dy dt with the heat kernel p(s, x, t, y) = (2π(t − s))^(−d/2) exp(−|y − x|²/(2(t − s))).

source.citation: S. R. S. Varadhan, Topics in probability: stochastic processes, lecture notes, Courant Institute, New York University, Spring 2011, Chapter 14, The general case.
source.revision: Lecture notes for Spring 2011 (PDF created 2011-04-03), posted on the author's home page.
source.module: Chapter 14, The general case
source.excerpt: Theorem 14.3. Let {a_{i,j}(s, x)} be continuous, positive definite for each (s, x) and satisfy the growth condition |a_{i,j}(s, x)| ≤ C(1 + |x|²), while {b_i(s, x)} are measurable and satisfy the growth condition |b_i(s, x)| ≤ C(1 + |x|). Then for every (s₀, x₀) there is a unique element P_{s₀,x₀} in C(a, b, s₀, x₀) which will be a Markov process with transition probability p(s, x, t, A) = P_{s,x}[x(t) ∈ A].
source.attribution: © S. R. S. Varadhan. Quoted from Topics in probability: stochastic processes (Courant Institute lecture notes) for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The authored statement writes out the martingale problem C(a, b, s₀, x₀) with the drift term, which the notes omit in their definition on p. 1. The outline follows the proof of Theorem 14.3 on p. 4 with Lemma 14.1 (localization, pp. 1-2) and Lemma 14.2 (perturbation, p. 3), and items 2, 3, 5 and 6 of Chapter 10 of the same notes. The original statement for bounded coefficients is Theorem 2.1 of Stroock and Varadhan (1972), p. 363.

source_references.citation: D. W. Stroock and S. R. S. Varadhan, Diffusion processes, Proceedings of the Sixth Berkeley Symposium on Mathematical Statistics and Probability, Vol. 3, University of California Press, 1972, 361–368.
source_references.revision: Scan of the proceedings article in the Berkeley digital collection.
source_references.module: Section 2, Existence and uniqueness: the general case
source_references.excerpt: THEOREM 2.1. The solution P_{s,x} to the martingale problem, starting from the point x at some s, exists and is unique for every s and x. Moreover, P is a strong Markov process with transition probabilities P(s, x, t, A) = P_{s,x}[x(t) ∈ A].
source_references.attribution: © D. W. Stroock and S. R. S. Varadhan. Quoted from Diffusion processes (Proceedings of the Sixth Berkeley Symposium) for identification of the cited result.
source_references.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source_references.alignment: Stroock and Varadhan assume a bounded, continuous and positive definite and b bounded and measurable, and they also state strong Markov property and continuous dependence. The article gives no proof and refers to their 1969 papers. The authored statement replaces boundedness by the growth conditions of Varadhan's Theorem 14.3.

results.proof_status: outline of the cited published proof. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of Theorem 14.3 in Varadhan's Spring 2011 notes, Chapter 14, p. 4, with Lemmas 14.1 and 14.2 and Chapter 10, items 2-6. Step s5 cites the L^p estimate of B. F. Jones from the source, and the source takes existence for bounded coefficients as known.

steps.text: Reduction to bounded coefficients. Modify a and b outside the ball {|x| ≤ ℓ} to bounded coefficients [a_ℓ, b_ℓ] with a unique solution P^ℓ from (s₀, x₀). Every solution P agrees with P^ℓ on F_(τ_ℓ), where τ_ℓ is the exit time from the ball, and τ_ℓ → ∞ because paths are continuous. So uniqueness for bounded coefficients gives uniqueness, without growth conditions.

Existence from a Lyapunov function. For u(x) = 1 + |x|², L_s u = tr a + 2⟨b, x⟩ ≤ C′u by the growth conditions. Itô's formula makes e^(−C′t) u(x(t)) a supermartingale up to τ_ℓ, so E^(P^ℓ)[e^(−C′τ_ℓ)] ≤ (1 + |x₀|²)/(1 + ℓ²) → 0, and P^ℓ[τ_ℓ ≤ t] → 0. For A ∈ F_t, |P^(ℓ₁)(A) − P^(ℓ₂)(A)| ≤ 2P^(ℓ₁∧ℓ₂)[τ_(ℓ₁∧ℓ₂) ≤ t] → 0, so P^ℓ converges to a solution P.

Uniform ellipticity and no drift. For uniqueness with bounded coefficients, modify a outside a large ball so that its eigenvalues lie between two positive constants. Then Girsanov's theorem, with the density exp(∫⟨a⁻¹b, dx⟩ − ½∫⟨b, a⁻¹b⟩ ds) on F_t, maps the solutions for [a, 0] one-to-one onto the solutions for [a, b] (Chapter 10, item 2). So it suffices to take b = 0.

Localization (Lemma 14.1). Assume that each (s, x) has coefficients that agree with [a, b] where |t − s| + |y − x| ≤ ε(s, x), with ε bounded below on compact sets, and that have exactly one solution. Two solutions P₁, P₂ agree on F_τ for the exit time τ from the ε(s₀, x₀)-neighbourhood. After τ, replace both by the unique modified solution from (τ, x(τ)) with regular conditional distributions. Both results solve the modified problem, so they agree. Induction over successive exit times τ_n gives P₁ = P₂ on F_(τ_n). Since τ_n → ∞, |P₁(A) − P₂(A)| ≤ P₁[τ_n ≤ t] + P₂[τ_n ≤ t] → 0.

Perturbation (Lemma 14.2). By continuity, near each (s, x) the matrix a stays close to ā = a(s, x), so the local coefficients of s4 can be close to the constant ā everywhere. After a linear change of variables ā = I. With the heat Green operator G, |Gf(s, x)| ≤ C(T − s)‖f‖_(κ*) for κ* > (d + 2)/2, and the estimate of B. F. Jones gives ‖u_t‖_p + ∑‖u_ij‖_p ≤ C_p‖f‖_p for u = Gf. If sup|a_ij − δ_ij| ≤ δ is small, the equation u_s + ½∑ a_ij u_ij = f on [0, T] × ℝ^d with u(T, ·) = 0 has the solution u = G(I + ½[a_ij − δ_ij](G·)_ij)⁻¹ f, with u ∈ W^(1,2)_p and sup|u| ≤ c(T)‖f‖_p.

Uniqueness and Markov property. For a solution P of the perturbed problem, Itô's formula for u gives E^P ∫_(s₀)^T f(t, x(t)) dt = −u(s₀, x₀) (Chapter 10, items 5 and 6). The source needs the a priori estimate that Λ(f) = E^P ∫ f(t, x(t)) dt is continuous on L^p to apply Itô's formula to u ∈ W^(1,2)_p. The right side does not depend on P, so all solutions have the same one-dimensional laws. Regular conditional distributions of a solution given F_t are again solutions (Chapter 10, item 3). So the finite-dimensional laws agree, and P_(s,x)[x(t₂) ∈ A | F_(t₁)] = p(t₁, x(t₁), t₂, A).

source.ref: S. R. S. Varadhan, Topics in probability: stochastic processes (Courant Institute lecture notes, Spring 2011), Chapter 14, Theorem 14.3 and its proof, p. 4, with Lemmas 14.1 (pp. 1-2) and 14.2 (p. 3).

applications.title: Colloid in a V-shaped potential
applications.inputs: A colloid on a line moves in the potential V(x) = θ|x| with θ = 1, with unit noise: L f = ½ f″ − θ sgn(x) f′. So a ≡ 1 and b(x) = −θ sgn(x), with sgn(0) = 0. It starts at x₀ = 0. The exit level is ℓ = 3.
applications.hypotheses: The diffusion coefficient a ≡ 1 is continuous and positive. The drift b is Borel with |b| ≤ θ ≤ C(1 + |x|). The drift is discontinuous at 0, so the theory of Lipschitz equations does not apply, but the theorem gives a unique Markov law P_x for every start x.

steps.text: Lyapunov bound of step s2: for u(x) = 1 + x², L u = 1 − 2θ|x| ≤ u, so C′ = 1 works. The bound E[e^(−τ_ℓ)] ≤ (1 + x₀²)/(1 + ℓ²) gives E[e^(−τ₃)] ≤ 1/10 from x₀ = 0.

Symmetry: b(−x) = −b(x) and a is even, so if P solves the martingale problem from 0, then the law of −x(·) under P solves it too. By uniqueness both laws are equal, so x(t) and −x(t) have the same law for every t.
Since b is bounded, Girsanov's theorem makes P_0 equivalent to Wiener measure on F_t, so P_0[x(t) = 0] = 0. With the symmetry, P_0[x(t) > 0] = (1 − 0)/2 = 1/2 for every t > 0.

applications.conclusion: The colloid in the V-shaped potential has a unique Markov law although its drift is discontinuous. From the bottom of the potential it is on each side with probability 1/2 at every time, and its exit time τ₃ from (−3, 3) satisfies E[e^(−τ₃)] ≤ 1/10.

limitations: Continuity of a cannot simply be dropped. In dimension d ≥ 3, Nadirashvili (1997) gave a measurable, bounded and uniformly elliptic a for which the martingale problem has more than one solution.
The theorem gives uniqueness in law only. A strong solution and pathwise uniqueness need further conditions, for example Lipschitz coefficients or the Yamada–Watanabe criterion in dimension one.
Without the growth conditions a solution may fail to exist, because the process can explode in finite time. Step s1 shows that uniqueness holds without them.

results.name: Dynkin's formula for Itô diffusions
results.statement: Let f: ℝⁿ → ℝⁿ and g: ℝⁿ → ℝ^(n×m) be Borel functions that are bounded on compact sets. Let W be an m-dimensional Brownian motion and let X be a continuous adapted process with X_t = x + ∫₀ᵗ f(X_s) ds + ∫₀ᵗ g(X_s) dW_s for all t ≥ 0. Put Lφ = ∑ᵢ fᵢ ∂ᵢφ + ½ ∑ᵢⱼ (g gᵀ)ᵢⱼ ∂ᵢ∂ⱼφ. Let τ be a stopping time with E τ < ∞, and let φ: ℝⁿ → ℝ be twice continuously differentiable with compact support. Then E φ(X_τ) = φ(x) + E ∫₀^τ (Lφ)(X_s) ds.
hypotheses: X is a continuous adapted solution of dX_t = f(X_t) dt + g(X_t) dW_t with X₀ = x, and f and g are Borel and bounded on compact sets.
τ is a stopping time for the filtration of W with E τ < ∞.
φ is twice continuously differentiable and has compact support.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 expands φ(X_t) with Itô's formula into a drift integral of Lφ and a stochastic integral.
Step s3 uses the Itô isometry: the stochastic integral of a bounded adapted integrand is a square-integrable martingale.
Step s3 applies the optional stopping theorem at the bounded stopping time τ ∧ N to get mean zero for the stopped stochastic integral.
Step s4 lets N → ∞ on both sides with the dominated convergence theorem, with the bounds sup|φ| and C τ.

definitions.name: generator of the diffusion
definitions.text: The second-order operator Lφ = ∑ᵢ fᵢ ∂ᵢφ + ½ ∑ᵢⱼ (g gᵀ)ᵢⱼ ∂ᵢ∂ⱼφ, which acts on twice continuously differentiable functions φ.

definitions.name: stopping time
definitions.text: A random time τ with values in [0, ∞] such that the event {τ ≤ t} is in F_t for every t ≥ 0.

source.citation: Nils Berglund, Long-time dynamics of stochastic differential equations, lecture notes of the summer school From kinetic equations to statistical mechanics (Saint Jean de Monts, 2021), arXiv:2106.12998.
source.revision: arXiv v2, version of August 24, 2021.
source.module: Chapter 1, Section 1.3.3 Dynkin's formula
source.excerpt: Proposition 1.3.12: Dynkin's formula Let {Xt}t⩾0 be a diffusion with generator L. Fix x ∈ Rⁿ, a stopping time τ such that Eˣ[τ] < ∞, and a compactly supported, twice continuously differentiable function ϕ : Rⁿ → R. Then Eˣ ϕ(Xτ) = ϕ(x) + Eˣ[∫₀^τ (Lϕ)(Xs) ds].
source.attribution: © Nils Berglund. Quoted from the author's lecture notes Long-time dynamics of stochastic differential equations for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states the formula for an Itô diffusion whose equation has a unique solution for all times, with the generator of Proposition 1.3.10. The authored statement needs only a continuous solution and coefficients that are bounded on compact sets, which makes Lφ bounded. The authored proof follows the proof on p. 23: Itô's formula and the vanishing mean of the stochastic integral through τ ∧ N. It stops the whole formula at τ ∧ N and passes to the limit with dominated convergence.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the proof of Proposition 1.3.12 in Berglund's notes. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement in all dimensions n and m.

steps.text: Apply Itô's formula to φ(X_t). The quadratic covariations of the coordinates are d⟨Xⁱ, Xʲ⟩_t = (g gᵀ)ᵢⱼ(X_t) dt. So φ(X_t) = φ(x) + ∫₀ᵗ (Lφ)(X_s) ds + M_t with M_t = ∫₀ᵗ h(X_s) dW_s, where h = (∇φ)ᵀ g is a row vector of length m.

Bounds. Let K be the compact support of φ. Then φ, ∇φ and the second derivatives vanish outside K. On K the functions f and g are bounded, and the derivatives of φ are bounded because they are continuous. Hence there is C with |Lφ(y)| ≤ C and |h(y)| ≤ C for all y ∈ ℝⁿ, and |φ| ≤ C as well.

Stopped formula. The integrand h(X_s) is adapted and bounded by C. By the Itô isometry E M_t² = E ∫₀ᵗ |h(X_s)|² ds ≤ C² t, so M is a square-integrable martingale. Fix N ∈ ℕ. The time τ ∧ N is a bounded stopping time, and the optional stopping theorem gives E M_(τ∧N) = E M₀ = 0. Evaluate step s1 at t = τ ∧ N and take expectations: E φ(X_(τ∧N)) = φ(x) + E ∫₀^(τ∧N) (Lφ)(X_s) ds.

Limit N → ∞. Since E τ < ∞, τ < ∞ almost surely, so τ ∧ N = τ for all large N. Hence X_(τ∧N) → X_τ and ∫₀^(τ∧N) (Lφ)(X_s) ds → ∫₀^τ (Lφ)(X_s) ds almost surely. The left side is bounded by C. The integral is bounded in absolute value by C τ, which is integrable. The dominated convergence theorem applies on both sides and gives E φ(X_τ) = φ(x) + E ∫₀^τ (Lφ)(X_s) ds.

applications.title: Mean escape time of a molecule from a channel
applications.inputs: A molecule diffuses in a channel of length ℓ = 10 µm, open at both ends, with diffusion coefficient D = 1 µm²/s. Its position is X_t = x + √(2D) W_t with x = 2 µm. It escapes at τ = inf{t : X_t ∉ (0, ℓ)}.
applications.hypotheses: X solves the equation with f = 0 and g = √(2D), so Lφ = D φ″. Put u(y) = y(ℓ − y)/(2D) and φ = u χ, where χ is smooth with compact support and χ = 1 on [−1, ℓ + 1]. Then φ is C² with compact support, φ = u ≥ 0 on [0, ℓ] and Lφ = −1 on [0, ℓ]. The time τ ∧ N is a stopping time with finite mean, so the formula applies to it.

steps.text: For s < τ ∧ N the molecule is in (0, ℓ), so (Lφ)(X_s) = −1. Dynkin's formula at τ ∧ N gives E φ(X_(τ∧N)) = φ(x) − E(τ ∧ N). Since X_(τ∧N) ∈ [0, ℓ] and φ ≥ 0 there, E(τ ∧ N) ≤ φ(x).
Monotone convergence as N → ∞ gives E τ ≤ φ(x) < ∞. Now Dynkin's formula applies at τ itself. At the exit time X_τ ∈ {0, ℓ}, so φ(X_τ) = 0 and E τ = φ(x) = x(ℓ − x)/(2D).
With x = 2 µm, ℓ = 10 µm and D = 1 µm²/s, E τ = 2 · (10 − 2)/(2 · 1) = 8 s.
The mean escape time is largest for a release at the centre x = ℓ/2, where it is ℓ²/(8D) = 100/8 = 25/2 s.

applications.conclusion: A molecule released at x in a channel (0, ℓ) escapes after a mean time x(ℓ − x)/(2D). For the given numbers this is 8 s, and the worst release point, the centre, gives 12.5 s.

limitations: The hypotheses cannot simply be dropped. For one-dimensional Brownian motion from 0 and τ = inf{t : W_t = 1}, the function φ(y) = y gives E φ(W_τ) = 1, while φ(0) + E ∫₀^τ ½φ″(W_s) ds = 0. Here φ has no compact support and E τ = ∞.

For a function without compact support, such as |x|², one first replaces it by a function with compact support that agrees with it on the region where the process stays before τ, as in the worked application.
To compute E τ or exit probabilities, one must also solve the boundary value problem Lu = −1 or Lu = 0 for the generator.

results.name: Ray–Knight theorem for Brownian local times
aliases: Ray–Knight theorem on local times at a hitting time
results.statement: Let B be a standard linear Brownian motion with B₀ = 0, let L(t, x) be its jointly continuous local time, normalized as the occupation density, and let τ = inf{t ≥ 0 : B_t = −1}. Put Z_x = L(τ, x) for x ≥ −1. Then Z_(−1) = 0, x ↦ Z_x is continuous, and Z is a Markov process in the level x with the following transition laws. For λ ≥ 0 and −1 ≤ a < b ≤ 0, E[e^(−λZ_b) | Z_y, −1 ≤ y ≤ a] = (1 + 2λ(b − a))^(−1) exp(−λZ_a/(1 + 2λ(b − a))). For λ ≥ 0 and 0 ≤ a < b, E[e^(−λZ_b) | Z_y, −1 ≤ y ≤ a] = exp(−λZ_a/(1 + 2λ(b − a))). These are the transition laws of the squared Bessel processes of dimension 2 and of dimension 0. So Z is a BESQ(2) process on [−1, 0] and a BESQ(0) process on [0, ∞). In particular, {L(τ, x) : −1 ≤ x ≤ 0} has the law of {|W(x + 1)|² : −1 ≤ x ≤ 0} for a standard planar Brownian motion W.
hypotheses: B is a standard linear Brownian motion with B₀ = 0.
L(t, x) is the jointly continuous local time of B, the density of the occupation measure.
τ is the first hitting time of the level −1.

prerequisites.reason: Steps s1 and s4 use that the excursions from a level form a Poisson point process with n(sup f > δ) = n(inf f < −δ) = 1/(2δ).
Step s2 adds the occupation densities of single excursions, and step s6 uses that L(τ, x) is continuous in x.
Step s6 uses that the finite-dimensional laws, a π-system of events, determine the law of a continuous process.

definitions.name: local time
definitions.text: L(t, x) is the density at x of the occupation measure A ↦ ∫₀ᵗ 1_A(B_s) ds, chosen continuous in (t, x). With this normalization |B_t − x| − L(t, x) is a martingale.

definitions.name: squared Bessel process BESQ(δ)
definitions.text: For δ ≥ 0, the nonnegative Markov process with E_z e^(−λZ_t) = (1 + 2λt)^(−δ/2) exp(−λz/(1 + 2λt)). It solves dZ = δ dt + 2√Z dW, and for an integer δ it is the squared norm of a δ-dimensional Brownian motion.

definitions.name: excursion from a
definitions.text: A piece of the path between two consecutive visits to the level a. It lies either above a or below a.

source.citation: L. C. G. Rogers, A guided tour through excursions, Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society 21 (1989), 305–341.
source.revision: Scan of the journal version (PDF created 2006-07-15), posted on the author's home page.
source.module: Section 3, Brownian local time and excursions
source.excerpt: THEOREM 4 (Ray, Knight). Let τ = inf{t : B_t = −1}. Then the process {L(τ, x) : x ≥ −1} is a time-inhomogeneous diffusion, behaving like a BESQ(2) process for −1 ≤ x ≤ 0, and like a BESQ(0) process for x > 0.
source.attribution: © L. C. G. Rogers. Quoted from A guided tour through excursions (Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society) for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: Rogers states the theorem for Brownian motion from 0 and the local time of his Section 3, for which |B| − L is a martingale. He remarks that the exact meaning of BESQ(n) is not important, because the proof finds the transition mechanism. The authored statement writes out these transition laws as Laplace transforms and adds the planar Brownian form on [−1, 0]. The proof in the source treats −1 < x < 0 and says that the case x > 0 is similar. The outline writes out that case and the identification that the source leaves to general results.

results.proof_status: outline of the cited published proof. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the excursion proof of THEOREM 4 in Rogers (1989), p. 315, which rests on Itô's excursion theorem and Proposition 2 of the source. The source proves the case −1 < x < 0 and says that the case x > 0 is similar. Step s5 writes out that case, and step s6 writes out the identification of the law that the source leaves to general results.

steps.text: Excursions from a level (the proof in the source, p. 315). Fix a ∈ (−1, 0) and let H_a = inf{t : B_t = a}. By the strong Markov property, the first piece {B_t : t ≤ H_a} is independent of B(H_a + ·), a Brownian motion from a. By Itô's excursion theorem, the excursions of B(H_a + ·) − a from 0, labelled by the local time L(·, a), form a Poisson point process with intensity Leb ⊗ n. Its restrictions Ξ₊ to excursions above a and Ξ₋ to excursions below a are independent Poisson point processes. By Proposition 2 of the source, n(sup f > δ) = n(inf f < −δ) = 1/(2δ) for δ > 0.

Splitting the local times. The time τ falls in the first excursion below a that reaches the depth 1 + a. Its label ℓ = L(τ, a) is a function of Ξ₋ alone, and it is exponential with mean 2(1 + a). By the occupation density formula, L(τ, x) is the sum of the local times at x of the first piece and of the excursions that start before τ. For x > a, only the first piece and the points of Ξ₊ with label below ℓ contribute. For −1 ≤ x ≤ a, only the points of Ξ₋ with label at most ℓ contribute, including the part of the last excursion before it hits −1. The first piece stays above a and adds nothing at x ≤ a.

Markov property (the source, p. 315). Ξ₊ is independent of Ξ₋, so given Ξ₋ the points of Ξ₊ with label below ℓ still form a Poisson point process, whose law depends only on ℓ. The first piece is independent of both. So {L(τ, x) : x ≥ a} and {L(τ, x) : −1 ≤ x ≤ a} are conditionally independent given L(τ, a) = ℓ. As a ∈ (−1, 0) is arbitrary, Z_x = L(τ, x) is a Markov process in the level x on [−1, 0].

Transition law on [−1, 0] (the source, p. 315). Let b = a + δ ≤ 0. Given ℓ, the number K of points of Ξ₊ with label below ℓ that reach b has the Poisson law with mean ℓ n(sup f > δ) = ℓ/(2δ). By the strong Markov property at the hitting time of b, each of them adds to L(τ, b) an independent amount with the law of the local time at 0 of a Brownian motion before it hits −δ. By step s1 this amount is exponential with rate n(inf f < −δ) = 1/(2δ), so its Laplace transform is (1 + 2δλ)^(−1). The first piece passes b on its way to a and adds one more such amount. So E[e^(−λL(τ, b)) | ℓ] = Σ_k e^(−ℓ/(2δ)) (ℓ/(2δ))^k/k! (1 + 2δλ)^(−k−1) = (1 + 2δλ)^(−1) exp(−λℓ/(1 + 2δλ)).

Levels x ≥ 0 (the source says that this case is similar). For a ≥ 0 the same splitting holds on the event H_a < τ, with one change: the first piece {B_t : t ≤ H_a} stays below a and adds nothing at levels b > a. On the event τ < H_a, L(τ, x) = 0 for all x ≥ a, which agrees with ℓ = 0. So the Markov property holds at a, and for b = a + δ the sum has no extra factor: E[e^(−λL(τ, b)) | ℓ] = exp(−λℓ/(1 + 2δλ)).

Identification (the source leaves it to general results). Z_(−1) = L(τ, −1) = 0, because τ is the first visit to −1. Steps s3 to s5 give the Markov property at every level and the transition Laplace transforms, which determine laws on [0, ∞). By induction over levels −1 < x₁ < … < x_m, the finite-dimensional laws of Z are those of the process with these kernels. For a planar Brownian motion W, each coordinate gives E e^(−λ(w + √t N)²) = (1 + 2λt)^(−1/2) exp(−λw²/(1 + 2λt)) for a standard normal N, so |W|² has the dimension-2 kernel. The map x ↦ L(τ, x) is continuous, so the finite-dimensional laws determine the law on path space.

source.ref: L. C. G. Rogers, A guided tour through excursions, Bull. London Math. Soc. 21 (1989), THEOREM 4 (Ray, Knight) and its proof, p. 315.

applications.title: Time that a diffusing tracer spends near a detector before absorption
applications.inputs: A tracer particle moves along a line as a standard Brownian motion B from 0. An absorbing wall at −1 removes it at the time τ. A detector at the level 1 measures L(τ, 1): the time that the particle spends in [1, 1 + h] before removal is about h L(τ, 1) for small h. Lengths and times are in the units in which B has variance t at time t.
applications.hypotheses: B is a standard Brownian motion from 0, τ is its first visit to −1, and L is its occupation density. So Z_x = L(τ, x) satisfies the theorem.

steps.text: On [−1, 0], Z is BESQ(2) from Z_(−1) = 0. So Z_0 = L(τ, 0) has the law of |W(1)|², which is exponential with mean 2, and E e^(−µZ_0) = 1/(1 + 2µ).
Let λ → ∞. Then P(L(τ, 1) = 0) = 1/2. This agrees with the gambler's ruin probability that B hits −1 before 1.

Given Z_0 = z, the BESQ(0) law at distance 1 has mean z and variance 4z, from the expansion of exp(−λz/(1 + 2λ)). So E Z_1 = E Z_0 = 2 and E Z_1² = E[Z_0² + 4Z_0] = 8 + 8 = 16. The variance of L(τ, 1) is 16 − 2² = 12.

applications.conclusion: The time density near the detector has mean 2 and variance 12. It is 0 with probability 1/2, so on the event that the particle reaches the detector its mean is 4.

limitations: The theorem depends on the stopping rule. The second Ray–Knight theorem stops B at an inverse local time at 0 and gives BESQ(0) processes on both sides of 0, and its generalized form is a separate row of this pack.

The level x plays the role of time, and the law changes at the starting point 0, where the dimension drops from 2 to 0. Mörters and Peres (Brownian Motion, Theorem 6.28) prove the part on [−1, 0], for Brownian motion from a stopped at 0, with downcrossing counts instead of excursion theory.

results.name: Itô's excursion theorem for Brownian motion
aliases: Poisson point process of Brownian excursions
Itô's theorem on the excursion point process
results.statement: Let B be a standard linear Brownian motion with B₀ = 0, and let L_t be its local time at 0, normalized so that |B_t| − L_t is a martingale. Let γ_ℓ = inf{u ≥ 0 : L_u > ℓ} and γ_ℓ− = lim_{s↑ℓ} γ_s for ℓ > 0. Let U be the set of excursions: continuous f : [0, ∞) → ℝ with f(0) = 0, ζ(f) = inf{t > 0 : f(t) = 0} ∈ (0, ∞) and f(t) = 0 for t ≥ ζ(f), with the σ-algebra of the coordinate maps. For each ℓ > 0 with γ_ℓ− < γ_ℓ, let e_ℓ(u) = B((γ_ℓ− + u) ∧ γ_ℓ) for u ≥ 0. Then the random measure Ξ = Σ δ_(ℓ, e_ℓ), summed over these ℓ, is a Poisson point process on (0, ∞) × U with intensity Leb ⊗ n for a σ-finite measure n on U, the excursion measure. That is, for disjoint measurable C₁, …, C_k ⊂ (0, ∞) × U, the counts Ξ(C₁), …, Ξ(C_k) are independent, and Ξ(C_i) has the Poisson law with mean (Leb ⊗ n)(C_i), where a count with mean ∞ is ∞ almost surely. Moreover, n(U) = ∞ and n({f : sup f > a}) = n({f : inf f < −a}) = 1/(2a) for every a > 0.
hypotheses: B is a standard linear Brownian motion with B₀ = 0.
L is the local time of B at 0, normalized so that |B| − L is a martingale.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 takes the local time L at 0 from Tanaka's formula, and step s6 uses that |B| − L is a martingale.
Step s5 uses monotone convergence to show that the mean measure E Ξ(·) is countably additive.
Step s6 applies optional sampling to the martingale |B| − L at the bounded stopping time H ∧ t.
Step s6 lets t → ∞ in E|B(H ∧ t)|, where |B(H ∧ t)| ≤ a gives the bound.

definitions.name: excursion
definitions.text: A piece of the path between two consecutive zeros: a continuous path f with f(0) = 0 that is nonzero on (0, ζ) and returns to 0 at the time ζ = ζ(f), its lifetime.

definitions.name: inverse local time
definitions.text: γ_ℓ = inf{u : L_u > ℓ}, the first time at which the local time at 0 exceeds ℓ. Its jumps (γ_ℓ−, γ_ℓ) are the excursion intervals.

definitions.name: Poisson point process with intensity µ
definitions.text: A random counting measure Ξ such that for disjoint sets C₁, …, C_k the counts Ξ(C_i) are independent Poisson variables with means µ(C_i).

definitions.name: excursion measure
definitions.text: The σ-finite measure n on U such that n(A) is the expected number of excursions in A per unit of local time at 0.

source.citation: L. C. G. Rogers, A guided tour through excursions, Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society 21 (1989), 305–341.
source.revision: Scan of the journal version (PDF created 2006-07-15), posted on the author's home page.
source.module: Section 3, Brownian local time and excursions
source.excerpt: THEOREM (Ito). The excursion point process is a POISSON point process with excursion measure Lebesgue × n, where the σ-finite measure n on U is called the excursion measure, or characteristic measure.
source.attribution: © L. C. G. Rogers. Quoted from A guided tour through excursions (Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society) for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: Rogers defines the excursion point process on p. 312: it has a point (ℓ, e) when B makes the excursion e at local time ℓ, and U is the space of excursions. The authored statement writes out this point process and the Poisson property, and it adds Proposition 2 of the source (p. 314), n(sup f > a) = 1/(2a). The proof in the source shows the renewal property and that one count is a Poisson process, and it refers to Itô (1972) for the rest. The outline completes it with Theorem 3.1 and Section 4 of K. Itô, Poisson point processes attached to Markov processes, Proc. Sixth Berkeley Symp. 3 (1972), 225-239.

results.proof_status: outline of the cited published proof. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of THEOREM (Ito) in Rogers (1989), p. 313, and the proof of Proposition 2, p. 314. For the joint Poisson law and the intensity the source refers to Itô (1972), and steps s4 and s5 follow Theorem 3.1 (p. 227) and Section 4 of that paper. Step s4 rests on the classical fact that the jump counts of a process with independent increments are independent Poisson variables.

steps.text: Inverse local time (set-up of the source, pp. 312-313). By Tanaka's formula, L is continuous and nondecreasing, and the measure dL is carried by the zero set Z = {t : B_t = 0}. In fact the support of dL is Z. So γ_ℓ = inf{u : L_u > ℓ} is a stopping time, finite because L_∞ = ∞, and B(γ_ℓ) = 0 because γ_ℓ is a point of right increase of L. The open intervals (γ_ℓ−, γ_ℓ) are exactly the components of {t : B_t ≠ 0}. So each excursion of B from 0 carries one label ℓ, the value of L during the excursion.

Regeneration (the proof in the source, p. 313). By the strong Markov property, B(γ_ℓ + ·) is a Brownian motion from 0 and is independent of F(γ_ℓ). Its local time at 0 is L(γ_ℓ + ·) − ℓ. The restriction of Ξ to (0, ℓ] × U is F(γ_ℓ)-measurable. The shifted process θ_ℓΞ, with a point (s − ℓ, e) for each point (s, e) of Ξ with s > ℓ, is the excursion process of B(γ_ℓ + ·). So θ_ℓΞ is independent of Ξ restricted to (0, ℓ] × U and has the same law as Ξ. In the words of Itô (1972), Ξ is a renewal point process.

One count is a Poisson process. Let U_m = {f ∈ U : ζ(f) > 1/m}. The excursion intervals before γ_t are disjoint subintervals of [0, γ_t], so at most mγ_t of them are longer than 1/m. Thus Ξ((0, t] × U_m) < ∞ for all t, and U is the union of the U_m (Itô calls this σ-discrete). For measurable A ⊂ U_m, the count N_t = Ξ((0, t] × A) is finite, nondecreasing and moves by jumps of size 1, because one local time carries at most one excursion. By step s2 it has stationary independent increments. So N is a Poisson process with a finite rate. The source proves this and refers to Itô (1972) for the rest.

Joint Poisson law (Itô 1972, Theorem 3.1, p. 227). Take disjoint measurable E₁, …, E_k ⊂ (0, ∞) × U_m and put Z_i(t) = Ξ(E_i ∩ ((0, t] × U)). By step s2, Z*(t) = Σ_i i Z_i(t) has independent increments. It is continuous in probability, because it jumps only when the Poisson process Ξ((0, t] × U_m) jumps. Z_i(t) counts the jumps of Z* of size i. For a process with independent increments that is continuous in probability, the counts of jumps of different sizes are independent Poisson variables. Let t → ∞. Then let m → ∞ as in (3.1) of Itô, where a Poisson variable with mean ∞ is ∞ almost surely.

Intensity (Itô 1972, Section 4). Put M(E) = E Ξ(E). Monotone convergence makes M a measure. By step s2, M does not change under shifts of the local-time coordinate, and M((0, t] × U_m) < ∞ by step s3. So t ↦ M((0, t] × A) is linear for A ⊂ U_m, and M = Leb ⊗ n for a unique σ-finite measure n on U. With step s4, each Ξ(E_i) has the Poisson law with mean (Leb ⊗ n)(E_i). The zeros of B accumulate at time 0 and γ₁ > 0, so B makes infinitely many excursions with labels in (0, 1]. Hence n(U) = ∞.

Value of n (Proposition 2 of the source, p. 314). Let A = {f : sup_t |f(t)| > a} and H = inf{t : |B_t| = a}. The first excursion in A has the label L_H. By step s5, P(L_H > ℓ) = P(Ξ((0, ℓ] × A) = 0) = exp(−ℓ n(A)), so E L_H = 1/n(A). Tanaka's formula makes |B| − L a martingale. Optional sampling at H ∧ t gives E L(H ∧ t) = E|B(H ∧ t)|. Monotone convergence on the left and bounded convergence on the right give E L_H = a. So n(A) = 1/a. The map B ↦ −B keeps the law of B and of L, so the disjoint sets {sup f > a} and {inf f < −a} each have measure 1/(2a).

source.ref: L. C. G. Rogers, A guided tour through excursions, Bull. London Math. Soc. 21 (1989), THEOREM (Ito) and its proof, p. 313, and Proposition 2, p. 314.

applications.title: Sensor counts of a diffusing tracer before it reaches a trap
applications.inputs: A tracer molecule moves along a channel as a standard Brownian motion B from the binding site 0. A sensor registers each excursion from 0 that goes above the level a = 1/2. A trap at the level −b = −2 absorbs the molecule. Lengths and times are in the units in which B has variance t at time t.
applications.hypotheses: B is a standard Brownian motion from 0, and the sets A = {f : sup f > 1/2} and C = {f : inf f < −2} of excursions are disjoint, because an excursion keeps one sign.

steps.text: The theorem gives n(A) = 1/(2a) = 1 and n(C) = 1/(2b) = 1/4. The molecule reaches the trap during the first excursion in C.
The local-time labels of the points in A and in C form independent Poisson processes with rates 1 and 1/4. So the local time at 0 before trapping is exponential with rate 1/4, and its mean is 4.

Each next point in A ∪ C is in A with probability n(A)/(n(A) + n(C)) = 4/5, independently of the earlier points. So the number M of sensor counts before trapping has P(M ≥ k) = (4/5)^k. For k = 1 this is P(H_(1/2) < H_(−2)) = b/(a + b) = 4/5, the gambler's ruin probability.
The mean number of sensor counts is E M = Σ_(k≥1) (4/5)^k = n(A)/n(C) = 4.

applications.conclusion: Before the trap absorbs it, the tracer makes on average 4 excursions that reach the sensor level, and it reaches the sensor at least once with probability 4/5.

limitations: The value of n depends on the normalization of the local time. If L is replaced by cL for a constant c > 0, the intensity of the excursion point process becomes Leb ⊗ (n/c).
The theorem describes the excursions as a whole, indexed by local time. The excursion that straddles a fixed time t is not a typical excursion: its length is size-biased, so it is longer on average.
Itô (1972) proves the Poisson structure for the excursions of a standard Markov process from a recurrent state. This record states only the case of linear Brownian motion and the state 0.

results.name: Lévy's arcsine law for the last zero of Brownian motion
aliases: first arcsine law for Brownian motion
arcsine law for the last zero of Brownian motion
results.statement: Let B be a standard linear Brownian motion with B(0) = 0, and let L = sup{t ∈ [0, 1] : B(t) = 0} be its last zero in [0, 1]. Almost surely B attains its maximum over [0, 1] at exactly one time M*. Then L and M* have the same law, the arcsine law: P(L ≤ s) = P(M* ≤ s) = (2/π) arcsin √s for every s ∈ [0, 1]. Equivalently, both have the density 1/(π√(s(1 − s))) on (0, 1).
hypotheses: B is a standard linear Brownian motion: B(0) = 0, the paths are continuous, and the increments are independent, with B(t) − B(r) of law N(0, t − r) for r < t.

prerequisites.reason: Step s2 uses the weak Markov property at the fixed time s: B(s + ·) − B(s) is a Brownian motion independent of the path up to time s.
Step s3 uses the reflection principle in the form M(r) has the same law as |B(r)| for the running maximum M at a fixed time r.
Step s4 changes the planar Gaussian density to polar coordinates to show that the angle of (Z₁, Z₂) is uniform.
Step s5 uses Lévy's identity that M − B and |B| have the same law as processes, to move from the maximiser M* to the last zero L.

definitions.name: arcsine distribution
definitions.text: The law on [0, 1] with distribution function (2/π) arcsin √s and density 1/(π√(s(1 − s))). The density is large near 0 and near 1.

definitions.name: last zero
definitions.text: L = sup{t ∈ [0, 1] : B(t) = 0}. The set is not empty because B(0) = 0, and it is closed because B is continuous.

definitions.name: running maximum
definitions.text: M(t) = max{B(r) : 0 ≤ r ≤ t}, the largest value of the path up to time t.

source.citation: Peter Mörters and Yuval Peres, Brownian Motion, Cambridge Series in Statistical and Probabilistic Mathematics 30, Cambridge University Press, 2010.
source.revision: Authors' version of the book (PDF created 2010-01-06), posted on the first author's home page.
source.module: Chapter 5, Section 5.4 The arcsine laws for random walk and Brownian motion
source.excerpt: L = sup{t ∈ [0, 1] : B(t) = 0}, the last zero of Brownian motion in [0, 1], is arcsine distributed, and (b) the random variable M* ∈ [0, 1], which is almost surely uniquely determined by B(M*) = max_{s∈[0,1]} B(s), is arcsine distributed.
source.attribution: © Peter Mörters and Yuval Peres. Quoted from the authors' version of Brownian Motion for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The authored statement is the source theorem with the distribution function and the density written out. The authored proof follows the proof of Theorem 5.26: time reversal at s, the reflection principle, scaling and polar coordinates for part (b), and Lévy's identity for part (a). It also proves the uniqueness of the maximiser, which the source takes from its Theorem 2.11.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the proof of Theorem 5.26 in Mörters and Peres. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement: uniqueness of the maximiser, the law of M*, the law of L and the density.

steps.text: The maximiser is unique. Take rationals 0 ≤ a < b < c < d ≤ 1. Then max_[c,d] B − max_[a,b] B = (B(c) − B(b)) + (max_[c,d] B − B(c)) − (max_[a,b] B − B(b)). The first term has law N(0, c − b) and is independent of the other two terms by independent increments. So the difference has a continuous law, and the two maxima are equal with probability 0. If the maximum over [0, 1] were attained at times t₁ < t₂, then rationals a ≤ t₁ ≤ b < c ≤ t₂ ≤ d would give equal maxima on [a, b] and [c, d]. There are countably many such quadruples, so M* is almost surely unique.

Fix s ∈ (0, 1). By step s1, {M* < s} = {max_[0,s] B > max_[s,1] B} up to a null event. Put B₁(t) = B(s − t) − B(s) for 0 ≤ t ≤ s and B₂(t) = B(s + t) − B(s) for 0 ≤ t ≤ 1 − s. B₁ is continuous and centred Gaussian, and Cov(B₁(t), B₁(u)) = (s − max(t, u)) − (s − t) − (s − u) + s = min(t, u). So B₁ is a Brownian motion on [0, s]. By the weak Markov property, B₂ is a Brownian motion independent of the path up to time s, hence independent of B₁. Subtract B(s) from both maxima: {M* < s} = {M₁(s) > M₂(1 − s)}, where Mᵢ is the running maximum of Bᵢ.

The reflection principle gives M₁(s) ~ |B₁(s)| and M₂(1 − s) ~ |B₂(1 − s)|, and the two maxima are independent. Brownian scaling gives B₁(s) ~ √s Z₁ and B₂(1 − s) ~ √(1 − s) Z₂, with Z₁ and Z₂ independent standard normal. Hence P(M* < s) = P(√s |Z₁| > √(1 − s) |Z₂|) = P(Z₂² < s(Z₁² + Z₂²)).

Write (Z₁, Z₂) = (R cos θ, R sin θ). The change of variables to polar coordinates turns the density (2π)⁻¹ e^(−(x² + y²)/2) dx dy into (2π)⁻¹ r e^(−r²/2) dr dθ. So θ is uniform on [0, 2π). The event of step s3 is {|sin θ| < √s}. With α = arcsin √s, this set of angles is [0, α) ∪ (π − α, π + α) ∪ (2π − α, 2π), of total length 4α. So P(M* < s) = 4α/(2π) = (2/π) arcsin √s. This function is continuous in s, so P(M* = s) = 0 and P(M* ≤ s) has the same value. Its derivative (2/π) · (1/√(1 − s)) · (1/(2√s)) = 1/(π√(s(1 − s))) is the density.

For part (a), Lévy's identity says that (M(t) − B(t))_{t ≤ 1} and (|B(t)|)_{t ≤ 1} have the same law on C[0, 1]. Let Λ(f) = sup{t ∈ [0, 1] : f(t) = 0} for continuous f with f(0) = 0. Λ is measurable, because {Λ ≥ s} = {min_[s,1] |f| = 0} is a closed set. Λ(|B|) = L. At t = M*, B(t) = M(t). For t ∈ (M*, 1], step s1 gives B(t) < B(M*) ≤ M(t). So Λ(M − B) = M*. Hence L has the same law as M*, which is the arcsine law of step s4.

applications.title: Last return of a diffusing tracer to its release plane
applications.inputs: A tracer particle moves along the x axis by free diffusion with coefficient D > 0, so X(t) = √(2D) B(t) with B a standard Brownian motion and X(0) = 0. The observation window is [0, T] with T = 60 s. Let g_T = sup{t ≤ T : X(t) = 0} be the last time the tracer is on its release plane x = 0.
applications.hypotheses: X/√(2D) = B is a standard Brownian motion. By Brownian scaling, B_T(u) = T^(−1/2) B(Tu), 0 ≤ u ≤ 1, is again a standard Brownian motion. Its last zero in [0, 1] is g_T/T, so the theorem applies to g_T/T.

steps.text: The zeros of X are the zeros of B. Scaling gives g_T/T ~ L, so P(g_T ≤ uT) = (2/π) arcsin √u for 0 ≤ u ≤ 1. The result depends neither on D nor on T.
First quarter: u = 1/4 and arcsin(1/2) = π/6. So P(g_T ≤ T/4) = (2/π) · (π/6) = 2/6 = 1/3.
Last quarter: arcsin(√3/2) = π/3, so P(g_T ≥ 3T/4) = 1 − (2/π) · (π/3) = 1 − 2/3 = 1/3. The middle half (T/4, 3T/4) gets the remaining probability 1 − 1/3 − 1/3 = 1/3.
With T = 60 s, the event g_T ≤ T/4 means that the tracer does not touch x = 0 during the last 45 s of observation. This event has probability 1/3, although Brownian motion is recurrent.

applications.conclusion: The last return time g_T has the U-shaped arcsine law on [0, T]. The first quarter of the window and the last quarter each hold probability 1/3, and the middle half holds only 1/3.

limitations: The law concerns a fixed time window. On [0, ∞) Brownian motion returns to 0 at arbitrarily large times, so there is no last zero.
Lévy's second arcsine law, for the time that B spends above 0 during [0, 1], gives the same law but needs a different proof.
For a simple random walk the arcsine law holds only in the limit of many steps, through Donsker's invariance principle.

results.name: Pitman's 2M − X theorem
aliases: Pitman's theorem on the three-dimensional Bessel process
results.statement: Let B be a standard linear Brownian motion with B(0) = 0 and M(t) = max_(0≤s≤t) B(s). Let ρ(t) = |W(t)| for a standard three-dimensional Brownian motion W with W(0) = 0 (the three-dimensional Bessel process started at 0), and let I(t) = inf_(s≥t) ρ(s) be its future infimum. Then the processes {(2M(t) − B(t), M(t)) : t ≥ 0} and {(ρ(t), I(t)) : t ≥ 0} have the same law as random elements of C([0, ∞), ℝ²). In particular 2M − B is a three-dimensional Bessel process, and almost surely M(t) = inf_(s≥t) (2M(s) − B(s)) for all t ≥ 0.
hypotheses: B is a standard linear Brownian motion started at 0, and M is its running maximum.
ρ = |W| for a standard three-dimensional Brownian motion W started at 0, and I is the future infimum of ρ.

prerequisites.reason: Step s7 uses Donsker's invariance principle to pass from the simple random walk S to the Brownian motion B.
Step s7 applies the continuous mapping theorem to the continuous map f ↦ (2 max f − f, max f) on path space.
Step s6 applies optional stopping to the martingale ρ(t)² − 3t at the embedding times to get E[τ_(j+1) − τ_j] = h².
Step s6 uses Doob's L² maximal inequality for the martingale τ_j − jh² to control the embedding times uniformly.

concepts: simple random walk conditioned to avoid zero

definitions.name: three-dimensional Bessel process
definitions.text: The process ρ(t) = |W(t)| for a three-dimensional Brownian motion W. Started at r > 0 it never hits 0, and it ever reaches a level a < r with probability a/r.

definitions.name: future infimum
definitions.text: I(t) = inf_(s≥t) ρ(s), the lowest value that ρ takes after time t. It is nondecreasing and continuous because ρ is continuous and tends to infinity.

definitions.name: walk conditioned to avoid zero
definitions.text: The Markov chain on {1, 2, …} that jumps from k to k + 1 with probability (k + 1)/(2k) and to k − 1 with probability (k − 1)/(2k). It is the Doob h-transform of simple random walk with h(x) = x.

source.citation: Peter Mörters and Yuval Peres, Brownian Motion, Cambridge Series in Statistical and Probabilistic Mathematics 30, Cambridge University Press, 2010.
source.revision: Authors' version of the book (PDF created 2010-01-06), posted on the first author's home page.
source.module: Chapter 5, Section 5.5 Pitman's 2M − B theorem
source.excerpt: … Also let {ρ(t) : t ⩾ 0} be a three-dimensional Bessel process and let {I(t) : t ⩾ 0} be the corresponding future infimum process given by I(t) = inf_(s⩾t) ρ(s). Then {(2M(t) − B(t), M(t)) : t ⩾ 0} =d {(ρ(t), I(t)) : t ⩾ 0}. In particular, {2M(t) − B(t) : t ⩾ 0} is a three-dimensional Bessel process.
source.attribution: © Peter Mörters and Yuval Peres. Quoted from the authors' version of Brownian Motion for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The excerpt omits the title 'Theorem 5.34 (Pitman's 2M − B theorem)' and the first sentence, which defines B and M = max B, because sp.py places excerpts in this long file several hundred characters too early. The record makes both starting points explicit and adds the almost sure identity M(t) = inf_(s≥t)(2M − B)(s), which follows from the equality in law. The outline follows the source proof, which is Pitman's discrete argument plus Donsker's invariance principle, with one correction: the discrete identity (5.18) needs the conditioned walk started at 1 and the shifted pair (2M̃ − S + 1, M̃ + 1). The original result is J. W. Pitman, Adv. Appl. Probab. 7 (1975) 511-526.

results.proof_status: outline of the cited published proof. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of Theorem 5.34 in Mörters and Peres (2010), Section 5.5, with Lemma 5.31, Lemma 5.32 and Proposition 5.33. Steps s1 to s5 prove the discrete identity by a comparison of transition probabilities, step s6 takes the embedding and scaling estimates from Lemma 5.32 and Proposition 5.33, and step s7 passes to the limit. Step s1 corrects the starting point of the discrete identity.

steps.text: Discrete objects and the corrected discrete identity. Let S be simple random walk on ℤ with S(0) = 0 and M̃(j) = max_(a≤j) S(a). Let ρ̃ be the walk on {1, 2, …} conditioned to avoid zero, with p(k, k + 1) = (k + 1)/(2k) and p(k, k − 1) = (k − 1)/(2k) as in (5.13), started at ρ̃(0) = 1, and let Ĩ(j) = min_(k≥j) ρ̃(k). The claim is (2M̃ − S + 1, M̃ + 1) =d (ρ̃, Ĩ) as processes indexed by j ≥ 0, or equivalently (S, M̃) =d (2Ĩ − ρ̃ − 1, Ĩ − 1). The source states (5.18) with ρ̃(0) = Ĩ(0) = 0 and no shift. That version fails at j = 1, because then ρ̃(1) = 1 and Ĩ(1) = 1 almost surely while M̃(1) is 0 or 1. The shifted form is Pitman's original one, and the computations of the source apply to it without change.

The chain (S, M̃) (equations (5.19) and (5.20)). It is a Markov chain on {(s, m) ∈ ℤ² : s ≤ m} started at (0, 0). If s < m, it moves to (s + 1, m) or (s − 1, m) with probability 1/2 each. If s = m, it moves to (s + 1, m + 1) or (s − 1, m) with probability 1/2 each.

Ĩ is the running maximum of 2Ĩ − ρ̃. For j ≤ k, 2Ĩ(j) − ρ̃(j) ≤ Ĩ(j) ≤ Ĩ(k), because Ĩ ≤ ρ̃ and Ĩ is nondecreasing. Let j* be the first index with Ĩ(j*) = Ĩ(k). If j* = 0 then ρ̃(0) = 1 = Ĩ(0). If j* > 0 then ρ̃(j* − 1) = Ĩ(j* − 1) < Ĩ(j*) ≤ ρ̃(j*), and steps of size 1 force ρ̃(j*) = Ĩ(j*). So 2Ĩ(j*) − ρ̃(j*) = Ĩ(k). The pair (s, m) = (2Ĩ − ρ̃ − 1, Ĩ − 1) therefore satisfies s ≤ m, with s = m exactly when ρ̃ = Ĩ, and it starts at (0, 0).

The conditional law of the future minimum (Lemma 5.31). The path probabilities of ρ̃ are (x_ℓ/x_0)·2^(−ℓ), that is x_ℓ/x_0 times those of simple random walk. Since simple random walk is recurrent, the walk ρ̃ started at k reaches i ∈ {1, …, k} with probability i/k. Hence P(Ĩ(j) = i | ρ̃(j) = k) = i/k − (i − 1)/k = 1/k, so Ĩ(j) is uniform on {1, …, k} given ρ̃(j) = k.

Matching transitions ((5.21)-(5.24)). Let G_j be generated by ρ̃(0), …, ρ̃(j) and Ĩ(j). The past of the pair is G_j-measurable, since Ĩ(a) = min(min_(a≤l≤j) ρ̃(l), Ĩ(j)) for a ≤ j. By the Markov property, conditional probabilities given G_j depend only on (ρ̃(j), Ĩ(j)) = (k, i). If i < k, then Ĩ(j + 1) = i and P(ρ̃(j + 1) = k − 1 | G_j) = ((k − 1)/(2k))·(1/(k − 1))/(1/k) = 1/2, so (s, m) moves to (s ± 1, m) with probability 1/2 each. If i = k, then ρ̃(j + 1) = k + 1 and P(Ĩ(j + 1) = k + 1 | G_j) = ((k + 1)/(2k))·(1/(k + 1))/(1/k) = 1/2, so (s, m) moves to (s + 1, m + 1) or (s − 1, m) with probability 1/2 each. These are the transitions of s2 from the same starting point, which proves the identity of s1.

Embedding and scaling (Lemma 5.32 and Proposition 5.33). Fix h > 0 and x_h ∈ ℝ³ with |x_h| = h, put ρ_h(t) = |x_h + W(t)|, τ_0 = 0 and τ_(j+1) = inf{t > τ_j : |ρ_h(t) − ρ_h(τ_j)| = h}. From radius kh, three-dimensional Brownian motion reaches radius (k − 1)h before (k + 1)h with probability (1/k − 1/(k + 1))/(1/(k − 1) − 1/(k + 1)) = (k − 1)/(2k) (Theorem 3.18 of the source), so by the strong Markov property (ρ_h(τ_j)/h)_j is the walk ρ̃ of s1. Optional stopping for ρ_h² − 3t gives E[τ_(j+1) − τ_j | F_(τ_j)] = h², Lemma 5.32 with Brownian scaling gives Var(τ_n − nh²) ≤ Cnh⁴, and Doob's inequality gives E[max_(j≤T/h²) (τ_j − jh²)²] ≤ 4CTh². By uniform continuity, max_(t≤T) |ρ_h(τ_⌊t/h²⌋) − ρ_h(t)| → 0 in probability. Between τ_k and τ_(k+1) the path stays within h of ρ_h(τ_k), so h·Ĩ(j) differs from inf_(s≥τ_j) ρ_h(s) by at most h. Finally |ρ_h − ρ| ≤ h and the future infima differ by at most h.

Passage to the limit. Fix T > 0. By Donsker's theorem the rescaled walk h·S(t/h²), linearly interpolated, converges in law in C[0, T] to B. The map f ↦ (2 max_[0,t] f − f(t), max_[0,t] f) is continuous on C[0, T], and the shift +1, the interpolation and the step versions change the processes by at most 2h in the supremum norm. So h·(2M̃ − S + 1, M̃ + 1)(t/h²) converges in law to (2M − B, M) by the continuous mapping theorem. By s5 the same process has the law of h·(ρ̃, Ĩ)(t/h²), and by s6 this converges to (ρ, I). Limits in law are unique, so the pairs agree in law on C([0, T], ℝ²) for every T, hence on C([0, ∞), ℝ²). The set of pairs (f, g) with g(t) = inf_(s≥t) f(s) for all rational t is Borel and carries the law of (ρ, I), hence also that of (2M − B, M), and continuity extends the identity to all t.

source.ref: P. Mörters and Y. Peres, Brownian Motion, Cambridge University Press 2010, Section 5.5, Lemma 5.31, Lemma 5.32, Proposition 5.33 and Theorem 5.34 with its proof, pp. 140-144.

applications.title: Running maximum and drawdown of a driftless log-price
applications.inputs: A driftless log-price X(t) = σB(t) with volatility σ = 1, its running maximum M(t), its drawdown D(t) = M(t) − X(t), and the horizon t = 4.
applications.hypotheses: B is a standard linear Brownian motion started at 0, so the theorem applies to (2M − B, M). Here 2M − B = M + D is the running maximum plus the drawdown. A three-dimensional Bessel process started at r > 0 reaches a level a < r with probability a/r, and by its Markov property at time t this gives P(I(t) ≤ a | ρ(t) = r) = a/r.

steps.text: By the theorem R(t) = M(t) + D(t) has the law of |W(t)| for a three-dimensional Brownian motion W, so E[R(t)²] = 3t = 12.

The pair (R(t), M(t)) has the law of (ρ(t), I(t)), so given R(t) = r the maximum M(t) is uniform on [0, r]. For example, given R(4) = 3, the probability that M(4) ≤ 1 is 1/3, and the drawdown D = R − M is also uniform on [0, 3].
Uniformity gives E[M(t)² | R(t)] = R(t)²/3, so E[M(4)²] = 12/3 = 4. This agrees with E[B(4)²] = 4, because M(t) has the law of |B(t)|.
Similarly E[M D | R] = R²/2 − R²/3 = R²/6, so E[M(4)D(4)] = 12/2 − 12/3 = 2. Since E[M(4)] = E[D(4)] = √(8/π), the covariance of the maximum and the drawdown is 2 − 8/π ≈ −0.55, which is negative.

applications.conclusion: At horizon 4 the sum of the running maximum and the drawdown has second moment 12, the maximum is uniform on [0, r] given that this sum equals r, and the maximum and the drawdown are negatively correlated with E[M D] = 2.

limitations: The theorem needs Brownian motion without drift. For B(t) + μt the analogue of 2M − B is a different diffusion (Rogers and Pitman, 1981), not the three-dimensional Bessel process.

The filtration of 2M − B is strictly smaller than that of B. Given the path of 2M − B up to time t, M(t) is still uniform on [0, 2M(t) − B(t)], so B is not a function of the past of the Bessel process.

results.name: Freedman's inequality
results.statement:
Let (Ω, F, P) be a probability space with a filtration F₀ ⊂ F₁ ⊂ F₂ ⊂ … ⊂ F, and write E_k for the conditional expectation given F_k. Let (Y_k)_{k≥0} be a real martingale with Y₀ = 0 and differences X_k = Y_k − Y_(k−1). Assume that there is a constant R > 0 with X_k ≤ R almost surely for every k ≥ 1. Let W₀ = 0 and W_k = ∑_{j=1}^k E_(j−1)[X_j²], with values in [0, ∞]. Then for all t ≥ 0 and σ² > 0,
P(there is k ≥ 0 with Y_k ≥ t and W_k ≤ σ²) ≤ exp(−(σ²/R²)·h(Rt/σ²)) ≤ exp(−(t²/2)/(σ² + Rt/3)),
where h(u) = (1 + u) log(1 + u) − u for u ≥ 0.
hypotheses: (Y_k)_{k≥0} is a real martingale for the filtration (F_k) with Y₀ = 0.
The differences are bounded above: X_k ≤ R almost surely for every k ≥ 1, with a constant R > 0.
W_k is the predictable quadratic variation ∑_{j≤k} E_(j−1)[X_j²]; the deviation is measured only on the event W_k ≤ σ².

prerequisites.reason: Step s4 applies optional stopping at the bounded stopping time τ ∧ n to the nonnegative supermartingale M_k, which gives E[M_(τ∧n)] ≤ M₀ = 1.

definitions.name: predictable quadratic variation
definitions.text: For a martingale with differences X_k, the process W_k = ∑_{j=1}^k E_(j−1)[X_j²]. Each term is known at time j − 1, so W_k is F_(k−1)-measurable.

definitions.name: Bennett function
definitions.text: The function h(u) = (1 + u) log(1 + u) − u on [0, ∞). It satisfies h(u) ≥ (u²/2)/(1 + u/3), and h(u) is close to u²/2 for small u.

source.citation: Joel A. Tropp, Freedman's inequality for matrix martingales, Electronic Communications in Probability 16 (2011), 262-270.
source.revision: arXiv:1101.3039v1 [math.PR], 16 Jan 2011.
source.module: Section 1.2 Freedman's Inequality
source.excerpt: Theorem 1.1 (Freedman). Consider a real-valued martingale {Y_k : k = 0, 1, 2, …} with difference sequence {X_k : k = 1, 2, 3, …}. Assume that the difference sequence is uniformly bounded: X_k ≤ R almost surely for k = 1, 2, 3, …. Define the predictable quadratic variation process of the martingale: W_k := ∑_{j=1}^k E_{j−1} X_j² for k = 1, 2, 3, …. Then, for all t ≥ 0 and σ² > 0, P{∃k ≥ 0 : Y_k ≥ t and W_k ≤ σ²} ≤ exp(−(t²/2)/(σ² + Rt/3)).
source.attribution: © Joel A. Tropp. Quoted from the arXiv version of Freedman's inequality for matrix martingales for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source quotes the scalar theorem of Freedman, Ann. Probab. 3 (1975), Theorem (1.6), in the Bernstein form. The authored statement adds the sharper Bennett form exp(−(σ²/R²)h(Rt/σ²)), which the source proves as Theorem 3.1. The authored proof is the scalar case of the source's proof of Theorems 2.3 and 3.1: an exponential supermartingale, a stopping time and an optimized parameter. The scalar case needs no matrix tools, and the authored proof gives the moment bound and the stopping argument in full.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the scalar case of the proof of Theorems 2.3 and 3.1 in Tropp, Freedman's inequality for matrix martingales. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement, both the Bennett form and the Bernstein form. For t = 0 the bound is 1 and there is nothing to prove, so the proof takes t > 0.

steps.text: A one-sided bound on the exponential. Fix λ > 0 and put g(λ) = (e^(λR) − 1 − λR)/R² ≥ 0. Taylor's formula with integral remainder gives e^y − 1 − y = y²·φ(y) with φ(y) = ∫₀¹ (1 − s) e^(sy) ds. The integrand increases with y, so φ is nondecreasing. For x ≤ R we have λx ≤ λR, so e^(λx) − 1 − λx = λ²x²φ(λx) ≤ λ²x²φ(λR) = x²·g(λ). Thus e^(λx) ≤ 1 + λx + g(λ)x² for every x ≤ R.

Conditional moment generating function. Put V_k = E_(k−1)[X_k²] ∈ [0, ∞], so W_k = V₁ + … + V_k. Apply s1 with x = X_k and take E_(k−1). The martingale property gives E_(k−1)[X_k] = 0, so E_(k−1)[e^(λX_k)] ≤ 1 + g(λ)V_k ≤ exp(g(λ)V_k), by 1 + a ≤ e^a.

An exponential supermartingale. Define M_k = exp(λY_k − g(λ)W_k), with exp(−∞) = 0. Then M₀ = 1 and M_k ≥ 0. Because Y_k ≤ kR and W_k ≥ 0, M_k ≤ e^(λkR), so M_k is integrable. W_k is F_(k−1)-measurable, so E_(k−1)[M_k] = M_(k−1)·exp(−g(λ)V_k)·E_(k−1)[e^(λX_k)] ≤ M_(k−1) by s2. On {V_k = ∞} we have M_k = 0, and the inequality also holds there. So (M_k) is a nonnegative supermartingale.

Stopping. Let τ = inf{k ≥ 0 : Y_k ≥ t and W_k ≤ σ²}, with inf ∅ = ∞. Y_k and W_k are F_k-measurable, so τ is a stopping time, and the event in the theorem is {τ < ∞}. Fix n. Optional stopping at the bounded time τ ∧ n gives E[M_(τ∧n)] ≤ M₀ = 1. On {τ ≤ n} we have Y_τ ≥ t and W_τ ≤ σ², so M_(τ∧n) = M_τ ≥ exp(λt − g(λ)σ²) because g(λ) ≥ 0. Since M ≥ 0, P(τ ≤ n)·exp(λt − g(λ)σ²) ≤ E[M_(τ∧n)] ≤ 1. Let n → ∞: P(τ < ∞) ≤ exp(−λt + g(λ)σ²) for every λ > 0.

Optimize λ to get the Bennett form. Put u = Rt/σ² > 0 and λ = (1/R) log(1 + u) > 0. Then e^(λR) = 1 + u, so g(λ)σ² = (σ²/R²)(u − log(1 + u)) and λt = (σ²/R²)·u log(1 + u). Hence −λt + g(λ)σ² = −(σ²/R²)[(1 + u) log(1 + u) − u] = −(σ²/R²)h(u), which is the first bound.

Compare h with the Bernstein function. Let q(u) = (u²/2)/(1 + u/3) = (3/2)(u − 3 + 9/(3 + u)). Then h(0) = q(0) = 0, h′(u) = log(1 + u) and q′(u) = (3/2)(1 − 9/(3 + u)²) are 0 at u = 0, and h″(u) = 1/(1 + u), q″(u) = 27/(3 + u)³. For u ≥ 0, (3 + u)³ = 27 + 27u + 9u² + u³ ≥ 27(1 + u), so h″ ≥ q″. Integrating twice from 0 gives h(u) ≥ q(u). With u = Rt/σ², (σ²/R²)q(u) = (t²/2)/(σ² + Rt/3), which gives the second bound.

applications.title: Adaptive stakes in a fair coin game
applications.inputs: A gambler bets on fair coin tosses ε₁, ε₂, … with P(ε_k = 1) = P(ε_k = −1) = 1/2, independent. Before toss k the gambler chooses a stake b_k ∈ [0, 1] from the past tosses by any rule, for example doubling after a loss up to the cap 1. The net gain is Y_k = ∑_{j≤k} b_j ε_j. Levels: t = 30 and σ² = 100.
applications.hypotheses: Let F_k be generated by ε₁, …, ε_k. The stake b_k is F_(k−1)-measurable and ε_k is independent of F_(k−1) with mean 0, so Y_k is a martingale with Y₀ = 0. The differences X_k = b_k ε_k satisfy X_k ≤ 1, so R = 1. Also E_(k−1)[X_k²] = b_k², so W_k = ∑_{j≤k} b_j², the total squared stake.

steps.text: Freedman's inequality with R = 1 bounds the probability that the gain ever reaches 30 while the total squared stake is still at most 100 by exp(−(t²/2)/(σ² + t/3)). The bound holds for every stake rule and for an unbounded time horizon.
Compute the Bernstein exponent: (t²/2)/(σ² + Rt/3) = (900/2)/(100 + 10) = 450/110 = 45/11.
So the probability is at most e^(−45/11) ≈ 0.0167. The Bennett form uses u = Rt/σ² = 3/10 and h(3/10) = 1.3 log 1.3 − 0.3 ≈ 0.04107, which gives the slightly smaller bound e^(−4.107) ≈ 0.0165.

The steps are dependent through the stakes, so Bernstein's inequality for independent sums does not apply. A fixed-time Azuma–Hoeffding bound with |X_k| ≤ 1 would need a fixed horizon n and would give exp(−t²/(2n)), which is useless for large n. Freedman's bound uses the realized variance W_k instead of n.

applications.conclusion: Whatever stake rule the gambler uses, the probability that the net gain ever reaches 30 before the total squared stake exceeds 100 is at most e^(−45/11) < 0.017.

limitations: Only the upper bound X_k ≤ R is used. The inequality controls the upper tail of Y_k. For the lower tail, apply it to −Y_k, which needs a bound X_k ≥ −R.
The bound holds only on the event W_k ≤ σ². Without control of the predictable quadratic variation, a bounded-increment martingale can still reach large values with high probability over long times.
Tropp's Theorem 1.2 extends the inequality to self-adjoint matrix martingales with an extra dimensional factor d.
