results.name: Reflection principle for Brownian motion
results.statement:
Let B = (B(t))_{t≥0} be a standard Brownian motion in ℝ^d with B(0) = 0, and let T be a stopping time for its right-continuous filtration (F⁺(t)), with values in [0, ∞]. Define the reflected process B*(t) = B(t) for t ≤ T and B*(t) = 2B(T) − B(t) for t > T. Then (a) B* is again a standard Brownian motion. (b) For d = 1, let M(t) = max_{0≤s≤t} B(s). For all t > 0, a > 0 and b ≤ a,
P(M(t) ≥ a, B(t) ≤ b) = P(B(t) ≥ 2a − b),
and in particular P(M(t) ≥ a) = 2P(B(t) ≥ a) = P(|B(t)| ≥ a).
hypotheses: B is a standard Brownian motion in ℝ^d with B(0) = 0.
T is a stopping time for the right-continuous filtration (F⁺(t)) of B, with values in [0, ∞].
For part (b): d = 1, t > 0, a > 0 and b ≤ a.
results.empty_prerequisites_reason: The proof rests on the strong Markov property of Brownian motion (Theorem 2.20 of the source, Theorem 2.16 of Mörters–Peres), which has no catalog or plan record. Steps s2 and s3 cite it, and the proof uses no other named result.

definitions.name: Brownian motion reflected at T
definitions.text: The process that follows B up to time T and then follows the mirror image of B in the point B(T): B*(t) = B(t) for t ≤ T and B*(t) = 2B(T) − B(t) for t > T.

definitions.name: strong Markov property
definitions.text: For every almost surely finite stopping time T, the process (B(T + s) − B(T))_{s≥0} is a standard Brownian motion independent of F⁺(T) (Theorem 2.20 of the source, Theorem 2.16 of Mörters–Peres).

definitions.name: running maximum
definitions.text: M(t) = max_{0≤s≤t} B(s) for a linear Brownian motion. The maximum exists because the path is continuous.

source.module: Chapter 2, Section 2.4 The Strong Markov Property of Brownian Motion
source.excerpt: Theorem (Reflection Principle). Let T be a stopping time with P[T < ∞] = 1. Define B_t^(T) := 2B_(T∧t) − B_t (t ⩾ 0). Then the process (B_t^(T))_(t⩾0) is a Brownian motion.

source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states part (a) for an almost surely finite stopping time and part (b) as Theorem 2.21 on pp. 17-18, with the same non-strict inequalities. The same result is Theorems 2.19 and 2.21 of Mörters and Peres, Brownian Motion (CUP 2010), pp. 44-45. The authored proof follows the source proofs: the strong Markov property (Theorem 2.20 of the source), a measurable concatenation map, and exact event identities for the hitting time of a. It adds the reduction from a general stopping time, possibly infinite, to bounded ones.

proof.scope: The full statement. Part (a) holds in every dimension d and for every stopping time, finite or not. Part (b) is for linear Brownian motion.

steps.text: Write both processes with one concatenation map. Let C = C([0, ∞), ℝ^d) with the topology of uniform convergence on compact sets. Its Borel σ-algebra is generated by the coordinate maps, so a continuous process is a random element of C. Define Ψ: C × [0, ∞) × C → C by Ψ(f, r, g)(t) = f(t) + g((t − r)⁺). Ψ is continuous, hence Borel measurable. Assume first that T is bounded. Let B^T(t) = B(t ∧ T) and W(s) = B(T + s) − B(T). For t ≤ T, (t − T)⁺ = 0 and W(0) = 0. For t > T, B(T) + W(t − T) = B(t) and B(T) − W(t − T) = 2B(T) − B(t). Hence B = Ψ(B^T, T, W) and B* = Ψ(B^T, T, −W).

Bounded T. By the strong Markov property (Theorem 2.20 of the source), W is a standard Brownian motion independent of F⁺(T). The stopped path B^T and the time T are F⁺(T)-measurable, because B is continuous and adapted. The process −W is also a standard Brownian motion, since negation keeps B(0) = 0, continuity, independence of increments and the centred normal law of each increment. So the triples (B^T, T, W) and (B^T, T, −W) have the same joint law, namely the law of (B^T, T) times the Wiener measure. Applying the measurable map Ψ gives B* = B in law as random elements of C. A continuous process with the law of a standard Brownian motion is a standard Brownian motion.

General T. Let T_n = T ∧ n, a bounded stopping time, and let B*_n be the reflection at T_n, which is a standard Brownian motion by s2. Fix ω and t. If T < ∞, then T_n = T for n ≥ T, so B*_n(t) = B*(t). If T = ∞, then B*(t) = B(t), and for n ≥ t we have t ≤ T_n, so B*_n(t) = B(t). Hence B*_n(t) → B*(t) for every t, and each finite-dimensional distribution of B* is the limit in law of the same distribution for a standard Brownian motion. B* is continuous, because both pieces equal B(T) at t = T, and B*(0) = 0. So B* is a standard Brownian motion, which proves (a).

An exact event identity for d = 1. Let τ = inf{s ≥ 0 : B(s) = a}, a stopping time because B is continuous and {a} is closed. Since B(0) = 0 < a, continuity gives B(s) < a for s < τ, and M(t) ≥ a if and only if τ ≤ t. Let B* be the reflection at τ. On {τ ≤ t} we have B*(t) = 2a − B(t), also when τ = t because then B(t) = a. Put E = {M(t) ≥ a, B(t) ≤ b} = {τ ≤ t, B(t) ≤ b}. On E, B*(t) = 2a − B(t) ≥ 2a − b. Conversely, if B*(t) ≥ 2a − b ≥ a, then τ ≤ t, because τ > t would give B*(t) = B(t) < a. So B(t) = 2a − B*(t) ≤ b. Hence E = {B*(t) ≥ 2a − b} exactly.

The laws. By (a), B*(t) has the law of B(t), so P(M(t) ≥ a, B(t) ≤ b) = P(B(t) ≥ 2a − b). For the maximum alone, split {M(t) ≥ a} into {B(t) > a} (where M(t) ≥ a holds) and {M(t) ≥ a, B(t) ≤ a}. The second part has probability P(B(t) ≥ a) by the case b = a. B(t) is normal with variance t > 0, so P(B(t) = a) = 0 and P(B(t) > a) = P(B(t) ≥ a). Thus P(M(t) ≥ a) = 2P(B(t) ≥ a). The law of B(t) is symmetric, so 2P(B(t) ≥ a) = P(B(t) ≥ a) + P(B(t) ≤ −a) = P(|B(t)| ≥ a).

applications.title: Ruin probability in a driftless Brownian risk model
applications.inputs: The surplus of an insurer is U(s) = u + σB(s) with initial capital u = 10, volatility σ = 5 per square-root year, a standard linear Brownian motion B and the horizon t = 4 years. Ruin is the event that U touches 0 before time t.
applications.hypotheses: B is a standard Brownian motion, so −B is one too. The first time that −B reaches the level a = u/σ = 2 is a stopping time, and part (b) applies to −B with t = 4 > 0, a = 2 > 0 and b ≤ a.

steps.text: U touches 0 before t if and only if min_{s≤t} B(s) ≤ −u/σ = −2, that is max_{s≤t}(−B(s)) ≥ 2. Part (b) for −B gives P(ruin before t) = P(|B(4)| ≥ 2).
B(4) has standard deviation √4 = 2, so the level 2 is 1 standard deviation: P(ruin before 4) = P(|Z| ≥ 1) = 2(1 − Φ(1)) ≈ 0.3173 for a standard normal Z with distribution function Φ.

The joint law answers a finer question. Continue the surplus path after it touches 0 (the insurer borrows). The probability that the path touches 0 and still ends at U(4) ≥ 10 is P(max(−B) ≥ 2, −B(4) ≤ 0) = P(−B(4) ≥ 2·2 − 0) = P(Z ≥ 4/2) = P(Z ≥ 2) ≈ 0.0228.

As t → ∞, P(|B(t)| ≥ 2) = P(|Z| ≥ 2/√t) → 1, so ruin is certain in the long run without positive drift. A naive estimate that checks only the end value, P(U(4) ≤ 0) = P(Z ≤ −1) ≈ 0.1587, is half of the correct ruin probability.

applications.conclusion: With capital 10 and volatility 5, the ruin probability within 4 years is 2(1 − Φ(1)) ≈ 0.317, twice the probability that the surplus is negative at the end of the period.

limitations: T must be a stopping time. For the time of the maximum on [0, 1], which is not a stopping time, the reflected process is not a Brownian motion and its law is singular to the Wiener measure (Mörters–Peres, Remark 2.20).
Part (b) is for driftless linear Brownian motion. With a drift μ, the reflection changes the drift sign, and the Girsanov change of measure gives the corrected law of the maximum.

results.name: Hewitt–Savage zero–one law
results.statement: Let (S, 𝒮) be a measurable space and let X₁, X₂, … be independent and identically distributed random elements of S. Let B ∈ 𝒮^⊗ℕ be a set of sequences that is invariant under every finite permutation: for every bijection π of ℕ = {1, 2, …} with π(i) = i for all but finitely many i, a sequence (s₁, s₂, …) is in B if and only if (s_π(1), s_π(2), …) is in B. Then P((X₁, X₂, …) ∈ B) is 0 or 1.
hypotheses: The random elements X₁, X₂, … of the measurable space (S, 𝒮) are independent and have the same law μ.
The measurable set B ⊂ S^ℕ does not change when finitely many coordinates of a sequence are permuted.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 identifies the law of the sequence and its invariance under permutations by agreement on cylinder sets, and step s2 shows that every measurable set is approximable by cylinder sets. Both use Dynkin's π-λ theorem.

concepts: independent and identically distributed random variables

definitions.name: finite permutation
definitions.text: A bijection π of ℕ = {1, 2, …} with π(i) = i for all but finitely many i. It acts on a sequence by T_π(s) = (s_π(1), s_π(2), …).

definitions.name: permutable set
definitions.text: A measurable set B ⊂ S^ℕ with T_π⁻¹(B) = B for every finite permutation π. The events {(X₁, X₂, …) ∈ B} for such B form the exchangeable σ-algebra.

definitions.name: cylinder set
definitions.text: A set of the form {s ∈ S^ℕ : (s₁, …, s_n) ∈ C} with n ≥ 1 and C ∈ 𝒮^⊗n. It depends only on the first n coordinates.

source.citation: Peter Mörters and Yuval Peres, Brownian Motion, Cambridge Series in Statistical and Probabilistic Mathematics 30, Cambridge University Press, 2010.
source.revision: Authors' version of the book (PDF created 2010-01-06), posted on the first author's home page.
source.module: Chapter 1, Section 1.3 Nondifferentiability of Brownian motion
source.excerpt: Lemma 1.25 (Hewitt–Savage 0-1 law) If E is an exchangeable event for an independent, identically distributed sequence, then P(E) is 0 or 1.
source.attribution: © Peter Mörters and Yuval Peres. Quoted from the authors' version of Brownian Motion for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states the law with Definition 1.24 of an exchangeable event and leaves the proof as Exercise 1.10. The authored statement makes the measurable set of sequences and its invariance under finite permutations explicit. The authored proof follows the proof of Theorem 2.5.4 in Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., pp. 82-83: approximation by cylinder events, a block swap of coordinates and independence of the two blocks. It also proves the approximation step with the π-λ theorem.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the proof of Theorem 2.5.4 in Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement for i.i.d. random elements of an arbitrary measurable space.

steps.text: Move to the sequence space. Let μ be the law of X₁ and Q the law of X = (X₁, X₂, …) on (S^ℕ, 𝒮^⊗ℕ). For a cylinder set C₁ × … × C_n × S × S × …, independence gives Q of it equal to μ(C₁)⋯μ(C_n). Cylinder sets form a π-system that generates 𝒮^⊗ℕ, so Q is the product measure μ^⊗ℕ by Dynkin's π-λ theorem. For a finite permutation π, T_π⁻¹ maps the cylinder set above to the set where coordinate π(i) lies in C_i for i ≤ n. Its Q-measure is again μ(C₁)⋯μ(C_n) because the indices π(1), …, π(n) are distinct. So Q ∘ T_π⁻¹ = Q, again by the π-λ theorem. Put p = Q(B) = P(X ∈ B).

Approximate B by cylinder sets. Let F_n be the σ-algebra of cylinder sets on the first n coordinates, and let G be the class of D ∈ 𝒮^⊗ℕ such that for every ε > 0 some E ∈ ∪_n F_n has Q(D Δ E) < ε. The union ∪_n F_n is an algebra, so it is a π-system, and it lies in G. G contains S^ℕ. G is closed under complements because D^c Δ E^c = D Δ E. G is closed under countable disjoint unions D = ∪_k D_k: choose m with Q(D \ (D₁ ∪ … ∪ D_m)) < ε/2 by continuity of Q, then E_k ∈ ∪_n F_n with Q(D_k Δ E_k) < ε/(2m), and use E = E₁ ∪ … ∪ E_m. The π-λ theorem gives G = 𝒮^⊗ℕ. Hence there are integers n_j and sets C_j ∈ 𝒮^⊗n_j such that B_j = {s : (s₁, …, s_n_j) ∈ C_j} satisfies Q(B Δ B_j) → 0.

Swap two blocks of coordinates. Fix j, write n = n_j, and let π exchange i and i + n for 1 ≤ i ≤ n and fix every i > 2n. Then T_π⁻¹(B_j) = B′_j := {s : (s_(n+1), …, s_2n) ∈ C_j}, and T_π⁻¹(B) = B because B is permutable. Since preimages commute with symmetric differences, T_π⁻¹(B Δ B_j) = B Δ B′_j. The invariance Q ∘ T_π⁻¹ = Q from step s1 gives Q(B Δ B′_j) = Q(B Δ B_j) → 0.

Use independence of the blocks. B_j depends on coordinates 1, …, n and B′_j on coordinates n + 1, …, 2n, so under the product measure Q(B_j ∩ B′_j) = μ^⊗n(C_j)² = Q(B_j)². The bound |Q(D) − Q(E)| ≤ Q(D Δ E) gives Q(B_j) → p. The inclusion (B_j ∩ B′_j) Δ B ⊂ (B_j Δ B) ∪ (B′_j Δ B) gives Q(B_j ∩ B′_j) → p. Therefore p = lim Q(B_j)² = p², so p is 0 or 1.

applications.title: Recurrence of the symmetric lattice random walk on ℤ
applications.inputs: Independent steps X₁, X₂, … with P(X_i = 1) = P(X_i = −1) = 1/2, the walk S_n = X₁ + … + X_n on the one-dimensional lattice ℤ, and L = limsup S_n in [−∞, +∞].
applications.hypotheses: The steps are i.i.d. random elements of S = {−1, 1}. For each real x, the set of step sequences with limsup of the partial sums at most x is measurable, and a permutation that fixes every index above m leaves the partial sums S_n unchanged for n ≥ m. So this set is permutable.

steps.text: The Hewitt–Savage law gives P(L ≤ x) ∈ {0, 1} for every real x. A nondecreasing function with values in {0, 1} jumps at one point c = inf{x : P(L ≤ x) = 1} in [−∞, +∞], so L = c almost surely.

The shifted sequence (X₂, X₃, …) has the same law as (X₁, X₂, …), so L′ = limsup (X₂ + … + X_(n+1)) is also equal to c almost surely. But S_(n+1) = X₁ + (X₂ + … + X_(n+1)), so L = X₁ + L′. If c were finite, then c = X₁ + c, so X₁ = 0 almost surely, which is false. Hence c = +∞ or c = −∞.
The steps are symmetric, so (−S_n) has the same law as (S_n). Thus limsup(−S_n) = c almost surely, that is liminf S_n = −c almost surely. Since liminf S_n ≤ limsup S_n, −c ≤ c, which leaves c = +∞.

So limsup S_n = +∞ and liminf S_n = −∞ almost surely. The walk moves by steps of size 1, so between a visit above k and a visit below k it passes through k. Hence every integer k is visited infinitely often.

applications.conclusion: The symmetric nearest-neighbour random walk on ℤ is recurrent: with probability 1 it visits every lattice site infinitely often. The proof uses no computation of return probabilities.

limitations: Independence and identical distribution are both necessary. For an exchangeable sequence that is a mixture of i.i.d. laws, the permutable events can have any probability, and de Finetti's theorem describes them.
The law gives only that the probability is 0 or 1. It does not say which value holds: in the application, a separate symmetry argument fixes the value.

results.name: Diaconis–Freedman finite de Finetti theorem
results.statement:
Let (Ω, 𝒜) be a measurable space, let N ≥ 1, and let μ_N be a symmetric probability measure on Ω^N: μ_N is invariant under every permutation of the N coordinates. For Z = (z₁, …, z_N) ∈ Ω^N let ρ̄_Z = N⁻¹ ∑_{j=1}^N δ_(z_j) be its empirical measure, let P be the law of ρ̄_Z when Z has law μ_N, and let μ̃_N = ∫ ρ^⊗N P(dρ), a mixture of i.i.d. laws. For 1 ≤ n ≤ N let μ_N^(n) and μ̃_N^(n) be the marginals on the first n coordinates. Then for every measurable A ⊂ Ω^n,
|μ_N^(n)(A) − μ̃_N^(n)(A)| ≤ 1 − N(N − 1)⋯(N − n + 1)/N^n ≤ n(n − 1)/(2N),
and the total variation norm satisfies ‖μ_N^(n) − μ̃_N^(n)‖ = ∫ d|μ_N^(n) − μ̃_N^(n)| ≤ n(n − 1)/N.
hypotheses: μ_N is a probability measure on the product Ω^N of a measurable space (Ω, 𝒜).
μ_N is symmetric: its law does not change when the N coordinates are permuted.
1 ≤ n ≤ N, and the comparison is between the n-coordinate marginals.
results.empty_prerequisites_reason: The proof is a direct computation: an expansion of a product of sums, an exchange of a finite sum with an integral, and an elementary product inequality proved by induction inside step s4. It uses no named theorem.

definitions.name: symmetric probability measure
definitions.text: A probability measure μ_N on Ω^N with μ_N(A₁ × … × A_N) = μ_N(A_σ(1) × … × A_σ(N)) for all measurable A_i and every permutation σ of {1, …, N}. It is the law of an exchangeable vector (X₁, …, X_N).

definitions.name: Diaconis–Freedman mixture
definitions.text: μ̃_N = ∫ ρ̄_Z^⊗N μ_N(dZ): draw Z from μ_N, then draw N points independently from the empirical measure of Z. Its n-marginal is ∫ ρ̄_Z^⊗n μ_N(dZ).

definitions.name: total variation norm
definitions.text: For a finite signed measure ν, ‖ν‖ = ∫ d|ν| = |ν|(Ω^n). For two probability measures, ‖μ − ν‖ = 2 sup_A |μ(A) − ν(A)|.

source.citation: Nicolas Rougerie, De Finetti theorems, mean-field limits and Bose-Einstein condensation, lecture notes (Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München, 2015), arXiv:1506.05263.
source.module: Chapter 2, Section 2.2 The Diaconis-Freedman theorem
source.excerpt: Theorem 2.2 (Diaconis-Freedman). Let µ_N ∈ P_s(Ω^N) be a symmetric probability measure. There exists P_µN ∈ P(P(Ω)) such that, setting µ̃_N := ∫ ρ^⊗N dP_µN(ρ) (2.13) we have ‖µ_N^(n) − µ̃_N^(n)‖_TV ≤ 2n(n − 1)/N. (2.14)
source.attribution: © Nicolas Rougerie. Quoted from the arXiv version of De Finetti theorems, mean-field limits and Bose-Einstein condensation for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states the theorem with the constant 2 in the norm ∫ d|µ| and remarks that the constant 1 is possible. The authored statement gives the mixing measure explicitly (the law of the empirical measure), the exact bound 1 − N(N−1)⋯(N−n+1)/N^n for every event, and the constant 1. The authored proof follows the second proof in the source, pp. 32-33 (expansion of the tensor power and the positive remainder ν_n), and it sums the product inequality to get the better constant. The original result is Diaconis and Freedman, Finite exchangeable sequences, Ann. Probab. 8 (1980) 745-764.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the second proof of Theorem 2.2 in Rougerie, De Finetti theorems, mean-field limits and Bose-Einstein condensation. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement, for an arbitrary measurable space Ω and all 1 ≤ n ≤ N.

steps.text: Expand the tensor power. For Z ∈ Ω^N and a map γ: {1, …, n} → {1, …, N} write Z_γ = (z_γ(1), …, z_γ(n)). Expanding the product of the sums ρ̄_Z = N⁻¹ ∑_j δ_(z_j) gives ρ̄_Z^⊗n = N^(−n) ∑_γ δ_(Z_γ), a sum over all N^n maps γ. Each map Z ↦ 1_A(Z_γ) is measurable, so Z ↦ ρ̄_Z^⊗n(A) is measurable, and the n-marginal of the mixture is μ̃_N^(n)(A) = ∫ ρ̄_Z^⊗n(A) μ_N(dZ) = N^(−n) ∑_γ ∫ 1_A(Z_γ) μ_N(dZ), because the n-marginal of ρ^⊗N is ρ^⊗n.

Injective maps give the true marginal. Let γ be injective. Choose a permutation σ of {1, …, N} with σ(i) = γ(i) for i ≤ n. Then Z_γ is the vector of the first n coordinates of Z∘σ = (z_σ(1), …, z_σ(N)). By symmetry Z∘σ has law μ_N, so ∫ 1_A(Z_γ) μ_N(dZ) = μ_N(A × Ω^(N−n)) = μ_N^(n)(A). There are (N)_n = N(N − 1)⋯(N − n + 1) injective maps.

Split off a positive remainder. Put c = (N)_n/N^n ∈ (0, 1] and ν(A) = N^(−n) ∑_{γ not injective} ∫ 1_A(Z_γ) μ_N(dZ). Then ν is a positive measure with total mass ν(Ω^n) = (N^n − (N)_n)/N^n = 1 − c, and s1 and s2 give μ̃_N^(n) = c·μ_N^(n) + ν. Hence μ_N^(n) − μ̃_N^(n) = (1 − c)μ_N^(n) − ν. For every A both (1 − c)μ_N^(n)(A) and ν(A) lie in [0, 1 − c], so |μ_N^(n)(A) − μ̃_N^(n)(A)| ≤ 1 − c. For the norm, the triangle inequality for |·| gives ∫ d|μ_N^(n) − μ̃_N^(n)| ≤ (1 − c)·1 + ν(Ω^n) = 2(1 − c).

Bound 1 − c. Write c = ∏_{j=1}^n (1 − a_j) with a_j = (j − 1)/N ∈ [0, 1). For numbers a_j ∈ [0, 1], the partial products p_m = ∏_{j≤m}(1 − a_j) lie in [0, 1], and p_(m+1) = p_m − p_m·a_(m+1) ≥ p_m − a_(m+1). By induction on m, p_m ≥ 1 − (a₁ + … + a_m). Hence 1 − c ≤ ∑_{j=1}^n (j − 1)/N = n(n − 1)/(2N). With s3 this gives the bound n(n − 1)/(2N) for every event and the bound n(n − 1)/N for the total variation norm.

applications.title: Survey sampling without replacement against sampling with replacement
applications.inputs: A population of N = 1000 distinct individuals z₁, …, z_N, each with a recorded answer. A survey interviews n = 10 individuals chosen without replacement, that is the first 10 entries of a uniformly random ordering of the population.
applications.hypotheses: Let σ be a uniform random permutation and X = (z_σ(1), …, z_σ(N)). The law μ_N of X is symmetric, because a fixed permutation of a uniform permutation is again uniform. The interviewed sample is the first n = 10 coordinates, with 10 ≤ 1000.

steps.text: Every ordering of the population has the same empirical measure ρ = N⁻¹ ∑_j δ_(z_j). So the mixing law P is the point mass at ρ, and μ̃_N^(n) = ρ^⊗n is the law of 10 independent draws with replacement from the population.
The theorem bounds the change of every event of the sample, for example the event that a test statistic exceeds a threshold, by n(n − 1)/(2N) = 90/2000 = 9/200 = 0.045.

The sharper bound is 1 − c with c = (1000·999⋯991)/1000^10 ≈ 0.9559, so 1 − c ≈ 0.0441. For the event A that the 10 interviewed individuals are all different, μ_N^(n)(A) = 1 and μ̃_N^(n)(A) = c. So the bound 1 − c is attained in this example.

For yes/no answers with a share p of yes in the population, the number of yes answers is hypergeometric under μ_N^(n) and binomial(10, p) under μ̃_N^(n). The theorem gives the uniform bound 0.045 between the two laws for every p.

applications.conclusion: Any statement about a sample of 10 out of 1000 that holds for independent draws with replacement holds for the survey sample with a probability error of at most 0.045, and the exact error bound 1 − c ≈ 0.044 cannot be improved for this population.

limitations: The bound is small only when n is small compared with √N, and this rate cannot be improved in general (Remark 2.4 (2) of the source, with examples of Diaconis and Freedman). For a finite set Ω = {1, …, d}, the original proof gives an error of order dn/N instead (Remark 2.4 (6) of the source).
For n = 1 the bound is 0: the one-coordinate marginals of μ_N and of the mixture are equal (Remark 2.3 of the source).
Letting N → ∞ with n fixed gives the Hewitt–Savage form of de Finetti's theorem for compact Ω, as in the proof of Theorem 2.1 of the source.

results.name: Quantum de Finetti theorem for symmetric states
results.statement: Let d ≥ 1 and let D_d be the set of density matrices on ℂ^d (positive semidefinite d × d matrices of trace 1), a compact set. Let (ρ^(n))_(n≥1) be a sequence such that each ρ^(n) is a density matrix on (ℂ^d)^⊗n, U_π ρ^(n) U_π* = ρ^(n) for every permutation π of the n tensor factors, and Tr_(n+1) ρ^(n+1) = ρ^(n) for every n, where Tr_(n+1) is the partial trace over the last factor. Then there is a unique Borel probability measure m on D_d such that ρ^(n) = ∫_(D_d) σ^⊗n m(dσ) for every n ≥ 1. If moreover ρ^(2) is supported by the symmetric subspace of (ℂ^d)^⊗2 (bosonic symmetry), then m is concentrated on the pure states σ = |u⟩⟨u|, so every ρ^(n) is a mixture of the bosonic product states |u^⊗n⟩⟨u^⊗n|.
hypotheses: The one-particle space ℂ^d has finite dimension d.
Each ρ^(n) is a density matrix on (ℂ^d)^⊗n that commutes with every permutation of the n tensor factors.
The sequence is consistent: Tr_(n+1) ρ^(n+1) = ρ^(n) for all n ≥ 1.
For the last sentence only: ρ^(2) is supported by the symmetric subspace of (ℂ^d)^⊗2.

prerequisites.reason: Step s2 applies the classical de Finetti theorem, existence and uniqueness of the mixing measure, to the exchangeable sequence of outcomes of an informationally complete measurement on each system.

definitions.name: infinitely exchangeable quantum state
definitions.text: A sequence (ρ^(n)) of permutation-invariant density matrices on (ℂ^d)^⊗n with Tr_(n+1) ρ^(n+1) = ρ^(n). It describes the first n systems of an infinite sequence of systems whose order does not matter.

definitions.name: minimal informationally complete POVM
definitions.text: Positive semidefinite operators E_1, …, E_(d²) on ℂ^d with ∑_α E_α = 1 that are linearly independent. Their probabilities p_α = Tr(ρE_α) determine every operator ρ, and every vector p comes from exactly one operator A_p.

source.citation: Nicolas Rougerie, De Finetti theorems, mean-field limits and Bose-Einstein condensation, lecture notes (Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München, 2015), arXiv:1506.05263.
source.module: Chapter 3, Section 3.4 Links between various structure theorems for bosonic states
source.excerpt: … Let H be a complex separable Hilbert space and (ω^(n))_(n∈ℕ) an abstract bosonic state with infinitely many particles built on H. There exists a unique probability measure µ ∈ P((B(H))*) on the dual of the space of bounded operators on H such that µ({ω ∈ (B(H))*, ω ≥ 0, ω(1_H) = 1}) = 1 (3.43) and ω^(n) = ∫ ω^⊗n dµ(ω) (3.44) for all n ≥ 0.

source.alignment: The excerpt starts after the title 'Theorem 3.16 (Abstract quantum de Finetti).'. The source theorem is for the abstract states of Definition 3.13, which have the permutation symmetry (3.39) and need not be bosonic, and the record states its case dim H = d < ∞, where every abstract state is a density matrix (Remark 3.17 (3)). The bosonic clause is the finite-dimensional case of Theorem 3.5 (Hudson and Moody) of the source. The outline follows the proof of Caves, Fuchs and Schack, Unknown quantum states: the quantum de Finetti representation, J. Math. Phys. 43 (2002) 4537, arXiv:quant-ph/0104088, Section IV.

proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of the quantum de Finetti representation theorem in Caves, Fuchs and Schack (2002), Section IV, equations (4.6)-(4.26), which reduces the quantum statement to the classical de Finetti theorem. Step s5 adds the uniqueness argument, and step s6 adds the bosonic clause with the swap-operator identity that Rougerie quotes from Hudson and Moody after Definition 3.4.

steps.text: A minimal informationally complete measurement (CFS (4.6)-(4.11)). Let (e_j) be an orthonormal basis of ℂ^d. Take the d² rank-one projections Π_α onto e_j (1 ≤ j ≤ d), onto (e_j + e_k)/√2 and onto (e_j + i e_k)/√2 (j < k). Their span contains every |e_j⟩⟨e_k|, so they are a basis of the d²-dimensional space of d × d matrices. G = ∑_α Π_α ≥ ∑_j |e_j⟩⟨e_j| = 1 is invertible, and E_α = G^(−1/2) Π_α G^(−1/2) are positive semidefinite, linearly independent and satisfy ∑_α E_α = 1.

The classical exchangeable sequence (CFS (4.12)-(4.13)). Put p^(N)(α_1, …, α_N) = Tr[ρ^(N) E_(α_1) ⊗ ⋯ ⊗ E_(α_N)]. These numbers are nonnegative because the tensor product of positive operators is positive, they are invariant under permutations of (α_1, …, α_N) because ρ^(N) is permutation invariant, and ∑_α E_α = 1 with Tr_(N+1) ρ^(N+1) = ρ^(N) makes them consistent in N. So they are the finite-dimensional laws of an infinite exchangeable sequence with values in {1, …, d²}. The classical de Finetti theorem gives a unique probability measure P on the simplex S = {p ∈ [0, 1]^(d²) : ∑_α p_α = 1} with p^(N)(α) = ∫_S p_(α_1) ⋯ p_(α_N) P(dp) for all N and α.

Lift to operators (CFS (4.14)-(4.19)). Because the E_α are a basis and the pairing (A, B) ↦ Tr(AB) is nondegenerate, each p ∈ S has a unique operator A_p with Tr(A_p E_α) = p_α for all α, and p ↦ A_p is linear and injective. Taking adjoints shows that A_p* solves the same equations, so A_p is Hermitian, and Tr A_p = ∑_α p_α = 1. Now Tr[A_p^⊗N E_(α_1) ⊗ ⋯ ⊗ E_(α_N)] = p_(α_1) ⋯ p_(α_N), so ρ^(N) and ∫_S A_p^⊗N P(dp) have the same pairing with each of the d^(2N) products E_(α_1) ⊗ ⋯ ⊗ E_(α_N). These products are a basis of the operators on (ℂ^d)^⊗N, hence ρ^(N) = ∫_S A_p^⊗N P(dp).

The mixing measure sees only density matrices (CFS (4.20)-(4.25)). Let q ∈ S be such that A_q has an eigenvalue −λ < 0, with unit eigenvector ψ, and let Π = 1 − |ψ⟩⟨ψ|. Then Tr(A_q Π) = 1 + λ, and B = {p ∈ S : Tr(A_p Π) > 1 + λ/2} is a relatively open neighbourhood of q. For even N the function Tr(A_p Π)^N is nonnegative on S, so 1 ≥ Tr[ρ^(N) Π^⊗N] = ∫_S Tr(A_p Π)^N P(dp) ≥ (1 + λ/2)^N P(B). Letting N → ∞ along even integers gives P(B) = 0. The set U of p for which A_p is not positive semidefinite is covered by such sets B, and countably many of them suffice because S ⊂ ℝ^(d²) is second countable. Hence P(U) = 0.

Existence and uniqueness of m. On S ∖ U the operator A_p is a density matrix, and the map T : D_d → S, T(σ) = (Tr σE_α)_α, is a continuous injection of a compact set with inverse p ↦ A_p. Let m be the image of P under p ↦ A_p. Then s3 and s4 give ρ^(n) = ∫ σ^⊗n m(dσ) for every n. If m′ also represents every ρ^(n), then ∫ ∏_i Tr(σE_(α_i)) m′(dσ) = Tr[ρ^(N) E_(α_1) ⊗ ⋯ ⊗ E_(α_N)] = p^(N)(α), so the image T(m′) is a de Finetti measure of the same exchangeable sequence. Uniqueness in the classical theorem gives T(m′) = P = T(m), and the injectivity of T gives m′ = m.

The bosonic clause. Let F be the swap of the two factors of (ℂ^d)^⊗2. Then Tr[F(A ⊗ B)] = Tr(AB), so Tr[F σ ⊗ σ] = Tr σ². The projection onto the antisymmetric subspace is (1 − F)/2. If ρ^(2) is supported by the symmetric subspace, then 0 = Tr[((1 − F)/2) ρ^(2)] = ∫ (1 − Tr σ²)/2 m(dσ). Since Tr σ² ≤ 1 with equality exactly for pure states, m-almost every σ is pure, σ = |u⟩⟨u|, and then σ^⊗n = |u^⊗n⟩⟨u^⊗n|.

source.ref: C. M. Caves, C. A. Fuchs and R. Schack, Unknown quantum states: the quantum de Finetti representation, J. Math. Phys. 43 (2002) 4537, arXiv:quant-ph/0104088v1, Section IV, pp. 14-19.

applications.title: Mean-field limit and symmetry breaking in the quantum Curie–Weiss model
applications.inputs: Spins 1/2 (d = 2) with Pauli matrices X, Z, the Hamiltonian H_N = −(1/(N − 1)) ∑_(i<j) Z_i Z_j − Γ ∑_i X_i with transverse field Γ = 1/2, its ground-state energy E_N, and the normalized projection ρ_N onto its ground space.
applications.hypotheses: H_N = (1/(N − 1)) ∑_(i<j) h_ij with h = −Z ⊗ Z − Γ(X ⊗ 1 + 1 ⊗ X). H_N commutes with the permutations of the spins, so ρ_N is permutation invariant. The space of density matrices on (ℂ²)^⊗k is compact, so a diagonal subsequence N_j has ρ_(N_j)^(k) → ρ^(k) for every k. The limits are density matrices, permutation invariant and consistent, because the partial trace is continuous. So the theorem applies to (ρ^(k)) with d = 2.

steps.text: Permutation invariance gives E_N/N = (1/2)Tr[h ρ_N^(2)], and a product trial state σ^⊗N gives E_N/N ≤ e_MF = min_σ (1/2)Tr[h σ ⊗ σ]. With the Bloch vector r of σ, (1/2)Tr[h σ ⊗ σ] = −r_z²/2 − Γ r_x.
On the Bloch ball the minimum needs r_y = 0 and r_z² = 1 − r_x², and then r_x = Γ = 1/2. So e_MF = −1/2 − Γ²/2 = −5/8, and the minimizers are exactly the two pure states σ_± with r = (1/2, 0, ±√3/2).

The theorem gives ρ^(2) = ∫ σ ⊗ σ m(dσ), so lim E_(N_j)/N_j = ∫ (1/2)Tr[h σ ⊗ σ] m(dσ) ≥ e_MF. With the upper bound, E_N/N → −5/8 for the whole sequence, and m-almost every σ is a minimizer, so m is carried by {σ_+, σ_−}.

The spin flip X^⊗N commutes with H_N, so every ρ^(k) is invariant under X^⊗k. Then the image of m under σ ↦ XσX also represents (ρ^(k)), and uniqueness forces m = (δ_(σ+) + δ_(σ−))/2. Hence ⟨Z_1⟩ → 0 while ⟨Z_1 Z_2⟩ → r_z² = 1 − (1/2)² = 3/4.

applications.conclusion: For Γ = 1/2 the ground-state energy per spin tends to −5/8, the two-spin correlation ⟨Z_1 Z_2⟩ tends to 3/4 although ⟨Z_1⟩ tends to 0, and the de Finetti measure is the equal mixture of the two magnetized product states. This is long-range order with symmetry breaking.

limitations: The proof uses a measurement with d² outcomes, so it needs finite dimension. For a separable infinite-dimensional space the theorem of Størmer and Hudson–Moody holds for abstract states, but the measure then lives on the dual of B(H), and states that are not normal can occur (Remark 3.17 of the source).

The whole infinite consistent sequence is necessary. A symmetric state of N systems without symmetric extensions need not be a mixture of product states, for example the GHZ state of three qubits (Caves, Fuchs and Schack, Eq. (3.17)). The finite quantum de Finetti theorem gives approximate versions.

results.name: Finite quantum de Finetti theorem
results.statement: Let d ≥ 1, let H = ℂ^d, and let 1 ≤ k ≤ N. Write Sym^N(H) ⊂ H^⊗N for the symmetric (bosonic) subspace, of dimension C(N + d − 1, d − 1), let du be the normalized uniform measure on the unit sphere S of H, and let ‖X‖₁ = Tr|X| be the trace norm. (a) Bosonic states. Let Γ_N be a density operator on Sym^N(H) with k-particle reduced density matrix γ^(k) = Tr_(k+1→N) Γ_N. Then µ_N(du) = dim Sym^N(H)·⟨u^⊗N, Γ_N u^⊗N⟩ du is a probability measure on S, and γ̃^(k) = ∫ |u^⊗k⟩⟨u^⊗k| µ_N(du) satisfies ‖γ^(k) − γ̃^(k)‖₁ ≤ 2kd/(N − kd) if N > kd, and ‖γ^(k) − γ̃^(k)‖₁ ≤ 4kd/N for all k ≤ N. (b) Permutation-invariant states. Let ξ_N be a density operator on H^⊗N with U_π ξ_N U_π* = ξ_N for every permutation π of the N factors, and ξ^(k) = Tr_(k+1→N) ξ_N. Then there is a probability measure m on the set of density operators on H such that ‖ξ^(k) − ∫ σ^⊗k m(dσ)‖₁ ≤ 4kd²/N. The measures µ_N and m do not depend on k.
hypotheses: The one-particle space H = ℂ^d has finite dimension d.
For (a): Γ_N is a density operator on the symmetric subspace Sym^N(H). For (b): ξ_N is a density operator on H^⊗N that commutes with every permutation of the factors.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 uses Schur's lemma for the irreducible action of the unitary group on Sym^N(ℂ^d) to prove Schur's formula dim Sym^N(H)·∫ |u^⊗N⟩⟨u^⊗N| du = 1, which steps s2 and s3 use again.

definitions.name: symmetric subspace
definitions.text: Sym^N(H) is the subspace of H^⊗N of vectors that every permutation of the N factors leaves unchanged. It is the state space of N bosons, and dim Sym^N(ℂ^d) = C(N + d − 1, d − 1).

definitions.name: CKMR measure
definitions.text: The probability measure µ_N(du) = dim Sym^N(H)·⟨u^⊗N, Γ_N u^⊗N⟩ du on the unit sphere. It is the lower symbol (Husimi function) of Γ_N in the coherent states u^⊗N.

definitions.name: reduced density matrix
definitions.text: γ^(k) = Tr_(k+1→N) Γ_N, the partial trace over the last N − k factors. It gives the expectation of every k-particle observable.

source.citation: Mathieu Lewin, Phan Thành Nam and Nicolas Rougerie, Remarks on the quantum de Finetti theorem for bosonic systems, Applied Mathematics Research eXpress (2015), arXiv:1310.2200.
source.revision: arXiv:1310.2200v3 [math-ph], 22 Aug 2014.
source.module: Section 2.2 A quantitative de Finetti theorem and an explicit formula
source.excerpt: … Let H be a Hilbert space of dimension d. For every state Γ_N on H^N, let γ̃_N^(k) be defined as in (2.5). Then for every k = 1, 2, ..., N we have Tr_(H^k)|γ_N^(k) − γ̃_N^(k)| ≤ 2 if N ≤ 2kd, and ≤ 2kd/(N − kd) if N > 2kd. (2.6)
source.attribution: © Mathieu Lewin, Phan Thành Nam and Nicolas Rougerie. Quoted from the arXiv version of Remarks on the quantum de Finetti theorem for bosonic systems for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The excerpt starts after the theorem title 'Theorem 2.1 (Quantitative quantum de Finetti in finite dimension).', where H^N is the bosonic space and γ̃_N^(k) is built from the CKMR measure (2.5). Part (a) is this theorem together with the bound 4kd/N of (2.7). Part (b) is Theorem II.7 of Christandl, König, Mitchison and Renner, Commun. Math. Phys. 273 (2007), arXiv:quant-ph/0602130, stated in the full trace norm (the paper uses half of it). The outline follows the proof in Section 3 of the source for (a), and the purification proof of Theorem II.7 and Lemma II.5 of CKMR for (b).

results.proof_status: outline of the cited published proof. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Outline: steps s1-s5 follow the proof of Theorem 2.1 in Section 3 of Lewin, Nam and Rougerie (equations (3.1)-(3.3)), and step s6 follows the proofs of Lemma II.5 and Theorem II.7 in Christandl, König, Mitchison and Renner. The outline covers both parts of the statement.

steps.text: Schur's formula and the CKMR measure. The operator ∫ |u^⊗N⟩⟨u^⊗N| du on Sym^N(H) commutes with V^⊗N for every unitary V, because du is invariant under V. The unitary group acts irreducibly on Sym^N(H), so by Schur's lemma the operator is a multiple of the identity, and taking traces gives dim Sym^N(H)·∫ |u^⊗N⟩⟨u^⊗N| du = 1_(Sym^N). Hence µ_N(S) = Tr Γ_N = 1, so µ_N is a probability measure. Both γ^(k) and γ̃^(k) are linear in Γ_N, so by the triangle inequality it suffices to treat a pure state Γ_N = |Ψ⟩⟨Ψ|.

A formula for the difference. Let P_u = |u⟩⟨u| and let A be a bounded operator on H^⊗k. Inserting Schur's formula next to Ψ gives Tr[A γ^(k)] = ⟨Ψ, (A ⊗ 1)Ψ⟩ = dim Sym^N ∫ ⟨Ψ, P_u^⊗N (A ⊗ 1)Ψ⟩ du. The definition of µ_N gives Tr[A γ̃^(k)] = dim Sym^N ∫ ⟨Ψ, P_u^⊗N (A ⊗ 1) P_u^⊗N Ψ⟩ du. So Tr[A(γ^(k) − γ̃^(k))] = dim Sym^N ∫ ⟨Ψ, P_u^⊗N (A ⊗ 1)(1 − P_u^⊗N)Ψ⟩ du, which is (3.1) of the source.

Split the integrand. With P = P_u^⊗k one has P_u^⊗N (A ⊗ 1)(1 − P_u^⊗N) = PA(1 − P) ⊗ P_u^⊗(N−k), and PA(1 − P) = A(1 − P) − (1 − P)A(1 − P). For Ψ ∈ Sym^N, Schur's formula on Sym^(N−k) and on Sym^N gives ∫ ⟨Ψ, (B ⊗ P_u^⊗(N−k))Ψ⟩ du = ⟨Ψ, (B ⊗ 1)Ψ⟩/dim Sym^(N−k), so ∫ (1 − P) ⊗ P_u^⊗(N−k) du acts on Ψ as c = 1/dim Sym^(N−k) − 1/dim Sym^N, which is (3.2). The first term is therefore c·⟨Ψ, (A ⊗ 1)Ψ⟩. The second term is ⟨Ψ, Q(A ⊗ 1)QΨ⟩ with the projection Q = (1 − P) ⊗ P_u^⊗(N−k), so its absolute value is at most ‖A‖⟨Ψ, QΨ⟩, and ∫ ⟨Ψ, QΨ⟩ du = c.

The bound (3.3). Steps s2 and s3 give |Tr[A(γ^(k) − γ̃^(k))]| ≤ 2‖A‖·dim Sym^N·c = 2‖A‖(dim Sym^N/dim Sym^(N−k) − 1). The trace norm is the supremum of |Tr[AX]| over ‖A‖ ≤ 1, so ‖γ^(k) − γ̃^(k)‖₁ ≤ 2(dim Sym^N(H)/dim Sym^(N−k)(H) − 1). By s1 the same bound holds for mixed Γ_N.

The dimension ratio. dim Sym^(N−k)/dim Sym^N = ∏_{j=1}^{d−1} (N − k + j)/(N + j) = ∏_{j=1}^{d−1} (1 − k/(N + j)) ≥ (1 − k/N)^(d−1) ≥ 1 − dk/N by Bernoulli's inequality. For N > dk this gives dim Sym^N/dim Sym^(N−k) − 1 ≤ dk/(N − dk), hence the bound 2kd/(N − kd). For N > 2kd, δ = kd/N < 1/2 and δ/(1 − δ) ≤ 2δ give 4kd/N. For N ≤ 2kd, ‖γ^(k) − γ̃^(k)‖₁ ≤ 2 ≤ 4kd/N because both operators are density operators. This proves (a).

General permutation-invariant states (CKMR, Lemma II.5 and Theorem II.7). Let K ≅ H with an orthonormal basis (e_i), Φ = (∑_i e_i ⊗ e_i)^⊗N ∈ (K ⊗ H)^⊗N and Ψ_ξ = (1 ⊗ √ξ_N)Φ. Since √ξ_N commutes with the permutations and Φ is invariant under the simultaneous permutation of the N pairs, Ψ_ξ ∈ Sym^N(K ⊗ H), and Tr_(K^⊗N)|Ψ_ξ⟩⟨Ψ_ξ| = √ξ_N·1·√ξ_N = ξ_N. Part (a) with one-particle dimension d² gives a measure µ on the unit sphere of K ⊗ H with ‖Γ^(k) − ∫ |w^⊗k⟩⟨w^⊗k| µ(dw)‖₁ ≤ 4kd²/N for the k-pair marginal Γ^(k) of Ψ_ξ. The partial trace over K^⊗k does not increase the trace norm, maps Γ^(k) to ξ^(k) and maps |w⟩⟨w|^⊗k to σ_w^⊗k with σ_w = Tr_K|w⟩⟨w|. So m, the image of µ under w ↦ σ_w, satisfies (b).

source.ref: M. Lewin, P. T. Nam and N. Rougerie, Remarks on the quantum de Finetti theorem for bosonic systems, arXiv:1310.2200v3, Theorem 2.1 and its proof in Section 3, pp. 5-9; M. Christandl, R. König, G. Mitchison and R. Renner, One-and-a-half quantum de Finetti theorems, arXiv:quant-ph/0602130v4, Lemma II.5 and Theorem II.7, pp. 3-4.

applications.title: Mean-field energy of the quantum Curie–Weiss model in a transverse field
applications.inputs: N = 1000 spins 1/2 (d = 2) with Hamiltonian H_N = −(1/(N − 1)) ∑_{i<j} Z_i Z_j − Γ ∑_i X_i and transverse field Γ = 1/2, where X and Z are Pauli matrices. Let E₀ be the ground-state energy of H_N.
applications.hypotheses: Since ∑_{i<j}(X_i + X_j) = (N − 1)∑_i X_i, H_N = (1/(N − 1))∑_{i<j} h_ij with the two-spin operator h = −Z ⊗ Z − Γ(X ⊗ 1 + 1 ⊗ X), and ‖h‖ ≤ 1 + 2Γ = 2. H_N commutes with the permutations, so the normalized projection ρ onto its ground space is a permutation-invariant density operator, and part (b) applies with k = 2.

steps.text: Permutation invariance gives Tr[H_N ρ] = (1/(N − 1))·(N(N − 1)/2)·Tr[h ρ^(2)], so E₀/N = (1/2)Tr[h ρ^(2)]. A product state σ^⊗N gives E₀/N ≤ (1/2)Tr[h σ ⊗ σ] for every σ, so E₀/N ≤ e_MF := min_σ (1/2)Tr[h σ ⊗ σ].
With the Bloch vector r of σ, (1/2)Tr[h σ ⊗ σ] = −r_z²/2 − Γ r_x. For Γ = 1/2 the minimum over |r| ≤ 1 is at r_x = 1/2, r_z² = 3/4, so e_MF = −1/2 + (1/2)(1/2)² − (1/2)(1/2) = −5/8.
So −5/8 − 4/125 ≤ E₀/N ≤ −5/8, that is −0.657 ≤ E₀/N ≤ −0.625. The error term 4kd²‖h‖/(2N) decreases like 1/N, so the mean-field energy is exact in the limit N → ∞.

applications.conclusion: For 1000 spins in the quantum Curie–Weiss model with transverse field 1/2, the ground-state energy per spin lies between −5/8 − 4/125 and −5/8. The finite de Finetti theorem turns the mean-field approximation into a bound with an explicit error.

limitations: The bounds grow with the one-particle dimension d, so they give nothing for infinite-dimensional H. CKMR show by examples that some dependence on d is necessary (Section II and Theorem II.10 of their paper).

Part (b) loses a factor d compared with part (a), because the purification doubles the local dimension to d². Chiribella's formula gives the sharper bosonic bound 2kd/N (Remark 4.2 of Rougerie's lecture notes, arXiv:1506.05263).

results.name: Aldous–Hoover representation of exchangeable arrays
aliases: representation theorem for exchangeable random graphs
Aldous–Hoover representation of jointly exchangeable symmetric arrays
results.statement: Let S be a countably infinite set and K a standard Borel space. Let (X_e) be a family of K-valued random variables indexed by the 2-element subsets e = {s, t} of S. Equivalently, (X_e) is a random K-coloured graph on S, or a symmetric array (X_st) with X_st = X_ts and no diagonal. Suppose that (X_e) is jointly exchangeable: (X_{g(s), g(t)}) has the same law as (X_{s, t}) for every permutation g of S that moves only finitely many points. Then there is a measurable function f : [0, 1]^4 → K with f(α, x, y, u) = f(α, y, x, u) with the following property. If ξ_∅, (ξ_s)_(s∈S) and (ξ_e)_(e⊂S, |e|=2) are independent random variables, each uniform on [0, 1], then the family (f(ξ_∅, ξ_s, ξ_t, ξ_{s,t}))_({s,t}) has the same law as (X_{s,t})_({s,t}). Conversely, every family of this form is jointly exchangeable.
hypotheses: The vertex set S is countably infinite.
The colour space K is a standard Borel space, for example a finite set of colours or the real line.
The family (X_e) is jointly exchangeable: its law does not change when the vertices are relabelled by a permutation of S that moves finitely many points.

prerequisites.reason: Step s5 applies de Finetti's theorem to the exchangeable sequence of vertex types to get a random directing measure ν on the type space.

definitions.name: vertex type
definitions.text: For a split S = S_1 ∪ S_2 into two infinite sets and a vertex s ∈ S_1, the type Y_s is the list of colours of all edges from s to S_2, together with the colours of all edges inside S_2.

definitions.name: noise outsourcing
definitions.text: The representation of a probability kernel P from X to a standard Borel space Y by a measurable map h : X × [0, 1] → Y such that h(x, U) has law P(x, ·) when U is uniform on [0, 1].

source.citation: Tim Austin, On exchangeable random variables and the statistics of large graphs and hypergraphs, Probability Surveys 5 (2008) 80–145.
source.revision: arXiv:0801.1698v3 [math.PR], 26 May 2008, which carries the journal pagination of Probability Surveys 5 (2008).

source.excerpt: … there is some measurable function f : [0, 1]^4 → K such that given any uniform [0, 1]-valued random variable ξ_∅ and uniform [0, 1]-valued processes (ξ_s)_(s∈S) and (ξ_e)_(e∈(S 2)), all independent, then the stochastic process (f(ξ_∅, ξ_s, ξ_t, ξ_{s,t}))_({s,t}∈(S 2)) has joint law µ.

source.alignment: The excerpt omits the opening words 'Theorem 3.6. For any exchangeable random K-coloured graph µ', because sp.py places excerpts in this long file several hundred characters too early. The record writes the random coloured graph as a family (X_e) on the 2-element subsets of S, makes the symmetry of f explicit, allows any standard Borel colour space K (the proof uses only this structure) and adds the easy converse. The outline follows the source proof of Corollary 3.5 through Lemma 3.2, Lemma 3.3 and Proposition 3.4 (pp. 100-104), and then the noise outsourcing Lemma 4.2 (p. 127), which the source names as the way from Corollary 3.5 to Theorem 3.6. The result is due to D. J. Aldous, J. Multivariate Anal. 11 (1981) 581–598, and D. N. Hoover (1979), and the source presents it as a special case of Theorem 14.11 in Aldous, Exchangeability and related topics (1985).

proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of Corollary 3.5 in Austin, Probability Surveys 5 (2008), pp. 100-104, through Lemma 3.2, Lemma 3.3 and Proposition 3.4, and then the passage from probability kernels to one function by the noise outsourcing Lemma 4.2, p. 127, which the source names on pp. 104 and 127. Step s5 writes out the common symmetric edge kernel, which the source states briefly, and step s6 writes out the transfer to the function f.

steps.text: Reduction to an induced graph. Split S = S_1 ∪ S_2 into two disjoint infinite sets and fix a bijection ψ : S → S_1. For finitely many edges of S, a permutation of S that moves finitely many points agrees with ψ on their end points. So by exchangeability the induced graph (X_{ψ(s), ψ(t)}) has the same law as (X_{s, t}). It is enough to represent the edges inside S_1. The vertices of S_2 serve as reference vertices.

Vertex types. For s ∈ S_1 let Y_s be the type of s: the colours of all edges {s, a} with a ∈ S_2, together with the colours of all edges inside S_2. Y_s takes values in the standard Borel space Z_1 = K^(S_2) × K^(2-subsets of S_2). A finitely supported permutation g of S_1, extended by the identity on S_2, maps Y_s to Y_(g(s)) and keeps the law. So (Y_s)_(s∈S_1) is an exchangeable sequence (Lemma 3.2 of the source). Let T be the σ-algebra generated by all Y_s. For an edge e = {s, t} ⊂ S_1 let T_e = σ(Y_s, Y_t), and let T_e^(S_3) be built in the same way from an infinite set S_3 ⊂ S_2 in place of S_2.

Energy squeeze (Lemma 3.3). Let e = {s, t} ⊂ S_1 and let φ be bounded and measurable on K. Since T_e^(S_3) ⊂ T_e, the conditional expectation E[φ(X_e) | T_e^(S_3)] is the orthogonal projection of E[φ(X_e) | T_e] in L². So the two are equal when their L² norms are equal. By martingale convergence, the squared norm of E[φ(X_e) | T_e] is the supremum over finite F ⊂ S_2 of the squared norms of the conditional expectations given the colours inside {s} ∪ F and inside {t} ∪ F. By exchangeability each term depends only on |F|, and S_3 has finite subsets of every size. So the norms agree, and E[φ(X_e) | T_e] = E[φ(X_e) | T_e^(S_3)] is a function of the colours at s, t and S_3 only.

Moving vertices into the reference set (Proposition 3.4). Let A ∈ T depend on finitely many types through finitely many edges, with edge e_1 = {s, t}. A finitely supported permutation g fixes s, t and a co-finite set S_3 ⊂ S_2, and moves every other vertex of S_1 that A involves into S_2. The permutation keeps φ(X_(e_1)) and maps A to an event in T_(e_1). By s3, E[φ(X_(e_1)) | T_(e_1)] is a function of the colours at s, t and S_3, which g does not move. Moving back gives E[φ(X_(e_1)) | T] = E[φ(X_(e_1)) | T_(e_1)]. With more edges e_2, …, e_r, the permutation also moves the end points of e_p outside e_1 into S_2, so each moved edge factor becomes T-measurable. The same steps then give E[∏_p φ_p(X_(e_p)) | T] = ∏_p E[φ_p(X_(e_p)) | T]. So the edge colours inside S_1 are conditionally independent given T.

Edge kernel and de Finetti. By exchangeability the triple (Y_s, Y_t, X_{s,t}) has the same law for all edges {s, t} ⊂ S_1, and the transposition of s and t maps it to (Y_t, Y_s, X_{s,t}). So one probability kernel P_2 from Z_1 × Z_1 to K gives the conditional law P_2(Y_s, Y_t, ·) of X_{s,t} given T_e, for every edge. The average of P_2(y, y′, ·) and P_2(y′, y, ·) is again such a kernel, so P_2 can be taken symmetric. By s4 the conditional law of the edge colours given T is the product of the laws P_2(Y_s, Y_t, ·). By de Finetti's theorem there is a random probability measure ν on Z_1 such that, given ν, the Y_s are i.i.d. with law ν (Theorem 3.1 and Corollary 3.5 of the source).

Transfer to one function (Lemma 4.2). For a probability kernel P into a standard Borel space, the quantile construction of the source gives a measurable h with h(x, U) of law P(x, ·) for U uniform, and h depends on x only through P(x, ·). Take h_0 with h_0(U) of the law of ν, h_1 with h_1(m, U) of law m, and h_2 with h_2(y, y′, U) of law P_2(y, y′, ·), so that h_2 is symmetric in (y, y′). Put f(α, x, y, u) = h_2(h_1(h_0(α), x), h_1(h_0(α), y), u). Then the types h_1(h_0(ξ_∅), ξ_s) have the law of (Y_s), and given them the values f(ξ_∅, ξ_s, ξ_t, ξ_{s,t}) are independent with laws P_2. By s4 and s5 this is the joint law of types and edges in S_1, and s1 gives the claim on S. Conversely, a finitely supported permutation of S maps the independent uniform family to a family with the same law, so every family of this form is exchangeable.

source.ref: T. Austin, On exchangeable random variables and the statistics of large graphs and hypergraphs, Probability Surveys 5 (2008) 80–145, Theorem 3.6, Corollary 3.5 and Lemma 4.2.

applications.title: Edges at a common vertex are not negatively correlated
applications.inputs: An exchangeable random graph on ℕ, coded as X_st ∈ {0, 1}. For numbers, the two-block graph: each vertex gets an independent fair type A or B, and given the types each edge is present independently with probability 3/4 between equal types and 1/4 between different types. For contrast, the random graph on {1, 2, 3, 4} with exactly one edge, chosen uniformly among the 6 possible edges.
applications.hypotheses: The two-block graph is jointly exchangeable on ℕ, because the types are i.i.d. and the edge law depends only on the two types. The colour set K = {0, 1} is finite, so it is standard Borel. So the theorem applies to the two-block graph and to every exchangeable random graph on ℕ.

steps.text: By the theorem, (X_st) has the law of (f(ξ_∅, ξ_s, ξ_t, ξ_st)). Put d(α, x) = P(f(α, x, ξ_2, ξ_12) = 1). Given ξ_∅ and ξ_1, the edges X_12 and X_13 use the independent noise (ξ_2, ξ_12) and (ξ_3, ξ_13). So they are conditionally independent, each with success probability d(ξ_∅, ξ_1). Hence P(X_12 = X_13 = 1) = E[d²] ≥ (E[d])² = P(X_12 = 1)² by Jensen's inequality.
In the two-block graph, the edge probability is P(X_12 = 1) = (1/2)(3/4) + (1/2)(1/4) = 1/2.

Given the type of vertex 1, each other vertex joins it with probability (1/2)(3/4) + (1/2)(1/4) = 1/2, independently. So P(X_12 = X_13 = 1) = (1/2)² = 1/4 = P(X_12 = 1)², and the bound of a1 holds with equality.

Triangles separate the two-block graph from the Erdős–Rényi graph with p = 1/2. The three types agree with probability 1/4, and then the triangle has probability (3/4)³. Otherwise two vertices share a type, and the triangle has probability (3/4)(1/4)². So P(triangle on 1, 2, 3) = 9/64, which is more than (1/2)³ = 8/64.

The single-edge graph on {1, 2, 3, 4} is exchangeable under the permutations of {1, 2, 3, 4}. It has P(X_12 = 1) = 1/6 and P(X_12 = X_13 = 1) = 0, which is less than (1/6)² = 1/36. So by a1 it is not the restriction of an exchangeable random graph on ℕ.

applications.conclusion: In every exchangeable random graph on ℕ, two edges at a common vertex satisfy P(X_12 = X_13 = 1) ≥ P(X_12 = 1)². The two-block graph meets this bound with equality at 1/4 and has triangle probability 9/64 > 1/8. The single-edge graph on 4 vertices violates the bound, so it does not extend to an exchangeable graph on ℕ.

limitations: The theorem needs an infinite vertex set. A finite exchangeable random graph need not have this form, as the single-edge graph on 4 vertices in worked-1 shows.
The function f is not unique. For example, f(α, T(x), T(y), u) gives the same law as f(α, x, y, u) for every measure-preserving map T of [0, 1].

The record treats symmetric arrays without diagonal, that is random coloured graphs. Hypergraphs, directed graphs and separately exchangeable arrays need the analogous Theorems 3.14, 3.21 and 3.25 of the source.

results.name: Kingman's paintbox representation of exchangeable random partitions
aliases: Kingman's representation theorem for exchangeable partitions
results.statement: Let Π be an exchangeable random partition of ℕ = {1, 2, …}, that is a random partition whose law does not change when the points are relabelled by any permutation of ℕ that moves finitely many points. Let Π_n be its restriction to {1, …, n}, and let N↓_(n,1) ≥ N↓_(n,2) ≥ … be the block sizes of Π_n in decreasing order, with N↓_(n,i) = 0 if Π_n has fewer than i blocks. Then for each i the limit P↓_i = lim_(n→∞) N↓_(n,i)/n exists almost surely, with P↓_1 ≥ P↓_2 ≥ … ≥ 0 and ∑_i P↓_i ≤ 1. Conditionally given P↓ = p, Π has the paintbox law of p: take disjoint intervals J_1, J_2, … ⊂ [0, 1] of lengths p_1, p_2, … and i.i.d. uniform points U_1, U_2, … in [0, 1], and put two distinct integers i and j in the same block exactly when U_i and U_j lie in the same interval J_k. So the law of Π is a mixture of paintbox laws, mixed over the law of P↓.
hypotheses: Π is a random partition of the infinite set ℕ, or equivalently a sequence of random partitions Π_n of {1, …, n} whose restrictions agree.
Π is exchangeable: σ(Π) has the same law as Π for every permutation σ of ℕ that moves finitely many points.

prerequisites.reason: Step s3 applies de Finetti's theorem to the exchangeable sequence of uniform marks that labels the blocks of Π.
Step s3 uses the Glivenko–Cantelli theorem, conditionally on the directing measure, to get uniform almost sure convergence of the empirical distribution functions.

definitions.name: paintbox partition
definitions.text: For ranked frequencies p_1 ≥ p_2 ≥ … ≥ 0 with ∑ p_k ≤ 1, the random partition of ℕ in which i and j share a block when independent uniform points U_i and U_j fall in the same interval J_k of length p_k. Points that fall outside all intervals are singletons.

definitions.name: ranked frequencies
definitions.text: The almost sure limits P↓_i of N↓_(n,i)/n, the asymptotic proportions of the largest, second largest, … block of Π. The quantity 1 − ∑ P↓_i is the asymptotic proportion of singletons.

source.citation: Jim Pitman, Combinatorial Stochastic Processes, Lecture Notes in Mathematics 1875 (École d'Été de Probabilités de Saint-Flour XXXII, 2002), Springer, 2006.

source.module: Chapter 2 Exchangeable random partitions, Section 2.2 Infinite partitions
source.excerpt: Theorem 2.2. (Kingman's representation [251, 253]) Let Π∞ := (Πn) be an exchangeable random partition of N, and let (N↓n,i, i ≥ 1) be the decreasing rearrangement of block sizes of Πn, with N↓n,i = 0 if Πn has fewer than i blocks. Then N↓n,i/n has an almost sure limit P↓i as n → ∞ for each i. Moreover the conditional distribution of Π∞ given (P↓i, i ≥ 1) is as if Π∞ were generated by random sampling from a random distribution with ranked atoms (P↓i, i ≥ 1).
source.attribution: © Jim Pitman. Quoted from the author's version of Combinatorial Stochastic Processes for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source describes the conditional law as random sampling from a distribution with ranked atoms P↓. The record states the same law as Kingman's paintbox, where the intervals J_k play the role of the atoms and the rest of [0, 1] plays the role of the continuous part. The outline follows the proof sketch of the source (pp. 44-45), which follows Aldous, Exchangeability and related topics (1985), p. 88. The original result is J. F. C. Kingman, J. London Math. Soc. (2) 18 (1978) 374-380.

proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof sketch of Theorem 2.2 in Pitman, Combinatorial Stochastic Processes (2006), pp. 44-45, which follows Aldous (1985), p. 88. Steps s2, s4 and s5 write out the exchangeability of the marks, the identification of the conditional law and the convergence of ranked atoms, which the sketch states briefly.

steps.text: Uniform marks. Enlarge the probability space by i.i.d. uniform variables U_1, U_2, … on [0, 1], independent of Π. Order the blocks of Π by their least elements, and put X_n = U_j when n lies in the j-th block. The U_j are distinct almost surely, so almost surely X_m = X_n exactly when m and n lie in the same block. Thus Π is the partition generated by the sequence (X_n).

The marks are exchangeable. Let σ be a permutation of ℕ that moves finitely many points, and Π′ = σ⁻¹(Π), which has the same law as Π. The block of σ(n) in Π is the image under σ of the block of n in Π′. So there is a bijection π of block indices, a function of (Π, σ), with X_(σ(n)) = U_(π(J′(n))), where J′(n) is the index of the block of n in Π′ in order of appearance. Conditionally on Π the variables U′_k = U_(π(k)) are again i.i.d. uniform, so (Π′, U′) has the law of (Π, U). The sequence (X_(σ(n))) is built from (Π′, U′) exactly as (X_n) is built from (Π, U), hence (X_(σ(n)))_n has the law of (X_n)_n.

Directing measure. By de Finetti's theorem there is a random probability measure F on [0, 1] such that, conditionally on F, the X_n are i.i.d. with law F. The Glivenko–Cantelli theorem, applied conditionally on F, gives sup_x |F_n(x) − F(x)| → 0 almost surely, where F_n(x) = n⁻¹ ∑_(m≤n) 1(X_m ≤ x) is the empirical distribution function (equation (2.12) of the source).

The conditional law is a paintbox. Let a_1 ≥ a_2 ≥ … be the ranked atom sizes of F. Conditionally on F, two i.i.d. draws X_i and X_j (i ≠ j) coincide with probability ∑_k a_k², and a.s. they coincide only when both hit the same atom, because the continuous part of F produces no ties. Map the k-th atom to an interval J_k of length a_k and the continuous part to [0, 1] ∖ ∪J_k. Since Π is the partition generated by (X_n), its conditional law given F is the paintbox law of (a_k). This law depends on F only through (a_k).

Ranked frequencies. The atoms of F_n sit at the distinct values of X_1, …, X_n, and by s1 their masses are the block sizes of Π_n divided by n. So N↓_(n,i)/n is the i-th largest jump of F_n. For each x the jumps satisfy |ΔF_n(x) − ΔF(x)| ≤ 2 sup_y |F_n(y) − F(y)|. The decreasing rearrangement is 1-Lipschitz in the supremum norm, because a↓_i = sup_(|A|=i) min_(x∈A) a(x). Hence N↓_(n,i)/n → a_i = P↓_i almost surely for every i. Since P↓ is a function of F and the conditional law given F depends only on P↓, the conditional law given P↓ is the paintbox law of P↓.

source.ref: J. Pitman, Combinatorial Stochastic Processes, Lecture Notes in Mathematics 1875, Springer 2006, Theorem 2.2 and its proof sketch, pp. 44-45.

applications.title: Allele frequencies in the infinite alleles model
applications.inputs: The Chinese restaurant process with parameter θ = 1, which gives the allelic partition of a sample of genes under the infinite alleles model (Ewens sampling formula). Gene n + 1 joins an existing allele class of size n_j with probability n_j/(n + θ) and starts a new class with probability θ/(n + θ).
applications.hypotheses: The process defines partitions Π_n of {1, …, n} whose restrictions agree. The probability of a given partition with block sizes n_1, …, n_k is θ^k ∏(n_i − 1)!/(θ(θ + 1)⋯(θ + n − 1)), which depends only on the block sizes. So the limit partition of ℕ is exchangeable and the theorem applies.

steps.text: In the paintbox, genes 1 and 2 share a class exactly when U_1 and U_2 fall in the same interval. So P(1 ∼ 2) = E[∑_k (P↓_k)²], the expected homozygosity. The process gives P(1 ∼ 2) = 1/(1 + θ) = 1/2.
Similarly P(1 ∼ 2 ∼ 3) = E[∑_k (P↓_k)³]. The process gives (1/(1 + θ))·(2/(2 + θ)) = 1/3 for θ = 1.
Gene 1 is still alone among the first n = 10 genes with probability ∏_(m=1)^(9) (m − 1 + θ)/(m + θ) = ∏_(m=1)^(9) m/(m + 1) = 1/10. This tends to 0 as n grows.

In the paintbox, gene 1 is a singleton of Π exactly when U_1 falls outside all intervals. So E[1 − ∑_k P↓_k] = P(1 is a singleton) = 0 by a3, and the frequencies are proper: ∑_k P↓_k = 1 almost surely.

applications.conclusion: For θ = 1 the allele frequencies P↓ exist as almost sure limits, they sum to 1, and E[∑ (P↓_k)²] = 1/2 and E[∑ (P↓_k)³] = 1/3. The sample partition is a paintbox sample from these random frequencies.

limitations: The theorem needs a partition of the infinite set ℕ. An exchangeable partition of {1, …, n} that does not extend need not be a mixture of paintboxes. Proposition 2.1 of the source gives the finite analogue by sampling without replacement.
The theorem identifies the mixing law only abstractly. Explicit laws of P↓, such as the Poisson–Dirichlet laws, need extra structure, for example the consistency of the Ewens sampling formula.

results.name: Ryll-Nardzewski theorem: spreadable sequences are exchangeable
results.statement: Let X = (X_1, X_2, …) be an infinite sequence of random variables with values in a standard Borel space E. Suppose that X is spreadable: for every strictly increasing sequence n_1 < n_2 < … of positive integers, (X_(n_1), X_(n_2), …) has the same law as X. Then X is exchangeable: (X_(π(1)), X_(π(2)), …) has the same law as X for every permutation π of ℕ that moves finitely many points. More precisely, let T = ∩_m σ(X_m, X_(m+1), …) be the tail σ-field. Then P(X_1 ∈ B_1, …, X_k ∈ B_k | T) = ∏_(i≤k) P(X_1 ∈ B_i | T) almost surely for all k and all measurable B_1, …, B_k ⊂ E, so the X_n are conditionally i.i.d. given T. Conversely, every exchangeable sequence is spreadable.
hypotheses: X = (X_n)_(n≥1) is an infinite sequence of random variables with values in a standard Borel space E, for example the real line.
X is spreadable: every subsequence (X_(n_1), X_(n_2), …) with n_1 < n_2 < … has the same law as X.

prerequisites.reason: Step s2 uses Lévy's upward theorem: E[Y | G_n] converges to E[Y | G] almost surely, hence in L² for bounded Y.
Step s3 uses the backward form of the martingale convergence theorem: E[φ(X_1) | X_m, X_(m+1), …] converges to E[φ(X_1) | T] as m → ∞.

definitions.name: spreadable sequence
definitions.text: An infinite sequence (X_n) such that every subsequence (X_(n_1), X_(n_2), …) with n_1 < n_2 < … has the same law as (X_n). Other names are spreading-invariant and contractable.

definitions.name: conditionally i.i.d. given T
definitions.text: For all k and measurable B_1, …, B_k, the conditional probability P(X_1 ∈ B_1, …, X_k ∈ B_k | T) equals ∏_(i≤k) P(X_1 ∈ B_i | T) almost surely.

source.citation: Claus Köstler, A noncommutative extended de Finetti theorem, J. Funct. Anal. 258 (2010) 1073–1120.
source.revision: arXiv:0806.3621v1 [math.OA], 23 June 2008.
source.module: Introduction and main result
source.excerpt: Theorem 0.1. Let X ≡ (X_n)_(n∈ℕ) : (Ω, Σ, µ) → (Ω_0, Σ_0) be a sequence of random variables, where (Ω, Σ) and (Ω_0, Σ_0) are standard Borel spaces and µ is a probability measure. Then the following conditions are equivalent: (a) X is exchangeable; (b) X is spreadable; (c) X is conditionally i.i.d.
source.attribution: © Claus Köstler. Quoted from A noncommutative extended de Finetti theorem (arXiv:0806.3621v1) for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The record states the implication (b) ⇒ (a) of Theorem 0.1, which the source attributes to Ryll-Nardzewski, Colloq. Math. 4 (1957) 149–156, together with (c) written as a product formula for conditional probabilities given the tail σ-field, and the easy converse (a) ⇒ (b). The source proves a noncommutative version and gives no proof of the classical theorem. The outline follows the proof of Theorem 6.1, property (A), in D. J. Aldous, Exchangeability and related topics (1985), pp. 42-45, through Lemma 6.3, Proposition 6.4 and Lemma 6.5.

proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of Theorem 6.1, property (A), in Aldous, Exchangeability and related topics, Saint-Flour XIII (1985), pp. 42-45. Step s2 is Lemma 6.3, steps s3 and s4 are Proposition 6.4 with the choice of indices that spreadability gives, and step s5 is Lemma 6.5. Step s1 writes out the easy directions.

steps.text: Easy directions. Let X be exchangeable and n_1 < … < n_k. Choose a permutation π of {1, …, n_k} with π(i) = n_i for i ≤ k. Then (X_(n_1), …, X_(n_k)) is the start of (X_(π(1)), …, X_(π(n_k))), which has the law of (X_1, …, X_(n_k)). So all finite-dimensional laws agree, and X is spreadable. Next, if X is conditionally i.i.d. given T, a permutation of the indices does not change the product ∏_i P(X_1 ∈ B_i | T). So the conditional law of every finite block, and hence the law of X, is invariant, and X is exchangeable. It remains to show that a spreadable X is conditionally i.i.d. given T.

Projection squeeze (Lemma 6.3). Let G_1 ⊂ G_2 ⊂ … be σ-fields with G = ∨_n G_n, let F ⊂ G, and let Y be bounded. Suppose that for each n there is F_n ⊂ F with E[Y | F_n] equal in law to E[Y | G_n]. Then ‖E[Y | G_n]‖₂ = ‖E[Y | F_n]‖₂ ≤ ‖E[Y | F]‖₂. Lévy's upward theorem gives E[Y | G_n] → E[Y | G] in L², so ‖E[Y | G]‖₂ ≤ ‖E[Y | F]‖₂. Since F ⊂ G, E[Y | F] is the orthogonal projection of E[Y | G], and ‖E[Y | G]‖₂² = ‖E[Y | F]‖₂² + ‖E[Y | G] − E[Y | F]‖₂². Hence E[Y | F] = E[Y | G] almost surely.

The first variable and the tail (Proposition 6.4). Fix m ≥ 2 and a bounded measurable φ on E. For n ≥ 2, spreadability gives (X_1, X_2, …, X_n) equal in law to (X_1, X_m, …, X_(m+n−2)). So E[φ(X_1) | X_2, …, X_n] and E[φ(X_1) | X_m, …, X_(m+n−2)] are the same measurable function of vectors with the same law, and they have the same law. Apply s2 with G_n = σ(X_2, …, X_n), G = σ(X_2, X_3, …), F = σ(X_m, X_(m+1), …) and F_n = σ(X_m, …, X_(m+n−2)). This gives E[φ(X_1) | X_2, X_3, …] = E[φ(X_1) | X_m, X_(m+1), …] for every m. As m → ∞, the backward martingale convergence theorem turns the right side into E[φ(X_1) | T]. Since T ⊂ σ(X_2, X_3, …), X_1 and σ(X_2, X_3, …) are conditionally independent given T.

All coordinates. For each j the shifted sequence (X_j, X_(j+1), …) is again spreadable and has the same tail σ-field T. So by s3, X_j and σ(X_(j+1), X_(j+2), …) are conditionally independent given T, for every j. Induction on k then gives P(X_1 ∈ B_1, …, X_k ∈ B_k | T) = ∏_(i≤k) P(X_i ∈ B_i | T) almost surely.

Equal conditional laws (Lemma 6.5). For n ≥ 2, both (X_1, X_(n+1), X_(n+2), …) and (X_n, X_(n+1), X_(n+2), …) are subsequences of X, so they have the same law. The conditioning variables X_(n+1), X_(n+2), … are the same in both, so E[φ(X_1) | X_(n+1), X_(n+2), …] = E[φ(X_n) | X_(n+1), X_(n+2), …] almost surely. Conditioning on T ⊂ σ(X_(n+1), X_(n+2), …) gives E[φ(X_n) | T] = E[φ(X_1) | T]. With s4 this is the product formula of the statement, so X is conditionally i.i.d. given T, and s1 gives exchangeability.

source.ref: D. J. Aldous, Exchangeability and related topics, École d'Été de Probabilités de Saint-Flour XIII—1983, Lecture Notes in Mathematics 1117, Springer 1985, Theorem 6.1 with Lemma 6.3, Proposition 6.4 and Lemma 6.5, pp. 42-45.

applications.title: Orderings and records in a spreadable sequence
applications.inputs: A spreadable sequence (X_n) of real random variables without ties: P(X_i = X_j) = 0 for i ≠ j. For example, X_n = Θ + ε_n with independent standard normal Θ, ε_1, ε_2, …. For contrast, the pair (X_1, X_2) = (U, U + 1/3 mod 1) with U uniform on [0, 1).
applications.hypotheses: The real line is a standard Borel space and (X_n) is an infinite spreadable sequence, so the theorem applies to it. The pair (U, U + 1/3 mod 1) has two uniform coordinates, so it is spreadable as a finite sequence of length 2.

steps.text: By the theorem, (X_n) is exchangeable. So the n! orderings of X_1, …, X_n have the same probability. Ties have probability 0, so each strict ordering has probability 1/n!. For n = 3 this gives P(X_1 < X_2 < X_3) = 1/6.
X_4 is a record when X_4 > max(X_1, X_2, X_3). By a1 exactly 3! of the 4! orderings put X_4 on top, so P(X_4 is a record) = 1/4. In the same way X_n is a record with probability 1/n.
By linearity of expectation, the expected number of records among X_1, …, X_4 is 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4 = 25/12.

Spreadability alone compares subsequences only in their original order. The swap (X_1, X_2) to (X_2, X_1) comes from the theorem and needs an infinite sequence. The pair (U, U + 1/3 mod 1) has no ties, but X_1 < X_2 exactly when U < 2/3, so P(X_1 < X_2) = 2/3 and not 1/2. So this pair is not the start of an infinite spreadable sequence.

applications.conclusion: In a spreadable real sequence without ties, every ordering of X_1, …, X_n has probability 1/n!, X_n is a record with probability 1/n, and the expected number of records among the first 4 terms is 25/12. The pair (U, U + 1/3 mod 1) has P(X_1 < X_2) = 2/3, so it does not extend to an infinite spreadable sequence.

limitations: The theorem needs an infinite sequence. For a finite sequence spreadability does not give exchangeability: the pair (U, U + 1/3 mod 1) is spreadable, but P(X_1 < X_2) = 2/3.
Stationarity, that is invariance under the shift only, is much weaker than spreadability. A stationary sequence, for example a stationary Markov chain, need not be exchangeable.
The theorem does not identify the mixing law. De Finetti's theorem then writes the law of X as a mixture of i.i.d. laws, directed by the conditional law of X_1 given T.

results.name: Lévy–Khintchine formula
aliases: Lévy–Khintchine representation of infinitely divisible distributions
results.statement: A probability measure on ℝ with characteristic function φ is infinitely divisible (for every n ≥ 1 it is the n-fold convolution power of some probability measure) if and only if φ(t) = exp(ict − σ²t²/2 + ∫_{ℝ∖{0}} (e^{itx} − 1 − itx/(1 + x²)) ν(dx)) for all t ∈ ℝ, where c ∈ ℝ, σ² ≥ 0 and ν is a measure on ℝ∖{0} with ∫ x²/(1 + x²) ν(dx) < ∞. The triple (c, σ², ν) is then uniquely determined by φ.
hypotheses: The law is a probability measure on ℝ. Infinite divisibility means that for every n ≥ 1 there is a probability measure μ_n with μ = μ_n * ⋯ * μ_n (n factors).
In the formula, c ∈ ℝ, σ² ≥ 0 and ν is a measure on ℝ∖{0} with ∫ x²/(1 + x²) ν(dx) < ∞.

prerequisites.reason: Steps s1 and s3 use Lévy's continuity theorem to show that pointwise limits of characteristic functions that are continuous at 0 are characteristic functions.
Steps s1 and s7 use dominated convergence with the bound |e^{itx} − 1 − itx/(1 + x²)| ≤ C(1 + t²) x²/(1 + x²) and its analogues.
Step s4 uses Bochner's theorem to turn the positive definite functions e^{−tψ} into laws of the increments.
Step s4 uses the Kolmogorov extension theorem to build a process from the consistent finite-dimensional laws.
Step s5 takes the characteristic exponent of the Lévy process from the independent pieces of the Lévy–Itô decomposition.
Step s7 uses that a finite measure on ℝ is determined by its Fourier transform.

definitions.name: infinitely divisible distribution
definitions.text: A probability measure μ on ℝ such that for every n ≥ 1 there is a probability measure μ_n with μ = μ_n^{*n}. Equivalently, a random variable with law μ has the law of a sum of n i.i.d. random variables for every n.

definitions.name: Lévy measure
definitions.text: The measure ν on ℝ∖{0} in the formula. It satisfies ∫ x²/(1 + x²) ν(dx) < ∞, which is equivalent to ∫ min(1, x²) ν(dx) < ∞.

source.citation: Rick Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th edition, Cambridge University Press, 2019.
source.revision: Author's online version of January 11, 2019 (PTE5_011119.pdf).
source.module: Chapter 3, Section 3.9 Infinitely Divisible Distributions
source.excerpt: where µ is a measure with µ({0}) = 0 and ∫ x²/(1+x²) µ(dx) < ∞. For a proof, see Breiman (1968), Section 9.5., or Feller II (1971), Section XVII.2. µ is called the Lévy measure of the distribution.

source.alignment: Theorem 3.9.6 (Lévy-Khinchin Theorem) states that Z has an infinitely divisible distribution if and only if log ϕ(t) = ict − σ²t²/2 + ∫(e^{itx} − 1 − itx/(1+x²)) µ(dx) with µ({0}) = 0 and ∫ x²/(1+x²) µ(dx) < ∞. The authored statement writes the same formula with exp instead of log, so that no choice of logarithm is needed, and adds the uniqueness of the triple, which part (D) of Theorem 3.12 in the second source proves. Durrett gives no proof. The outline follows the second source, whose formula uses the compensator itx 1(|x| < 1). Step s6 converts it to Durrett's compensator itx/(1 + x²).

source_references.citation: J. L. Bretagnolle, The Lévy–Itô Decomposition Theorem, free translation with notes by P. Ouwehand of 'Processus à accroissements indépendants, Chapitre I: La décomposition de Paul Lévy' (École d'Été de Probabilités de Saint-Flour, Lecture Notes in Mathematics 307, Springer, 1973), arXiv:1506.06624, 2015.
source_references.excerpt: where Q is a positive definite quadratic form on Rn , a ∈ Rn , and ν(dx) is as in (A). (C) Conversely, given Q, a, ν as in (B), here exists a Lévy process whose law is given by the formula in (B). (D) The representation in (B) is unique.
source_references.attribution: © J. L. Bretagnolle and P. Ouwehand. Quoted from the arXiv translation for identification of the cited result.
source_references.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof outline and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source_references.alignment: Parts (B)-(D) of Theorem 3.12 give the characteristic exponent ψ(u) = ½Q(u) − i⟨a, u⟩ + ∫_{|x|≥1} (1 − e^{i⟨u,x⟩}) ν(dx) + ∫_{|x|<1} (1 − e^{i⟨u,x⟩} + i⟨u,x⟩) ν(dx) of an n-dimensional Lévy process, its converse and its uniqueness. The abstract of the source says that the Lévy–Khintchine representation of infinitely divisible distributions follows as a by-product. Steps s2-s4 of the outline supply the passage from an infinitely divisible law to a Lévy process. The source calls Q positive definite. Footnote 40 identifies Q(u) = uᵀΣu with the covariance matrix Σ of the Gaussian part, which is only nonnegative definite in general.
