source_references.alignment: Theorem 18 extends the case k ≡ 0 of Lamperti's theorem to random fields indexed by ℝ^d_+ with diagonal normalizations. Its proof, which the source says follows Lamperti's proof, applies Lamperti's lemma on types to get lim f(at)/f(a), identifies the limit as a power, and proves self-similarity by a double limit. For d = m = 1 these are steps s1-s3 of the outline. The source states H > 0 without the hypothesis f → ∞. Step s4 of the outline uses f → ∞ and continuity at t = 0 for this.

results.proof_status: outline of the cited published proof. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of Theorem 18 in Davydov and Paulauskas (arXiv:1705.00182) for d = m = 1, which the authors say follows Lamperti's 1962 proof of Theorem 3. Step s1 takes the lemma on types from Lamperti (p. 71 of his paper) as cited by the source. Steps s2 and s4 replace the citation of the theory of regularly varying functions by short direct arguments. The centering k(a) of Lamperti's general theorem is not treated.

steps.text: Convergence of types. Fix b > 0 and a sequence a_n → ∞. The one-dimensional laws give W_n = Y(a_n b)/f(a_n b) ⇒ X(1), because a_n b → ∞, and α_n W_n = Y(a_n b)/f(a_n) ⇒ X(b) with α_n = f(a_n b)/f(a_n) > 0. Both limits are nondegenerate because X is proper. The lemma on types that the source takes from Lamperti (p. 71) gives α_n → l(b) ∈ (0, ∞) and X(b) = l(b) X(1) in law. Two quantiles of X(1) and X(b) fix l(b), so the limit does not depend on the sequence, and f(ab)/f(a) → l(b) as a → ∞.

The limit is a power. Since ab → ∞ when a → ∞, l(bc) = lim [f(abc)/f(ab)] [f(ab)/f(a)] = l(c) l(b). As b → b_0 > 0, continuity in probability gives l(b) X(1) = X(b) ⇒ X(b_0) = l(b_0) X(1) in law, and the lemma on types gives l(b) → l(b_0). So g(x) = log l(e^x) is continuous and additive, hence linear, and l(b) = b^H with H = log l(e). Then L(a) = f(a) a^{−H} satisfies L(ab)/L(a) → 1, so L is slowly varying. The source reaches the same conclusion with its Proposition 9 on regularly varying functions.

Self-similarity by a double limit. Fix a > 0 and times t_1, …, t_k. As b → ∞, the finite-dimensional convergence at the times a t_i gives (Y(a b t_i)/f(b))_i ⇒ (X(a t_i))_i. At the times t_i with the scale ab it gives (Y(a b t_i)/f(ab))_i ⇒ (X(t_i))_i, and multiplication by f(ab)/f(b) → a^H with Slutsky's theorem gives (Y(a b t_i)/f(b))_i ⇒ (a^H X(t_i))_i. Limits in distribution are unique, so (X(a t_i))_i and (a^H X(t_i))_i have the same law. This is the last part of the proof of Theorem 18 in the source.

The index is positive and X(0) = 0. The variable Y(0) does not depend on a and f(a) → ∞, so Y(0)/f(a) → 0 in probability and X(0) = 0. If H < 0, then f(2^n)/f(2^{n−1}) → 2^H < 1 forces f(2^n) → 0, which contradicts f → ∞. If H = 0, then s1 gives X(t) = X(1) in law for all t > 0. Continuity in probability at 0 gives X(t) → X(0) = 0 as t ↓ 0, so X(1) = 0 almost surely, which contradicts properness. Hence H > 0.

Converse. If X is H-self-similar with H > 0, put Y = X and f(a) = a^H, which tends to ∞. Then (Y(at)/f(a))_t = (a^{−H} X(at))_t has the finite-dimensional laws of (X(t))_t for every a, so the convergence holds trivially. Lamperti's theorem therefore identifies the class of proper, stochastically continuous scaling limits with the class of self-similar processes of positive index.

source.ref: Y. Davydov and V. Paulauskas, Lamperti type theorems for random fields, arXiv:1705.00182v1 (2017), Theorem 3 (pp. 2-3) and the proof of Theorem 18 (pp. 20-21), which follows J. Lamperti, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 104 (1962), 62-78.

applications.title: Subdiffusive scaling of a tagged particle in single-file diffusion
applications.inputs: In single-file diffusion, particles on a line cannot pass each other, and the displacement Y(t) of a tagged particle grows like t^{1/4}. Assume that Y(at)/f(a) converges in finite-dimensional distributions to a proper process X that is continuous in probability, with f(a) = a^{1/4} in units where the mean square of X(1) is σ² = 1.
applications.hypotheses: f(a) = a^{1/4} is positive and tends to ∞. X is proper and continuous in probability by assumption. So the theorem applies.

steps.text: The index is fixed by f: f(16a)/f(a) = 16^{1/4} = 2, so l(16) = 2 and 16^H = 2. Since 2⁴ = 16, H = 1/4.
Self-similarity gives X(81t) = 81^{1/4} X(t) = 3X(t) in law, because 3⁴ = 81.
Mean squares scale with the square of the factor: E[X(81)²] = 3² E[X(1)²] = 9. In general E[X(t)²] = t^{2H} = t^{1/2}, a subdiffusive mean-square displacement.
X(0) = 0 almost surely, and the theorem rules out any proper limit X with a scaling exponent different from 1/4. For example, a factor 16 in time must multiply the mean square by 16^{1/2} = 4 = 2².

applications.conclusion: Any proper, stochastically continuous scaling limit of the tagged-particle displacement with normalization t^{1/4} is self-similar with index H = 1/4. Its mean-square displacement grows like t^{1/2}, which is the subdiffusive law of single-file diffusion.

limitations: The theorem gives the scaling of the limit but not its law. Brownian motion, fractional Brownian motion and stable Lévy processes are all possible limits with different indices.
Without continuity in probability or properness the conclusion H > 0 can fail. For example Y(t) = log(t) Z for t ≥ 1 with f(a) = log a gives the limit X(t) = Z for t > 0, which is constant in t.
The record omits the centering function k(a) of Lamperti's general theorem, which changes only the location of X(0).

results.name: Marcinkiewicz–Zygmund strong law of large numbers
aliases: Marcinkiewicz strong law of large numbers
results.statement: Let 1 < p < 2 and let X_1, X_2, … be i.i.d. real random variables with E X_1 = 0 and E|X_1|^p < ∞. Put S_n = X_1 + ⋯ + X_n. Then S_n / n^(1/p) → 0 almost surely.
hypotheses: The variables X_1, X_2, … are independent and identically distributed.
E|X_1|^p < ∞ for some p with 1 < p < 2.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 uses the Borel–Cantelli lemma to show that X_k equals its truncation Y_k for all large k, almost surely.
Step s2 exchanges the sum over m and the expectation of a nonnegative series (Tonelli) to bound the variance series.
Step s3 uses the sufficiency part of Kolmogorov's series criterion: centered independent terms with summable variances give an almost surely convergent series.
Step s4 uses dominated convergence to show that E[|X_1|^p 1(|X_1| > m^(1/p))] tends to 0 as m grows.

definitions.name: truncation
definitions.text: Y_k = X_k 1(|X_k| ≤ k^(1/p)) keeps X_k when |X_k| ≤ k^(1/p) and replaces it by 0 otherwise. The truncated variables have finite variance.

definitions.name: Kronecker's lemma
definitions.text: If 0 < a_n ↑ ∞ and the series Σ x_m/a_m converges, then a_n^(−1) Σ_{m≤n} x_m → 0.

source.excerpt: If we let µm = EYm and apply Theorem 2.5.6 and Theorem 2.5.9 it follows that n^{−1/p} Σ_{m=1}^n (Ym − µm) → 0 a.s. To estimate µm, we note that since EXm = 0, µm = −E(Xi; |Xi| > m^{1/p}), so |µm| ≤ E(|X|; |Xi| > m^{1/p})

source.alignment: The authored statement is the statement of Theorem 2.5.12 on p. 87, and the excerpt quotes a step of its proof on p. 88. The authored proof follows the proof in the source with truncation at k^(1/p), the Borel–Cantelli lemma, a variance series, Theorem 2.5.6 with Kronecker's lemma (Theorem 2.5.9) and a bound on the truncated means. The variance series is bounded by a direct Tonelli argument and not by the tail integral of the source.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the proof of Theorem 2.5.12 in Durrett's Probability: Theory and Examples. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement for 1 < p < 2. The cases 0 < p < 1 and p = 1 are not treated.

steps.text: Truncate. Put Y_k = X_k 1(|X_k| ≤ k^(1/p)) and T_n = Y_1 + ⋯ + Y_n. Since the X_k have the law of X_1, Σ_k P(Y_k ≠ X_k) = Σ_{k≥1} P(|X_1|^p > k) ≤ ∫_0^∞ P(|X_1|^p > u) du = E|X_1|^p < ∞. By the Borel–Cantelli lemma, almost surely X_k = Y_k for all k larger than some random K. Then S_n − T_n is eventually constant, so (S_n − T_n)/n^(1/p) → 0 almost surely. It remains to show T_n/n^(1/p) → 0 almost surely.

Bound the variances. Let q = 2/p > 1. For an integer M ≥ 1, Σ_{m≥M} m^(−q) ≤ M^(−q) + ∫_M^∞ x^(−q) dx ≤ C_p M^(1−q) with C_p = 1 + p/(2 − p). By Tonelli, Σ_m Var(Y_m)/m^q ≤ Σ_m E[Y_m²]/m^q = E[X_1² Σ_{m ≥ 1, m ≥ |X_1|^p} m^(−q)]. The smallest admissible m is at least max(1, |X_1|^p), and 1 − q < 0, so the inner sum is at most C_p max(1, |X_1|^p)^(1−q). If |X_1| ≤ 1 the integrand is at most C_p. If |X_1| > 1 it is at most C_p X_1² |X_1|^(p−2) = C_p |X_1|^p. Hence Σ_m Var(Y_m/m^(1/p)) ≤ C_p (1 + E|X_1|^p) < ∞.

Center and sum. Let μ_m = E Y_m. The variables (Y_m − μ_m)/m^(1/p) are independent, centered and have summable variances by s2. So Kolmogorov's criterion gives that Σ_m (Y_m − μ_m)/m^(1/p) converges almost surely. Kronecker's lemma with a_m = m^(1/p) then gives n^(−1/p) Σ_{m≤n} (Y_m − μ_m) → 0 almost surely. Kronecker's lemma follows by summation by parts: with b_n = Σ_{m≤n} x_m/a_m → b and a_0 = 0, a_n^(−1) Σ_{m≤n} x_m = b_n − a_n^(−1) Σ_{m<n} (a_{m+1} − a_m) b_m, and the last average of the b_m with weights a_{m+1} − a_m ≥ 0 also tends to b.

Control the means. Since E X_1 = 0, μ_m = −E[X_1; |X_1| > m^(1/p)]. On the event |X_1| > m^(1/p) we have |X_1| = |X_1|^p |X_1|^(1−p) ≤ |X_1|^p m^((1−p)/p), because 1 − p < 0. So |μ_m| ≤ m^(1/p − 1) ε_m with ε_m = E[|X_1|^p; |X_1| > m^(1/p)]. Dominated convergence gives ε_m → 0. The function x ↦ x^(1/p − 1) decreases, so Σ_{m≤n} m^(1/p − 1) ≤ ∫_0^n x^(1/p − 1) dx = p n^(1/p). Fix M. Then n^(−1/p) Σ_{m≤n} |μ_m| ≤ n^(−1/p) Σ_{m≤M} |μ_m| + p sup_{m>M} ε_m. Let n → ∞ and then M → ∞: n^(−1/p) Σ_{m≤n} μ_m → 0.
Combine. S_n/n^(1/p) = (S_n − T_n)/n^(1/p) + n^(−1/p) Σ_{m≤n} (Y_m − μ_m) + n^(−1/p) Σ_{m≤n} μ_m. The three terms tend to 0 almost surely by s1, s3 and s4. Hence S_n/n^(1/p) → 0 almost surely.

applications.title: The clock of a trap model with heavy-tailed trapping times
applications.inputs: In the mean-field version of Bouchaud's trap model, a walker visits a new trap at each step. A trap of depth E holds the walker for the time τ = e^(E/T), and the depths are exponential with P(E > x) = e^(−x/T_g). Then P(τ > t) = t^(−T/T_g) for t ≥ 1. Take T = 3T_g/2, so P(τ > t) = t^(−3/2). The trapping times τ_1, τ_2, … are i.i.d., and T_n = τ_1 + ⋯ + τ_n is the time of the n-th exit.
applications.hypotheses: Put X_k = τ_k − E τ_k and p = 5/4. The X_k are i.i.d. with mean 0. Step a2 shows E|X_1|^p < ∞, and 1 < 5/4 < 2.

steps.text: The mean is E τ = 1 + ∫_1^∞ t^(−3/2) dt = 1 + 1/(3/2 − 1) = 3. The second moment is infinite because ∫_1^∞ 2t · t^(−3/2) dt diverges. So the classical central limit theorem does not apply.
The theorem with p = 5/4 gives (T_n − 3n)/n^(4/5) → 0 almost surely. So the exit times satisfy T_n = 3n + o(n^(4/5)) on almost every path.
The same argument works for every p < 3/2. Since 1/p decreases to 2/3 as p increases to 3/2, T_n − 3n = o(n^(2/3 + δ)) almost surely for every δ > 0.

applications.conclusion: On almost every path the trap-model clock grows like 3n with an error o(n^(2/3+δ)) for every δ > 0, although the trapping times have infinite variance.

limitations: The theorem does not give a limit law for (T_n − nE τ)/n^(1/p). The generalized central limit theorem gives a stable limit on the scale n^(1/α) under a regular variation assumption.
For 0 < p < 1 the same conclusion holds without centering, and p = 1 is Kolmogorov's strong law. These cases are not proved here.
The converse also holds: if S_n/n^(1/p) → 0 almost surely, then E|X_1|^p < ∞. The converse is not proved here.

results.name: Two-sided Jensen gap bounds from curvature
results.statement: Let −∞ ≤ a < b ≤ ∞ and let φ: (a, b) → ℝ be twice differentiable. Let X be a real random variable with P(X ∈ (a, b)) = 1 and E[X²] < ∞, and put μ = E[X]. Then μ ∈ (a, b). For x ∈ (a, b) with x ≠ μ put h(x) = (φ(x) − φ(μ) − φ′(μ)(x − μ))/(x − μ)², and let m and M be the infimum and the supremum of h over (a, b) ∖ {μ}. Then m < ∞ and M > −∞. (i) If m > −∞, then E[φ(X)] exists in (−∞, ∞] and E[φ(X)] − φ(μ) ≥ m Var(X). (ii) If M < ∞, then E[φ(X)] exists in [−∞, ∞) and E[φ(X)] − φ(μ) ≤ M Var(X). (iii) inf_{(a,b)} φ″/2 ≤ m and M ≤ sup_{(a,b)} φ″/2. In particular, if c ≤ φ″ ≤ C on (a, b) with real c and C, then (c/2) Var(X) ≤ E[φ(X)] − φ(E[X]) ≤ (C/2) Var(X). Both bounds are equalities when φ is a quadratic polynomial.
hypotheses: φ is twice differentiable on the open interval (a, b), where −∞ ≤ a < b ≤ ∞.
X is a real random variable with P(X ∈ (a, b)) = 1 and E[X²] < ∞.

prerequisites.reason: Step s4 uses Taylor's theorem with the Lagrange form of the remainder to write h(x) = φ″(ξ)/2 for a point ξ between μ and x.

definitions.name: Jensen gap
definitions.text: The difference E[φ(X)] − φ(E[X]). Jensen's inequality says that it is nonnegative when φ is convex.

definitions.name: slope function h
definitions.text: h(x) = (φ(x) − φ(μ) − φ′(μ)(x − μ))/(x − μ)² for x ≠ μ. It is the coefficient of (x − μ)² in the exact second-order expansion of φ about μ.

source.citation: J. G. Liao and Arthur Berg, Sharpening Jensen's Inequality, The American Statistician 73(3), 278–281, 2019.
source.revision: arXiv:1707.08644v2 of 24 October 2017
source.module: Section 2, Main result
source.excerpt: Theorem 1. Let X be a one-dimensional random variable with mean µ, and P(X ∈ (a, b)) = 1, where −∞ ≤ a < b ≤ ∞. Let ϕ(x) is a twice differentiable function on (a, b), and define function h(x; ν) ≜ (ϕ(x) − ϕ(ν))/(x − ν)² − ϕ′(ν)/(x − ν). Then inf_{x∈(a,b)} {h(x; µ)} var(X) ≤ E[ϕ(X)] − ϕ(E[X]) ≤ sup_{x∈(a,b)} {h(x; µ)} var(X).
source.attribution: © J. G. Liao and Arthur Berg. Quoted from the arXiv preprint for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source takes the infimum and the supremum of h over (a, b) and leaves the point x = μ and the integrability of φ(X) implicit. The authored statement excludes x = μ, assumes E[X²] < ∞, and states each bound separately with the exact condition under which E[φ(X)] exists. Part (iii) is the remark that follows Theorem 1 in the source. The authored proof follows the source proof, which integrates the exact second-order expansion φ(x) = φ(μ) + φ′(μ)(x − μ) + h(x)(x − μ)² against the law of X.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the proof of Theorem 1 in Liao and Berg. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement: the location of μ, the one-sided bounds (i) and (ii) with the existence of E[φ(X)], the comparison (iii) with the bounds of φ″, and the equality case for quadratic φ.

steps.text: Location of the mean. E[X²] < ∞ makes X integrable, so μ is a real number. If a > −∞, then X − a > 0 almost surely. A nonnegative random variable with mean 0 is 0 almost surely, so E[X − a] > 0 and μ > a. In the same way μ < b if b < ∞. Hence μ ∈ (a, b), and φ(μ) and φ′(μ) are defined. The set (a, b) ∖ {μ} is not empty, so m ≤ h(x) ≤ M for some real h(x), which gives m < ∞ and M > −∞.

Exact expansion. Put H(x) = φ(x) − φ(μ) − φ′(μ)(x − μ) for x ∈ (a, b). By the definition of h, H(x) = h(x)(x − μ)² for x ≠ μ, and H(μ) = 0. Hence, for every x ∈ (a, b), H(x) ≥ m(x − μ)² when m > −∞, and H(x) ≤ M(x − μ)² when M < ∞. The function φ is continuous, so φ(X) and H(X) are random variables, and φ(X) = φ(μ) + φ′(μ)(X − μ) + H(X) almost surely.

Integration. Assume m > −∞. Then H(X) ≥ m(X − μ)², and (X − μ)² is integrable, so the negative part of H(X) is integrable. The term φ′(μ)(X − μ) is integrable with mean 0. So the negative part of φ(X) is integrable, E[φ(X)] exists in (−∞, ∞], and E[φ(X)] − φ(μ) = E[H(X)] ≥ m E[(X − μ)²] = m Var(X). This is (i). If M < ∞, the same argument with H(X) ≤ M(X − μ)² and the positive parts gives (ii).

Comparison with φ″. Fix x ∈ (a, b) with x ≠ μ. The function φ′ is differentiable, hence continuous, on the closed interval between μ and x, and φ″ exists inside it. Taylor's theorem with the Lagrange remainder gives a point ξ strictly between μ and x with φ(x) = φ(μ) + φ′(μ)(x − μ) + φ″(ξ)(x − μ)²/2. So h(x) = φ″(ξ)/2, which lies between inf φ″/2 and sup φ″/2. Taking the infimum and the supremum over x gives (iii). If c ≤ φ″ ≤ C, then c/2 ≤ m and M ≤ C/2 are finite, and (i) and (ii) give the two-sided bound with E[φ(X)] finite.
Equality case. If φ(x) = αx² + βx + γ, then H(x) = α(x − μ)², so h is the constant α and m = M = α. Step s3 gives E[φ(X)] − φ(μ) = α Var(X) from both sides, so both bounds are equalities.

applications.title: Excess resistivity of a random layered conductor
applications.inputs: A conductor is a stack of many layers of equal thickness. Current flows across the layers, so the effective resistivity is the mean E[1/X] of the layer resistivities, where X is the conductivity of a layer chosen uniformly at random. Half of the layers have X = 5/4 and half have X = 7/4, in units of a reference conductivity. Take φ(x) = 1/x on (a, b) = (1, 2).
applications.hypotheses: φ(x) = 1/x is twice differentiable on (1, 2). The layer conductivity X takes values in (1, 2), so P(X ∈ (1, 2)) = 1, and E[X²] < ∞ because X is bounded.

steps.text: The mean is μ = (5/4 + 7/4)/2 = 3/2, and the variance is Var(X) = (7/4 − 3/2)² = 1/16.
For φ(x) = 1/x, the numerator of h is 1/x − 1/μ + (x − μ)/μ² = (x − μ)²/(xμ²). So h(x) = 1/(xμ²) = 4/(9x). On (1, 2) ∖ {3/2} its infimum is m = 2/9 and its supremum is M = 4/9.
The theorem gives m Var(X) ≤ E[1/X] − 1/μ ≤ M Var(X). The lower bound is (2/9)(1/16) = 1/72, and the upper bound is (4/9)(1/16) = 1/36.
The cruder part (iii) uses φ″(x)/2 = 1/x³, which lies in (1/8, 1) on (1, 2). It gives only 1/128 ≤ gap ≤ 1/16, a window of width 7/128, which is 63/16 times the width 1/72 of the window from h.

applications.conclusion: The effective resistivity of the stack exceeds the resistivity 2/3 of a homogeneous medium with the mean conductivity by an amount between 1/72 and 1/36, without computing E[1/X] exactly. The exact excess is 2/105.

limitations: The bounds are informative only when h is bounded on the relevant side. For φ = exp on ℝ the supremum M is infinite, and only the lower bound remains.
The constants m and M use all of (a, b), not only the values that X takes. A narrower interval that still carries X gives sharper constants.

results.name: Conditional expectation minimizes every Bregman divergence
aliases: Bregman optimality of the conditional mean
results.statement: Let U ⊆ ℝ^d be a nonempty open convex set and let φ: U → ℝ be strictly convex and differentiable. For x, y ∈ U let d_φ(x, y) = φ(x) − φ(y) − ⟨∇φ(y), x − y⟩. Let X be an integrable random vector with values in U, let G be a sub-σ-algebra, and assume that Z = E[X | G] takes values in U almost surely (this holds automatically when U = ℝ^d). Then for every G-measurable random vector Y with values in U, E[d_φ(X, Y)] = E[d_φ(X, Z)] + E[d_φ(Z, Y)], as an identity in [0, ∞]. Hence E[d_φ(X, Y)] ≥ E[d_φ(X, Z)], so Z minimizes Y ↦ E[d_φ(X, Y)] over all G-measurable U-valued Y. If E[d_φ(X, Z)] < ∞, then every minimizer Y equals Z almost surely. For the trivial σ-algebra this says that the constant E[X] is the unique minimizer of s ↦ E[d_φ(X, s)].
hypotheses: U ⊆ ℝ^d is a nonempty open convex set, and φ: U → ℝ is strictly convex and differentiable.
X is an integrable random vector with values in U.
G is a sub-σ-algebra, and Z = E[X | G] takes values in U almost surely.

prerequisites.reason: Step s3 uses the dominated convergence theorem to pass from indicators of events in G to bounded G-measurable weights in the defining property of the conditional expectation.
Step s5 uses the monotone convergence theorem to remove the truncation sets A_k from the three nonnegative expectations.

definitions.name: Bregman divergence
definitions.text: d_φ(x, y) = φ(x) − φ(y) − ⟨∇φ(y), x − y⟩ for a strictly convex differentiable φ. Squared Euclidean distance (φ(x) = |x|²), the generalized Kullback–Leibler divergence (φ(x) = Σ xᵢ log xᵢ − xᵢ) and the Itakura–Saito divergence (φ(x) = −log x) are examples.

definitions.name: three-point identity
definitions.text: d_φ(x, y) = d_φ(x, z) + d_φ(z, y) + ⟨∇φ(z) − ∇φ(y), x − z⟩ for all x, y, z ∈ U.

source.citation: Arindam Banerjee, Srujana Merugu, Inderjit S. Dhillon and Joydeep Ghosh, Clustering with Bregman Divergences, Journal of Machine Learning Research 6, 1705–1749, 2005.
source.revision: Journal version, published 10/05
source.module: Section 3, Bregman Hard Clustering, Section 3.1 Bregman Information
source.excerpt: Proposition 1 Let X be a random variable that take values in X = {x_i}_{i=1}^n ⊂ S ⊆ ℝ^d following a positive probability measure ν such that E_ν[X] ∈ ri(S). Given a Bregman divergence d_φ : S × ri(S) ↦ [0, ∞), the problem min_{s∈ri(S)} E_ν[d_φ(X, s)] has a unique minimizer given by s† = µ = E_ν[X].
source.attribution: © Arindam Banerjee, Srujana Merugu, Inderjit S. Dhillon and Joydeep Ghosh. Quoted from the journal version for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source proves the unconditional statement for a random variable with finitely many values. The authored statement conditions on a sub-σ-algebra, allows any integrable law, and states the exact excess-risk identity in [0, ∞], from which the source statement follows with the trivial σ-algebra. The authored proof follows the source proof, which expands J(s) − J(μ) and finds d_φ(μ, s). The authored proof writes this as the three-point identity and adds a truncation argument for the cross term, because a general law does not give finite sums.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the proof of Proposition 1 in Banerjee, Merugu, Dhillon and Ghosh. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement: the identity in [0, ∞] for every G-measurable U-valued Y, the minimizing property of Z, and uniqueness when E[d_φ(X, Z)] < ∞.

steps.text: Properties of d_φ. Fix x ≠ y in U and put g(t) = φ(y + t(x − y)) for t ∈ [0, 1]. The function g is strictly convex and differentiable, with g′(0) = ⟨∇φ(y), x − y⟩. Convexity gives g′(0) ≤ (g(1/2) − g(0))/(1/2), and strict convexity gives g(1/2) < (g(0) + g(1))/2. Together, g′(0) < g(1) − g(0), that is, d_φ(x, y) > 0. Also d_φ(x, x) = 0. So d_φ ≥ 0, with equality exactly when x = y. The gradient ∇φ is a pointwise limit of continuous difference quotients, so it is Borel, and d_φ(X, Y) is a nonnegative random variable.

Three-point identity. For x, y, z ∈ U, expand both sides with the definition of d_φ. The terms φ(z) cancel, and d_φ(x, y) − d_φ(x, z) − d_φ(z, y) = ⟨∇φ(z), x − z⟩ + ⟨∇φ(y), z − y⟩ − ⟨∇φ(y), x − y⟩ = ⟨∇φ(z) − ∇φ(y), x − z⟩. Change Z on a G-measurable null set so that Z takes values in U everywhere. With W = ∇φ(Z) − ∇φ(Y), this gives d_φ(X, Y) = d_φ(X, Z) + d_φ(Z, Y) + ⟨W, X − Z⟩ pointwise.

The cross term vanishes on truncation sets. By definition, E[1_B (X − Z)] = 0 for every B ∈ G. By linearity, E[⟨V, X − Z⟩] = 0 for every G-measurable simple random vector V. A bounded G-measurable random vector V is a uniform limit of G-measurable simple V_n with |V_n| ≤ |V|. Since |⟨V_n, X − Z⟩| ≤ sup|V| · |X − Z|, which is integrable, the dominated convergence theorem gives E[⟨V, X − Z⟩] = 0. The vector W is G-measurable and finite, so A_k = {|W| ≤ k} lies in G, and V = 1_{A_k} W is bounded. Hence E[1_{A_k} ⟨W, X − Z⟩] = 0 for every k.

Truncated identity. Multiply the pointwise identity of step s2 by 1_{A_k}. The terms 1_{A_k} d_φ(X, Z) and 1_{A_k} d_φ(Z, Y) are nonnegative, and 1_{A_k} ⟨W, X − Z⟩ is integrable because it is bounded by k |X − Z|. The expectation of a nonnegative variable plus an integrable variable is the sum of the expectations in (−∞, ∞]. With step s3 this gives E[1_{A_k} d_φ(X, Y)] = E[1_{A_k} d_φ(X, Z)] + E[1_{A_k} d_φ(Z, Y)] in [0, ∞].

Limit and conclusions. The sets A_k increase to the whole space as k → ∞, because W is finite. The monotone convergence theorem applies to each of the three nonnegative terms and gives E[d_φ(X, Y)] = E[d_φ(X, Z)] + E[d_φ(Z, Y)]. Since E[d_φ(Z, Y)] ≥ 0, Z is a minimizer. If E[d_φ(X, Z)] < ∞ and Y is also a minimizer, then E[d_φ(Z, Y)] = 0, so d_φ(Z, Y) = 0 almost surely, and step s1 gives Y = Z almost surely. For the trivial σ-algebra, Z = E[X] and the G-measurable Y are the constants s ∈ U.

applications.title: Predicting the kinetic energy of a molecule from the bath temperature
applications.inputs: A molecule of an ideal gas is in contact with a heat bath of temperature T. With probability 1/2 the bath has T = 1, and with probability 1/2 it has T = 2, in units with Boltzmann constant 1. Given T, the kinetic energy X has the Maxwell–Boltzmann law Gamma(3/2, scale T), with mean 3T/2. A forecaster knows T and predicts X with a function Y = g(T) > 0. Two losses are used: the squared error (φ(x) = x²) and the Itakura–Saito divergence d(x, y) = x/y − log(x/y) − 1 (φ(x) = −log x on U = (0, ∞)).
applications.hypotheses: U = (0, ∞) is open and convex, and both choices of φ are strictly convex and differentiable on U. X > 0 is integrable. G = σ(T), and Z = E[X | T] = 3T/2 is positive. Also E[d(X, Z)] < ∞ for both losses, because the Gamma law has finite second moment and E|log X| < ∞.

steps.text: The theorem gives the same optimal forecast for both losses: Z = 3T/2, that is, 3/2 when T = 1 and 3 when T = 2. No other forecast g(T) does as well for either loss.

Compare the forecast that ignores T: the constant Y = E[X] = (3/2 + 3)/2 = 9/4. By the identity, its excess loss is E[d(Z, 9/4)], which needs only the two values of Z and no integral over the Gamma law.
For squared error the excess is E[(Z − 9/4)²] = ((3/2 − 9/4)² + (3 − 9/4)²)/2 = 9/16.
For the Itakura–Saito loss the ratios are Z/Y = (3/2)/(9/4) = 2/3 and 3/(9/4) = 4/3. The excess is ((2/3 − log(2/3) − 1) + (4/3 − log(4/3) − 1))/2 = (1/2) log(9/8) ≈ 0.0589.

applications.conclusion: The conditional mean 3T/2 is the best forecast of the kinetic energy for the squared error and for the Itakura–Saito loss at the same time. The forecast that ignores the temperature loses exactly 9/16 in squared error and (1/2) log(9/8) in Itakura–Saito loss.

limitations: The conditional mean is optimal only for losses that are Bregman divergences in this argument order. For the absolute error the optimal forecast is a conditional median, and for d_φ(Y, X) with the arguments swapped the optimum is in general not the conditional mean.
Uniqueness needs E[d_φ(X, Z)] < ∞. If this expectation is infinite, every forecast has infinite expected loss and the comparison is empty.

results.name: Banerjee–Guo–Wang characterization of Bregman losses
aliases: Savage characterization of scoring functions consistent for the mean
characterization of losses with the mean as optimal forecast
results.statement: Let U ⊆ ℝ^d be a nonempty open convex set. Let F: U × U → [0, ∞) satisfy F(x, x) = 0 for every x ∈ U, and assume that for each x ∈ U the map y ↦ F(x, y) is continuously differentiable on U. Here x is the outcome and y is the forecast. Then the following are equivalent. (a) For every random vector X with finitely many values in U, the mean E[X] minimizes y ↦ E[F(X, y)] over U. (b) There is a convex differentiable function φ: U → ℝ with F(x, y) = φ(x) − φ(y) − ⟨∇φ(y), x − y⟩ for all x, y ∈ U. In that case φ = F(·, y₀) works for every y₀ ∈ U, and φ is unique up to an affine function. Moreover, E[X] is the unique minimizer for every such X if and only if φ is strictly convex. It suffices to check (a) and the uniqueness for laws with at most three values.
hypotheses: U ⊆ ℝ^d is a nonempty open convex set.
F: U × U → [0, ∞) satisfies F(x, x) = 0 for every x ∈ U.
For each x ∈ U the map y ↦ F(x, y) is continuously differentiable on U.

prerequisites.reason: Step s2 applies Fermat's theorem on stationary points to the differentiable function z ↦ Σᵢ νᵢ F(xᵢ, z), which has an interior minimum at the mean.
Step s5 uses the fundamental theorem of calculus for the continuously differentiable map t ↦ F(x, y₀ + t(y − y₀)) on [0, 1].
Step s5 uses the dominated convergence theorem to show that the integral A(y) of the continuous matrix function M along the segment from y₀ to y is continuous in y.

definitions.name: Bregman divergence
definitions.text: d_φ(x, y) = φ(x) − φ(y) − ⟨∇φ(y), x − y⟩ for a convex differentiable φ. It is nonnegative and vanishes at x = y.

definitions.name: consistent loss
definitions.text: A loss F(outcome, forecast) is consistent for the mean on a class of laws if, for every law in the class, the mean of the outcome minimizes the expected loss. It is strictly consistent if the mean is the only minimizer.

source.citation: Tilmann Gneiting, Making and evaluating point forecasts, Journal of the American Statistical Association 106(494), 746–762, 2011.
source.revision: arXiv:0912.0902v2 of 7 March 2010
source.module: Section 3, Examples, Section 3.1 Expectations
source.excerpt: Theorem 3.1 (Savage). Let F be the class of the probability measures on the interval I ⊆ ℝ with finite first moment. Then the following holds. … (b) Suppose that the scoring function S satisfies assumptions (S0), (S1) and (S2) on the PO domain D = I × I. Then S is consistent for the mean functional relative to the class of the compactly supported probability measures on I if, and only if, it is of the form S(x, y) = φ(y) − φ(x) − φ′(x)(y − x), (18) where φ is a convex function with subgradient φ′ on I.
source.attribution: © Tilmann Gneiting. Quoted from the arXiv version of the article for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states Savage's characterization on an interval of ℝ, writes the forecast as the first argument, and assumes continuity and differentiability in the forecast away from the diagonal. The authored statement is the d-dimensional version in the form of Banerjee, Guo and Wang, cited in the source: the outcome comes first, the loss is continuously differentiable in the forecast, finitely supported laws are tested, and strict convexity corresponds to a unique minimizer as in part (c) of the source. The authored proof follows Osband's principle of Section 2.4 of the source, which the source applies in its proof of Theorem 3.2 (Appendix A, p. 30). Two-point laws give the proportionality of the gradient to x − y, and the authored proof adds three-point laws, which give linearity in d dimensions.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows Osband's principle as used in the source's proof of Theorem 3.2, extended to d dimensions. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement: both directions of the equivalence, the choice φ = F(·, y₀), uniqueness of φ up to affine functions, the characterization of a unique minimizer by strict convexity, and the reduction to laws with at most three values.

steps.text: From (b) to (a). Let X take the values xᵢ ∈ U with probabilities νᵢ, and let m = Σᵢ νᵢ xᵢ, which lies in U by convexity. Expanding the definition, Σᵢ νᵢ d_φ(xᵢ, y) − Σᵢ νᵢ d_φ(xᵢ, m) = φ(m) − φ(y) − ⟨∇φ(y), m − y⟩ = d_φ(m, y), because the terms φ(xᵢ) cancel and Σᵢ νᵢ (xᵢ − m) = 0. Convexity of φ gives d_φ(m, y) ≥ 0, so m is a minimizer. If φ is strictly convex, then d_φ(m, y) > 0 for y ≠ m: along the segment from y to m, strict convexity makes the slope at y strictly smaller than the chord slope. So m is the unique minimizer.

First-order condition. Assume (a), at least for laws with at most three values. Fix y ∈ U and put G(x) = ∇_y F(x, y) for x ∈ U. Let X take the values xᵢ ∈ U with probabilities νᵢ > 0 and mean y. The function z ↦ Σᵢ νᵢ F(xᵢ, z) is differentiable on the open set U and has a minimum at y, so Fermat's theorem gives Σᵢ νᵢ G(xᵢ) = 0. The one-point law gives G(y) = 0.

Osband step. Put h(v) = G(y + v) and choose ρ > 0 with B(y, 2ρ) ⊆ U. If y + v ∈ U and y − sv ∈ U with s > 0, the law with values y + v and y − sv and weights s/(1 + s) and 1/(1 + s) has mean y, so s h(v) + h(−sv) = 0. With s = 1 this gives h(−w) = −h(w) for |w| < 2ρ, and then h(tv) = t h(v) whenever |v| < ρ and |tv| < ρ. For |u|, |v| < ρ, the law with values y + u, y + v and y − u − v, each with weight 1/3, has mean y, so h(u) + h(v) + h(−u − v) = 0, that is, h(u + v) = h(u) + h(v). Put L(w) = h(εw)/ε for any ε > 0 with |εw| < ρ. By homogeneity L does not depend on ε, it is additive and homogeneous, hence linear, and L = h on the ball of radius ρ. For any v with y + v ∈ U, take s > 0 so small that |sv| < ρ. The two-point identity gives h(v) = −h(−sv)/s = L(v). So there is a d × d matrix M(y) with ∇_y F(x, y) = M(y)(x − y) for all x, y ∈ U.

Continuity of M. Fix x ∈ U and a coordinate vector eⱼ, and take ε > 0 with x + εeⱼ ∈ U. Then M(y)eⱼ = (∇_y F(x + εeⱼ, y) − ∇_y F(x, y))/ε for every y ∈ U. The right side is continuous in y by hypothesis, so each column of M, and hence M, is continuous on U.

Bregman form. Fix y₀ ∈ U and put φ(x) = F(x, y₀). For y ∈ U let y_t = y₀ + t(y − y₀), which lies in U. The map t ↦ F(x, y_t) is continuously differentiable on [0, 1], so the fundamental theorem of calculus and step s3 give F(x, y) = φ(x) + ⟨A(y), x⟩ + B(y), with A(y) = ∫₀¹ M(y_t)ᵀ(y − y₀) dt and B(y) = −∫₀¹ ⟨M(y_t)y_t, y − y₀⟩ dt. As y′ → y, the integrands of A(y′) converge pointwise and stay bounded, because M is continuous on a compact neighborhood in U of the segments involved. Dominated convergence shows that A is continuous. The condition F(y, y) = 0 gives B(y) = −φ(y) − ⟨A(y), y⟩, so F(x, y) = φ(x) − φ(y) + ⟨A(y), x − y⟩.

Convexity and differentiability of φ. Put g(y) = −A(y). Since F ≥ 0, φ(x) ≥ φ(y) + ⟨g(y), x − y⟩ for all x, y ∈ U, with equality at x = y. So φ is the supremum of these affine functions, hence convex. For y + w ∈ U the two subgradient inequalities give ⟨g(y), w⟩ ≤ φ(y + w) − φ(y) ≤ ⟨g(y + w), w⟩. Hence |φ(y + w) − φ(y) − ⟨g(y), w⟩| ≤ |g(y + w) − g(y)| |w|, which is o(|w|) because g is continuous. So φ is differentiable with ∇φ = g, and F(x, y) = φ(x) − φ(y) − ⟨∇φ(y), x − y⟩. If ψ is another such function, then χ = φ − ψ satisfies χ(x) = χ(y) + ⟨∇χ(y), x − y⟩ for all x, y, so χ is affine.

Strict convexity from uniqueness. Assume that the minimizer is unique for laws with two values, and suppose that φ is not strictly convex. Then φ((1 − λ)a + λb) = (1 − λ)φ(a) + λφ(b) for some a ≠ b and λ ∈ (0, 1). The convex function t ↦ φ(a + t(b − a)) on [0, 1] lies below its chord and meets it at the interior point λ, so it equals the chord, and φ is affine on the segment [a, b]. Since φ is differentiable, its directional derivatives along the segment equal the slope of this affine function, so d_φ(b, a) = 0 and d_φ(a, m) = d_φ(b, m) = 0 for the midpoint m. For X equal to a or b with probability 1/2 each, E[F(X, m)] = 0 = (1/2)F(a, a) + (1/2)F(b, a) = E[F(X, a)]. So both m and a ≠ m minimize, which contradicts uniqueness. With step s1, uniqueness for all finitely supported laws holds exactly when φ is strictly convex.

applications.title: Which losses reward reporting the thermal mean energy
applications.inputs: The energy X of a two-level system at infinite temperature takes the values 1 and 3 with probability 1/2 each, so E[X] = 2. An analyst reports a forecast y > 0 and pays a loss F(x, y) on U = (0, ∞). Two losses are compared: the relative squared error F₁(x, y) = (x − y)²/y and the Itakura–Saito loss F₂(x, y) = x/y − log(x/y) − 1.
applications.hypotheses: U = (0, ∞) is open and convex. Both losses are nonnegative, vanish at x = y, and are continuously differentiable in y on U. The law of X has two values in U.

steps.text: For F₁, ∂_y F₁(x, y) = −(x − y)(x + y)/y². The factor x + y depends on the outcome x, so ∂_y F₁ is not of the form M(y)(x − y) of step s3. Hence F₁ is not a Bregman divergence, and the theorem predicts a law with at most three values whose mean is not optimal.
For the two-level law, the mean forecast y = 2 has expected loss E[F₁(X, 2)] = ((1 − 2)² + (3 − 2)²)/2/2 = 1/2.

The forecast y = 9/4 has expected loss ((1 − 9/4)² + (3 − 9/4)²)/2/(9/4) = 17/36, which is less than 1/2. So F₁ rewards a forecast above the mean. The exact optimum is √(E[X²]) = √5, with E[X²] = (1 + 9)/2 = 5.

For F₂, ∂_y F₂(x, y) = −(x − y)/y², which is of the form M(y)(x − y) with M(y) = −1/y². Indeed F₂ = d_φ with φ(x) = −log x, which is strictly convex. So E[F₂(X, y)] has the unique minimizer y = 2, and E[F₂(X, y)] − E[F₂(X, 2)] = 2/y − log(2/y) − 1.

applications.conclusion: The Itakura–Saito loss rewards the honest report of the mean energy 2, but the relative squared error rewards the larger report √5. The theorem explains the difference: only Bregman losses make the mean the optimal forecast for every law.

limitations: The theorem assumes that the loss is continuously differentiable in the forecast. Without smoothness, Savage's form needs a subgradient in place of the gradient, as in the source.

The characterization concerns the mean only. Other functionals, such as quantiles or expectiles, have their own classes of consistent losses, and some functionals, such as the variance, have no consistent loss at all.

results.name: Generalized Pythagorean inequality for Bregman projections
results.statement: Let U ⊆ ℝ^d be a nonempty open convex set and let φ: U → ℝ be strictly convex and differentiable, with Bregman divergence d_φ(x, y) = φ(x) − φ(y) − ⟨∇φ(y), x − y⟩. Let C ⊆ U be a nonempty convex set and y ∈ U. Suppose that x* ∈ C minimizes x ↦ d_φ(x, y) over C. Then, for every x ∈ C, ⟨∇φ(y) − ∇φ(x*), x − x*⟩ ≤ 0 and d_φ(x, y) ≥ d_φ(x, x*) + d_φ(x*, y). The minimizer x* is unique. Conversely, a point x* ∈ C that satisfies the first inequality for every x ∈ C is the minimizer. If C = U ∩ L for an affine subspace L of ℝ^d, then both inequalities are equalities for every x ∈ C.
hypotheses: U ⊆ ℝ^d is a nonempty open convex set, and φ: U → ℝ is strictly convex and differentiable.
C ⊆ U is a nonempty convex set and y ∈ U.
x* ∈ C minimizes d_φ(·, y) over C.

prerequisites.reason: Step s5 uses Fermat's theorem on stationary points at the interior minimum t = 0 of g(t) = d_φ(x* + t(x − x*), y) in the affine case.

definitions.name: Bregman divergence
definitions.text: d_φ(x, y) = φ(x) − φ(y) − ⟨∇φ(y), x − y⟩. It is nonnegative, and it is zero only when x = y, because φ is strictly convex.

definitions.name: Bregman projection
definitions.text: A minimizer over C of x ↦ d_φ(x, y). The projection is taken in the first argument of d_φ.

source.citation: Sébastien Bubeck, Convex Optimization: Algorithms and Complexity, Foundations and Trends in Machine Learning 8(3-4), 231–358, 2015.

source.module: Chapter 4, Section 4.1 Mirror maps
source.excerpt: Lemma 4.1. Let x ∈ X ∩ D and y ∈ D, then (∇Φ(Π^Φ_X(y)) − ∇Φ(y))^⊤(Π^Φ_X(y) − x) ≤ 0, which also implies D_Φ(x, Π^Φ_X(y)) + D_Φ(Π^Φ_X(y), y) ≤ D_Φ(x, y). … the fact that ∇_x D_Φ(x, y) = ∇Φ(x) − ∇Φ(y).

source.alignment: The source states the lemma for a mirror map Φ, whose gradient is onto ℝ^n and blows up at the boundary, so that the projection exists. The authored statement keeps only strict convexity and differentiability, assumes that the minimizer exists, and adds uniqueness, the converse and the equality case for affine sets. The authored proof follows the source proof: the first-order optimality condition for x ↦ d_φ(x, y), with gradient ∇φ(x) − ∇φ(y), gives the first inequality, and the three-point identity (4.1) turns it into the second.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the proof of Lemma 4.1 in Bubeck. No local formal verification.

proof.scope: The full statement: the variational inequality, the Pythagorean inequality, uniqueness, the converse, and the equality case for affine C. Existence of the minimizer is a hypothesis.

steps.text: Three-point identity. For x, y, z ∈ U, expand the three divergences with the definition. The terms φ(z) cancel, and d_φ(x, y) − d_φ(x, z) − d_φ(z, y) = ⟨∇φ(z) − ∇φ(y), x − z⟩. With z = x*, the Pythagorean inequality d_φ(x, y) ≥ d_φ(x, x*) + d_φ(x*, y) is equivalent to ⟨∇φ(y) − ∇φ(x*), x − x*⟩ ≤ 0. Also d_φ(u, v) > 0 for u ≠ v: along the segment from v to u, convexity bounds the slope at v by the chord slope over half the segment, and strict convexity makes the chord bound strict.

Variational inequality. Fix x ∈ C. By convexity of C, x_t = x* + t(x − x*) lies in C for t ∈ [0, 1]. Put g(t) = d_φ(x_t, y) = φ(x_t) − φ(y) − ⟨∇φ(y), x_t − y⟩. By the chain rule, g has the right derivative g′(0+) = ⟨∇φ(x*) − ∇φ(y), x − x*⟩ at 0. Since x* minimizes d_φ(·, y) over C, g(t) ≥ g(0) for t ∈ (0, 1], so the difference quotients (g(t) − g(0))/t are nonnegative and g′(0+) ≥ 0. This is ⟨∇φ(y) − ∇φ(x*), x − x*⟩ ≤ 0, and step s1 gives the Pythagorean inequality.

Uniqueness. Let x₁ and x₂ be two minimizers. Step s2 with x* = x₁ and x = x₂ gives d_φ(x₂, y) ≥ d_φ(x₂, x₁) + d_φ(x₁, y). The two minimal values are equal, so d_φ(x₂, x₁) ≤ 0. Step s1 gives d_φ(x₂, x₁) ≥ 0 with equality only for x₂ = x₁. Hence x₂ = x₁.

Converse. Let x* ∈ C satisfy ⟨∇φ(y) − ∇φ(x*), x − x*⟩ ≤ 0 for every x ∈ C. By step s1, d_φ(x, y) ≥ d_φ(x, x*) + d_φ(x*, y) ≥ d_φ(x*, y) for every x ∈ C, because d_φ(x, x*) ≥ 0. So x* minimizes d_φ(·, y) over C.

Affine case. Let C = U ∩ L with L affine, and fix x ∈ C. The points x_t = x* + t(x − x*) lie in L for every real t. Since U is open, x_t lies in U, and hence in C, for t in an open interval around 0. So g from step s2 is defined near 0 and has a minimum at the interior point t = 0. Fermat's theorem gives g′(0) = 0, so the inner product in step s2 is 0, and the identity of step s1 gives d_φ(x, y) = d_φ(x, x*) + d_φ(x*, y).

applications.title: Minimum relative entropy update of a three-level system
applications.inputs: A three-level system has the uniform prior law y = (1/3, 1/3, 1/3), the infinite-temperature state. A measurement shows that the probability of level 1 is at least 1/2. Take U = (0, ∞)³ and φ(x) = Σᵢ (xᵢ log xᵢ − xᵢ). Then d_φ(x, y) = Σᵢ (xᵢ log(xᵢ/yᵢ) − xᵢ + yᵢ), which equals the Kullback–Leibler divergence D(x‖y) for two probability vectors. Let C = {x ∈ U : x₁ + x₂ + x₃ = 1, x₁ ≥ 1/2}.
applications.hypotheses: U is open and convex, and φ is strictly convex and differentiable on U. C is a nonempty convex subset of U, and y ∈ U. The candidate point is x* = (1/2, 1/4, 1/4) ∈ C.

steps.text: The candidate splits the remaining mass 1 − 1/2 equally between levels 2 and 3, so x₂* = x₃* = 1/4.

Here ∇φ(x) = (log x₁, log x₂, log x₃). So ∇φ(y) − ∇φ(x*) = (log(2/3), log(4/3), log(4/3)). For x ∈ C, the coordinates of x − x* sum to 0, and x₂ + x₃ − 1/2 = 1/2 − x₁. The inner product is (x₁ − 1/2)(log(2/3) − log(4/3)) = −(x₁ − 1/2) log 2 ≤ 0.
By the converse part, x* = (1/2, 1/4, 1/4) is the minimum relative entropy law in C. Its divergence from the prior is D(x*‖y) = (1/2) log(3/2) + (1/2) log(3/4) = (1/2) log(9/8) ≈ 0.0589 nats.

For the law x = (3/4, 1/8, 1/8) in C, step s1 of the proof gives D(x‖y) − D(x‖x*) − D(x*‖y) = (x₁ − 1/2) log 2 = (1/4) log 2. So the Pythagorean inequality is strict, with gap (1/4) log 2 ≈ 0.173 nats.

applications.conclusion: The minimum relative entropy update of the uniform law under the constraint p₁ ≥ 1/2 is (1/2, 1/4, 1/4). Every other law p in the constraint set satisfies D(p‖uniform) ≥ D(p‖x*) + (1/2) log(9/8), with excess (p₁ − 1/2) log 2.

limitations: The theorem assumes that the minimizer exists. Existence needs more, for example a compact C, or a closed C together with a Legendre-type φ as in the mirror maps of the source.
The projection is in the first argument of d_φ. For the minimizer of d_φ(y, ·) over C the Pythagorean inequality fails in general.

results.name: Csiszár's I-projection theorem
results.statement: Let P be a probability measure on a measurable space (Ω, F). For a probability measure Q on (Ω, F), let D(Q‖P) = ∫ log(dQ/dP) dQ (natural logarithm) if Q ≪ P, and D(Q‖P) = ∞ otherwise. Let E be a convex set of probability measures on (Ω, F) with D* = inf_{Q∈E} D(Q‖P) < ∞. (a) If Q* ∈ E and D(Q*‖P) = D*, then D(Q‖P) ≥ D(Q‖Q*) + D(Q*‖P) for every Q ∈ E. In particular, every Q ∈ E with D(Q‖P) < ∞ is absolutely continuous with respect to Q*. (b) Conversely, if Q* ∈ E satisfies this inequality for every Q ∈ E, then D(Q*‖P) = D*. At most one Q* ∈ E has D(Q*‖P) = D*. (c) If E is closed in total variation distance, then some Q* ∈ E has D(Q*‖P) = D*. This unique minimizer is the I-projection of P onto E.
hypotheses: P is a probability measure on the measurable space (Ω, F).
E is a convex set of probability measures on (Ω, F).
D* = inf_{Q∈E} D(Q‖P) is finite.
For the existence part (c), E is closed in total variation distance.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 uses the Radon–Nikodym theorem to write every Q with finite divergence as Q(A) = ∫_A f dP with a density f = dQ/dP.
Steps s1, s4, s5 and s6 use Gibbs' inequality D(Q‖R) ≥ 0, for the sign and finiteness of the divergences and for the converse in part (b).
Step s2 applies the monotone convergence theorem to the decreasing difference quotients of the convex function t log t, and step s6 uses it to sum the series of L¹ distances.
Steps s4 and s6 use Pinsker's inequality TV(Q, R) ≤ √(D(Q‖R)/2) to turn small divergences into small total variation distances.
Step s6 applies Fatou's lemma to identify the L¹ limit of the densities and to show that the limit measure has divergence at most D*.

definitions.name: relative entropy
definitions.text: D(Q‖P) = ∫ log(dQ/dP) dQ if Q ≪ P, and D(Q‖P) = ∞ otherwise. It is also called the Kullback–Leibler divergence or I-divergence.

definitions.name: I-projection
definitions.text: A Q* ∈ E with D(Q*‖P) = inf_{Q∈E} D(Q‖P). It is the element of E that is closest to P in relative entropy.

definitions.name: total variation distance
definitions.text: TV(Q₁, Q₂) = sup_A |Q₁(A) − Q₂(A)|. For densities f₁, f₂ with respect to P it equals (1/2)∫|f₁ − f₂| dP. E is closed in total variation if every TV limit of elements of E is in E.

source.citation: Imre Csiszár and Paul C. Shields, Information Theory and Statistics: A Tutorial, Foundations and Trends in Communications and Information Theory, Vol. 1, No. 4 (2004), pp. 417-528.

source.excerpt: Theorem 3.1. S(P*) = S(Π), and D(P‖Q) ≥ D(P‖P*) + D(P*‖Q) for all P ∈ Π. Of course, if the asserted inequality holds for some P* ∈ Π and all P ∈ Π then P* must be the I-projection of Q onto Π.

source.alignment: The source works on a finite alphabet A with a reference distribution Q of full support and a closed convex set Π, and it swaps the roles of the letters P and Q. The authored statement works on a general measurable space, replaces the support statement S(P*) = S(Π) by absolute continuity, and proves uniqueness and existence under closedness in total variation. The proof of part (a) follows the proof of Theorem 3.1: the one-sided derivative of the divergence along the segment from the minimizer to another element is nonnegative. The general space needs monotone difference quotients instead of the mean value theorem. The existence proof uses the parallelogram identity for relative entropy and Pinsker's inequality.

Its proof computes the derivative at λ = 0 of D(Q_λ‖P) and refers to Csiszár's 1975 paper I-divergence geometry of probability distributions for the exchange of derivative and integral. Steps s2 and s3 of the authored proof carry out that exchange with monotone convergence.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Parts (a), (b) and (c) of the statement, for every probability measure P on every measurable space and every convex set E with finite D*.

steps.text: Densities and convexity. Let φ(t) = t log t for t > 0 and φ(0) = 0. Then φ is continuous and convex on [0, ∞), and φ ≥ −1/e. If D(Q‖P) < ∞, then Q ≪ P, and the Radon–Nikodym theorem gives a density f = dQ/dP ≥ 0 with ∫ f dP = 1 and D(Q‖P) = ∫ φ(f) dP. This integral is well defined because φ ≥ −1/e and P(Ω) = 1, and Gibbs' inequality gives D(Q‖P) ≥ 0. If Q₀ and Q₁ have finite divergence and densities f₀, f₁, then (1 − λ)Q₀ + λQ₁ has density (1 − λ)f₀ + λf₁ for λ ∈ [0, 1]. Pointwise convexity of φ gives D((1 − λ)Q₀ + λQ₁‖P) ≤ (1 − λ)D(Q₀‖P) + λD(Q₁‖P) < ∞.

One-sided derivative. Let Q* ∈ E with D(Q*‖P) = D* and density f*. Let Q ∈ E. If D(Q‖P) = ∞, part (a) holds for Q. So let D(Q‖P) < ∞, with density f. For λ ∈ (0, 1], Q_λ = (1 − λ)Q* + λQ is in E because E is convex, and its density is f_λ = f* + λ(f − f*). Let q_λ = (φ(f_λ) − φ(f*))/λ pointwise. By step s1 both φ(f_λ) and φ(f*) are integrable, and ∫ q_λ dP = (D(Q_λ‖P) − D*)/λ ≥ 0 because D* is the infimum over E. At each point, q_λ is the slope of a chord of a convex function from a fixed end point, so q_λ is nondecreasing in λ. As λ = 1/k decreases to 0, q_λ decreases to q₀, where q₀ = (1 + log f*)(f − f*) on {f* > 0}, q₀ = −∞ on {f* = 0 < f}, and q₀ = 0 on {f* = 0 = f}. The functions q₁ − q_{1/k} ≥ 0 increase to q₁ − q₀, and q₁ = φ(f) − φ(f*) is integrable. The monotone convergence theorem gives ∫ q_{1/k} dP → ∫ q₀ dP. So ∫ q₀ dP ≥ 0. In particular q₀ > −∞ almost everywhere, so P(f* = 0 < f) = 0, and q₀ is integrable because q₀ ≤ q₁.

Pythagorean inequality. By step s2, f = 0 almost everywhere on {f* = 0}. So Q ≪ Q* with dQ/dQ* = f/f* on {f* > 0}, and ∫_{f*>0} (f − f*) dP = 1 − 1 = 0. On {f* > 0}, (f − f*) log f* = q₀ − (f − f*) is integrable, and its integral is ∫ q₀ dP ≥ 0. Since φ(f*) is integrable, f log f* = (f − f*) log f* + φ(f*) is integrable on {f* > 0}, and ∫_{f*>0} f log f* dP ≥ ∫ φ(f*) dP = D(Q*‖P). Then D(Q‖Q*) = ∫_{f>0} f log(f/f*) dP = ∫ φ(f) dP − ∫_{f*>0} f log f* dP ≤ D(Q‖P) − D(Q*‖P). This proves part (a).

Converse and uniqueness. Suppose Q* ∈ E satisfies the inequality of part (a) for every Q ∈ E. Gibbs' inequality gives D(Q‖Q*) ≥ 0, so D(Q‖P) ≥ D(Q*‖P) for every Q ∈ E. Since Q* ∈ E, D(Q*‖P) = D*. Now let Q₁, Q₂ ∈ E both have divergence D*. Part (a) with Q* = Q₁ and Q = Q₂ gives D* ≥ D(Q₂‖Q₁) + D*. Since D* < ∞, D(Q₂‖Q₁) = 0. Pinsker's inequality gives TV(Q₂, Q₁) ≤ √(0/2) = 0, so Q₂ = Q₁. This proves part (b).

Parallelogram identity. Let Q₁, Q₂ have finite divergence from P, with densities f₁, f₂, and let M = (Q₁ + Q₂)/2 with density m = (f₁ + f₂)/2. Then Q_i ≪ M with dQ_i/dM = f_i/m ≤ 2. The integrand f_i log(f_i/m) is at most f_i log 2, and its integral D(Q_i‖M) is at least 0, so it is integrable. Hence f_i log m = φ(f_i) − f_i log(f_i/m) on {f_i > 0} (and 0 on {f_i = 0}) is integrable. Since f₁ log m + f₂ log m = 2φ(m), integration gives D(Q₁‖P) + D(Q₂‖P) = 2D(M‖P) + D(Q₁‖M) + D(Q₂‖M), with every term finite.

Existence. Let E be closed in total variation and take Q_n ∈ E with D(Q_n‖P) → D*, all finite, with densities f_n. For m and n, M = (Q_m + Q_n)/2 is in E, so D(M‖P) ≥ D*. Step s5 gives D(Q_m‖M) + D(Q_n‖M) ≤ D(Q_m‖P) + D(Q_n‖P) − 2D*, which tends to 0 as m, n → ∞. Both terms are nonnegative by Gibbs' inequality. Since Q_m − Q_n = 2(Q_m − M), Pinsker's inequality gives TV(Q_m, Q_n) = 2TV(Q_m, M) ≤ 2√(D(Q_m‖M)/2) → 0. So ∫|f_m − f_n| dP → 0. Choose n₁ < n₂ < … with ∫|f_{n_{k+1}} − f_{n_k}| dP ≤ 2^(−k). By monotone convergence, Σ_k |f_{n_{k+1}} − f_{n_k}| has integral at most 1, so it is finite almost everywhere, and f_{n_k} converges almost everywhere to some f ≥ 0. Fatou's lemma gives ∫|f − f_{n_k}| dP ≤ liminf_j ∫|f_{n_j} − f_{n_k}| dP → 0 as k → ∞. So ∫ f dP = 1, Q*(A) = ∫_A f dP is a probability measure, and TV(Q_n, Q*) → 0 because (Q_n) is Cauchy in total variation. Closedness gives Q* ∈ E. Finally φ(f_{n_k}) + 1/e ≥ 0 converges almost everywhere to φ(f) + 1/e, and Fatou's lemma gives D(Q*‖P) = ∫ φ(f) dP ≤ liminf_k D(Q_{n_k}‖P) = D*. So D(Q*‖P) = D*. With step s4 this proves part (c).

applications.title: The Gibbs law of a three-level system is the I-projection under a mean-energy constraint
applications.inputs: A single site has energy levels H(k) = k for k ∈ {0, 1, 2}. The reference law P is uniform, P(k) = 1/3 (infinite temperature). The constraint set is E = {Q : E_Q[H] ≤ 4/7}. The candidate is the Gibbs law Q*(k) = 2^(−k)/Z with Z = 1 + 1/2 + 1/4, which is the Boltzmann factor e^(−βk) with β = ln 2. Divergences are in bits.
applications.hypotheses: P is a probability measure on {0, 1, 2}. E is convex, because Q ↦ E_Q[H] is linear. E is closed in total variation, because on a finite set total variation convergence is convergence of the three masses. D* is finite, because P has full support and so D(Q‖P) ≤ log₂ 3 for every Q.

steps.text: The partition function is Z = 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 = 7/4, so Q* = (4/7, 2/7, 1/7).
The mean energy of Q* is (0 · 4 + 1 · 2 + 2 · 1)/7 = 4/7. So Q* ∈ E and the constraint is active.

For each k, log₂(Q*(k)/P(k)) = log₂(3/Z) − k. Q* has full support, so for every Q, D(Q‖P) = D(Q‖Q*) + Σ_k Q(k) log₂(Q*(k)/P(k)) = D(Q‖Q*) + log₂(3/Z) − E_Q[H]. The same formula for Q = Q* gives D(Q*‖P) = log₂(12/7) − 4/7 ≈ 0.206 bits. So D(Q‖P) − D(Q‖Q*) − D(Q*‖P) = 4/7 − E_Q[H] ≥ 0 for every Q ∈ E. By part (b), Q* is the I-projection, and it is the only minimizer.
For the competitor Q = (5/7, 1/7, 1/7), E_Q[H] = (0 · 5 + 1 · 1 + 2 · 1)/7 = 3/7. Its Pythagorean gap is 4/7 − 3/7 = 1/7 bit, so D(Q‖P) exceeds D(Q‖Q*) + D(Q*‖P) by exactly 1/7 bit.

applications.conclusion: Among all laws of the three-level system with mean energy at most 4/7, the Gibbs law at β = ln 2 is the unique one closest to the uniform law in relative entropy. Since D(Q‖P) = log₂ 3 − H(Q) for uniform P, it is also the unique law of maximum entropy under the constraint.

limitations: Without closedness the infimum need not be attained. For P uniform on {0, 1} and E = {Q : Q(1) > 1/2}, D* = 0 but P is not in E.
For a linear family the inequality of part (a) is an identity, and the I-projection is an exponential tilt of P (Theorem 3.2 of Csiszár and Shields). Part (a) alone does not give this form.

results.name: Joint convexity of f-divergences
results.statement: Let f: (0, ∞) → ℝ be convex with f(1) = 0. Put f(0) = lim_{x↓0} f(x) ∈ (−∞, ∞] and M_f = lim_{t→∞} f(t)/t ∈ (−∞, ∞]. For probability measures P and Q on a measurable space (Ω, F), let P = P_ac + P_sing be the Lebesgue decomposition of P with respect to Q, and put D_f(P‖Q) = ∫ f(dP_ac/dQ) dQ + P_sing(Ω) M_f, with 0 · ∞ = 0. Then D_f(P‖Q) is well defined in (−∞, ∞]. For all probability measures P₁, P₂, Q₁, Q₂ on (Ω, F) and every λ ∈ [0, 1], D_f((1 − λ)P₁ + λP₂ ‖ (1 − λ)Q₁ + λQ₂) ≤ (1 − λ) D_f(P₁‖Q₁) + λ D_f(P₂‖Q₂). In particular, D_f(P‖Q) is convex in P for fixed Q and convex in Q for fixed P.
hypotheses: f: (0, ∞) → ℝ is convex and f(1) = 0.
P₁, P₂, Q₁ and Q₂ are probability measures on the same measurable space (Ω, F), and λ ∈ [0, 1].
results.empty_prerequisites_reason: The proof uses only the definition of convexity, the Lebesgue decomposition written with densities, and linearity of the integral for functions with integrable negative parts.

definitions.name: f-divergence
definitions.text: D_f(P‖Q) = ∫ f(dP_ac/dQ) dQ + P_sing(Ω) M_f. The choices f(x) = x log x, (x − 1)², |x − 1|/2 and (√x − 1)² give the Kullback–Leibler divergence, the χ²-divergence, the total variation distance and the squared Hellinger distance.

definitions.name: perspective function
definitions.text: g(a, b) = b f(a/b) for a ≥ 0 and b > 0, extended by g(a, 0) = a M_f. It is positively homogeneous of degree 1.

definitions.name: maximal slope
definitions.text: M_f = lim_{t→∞} f(t)/t. It is the limit of the chord slopes of f to the right, and it is the cost per unit of mass of P that Q does not charge.

source.citation: Sébastien Gerchinovitz, Pierre Ménard and Gilles Stoltz, Fano's inequality for random variables, Statistical Science 35(2), 178–201, 2020.
source.revision: arXiv:1702.05985v3 of 10 June 2019
source.module: Section 2.3, The data-processing inequality and two major consequences
source.excerpt: Corollary 3 (Joint convexity of Div_f). All f–divergences Div_f are jointly convex, i.e., for all probability distributions P1, P2 and Q1, Q2 on the same measurable space (Ω, F), and all λ ∈ (0, 1), Div_f((1 − λ)P1 + λP2, (1 − λ)Q1 + λQ2) ⩽ (1 − λ) Div_f(P1, Q1) + λ Div_f(P2, Q2). … we derive Corollary 3 as an elementary consequence of Lemma 1 applied to an augmented probability space.
source.attribution: © Sébastien Gerchinovitz, Pierre Ménard and Gilles Stoltz. Quoted from the arXiv preprint for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The authored statement uses the same definition (3) of the f-divergence, with the maximal slope M_f for the singular part, and the same conclusion. It adds that the divergence is well defined in (−∞, ∞] and that convexity in each argument follows. The source derives the corollary from the data processing inequality on an augmented space and gives the proof only in an extended version. The authored proof is a different, direct proof: it shows that the perspective function of f is jointly convex on [0, ∞)² and integrates this inequality.

results.proof_status: authored proof by joint convexity of the perspective function of f, a direct route that differs from the data processing proof of the source. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement, for every convex f with f(1) = 0, including f with f(0) = ∞ or M_f = ∞ and measures with singular parts.

steps.text: Slopes of f. Fix x > 0. By convexity the chord slope (f(t) − f(x))/(t − x) is nondecreasing in t > x, so it has a limit in (−∞, ∞] as t → ∞. Since f(t)/t = ((f(t) − f(x))/(t − x)) · (t − x)/t + f(x)/t, this limit is M_f. Hence f(x + y) ≤ f(x) + y M_f for x > 0 and y ≥ 0, and letting x ↓ 0 gives the same bound for x = 0. Let c be a subgradient of f at 1, so that f(x) ≥ c(x − 1) for x > 0, and also for x = 0 by the limit. The chord slopes from 1 are at least c, so M_f ≥ c. The convexity inequality f((1 − s)x + sy) ≤ (1 − s)f(x) + s f(y) also holds for x = 0 or y = 0, by letting the variable tend to 0.

Perspective function. Define g on [0, ∞)² by g(a, b) = b f(a/b) for b > 0 and g(a, 0) = a M_f, with 0 · ∞ = 0. Then g(a, b) ≥ c(a − b) for all a, b ≥ 0: for b > 0 this is b f(a/b) ≥ b c(a/b − 1), and for b = 0 it is a M_f ≥ c a. Let μ be a measure that dominates P and Q, for example μ = P + Q, and let p = dP/dμ and q = dQ/dμ. The measures P(· ∩ {q > 0}) and P(· ∩ {q = 0}) are absolutely continuous and singular with respect to Q, so by uniqueness of the Lebesgue decomposition they are P_ac and P_sing, and dP_ac/dQ = p/q on {q > 0}. Hence ∫ f(dP_ac/dQ) dQ = ∫_{q>0} q f(p/q) dμ and P_sing(Ω) M_f = ∫_{q=0} p M_f dμ. Since g(p, q) ≥ c(p − q) and ∫|p − q| dμ ≤ 2, both integrals have integrable negative parts, and D_f(P‖Q) = ∫ g(p, q) dμ is well defined in (−∞, ∞] for every such μ.

Joint convexity of g. Let (a₁, b₁), (a₂, b₂) ∈ [0, ∞)², λ ∈ (0, 1), a = (1 − λ)a₁ + λa₂ and b = (1 − λ)b₁ + λb₂. If b₁, b₂ > 0, put s = λb₂/b. Then a/b = (1 − s)(a₁/b₁) + s(a₂/b₂), and convexity of f gives g(a, b) = b f(a/b) ≤ (1 − λ)b₁ f(a₁/b₁) + λb₂ f(a₂/b₂). If b₁ = 0 < b₂, then b = λb₂ and a/b = a₂/b₂ + (1 − λ)a₁/(λb₂). Step s1 gives f(a/b) ≤ f(a₂/b₂) + ((1 − λ)a₁/(λb₂)) M_f, and multiplication by λb₂ gives g(a, b) ≤ λ g(a₂, b₂) + (1 − λ) a₁ M_f = (1 − λ)g(a₁, b₁) + λg(a₂, b₂). The case b₂ = 0 < b₁ is symmetric. If b₁ = b₂ = 0, then g(a, 0) = a M_f = (1 − λ)a₁ M_f + λa₂ M_f, also when M_f = ∞. So g((1 − λ)(a₁, b₁) + λ(a₂, b₂)) ≤ (1 − λ)g(a₁, b₁) + λg(a₂, b₂) in all cases.

Integration. For λ ∈ {0, 1} there is nothing to prove, so let λ ∈ (0, 1). Let μ = P₁ + P₂ + Q₁ + Q₂, with densities pᵢ = dPᵢ/dμ and qᵢ = dQᵢ/dμ. The mixtures P = (1 − λ)P₁ + λP₂ and Q = (1 − λ)Q₁ + λQ₂ have the densities p = (1 − λ)p₁ + λp₂ and q = (1 − λ)q₁ + λq₂. Step s3 gives g(p, q) ≤ (1 − λ)g(p₁, q₁) + λg(p₂, q₂) pointwise. All three functions have integrable negative parts by the lower bound of step s2, so the integral is monotone and linear for them. Integration and step s2 give D_f(P‖Q) ≤ (1 − λ)D_f(P₁‖Q₁) + λD_f(P₂‖Q₂). With Q₁ = Q₂ or with P₁ = P₂ this gives convexity in each argument.

applications.title: Losing the label of the magnet loses information about the field
applications.inputs: A spin is measured in one of two magnets, chosen by a fair coin, so λ = 1/2. Under hypothesis H (field on) the spin is up with probability 3/4 in magnet A and 1/2 in magnet B. Under hypothesis K (field off) it is up with probability 1/2 in magnet A and 1/4 in magnet B. So P₁ = Ber(3/4), Q₁ = Ber(1/2), P₂ = Ber(1/2) and Q₂ = Ber(1/4). The record of the magnet is lost. Use the χ²-divergence, f(x) = (x − 1)², for which χ²(Ber(p)‖Ber(q)) = (p − q)²/(q(1 − q)).
applications.hypotheses: f(x) = (x − 1)² is convex with f(1) = 0. The four laws are probability measures on {0, 1}, and λ = 1/2 ∈ [0, 1].

steps.text: Without the label, the spin is up with probability (3/4 + 1/2)/2 = 5/8 under H and (1/2 + 1/4)/2 = 3/8 under K. So χ²(Ber(5/8)‖Ber(3/8)) = (1/4)²/((3/8)(5/8)) = 4/15.
Joint convexity predicts 4/15 ≤ 7/24, and indeed 4/15 ≈ 0.267 < 0.292 ≈ 7/24. The difference is 7/24 − 4/15 = 1/40.

applications.conclusion: With the magnet label, the χ²-divergence of the pair (magnet, spin) under H and K is the average 7/24, because the label has the same law under both hypotheses. Without the label, the divergence drops to 4/15. Joint convexity guarantees that the loss of the label can never increase the divergence.

limitations: The theorem gives no lower bound for the divergence of the mixtures. Mixtures of far-apart pairs can have a divergence much smaller than the average.
The mixtures in the two arguments must use the same weights. For mixtures with different weights the theorem gives no bound.

results.name: Pinsker's inequality
results.statement: Let P and Q be probability measures on the same measurable space. Let TV(P, Q) = sup_A |P(A) − Q(A)|, where A runs over the measurable sets. Let D(P‖Q) = ∫ log(dP/dQ) dP (natural logarithm) when P is absolutely continuous with respect to Q, and D(P‖Q) = ∞ otherwise. Then D(P‖Q) ≥ 2 TV(P, Q)², that is, TV(P, Q) ≤ √(D(P‖Q)/2). The constant 2 cannot be made larger.
hypotheses: P and Q are probability measures on the same measurable space.
The divergence D(P‖Q) uses the natural logarithm. In base b the inequality reads D_b(P‖Q) ≥ (2 log_b e) TV(P, Q)².

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 applies the data processing inequality for relative entropy to the measurable map ω ↦ 1_A(ω), which sends P and Q to two Bernoulli laws.
Step s4 uses that D(P‖Q) ≥ 0 and the case analysis of step s1 to dispose of the events with Q(A) ∈ {0, 1}.

definitions.name: relative entropy
definitions.text: D(P‖Q) = ∫ log(dP/dQ) dP if P ≪ Q, and D(P‖Q) = ∞ otherwise. It is also called the Kullback–Leibler divergence.

definitions.name: total variation distance
definitions.text: TV(P, Q) = sup_A |P(A) − Q(A)| = (1/2)∫|p − q| dμ, where p and q are densities of P and Q with respect to a common dominating measure μ.

definitions.name: binary divergence
definitions.text: d(p‖q) = p log(p/q) + (1 − p) log((1 − p)/(1 − q)) for p, q ∈ [0, 1], with 0 log 0 = 0. It equals D(Ber(p)‖Ber(q)).

source.citation: Clément L. Canonne, A short note on an inequality between KL and TV, arXiv:2202.07198 [math.PR], 2022.
source.revision: arXiv v2 of 2 August 2023
source.module: Section 1, Pinsker's inequality
source.excerpt: Lemma 2 (Pinsker’s Inequality). For every p, q on Ω, dTV(p, q) ≤ √(½ KL(p ‖ q)). … Proof. Consider first the binary case, i.e., where p, q are Bernoulli distributions Bern(p) and Bern(q), respectively.
source.attribution: © Clément L. Canonne. Quoted from the arXiv preprint for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states the inequality for distributions p and q on a domain Ω, with KL in nats. The authored statement uses probability measures, writes the definitions of TV and D explicitly, and includes the sharpness of the constant, which the source shows after the proof. The authored proof follows the source proof. It first proves the Bernoulli case with the integral of f'(x) = (p − x)/(x(1 − x)) and the bound x(1 − x) ≤ 1/4. Then data processing for the indicator of an event and a supremum over events give the general case. The authored proof also writes out the cases with Q(A) in {0, 1}, which the source leaves to the reader.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the proof of Lemma 2 in Canonne's note. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement, for all probability measures P and Q, including the case D(P‖Q) = ∞ and the sharpness of the constant 2.

steps.text: If D(P‖Q) = ∞ there is nothing to prove, so assume D(P‖Q) < ∞. Then P ≪ Q. Fix a measurable set A and put p = P(A), q = Q(A). The measurable map ω ↦ 1_A(ω) sends P to Ber(p) and Q to Ber(q). The data processing inequality for relative entropy gives D(P‖Q) ≥ d(p‖q), where d is the binary divergence. If q = 0, then p = 0 because P ≪ Q. If q = 1, then Q(A^c) = 0, so P(A^c) = 0 and p = 1. In both cases p = q.

Fix q ∈ (0, 1). For p ∈ [0, 1] put R(p) = ∫_q^p (p − t)/(t(1 − t)) dt. The integrand is bounded on the interval between q and p, also when p ∈ {0, 1}, because the factor p − t cancels the zero of t(1 − t) at t = p. Differentiation under the integral sign gives R'(p) = ∫_q^p dt/(t(1 − t)) = log(p/(1 − p)) − log(q/(1 − q)) for p ∈ (0, 1), and this is also ∂_p d(p‖q). Both R and d(·‖q) vanish at p = q and are continuous on [0, 1]. Hence d(p‖q) = R(p) for every p ∈ [0, 1].

For t ∈ (0, 1), t(1 − t) ≤ 1/4, so 1/(t(1 − t)) ≥ 4. If p ≥ q, the factor p − t is nonnegative on [q, p], so R(p) ≥ 4∫_q^p (p − t) dt = 2(p − q)². If p < q, then R(p) = ∫_p^q (t − p)/(t(1 − t)) dt with a nonnegative factor t − p, so R(p) ≥ 4∫_p^q (t − p) dt = 2(p − q)². Thus d(p‖q) ≥ 2(p − q)² for all p ∈ [0, 1] and q ∈ (0, 1).

Combine the steps. For q ∈ (0, 1), steps s1 and s3 give D(P‖Q) ≥ d(p‖q) ≥ 2(P(A) − Q(A))². For q ∈ {0, 1}, step s1 gives P(A) = Q(A), and D(P‖Q) ≥ 0 by Gibbs' inequality, so the same bound holds. Take the supremum over A: D(P‖Q) ≥ 2 sup_A (P(A) − Q(A))² = 2 TV(P, Q)².

Sharpness. Let P = Ber(1/2 + ε) and Q = Ber(1/2) with 0 < ε < 1/2. Then TV(P, Q) = ε. A Taylor expansion of d(1/2 + ε‖1/2) = (1/2 + ε) log(1 + 2ε) + (1/2 − ε) log(1 − 2ε) in ε gives 2ε² + (4/3)ε⁴ + O(ε⁶). So D(P‖Q)/TV(P, Q)² → 2 as ε → 0, and no constant larger than 2 is valid.

applications.title: Two positions of an optical trap cannot be told apart from 50 measurements
applications.inputs: A colloidal particle in a harmonic optical trap has the stationary position law N(m, 1) in units of the thermal length. Under hypothesis H0 the trap center is m = 0, and under H1 it is m = δ = 1/10. The experimenter records n = 50 independent stationary positions X₁, …, X₅₀. Let P₀ and P₁ be the laws of (X₁, …, X₅₀) under H0 and H1.
applications.hypotheses: P₀ = N(0, 1)^⊗50 and P₁ = N(1/10, 1)^⊗50 are probability measures on ℝ⁵⁰. They have positive densities, so P₁ ≪ P₀ and the divergence is finite.

steps.text: The log-likelihood ratio is log(dP₁/dP₀)(x) = Σᵢ (δxᵢ − δ²/2). Its mean under P₁ is n(δ² − δ²/2) = nδ²/2. So D(P₁‖P₀) = nδ²/2.
Pinsker's inequality gives TV(P₀, P₁)² ≤ D(P₁‖P₀)/2 = 1/8, so TV(P₀, P₁) ≤ √(1/8) < 0.3536.
For every test with rejection region A, the two error probabilities satisfy P₀(A) + P₁(A^c) = 1 − (P₁(A) − P₀(A)) ≥ 1 − TV(P₀, P₁) > 0.646. So at least one of the two errors is larger than 0.32.

applications.conclusion: No test based on 50 positions decides between the two trap centers with both error probabilities below 0.32. The sum of the two errors is larger than 0.646 for every test.

limitations: The bound is useless when D(P‖Q) ≥ 2, because TV ≤ 1 always. The Bretagnolle–Huber inequality TV ≤ √(1 − e^(−D)) stays informative for large D.
The constant 2 is optimal only as TV → 0. The optimal lower bound of D as a function of TV (Vajda's bound) is strictly larger than 2 TV² for TV > 0.

results.name: Bretagnolle–Huber inequality
results.statement: Let P and Q be probability measures on the same measurable space (Ω, F). Let TV(P, Q) = sup_{A∈F} |P(A) − Q(A)|. Let D(P‖Q) = ∫ log(dP/dQ) dP (natural logarithm) when P is absolutely continuous with respect to Q, and D(P‖Q) = ∞ otherwise, with e^(−∞) = 0. Then TV(P, Q) ≤ √(1 − e^(−D(P‖Q))). Consequently, for every event A ∈ F, P(A) + Q(A^c) ≥ 1 − TV(P, Q) ≥ (1/2) e^(−D(P‖Q)).
hypotheses: P and Q are probability measures on the same measurable space (Ω, F).
The divergence D(P‖Q) uses the natural logarithm, and D(P‖Q) = ∞ when P is not absolutely continuous with respect to Q.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 uses the Radon–Nikodym theorem to get densities p and q of P and Q with respect to ν = P + Q, and dP/dQ = p/q P-almost surely.
Step s2 applies the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality to √(pq) = √(min(p, q)) · √(max(p, q)) in L²(ν).
Step s3 applies Jensen's inequality to the convex function exp under P to bound the Hellinger affinity ∫√(pq) dν below by e^(−D/2).

definitions.name: relative entropy
definitions.text: D(P‖Q) = ∫ log(dP/dQ) dP if P ≪ Q, and D(P‖Q) = ∞ otherwise. It is also called the Kullback–Leibler divergence.

definitions.name: total variation distance
definitions.text: TV(P, Q) = sup_A |P(A) − Q(A)| = (1/2)∫|p − q| dν = 1 − ∫ min(p, q) dν, where p and q are densities of P and Q with respect to a common dominating measure ν.

definitions.name: Hellinger affinity
definitions.text: The number ∫ √(pq) dν ∈ [0, 1]. It does not depend on the choice of the dominating measure ν.

source.excerpt: Lemma 3 (The BH Bound). For every p, q on Ω, dTV(p, q) ≤ √(1 − e^(−KL(p ‖ q))). Proof. We follow the original argument of [BH78, Lemma 2.1]: fixing p, q, we define, for X distributed according to p, the random variables U := q(X)/p(X)

source.alignment: The source states the bound for distributions p and q on a domain Ω, with KL in nats. The authored statement uses general probability measures, makes the case D = ∞ explicit, and adds the event form P(A) + Q(A^c) ≥ (1/2)e^(−D), which is Theorem 14.2 of Lattimore and Szepesvári. The authored proof follows the second proof of Lemma 3 in the source, from the argument of Tsybakov's Lemma 2.6: Cauchy–Schwarz gives 1 − TV² ≥ (∫√(pq))², and Jensen's inequality gives (∫√(pq))² ≥ e^(−D). The last step uses √(1 − x) ≤ 1 − x/2, as in the source's Corollary 4.

source_references.excerpt: Theorem 14.2 (Bretagnolle–Huber inequality). Let P and Q be probability measures on the same measurable space (Ω, F), and let A ∈ F be an arbitrary event. Then, P(A) + Q(A^c) ≥ (1/2) exp(−D(P, Q)), where A^c = Ω \ A is the complement of A.
source_references.attribution: © Tor Lattimore and Csaba Szepesvári. Quoted from the authors' online version of the book for identification of the cited result.
source_references.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source_references.alignment: The source states the event form of the inequality, which is the second conclusion of the authored statement. Its proof proves ∫ min(p, q) ≥ (1/2)(∫√(pq))² ≥ (1/2)e^(−D) with the same Cauchy–Schwarz and Jensen steps, but it bounds ∫ max(p, q) by 2 and so does not give the total variation form.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the second proof of Lemma 3 in Canonne's note, from the argument of Lemma 2.6 of Tsybakov. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement, for all probability measures P and Q, including the case D(P‖Q) = ∞.

steps.text: If D(P‖Q) = ∞, then e^(−D) = 0. The first bound reads TV ≤ 1, and the second reads P(A) + Q(A^c) ≥ 1 − TV ≥ 0. Both are true, because Q(A) − P(A) ≤ TV ≤ 1. So assume D(P‖Q) < ∞, which means P ≪ Q. Let ν = P + Q. By the Radon–Nikodym theorem, P and Q have densities p, q ≥ 0 with respect to ν. Since Q({q = 0}) = 0 and P ≪ Q, also P({q = 0}) = 0, and dP/dQ = p/q holds P-almost surely. Write m = min(p, q) and M = max(p, q). Then m + M = p + q and M − m = |p − q|. For an event A, P(A) − Q(A) = ∫_A (p − q) dν ≤ ∫_{p>q} (p − q) dν, and the same bound holds for Q(A) − P(A) because ∫ (p − q) dν = 0. Equality holds for A = {p > q}. So TV = (1/2)∫|p − q| dν, ∫ m dν = 1 − TV and ∫ M dν = 1 + TV.
Cauchy–Schwarz step. Pointwise √(pq) = √m · √M. The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality in L²(ν) gives (∫√(pq) dν)² ≤ (∫ m dν)(∫ M dν) = (1 − TV)(1 + TV) = 1 − TV².

Jensen step. Let Z = (1/2) log(q/p), which is defined and finite P-almost surely by step s1. Since D(P‖Q) < ∞, log(p/q) is P-integrable: its negative part is integrable because ∫ (x log x)_− dQ ≤ 1/e with x = dP/dQ, and E_P[log(p/q)] = D(P‖Q). So E_P[Z] = −D(P‖Q)/2. The set {p = 0} is P-null, so ∫√(pq) dν = ∫_{p>0} p √(q/p) dν = E_P[e^Z]. The function exp is convex, and Jensen's inequality gives E_P[e^Z] ≥ e^(E_P[Z]) = e^(−D/2). Hence (∫√(pq) dν)² ≥ e^(−D(P‖Q)).
Total variation form. Steps s2 and s3 give 1 − TV² ≥ e^(−D(P‖Q)). So TV² ≤ 1 − e^(−D), and TV ≤ √(1 − e^(−D(P‖Q))).

applications.title: A weak field on a paramagnet stays hard to detect when Pinsker's inequality is vacuous
applications.inputs: An experimenter reads the magnetization of a paramagnetic sample n = 800 times. Each reading is the true value m plus independent Gaussian noise with variance 1. Under H0 the applied field is off and m = 0. Under H1 it is on and m = 1/10. Let P₀ = N(0, 1)^⊗800 and P₁ = N(1/10, 1)^⊗800 be the laws of the 800 readings.
applications.hypotheses: P₀ and P₁ are probability measures on ℝ⁸⁰⁰. They have positive densities, so P₁ ≪ P₀ and D(P₁‖P₀) is finite.

steps.text: The log-likelihood ratio is log(dP₁/dP₀)(x) = Σᵢ (m xᵢ − m²/2) with m = 1/10. Its mean under P₁ is n m²/2. So D(P₁‖P₀) = n m²/2.
Pinsker's inequality gives only TV² ≤ D/2 = 2. This bound is vacuous, because TV ≤ 1 always.

The Bretagnolle–Huber inequality gives TV(P₁, P₀) ≤ √(1 − e^(−4)). Since e^(−4) > 0.0183, this is less than √0.9817 < 0.9909. For every test with rejection region A, P₀(A) + P₁(A^c) ≥ 1 − TV > 0.0091.

applications.conclusion: No test based on 800 readings has both error probabilities below 0.0045. Pinsker's inequality cannot show this, because it is vacuous at D = 4.

limitations: For small D the bound TV ≤ √(1 − e^(−D)) ≈ √D is weaker than Pinsker's bound √(D/2) by the factor √2.
The event form gives only the sum of the two error probabilities. It does not say which of the two errors is large.

results.name: Le Cam's two-point lower bound
aliases: two-point lower bound for minimax risk
results.statement: Let (Θ, d) be a metric space, let 𝒫 be a set of probability measures on a measurable space (𝒳, 𝒜), and let θ: 𝒫 → Θ. Let Φ: [0, ∞) → [0, ∞) be nondecreasing and fix n ≥ 1. For P ∈ 𝒫, Pⁿ is the law of n independent observations X = (X₁, …, X_n) with law P, and E_P is the expectation under Pⁿ. An estimator is a measurable map θ̂: 𝒳ⁿ → Θ. Let P₀, P₁ ∈ 𝒫 and s = d(θ(P₀), θ(P₁)). Then every estimator θ̂ satisfies max_{j=0,1} E_{P_j}[Φ(d(θ̂(X), θ(P_j)))] ≥ (Φ(s/2)/2)(1 − TV(P₀ⁿ, P₁ⁿ)), where TV(P, Q) = sup_A |P(A) − Q(A)|. Hence the minimax risk R_n = inf_θ̂ sup_{P∈𝒫} E_P[Φ(d(θ̂(X), θ(P)))] is at least (Φ(s/2)/2)(1 − TV(P₀ⁿ, P₁ⁿ)). For Φ(t) = t the bound is (s/4)(1 − TV(P₀ⁿ, P₁ⁿ)).
hypotheses: d is a metric on the parameter set Θ.
Φ: [0, ∞) → [0, ∞) is nondecreasing.
P₀ and P₁ belong to the model 𝒫, and the data are n independent observations from one P ∈ 𝒫.
Estimators are measurable maps from 𝒳ⁿ to Θ with its Borel σ-algebra.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 applies Markov's inequality to the nonnegative variable Φ(d(θ̂, θ_j)) to bound its mean below by Φ(s/2) times the probability that the error is at least s/2.

definitions.name: minimax risk
definitions.text: R_n = inf_θ̂ sup_{P∈𝒫} E_P[Φ(d(θ̂(X), θ(P)))], the smallest worst-case expected loss that an estimator from n observations can have.

definitions.name: total variation distance
definitions.text: TV(P, Q) = sup_A |P(A) − Q(A)|. If p and q are densities with respect to a common measure ν, then 1 − TV(P, Q) = ∫ min(p, q) dν.

definitions.name: two-point method
definitions.text: A lower bound on the minimax risk from two models P₀ and P₁ whose parameters are far apart but whose sample laws are close.

source.module: Section 5, Lower Bound Method 1: Le Cam
source.excerpt: Theorem 4 Let 𝒫 be a set of distributions. For any pair P₀, P₁ ∈ 𝒫, inf_θ̂ sup_{P∈𝒫} E_P[d(θ̂, θ(P))] ≥ (s/4) ∫ [p₀ⁿ(x) ∧ p₁ⁿ(x)] dx = (s/4)[1 − TV(P₀ⁿ, P₁ⁿ)] (9) where s = d(θ(P₀), θ(P₁)).
