The source cites its Theorem 14 (large deviations of tilted measures) for Proposition 3. Steps s1 and s2 give that argument for the function −βu in full. The macrostate level of the source is not covered.

steps.text: Lower bound on open sets. Let O be open, u ∈ O with s(u) > −∞, and ε > 0 with (u − ε, u + ε) ⊂ O. On that interval e^(−βN h_N) ≥ e^(−N(βu + |β|ε)). So ∫_{h_N∈O} e^(−βN h_N) dP_N ≥ e^(−N(βu + |β|ε)) P_N(|h_N − u| < ε). The lower bound of hypothesis (i) gives liminf N⁻¹ log P_N(|h_N − u| < ε) ≥ s(u). Let ε → 0 and take the supremum over u: liminf N⁻¹ log ∫_{h_N∈O} e^(−βN h_N) dP_N ≥ sup_O (s(u) − βu).

Upper bound on closed sets. Let C be closed, M > 0 and ε > 0. On {h_N > M}, e^(−βN h_N) ≤ e^(−NM) e^(−(β−1)N h_N), so this part of the integral is at most e^(−NM) Z_N(β − 1), whose exponential rate is −M − φ(β − 1). In the same way {h_N < −M} contributes at most e^(−NM) Z_N(β + 1). Cover [−M, M] by finitely many closed intervals K_i of length at most ε/(1 + |β|). Then βu varies by at most ε on K_i, and the upper bound of (i) for the closed set K_i ∩ C gives the rate sup_{K_i∩C} (s(u) − βu) + ε for the part in K_i ∩ C. The rate of a finite sum is the maximum of the rates. So limsup N⁻¹ log ∫_{h_N∈C} e^(−βN h_N) dP_N ≤ max(sup_C (s(u) − βu) + ε, −M − φ(β − 1), −M − φ(β + 1)). Let M → ∞ and ε → 0.

Part (a). Steps s1 and s2 with O = C = ℝ give lim N⁻¹ log Z_N(β) = sup_u (s(u) − βu). By (ii) this limit is −φ(β), so φ(β) = inf_u (βu − s(u)). As an infimum of affine functions of β, φ is concave. This is the transform (21) of the source.

Part (b). By (a), βu − φ(β) ≥ s(u) for all β and u, so s** ≥ s. Apply the Fenchel–Moreau theorem to f = −s, which is proper because sup s = 0, and has the affine minorant 0. Its conjugate is f*(y) = −φ(−y), and f** = −s**. So −s** is the largest lower semicontinuous convex function below −s. Equivalently, s** is the smallest concave upper semicontinuous function above s. Since s is upper semicontinuous, s = s** exactly when s is concave. If β ∈ ∂s(u), the line v ↦ s(u) + β(v − u) is one such function, so s**(u) ≤ s(u). Hence s(u) < s**(u) forces ∂s(u) = ∅.

Part (c). P_{N,β}(h_N ∈ A) = Z_N(β)⁻¹ ∫_{h_N∈A} e^(−βN h_N) dP_N, and N⁻¹ log Z_N(β) → −φ(β). Steps s1 and s2 give limsup N⁻¹ log P_{N,β}(h_N ∈ C) ≤ sup_C (s(u) − βu) + φ(β) = −inf_C J_β for closed C, and the matching lower bound for open sets. J_β ≥ 0 by (a), and J_β is lower semicontinuous because s is upper semicontinuous. By (a), −s(v) ≥ φ(β′) − β′v for every β′. With β′ = β ∓ 1 this gives J_β(v) ≥ |v| − c, where c = max(φ(β) − φ(β − 1), φ(β) − φ(β + 1)). So the level sets of J_β are closed and bounded, and J_β is a good rate function.

Part (d), which is Proposition 4 of the source. If s(u) = −∞, then J_β(u) = ∞ and ∂s(u) = ∅, because sup s = 0. If s(u) > −∞, then J_β(u) = 0 means βu − s(u) = inf_v (βv − s(v)), that is, s(v) ≤ s(u) + β(v − u) for all v, which is β ∈ ∂s(u). If the inequality is strict for v ≠ u, then J_β(v) > 0 for v ≠ u. Let δ > 0. The closed set {v : |v − u| ≥ δ} meets the compact level sets of J_β, so the infimum a of J_β on it is attained or infinite, and a > 0. Part (c) gives limsup N⁻¹ log P_{N,β}(|h_N − u| ≥ δ) ≤ −a < 0.

source.ref: H. Touchette, Equivalence and nonequivalence of ensembles: thermodynamic, macrostate, and measure levels, J. Stat. Phys. 159 (2015) 987-1016, arXiv:1403.6608v2, Section III, Propositions 3 and 4, pp. 10-13.

applications.title: A paramagnet of two-level atoms
applications.inputs: N independent atoms, each in the ground level (energy 0) or the excited level (energy 1), with the uniform prior P_N on {0, 1}^N. The mean energy h_N is the fraction of excited atoms. The microcanonical mean energy is u = 1/4.
applications.hypotheses: P_N is a probability measure. Under P_N, h_N is the mean of N independent fair Bernoulli variables. Cramér's theorem gives the large deviation principle with s(u) = −u log u − (1 − u) log(1 − u) − log 2 for u ∈ [0, 1] and s(u) = −∞ otherwise. This s is continuous on [0, 1], so it is upper semicontinuous, and s ≤ 0. Also Z_N(β) = ((1 + e^(−β))/2)^N exactly, so φ(β) = log 2 − log(1 + e^(−β)) is finite for every β.

steps.text: On (0, 1), s′(u) = log((1 − u)/u) and s″(u) = −1/(u(1 − u)) < 0. So s is strictly concave on [0, 1], and the tangent at u touches the graph only at u. At u = 1/4 the slope is log 3, because (1 − 1/4)/(1/4) = 3. So ∂s(1/4) = {log 3}.

Part (d) says that β = log 3 is the only inverse temperature whose canonical ensemble has the equilibrium mean energy 1/4. Directly, the canonical probability of the excited level is e^(−β)/(1 + e^(−β)) = (1/3)/(1 + 1/3) = 1/4.

Part (a) at β = log 3: φ(log 3) = log 2 − log(4/3) = log(3/2). The infimum of βu − s(u) is at u = 1/4, where (1/4) log 3 + (1/4) log(1/4) + (3/4) log(3/4) + log 2 = log 3 − log 2 = log(3/2). The two values agree. The partition function per atom is e^(−φ) = (1 + 1/3)/2 = 2/3.

Part (c): J_{log 3}(u) = u log 3 + u log u + (1 − u) log(1 − u) + log(4/3) = u log(4u) + (1 − u) log(4(1 − u)/3). This is the relative entropy of the Bernoulli(u) law with respect to the Bernoulli(1/4) law. At u = 1/2 it is (1/2) log 2 + (1/2) log(2/3) = (1/2) log(4/3) ≈ 0.1438.

applications.conclusion: The microcanonical ensemble at mean energy 1/4 and the canonical ensemble at β = log 3 are equivalent: the entropy is concave, φ and s are Legendre transforms of each other, and the canonical mean energy concentrates at 1/4. For example, the canonical probability that at least half of the atoms are excited decays like e^(−N (1/2) log(4/3)) on the exponential scale.

limitations: Systems with long-range interactions can have a nonconcave entropy. Then energies u with s(u) < s**(u) are not seen in the canonical ensemble at any temperature, and the canonical ensemble has a first-order phase transition in their place.

The record covers the thermodynamic level and the equilibrium energies. Equivalence of equilibrium macrostates and of the measures themselves needs more assumptions, as in Theorems 7, 10 and 12 of the source.

results.name: Jarzynski equality
results.statement: Let S be a finite set, β > 0 and N ≥ 1. Let X = (X_0, …, X_N) be a Markov chain on S with initial law p_0 and transition matrices M_1, …, M_N, where (M_n)_{xy} = P(X_n = x | X_{n−1} = y). Assume that p_0 has positive entries and that each M_n has a stationary distribution p_n (M_n p_n = p_n) with positive entries. This holds, with p_n unique, when M_n is irreducible. For n = 0, …, N let E_n: S → ℝ be an energy function of p_n, that is, p_n(x) = e^(−βE_n(x))/Z_n with Z_n = Σ_{x∈S} e^(−βE_n(x)), and let F_n = −β⁻¹ log Z_n. Let W = Σ_{n=0}^{N−1} (E_{n+1}(X_n) − E_n(X_n)) be the work and ΔF = F_N − F_0. Then E[e^(−β(W − ΔF))] = 1. In particular E[W] ≥ ΔF.
hypotheses: S is a finite set, β > 0, and X = (X_0, …, X_N) is a Markov chain on S with transition matrices M_1, …, M_N.
The initial law p_0 has positive entries.
Each M_n has a stationary distribution p_n with positive entries, for example because M_n is irreducible.
E_n is an energy function of p_n: p_n(x) = e^(−βE_n(x))/Z_n for n = 0, …, N.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 uses the Perron–Frobenius theorem to show that an irreducible transition matrix has a unique stationary distribution with positive entries.
Step s3 conditions on X_0, …, X_n and uses the tower property to get the one-step recursion for the weighted occupation ρ_n.
Step s6 applies Jensen's inequality to the convex exponential function to derive E[W] ≥ ΔF from the equality.

definitions.name: work
definitions.text: W = Σ_{n=0}^{N−1} (E_{n+1}(X_n) − E_n(X_n)): the energy put into the system when the energy function changes from E_n to E_{n+1} while the state X_n stays fixed.

definitions.name: free energy
definitions.text: F_n = −β⁻¹ log Z_n, where Z_n = Σ_x e^(−βE_n(x)) is the partition function of the energy E_n.

definitions.name: stationary distribution
definitions.text: A probability vector p with M p = p, that is, Σ_y (M)_{xy} p(y) = p(x) for every x.

source.citation: Pedro Hack, Sebastian Gottwald, Daniel A. Braun, Jarzyski's equality and Crooks' fluctuation theorem for general Markov chains with application to decision-making systems, arXiv:2202.05576.
source.revision: arXiv:2202.05576v2 [cond-mat.stat-mech], 25 Nov 2022, 26 pages.
source.module: Section 3 Jarzynski's equality for Markov chains
source.excerpt: Theorem 1 (Jarzynski's equality for Markov chains). If X = (Xn)Nn=0 is a Markov chain on a finite state space S whose initial distribution p0 has non-zero entries and whose transition matrices (Mn)Nn=1 are irreducible, then we have, for any family of energies E = (En)Nn=0 of X, ⟨e−β(W(X)−∆F)⟩ = 1, (10) where W = WX,E and ∆F = ∆FX,E.
source.attribution: © Pedro Hack, Sebastian Gottwald, Daniel A. Braun. Quoted from the arXiv preprint for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source defines the work (4), the energies and the free energies in Section 2.1 on pp. 5-6, with E_0 an energy function of the initial law p_0. The source assumes irreducible transition matrices. The authored statement assumes only a stationary distribution with positive entries for each M_n, which irreducibility gives, because the proof uses nothing more. The source proves the equality with an auxiliary reversed chain on pp. 8-9. The authored proof uses an induction on the weighted occupation E[e^(−βW_n); X_n = x], which rests on the same cancellation. The inequality E[W] ≥ ΔF is (22) on p. 17 of the source. The title of the source prints 'Jarzyski'.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the proof of Theorem 1 in Hack, Gottwald and Braun (arXiv:2202.05576). No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement, for any finite state space, any β > 0 and any protocol of energies whose Boltzmann laws are stationary for the corresponding transition matrices.

steps.text: Existence of the energies. If M_n is irreducible, it is a nonnegative irreducible matrix with column sums 1, so the all-ones row vector is a positive left eigenvector for the eigenvalue 1. By the Perron–Frobenius theorem the only eigenvalue with a positive eigenvector is the spectral radius, which is therefore 1, and its right eigenvector is positive and unique up to a factor. Normalizing gives the unique stationary distribution p_n, and its entries are positive. For any positive p_n, E_n = −β⁻¹ log p_n is an energy function with Z_n = 1. Any other energy function differs from it by a constant.

Partial work and the base case. Let W_0 = 0 and W_n = Σ_{k=0}^{n−1} (E_{k+1}(X_k) − E_k(X_k)) for 1 ≤ n ≤ N, so W_N = W. W_n is a function of X_0, …, X_{n−1}. Define ρ_n(x) = E[e^(−βW_n) 1{X_n = x}] for x ∈ S. Since S is finite, all these expectations are finite sums. At n = 0, ρ_0(x) = P(X_0 = x) = p_0(x) = e^(−βE_0(x))/Z_0.

One-step recursion. W_{n+1} = W_n + E_{n+1}(X_n) − E_n(X_n) is a function of X_0, …, X_n. By the Markov property, P(X_{n+1} = y | X_0, …, X_n) = (M_{n+1})_{y X_n}. The tower property, conditioning on X_0, …, X_n, gives ρ_{n+1}(y) = E[e^(−βW_n) e^(−β(E_{n+1}(X_n) − E_n(X_n))) (M_{n+1})_{y X_n}] = Σ_{x∈S} ρ_n(x) e^(−β(E_{n+1}(x) − E_n(x))) (M_{n+1})_{yx}.

Induction. Assume ρ_n(x) = e^(−βE_n(x))/Z_0 for all x. Then the factor e^(−βE_n(x)) cancels in step s3, and ρ_{n+1}(y) = Z_0⁻¹ Σ_x e^(−βE_{n+1}(x)) (M_{n+1})_{yx} = (Z_{n+1}/Z_0) Σ_x (M_{n+1})_{yx} p_{n+1}(x). Since p_{n+1} is stationary for M_{n+1}, the last sum is p_{n+1}(y). So ρ_{n+1}(y) = (Z_{n+1}/Z_0) p_{n+1}(y) = e^(−βE_{n+1}(y))/Z_0. By induction from step s2, ρ_n = e^(−βE_n)/Z_0 for every n = 0, …, N.

The equality. Sum ρ_N over S: E[e^(−βW)] = Σ_x ρ_N(x) = Σ_x e^(−βE_N(x))/Z_0 = Z_N/Z_0. Since F_n = −β⁻¹ log Z_n, Z_N/Z_0 = e^(−β(F_N − F_0)) = e^(−βΔF). Multiplying by the constant e^(βΔF) gives E[e^(−β(W − ΔF))] = 1.

The second law. W takes finitely many values, so E[W] is finite. The function t ↦ e^(−βt) is convex, and Jensen's inequality gives e^(−β(E[W] − ΔF)) ≤ E[e^(−β(W − ΔF))] = 1. Since β > 0, taking logarithms gives −β(E[W] − ΔF) ≤ 0, that is, E[W] ≥ ΔF.

applications.title: A two-level atom with a ramped excitation energy
applications.inputs: A two-level atom with states S = {0, 1} at β = 1. The excited level has energy a_n, and the protocol is a_0 = 0, a_1 = log 2, a_2 = log 4, so E_n(0) = 0 and E_n(1) = a_n, with N = 2. The atom starts in equilibrium, p_0 = (1/2, 1/2). Between changes it relaxes partly: M_n = (1/2) I + (1/2) p_n 1ᵀ, where p_n is the Boltzmann law of E_n.
applications.hypotheses: S is finite and β = 1 > 0. p_0 = (1/2, 1/2) has positive entries and is the Boltzmann law of E_0 = 0. Each M_n has positive entries, so it is irreducible, and M_n p_n = (1/2) p_n + (1/2) p_n = p_n, so p_n is its stationary distribution. Here p_1 = (2/3, 1/3) and p_2 = (4/5, 1/5), and E_n is an energy function of p_n.

steps.text: The partition functions are Z_0 = 2, Z_1 = 1 + 1/2 = 3/2 and Z_2 = 1 + 1/4 = 5/4. So the theorem predicts E[e^(−W)] = e^(−ΔF) = Z_2/Z_0 = 5/8.

Each change of the energy raises the excited level by log 2, so W = log 2 · (X_0 + X_1) and e^(−W) = 2^(−(X_0 + X_1)). From M_1 = (1/2) I + (1/2) p_1 1ᵀ, P(X_1 = 1 | X_0 = 0) = (1/2)(1/3) = 1/6 and P(X_1 = 1 | X_0 = 1) = 1/2 + (1/2)(1/3) = 2/3.

The mean work is E[W] = log 2 · (P(X_0 = 1) + P(X_1 = 1)) = log 2 · (1/2 + 5/12) = (11/12) log 2 ≈ 0.635, because P(X_1 = 1) = (1/2)(1/6) + (1/2)(2/3) = 5/12. The free energy change is ΔF = log(8/5) ≈ 0.470, so E[W] ≥ ΔF holds with a dissipated work of about 0.165.

applications.conclusion: For this protocol E[e^(−W)] = 5/8 = e^(−ΔF), although the atom is never in equilibrium with the current energy after the first change. The mean work (11/12) log 2 is larger than ΔF = log(8/5), as the second law requires.

limitations: The equality needs the initial law to be the Boltzmann law of E_0. If the system does not start in equilibrium, it fails in general.
The average of e^(−βW) is dominated by rare trajectories with small work, so estimates of ΔF from few samples can have a large bias.
Crooks' fluctuation theorem gives the full ratio of forward and reverse work distributions under detailed balance, and it implies this equality.

results.name: Lebowitz–Spohn fluctuation symmetry
aliases: Gallavotti–Cohen symmetry for Markov jump processes
fluctuation relation for the action functional of a Markov chain
results.statement: Let (X_t)_{t≥0} be an irreducible continuous-time Markov chain on a finite set S with at least two states and jump rates k(σ, σ′) ≥ 0 for σ ≠ σ′, such that k(σ, σ′) > 0 if and only if k(σ′, σ) > 0. Split the rates as k = Σ_{i=1}^m k^(i), with k^(i)(σ, σ′) ≥ 0 and k^(i)(σ, σ′) > 0 if and only if k^(i)(σ′, σ) > 0, and let a jump from σ to σ′ carry the label i with rate k^(i)(σ, σ′). Let W^(i)(t) be the sum of w^(i)(σ, σ′) = log(k^(i)(σ, σ′)/k^(i)(σ′, σ)) over the jumps σ → σ′ with label i up to time t. For λ ∈ ℝ^m let L_λ be the S × S matrix with off-diagonal entries L_λ(σ, σ′) = Σ_{i: k^(i)(σ,σ′)>0} k^(i)(σ, σ′)^(1−λ_i) k^(i)(σ′, σ)^(λ_i) and diagonal entries −r(σ) = −Σ_{σ′≠σ} k(σ, σ′). Then for every initial law ν and every λ ∈ ℝ^m: (a) the limit e(λ) = −lim_{t→∞} t⁻¹ log E_ν exp(−Σ_i λ_i W^(i)(t)) exists, is finite and does not depend on ν, and −e(λ) is the largest real eigenvalue of L_λ. (b) e(λ_1, …, λ_m) = e(1 − λ_1, …, 1 − λ_m). (c) The Legendre transform I(z) = sup_{λ∈ℝ^m} (e(λ) − ⟨λ, z⟩) satisfies I(−z) = I(z) + Σ_i z_i for every z ∈ ℝ^m. (d) Under P_ν, W(t)/t = (W^(1)(t), …, W^(m)(t))/t satisfies the large deviation principle as t → ∞ with speed t and the good rate function I. For m = 1, W(t) is the Lebowitz–Spohn action functional, and (c) is the Gallavotti–Cohen symmetry of its rate function.
hypotheses: (X_t) is an irreducible continuous-time Markov chain on a finite set S with at least two states.
The jump rates satisfy k(σ, σ′) > 0 if and only if k(σ′, σ) > 0.
The rates split as k = Σ_i k^(i) with k^(i) ≥ 0, and k^(i)(σ, σ′) > 0 if and only if k^(i)(σ′, σ) > 0 for each i.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 uses the Dyson formula (the time-ordered expansion of e^(t(A+B)) in powers of B) to identify the path expansion with e^(tL_λ).
Step s1 uses the monotone convergence theorem to sum the nonnegative contributions of the paths with n jumps over all n.
Steps s2 and s4 use the Perron–Frobenius theorem for the irreducible nonnegative matrix L_λ + aI: a simple dominant eigenvalue with a positive eigenvector.
Step s6 uses the implicit function theorem at the simple Perron root to show that e is differentiable in λ.
Step s7 applies the Gärtner–Ellis theorem to W(t)/t, whose scaled cumulant generating function −e(−λ) is finite and differentiable.

definitions.name: action functional
definitions.text: W(t) = Σ over the jumps σ → σ′ up to time t of log(k(σ, σ′)/k(σ′, σ)). It compares the probability of a path with the probability of its time reversal, and in physical models it is the entropy production in units of k_B.

definitions.name: tilted generator
definitions.text: L_λ is the generator L in which each rate k^(i)(σ, σ′) is multiplied by e^(−λ_i w^(i)(σ, σ′)). This gives k^(i)(σ, σ′)^(1−λ_i) k^(i)(σ′, σ)^(λ_i). L_λ is not a Markov generator when λ ≠ 0, because its rows need not sum to 0.

definitions.name: scaled cumulant generating function
definitions.text: Λ(λ) = lim t⁻¹ log E e^(⟨λ, W(t)⟩). Here Λ(λ) = −e(−λ).

source.citation: Alessandra Faggionato, Daniele Di Pietro, Gallavotti–Cohen-type symmetry related to cycle decompositions for Markov chains and biochemical applications, Journal of Statistical Physics 143 (2011) 11–32.
source.revision: arXiv:1009.4550v2 [math-ph], 21 Feb 2011, 23 pages.
source.module: Section 2 Fluctuation Theorem for sums of Markov generators
source.excerpt: Theorem 2.1. Given a distribution ν on S, for each λ1, . . . , λm ∈ R the limit e(λ1, . . . , λm) := lim_{t→∞} −(1/t) ln Eν[e^{−Σ_{i=1}^m λi W^(i)(t)}] (2.5) exists, is finite and does not depend on ν. Moreover, the following fluctuation relation is valid: e(λ1, . . . , λm) = e(1 − λ1, . . . , 1 − λm). (2.6)
source.attribution: © Alessandra Faggionato and Daniele Di Pietro. Quoted from the arXiv preprint of the article for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: Parts (a) and (b) are Theorem 2.1 of the source, which extends Section 2.3 of Lebowitz and Spohn (J. Stat. Phys. 95, 1999) and gives its own proof in Section 5.1, pp. 17-19. The source states (c) as (2.7) and (d) on p. 6 with references to the theory of large deviations. The authored proof gives both. The source obtains the formula E_ν e^(−⟨λ, W(t)⟩) = (ν, e^(tL_λ) 1) from a differential equation for t ↦ E_σ e^(−⟨λ, W(t)⟩). Step s1 obtains it from the path expansion instead. The limit, the Perron–Frobenius bounds and the transpose identity follow the source.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement for finite state spaces, every splitting of the rates and every initial law.

steps.text: Path expansion. Irreducibility with |S| ≥ 2 gives r(σ) > 0. Started at σ, the chain stays at σ for an exponential time with rate r(σ) and then jumps to σ′ with label i with probability k^(i)(σ, σ′)/r(σ). So the paths with exactly n jumps up to time t, through σ_0 = σ, σ_1, …, σ_n with labels i_1, …, i_n at times s_1 < … < s_n, have the density Π_j [e^(−r(σ_{j−1})(s_j − s_{j−1})) k^(i_j)(σ_{j−1}, σ_j)] · e^(−r(σ_n)(t − s_n)), with s_0 = 0. The weight e^(−λ_i w^(i)(σ, σ′)) turns k^(i)(σ, σ′) into k^(i)(σ, σ′)^(1−λ_i) k^(i)(σ′, σ)^(λ_i), and the sum over labels gives K_λ(σ, σ′), the off-diagonal part of L_λ. With R = diag(r), the n-jump term of E_σ[e^(−⟨λ, W(t)⟩); X_t = σ′] is ∫_{0<s_1<…<s_n<t} (e^(−s_1R) K_λ e^(−(s_2−s_1)R) ⋯ K_λ e^(−(t−s_n)R))(σ, σ′) ds. The number of jumps up to time t is finite almost surely, and all terms are nonnegative. So monotone convergence and the Dyson formula for e^(t(−R + K_λ)) give E_ν e^(−⟨λ, W(t)⟩) = (ν, e^(tL_λ) 1), where 1 is the all-ones vector.

The Perron eigenvector. The off-diagonal entries of L_λ are nonnegative, and L_λ(σ, σ′) > 0 exactly when k(σ, σ′) > 0, by the positivity relations. Take a ≥ max_σ r(σ). Then M = L_λ + aI is a nonnegative matrix, and it is irreducible because the chain is irreducible. By the Perron–Frobenius theorem its spectral radius ρ is an algebraically simple eigenvalue with an eigenvector v whose entries are all positive. Every real eigenvalue μ of M satisfies μ ≤ |μ| ≤ ρ. Put −e(λ) = ρ − a. Then L_λ v = −e(λ) v, and −e(λ) is the largest real eigenvalue of L_λ.

Part (a). e^(tL_λ) = e^(−ta) e^(tM) has nonnegative entries, and e^(tL_λ) v = e^(−te(λ)) v. With v_min = min v and v_max = max v, the vectors satisfy v/v_max ≤ 1 ≤ v/v_min entrywise. So v_max⁻¹ e^(−te(λ)) (ν, v) ≤ (ν, e^(tL_λ) 1) ≤ v_min⁻¹ e^(−te(λ)) (ν, v). Since (ν, v) > 0, taking −t⁻¹ log and t → ∞ gives the limit e(λ) for every initial law ν.

Part (b). For σ ≠ σ′, L_{1−λ}(σ′, σ) = Σ_i k^(i)(σ′, σ)^(λ_i) k^(i)(σ, σ′)^(1−λ_i) = L_λ(σ, σ′), where the sums run over the same labels by the positivity relation for k^(i). The diagonals are both −r. So the transpose of L_{1−λ} is L_λ. A matrix and its transpose have the same eigenvalues, so they have the same largest real eigenvalue, and step s2 gives e(1 − λ) = e(λ).

Part (c). Substitute λ = 1 − µ, where 1 is the vector with all entries 1: I(−z) = sup_λ (e(λ) + ⟨λ, z⟩) = sup_µ (e(1 − µ) + ⟨1 − µ, z⟩) = sup_µ (e(µ) − ⟨µ, z⟩) + Σ_i z_i = I(z) + Σ_i z_i. The middle equality uses part (b). The identity holds in (−∞, ∞].

Differentiability. The entries of L_λ are k^(i)(σ, σ′) e^(λ_i log(k^(i)(σ′, σ)/k^(i)(σ, σ′))), which are smooth in λ, so the characteristic polynomial p(λ, x) = det(xI − L_λ) has smooth coefficients. At λ_0 the root x_0 = −e(λ_0) is simple by step s2, so ∂p/∂x ≠ 0 there, and the implicit function theorem gives a smooth root x(λ) near λ_0. The other eigenvalues of L_{λ_0} have real parts smaller than x_0. Eigenvalues depend continuously on λ, so for λ near λ_0 exactly one eigenvalue lies near x_0, it is real, and it is the largest real eigenvalue. Hence −e(λ) = x(λ) near λ_0, and e is differentiable on ℝ^m.

Part (d). By part (a), Λ(λ) = lim t⁻¹ log E_ν e^(⟨λ, W(t)⟩) = −e(−λ) exists and is finite for every λ, and by step s6 it is differentiable. So Λ is continuous and essentially smooth with domain ℝ^m. The Gärtner–Ellis theorem, whose proof is unchanged when the speed N is replaced by a sequence t_n → ∞, gives along every such sequence the large deviation principle for W(t_n)/t_n with the good rate function Λ*(z) = sup_λ (⟨λ, z⟩ + e(−λ)) = I(z). If a bound failed as t → ∞, it would fail along some sequence t_n → ∞, so the bounds hold as t → ∞.

applications.title: Entropy production of a driven three-state ring
applications.inputs: A molecular motor with three states 0, 1, 2 on a ring. It steps forward σ → σ + 1 (mod 3) with rate 2 and backward σ → σ − 1 with rate 1. Take m = 1. Each forward jump adds w = log 2 to W(t) and each backward jump adds −log 2, so W(t) = (log 2)(N₊(t) − N₋(t)), where N₊ and N₋ count the forward and backward jumps. The test value is z = (7/2) log 2, a net current of 7/2 steps per unit time.
applications.hypotheses: S is finite with three states. All rates are positive, so the chain is irreducible, and each rate has a positive reverse rate. With m = 1 the splitting is k^(1) = k.

steps.text: L_λ has diagonal −3, forward entries 2^(1−λ)·1^λ = 2^(1−λ) and backward entries 1^(1−λ)·2^λ = 2^λ. Its rows have the same sum, so the all-ones vector is a positive eigenvector with eigenvalue 2^(1−λ) + 2^λ − 3. By Perron–Frobenius it is the Perron eigenvalue, so e(λ) = 3 − 2^(1−λ) − 2^λ. The formula is unchanged under λ ↦ 1 − λ, as part (b) states.
At λ = −1 and at its mirror λ = 2: e(−1) = 3 − 4 − 1/2 = −3/2 and e(2) = 3 − 1/2 − 4 = −3/2. The mean of W(t)/t is e′(0) = (log 2)(2 − 1) = log 2, the entropy produced per unit time.

e″(λ) = −(log 2)²(2^(1−λ) + 2^λ) < 0, so e is concave and the supremum in I(z) is at e′(λ) = z, that is, (log 2)(2^(1−λ) − 2^λ) = z. For z = (7/2) log 2 this holds at λ = −1, because 4 − 1/2 = 7/2. So I(z) = e(−1) + z = (7/2) log 2 − 3/2 ≈ 0.926.
For −z the condition holds at λ = 2, because 1/2 − 4 = −7/2. So I(−z) = e(2) + 2z = 7 log 2 − 3/2 ≈ 3.352. Then I(−z) − I(z) = (7/2) log 2 = z, which is part (c) with m = 1.

applications.conclusion: On the exponential scale, P(W(t)/t ≈ −(7/2) log 2) / P(W(t)/t ≈ (7/2) log 2) ≈ e^(−t(I(−z) − I(z))) = 2^(−7t/2). A net backward current of 7/2 steps per unit time is less probable than the same forward current by the factor 2^(−7t/2), and this ratio does not depend on the details of the rate function.

limitations: The theorem needs a finite state space and the positivity relation for each pair of reverse jumps. With an unbounded state space or with unbounded weights, the symmetry can fail for some currents and needs extra conditions.
The symmetry (c) fixes only the odd part of the rate function. The rate function itself depends on the model and is usually known only through the Perron eigenvalue.

results.name: Kolmogorov's criterion for reversibility
results.statement: Let S be a countable set and let p be an irreducible transition probability on S. A reversible measure is a function μ: S → [0, ∞), not identically zero, with μ(x)p(x, y) = μ(y)p(y, x) for all x, y ∈ S. A reversible measure exists if and only if (i) p(x, y) > 0 implies p(y, x) > 0, and (ii) every loop x₀, x₁, …, x_n = x₀ with p(x_i, x_{i−1}) > 0 for 1 ≤ i ≤ n satisfies ∏_{i=1}^n p(x_{i−1}, x_i) = ∏_{i=1}^n p(x_i, x_{i−1}). In that case the reversible measure is positive everywhere and unique up to a constant factor. If its total mass is finite, its normalization π is a stationary distribution that satisfies detailed balance.
hypotheses: The state space S is countable and p is a transition probability on S.
p is irreducible: for all x, y ∈ S there is n ≥ 1 with p^n(x, y) > 0.

prerequisites.reason: Steps s1 and s3 expand p^n(x, y) > 0 as a sum over paths and so obtain a path with positive one-step probabilities.

definitions.name: reversible measure
definitions.text: A function μ: S → [0, ∞), not identically zero, that satisfies the detailed balance equations μ(x)p(x, y) = μ(y)p(y, x) for all x, y.

definitions.name: loop
definitions.text: A finite sequence of states x₀, x₁, …, x_n with x_n = x₀. The cycle condition compares the probability of going around it forward with the probability of going around it backward.

source.citation: Rick Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, fifth edition, Cambridge University Press, 2019.
source.revision: Author's online version 5 of January 11, 2019 (PDF created 2019-03-29), 490 pages.
source.module: Chapter 5, Section 5.5 Stationary Measures
source.excerpt: Theorem 5.5.6. Kolmogorov’s cycle condition. Suppose p is irreducible. A necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of a reversible measure is that (i) p(x, y) > 0 implies p(y, x) > 0, and (ii) for any loop x0, x1, . . . , xn = x0 with ∏_{1≤i≤n} p(xi, xi−1) > 0, ∏_{i=1}^{n} p(xi−1, xi)/p(xi, xi−1) = 1.
source.attribution: © Rick Durrett. Quoted from Probability: Theory and Examples, fifth edition, for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states Theorem 5.5.6 for an irreducible chain on a countable set, with the same conditions (i) and (ii), and writes (ii) as a product of ratios equal to 1. The authored statement adds positivity and uniqueness of the reversible measure and the normalized case. The authored proof follows the proof of Theorem 5.5.6 and makes explicit why the definition by path weights does not depend on the path.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the proof of Theorem 5.5.6 in Durrett. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement: both directions of the criterion, positivity and uniqueness of the reversible measure, and the normalized case.

steps.text: Positivity and uniqueness. By the Chapman–Kolmogorov equation, p^n(x, y) is a sum over paths of products of one-step probabilities. So irreducibility gives, for all x and y, a path x = y₀, …, y_n = y with p(y_{j−1}, y_j) > 0 for each j. Let μ be reversible. If μ(u) > 0 and p(u, v) > 0, then μ(v)p(v, u) = μ(u)p(u, v) > 0, so μ(v) > 0 and p(v, u) > 0. Some state has μ > 0, and induction along paths from it gives μ > 0 everywhere. If ν is also reversible and p(u, v) > 0, then ν(v)/ν(u) = p(u, v)/p(v, u) = μ(v)/μ(u). So ν/μ is constant along each step of positive probability, and paths connect all states. Hence ν = cμ for a constant c > 0.

Necessity. Let μ be reversible. Step s1 shows that p(x, y) > 0 implies p(y, x) > 0, which is (i). Take a loop with p(x_i, x_{i−1}) > 0 for each i. By (i), also p(x_{i−1}, x_i) > 0. Because μ > 0, detailed balance gives p(x_{i−1}, x_i)/p(x_i, x_{i−1}) = μ(x_i)/μ(x_{i−1}) for each i. The product over i telescopes to μ(x_n)/μ(x₀) = 1, which is (ii).

Path weights. Assume (i) and (ii). Call a path admissible when each step x_{i−1} → x_i has p(x_{i−1}, x_i) > 0. By (i), each backward step also has positive probability, so the reversed path is admissible and (ii) applies to every admissible loop. Define the weight w(γ) = ∏_i p(x_{i−1}, x_i)/p(x_i, x_{i−1}) ∈ (0, ∞). The weight of a concatenation is the product of the weights, and the reversed path has weight 1/w(γ). Fix a ∈ S. Irreducibility gives an admissible path from a to every x. If γ and γ′ are admissible paths from a to x, then γ followed by the reverse of γ′ is an admissible loop, so (ii) gives w(γ)/w(γ′) = 1. So μ(x) = w(γ) does not depend on γ, and μ(x) ∈ (0, ∞).

Detailed balance. Let x, y ∈ S with p(x, y) > 0. Append the step x → y to an admissible path γ from a to x. The new path is admissible, ends at y and has weight w(γ)p(x, y)/p(y, x). By step s3, μ(y) = μ(x)p(x, y)/p(y, x), that is μ(x)p(x, y) = μ(y)p(y, x). If p(x, y) = 0, then p(y, x) = 0 too, because p(y, x) > 0 would give p(x, y) > 0 by (i). Then both sides are 0. So μ is a reversible measure.

Normalization. Suppose Z = ∑_x μ(x) < ∞ and set π = μ/Z. Sum the detailed balance equations over x: ∑_x π(x)p(x, y) = π(y) ∑_x p(y, x) = π(y). So π is a stationary distribution that satisfies detailed balance. By step s1 it is the only normalized reversible measure.

applications.title: A driven particle on a ring has no reversible measure
applications.inputs: A particle hops on a ring of 3 sites 0, 1, 2 under a constant driving force. At each step it moves one site clockwise with probability 2/3 and one site counterclockwise with probability 1/3. So p(0, 1) = p(1, 2) = p(2, 0) = 2/3 and p(1, 0) = p(2, 1) = p(0, 2) = 1/3.
applications.hypotheses: The state space is finite, so it is countable. The chain is irreducible because 0 → 1 → 2 → 0 has positive probabilities. Condition (i) holds because every step and its reverse have positive probability.

steps.text: Take the loop 0 → 1 → 2 → 0. The forward product is p(0, 1)p(1, 2)p(2, 0) = (2/3)³ = 8/27. The backward product is p(1, 0)p(2, 1)p(0, 2) = (1/3)³ = 1/27.
The ratio of the two products is 8, not 1. So condition (ii) fails, and by the criterion the chain has no reversible measure.
Each column of p sums to 2/3 + 1/3 = 1, so p is doubly stochastic and the uniform law π = (1/3, 1/3, 1/3) is stationary. A stationary distribution exists, but it does not satisfy detailed balance.
The net probability current from 0 to 1 is J = π(0)p(0, 1) − π(1)p(1, 0) = 2/9 − 1/9 = 1/9. A reversible chain has J = 0 on every edge.

With no force, both hop probabilities equal 1/2. Then the loop ratio is 1, and the uniform measure satisfies detailed balance. The logarithm of the loop ratio, log 8 = 3 log 2, measures the entropy produced in one turn around the ring.

applications.conclusion: The driven ring has the uniform stationary law but no reversible measure, because its loop ratio is 8 and not 1. It is a nonequilibrium steady state with a probability current of 1/9 per step around the ring.

limitations: Condition (ii) must hold for every loop. On a large state space a direct check is not practical, and one usually guesses μ and checks detailed balance instead.
A reversible measure can have infinite total mass. For example, simple symmetric random walk on ℤ has the reversible measure μ ≡ 1 and no stationary distribution.

results.name: Reversibility of the Metropolis–Hastings chain
results.statement: Let X be a countable set, let π be a probability distribution on X with π(x) > 0 for every x, and let Ψ be a transition matrix on X. For x ≠ y with Ψ(x, y) > 0 put a(x, y) = min{1, π(y)Ψ(y, x)/(π(x)Ψ(x, y))}, and put a(x, y) = 0 when Ψ(x, y) = 0. Define P(x, y) = Ψ(x, y)a(x, y) for y ≠ x and P(x, x) = 1 − ∑_{z≠x} P(x, z). Then P is a transition matrix and π(x)P(x, y) = π(y)P(y, x) for all x, y ∈ X. Hence π is a stationary distribution of P, and the chain started from π has the same law forward and backward in time. If Ψ is irreducible and Ψ(x, y) > 0 exactly when Ψ(y, x) > 0, then P is irreducible.
hypotheses: The state space X is countable and the target π is a probability distribution with π(x) > 0 for every x ∈ X.
The proposal Ψ is a transition matrix on X.
For the irreducibility claim only: Ψ is irreducible and Ψ(x, y) > 0 exactly when Ψ(y, x) > 0.
results.empty_prerequisites_reason: The proof is a direct computation with the definition of P. It uses no named result.

definitions.name: Metropolis–Hastings chain
definitions.text: From state x, propose y with probability Ψ(x, y). Accept the move with probability a(x, y). Otherwise stay at x.

definitions.name: detailed balance
definitions.text: The equations π(x)P(x, y) = π(y)P(y, x) for all states x and y. In equilibrium, the flow of probability from x to y equals the flow from y to x.

source.citation: David A. Levin and Yuval Peres, with contributions by Elizabeth L. Wilmer, Markov Chains and Mixing Times, second edition, American Mathematical Society, 2017.
source.revision: Second edition, authors' online version (PDF created 2017-03-21), 461 pages.
source.module: Chapter 3, Exercises (the chain is defined in Section 3.2.2 General base chain, (3.5), p. 41)
source.excerpt: Exercise 3.1. Let Ψ be an irreducible transition matrix on X, and let π be a probability distribution on X. Show that the transition matrix P(x, y) = Ψ(x, y)[π(y)Ψ(y, x)/(π(x)Ψ(x, y)) ∧ 1] if y ≠ x, 1 − ∑_{z: z≠x} Ψ(x, z)[π(z)Ψ(z, x)/(π(x)Ψ(x, z)) ∧ 1] if y = x defines a reversible Markov chain with stationary distribution π.
source.attribution: © David A. Levin and Yuval Peres. Quoted from Markov Chains and Mixing Times, second edition, for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source poses the result as an exercise for a finite state space and leaves implicit that π > 0 and the convention a(x, y) = 0 when Ψ(x, y) = 0. The authored statement makes these explicit, allows a countable state space, adds the reversal of the path law, and adds a condition under which P is irreducible. The source gives no proof. The authored proof is the standard computation of π(x)P(x, y) as a minimum that is symmetric in x and y.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the standard detailed balance computation for the chain (3.5) of Levin and Peres. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement: P is stochastic, detailed balance, stationarity, reversal of the path law, and irreducibility under the extra condition.

steps.text: P is a transition matrix. For y ≠ x, 0 ≤ a(x, y) ≤ 1, so 0 ≤ P(x, y) ≤ Ψ(x, y). Hence ∑_{z≠x} P(x, z) ≤ ∑_{z≠x} Ψ(x, z) ≤ 1, which gives 0 ≤ P(x, x) ≤ 1. Each row of P sums to 1 by the definition of P(x, x).

The flow identity. For x ≠ y, π(x)P(x, y) = min{π(x)Ψ(x, y), π(y)Ψ(y, x)}. If Ψ(x, y) > 0, then c = π(x)Ψ(x, y) is positive and c · min{1, b/c} = min{c, b} with b = π(y)Ψ(y, x) ≥ 0. If Ψ(x, y) = 0, then the left side is 0 by the convention a(x, y) = 0, and the right side is min{0, b} = 0.

Detailed balance. The right side of the flow identity does not change when x and y are exchanged. So π(x)P(x, y) = π(y)P(y, x) for x ≠ y. For x = y the equation is trivial. Summing over x ∈ X, which is allowed because all terms are nonnegative, gives ∑_x π(x)P(x, y) = π(y) ∑_x P(y, x) = π(y). So πP = π.

Reversal of the path law. Start the chain from π. For states x₀, …, x_n, P(X₀ = x₀, …, X_n = x_n) = π(x₀)P(x₀, x₁)⋯P(x_{n−1}, x_n). Apply detailed balance to the first factor pair, π(x₀)P(x₀, x₁) = π(x₁)P(x₁, x₀), then to π(x₁)P(x₁, x₂), and so on n times. The result is π(x_n)P(x_n, x_{n−1})⋯P(x₁, x₀) = P(X₀ = x_n, …, X_n = x₀). So (X₀, …, X_n) and (X_n, …, X₀) have the same law.

Irreducibility. Assume that Ψ is irreducible and that Ψ(x, y) > 0 exactly when Ψ(y, x) > 0. For x ≠ y with Ψ(x, y) > 0, also π(y)Ψ(y, x) > 0, so a(x, y) > 0 and P(x, y) > 0. Irreducibility of Ψ gives, for any x and y, a path with Ψ-positive steps from x to y. We may delete steps that stay in place, so each step has P-positive probability, and P is irreducible.

applications.title: Metropolis–Hastings sampling of a three-level system
applications.inputs: A system has three levels 0, 1, 2 with energies 0, ε and 2ε, at inverse temperature β with e^(−βε) = 1/2. The Boltzmann law is π ∝ (1, 1/2, 1/4), so π = (4/7, 2/7, 1/7). The proposal is the reflecting walk Ψ(0, 1) = 1, Ψ(1, 0) = Ψ(1, 2) = 1/2, Ψ(2, 1) = 1. It is not symmetric.
applications.hypotheses: The state space is finite and π > 0 everywhere. Ψ is a transition matrix. Ψ is irreducible and Ψ(x, y) > 0 exactly when Ψ(y, x) > 0, so the irreducibility claim also applies.

steps.text: Detailed balance on the edge {1, 2}: π(1)P(1, 2) = (2/7)(1/2) = 1/7 = π(2)P(2, 1). Stationarity at level 0 follows: π(0)P(0, 0) + π(1)P(1, 0) = 3/7 + 1/7 = 4/7 = π(0).

The Hastings factor Ψ(y, x)/Ψ(x, y) is necessary here. The plain Metropolis rule min{1, π(y)/π(x)} gives P(0, 1) = P(1, 0) = 1/2, P(1, 2) = 1/4 and P(2, 1) = 1. This birth-death chain has stationary law ∝ (1, 1, 1/4) = (4/9, 4/9, 1/9), which is not the Boltzmann law.

applications.conclusion: The Metropolis–Hastings chain with the asymmetric reflecting proposal satisfies detailed balance with the Boltzmann law (4/7, 2/7, 1/7). It is irreducible, and P(0, 0) > 0 makes it aperiodic. Without the Hastings factor the chain samples the wrong law (4/9, 4/9, 1/9).

limitations: The theorem gives the correct stationary law but no rate of convergence. A poor proposal can make the chain mix very slowly.
Irreducibility of Ψ alone is not enough for irreducibility of P. If Ψ(x, y) > 0 but Ψ(y, x) = 0, the move x → y is always rejected.

results.name: Kipnis–Varadhan central limit theorem for reversible Markov processes
results.statement: Let (η_t)_{t≥0} be a Markov process on a state space Ω with semigroup P_t and generator L on L²(μ). Suppose that the process starts from an invariant probability measure μ that is reversible and ergodic. Let f ∈ L²(μ) satisfy ∫ f dμ = 0 and σ_f² = 2∫_0^∞ ⟨P_s f, f⟩_μ ds < ∞. Then t^(−1/2) ∫_0^t f(η_s) ds converges in distribution to the normal law N(0, σ_f²) as t → ∞. Moreover σ_f² = 2‖f‖²_{−1}, where ‖f‖²_{−1} = sup_ψ (2⟨f, ψ⟩_μ − ⟨ψ, −Lψ⟩_μ).
hypotheses: (η_t) is a Markov process started from an invariant probability measure μ, and each P_t is self-adjoint on L²(μ), so μ is reversible.
μ is ergodic for the process.
f ∈ L²(μ), ∫ f dμ = 0 and σ_f² = 2∫_0^∞ ⟨P_s f, f⟩_μ ds is finite.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 uses the spectral theorem for the nonnegative self-adjoint operator −L to write the Laplace transform of ⟨P_s f, f⟩_μ as ⟨f, (λ − L)^(−1) f⟩_μ.
Step s1 lets λ ↓ 0 in the Laplace transform of the nonnegative function s ↦ ⟨P_s f, f⟩_μ by monotone convergence.
Step s3 takes a weakly convergent subsequence of the bounded family u_λ in the Hilbert space H_1.
Step s6 adds a remainder that tends to 0 in probability to a sequence that converges in distribution.

definitions.name: additive functional
definitions.text: A_f(t) = ∫_0^t f(η_s) ds, the time integral of an observable f along the path of the process.

definitions.name: H_1 and H_{−1} norms
definitions.text: ‖ψ‖²_1 = ⟨ψ, −Lψ⟩_μ is the Dirichlet form. ‖f‖_{−1} = sup{⟨f, ψ⟩_μ / ‖ψ‖_1}, which equals the square root of lim_{λ↓0} ⟨f, (λ − L)^(−1) f⟩_μ.

definitions.name: asymptotic variance
definitions.text: σ_f² = lim_{t→∞} t^(−1) Var A_f(t) = 2∫_0^∞ ⟨P_s f, f⟩_μ ds under the stationary law.

source.excerpt: Theorem 9.3.1. Consider an L2(µ) Markov process ηt begun with ergodic, reversible invariant measure µ. Let f : Ω → R be an L2(µ) function such that σf² < ∞. Then, (1/√t) ∫_0^t f(ηs) ds ⇒ N(0, σf²).

The source takes f with mean zero, as in Section 9.2, and the authored statement writes this condition explicitly. The identity σ_f² = 2‖f‖²_{−1} is Lemma 9.3.4 of the source.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of Theorem 9.3.1 in Sethuraman's notes (arXiv:2608.20252), Section 9.3, pp. 83-88. Steps s1, s3, s5 and s6 take Lemma 9.3.4, Proposition 9.3.6 with Lemma 9.3.7, Proposition 9.3.2 and the martingale central limit theorem Proposition 9.1.1 from the source.

steps.text: Variance and the H_{−1} norm. By stationarity Var A_f(t) = 2∫_0^t (t − s)⟨P_s f, f⟩_μ ds (Section 9.2 of the source, p. 80). Reversibility gives ⟨P_s f, f⟩_μ = ‖P_{s/2} f‖² ≥ 0, so t^(−1) Var A_f(t) increases to σ_f². The spectral theorem gives ∫_0^∞ e^(−λs)⟨P_s f, f⟩_μ ds = ⟨f, (λ − L)^(−1) f⟩_μ = ‖f‖²_{−1,λ}, and monotone convergence as λ ↓ 0 gives σ_f² = 2‖f‖²_{−1}. Lemma 9.3.4 of the source (p. 85) records this identity, so the hypothesis σ_f² < ∞ means f ∈ H_{−1}.

Resolvent bounds. For λ > 0 let u_λ = (λ − L)^(−1) f = ∫_0^∞ e^(−λt) P_t f dt, so λu_λ − Lu_λ = f, which is (9.3.2) of the source. Pairing with u_λ gives λ‖u_λ‖²_{L²} + ‖u_λ‖²_1 = ⟨f, u_λ⟩_μ ≤ ‖f‖_{−1}‖u_λ‖_1. Section 9.3.2 of the source (p. 85) deduces ‖u_λ‖_1 ≤ ‖f‖_{−1} and λ‖u_λ‖²_{L²} ≤ ‖f‖²_{−1} uniformly in λ, and ‖Lu_λ‖_{−1} ≤ ‖u_λ‖_1.

Strong limit of the resolvent. Proposition 9.3.6 of the source (p. 85, proof pp. 87-88) proves λ‖u_λ‖²_{L²} → 0 and u_λ → w strongly in H_1 as λ ↓ 0, with ‖w‖²_1 = ⟨w, f⟩_μ. The proof takes a weakly convergent subsequence u_{λ_n} → w in H_1. Mazur's lemma (Lemma 9.3.7) gives convex combinations v_n → w strongly, and −Lv_n → f strongly in H_{−1}, so ‖w‖²_1 = ⟨w, f⟩_μ. Then ‖w‖²_1 ≤ lim inf (λ_n‖u_{λ_n}‖² + ‖u_{λ_n}‖²_1) = ⟨f, w⟩_μ = ‖w‖²_1 forces ‖u_{λ_n}‖_1 → ‖w‖_1. Two subsequential limits w and w′ satisfy ‖w − w′‖²_1 = lim ⟨u_{λ_n} − u_{λ′_n}, −λ_n u_{λ_n} + λ′_n u_{λ′_n}⟩_μ = 0.

Martingale decomposition. By Dynkin's formula M_λ(t) = u_λ(η_t) − u_λ(η_0) − ∫_0^t Lu_λ(η_s) ds is a martingale. Since Lu_λ = λu_λ − f, A_f(t) = M_λ(t) + ζ_λ(t) with ζ_λ(t) = λ∫_0^t u_λ(η_s) ds + u_λ(η_0) − u_λ(η_t). The source computes E_μ M_λ(t)² = 2t‖u_λ‖²_1 from stationary increments and (9.3.4), p. 86. Hence E_μ(M_λ(t) − M_θ(t))² = 2t‖u_λ − u_θ‖²_1 → 0 by step s3, and the L² limit M(t) is a martingale with stationary ergodic increments. Its variance is E_μ M(1)² = 2‖w‖²_1 = 2 lim ⟨u_λ, f⟩_μ = 2‖f‖²_{−1} = σ_f² by step s1.

The remainder is small. Put ζ(t) = A_f(t) − M(t) = ζ_λ(t) + M_λ(t) − M(t). Cauchy–Schwarz and stationarity give E_μ ζ_λ(t)² ≤ 3(λ²t² + 2)‖u_λ‖²_{L²}. With λ = 1/t this is t^(−1) E_μ ζ_λ(t)² ≤ 9λ‖u_λ‖²_{L²} → 0 by step s3. Also t^(−1) E_μ(M_λ(t) − M(t))² = 2‖u_λ − w‖²_1 → 0. So t^(−1) E_μ ζ(t)² → 0, which is Proposition 9.3.2 of the source (p. 83, proof pp. 86-87).

Central limit theorem. Write t^(−1/2) A_f(t) = t^(−1/2) M(t) + t^(−1/2) ζ(t). The second term tends to 0 in L²(P_μ) by step s5. The martingale central limit theorem for martingales with stationary ergodic increments, Proposition 9.1.1 of the source (p. 79), gives t^(−1/2) M(t) ⇒ N(0, E_μ M(1)²) = N(0, σ_f²). Slutsky's theorem then gives t^(−1/2) A_f(t) ⇒ N(0, σ_f²), as in Section 9.3.4 of the source (p. 87).

source.ref: S. Sethuraman, Notes on hydrodynamic limits and related topics, arXiv:2608.20252v1 (2026), Theorem 9.3.1, p. 83, with Proposition 9.3.2, Lemma 9.3.4, Proposition 9.3.6 and Lemma 9.3.7, pp. 83-88.

applications.title: Effective diffusion of a run-and-reverse swimmer
applications.inputs: A bacterium swims along a line at speed v and reverses its direction at rate γ. Its direction η_t ∈ {−1, +1} is a two-state Markov process with generator Lg(x) = γ(g(−x) − g(x)). Its position is X(t) = v∫_0^t η_s ds, so X(t) = v A_f(t) with f(x) = x. Take v = 20 μm/s and γ = 1 per second.
applications.hypotheses: The uniform law μ on {−1, +1} satisfies μ(+1)γ = μ(−1)γ, so it is invariant and reversible. The chain is irreducible on two points, so μ is ergodic. The function f(x) = x is bounded and has mean 0 under μ.

steps.text: Lf(x) = γ(−x − x) = −2γf(x), so P_s f = e^(−2γs) f and ⟨P_s f, f⟩_μ = e^(−2γs). The asymptotic variance is σ_f² = 2∫_0^∞ e^(−2γs) ds = 1/γ.
The H_{−1} route of the proof gives the same value. The resolvent is u_λ = f/(λ + 2γ), and it converges to w = f/(2γ), which solves −Lw = f. So σ_f² = 2⟨w, f⟩_μ = 2 · 1/(2γ) = 1/γ.
Here the martingale is M(t) = w(η_t) − w(η_0) + A_f(t), so the remainder ζ(t) = w(η_0) − w(η_t) is bounded by 2/(2γ) = 1/γ for all t. The theorem then gives A_f(t)/√t ⇒ N(0, 1/γ).

So X(t)/√t ⇒ N(0, v²/γ). A diffusion with coefficient D has variance 2Dt, so the swimmer has the effective diffusion coefficient D = v²/(2γ). With v = 20 μm/s and γ = 1 per second, D = 400/2 = 200 μm²/s.
A direct check of the variance: Var X(t) = 2v²∫_0^t (t − s)e^(−2γs) ds = (v²/γ)(t − (1 − e^(−2γt))/(2γ)). The ratio Var X(t)/t tends to v²/γ = 2D, as the theorem says.

applications.conclusion: On time scales much longer than 1/γ, the run-and-reverse swimmer behaves like a Brownian particle with diffusion coefficient v²/(2γ), which is 200 μm²/s for the given values.

limitations: The proof uses reversibility in an essential way. Section 9.4 of the source states that a central limit theorem under the symmetrized H_{−1} condition alone is open in the general nonreversible case.
The process starts from the invariant law μ, and the theorem gives no rate of convergence. Other starting laws need further arguments.

results.name: Hydrodynamic limit of the symmetric simple exclusion process
aliases: Heat equation limit of symmetric exclusion
results.statement: Let p be a symmetric probability on ℤ^d with finite range, and let C_{ij} = ∑_z z_i z_j p(z). For N ≥ 1 let (η_t) be the symmetric exclusion process on the discrete torus T_N^d = (ℤ/Nℤ)^d with generator Lf(η) = ½ ∑_{x,y} p(y)(f(η^{x,x+y}) − f(η)), where η^{x,x+y} exchanges the occupation variables at x and x + y. Let ρ_0 : T^d → [0, 1] be continuous and start the process from the product measure μ^N = ⊗_x Bern(ρ_0(x/N)). Let π^N_t = N^(−d) ∑_x η_t(x) δ_{x/N}. Then for every t ≥ 0 and every continuous G : T^d → ℝ, ⟨G, π^N_{N²t}⟩ converges in probability to ∫ G(u)ρ(t, u) du, where ρ is the unique bounded weak solution of ∂_t ρ = ½ ∑_{i,j} C_{ij} ∂_i ∂_j ρ with ρ(0, ·) = ρ_0.
hypotheses: The jump probability p on ℤ^d is symmetric, p(y) = p(−y), and has finite range R.
The process is the symmetric exclusion process on T_N^d, run on the diffusive time scale N²t.
The initial law is the product Bernoulli measure with a continuous profile ρ_0 : T^d → [0, 1].

prerequisites.reason: Steps s4 and s5 bound the supremum of the martingale M^N(G) over a time interval by its second moment at the end of the interval.
Step s2 expands the discrete second differences of the test function to second order.
Step s3 proves the law of large numbers for the initial empirical measure from its variance bound.
Step s6 uses that the Fourier coefficients of a bounded function on the torus determine the function.

definitions.name: symmetric exclusion process
definitions.text: Each particle on T_N^d waits an exponential time of rate 1, picks a displacement y with probability p(y) = p(−y), and jumps from x to x + y only if x + y is empty.

definitions.name: empirical measure
definitions.text: π^N_t = N^(−d) ∑_x η_t(x) δ_{x/N}, the measure on the continuous torus T^d = ℝ^d/ℤ^d with mass N^(−d) at x/N for each occupied site x.

definitions.name: weak solution
definitions.text: A bounded measurable ρ with ∫ G(t, u)ρ(t, u) du − ∫ G(0, u)ρ_0(u) du = ∫_0^t ∫ (∂_s + ½Δ_C)G(s, u) ρ(s, u) du ds for every G ∈ C^{1,2}([0, T] × T^d), where Δ_C = ∑_{i,j} C_{ij} ∂_i ∂_j.

source.citation: Sunder Sethuraman, Notes on hydrodynamic limits and related topics, arXiv:2608.20252v1 [math.PR], 2026.
source.revision: arXiv version 1, 20 August 2026, 133 pages.
source.module: Section 3 Proof of hydrodynamics for symmetric exclusion processes, Subsection 3.1 Statement of hydrodynamics
source.excerpt: Consider the symmetric exclusion process with finite-range translation-invariant jump probabilities. Then, starting from the local equilibrium measure µN, associated with continuous profile ρ0(·), the empirical measure π^N_{N²t} converges in probability to the measure ρ(t, u)du where ρ(t, u) satisfies the hydrodynamic equation
source.attribution: © Sunder Sethuraman. Quoted from Notes on Hydrodynamic Limits and Related Topics for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: Theorem 3.1.1 of the source states the limit for finite-range translation-invariant symmetric p, started from μ^N = ⊗_x Bern(ρ_0(x/N)) with continuous ρ_0, with the hydrodynamic equation (3.1.1) ∂_t ρ = ½Δ_C ρ. The authored statement writes the convergence of measures in probability as convergence of each pairing with a continuous G, which is the meaning in the source. It takes ρ_0 with values in [0, 1], which the Bernoulli marginals need. The source quotes the uniqueness of bounded weak solutions, and the authored step s6 adds a short Fourier proof of it.

results.proof_status: outline of the cited published proof. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of Theorem 3.1.1 in Sethuraman's notes (arXiv:2608.20252), Sections 2.3-2.4 and 3.1-3.4. Steps s1, s2, s4 and s6 take Proposition 2.3.2, the bound (2.4.1), the summation by parts of Section 2.4.1, Propositions 3.2.5 and 3.2.7, the estimate (3.3.1) and the Portmanteau argument of Section 3.4 from the source.

steps.text: Martingale. For G ∈ C^{1,2}([0, T] × T^d), Proposition 2.3.2 of the source makes M^N_t(G) = ⟨G_t, π^N_{N²t}⟩ − ⟨G_0, π^N_0⟩ − ∫_0^t (∂_s + N²L)⟨G_s, π^N_{N²s}⟩ ds a martingale. By (2.4.1) of the source, E(M^N_t(G))² = E ∫_0^{N²t} N^(−2d−2) ∑_{x,y} (∇^N_{x,x+y}G)² p(y) η_s(x)(1 − η_s(x + y)) ds, with ∇^N_{u,v}G = N(G(u/N) − G(v/N)). The occupation variables are at most 1 and p has finite range, so E(M^N_t(G))² = O(t N^(−d)).

Closed drift. For symmetric p, Section 2.4.1 of the source sums by parts twice and gets N²L⟨G, π^N⟩ = (2N^d)^(−1) ∑_{x,y} p(y) η(x) Δ^N_{x,y}G with Δ^N_{x,y}G = N²(G((x + y)/N) − 2G(x/N) + G((x − y)/N)). This drift is linear in η. Taylor's theorem gives ∑_y p(y)Δ^N_{x,y}G = Δ_C G(x/N) + o(1) uniformly in x. Hence ⟨G_t, π^N_{N²t}⟩ = ⟨G_0, π^N_0⟩ + ∫_0^t ⟨(∂_s + ½Δ_C)G_s, π^N_{N²s}⟩ ds + M^N_t(G) + o(1).

Initial law of large numbers. Under μ^N the variables η_0(x) are independent Bernoulli(ρ_0(x/N)). So E⟨G, π^N_0⟩ = N^(−d) ∑_x G(x/N)ρ_0(x/N) → ∫ Gρ_0 as a Riemann sum, and Var⟨G, π^N_0⟩ ≤ N^(−d)‖G‖²_∞. By Chebyshev's inequality, ⟨G, π^N_0⟩ → ∫ Gρ_0 in probability.

Tightness. Let Q^N be the law of (π^N_{N²t})_{t≤T} on D([0, T], M_+(T^d)). By Proposition 3.2.7 of the source, it is enough to check conditions (1) and (2′) of Proposition 3.2.5 for each real process ⟨G, π^N_{N²t}⟩ with G ∈ C²(T^d). Condition (1) holds because |⟨G, π^N⟩| ≤ ‖G‖_∞. In (2′) the drift changes by at most γR‖ΔG‖_∞ on a time interval of length γ. For the martingale, Section 3.3 of the source applies Doob's inequality on the intervals of a partition of mesh γ, which gives (3.3.1): P(sup_{|t−s|≤γ} |M^N_t − M^N_s| > λ) ≤ 9λ^(−2) ∑_k E|M^N_{l_{k+1}} − M^N_{l_k}|² = O(λ^(−2)TN^(−d)). So {Q^N} is tight in the uniform topology, and its limit points charge only continuous trajectories.

Identification. Let Q be a limit point. The functional sup_{t≤T} |⟨G_t, π_t⟩ − ⟨G_0, π_0⟩ − ∫_0^t ⟨(∂_s + ½Δ_C)G_s, π_s⟩ ds| is continuous at continuous trajectories. Under Q^N it equals sup_t |M^N_t(G)| + o(1), which tends to 0 in probability by steps s1 and s2 and Doob's inequality. With step s3, Q-almost surely ⟨G_t, π_t⟩ − ⟨G_0, ρ_0⟩ = ∫_0^t ⟨(∂_s + ½Δ_C)G_s, π_s⟩ ds, which is (3.1.2) of the source, for G in a countable dense set and then for all G.

Density and uniqueness. Each site holds at most one particle, so |⟨G, π^N_t⟩| ≤ N^(−d) ∑_x |G(x/N)| → ‖G‖_{L¹}. Section 3.4 of the source passes this bound to Q with the Portmanteau theorem, so π_t = ρ(t, u)du with 0 ≤ ρ ≤ 1. By step s5, ρ is a bounded weak solution. For k ∈ ℤ^d the test function G(s, u) = e^(−2π²(k·Ck)(t−s)) e^(2πik·u) has (∂_s + ½Δ_C)G = 0, so its real and imaginary parts give ρ̂(t, k) = e^(−2π²(k·Ck)t) ρ̂_0(k). The Fourier coefficients determine ρ(t, ·), so every limit point is the point mass at one deterministic continuous trajectory. Projection at a fixed time t then gives convergence in law to the constant ρ(t, u)du, hence convergence in probability.

source.ref: S. Sethuraman, Notes on hydrodynamic limits and related topics, arXiv:2608.20252v1 (2026), Theorem 3.1.1, p. 20, with Sections 2.3-2.4 and 3.1-3.4, pp. 13-25.

applications.title: Relaxation of a density wave in a one-dimensional lattice gas
applications.inputs: Particles sit on a ring of N sites with at most one particle per site. Each particle has a rate-1 clock. When it rings, the particle picks a displacement ±1 or ±2, each with probability 1/4, and jumps only if the target site is empty. The initial density profile is ρ_0(u) = 1/2 + (1/4)cos(2πu), so the sites are filled independently with probabilities between 1/4 and 3/4.
applications.hypotheses: The jump law p(±1) = p(±2) = 1/4 is symmetric with range 2. The profile ρ_0 is continuous with values in [1/4, 3/4] ⊂ [0, 1], and the initial law is the product Bernoulli measure.

steps.text: In dimension one the matrix C is the number C = ∑_z z²p(z) = 2 · (1/4) · 1² + 2 · (1/4) · 2² = 5/2.
The hydrodynamic equation is ∂_t ρ = ½Cρ'' = (5/4)ρ''. Its coefficient is C/2 = 5/4.

The solution is ρ(t, u) = 1/2 + (1/4)e^(−5π²t)cos(2πu). Indeed ∂_t of the second term is −5π² times it, and (5/4) times its second derivative is (5/4)(−4π²) = −5π² times it. This agrees with the Fourier formula of step s6 with k = 1 and 2π²C = 5π².

Macroscopic time t is microscopic time N²t. The amplitude of the wave halves at t = ln 2/(5π²) ≈ 0.014, so on a ring of N = 1000 sites the wave halves after about 14000 time units of the particle clocks.

The total mass ∫ρ(t, u) du = 1/2 does not change, as the conservation of particles requires. The same equation holds for independent walkers with the same p, so the exclusion rule does not change the diffusion of the density, as Section 2.4.1 of the source remarks.

applications.conclusion: On the diffusive time scale, the density wave of the lattice gas decays like a solution of the heat equation with coefficient 5/4, at the rate e^(−5π²t), with no trace of the exclusion rule in the macroscopic equation.

limitations: The proof uses that the drift of ⟨G, π^N⟩ is linear in η, which holds only for symmetric exclusion. Asymmetric or interacting gradient systems need the entropy method and replacement lemmas, as in Sections 4-6 of the source.
The theorem is a law of large numbers. It says nothing about the fluctuations of the density, and on the time scale N²t it says nothing about the motion of one tagged particle.

results.name: Eyring–Kramers formula for metastable exit times of reversible diffusions
results.statement: Let F ∈ C³(ℝ^d) satisfy lim inf_{|x|→∞} |∇F(x)| = ∞ and lim inf_{|x|→∞} (|∇F(x)| − 2ΔF(x)) = ∞. Suppose that F has finitely many local minima, that the gate between any two local minima is a unique finite set of points, and that the Hessian of F is non-degenerate at all local minima and at these saddle points. For ε > 0 let X solve dX_t = −∇F(X_t) dt + √(2ε) dW_t. Let x be a local minimum, and let M_x be the nonempty set of the other local minima y with F(y) ≤ F(x). Suppose that the set of saddle points between x and M_x is one point z*, and that ∇²F(z*) has exactly one negative eigenvalue λ_1(z*). Fix ρ_0 > 0 such that, for each y ∈ M_x, F < F(z*) on the closed ball B̄_{ρ_0}(y) and y is the only critical point of F in it. Let D = ⋃_{y∈M_x} B̄_ρ(y) with ε ≤ ρ ≤ ρ_0. Then, as ε ↓ 0, the hitting time τ_D of D satisfies E_x τ_D = (2π/|λ_1(z*)|) √(|det ∇²F(z*)| / det ∇²F(x)) e^((F(z*) − F(x))/ε) (1 + O(ε^(1/2)|ln ε|)).
hypotheses: F ∈ C³(ℝ^d) with lim inf_{|x|→∞} |∇F(x)| = ∞ and lim inf_{|x|→∞} (|∇F(x)| − 2ΔF(x)) = ∞, and F has finitely many local minima.
The gate between any two local minima is a unique finite set of saddle points, and the Hessian of F is non-degenerate at the local minima and at these saddle points.
The saddle set between the minimum x and the set M_x of the other minima y with F(y) ≤ F(x) is one point z*, and ∇²F(z*) has exactly one negative eigenvalue.
D = ⋃_{y∈M_x} B̄_ρ(y) with ε ≤ ρ ≤ ρ_0, where ρ_0 > 0 is fixed so that F < F(z*) on each ball B̄_{ρ_0}(y) and y is the only critical point of F in it.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 exchanges the integrals over the Green function and the equilibrium measure to get the identity (2.27) of the source.
Step s5 expands F to second order near the saddle point to evaluate the Gaussian integrals.

definitions.name: equilibrium potential
definitions.text: h_{A,D}(y) = P_y[τ_A < τ_D], the solution of L_ε h = 0 off A ∪ D with h = 1 on A and h = 0 on D, where L_ε = −εΔ + ∇F · ∇.

definitions.name: capacity
definitions.text: cap_A(D) = inf {ε ∫ e^(−F(y)/ε) |∇h(y)|² dy : h = 1 on A, h = 0 on D}. The equilibrium potential attains the infimum.

definitions.name: saddle height
definitions.text: F̂(A, B) = inf over continuous paths ω from A to B of sup_t F(ω(t)). The saddle points between A and B are the points at this height that every minimal path must pass.

source.citation: Anton Bovier, Michael Eckhoff, Véronique Gayrard and Markus Klein, Metastability in reversible diffusion processes I. Sharp asymptotics for capacities and exit times, Journal of the European Mathematical Society 6 (2004), 399–424.

source.module: Section 3 Results
source.excerpt: Let x_i be a minimum of F and let D be any closed subset of R^d such that: (i) if M_i ≡ {y_1, …, y_k} ⊂ M enumerates all those minima of F such that F(y_j) ≤ F(x_i), then ⋃_{j=1}^k B_ε(y_j) ⊂ D, (ii) dist(S(x_i, M_i), D) ≥ δ > 0 for some δ independent of ε.

source.alignment: Theorem 3.2 of the source (p. 407) gives E_{x_i}τ_D for several saddle points, and the Remark after it (formula (3.3), p. 408) reduces it to the classical single-saddle Eyring formula, which is the authored statement. The source assumes (H.1), (ND) and (IB) throughout, and the authored statement writes them for Ω = ℝ^d. The source writes F(x_j) in the exponent of (3.2) and (3.3), and the authored statement reads it as F(x_i), the value at the starting minimum, as the proof in Section 6 shows. The set M_i is read as the other minima, because a ball around x_i itself in D would make τ_D = 0. The source allows any closed D with (i) and (ii), but its proof also needs the saddle between x_i and D to be the saddle between x_i and M_i. A set D that enters the valley of x_i below the saddle height keeps (i) and (ii) and makes τ_D much shorter. So the authored statement takes D to be a union of small balls around the minima in M_x, as in Theorem 6.2 of the source, and these balls satisfy (i) and (ii).

proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of Theorem 3.2 in Bovier, Eckhoff, Gayrard and Klein (2004), Sections 2 and 4-6, for one saddle point and for D a union of small balls around the lower minima. The outline takes from the source Proposition 6.1, Proposition 4.7, Corollary 4.8, Theorem 6.2, Theorem 3.1 with its proof in Section 5, and the iteration in the proof of Theorem 3.2, with the Harnack and Hölder estimates of Lemmas 4.1-4.2.

steps.text: Potential theory. Let L_ε = −εΔ + ∇F · ∇. The mean hitting time w_D(y) = E_y τ_D solves L_ε w_D = 1 off D, so w_D(y) = ∫_{D^c} G_{D^c}(y, z) dz by (2.25)-(2.26). The capacity cap_A(D) = ∫_{∂A} e^(−F/ε) de_{A,D} is the infimum of the Dirichlet form ε∫e^(−F/ε)|∇h|² over h = 1 on A, h = 0 on D, by (2.13)-(2.16). The symmetry (2.4) of G, the representation (2.10) of h_{A,D} and Fubini give (2.27): ∫_{∂B_ρ(x)} e^(−F(z)/ε) E_z τ_D e_{B_ρ(x),D}(dz) = ∫_{D^c} e^(−F(y)/ε) h_{B_ρ(x),D}(y) dy.

From an average to the point x. Proposition 6.1 of the source takes ρ = ε. Near the critical point x the drift is small, so the Harnack inequality (Lemma 4.1) and the Hölder estimate (Lemma 4.2), both from Gilbarg and Trudinger, have constants independent of ε on B_√ε(x). With (2.26) and Lemma 4.6 they give |w_D(y) − w_D(x)| ≤ Cε^(α/2) w_D(x) + Cε^(1/2+α/2) on B_ε(x), which is (6.5). Insert this in (2.27) and use ∫ e^(−F/ε) de_{B_ε(x),D} = cap_{B_ε(x)}(D). This gives (6.1): E_x τ_D = ∫_{D^c} e^(−F(y)/ε) h_{B_ε(x),D}(y) dy / cap_{B_ε(x)}(D) · (1 + O(ε^(α/2))).

Rough bounds. Proposition 4.7 of the source bounds cap_{B_ρ(x)}(D) below by C(‖∇F(z*)‖ + √ε)ρ^(d−1) e^(−F(z*)/ε), with a tube around a path below the saddle height and the one-dimensional problems (4.24)-(4.26), and above by Cρ^(d−2) e^(−F(z*)/ε). With the renewal bound of Proposition 4.3, from Lemmas 4.4-4.6, this gives Corollary 4.8: h_{A,D}(y) ≤ Cε^(−1/2) e^(−[F(z*(y,A)) − F(z*(y,D))]/ε).

Laplace asymptotics. The proof of Theorem 6.2 of the source splits ∫_{D^c} e^(−F/ε) h_{B_ε(x),D} dy into a high set of F, which (1.3) makes exponentially small, and the components of a sublevel set. In the component of x, Corollary 4.8 for h_{D,B_ε(x)} = 1 − h_{B_ε(x),D} makes h_{B_ε(x),D} exponentially close to 1, and Laplace's method at the non-degenerate minimum gives (6.13). The other minima outside D lie higher than x, so by (6.12)-(6.15) the other components add exponentially less. This gives (6.9): E_x τ_D = (2πε)^(d/2) e^(−F(x)/ε) / (√(det ∇²F(x)) cap_{B_ε(x)}(D)) · (1 + O(ε^(1/2)|ln ε|, ε^(α/2))).

Sharp capacity. Theorem 3.1 of the source, with the proof of Theorem 5.1, gives cap_{B_ε(x)}(D) = e^(−F(z*)/ε) ((2πε)^(d/2)/(2π)) |λ_1(z*)| / √|det ∇²F(z*)| · (1 + O(√ε|ln ε|)). With z* = 0, F(z) = F(0) − |λ_1|z_1²/2 + ∑_{i≥2} λ_i z_i²/2 + O(|z|³) by (5.4). For the upper bound, the test function is the one-dimensional equilibrium potential (5.8) in z_1 on a box C_δ with δ² = Kε|ln ε|, and Gaussian integrals give (5.15). For the lower bound, (5.18) keeps only ∂h/∂z_1 on a box and minimizes on each fibre, and Lemma 5.2, from Corollary 4.8, puts the true equilibrium potential near 1 and near 0 on the two faces. The bounds agree to leading order.

Conclusion. Insert the capacity of step s5 into (6.9). The factors (2πε)^(d/2) cancel and leave E_x τ_D = (2π/|λ_1(z*)|) √(|det ∇²F(z*)|/det ∇²F(x)) e^((F(z*) − F(x))/ε) (1 + O(ε^(1/2)|ln ε|, ε^(α/2))). To remove the ε^(α/2) error, the proof of Theorem 3.2 repeats the argument for starting points in B_√ε(x), which gives the oscillation bound (6.16). This improves the input of the Hölder estimate, and iteration lowers the error to the order ε^(1/2)|ln ε|.

source.ref: A. Bovier, M. Eckhoff, V. Gayrard and M. Klein, Metastability in reversible diffusion processes I, J. Eur. Math. Soc. 6 (2004) 399–424, Theorem 3.2 and formula (3.3), pp. 407-408, with Sections 4-6, pp. 408-422.

applications.title: Transition time in a symmetric double well
applications.inputs: A particle moves by overdamped Langevin dynamics dX_t = −∇F(X_t) dt + √(2ε) dW_t in the plane, with F(x, y) = x⁴/4 − x²/2 + y²/2 and temperature ε. It starts in the left well at (−1, 0). The target D is the closed disk of radius 1/4 around the right well (1, 0).
applications.hypotheses: ∇F = (x³ − x, y) and ΔF = 3x². Since |∇F| ≥ (|x³ − x| + |y|)/2, we get |∇F| − 2ΔF ≥ (|x|³ − |x|)/2 − 6x² + |y|/2, and the cubic term makes the right side tend to infinity as |(x, y)| → ∞. The other minimum (1, 0) has the same height, so M_x = {(1, 0)}. With x = 1 + u, F = −1/4 + u² + u³ + u⁴/4 + y²/2 ≤ −1/4 + 1/16 + 1/64 + 1/1024 < 0 = F(0, 0) on D, and (1, 0) is the only critical point in D. So ρ = ρ_0 = 1/4 is allowed for ε ≤ 1/4.

steps.text: The critical points are (−1, 0), (0, 0) and (1, 0). The Hessian is diag(3x² − 1, 1). At (±1, 0) it is diag(2, 1), so the minima are non-degenerate with determinant 2. At (0, 0) it is diag(−1, 1), a saddle with λ_1 = −1 and |det| = 1.

Every path from (−1, 0) to (1, 0) crosses the line x = 0, where F(0, y) = y²/2 ≥ 0 with equality only at y = 0. So the saddle height is 0 and z* = (0, 0) is the only saddle point. The barrier is F(z*) − F(−1, 0) = 0 − (1/4 − 1/2) = 1/4.
The prefactor is (2π/|λ_1|) √(|det ∇²F(z*)| / det ∇²F(x)) = 2π √(1/2) = √2 π ≈ 4.44. As a check, (prefactor/π)² = (2/1)² · (1/2) = 2.
So E τ_D ≈ √2 π e^(1/(4ε)). At ε = 1/20 the exponent is (1/4)/(1/20) = 5, and E τ_D ≈ 4.44 · 148.4 ≈ 659 time units.

At ε = 1/40 the exponent doubles to 10, so the mean time grows by the factor e^5 ≈ 148 to about 97 900 time units. To leading order, the logarithm of the rate 1/E τ_D is linear in 1/ε with slope −1/4, which is the Arrhenius law with activation energy 1/4.

applications.conclusion: A particle in the symmetric double well needs on average about √2 π e^(1/(4ε)) time units to reach the other well. The barrier height sets the exponential rate, and the curvatures at the minimum and at the saddle set the prefactor √2 π.

limitations: The theorem gives the mean exit time only. That the exit time is asymptotically exponential, and the link with the small eigenvalues of L_ε, are in the follow-up paper of the same authors.
The formula needs non-degenerate critical points and a gradient drift. Degenerate saddles change the prefactor, and non-reversible drifts are outside the potential theory of the source.

results.name: Propp–Wilson coupling from the past
results.statement: Let X be a finite set and let P be an irreducible aperiodic transition matrix on X with stationary distribution π. Let f_{−1}, f_{−2}, … be independent random maps from X to X such that, for each t, the values f_t(x) with x ∈ X are independent and P(f_t(x) = y) = P(x, y). Put F_0 = id and F_{−T} = f_{−1} ∘ f_{−2} ∘ ⋯ ∘ f_{−T} for T ≥ 1. Then, with probability 1, there is a finite T₀ such that F_{−T} is a constant map for every T ≥ T₀, and all these constant maps have the same value Y. The law of Y is π.
hypotheses: The state space X is finite and P is a stochastic matrix on X.
P is irreducible and aperiodic.
The random maps f_{−1}, f_{−2}, … are independent. For each t the values f_t(x), x ∈ X, are independent, and f_t(x) has the law P(x, ·).

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 takes a positive stationary distribution and the convergence of P^t(x, ·) to π from the convergence theorem, and deduces that some power P^r has only positive entries.
Step s2 writes P^j(w, z) = ∑_u P(w, u)P^(j−1)(u, z) to choose the next state of each coalescing map.

definitions.name: coupling from the past
definitions.text: The algorithm that composes the random maps f_{−1}, f_{−2}, … backward in time until the composition F_{−T} is a constant map, and then returns the value of that constant map.

definitions.name: constant map
definitions.text: A map F : X → X with F(x) = F(x′) for all x, x′ ∈ X. Its value is the single point of its image.

definitions.name: coalescence time
definitions.text: T₀ = min{T ≥ 0 : F_{−T} is constant}, the number of steps that the algorithm looks back into the past.

source.citation: James Gary Propp and David Bruce Wilson, Exact sampling with coupled Markov chains and applications to statistical mechanics, Random Structures & Algorithms 9 (1996), 223–252.
source.revision: Authors' preprint dated July 16, 1996, 27 pages.
source.module: Section 2.1 Coupling from the past
source.excerpt: Theorem 1 With probability 1 the coupling-from-the-past protocol returns a value, and this value is distributed according to the stationary distribution of the Markov chain.
source.attribution: © James Gary Propp and David Bruce Wilson. Quoted from Exact Sampling with Coupled Markov Chains and Applications to Statistical Mechanics for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states Theorem 1 for the procedure of Section 2.1, in which each random map has independent coordinates f_t(i) = Markov(i) with law p_{i,·}. The authored statement writes this procedure with explicit random maps. The authored proof follows the proof of Theorem 1. It adds an explicit construction for the claim that a block of maps is constant with positive probability, and it proves the claim about the law of the output with the argument of the proof of Theorem 3 on pp. 6-7.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the proofs of Theorems 1 and 3 in Propp and Wilson. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement: almost sure coalescence, persistence of the constant value, and the law π of the output.

steps.text: A positive power. By the convergence theorem, π(y) > 0 for every y and max_x ‖P^t(x, ·) − π‖_TV ≤ Cα^t with α < 1. A single entry differs by at most the total variation distance, so P^t(x, y) ≥ π(y) − Cα^t. Since X is finite, there is r ≥ 1 with P^r(x, y) > 0 for all x, y ∈ X.

A coalescing choice of maps. Fix z ∈ X and let A_j = {u ∈ X : P^j(u, z) > 0} for 0 ≤ j ≤ r. Then A_r = X by step s1 and A_0 = {z}. If w ∈ A_j with j ≥ 1, then P^j(w, z) = ∑_u P(w, u)P^(j−1)(u, z) > 0, so some u ∈ A_(j−1) has P(w, u) > 0. So for k = 1, …, r there is a map g_k : X → X with P(w, g_k(w)) > 0 for every w and g_k(A_(r−k+1)) ⊂ A_(r−k). The composition g_r ∘ ⋯ ∘ g_1 sends X into {z}, so it is constant. All coordinates of all the maps are independent, so the event {f_{−r} = g_1, f_{−r+1} = g_2, …, f_{−1} = g_r} has probability ∏_{k=1}^{r} ∏_{w∈X} P(w, g_k(w)) > 0. On this event F_{−r} = g_r ∘ ⋯ ∘ g_1. Thus ε = P(F_{−r} is constant) > 0.

Almost sure coalescence. For k ≥ 1 let G_k = f_{−(k−1)r−1} ∘ ⋯ ∘ f_{−kr}, so F_{−kr} = G_1 ∘ ⋯ ∘ G_k. The blocks use disjoint families of maps, so G_1, G_2, … are independent, and each has the law of G_1 = F_{−r}. A composition is constant when one of its factors is constant. So F_{−kr} is not constant only if no G_j with j ≤ k is constant, and P(F_{−kr} is not constant) ≤ (1 − ε)^k. Also F_{−T−1} = F_{−T} ∘ f_{−T−1}, so if F_{−T} is constant with value c, then every F_{−T′} with T′ ≥ T is constant with value c. Let T₀ be the least T with F_{−T} constant. Then P(T₀ > kr) ≤ (1 − ε)^k → 0. So T₀ is finite almost surely, and the value Y of F_{−T₀} is the value of every F_{−T} with T ≥ T₀.

A stationary start stays stationary. Let X₀ have the law π and be independent of all the maps, and put Z_T = F_{−T}(X₀). Induction on T shows that Z_T has the law π. The case T = 0 is clear. The variable W = f_{−T−1}(X₀) depends only on X₀ and f_{−T−1}, so W is independent of f_{−1}, …, f_{−T}, and P(W = y) = ∑_x π(x)P(x, y) = π(y). So (W, f_{−1}, …, f_{−T}) has the same joint law as (X₀, f_{−1}, …, f_{−T}). Hence Z_(T+1) = F_{−T}(W) has the same law as Z_T = F_{−T}(X₀), which is π.

The output has the law π. On the event {T₀ ≤ T}, the map F_{−T} is constant with value Y, so Z_T = Y. Hence, for every y ∈ X, |P(Y = y) − π(y)| = |P(Y = y) − P(Z_T = y)| ≤ P(Y ≠ Z_T) ≤ P(T₀ > T). The right side tends to 0 as T → ∞ by step s3, so P(Y = y) = π(y). The law of Y depends only on the maps. So the same argument with any stationary π′ in place of π gives π′ = π, which shows again that π is unique.

applications.title: Exact sampling of a three-state reflecting walk
applications.inputs: The state space is {0, 1, 2}. A fair coin moves the walk from i to min(i + 1, 2) on heads and to max(i − 1, 0) on tails. So P(0, 0) = P(0, 1) = 1/2, P(1, 0) = P(1, 2) = 1/2 and P(2, 1) = P(2, 2) = 1/2. The source uses this chain with one shared coin in a remark on p. 6. Here each state has its own coin, as in Theorem 1. So a random map f has independent coordinates f(0) ∈ {0, 1}, f(1) ∈ {0, 2} and f(2) ∈ {1, 2}, each value with probability 1/2, and each of the 8 maps has probability 1/8.
applications.hypotheses: The state space is finite. The chain is irreducible because 0 → 1 → 2 → 1 → 0 has positive probabilities, and aperiodic because P(0, 0) = 1/2 > 0. The coordinates of each map are independent and have the laws P(x, ·).

steps.text: Each column of P sums to 1, for example P(0, 1) + P(2, 1) = 1/2 + 1/2 = 1. So the uniform law π = (1/3, 1/3, 1/3) is stationary. All entries of P² are positive, for example P²(0, 2) = P(0, 1)P(1, 2) = 1/4, so r = 2 works in step s1.
A single map is never constant. The equality f(0) = f(1) forces the value 0, because f(0) ∈ {0, 1} and f(1) ∈ {0, 2}, but f(2) ∈ {1, 2}. So T₀ ≥ 2 for every outcome.

Write a map as the list (f(0), f(1), f(2)). Of the 8 maps for f_{−2}, two are bijections, (0, 2, 1) and (1, 0, 2), and after them F_{−2} is not constant by step a2. The other 6 maps have an image with 2 points. The map f_{−1} merges {0, 1} only if f(0) = f(1) = 0, merges {0, 2} only if f(0) = f(2) = 1, and merges {1, 2} only if f(1) = f(2) = 2, each with probability 1/4. So ε = P(F_{−2} is constant) = 6 · (1/8) · (1/4) = 3/16. The construction of step s2 for one target state guarantees only (1/2)^6 = 1/64.
Step s3 gives P(T₀ > 2k) ≤ (13/16)^k. Since P(T₀ > T) decreases in T, E[T₀] = ∑_{T≥0} P(T₀ > T) ≤ 2 ∑_{k≥0} (13/16)^k = 32/3. So on average the algorithm looks back fewer than 11 steps.

The theorem says that the returned state is uniform on {0, 1, 2}. Enumeration of the 64 pairs (f_{−1}, f_{−2}) agrees at the first possible stopping time: 12 pairs give a constant F_{−2}, and each state is the value for 4 of them, so each state has probability 4/64 = 1/16 of being returned at T₀ = 2.

applications.conclusion: Coupling from the past returns an exact uniform sample of the three-state walk. It never stops before 2 steps, it stops at 2 steps with probability 3/16, and on average it looks back at most 32/3 steps.

limitations: The theorem gives no useful bound on the running time in general. The proof gives E[T₀] ≤ r/ε, and ε can be exponentially small in the number of states. Practical use needs a better coupling, for example a monotone coupling that follows only the top and the bottom states, as in Section 3 of the source.

The direction of time matters. If the coupled chains run forward from time 0 and the algorithm returns the state where they first meet, the sample can be biased, as the source remarks. New random numbers at each restart further into the past can also bias the sample, and the source gives a three-state example.
