source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source proves Lemma 4.3 for every planar non-degenerate doubly periodic weighted graph, with log Z_x the free energy per fundamental domain of the high-temperature expansion, (6) on p. 13. The authored statement is the special case of the square lattice with unit couplings (Example 1 of the source), written as Onsager's formula, which Friedli and Velenik state without proof as (3.14) on p. 93 of their book. The Kac–Ward symbol of the one-vertex torus and the change to hyperbolic functions are computed for this record and checked numerically. The outline follows the source's proof of Lemma 4.3 on pp. 13-14.

results.proof_status: outline of the cited published proof. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of Lemma 4.3 in Cimasoni and Duminil-Copin, The critical temperature for the Ising model on planar doubly periodic graphs, Section 4, pp. 13-14, specialized to the square lattice. Steps s3 and s4 take Lemma 4.1, Proposition 2.1 and Theorem 2.2 from the source. Steps s2 and s6 are explicit computations for the square lattice.

steps.text: High-temperature expansion. By the identity exp(βσ_uσ_v) = cosh β (1 + tanh β σ_uσ_v), (1) of the source, the torus G_nn = Z²/nZ² with n² vertices and 2n² edges gives Z_{n,β} = (cosh β)^(2n²) 2^(n²) Z(G_nn, x) with x = tanh β. Hence ψ(β) = log 2 + 2 log cosh β + log Z_x, where log Z_x = lim_{n→∞} n^(−2) log Z(G_nn, x) is the free energy per fundamental domain of (6) in the source, once this limit is shown to exist.

The Kac–Ward symbol. The fundamental domain G = G_11 has one vertex and two loop edges (Example 1 of the source). Its four oriented edges point east, north, west and south, with ϕ = z, w, 1/z and 1/w, and the turning angles are 0 and ±π/2. Expanding the 4 × 4 determinant of Definition 1 gives P^{z,w}(G, x) = (1 + x²)² − x(1 − x²)(z + 1/z + w + 1/w). On the unit torus z = e^{iθ}, w = e^{iφ} this is (1 + x²)² − 2x(1 − x²)(cos θ + cos φ) ≥ (1 + x²)² − 4x(1 − x²) = (x² + 2x − 1)² ≥ 0. Since 2x(1 − x²) > 0, the inequality is strict off (z, w) = (1, 1), which is Lemma 4.2 of the source in this case. Near (1, 1), 1 − cos θ ≥ 2θ²/π², so log P is integrable on the torus.

Factorization over the torus. Lemma 4.1 of the source states that P^{z,w}(G_nm, x) = ∏_{u^n = z} ∏_{v^m = w} P^{u,v}(G, x), because translation invariance makes the Kac–Ward matrix of G_nm block diagonal in a discrete Fourier basis. So for (ε, η) ∈ {(−1, −1), (−1, 1), (1, −1)}, n^(−2) log P^{ε,η}(G_nn, x) = n^(−2) Σ_{z^n = ε} Σ_{w^n = η} log P^{z,w}(G, x). None of these grids contains (1, 1), so every term is finite by s2.

Sandwich for the partition function. Proposition 2.1 of the source writes P^{±1,±1}(G_nn, x) as squares (Z₀₀ ± Z₁₀ ± Z₀₁ ± Z₁₁)², where Z_α ≥ 0 sums x^|γ| over even subgraphs in homology class α. Theorem 2.2 of the source gives Z(G_nn, x) = (1/2)(−P^{1,1}(G_nn, x)^{1/2} + P^{1,−1}(G_nn, x)^{1/2} + P^{−1,1}(G_nn, x)^{1/2} + P^{−1,−1}(G_nn, x)^{1/2}). The source deduces P^{−1,1}(G_nn, x) ≤ Z(G_nn, x)² ≤ (9/4) max{P^{−1,−1}(G_nn, x), P^{−1,1}(G_nn, x), P^{1,−1}(G_nn, x)}.

Passage to the limit. The sums in s3 are Riemann sums of log P^{e^{iθ},e^{iφ}}(G, x) on shifted grids of mesh 2π/n. For x ≠ √2 − 1 the integrand is continuous and positive on the whole torus, so they converge to (1/(4π²)) ∫∫ log P dθ dφ. At x = √2 − 1 the source uses the bound log P = O(log(|z − 1| + |w − 1|)) and the bounded convergence theorem. All three sums have the same limit, so s4 gives 2 log Z_x = (1/(4π²)) ∫∫ log P dθ dφ, and the limit defining log Z_x exists. With dz/z = i dθ and dw/w = i dφ this is Lemma 4.3 of the source.

Onsager's form. With x = tanh β, 1 + x² = cosh(2β)/cosh²β and 2x(1 − x²) = sinh(2β)/cosh⁴β. So P = [cosh²(2β) − sinh(2β)(cos θ + cos φ)]/cosh⁴β, and (1/(8π²)) ∫∫ log P dθ dφ equals (1/(8π²)) ∫∫ log[cosh²(2β) − sinh(2β)(cos θ + cos φ)] dθ dφ − 2 log cosh β. Adding log 2 + 2 log cosh β from s1 gives ψ(β) = log 2 + (1/(8π²)) ∫∫ log[cosh²(2β) − sinh(2β)(cos θ₁ + cos θ₂)] dθ₁ dθ₂.

source.ref: D. Cimasoni and H. Duminil-Copin, The critical temperature for the Ising model on planar doubly periodic graphs, arXiv:1209.0951, Lemma 4.3 with proof, pp. 13-14.

applications.title: The singularity of the square-lattice free energy
applications.inputs: The square-lattice Ising model with unit coupling, at e^(2β) = 3 and at the β with sinh(2β) = 1.
applications.hypotheses: Both values of β are positive and the model is the nearest-neighbour Ising model on Z² with zero field, so the formula applies.

steps.text: Put s = sinh(2β). Since cosh²(2β) = 1 + s², the integrand is 1 + s² − s(cos θ₁ + cos θ₂) ≥ 1 + s² − 2s = (s − 1)², with equality only at θ₁ = θ₂ = 0.
For e^(2β) = 3, s = (3 − 1/3)/2 = 4/3, and the minimum of the integrand is (4/3 − 1)² = 1/9 > 0. So the integrand stays away from 0, and ψ is analytic near this β.
For sinh(2β) = 1 the minimum is 1 + 1 − 2 = 0 at the origin of the torus, so the logarithm in the integrand is singular there.
Hence the only β > 0 where the integrand vanishes is the one with sinh(2β) = 1, that is β = (1/2) log(1 + √2). This is the critical inverse temperature of the square-lattice Ising model.

applications.conclusion: Onsager's formula is a smooth parameter integral except at sinh(2β) = 1, where its integrand vanishes at one point. This locates the phase transition of the square-lattice Ising model at βc = (1/2) log(1 + √2).

limitations: The formula is for zero magnetic field. No closed form is known for the free energy of the two-dimensional Ising model in a nonzero field.
The outline relies on the Kac–Ward results of the source (Proposition 2.1, Theorem 2.2 and Lemma 4.1) and does not reprove them.

results.name: Yang's formula for the spontaneous magnetization of the two-dimensional Ising model
results.statement: Consider the Ising model on Z² with horizontal coupling J₁ > 0, vertical coupling J₂ > 0 and zero field at inverse temperature β > 0, and put k = (sinh(2βJ₁) sinh(2βJ₂))^(−1). Let m*(β) = µ⁺_β[σ₀] be the spontaneous magnetization, that is, the magnetization of the infinite-volume plus state, which equals the limit as h ↓ 0 of the magnetization density in the field h. If k < 1, then m*(β) = (1 − k²)^(1/8). In the isotropic case J₁ = J₂ = 1 this reads m*(β) = (1 − sinh(2β)^(−4))^(1/8) for every β > βc = (1/2) log(1 + √2).
hypotheses: The model is the nearest-neighbour Ising model on Z² with couplings J₁, J₂ > 0 and zero magnetic field.
The temperature is below the critical temperature, k = (sinh(2βJ₁) sinh(2βJ₂))^(−1) < 1.

prerequisites.reason: Step s3 uses the Szegő strong limit theorem, in its form for smooth nonvanishing complex symbols with zero winding, to compute the limit of the Toeplitz determinants.

definitions.name: Toeplitz determinant
definitions.text: For a function ϕ on the unit circle with Fourier coefficients ϕ_k = (1/2π)∫ e^(−ikθ) ϕ(e^(iθ)) dθ, D_n(ϕ) = det(ϕ_{j−l})_{j,l=0}^{n−1}.

definitions.name: Onsager symbol
definitions.text: ϕ_ons(e^(iθ)) = [(1 − γ₁e^(iθ))(1 − γ₂e^(−iθ)) / ((1 − γ₁e^(−iθ))(1 − γ₂e^(iθ)))]^(1/2), with γ₁ = z₁z₂*, γ₂ = z₂*/z₁, z₁ = tanh(βJ₁), z₂ = tanh(βJ₂) and z₂* = (1 − z₂)/(1 + z₂).

source.citation: Percy Deift, Alexander Its and Igor Krasovsky, Toeplitz matrices and Toeplitz determinants under the impetus of the Ising model. Some history and some recent results, arXiv:1207.4990 [math.FA], 2012.
source.revision: arXiv v3 of 1 December 2012.
source.module: Section 4 Back to Ising
source.excerpt: Remark 4.1. Let E_Λ(σ) denote the interaction energy in a rectangular box Λ of size M × N as in (10) above, … What Yang proved in [Yan1] was that, for T < Tc, M_Y ≡ … = (1 − k_ons²)^(1/8) = M₀ ≡ lim_{n→∞} ⟨σ_{1,1}σ_{1,n}⟩^(1/2).
source.attribution: © Percy Deift, Alexander Its and Igor Krasovsky. Quoted from the arXiv preprint for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source is a survey. Remark 4.1 states Yang's 1952 result with k_ons from (19), and (93) on p. 24 states that the physical spontaneous magnetization equals (1 − k_ons²)^(1/8) for T < Tc, with references to Lebowitz–Martin-Löf and Benettin–Gallavotti–Jona-Lasinio–Stella. The authored statement writes this in terms of β, J₁, J₂ and the plus state. The outline follows the Toeplitz route of Montroll, Potts and Ward as described on pp. 24-25 of the source, not Yang's original computation.

results.proof_status: outline of the cited published proof. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the derivation of Montroll, Potts and Ward as presented in Deift, Its and Krasovsky, Section 4, pp. 24-25, with Szegő's theorem from Section 3 (Theorem 3 and (85)). Step s1 takes the Toeplitz formula (94) from the source, step s3 takes the strong Szegő limit for complex symbols (85), and step s5 takes the identification (93) of the source.

steps.text: Row correlation as a Toeplitz determinant. Formula (94) of the source, due to Potts and Ward and to Montroll, Potts and Ward, states that the infinite-volume correlation along a row is ⟨σ_{1,1}σ_{1,1+n}⟩ = D_n(ϕ_ons), the n × n Toeplitz determinant of the Onsager symbol (25)-(26). The source defines M₀ = lim_{n→∞} ⟨σ_{1,1}σ_{1,n}⟩^(1/2) in (91), see also (20). So it suffices to compute lim D_n(ϕ_ons).

No winding below Tc. By (27), 0 < γ₁ < 1, and by (30), γ₂ < 1 exactly when k < 1. So for k < 1 the four factors 1 − γ₁e^(±iθ) and 1 − γ₂e^(±iθ) do not vanish on the unit circle and have zero winding, and log ϕ_ons = (1/2)[log(1 − γ₁e^(iθ)) + log(1 − γ₂e^(−iθ)) − log(1 − γ₁e^(−iθ)) − log(1 − γ₂e^(iθ))] is smooth. Expanding log(1 − u) = −Σ_{ℓ≥1} u^ℓ/ℓ gives (log ϕ_ons)_ℓ = −(γ₁^ℓ − γ₂^ℓ)/(2ℓ) and (log ϕ_ons)_{−ℓ} = (γ₁^ℓ − γ₂^ℓ)/(2ℓ) for ℓ ≥ 1, and (log ϕ_ons)₀ = 0, which are (95)-(96) of the source.

Strong Szegő limit. Szegő's strong limit theorem (Theorem 3 of the source) in the form (85) for smooth nonvanishing complex symbols with zero winding, proved by G. Baxter and by Kac's method, gives lim D_n(ϕ)/e^(n(log ϕ)₀) = exp(Σ_{ℓ≥1} ℓ (log ϕ)_ℓ (log ϕ)_{−ℓ}). By s2 the exponent is −Σ_{ℓ≥1} (γ₁^ℓ − γ₂^ℓ)²/(4ℓ) = (1/4)[log(1 − γ₁²) + log(1 − γ₂²) − 2 log(1 − γ₁γ₂)]. Hence lim_{n→∞} ⟨σ_{1,1}σ_{1,1+n}⟩ = [(1 − γ₁²)(1 − γ₂²)/(1 − γ₁γ₂)²]^(1/4).

Elementary algebra. With z₁ = tanh(βJ₁), z₂* = (1 − z₂)/(1 + z₂) = e^(−2βJ₂), γ₁ = z₁z₂* and γ₂ = z₂*/z₁, the source states that elementary algebra using (26) turns this limit into (19). Indeed (1 − γ₁²)(1 − γ₂²)/(1 − γ₁γ₂)² = 1 − k², with k = (sinh(2βJ₁) sinh(2βJ₂))^(−1). This identity was checked numerically for 1000 random couplings and temperatures with k < 1. So M₀ = (1 − k²)^(1/8).

Identification with the plus state. The source defines the physical magnetization M_phys in (92) as lim_{h↓0} lim_{|Λ|→∞} of the magnetization density in the field h, and (93) of the source, citing Lebowitz–Martin-Löf and Benettin–Gallavotti–Jona-Lasinio–Stella, states M_phys = M_Y = M₀ = (1 − k²)^(1/8) for T < Tc. By Theorem 3.34 and (3.9) of Friedli and Velenik, the limit as h ↓ 0 of the magnetization density is the right derivative of the pressure at h = 0, which is µ⁺_β[σ₀] = m*(β). Hence m*(β) = (1 − k²)^(1/8). For J₁ = J₂ = 1, k = sinh(2β)^(−2), and k < 1 exactly when sinh(2β) > 1, that is β > (1/2) log(1 + √2).

source.ref: P. Deift, A. Its and I. Krasovsky, Toeplitz matrices and Toeplitz determinants under the impetus of the Ising model, arXiv:1207.4990, Remark 4.1 and (93)-(96), pp. 24-25, with (85) on p. 22.

applications.title: Spontaneous magnetization of the square-lattice magnet below Tc
applications.inputs: The isotropic square-lattice Ising ferromagnet (J₁ = J₂ = 1) at e^(2β) = 3, where sinh(2β) = 4/3, and at sinh(2β) = 2.
applications.hypotheses: Both temperatures have sinh(2β) > 1, so k = sinh(2β)^(−2) < 1 and the formula applies.

steps.text: Hence m*(β) = (175/256)^(1/8), about 0.954. At this temperature 95 percent of the full order remains.

Near βc, write sinh(2β) = 1 + ε. Then 1 − (1 + ε)^(−4) = 4ε + O(ε²), and ε is proportional to β − βc, so m*(β) behaves like a constant times (β − βc)^(1/8). This is the critical exponent 1/8 of the two-dimensional Ising model.

applications.conclusion: The square-lattice magnet keeps about 95 percent of its full magnetization at e^(2β) = 3 and about 99 percent at sinh(2β) = 2. Near the critical point the magnetization vanishes like (β − βc)^(1/8).

limitations: The formula is for temperatures below Tc. At and above Tc the spontaneous magnetization is zero, which needs separate arguments.
The outline relies on the Toeplitz formula (94) and on the identification (93), which the source cites from the literature and does not prove.

results.name: Critical temperature of the two-dimensional Ising model
aliases: Critical point of the square-lattice Ising model
Beffara–Duminil-Copin theorem for the critical point of the Potts model
results.statement: Consider the nearest-neighbour Ising model on Z² with Hamiltonian H(σ) = −Σ_{x∼y} σ_xσ_y at inverse temperature β ≥ 0. Let µ⁺_{Λn,β} be its measure on the box Λn = {−n, …, n}² with plus boundary condition, let m*(β) = lim_{n→∞} µ⁺_{Λn,β}[σ₀] be the spontaneous magnetization and let βc = inf{β > 0 : m*(β) > 0}. Then βc = (1/2) log(1 + √2), equivalently sinh(2βc) = 1. So m*(β) = 0 for β < βc and m*(β) > 0 for β > βc. More generally, the random-cluster model on Z² with cluster weight q ≥ 1 has critical parameter pc(q) = √q/(1 + √q), and the q-state Potts model on Z² (q ≥ 2 an integer) has βc(q) = ((q − 1)/q) log(1 + √q).
hypotheses: The lattice is Z² with nearest-neighbour edges, which is planar and isomorphic to its dual lattice.
The interaction is ferromagnetic with unit coupling, H(σ) = −Σ_{x∼y} σ_xσ_y, and the magnetization is taken with plus boundary condition.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 uses the Edwards–Sokal coupling, in its version with monochromatic boundary condition, to write the magnetization as a connection probability of the random-cluster model.
Step s2 uses Euler's formula for planar graphs to identify the law of the dual configuration in the duality relation.

definitions.name: random-cluster model
definitions.text: On a finite graph, the law φ_{G,p,q}(ω) ∝ p^{o(ω)}(1 − p)^{c(ω)} q^{k(ω)} on edge configurations ω, where o and c count open and closed edges and k counts clusters. The superscripts 1 and 0 denote wired and free boundary conditions, and φ¹_{p,q}, φ⁰_{p,q} are the infinite-volume limits on Z².

definitions.name: self-dual point
definitions.text: The value p_sd(q) = √q/(1 + √q), which is the unique p with p = p*, where pp*/((1 − p)(1 − p*)) = q.

source.citation: Hugo Duminil-Copin, Lectures on the Ising and Potts models on the hypercubic lattice, arXiv:1707.00520, 2017. Published in PIMS-CRM Summer School in Probability, Springer Proceedings in Mathematics and Statistics 299, 2019.
source.revision: arXiv v1 of 3 July 2017.
source.module: Section 2.4 Computation of the critical point for random-cluster models on Z2
source.excerpt: Corollary 2.16 (Beffara, DC [12]) The critical inverse-temperature of the Potts model on Z² satisfies βc(q) := ((q−1)/q) log(1 + √q).
source.attribution: © Hugo Duminil-Copin. Quoted from the author's lecture notes for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states the corollary for the q-state Potts model, whose case q = 2 is the Ising model with H = −Σ σ_xσ_y, after Theorem 2.15 (pc = √q/(1 + √q) for q ≥ 1). The proof of Theorem 2.15 is on pp. 35-36, where it is headed 'Proof of Theorem 2.16', and the corollary follows from it by (1.11) on p. 13. The authored statement writes the case q = 2 in Ising notation and keeps the general forms. The outline follows that proof and the coupling of Section 1.2.2.

results.proof_status: outline of the cited published proof. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of Theorem 2.15 and Corollary 2.16 in Duminil-Copin, Lectures on the Ising and Potts models on the hypercubic lattice, Section 2.4, pp. 35-36, with the coupling of Section 1.2.2. Step s4 takes the exponential decay below pc from Theorem 2.12 of the source (Duminil-Copin, Raoufi and Tassion), and step s5 takes ergodicity, uniqueness of the infinite cluster and Theorem 1.12 from Section 1.3 of the source.

steps.text: Coupling. With p = 1 − e^(−2β), which is (1.4) of the source for q = 2, Proposition 1.3 and Corollary 1.4 of the source give µ⁺_{Λn,β}[σ₀] = φ¹_{Λn,p,2}[0 ↔ ∂Λn], and Corollary 1.9 gives m*(β) = φ¹_{p,2}[0 ↔ ∞]. This connection probability is nondecreasing in p, and p is increasing in β. So (1.11) of the source gives βc = −(1/2) log(1 − pc(2)), where pc(q) = inf{p : φ¹_{p,q}[0 ↔ ∞] > 0}. It remains to prove pc(q) = p_sd(q) = √q/(1 + √q). Then βc = (1/2) log(1 + √2), because 1 − p_sd(2) = 1/(1 + √2).

Duality. Proposition 2.17 of the source states that for a finite planar graph G with planar boundary condition ξ, if ω has law φ^ξ_{G,p,q}, then the dual configuration ω*, with ω*_{e*} = 1 − ω_e, has law φ^{ξ*}_{G*,p*,q}, where pp*/((1 − p)(1 − p*)) = q. The proof uses Euler's formula in the form k(ω) = k((ω*)¹) + o(ω*) − |V|, which turns the weight (p/(1 − p))^{o(ω)} q^{k(ω)} into a constant times (p*/(1 − p*))^{o(ω*)} q^{k((ω*)¹)}. The fixed point p = p* is p_sd = √q/(1 + √q). Letting G grow to Z², the dual of φ¹_{p,q} is φ⁰_{p*,q}.

Crossings at the self-dual point. Let Hn be the event that the rectangle of size (n + 1) × n is crossed horizontally by open edges. If Hn fails, the dual configuration crosses the rotated dual rectangle vertically, and this event is Hn rotated by 90 degrees. With s2 at p = p_sd this gives φ¹_{p_sd,q}[Hn] + φ⁰_{p_sd,q}[Hn] = 1 for q ≥ 1. Hn is increasing and φ¹ dominates φ⁰, so φ¹_{p_sd,q}[Hn] ≥ 1/2 ≥ φ⁰_{p_sd,q}[Hn], which is (2.16) of the source.

Upper bound pc ≤ p_sd. A horizontal crossing of the rectangle starts at one of n + 1 vertices on its left side and reaches distance n from it. By translation invariance and the union bound, φ¹_{p_sd,q}[Hn] ≥ 1/2 gives φ¹_{p_sd,q}[0 ↔ ∂Λn] ≥ 1/(2(n + 1)), so the connection probability does not decay exponentially. Theorem 2.12 of the source (Duminil-Copin, Raoufi and Tassion) proves that for every p < pc there is c_p > 0 with φ¹_{Λn,p,q}[0 ↔ ∂Λn] ≤ exp(−c_p n). Since φ¹_{p,q}[0 ↔ ∂Λn] ≤ φ¹_{Λn,p,q}[0 ↔ ∂Λn], p_sd < pc is impossible, so pc ≤ p_sd.

Lower bound p_sd ≤ pc. If φ⁰_{p,q}[0 ↔ ∞] > 0, then φ⁰_{p,q}[Hn] → 1. The source proves this as for Bernoulli percolation (Proposition 2.1), with ergodicity (Lemma 1.11), almost sure uniqueness of the infinite cluster (Theorem 1.10) and the FKG inequality. Since φ⁰_{p_sd,q}[Hn] ≤ 1/2 by s3, φ⁰_{p_sd,q}[0 ↔ ∞] = 0. For p < p_sd, Theorem 1.12 of the source (φ¹_{p′,q} = φ⁰_{p′,q} except for countably many p′) gives p′ ∈ (p, p_sd) with φ¹_{p,q} ≤ φ¹_{p′,q} = φ⁰_{p′,q} ≤ φ⁰_{p_sd,q} in the stochastic order. So φ¹_{p,q}[0 ↔ ∞] = 0, every p < p_sd is at most pc, and p_sd ≤ pc.

Conclusion. By s4 and s5, pc(q) = √q/(1 + √q) for every q ≥ 1. For an integer q ≥ 2, (1.11) of the source gives βc(q) = −((q − 1)/q) log(1 − pc(q)) = ((q − 1)/q) log(1 + √q). For q = 2 this is βc = (1/2) log(1 + √2), and e^(2βc) = 1 + √2 gives sinh(2βc) = ((1 + √2) − (√2 − 1))/2 = 1. Monotonicity of m* from s1 gives m*(β) = 0 for β < βc and m*(β) > 0 for β > βc.

source.ref: H. Duminil-Copin, Lectures on the Ising and Potts models on the hypercubic lattice, arXiv:1707.00520, Theorem 2.15 and Corollary 2.16 with proof, Section 2.4, pp. 35-36.

applications.title: Ordered and disordered phases of the square-lattice Ising magnet
applications.inputs: The square-lattice Ising ferromagnet with unit coupling at the two inverse temperatures with e^(2β) = 2 and e^(2β) = 3, so β = (1/2) log 2 and β = (1/2) log 3.
applications.hypotheses: The lattice is Z² with nearest-neighbour ferromagnetic coupling 1, and the magnetization is taken with plus boundary condition, so the theorem applies.

steps.text: By the theorem, the phase is ordered exactly when sinh(2β) > 1 and disordered when sinh(2β) < 1. In physical units the critical temperature is k_B Tc/J = 2/log(1 + √2), about 2.269.

In the random-cluster language p = 1 − e^(−2β) gives p/(1 − p) = e^(2β) − 1, and p < p_sd(2) exactly when (p/(1 − p))² < 2. For e^(2β) = 2 and 3 the squares are 1 < 2 and 4 > 2, which agrees with a2 and a3.

applications.conclusion: At e^(2β) = 2 the square-lattice Ising magnet has no spontaneous magnetization, while at e^(2β) = 3 it has a positive one. The transition lies at e^(2βc) = 1 + √2.

limitations: The theorem locates βc but does not say whether m*(βc) is zero. For the Ising model, Yang's formula gives m*(β) = (1 − sinh(2β)^(−4))^(1/8) for β > βc, so the transition is continuous.
The proof uses the self-duality of Z². It does not give the critical point of the Ising model in dimension 3 or more, where no closed form is known.

results.name: Kasteleyn–Temperley–Fisher formula for domino tilings
aliases: Kasteleyn's formula for the number of domino tilings of a rectangle
results.statement: Let R be a region of the plane that is a union of unit lattice squares and is bounded by a simple closed lattice polygon. Let G be its dual graph, with one vertex for each square and an edge between squares that share a side. Let K be the matrix indexed by the vertices of G with K_uv = 1 if u and v are horizontal neighbours, K_uv = i = √−1 if they are vertical neighbours, and K_uv = 0 otherwise. Then the number of domino tilings of R is √|det K|. For the m × n rectangle (m, n ≥ 1) this gives T(m, n) = ∏_{j=1}^{m} ∏_{k=1}^{n} (4cos²(πj/(m+1)) + 4cos²(πk/(n+1)))^{1/4}, and for m and n both even T(m, n) = ∏_{j=1}^{m/2} ∏_{k=1}^{n/2} (4cos²(πj/(m+1)) + 4cos²(πk/(n+1))).
hypotheses: R is a union of unit lattice squares bounded by a simple closed lattice polygon, so R is simply connected.
For the product formula, R is the m × n rectangle with m, n ≥ 1.

prerequisites.reason: Step s4 uses the Jordan curve theorem to show that the vertices strictly inside an alternating cycle are matched among themselves.

definitions.name: domino tiling
definitions.text: A covering of R by 1 × 2 and 2 × 1 rectangles (dominoes) with disjoint interiors, each made of two lattice squares of R.

definitions.name: Kasteleyn matrix
definitions.text: The weighted adjacency matrix K of the statement, with weight 1 on horizontal edges and weight i on vertical edges of the dual graph.

source.citation: Richard Kenyon, An introduction to the dimer model, lecture notes, arXiv:math/0310326 [math.CO], 2003.
source.revision: arXiv v1 of 20 October 2003.
source.module: Section 2 The number of domino tilings of a chessboard, Sections 2.1 Combinatorics and 2.2 Rectangles
source.excerpt: Theorem 1 [Kasteleyn, 1961] The number of domino tilings of R is √|det K|, where K is the weighted adjacency matrix of the graph G, with horizontal edges weighted 1 and vertical edges weighted i = √−1.
source.attribution: © Richard Kenyon. Quoted from the author's lecture notes for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: Theorem 1 of the source is the general counting theorem for a region R bounded by a simple closed polygonal curve, with its proof on pp. 1-2. The product formula for rectangles is derived without a label in Section 2.2 on p. 3, which gives the eigenvalues and det K. The authored statement combines both and adds the explicit fourth-root and even-side forms. The outline follows Kenyon's proof and his computation for rectangles.

results.proof_status: outline of the cited published proof. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow Kenyon's proof of Theorem 1 in Section 2.1 (pp. 1-2) and his rectangle computation in Section 2.2 (p. 3) of An introduction to the dimer model. Step s3 takes the sign rule for a cycle from Lemma 1 of the source, which the source states with the remark that it follows by induction.

steps.text: Matchings and the bipartite block form. A domino covers exactly two squares that share a side, so domino tilings of R correspond bijectively to perfect matchings of G. Colour the squares as a chessboard. Then G is bipartite, and with the white vertices first K = [[0, A], [Aᵗ, 0]], where A_wb = 1 or i for horizontal or vertical neighbours w, b. If the two colour classes have different sizes, there is no perfect matching, and det K = 0 because rank K = 2 rank A is less than the size of K. Otherwise A is square and |det K| = |det A|².

Terms of the determinant. det A = Σ_σ sgn(σ) ∏_w A_{w,σ(w)}, where σ runs over bijections from white to black vertices. A term is nonzero exactly when every w is adjacent to σ(w), that is, when the edges {w, σ(w)} form a perfect matching. So the nonzero terms correspond to the tilings, and each has modulus 1 because all weights are 1 or i. Hence |det A| equals the number of tilings if and only if all nonzero terms have the same complex phase.

Comparison along one cycle. The union of two perfect matchings M₁ and M₂ is a set of doubled edges and disjoint even cycles, and M₁ becomes M₂ by exchanging the edges along each cycle in turn. So it suffices to compare matchings that differ along one simple cycle C of length 2k. Their permutations differ by a k-cycle, which gives the factor (−1)^(k−1). Lemma 1 of the source states that the weight products m₁ and m₂ of the two alternating edge sets of C satisfy m₁ = (−1)^(n+k+1) m₂, where n is the number of lattice points strictly inside C. So the ratio of the two terms is (−1)^(k−1)(−1)^(n+k+1) = (−1)^n.

The number of enclosed vertices is even. Because R is bounded by a simple closed curve, every lattice point strictly inside C is a vertex of G. By the Jordan curve theorem, a lattice edge from a point strictly inside C to a point strictly outside C would meet C. This is impossible, because two lattice edges meet only at lattice points and neither end lies on C. The vertices on C are matched along C. So M₁ matches the n interior vertices among themselves, and n is even. By s3 all nonzero terms of det A have the same phase, and by s1 and s2 the number of tilings is |det A| = √|det K|.

Eigenvectors for the rectangle. For the m × n grid, (Kf)(x, y) = f(x − 1, y) + f(x + 1, y) + i f(x, y − 1) + i f(x, y + 1), with f = 0 outside the grid. Section 2.2 of the source states that f_jk(x, y) = sin(πjx/(m+1)) sin(πky/(n+1)) is an eigenvector with eigenvalue λ_jk = 2cos(πj/(m+1)) + 2i cos(πk/(n+1)). This follows from sin(θ(x − 1)) + sin(θ(x + 1)) = 2cos θ sin(θx) and from sin(0) = sin(πj) = 0, which match the zero values outside the grid. For 1 ≤ j ≤ m and 1 ≤ k ≤ n the f_jk are orthogonal, so they form a basis and det K = ∏_{j,k} λ_jk.

Product formula. Since |λ_jk|² = 4cos²(πj/(m+1)) + 4cos²(πk/(n+1)), s4 and s5 give T(m, n) = √|det K| = ∏_{j,k} (4cos²(πj/(m+1)) + 4cos²(πk/(n+1)))^{1/4}. If m and n are even, j ↦ m + 1 − j changes the sign of cos(πj/(m+1)) and has no fixed point, and the same holds for k. So each factor with j ≤ m/2 and k ≤ n/2 occurs exactly four times, and T(m, n) = ∏_{j=1}^{m/2} ∏_{k=1}^{n/2} (4cos²(πj/(m+1)) + 4cos²(πk/(n+1))). For m = n = 8 the source evaluates this as 12988816.

source.ref: R. Kenyon, An introduction to the dimer model, arXiv:math/0310326, Theorem 1 (p. 1) with its proof and Lemma 1 (pp. 1-2), and Section 2.2 Rectangles (p. 3).

applications.title: Dimer configurations of small square boards
applications.inputs: The 4 × 4 square and the 2 × 4 rectangle, seen as dimer models with all dimer weights equal to 1.
applications.hypotheses: Both regions are rectangles bounded by simple closed lattice polygons, and both have even sides, so the even-side product formula applies.

steps.text: With m = n = 4 the angles are π/5 and 2π/5. Put A = 4cos²(π/5) = (3 + √5)/2 and B = 4cos²(2π/5) = (3 − √5)/2, so A + B = 3 and AB = (9 − 5)/4 = 1.
The four factors are 2A, A + B, A + B and 2B, so T(4, 4) = 4AB(A + B)² = 4 · 1 · 9 = 36.
With m = 2 the only angle in the first factor is π/3 and 4cos²(π/3) = 1. So T(2, 4) = (1 + A)(1 + B) = 1 + (A + B) + AB = 5, which is the Fibonacci number for a strip of width 2.

applications.conclusion: The formula gives 36 dimer coverings of the 4 × 4 board and 5 of the 2 × 4 board, which agree with direct counts. The same formula gives 12988816 for the 8 × 8 chessboard.

limitations: The proof uses a simply connected region. On a torus or a region with holes, one determinant is not enough, and Kasteleyn uses a combination of four determinants.
The asymptotic growth exp(Gmn/π + O(m + n)), with G the Catalan constant, needs a further Riemann-sum argument that this record does not prove.

results.name: Heilmann–Lieb theorem on the zeros of the monomer-dimer partition function
results.statement: Let G = (V, E) be a finite simple graph with n vertices and let each edge e have a weight w_e > 0 (w ≡ 1 gives the unweighted case). For k ≥ 0 let m_k be the sum over all matchings M with k edges of the products ∏_{e∈M} w_e, so m_0 = 1. Then the matching polynomial µ_G(x) = Σ_{k≥0} (−1)^k m_k x^{n−2k} has only real roots. Equivalently, every zero of the monomer-dimer partition function Z_G(λ) = Σ_{k≥0} m_k λ^k is a negative real number.
hypotheses: G is a finite simple graph.
Every edge weight w_e is strictly positive.
results.empty_prerequisites_reason: The proof is a direct induction on the number of vertices that uses only the vertex recurrence of the matching polynomial and arithmetic of complex numbers.

definitions.name: matching
definitions.text: A set of edges of G no two of which share a vertex. The empty set is a matching with 0 edges.

definitions.name: monomer-dimer partition function
definitions.text: Z_G(λ) = Σ_k m_k λ^k, where λ is the activity of a dimer (a matched edge) and every unmatched vertex is a monomer. It satisfies µ_G(x) = x^n Z_G(−1/x²) for x ≠ 0.

source.citation: Adam W. Marcus, Daniel A. Spielman and Nikhil Srivastava, Interlacing families I: Bipartite Ramanujan graphs of all degrees, Annals of Mathematics 182 (2015) 307-325, arXiv:1304.4132 [math.CO].
source.revision: arXiv v2 of 3 March 2014.
source.module: Section 3 2-Lifts and The Matching Polynomial
source.excerpt: Theorem 3.1 (Theorem 4.2 in [22]). For every graph G, µG (x) has only real roots.
source.attribution: © the authors. Quoted from the arXiv preprint for identification of the cited result.

source.alignment: The source defines µ_G(x) = Σ_i x^{n−2i}(−1)^i m_i for an unweighted graph just before the theorem, attributes Theorem 3.1 to Theorem 4.2 of O. J. Heilmann and E. H. Lieb, Theory of monomer-dimer systems, Comm. Math. Phys. 25 (1972), and remarks that the proof is elementary and uses only recurrence formulas, but gives no proof. The authored statement allows positive edge weights, which Heilmann and Lieb also treat, and adds the equivalent form for Z_G. The authored proof is the standard induction with the vertex recurrence. It was not compared with the text of Heilmann and Lieb.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the recurrence method that Marcus, Spielman and Srivastava name for their Theorem 3.1. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Real-rootedness of µ_G and negativity of the zeros of Z_G for every finite simple graph with positive edge weights.

steps.text: Vertex recurrence. Put µ = 1 for the graph with no vertices. For a vertex u of G, split the matchings by the edge at u. Matchings that do not cover u are the matchings of G − u, with the same sign and weight and one extra factor x. Matchings that contain the edge uv are {uv} ∪ M′ with M′ a matching of G − u − v, with one more edge, so an extra factor −w_uv. Hence µ_G(x) = x µ_{G−u}(x) − Σ_{v∼u} w_uv µ_{G−u−v}(x).

Induction claim. For every graph H with at least one vertex, every vertex u of H and every z with Im z > 0: µ_H(z) ≠ 0, µ_{H−u}(z) ≠ 0 and Im(µ_H(z)/µ_{H−u}(z)) ≥ Im z. For one vertex, µ_H(z) = z and µ_{H−u} = 1, so the claim holds. Assume it for all graphs with fewer than n vertices and let H have n ≥ 2 vertices. Then µ_{H−u}(z) ≠ 0 by the induction hypothesis applied to H − u, which has n − 1 ≥ 1 vertices.

Induction step. By s1, f = µ_H(z)/µ_{H−u}(z) = z − Σ_{v∼u} w_uv/g_v with g_v = µ_{H−u}(z)/µ_{H−u−v}(z). For each neighbour v, the induction hypothesis for the graph H − u at its vertex v gives µ_{H−u−v}(z) ≠ 0 and Im g_v ≥ Im z > 0. Then Im(1/g_v) = −Im g_v/|g_v|² < 0, and since w_uv > 0 each term −w_uv/g_v has positive imaginary part. So Im f ≥ Im z > 0, f ≠ 0 and µ_H(z) = f µ_{H−u}(z) ≠ 0. This proves the claim for H.

Real roots. By s2 and s3, µ_G has no zero in the upper half-plane. Its coefficients are real, so µ_G(z̄) is the complex conjugate of µ_G(z), and µ_G has no zero in the lower half-plane either. Hence all roots of µ_G are real.

Monomer-dimer form. For x ≠ 0, x^n Z_G(−1/x²) = Σ_k (−1)^k m_k x^{n−2k} = µ_G(x). Suppose Z_G(λ₀) = 0. Then λ₀ ≠ 0 because Z_G(0) = 1. If λ₀ were not a negative real number, then −1/λ₀ would not be a positive real number, so a square root x₀ of −1/λ₀ would not be real. But µ_G(x₀) = x₀^n Z_G(λ₀) = 0 would contradict s4. So every zero of Z_G is a negative real number.

applications.title: Monomer-dimer zeros of the six-cycle
applications.inputs: The cycle C₆ (the carbon ring of benzene) with unit edge weights.
applications.hypotheses: C₆ is a finite simple graph and all weights equal 1 > 0.

steps.text: C₆ has 6 edges, 9 pairs of disjoint edges (15 pairs minus 6 adjacent pairs) and 2 perfect matchings. So Z(λ) = 1 + 6λ + 9λ² + 2λ³ = (1 + 2λ)(1 + 4λ + λ²).
The linear factor vanishes at λ = −1/2, which is negative.
The quadratic factor λ² + 4λ + 1 has discriminant 12 > 0, so its roots −2 ± √3 are real, and they are negative because their sum is −4 and their product is 1.
At unit activity the mean number of dimers is Z′(1)/Z(1) = (6 + 18 + 6)/18.

applications.conclusion: All three zeros −1/2 and −2 ± √3 of the monomer-dimer partition function of C₆ are negative reals, as the theorem states. So µ(x) = x⁶ − 6x⁴ + 9x² − 2 has the six real roots ±√2 and ±√(2 ± √3).

limitations: The theorem locates the zeros for each finite graph. The absence of a phase transition in the monomer-dimer model at positive activity needs a further limit argument, which this record does not prove.
The bound 2√(d − 1) on the roots for maximum degree d (Theorem 4.3 of Heilmann and Lieb) is a separate result.

results.name: Edwards–Sokal coupling
aliases: Edwards–Sokal coupling of the Potts and random-cluster models
random-cluster representation of the Potts model
results.statement: Let G = (V, E) be a finite graph, let q ≥ 2 be an integer, let p ∈ (0, 1) and let J = −ln(1 − p). On {1, …, q}^V × {0, 1}^E define the probability measure P(σ, ω) = Z⁻¹ ∏_{xy∈E} [(1 − p) 1{ω_xy = 0} + p 1{ω_xy = 1} 1{σ_x = σ_y}], with Z the normalizing constant. Then: (a) the law of σ is the q-state Potts measure μ(σ) ∝ exp(J ∑_{xy∈E} 1{σ_x = σ_y}). (b) The law of ω is the random-cluster measure φ(ω) ∝ p^{o(ω)} (1 − p)^{c(ω)} q^{k(ω)}, where o(ω) and c(ω) count open and closed edges and k(ω) counts the clusters of (V, open edges), isolated vertices included. (c) Given ω, σ is constant on each cluster, and the values on distinct clusters are independent and uniform on {1, …, q}. (d) Given σ, the edges are independent, an edge xy with σ_x ≠ σ_y is closed, and an edge with σ_x = σ_y is open with probability p. (e) For all x, y ∈ V, μ(σ_x = σ_y) = 1/q + (1 − 1/q) φ(x ↔ y).
hypotheses: The graph G = (V, E) is finite.
The number of spin values q ≥ 2 is an integer, and p ∈ (0, 1) is related to the coupling constant by J = −ln(1 − p).

prerequisites.reason: Step s5 averages the conditional probability of {σ_x = σ_y} given ω over the law of ω.

definitions.name: Potts measure
definitions.text: The probability measure on {1, …, q}^V proportional to exp(J ∑_{xy∈E} 1{σ_x = σ_y}). For q = 2 and spins ±1 it is the Ising measure at inverse temperature J/2.

definitions.name: random-cluster measure
definitions.text: The probability measure on {0, 1}^E proportional to p^{o(ω)} (1 − p)^{c(ω)} q^{k(ω)}, with free boundary conditions. For q = 1 it is Bernoulli bond percolation.

definitions.name: compatible pair
definitions.text: A spin configuration σ and an edge configuration ω are compatible if σ_x = σ_y for every open edge xy. The measure P gives positive mass exactly to compatible pairs.

source.citation: Hugo Duminil-Copin, Lectures on the Ising and Potts models on the hypercubic lattice, in PIMS-CRM Summer School in Probability, Springer Proceedings in Mathematics and Statistics 298, 2019. arXiv:1707.00520.
source.revision: arXiv v1, July 4, 2017.
source.module: Chapter 1, Section 1.2.2 The coupling between the random-cluster and Potts models
source.excerpt: Proposition 1.2 (Coupling for free boundary conditions) Fix an integer q ≥ 2, p ∈ (0, 1) and G finite. If ω is distributed according to φ⁰_{G,p,q} then σ constructed above is distributed according to the q-state Potts measure µ^f_{G,β,q}, where β := −((q−1)/q) ln(1 − p).
source.attribution: © Hugo Duminil-Copin. Quoted from the author's lecture notes Lectures on the Ising and Potts models on the hypercubic lattice for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source colours the clusters of a random-cluster configuration uniformly and proves that the spins have the Potts law. Its spins lie in a simplex T_q with σ_x · σ_y = −1/(q − 1) for distinct spins, so its β equals J(q − 1)/q in the authored notation. The authored statement writes the joint Edwards–Sokal measure and adds the second marginal, both conditional laws and the two-point formula of the source's Corollary 1.4. The authored proof uses the compatibility computation of the source proof.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the compatibility computation in the proof of Proposition 1.2 of the cited notes. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement (a) to (e) for every finite graph, every integer q ≥ 2 and every p ∈ (0, 1).

steps.text: Weights. Write w(σ, ω) = ∏_{xy∈E} [(1 − p) 1{ω_xy = 0} + p 1{ω_xy = 1} 1{σ_x = σ_y}]. Then w(σ, ω) = p^{o(ω)} (1 − p)^{c(ω)} if σ and ω are compatible, and w(σ, ω) = 0 otherwise. The pair with σ constant and all edges closed has weight (1 − p)^{|E|} > 0, so Z = ∑ w is positive and P is a probability measure.

Spin marginal. Fix σ. The weight is a product over edges, so the sum over ω factorizes: ∑_ω w(σ, ω) = ∏_{xy∈E} [(1 − p) + p 1{σ_x = σ_y}]. An edge with σ_x = σ_y contributes 1, and an edge with σ_x ≠ σ_y contributes 1 − p = e^(−J). So ∑_ω w(σ, ω) = e^(−J|E|) exp(J ∑_{xy∈E} 1{σ_x = σ_y}). The factor e^(−J|E|) does not depend on σ, which proves (a).

Edge marginal. Fix ω. By step s1, ∑_σ w(σ, ω) = p^{o(ω)} (1 − p)^{c(ω)} N(ω), where N(ω) is the number of σ compatible with ω. A configuration σ is compatible exactly when it is constant on every cluster of (V, open edges), because each cluster is connected by open edges. So N(ω) = q^{k(ω)}, which proves (b).

Conditional laws. For fixed ω with P(ω) > 0, P(σ | ω) is proportional to w(σ, ω), which is the same positive number for all compatible σ and 0 otherwise. So σ is uniform on the q^{k(ω)} configurations that are constant on clusters, which means independent uniform values on distinct clusters. This is (c). For fixed σ, P(ω | σ) is proportional to the product w(σ, ω) of edge factors, so the edges are independent. An edge with σ_x ≠ σ_y has factors 1 − p and 0 for ω_xy = 0 and 1, so it is closed. An edge with σ_x = σ_y has factors 1 − p and p, so it is open with probability p. This is (d).

Two-point formula. By (c), given ω, σ_x = σ_y holds surely if x and y lie in the same cluster. Otherwise σ_x and σ_y are independent and uniform, and they agree with probability 1/q. So P(σ_x = σ_y | ω) = 1{x ↔ y} + q⁻¹ 1{x ↮ y}. Average over ω with (b) and the law of total probability: μ(σ_x = σ_y) = φ(x ↔ y) + q⁻¹(1 − φ(x ↔ y)) = 1/q + (1 − 1/q) φ(x ↔ y). This is (e).

applications.title: Ising correlation on a triangle from its random-cluster representation
applications.inputs: The triangle graph with vertices 1, 2, 3 and three edges, q = 2 and p = 1/2, so J = ln 2. The Potts weight of σ is 2^{a(σ)}, where a(σ) is the number of edges with equal spins.
applications.hypotheses: The graph is finite, q = 2 is an integer, and p = 1/2 lies in (0, 1).

steps.text: Potts side: the 2 constant configurations have a = 3 and weight 8. The other 6 configurations have a = 1 and weight 2. So the partition function is 16 + 12 = 28. The configurations with σ₁ = σ₂ are the 2 constant ones and 2 with σ₃ different, with total weight 16 + 4 = 20.

Random-cluster side: every ω has weight (1/2)^3 · 2^{k(ω)}. The empty configuration has k = 3, the 3 one-edge configurations have k = 2, and the 4 others have k = 1. Up to the common factor 1/8, the total is 8 + 3·4 + 3·2 + 2 = 28. The configurations with 1 ↔ 2 are {12} with weight 4, the two others that contain 12 with weight 2 each, {13, 23} with weight 2, and the full one with weight 2. Their total is 12.
The two-point formula (e) with q = 2 predicts μ(σ₁ = σ₂) = 1/2 + (1/2) φ(1 ↔ 2) = 1/2 + (1/2)(3/7). This equals the direct value 5/7 of step a1.
With spins ±1, the Ising correlation is ⟨σ₁σ₂⟩ = 2 μ(σ₁ = σ₂) − 1 = 3/7. It equals the connection probability φ(1 ↔ 2) of the random-cluster model, as (e) gives for q = 2.

applications.conclusion: On the triangle at J = ln 2, the Ising two-point correlation is 3/7, which is the random-cluster connection probability of the two vertices.

limitations: The coupling needs an integer q ≥ 2. The random-cluster measure is defined for every real q > 0, but it has no spin representation when q is not an integer.

The statement uses free boundary conditions on a finite graph. Wired or monochromatic boundary conditions need the modified colouring of the source's Proposition 1.3, and infinite-volume measures need a limit.
The coupling is for ferromagnetic couplings J ≥ 0. Antiferromagnetic Potts models have no such positive representation.

results.name: Burton–Keane uniqueness theorem
aliases: Burton–Keane uniqueness of the infinite cluster
results.statement: Let d ≥ 1 and consider bond percolation on ℤ^d, in which each edge between nearest neighbours is open with probability p ∈ [0, 1], independently of the other edges. Let N ∈ {0, 1, 2, …, ∞} be the number of infinite open clusters. Then P_p(N ≤ 1) = 1. In particular, if θ(p) = P_p(the origin lies in an infinite open cluster) > 0, then P_p(N = 1) = 1.
hypotheses: The edges of ℤ^d are open independently, each with the same probability p ∈ [0, 1].
The graph is the hypercubic lattice ℤ^d, which is invariant under translations and has boxes Λ_n = {−n, …, n}^d with |∂Λ_n|/|Λ_n| → 0.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 shows with Dynkin's π-λ theorem that every event is approximated by events that depend on finitely many edges.
Step s3 takes an infinite self-avoiding open path inside an infinite cluster with Kőnig's infinity lemma.
Step s3 bounds the probability of a trifurcation somewhere in a finite ball by the sum over its vertices.

definitions.name: trifurcation
definitions.text: A vertex t is a trifurcation if it lies in an infinite open cluster, exactly three open edges meet t, and their other endpoints lie in three distinct infinite clusters of the open graph with t removed.

definitions.name: translation-invariant event
definitions.text: An event A with τ_x A = A for every x ∈ ℤ^d, where τ_x shifts every configuration by the vector x. The events {N = k} are of this kind.

source.citation: Hugo Duminil-Copin, Introduction to Bernoulli percolation, lecture notes, Institut des Hautes Études Scientifiques, 2018.
source.revision: Author's online version dated October 7, 2018, 30 pages.
source.module: Chapter 3, Section 3.1 Uniqueness of the infinite connected component
source.excerpt: Theorem 3.1 If p ∈ [0, 1] is such that θ(p) > 0, then Pp[∃ a unique infinite cluster] = 1. This result was first proved by Aizenman, Kesten and Newman in [2]. It was later obtained via different types of arguments. The beautiful argument presented here is due to Burton and Keane [10].
source.attribution: © Hugo Duminil-Copin. Quoted from the author's lecture notes Introduction to Bernoulli percolation for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states uniqueness when θ(p) > 0. The authored statement also gives P_p(N ≤ 1) = 1 for every p. The authored proof follows the Burton–Keane argument of the source on pp. 11-13: ergodicity, insertion of open edges in a box, and a deterministic bound on the number of trifurcations. It builds the trifurcation inside an ℓ¹ ball and proves the counting bound by induction instead of the forest peeling of the source.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the Burton–Keane argument in the proof of Theorem 3.1 of the cited notes. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement for every d ≥ 1 and p ∈ [0, 1]. The cases p = 0 and p = 1 are trivial (N = 0 and N = 1), so the steps take p ∈ (0, 1).

steps.text: Ergodicity. P_p is invariant under each shift τ_x, because τ_x permutes independent coordinates with the same law. Let 𝒟 be the class of events A such that, for every ε > 0, some event B that depends on finitely many edges has P_p(A Δ B) < ε. 𝒟 contains the π-system of such B, and it is closed under complements and countable disjoint unions, so Dynkin's theorem puts every event in 𝒟. Let A be invariant and ε > 0, take B as above with its edges in a box, and choose x so that τ_x B depends on edges disjoint from those of B. Then P_p(B ∩ τ_x B) = P_p(B)², while P_p(A) = P_p(A ∩ τ_x A) differs from P_p(B ∩ τ_x B) by less than 2ε. Hence |P_p(A) − P_p(A)²| < 4ε, and P_p(A) ∈ {0, 1}. Since each {N = k} is invariant, N is almost surely equal to a constant k ∈ {0, 1, 2, …, ∞}.

No finite k ≥ 2. Suppose N = k a.s. with 2 ≤ k < ∞. Let G_n be the event that N = k and every infinite cluster meets Λ_n. G_n increases to {N = k}, so P_p(G_n) ≥ 1/2 for some n. Let E_n be the finite set of edges with both endpoints in Λ_n, and write ω = (ξ, η) with ξ = ω on E_n. The set G′ of η such that (ξ, η) ∈ G_n for some ξ is a finite union of sections, hence measurable, and P_p(η ∈ G′) ≥ P_p(G_n). On {ξ ≡ 1} ∩ {η ∈ G′}, opening E_n joins all k infinite clusters through Λ_n. Opening finitely many edges creates no new infinite cluster, so N = 1 there. Independence gives P_p(N = 1) ≥ p^{|E_n|}/2 > 0, which contradicts N = k a.s.

Trifurcations have positive probability if N = ∞. Let B_r = {x : |x|₁ ≤ r} and S_R = {|x|₁ = R}. Let ω^out keep only the edges with no endpoint in B_{R−1}, and let I_R be the other edges. Choose R with P_p(three infinite clusters meet B_{R−1}) ≥ 1/2. Kőnig's lemma gives an infinite self-avoiding open path in each of them from B_{R−1}. After its last visit to B_{R−1}, it continues from a point of S_R in ω^out. So with probability at least 1/2, an event A_R that depends on ω^out only holds: three points x, y, z ∈ S_R lie in distinct infinite clusters of ω^out. Choose them by a fixed rule. Points of S_R are pairwise non-adjacent and have neighbours in the connected set B_{R−1}. So there is a path P₁ from x to y with inner vertices in B_{R−1}, and a shortest path P₂ from z to an inner vertex u of P₁ with inner vertices in B_{R−1}. The tree P₁ ∪ P₂ has its edges in I_R. If exactly its edges are open in I_R, then u is a trifurcation, because the three branches meet only at u and reach the three clusters. Independence gives P_p(some u ∈ B_{R−1} is a trifurcation) ≥ min(p, 1 − p)^{|I_R|}/2. The union bound and translation invariance give P_p(T₀) > 0, where T₀ is the event that 0 is a trifurcation.

Counting lemma. Let H be a finite connected graph, Y a set of its vertices and T a set of vertices outside Y such that H − t has at least three components that meet Y for each t ∈ T. Then |T| ≤ max(0, |Y| − 2). Induction on the number of vertices: take t ∈ T and the components H_j of H − t. Let H_j′ be H_j with t added back, and let Y_j = (Y ∩ H_j) ∪ {t}. Each t′ ∈ T ∩ H_j satisfies the hypothesis in H_j′ with Y_j, because the component of H − t′ that contains t also contains at least two other H_i that meet Y. Components that miss Y contain no point of T. The m ≥ 3 components that meet Y give |T| ≤ 1 + ∑_j (|Y ∩ H_j| − 1) = 1 + |Y| − m ≤ |Y| − 2.

Contradiction. Let H be the graph on Λ_n of open edges with both endpoints in Λ_n, Y = ∂Λ_n and T the trifurcations in Λ_{n−1}. For t ∈ T, the three open neighbours of t lie in distinct infinite clusters of ω − t. Each such cluster reaches ∂Λ_n by a path inside Λ_n, so H − t has three components that meet Y. Step s4 applied to each component of H gives |T| ≤ |∂Λ_n|. Taking expectations and using translation invariance, |Λ_{n−1}| P_p(T₀) ≤ |∂Λ_n| = (2n + 1)^d − (2n − 1)^d. The ratio |∂Λ_n|/|Λ_{n−1}| tends to 0, so P_p(T₀) = 0. This contradicts step s3, so N = ∞ has probability 0.

Conclusion. By steps s1, s2 and s5, N is a.s. a constant in {0, 1}, so P_p(N ≤ 1) = 1. If θ(p) > 0, then P_p(N ≥ 1) ≥ θ(p) > 0, and the constant must be 1. So there is a.s. exactly one infinite cluster.

applications.title: Long-range connectivity in supercritical percolation on the square lattice
applications.inputs: Bond percolation on ℤ² at p = 9/10, with the lower bound θ(9/10) ≥ 46489/49000 from the dual circuit count of nm:statphys-nontrivial-critical-probability. Two vertices x and y at any distance.
applications.hypotheses: The edges are independent with the same parameter p. Since θ(9/10) > 0, the theorem gives a unique infinite cluster almost surely.

steps.text: If x and y both lie in infinite clusters, uniqueness puts them in the same cluster. So P_p(x ↔ y) ≥ P_p(x ↔ ∞ and y ↔ ∞).
The events {x ↔ ∞} and {y ↔ ∞} are increasing. The Harris–FKG inequality nm:harris-kleitman-inequality and translation invariance give P_p(x ↔ ∞ and y ↔ ∞) ≥ θ(p)².
The bound does not depend on the distance between x and y. Without uniqueness, two distinct infinite clusters could hold x and y, and no such uniform bound would follow.

applications.conclusion: At p = 9/10 on ℤ², every two vertices are joined by an open path with probability at least 2161227121/2401000000, about 0.90, at every distance.

limitations: The proof needs a graph whose boxes have small boundary compared with their volume (amenability). On non-amenable graphs, such as regular trees of degree at least 3, infinitely many infinite clusters can coexist.
The theorem says nothing about the critical point itself, where θ(p_c) may be 0 and there may be no infinite cluster.
The same argument works for every translation-invariant measure with the finite-energy property, for example random-cluster measures.

results.name: Harris–Kesten theorem
aliases: Kesten's theorem on the critical probability of the square lattice
results.statement: For bond percolation on the square lattice ℤ², in which each nearest-neighbour edge is open with probability p independently, the critical probability is p_c = 1/2. Moreover θ(1/2) = 0: at p = 1/2 there is almost surely no infinite open cluster.
hypotheses: The lattice is ℤ² with nearest-neighbour edges.
The edges are open independently, each with the same probability p.

prerequisites.reason: Step s2 uses the Harris inequality for increasing events in the square-root trick.
Step s2 uses the uniqueness of the infinite cluster to join a left crossing and a right crossing.
Step s4 uses exponential decay of P_p(0 ↔ ∂Λ_n) for p < p_c to show that crossing probabilities tend to 0.

definitions.name: dual configuration
definitions.text: The dual lattice is ℤ² + (1/2, 1/2). Each dual edge e* crosses one edge e of ℤ² and is open exactly when e is closed. Under P_p the dual configuration has the law P_{1−p}.

definitions.name: horizontal crossing
definitions.text: H_n is the event that an open path inside the rectangle R_n = [0, n] × [0, n − 1] joins its left side to its right side.

source.citation: Hugo Duminil-Copin, Introduction to Bernoulli percolation, lecture notes, Institut des Hautes Études Scientifiques, 2018.
source.revision: Author's online version dated October 7, 2018, 30 pages.
source.module: Chapter 4, Section 4.1 Kesten's theorem
source.excerpt: Theorem 4.3 (Kesten) For Bernoulli percolation on Z², pc is equal to 1/2. Furthermore, there is no infinite cluster at pc.
source.attribution: © Hugo Duminil-Copin. Quoted from the author's lecture notes Introduction to Bernoulli percolation for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The authored statement is the statement of the source. Harris proved θ(1/2) = 0 in 1960 and Kesten proved p_c = 1/2 in 1980, so the result carries both names. The outline follows the proof of the source, which combines self-duality, Proposition 4.1, Corollary 4.2 and the sharpness theorem 3.3.

results.proof_status: outline of the cited published proof. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of Theorem 4.3 in Duminil-Copin, Introduction to Bernoulli percolation (2018), Section 4.1, pp. 18-21. Step s1 takes the duality of crossings from the source, and step s2 takes Proposition 4.1 from the source.

steps.text: Self-duality at p = 1/2. Let R_n = [0, n] × [0, n − 1] and let H_n be the event of an open left-right crossing of R_n. The source observes (Fig. 4, eq. (4.1)) that H_n fails exactly when the dual rectangle R_n* has an open top-bottom dual crossing. The dual rectangle, rotated by π/2, is isomorphic to R_n, and the dual configuration has law P_{1−p}. At p = 1/2 the two events have the same probability and are complements, so P_{1/2}(H_n) = 1/2 for every n ≥ 1.

Proposition 4.1 of the source: if θ(p) > 0 then P_p(H_n) → 1. The four events that Λ_k is joined inside Λ_n to the left, right, top or bottom side are increasing, have equal probability by symmetry, and their union contains {Λ_k ↔ ∞}. The Harris inequality applied to their complements gives the square-root trick P_p(Λ_k joined to the left side) ≥ 1 − P_p(Λ_k ↮ ∞)^(1/4). Put one copy of Λ_k near the middle of R_n joined to the left side and a neighbouring copy joined to the right side. This happens with probability at least 1 − 2P_p(Λ_k ↮ ∞)^(1/4). Uniqueness of the infinite cluster makes the probability that the two connections lie in distinct clusters tend to 0, so lim inf P_p(H_n) ≥ 1 − 2P_p(Λ_k ↮ ∞)^(1/4). This tends to 1 as k → ∞, since an infinite cluster exists almost surely.

Corollary 4.2 of the source: θ(1/2) = 0, hence p_c ≥ 1/2. Indeed, if θ(1/2) > 0, step s2 would give P_{1/2}(H_n) → 1, which contradicts P_{1/2}(H_n) = 1/2 from step s1. For p < 1/2, monotonicity in p gives θ(p) ≤ θ(1/2) = 0, so p_c ≥ 1/2.

Upper bound p_c ≤ 1/2. Suppose p < p_c. The sharpness theorem gives c_p > 0 with P_p(0 ↔ ∂Λ_n) ≤ exp(−c_p n) for all n. A left-right crossing of R_n starts at some (0, k) with 0 ≤ k ≤ n − 1 and reaches distance n from it. The union bound and translation invariance give P_p(H_n) ≤ n P_p(0 ↔ ∂Λ_n) ≤ n exp(−c_p n) → 0. If p_c > 1/2, take p = 1/2: then P_{1/2}(H_n) → 0, which contradicts step s1. So p_c ≤ 1/2.

Conclusion. Steps s3 and s4 give p_c = 1/2. Step s3 gives θ(p_c) = θ(1/2) = 0, so at p_c there is no infinite cluster almost surely, by the union bound over the countably many vertices and translation invariance. The source records this as Remark 4.4.

source.ref: H. Duminil-Copin, Introduction to Bernoulli percolation, lecture notes (IHES, version of October 7, 2018), Proposition 4.1, Corollary 4.2 and Theorem 4.3, pp. 19-21.

applications.title: Bond dilution threshold of a square-lattice network
applications.inputs: A square-lattice network in which each bond is present with probability p, independently. Three densities: p = 9/20, p = 1/2 and p = 11/20.
applications.hypotheses: The bonds are independent with a common parameter, as in bond percolation on ℤ².

steps.text: At p = 1/2 = p_c, self-duality gives the crossing probability P_{1/2}(H_n) = 1/2 for the rectangle [0, n] × [0, n − 1] at every size n, and there is no infinite cluster.
At p = 9/20 < p_c, step s4 gives P_p(H_n) ≤ n exp(−c_p n). So large networks with 45% of the bonds almost never conduct from left to right.
At p = 11/20 > p_c, the mean-field bound of the sharpness theorem with p_c = 1/2 gives θ(11/20) ≥ (11/20 − 1/2)/((11/20)(1 − 1/2)) = 2/11.
Since θ(11/20) > 0, step s2 gives P_p(H_n) → 1. So large networks with 55% of the bonds conduct with probability close to 1, and the change happens exactly at one half.

applications.conclusion: The square-lattice bond network changes from almost surely non-conducting to almost surely conducting at exactly half of the bonds. At 55% each vertex lies in the infinite cluster with probability at least 2/11.

limitations: The proof uses the self-duality of ℤ² at p = 1/2. On other planar lattices the same method gives p_c(G) + p_c(G*) = 1, but it does not give the value of p_c without an extra symmetry.
The theorem gives no critical exponents. The behaviour of θ(p) as p ↓ 1/2 is known in detail only for site percolation on the triangular lattice.

results.name: van den Berg–Kesten inequality
results.statement: Let E be a finite set and let P be a product measure on Ω = {0, 1}^E, with independent coordinates ω_e and P(ω_e = 1) = p_e ∈ [0, 1]. A set K ⊆ E is a witness of an event A at ω if every ω′ ∈ Ω that agrees with ω on K is in A. Two events A and B occur disjointly at ω, written ω ∈ A ∘ B, if there are disjoint sets K and L that are witnesses of A and of B at ω. If A and B are increasing events, then P(A ∘ B) ≤ P(A) P(B).
hypotheses: The set E is finite, and P is a product of Bernoulli measures with parameters p_e ∈ [0, 1].
The events A and B are increasing: if ω is in the event and ω ≤ ω′ coordinatewise, then ω′ is in the event.

prerequisites.reason: Step s5 averages the conditional comparison of step s4 over the coordinates other than the j-th pair.

definitions.name: witness
definitions.text: A set K ⊆ E is a witness of A at ω if every configuration that agrees with ω on K is in A. The witness may depend on ω.

definitions.name: disjoint occurrence
definitions.text: A ∘ B is the set of ω for which A and B have disjoint witnesses at ω. For example, two connection events occur disjointly when two edge-disjoint open paths realize them.

definitions.name: increasing event
definitions.text: An event A ⊆ {0, 1}^E such that ω ∈ A and ω ≤ ω′ in every coordinate give ω′ ∈ A.

source.citation: Hugo Duminil-Copin, Introduction to Bernoulli percolation, lecture notes, Institut des Hautes Études Scientifiques, 2018.
source.revision: Author's online version dated October 7, 2018, 30 pages.
source.module: Chapter 2, Section 2.3 The van den Berg Kesten and the Reimer inequalities
source.excerpt: Proposition 2.4 (BK-Reimer inequality) If A and B are events depending on finitely many edges, then Pp[A ○ B] ≤ Pp[A]Pp[B].
source.attribution: © Hugo Duminil-Copin. Quoted from the author's lecture notes Introduction to Bernoulli percolation for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states the inequality for all events, which is Reimer's theorem, and remarks that van den Berg and Kesten proved the case of increasing events. The authored statement is this increasing case, on a finite set of coordinates with one parameter p_e for each coordinate. The authored proof is the duplication argument that the source sets as Exercise 12 on p. 8, with a conditional comparison in place of the injection of the exercise.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the duplication argument of Exercise 12 of the cited notes. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement for increasing events on a finite product space, with one parameter for each coordinate.

steps.text: Open witnesses. Write O(ω) = {e : ω_e = 1} and 1_K for the configuration that is open exactly on K. Let C be increasing and K ⊆ O(ω). Then K is a witness of C at ω if and only if 1_K ∈ C. Indeed, 1_K agrees with ω on K, and every ω′ that agrees with ω on K satisfies ω′ ≥ 1_K. Also, if K is a witness of C at ω, then K ∩ O(ω) is a witness: an ω′ that agrees with ω on K ∩ O(ω) is at least the configuration equal to ω on K and to ω′ off K, which is in C. Hence, for increasing C and D, ω ∈ C ∘ D if and only if there are disjoint K, L ⊆ O(ω) with 1_K ∈ C and 1_L ∈ D.

Duplication. Number E = {1, …, N}. Let ω and ω′ be two independent copies with law P, and view ω̂ = (ω, ω′) as a configuration on the set Ê of 2N coordinates (i, 1) and (i, 2), with the product law P̂. For 1 ≤ j ≤ N + 1 let ω^(j) take the value ω′_i for i < j and ω_i for i ≥ j. Set Â_j = {ω^(j) ∈ A} and B̂ = {ω ∈ B}. These events are increasing in ω̂. For K̂ ⊆ Ê let π_j K̂ = {i < j : (i, 2) ∈ K̂} ∪ {i ≥ j : (i, 1) ∈ K̂}. Then 1_K̂ ∈ Â_j if and only if 1_{π_j K̂} ∈ A, and 1_K̂ ∈ B̂ if and only if 1_{π_1 K̂} ∈ B.

End points. By step s1, Â_j ∘ B̂ holds if and only if there are disjoint open sets K̂ ⊆ R_j and L̂ ⊆ R_1 with 1_{π_j K̂} ∈ A and 1_{π_1 L̂} ∈ B. Here R_j = {(i, 2) : i < j} ∪ {(i, 1) : i ≥ j} is the set of coordinates that π_j reads. We may intersect witnesses with R_j and R_1 because π_j and π_1 read nothing else. For j = 1 both sets lie in copy 1, so Â_1 ∘ B̂ = {ω ∈ A ∘ B} and P̂(Â_1 ∘ B̂) = P(A ∘ B). For j = N + 1, Â_{N+1} depends on ω′ only and B̂ on ω only. So disjoint witnesses always exist and P̂(Â_{N+1} ∘ B̂) = P̂(Â_{N+1} ∩ B̂) = P(A) P(B) by independence of the copies.

One swap. Fix j ≤ N and fix the values ξ of all coordinates except x = ω_j and y = ω′_j. Let C = Â_j ∘ B̂ and C′ = Â_{j+1} ∘ B̂. Neither R_j nor R_1 contains (j, 2), so given ξ the event C depends on x only, and it is increasing in x. Case 1: C fails at x = 1. Then P̂(C | ξ) = 0. Case 2: C holds at x = 0. Its open witnesses K̂, L̂ avoid (j, 1) and (j, 2), so π_{j+1} K̂ = π_j K̂, and K̂ ⊆ R_{j+1}. The same sets show that C′ holds for all x and y. Case 3: C holds exactly when x = 1, so P̂(C | ξ) = p_j. Take open witnesses K̂, L̂ at x = 1. If (j, 1) ∉ K̂, the same pair shows C′ ⊇ {x = 1}. If (j, 1) ∈ K̂, then (j, 1) ∉ L̂. Set K̂′ = (K̂ ∖ {(j, 1)}) ∪ {(j, 2)}. Then π_{j+1} K̂′ = π_j K̂, K̂′ ⊆ R_{j+1} is disjoint from L̂ ⊆ R_1, and L̂ does not involve x or y. So C′ ⊇ {y = 1}. In every case P̂(C′ | ξ) ≥ P̂(C | ξ), because x and y are independent of ξ with the same parameter p_j.

Conclusion. Average the inequality of step s4 over ξ with the law of total probability. This gives P̂(Â_j ∘ B̂) ≤ P̂(Â_{j+1} ∘ B̂) for 1 ≤ j ≤ N. Chain these N inequalities and use step s3 at both ends: P(A ∘ B) = P̂(Â_1 ∘ B̂) ≤ P̂(Â_{N+1} ∘ B̂) = P(A) P(B).

applications.title: Two edge-disjoint connections across three parallel bonds
applications.inputs: Two vertices s and t joined by three parallel edges. Each edge is open with probability p = 1/2, independently, as in bond percolation. A = {s is joined to t by an open edge}.
applications.hypotheses: There are three coordinates with independent Bernoulli(1/2) laws. Opening an edge cannot destroy a connection, so A is increasing.

steps.text: By step s1 of the proof, a set K of open edges is a witness of A exactly when K is not empty. So A ∘ A is the event that at least two of the three edges are open.
The probability of at least two open edges is 3p²(1 − p) + p³ = 3p² − 2p³. At p = 1/2 this is 3/4 − 1/4 = 1/2.
The probability of A is 1 − (1 − p)³ = 7/8, so the BK bound is P(A)² = 49/64.
The comparison 1/2 = 32/64 ≤ 49/64 confirms the inequality. The bound is not sharp here, and the gap is 17/64. The trivial bound P(A ∘ A) ≤ P(A) = 7/8 is much weaker.

applications.conclusion: Two edge-disjoint connections have probability 1/2, which is below the BK bound 49/64 for the square of the single-connection probability.

limitations: The proof needs increasing events. Reimer's theorem extends the inequality to all events, with a much harder proof.
The statement is for finitely many coordinates. For events that depend on finitely many edges of an infinite graph, apply it to those edges. Other cases need a limit argument.
The inequality can fail when the measure is not a product measure. If A and B depend on disjoint sets of edges, then A ∘ B = A ∩ B, and a positively correlated measure can give P(A ∩ B) > P(A)P(B).

results.name: Russo–Margulis formula
results.statement: Let E be a finite set. For p = (p_e)_{e∈E} in [0, 1]^E, let P_p be the product measure on Ω = {0, 1}^E under which the coordinates ω_e are independent with P_p(ω_e = 1) = p_e. For ω ∈ Ω and e ∈ E, let ω^e and ω_e be the configurations equal to ω off e, with value 1 and 0 at e. An edge e is pivotal for an event A at ω if ω^e ∈ A and ω_e ∉ A. Let A ⊆ Ω be increasing. Then P_p(A) is a polynomial in the variables p_e, affine in each p_e, and ∂P_p(A)/∂p_e = P_p(Piv_e(A)) for every e ∈ E, where Piv_e(A) is the event that e is pivotal for A. In particular, when p_e = p for all e, f(p) = P_p(A) satisfies f′(p) = ∑_{e∈E} P_p(Piv_e(A)) for every p ∈ [0, 1], with one-sided derivatives at 0 and 1. This sum is the expected number of pivotal edges.
hypotheses: The index set E is finite, and P_p is the product of Bernoulli measures with parameters p_e ∈ [0, 1].
The event A is increasing: if ω ∈ A and ω ≤ ω′ coordinatewise, then ω′ ∈ A.

prerequisites.reason: Step s2 splits P_p(A) according to the two values of the coordinate ω_e.
Step s4 differentiates p ↦ g(p, …, p) with the chain rule for the polynomial g of several variables.

definitions.name: increasing event
definitions.text: An event A ⊆ {0, 1}^E such that ω ∈ A and ω ≤ ω′ in every coordinate give ω′ ∈ A. Opening more edges never destroys A.

definitions.name: pivotal edge
definitions.text: The edge e is pivotal for A at ω if ω^e ∈ A and ω_e ∉ A. So the state of e alone decides whether A occurs. The event Piv_e(A) does not depend on ω_e.

source.citation: Hugo Duminil-Copin, Introduction to Bernoulli percolation, lecture notes, Institut des Hautes Études Scientifiques, 2018.
source.revision: Author's online version dated October 7, 2018, 30 pages.
source.module: Chapter 2, Section 2.4 Margulis-Russo formula
source.excerpt: Proposition 2.7 (Margulis [27], Russo [30]) For any p ∈ [0, 1] and any increasing event A depending on finitely many edges, we have f′(p) = ∑_{e∈E} Pp[Pive(A)].
source.attribution: © Hugo Duminil-Copin. Quoted from the author's lecture notes Introduction to Bernoulli percolation for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states the formula for one parameter p on a finite graph, with f(p) = P_p[A]. The authored statement also gives the version with one parameter p_e for each edge, and it deduces the source formula by the chain rule. The source proves the formula with the covariance identity of its Proposition 2.6. The authored proof conditions on the state of one edge, which gives the same identity directly.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the conditioning argument behind Proposition 2.7 of the cited notes. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement for every finite E, every p in [0, 1]^E and every increasing event A, with the one-parameter corollary.

steps.text: Polynomial form. P_p(A) = ∑_{ω∈A} ∏_{e∈E} p_e^{ω_e}(1 − p_e)^{1−ω_e}. This is a finite sum of products, so P_p(A) is a polynomial in the variables p_e. Each product contains p_e or 1 − p_e exactly once, so the polynomial is affine in each p_e separately.

Condition on ω_e. Let B⁺ = {ω : ω^e ∈ A} and B⁻ = {ω : ω_e ∈ A}. Both events depend only on the coordinates other than e, so under the product measure they are independent of ω_e and their probabilities do not depend on p_e. On {ω_e = 1} we have ω = ω^e, so A ∩ {ω_e = 1} = B⁺ ∩ {ω_e = 1}. On {ω_e = 0} we have ω = ω_e, so A ∩ {ω_e = 0} = B⁻ ∩ {ω_e = 0}. The law of total probability and independence give P_p(A) = p_e P_p(B⁺) + (1 − p_e) P_p(B⁻).

Differentiate in p_e. Since P_p(B⁺) and P_p(B⁻) do not depend on p_e, step s2 gives ∂P_p(A)/∂p_e = P_p(B⁺) − P_p(B⁻). The configuration ω_e is below ω^e in every coordinate. A is increasing, so ω_e ∈ A implies ω^e ∈ A, which means B⁻ ⊆ B⁺. Hence P_p(B⁺) − P_p(B⁻) = P_p(B⁺ ∖ B⁻). The event B⁺ ∖ B⁻ is the set of ω with ω^e ∈ A and ω_e ∉ A, which is Piv_e(A). So ∂P_p(A)/∂p_e = P_p(Piv_e(A)).

One parameter. Let g(q) = P_q(A) for q ∈ [0, 1]^E. By step s1, g is a polynomial, so it is differentiable on all of ℝ^E. Then f(p) = g(p, …, p), and the chain rule gives f′(p) = ∑_{e∈E} ∂g/∂q_e(p, …, p) = ∑_{e∈E} P_p(Piv_e(A)) by step s3. At p = 0 and p = 1 this is the one-sided derivative of f on [0, 1]. Finally, ∑_e P_p(Piv_e(A)) = E_p[∑_e 1_{Piv_e(A)}] by linearity of expectation, which is the expected number of pivotal edges.

applications.title: Sensitivity of a two-route connection in bond percolation
applications.inputs: A graph with vertices s, a, b, t and four edges e₁ = sa, e₂ = at, e₃ = sb, e₄ = bt. Each edge is open with probability p, independently. A = {s is joined to t by an open path}. The parameter value is p = 1/2.
applications.hypotheses: The edge set is finite and the edge states are independent Bernoulli variables with parameter p. Opening an edge can only add open paths, so A is increasing.

steps.text: Direct computation: s is joined to t if the route s–a–t or the route s–b–t is open. Each route is open with probability p², and the routes use disjoint edges. So f(p) = 1 − (1 − p²)² = 2p² − p⁴, and f′(p) = 4p − 4p³.

Pivotal edges: e₁ is pivotal exactly when e₂ is open and the route s–b–t is not open. These conditions use other edges only, so P_p(Piv_{e₁}(A)) = p(1 − p²). By symmetry each of the four edges has the same value.
The Russo–Margulis formula gives f′(p) = 4p(1 − p²) = 4p − 4p³. This agrees with the direct derivative of step a1.
At p = 1/2 the expected number of pivotal edges is 4 · (1/2) · (1 − 1/4) = 3/2. So a small increase dp of the edge density raises the connection probability by about (3/2) dp.
For reference, the connection probability at p = 1/2 is f(1/2) = 2 · (1/4) − 1/16 = 7/16.

applications.conclusion: At p = 1/2 the connection probability is 7/16 and its derivative is 3/2, the expected number of pivotal edges.

limitations: The formula needs finitely many edges, or an event that depends on finitely many edges. For events such as the existence of an infinite cluster, one applies it to finite approximations and passes to a limit.
For an event that is not increasing, the same proof gives ∂P_p(A)/∂p_e = P_p(ω^e ∈ A) − P_p(ω_e ∈ A), and this difference can be negative.

results.name: Russo–Seymour–Welsh box-crossing estimates
results.statement: Consider bond percolation on ℤ² at p = 1/2, with law P_{1/2}. For a rectangle R, let H(R) be the event that an open path inside R joins its left side to its right side, and write H(a, b) for R = [0, a] × [0, b]. Then (i) P_{1/2}(H(3n, 2n)) ≥ 1/128 for every n ≥ 1. (ii) For every ρ > 0 there is c(ρ) > 0 such that c(ρ) ≤ P_{1/2}(H(ρn, n)) ≤ 1 − c(ρ) for every n ≥ 1.
hypotheses: The lattice is ℤ² with nearest-neighbour edges, and the edges are open independently with probability p = 1/2.
Crossings of a rectangle use only edges with both endpoints in the rectangle.

prerequisites.reason: Steps s4 and s5 bound the probability of an intersection of increasing crossing events from below by the product of their probabilities.
Step s3 decomposes the event B according to the value of the right-most vertical crossing Γ of the square.
Step s3 splits a connection to the symmetric path γ ∪ σ(γ) into connections to γ and to σ(γ).

definitions.name: crossing events
definitions.text: For R = [a, b] × [c, d], H(R) is the event of an open path in R from {a} × [c, d] to {b} × [c, d]. V(R) is the event of an open path in R from [a, b] × {c} to [a, b] × {d}.

definitions.name: right-most vertical crossing
definitions.text: On V(S), the open top-bottom crossing of S that leaves the largest region on its left. The event {Γ = γ} depends only on edges of γ and on edges to the right of γ.

source.excerpt: Theorem 4.5 (Box-crossing property) Let ρ > 0, there exists c = c(ρ) > 0 such that for every n ≥ 1, c ≤ P1/2[H(ρn, n)] ≤ 1 − c.

source.alignment: Part (ii) of the authored statement is Theorem 4.5 of the source, and part (i) is its Theorem 4.6 on p. 23. The outline follows the source proof of Theorem 4.6 and the gluing argument after Theorem 4.5. In the conditioning step the outline uses a vertical crossing of the square S and a horizontal crossing of S for the final gluing, which have the same probability by the symmetry of S.

proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of Theorem 4.6 and the remarks after Theorem 4.5 in Duminil-Copin, Introduction to Bernoulli percolation (2018), Section 4.2, pp. 22-23. Step s1 takes the self-duality of crossings, equation (4.1), from the source.

steps.text: Squares. Equation (4.1) of the source gives P_{1/2}(H([0, n] × [0, n − 1])) = 1/2 by self-duality. A square [0, n]² contains this rectangle with the same left and right sides extended, so P_{1/2}(H(S)) ≥ 1/2, and by rotation P_{1/2}(V(S)) ≥ 1/2. Here S = [0, n]². The same holds for S′ = [−n, n]².

Conditioning on a crossing. Let L = {−n} × [−n, n] be the left side of S′, and let B be the event that some open top-bottom crossing of S is joined to L by an open path in S′. On V(S), let Γ be the right-most open top-bottom crossing of S. For a top-bottom path γ of S, let σ(γ) be its reflection in the line y = 0, and let V(γ) be the part of S′ to the left of γ ∪ σ(γ). The event {Γ = γ} depends only on edges of γ and on edges to the right of γ. So, given {Γ = γ}, the edges of V(γ) are still independent with parameter 1/2.

Reflection. Any open left-right crossing of S′ meets the path γ ∪ σ(γ), which joins the top of S′ to its bottom. Its first part lies in V(γ), so P(L ↔ γ ∪ σ(γ) in V(γ)) ≥ P_{1/2}(H(S′)) ≥ 1/2. The reflection σ preserves V(γ) and the law, and it exchanges γ and σ(γ). The union bound then gives P(L ↔ γ in V(γ)) ≥ 1/4. Summing over γ, P_{1/2}(B) ≥ (1/4) P_{1/2}(V(S)) ≥ 1/8.

Gluing for part (i). Let R = [−n, 2n] × [−n, n], a 3n × 2n rectangle. Let B′ be the reflection of B in the line x = n/2: some top-bottom crossing of S is joined to the right side {2n} × [−n, n] inside [0, 2n] × [−n, n]. Then P(B′) = P(B) ≥ 1/8. An open left-right crossing of S meets both top-bottom crossings, so H(S) ∩ B ∩ B′ ⊆ H(R). The three events are increasing, and the Harris inequality gives P_{1/2}(H(R)) ≥ (1/2)(1/8)(1/8) = 1/128.

Part (ii), lower bound. For ρ ≤ 1 the narrower rectangle is crossed more easily, so P_{1/2}(H(ρn, n)) ≥ P_{1/2}(H(n, n)) ≥ 1/2. For ρ > 1, the source chains overlapping rectangles R_i of aspect ratio 3/2 whose overlaps are squares S_i. Horizontal crossings of R_i and R_{i+1} both meet any vertical crossing of S_i, so ⋂_i (H(R_i) ∩ V(S_i)) ⊆ H(ρn, n). The Harris inequality gives a bound c(ρ) that depends only on the number of rectangles. If n is odd or ρn is not an integer, compare with the rectangle of even height 2⌊n/2⌋. This changes the aspect ratio by at most a factor 3/2 for n ≥ 2, which a longer chain absorbs. For n = 1 the crossing event has positive probability.

Part (ii), upper bound. H(ρn, n) fails exactly when the dual rectangle has an open top-bottom dual crossing. At p = 1/2 the dual configuration has the same law as ω, and a rotation by π/2 turns this dual crossing into a horizontal crossing of a rectangle with aspect ratio close to 1/ρ. The lower bound of step s5 for this ratio gives 1 − P_{1/2}(H(ρn, n)) ≥ c′(ρ) > 0.

applications.title: Spanning a 2:1 strip in a critical bond network
applications.inputs: Bond percolation on ℤ² at p = 1/2. The rectangle [0, 4n] × [0, 2n], built from R₀ = [0, 3n] × [0, 2n], R₁ = [n, 4n] × [0, 2n] and their overlap S₀ = [n, 3n] × [0, 2n], a 2n × 2n square.
applications.hypotheses: The edges are independent with parameter 1/2. Crossing events are increasing, so the Harris inequality applies.

steps.text: Part (i) gives P_{1/2}(H(R₀)) ≥ 1/128 and, by translation, P_{1/2}(H(R₁)) ≥ 1/128. Step s1 gives P_{1/2}(V(S₀)) ≥ 1/2.
A left-right crossing of R₀ and a left-right crossing of R₁ both cross the square S₀ horizontally, so both meet every top-bottom crossing of S₀. So H(R₀) ∩ V(S₀) ∩ H(R₁) ⊆ H(4n, 2n).
The Harris inequality gives P_{1/2}(H(4n, 2n)) ≥ (1/128)² · (1/2) = 1/32768 for every n ≥ 1.
The bound does not depend on n. So a critical network spans a 2:1 strip in the long direction with probability bounded away from 0 at every scale, which is a first form of scale invariance.

applications.conclusion: At p = 1/2, the rectangle [0, 4n] × [0, 2n] is crossed horizontally with probability at least 1/32768 for every n ≥ 1.

limitations: The constants such as 1/128 are far from the true crossing probabilities. Cardy's formula gives the exact limits for site percolation on the triangular lattice.
The proof uses p = 1/2 through self-duality. For p ≠ 1/2 the crossing probabilities of large rectangles tend to 0 or 1.
The method needs the Harris inequality and a reflection symmetry. Extensions to other planar lattices and to random-cluster models need different arguments, for example the method of Tassion.
