results.name: Sharpness of the phase transition for Bernoulli percolation
results.statement: Let d ≥ 2 and consider bond percolation on ℤ^d with parameter p ∈ [0, 1], with law P_p. Let Λ_n = {−n, …, n}^d, let ∂Λ_n = {x : |x|_∞ = n}, let θ(p) = P_p(0 is in an infinite open cluster) and let p_c = inf{p : θ(p) > 0}. For a finite set S ∋ 0 let φ_p(S) = p ∑ P_p(0 is joined to x by an open path inside S), where the sum runs over the edges xy with x ∈ S and y ∉ S. Then (i) p_c = sup{p ∈ [0, 1] : φ_p(S) < 1 for some finite S ∋ 0}. (ii) For every p < p_c there is c_p > 0 such that P_p(0 ↔ ∂Λ_n) ≤ exp(−c_p n) for all n ≥ 1. (iii) For every p > p_c, θ(p) ≥ (p − p_c)/(p(1 − p_c)).
hypotheses: The edges of ℤ^d, d ≥ 2, are open independently, each with the same probability p.
The connection events use open paths of nearest-neighbour edges of ℤ^d.

prerequisites.reason: Step s2 computes the derivative of θ_n with the Russo–Margulis formula, and step s4 uses it to show that φ_p(S) is nondecreasing in p.
Steps s1 and s3 partition a connection event according to the value of a random set of vertices.
Step s1 bounds the connection event by a sum over the boundary edges xy of S and over the possible clusters C.
Step s5 integrates a differential inequality for the polynomial θ_n(p) between two parameter values.

definitions.name: θ_n(p)
definitions.text: θ_n(p) = P_p(0 ↔ ∂Λ_n), the probability that an open path joins the origin to the boundary of the box Λ_n. It decreases to θ(p) as n → ∞.

definitions.name: φ_p(S)
definitions.text: For a finite set S that contains 0, φ_p(S) = p ∑_{xy∈ΔS} P_p(0 ↔ x inside S), where ΔS is the set of edges xy with x ∈ S and y ∉ S. Set φ_p(S) = 0 if 0 ∉ S.

source.excerpt: Theorem 3.3 (Exponential decay in diameter) Fix d ≥ 2. For every p < pc, there exists cp > 0 such that for all n ≥ 1, Pp[0 ↔ ∂Λn] ≤ exp(−cp n). Furthermore, there exists c > 0 such that for p > pc, θ(p) ≥ c(p − pc).

The authored statement adds the explicit constant of the source proof and the characterization of p_c through φ_p(S), which the source proves on pp. 14-16. The authored proof follows the source proof by Duminil-Copin and Tassion, with Claim 1 proved by the cluster decomposition that the source uses for Corollary 2.5.

proof.scope: The full statement (i), (ii) and (iii) for bond percolation on ℤ^d with d ≥ 2.

steps.text: Claim 1: if S ∋ 0 is finite, S ⊆ Λ_{L−1} and φ = φ_p(S) < 1, then θ_n(p) ≤ φ θ_{n−L}(p) for n ≥ L, with θ_0 = 1. Let 𝒞 be the set of vertices joined to 0 by an open path inside S. On {0 ↔ ∂Λ_n}, let w be the last vertex of an open path from 0 to ∂Λ_n that lies in 𝒞, and let y be the next vertex. Then wy is open and y ∉ S, since otherwise y ∈ 𝒞. The rest of the path joins y to ∂Λ_n off 𝒞. For fixed C ∋ x, the events {𝒞 = C}, {ω_xy = 1} and {y ↔ ∂Λ_n off C} depend on disjoint sets of edges. Since |y|_∞ ≤ L, a path from y to ∂Λ_n reaches y + ∂Λ_{n−L}, so the last event has probability at most θ_{n−L}(p) by translation invariance. The union bound and independence give θ_n ≤ ∑_{xy∈ΔS} ∑_{C∋x} P_p(𝒞 = C) p θ_{n−L} = φ θ_{n−L}. So θ_{kL} ≤ φ^k. Since θ_n decreases in n and θ_1 < 1 when φ < 1 (then p < 1), there is c_p > 0 with θ_n ≤ exp(−c_p n) for all n ≥ 1.

Russo step. The event {0 ↔ ∂Λ_n} depends only on the finite set E_n of edges inside Λ_n, so θ_n is a polynomial. The Russo–Margulis formula gives θ_n′(p) = ∑_{e∈E_n} P_p(Piv_e). The pivotal event is independent of ω_e, so P_p(Piv_e) = P_p(Piv_e, ω_e = 0)/(1 − p). An edge e = xy is closed and pivotal exactly when 0 ↔ x, y ↔ ∂Λ_n and 0 is not joined to ∂Λ_n, for one of the two orders of x and y. Indeed, a self-avoiding open path from 0 to ∂Λ_n after e is opened uses e once, and its two parts give the two connections. Conversely, these connections force e to be closed, and opening e joins 0 to ∂Λ_n. The two orders give disjoint events, because 0 ↔ x and x ↔ ∂Λ_n cannot both hold when 0 ↮ ∂Λ_n. So θ_n′(p) = (1 − p)^(−1) ∑_{(x,y)} P_p(0 ↔ x, y ↔ ∂Λ_n, 0 ↮ ∂Λ_n), summed over ordered pairs with xy ∈ E_n.

Claim 2: θ_n′(p) = E_p[φ_p(𝒮)]/(p(1 − p)) for p ∈ (0, 1), where 𝒮 = {z ∈ Λ_n : z ↮ ∂Λ_n} ⊆ Λ_{n−1}. On {𝒮 = S} with 0 ∈ S, the event in step s2 means that xy ∈ ΔS and 0 is joined to x inside S, because a path from 0 cannot leave S without reaching ∂Λ_n. For S ⊆ Λ_{n−1}, {𝒮 = S} holds exactly when all edges from S to Λ_n ∖ S are closed and every vertex of Λ_n ∖ S is joined to ∂Λ_n inside Λ_n ∖ S. So it depends only on edges with an endpoint outside S, while {0 ↔ x inside S} depends only on edges inside S. Independence and a partition over S give θ_n′ = (1 − p)^(−1) ∑_S P_p(𝒮 = S) ∑_{xy∈ΔS} P_p(0 ↔ x inside S) = E_p[φ_p(𝒮)]/(p(1 − p)).

Below p̃_c. Let p̃_c = sup{p : φ_p(S) < 1 for some finite S ∋ 0}. For a fixed finite S, each P_p(0 ↔ x inside S) has a nonnegative derivative by the Russo–Margulis formula, so φ_p(S) is nondecreasing in p. If p < p̃_c, there is p′ > p and S with φ_{p′}(S) < 1, hence φ_p(S) < 1. Step s1 gives exponential decay at p, so θ(p) = 0. Hence p̃_c ≤ p_c.

Above p̃_c. Let p̃_c < p′ < q < 1. Then φ_q(S) ≥ 1 for every finite S ∋ 0, and φ_q(S) = 0 when 0 ∉ S. Step s3 gives θ_n′(q) ≥ P_q(0 ∈ 𝒮)/(q(1 − q)) = (1 − θ_n(q))/(q(1 − q)). Here 1 − θ_n(q) ≥ (1 − q)^(2d) > 0. So the derivative of −log(1 − θ_n) is at least the derivative of log(q/(1 − q)). Integrate from p′ to p < 1: (1 − θ_n(p)) ≤ (1 − θ_n(p′)) p′(1 − p)/(p(1 − p′)) ≤ p′(1 − p)/(p(1 − p′)). This gives θ_n(p) ≥ (p − p′)/(p(1 − p′)). Let p′ ↓ p̃_c and then n → ∞. Since {0 ↔ ∞} is the decreasing intersection of the events {0 ↔ ∂Λ_n}, θ(p) ≥ (p − p̃_c)/(p(1 − p̃_c)) > 0. The case p = 1 is trivial because θ(1) = 1.

Conclusion. Step s5 shows θ(p) > 0 for every p > p̃_c, so p_c ≤ p̃_c. With step s4, p_c = p̃_c, which is (i). Then (ii) is step s4 with step s1, and (iii) is the bound of step s5 with p̃_c replaced by p_c.

applications.title: Exponential decay of connections at low density on the square lattice
applications.inputs: Bond percolation on ℤ² at p = 1/5, the one-point set S = {0} with L = 1, and the box radius n = 10. For the supercritical side, p = 3/5 and the value p_c = 1/2 of the Harris–Kesten theorem.
applications.hypotheses: The edges are independent with a common parameter p. The set S = {0} is finite, contains 0 and lies in Λ_0.

steps.text: For S = {0}, the four edges at the origin form ΔS, and 0 is joined to itself inside S with probability 1. So φ_p({0}) = 4p = 4/5 < 1. In general dimension φ_p({0}) = 2dp, so (i) gives p_c(d) ≥ 1/(2d).
Step s1 with L = 1 gives θ_n(p) ≤ (4/5) θ_{n−1}(p), so θ_n(1/5) ≤ (4/5)^n for every n ≥ 1.
At n = 10 the bound is (4/5)^10 = 1048576/9765625, which is about 0.107. Each additional unit of radius multiplies the bound by 4/5.
On the supercritical side, (iii) with p_c = 1/2 gives θ(3/5) ≥ (3/5 − 1/2)/((3/5)(1 − 1/2)) = 1/3.

applications.conclusion: At p = 1/5 on ℤ², the probability that the origin reaches distance 10 is at most 1048576/9765625. At p = 3/5, the origin lies in an infinite cluster with probability at least 1/3.

limitations: The theorem gives no information at p = p_c itself. Whether θ(p_c) = 0 is open for 3 ≤ d ≤ 10.
The constant c_p in (ii) tends to 0 as p ↑ p_c, and the theorem gives no rate for this.
The method extends to percolation on transitive graphs, and a variant of it proves sharpness for the Ising model.

results.name: Non-trivial critical probability for percolation on the hypercubic lattice
results.statement: Let d ≥ 2. In bond percolation on ℤ^d, each edge between nearest neighbours is open with probability p ∈ [0, 1], independently of the other edges. Let θ_d(p) be the probability that the open cluster of the origin is infinite, and let p_c(d) = inf{p ∈ [0, 1] : θ_d(p) > 0}. Then θ_d(p) = 0 for p < 1/(2d − 1), and θ_d(p) ≥ 3/8 for p ≥ 5/6. Hence 1/(2d − 1) ≤ p_c(d) ≤ 5/6, and in particular 0 < p_c(d) < 1.
hypotheses: The dimension satisfies d ≥ 2.
The edge states of ℤ^d are independent, and each edge is open with the same probability p.

prerequisites.reason: Steps s1 and s5 bound the probability of a countable union of path events or circuit events by the sum of their probabilities.

definitions.name: open cluster
definitions.text: The open cluster of a vertex x is the set of vertices joined to x by a path of open edges. θ_d(p) is the probability that the cluster of the origin is infinite.

definitions.name: dual lattice
definitions.text: The dual lattice of ℤ² is ℤ² + (1/2, 1/2). Each edge e of ℤ² crosses exactly one dual edge e*, at its midpoint. The dual edge e* is called open when e is closed.

definitions.name: edge boundary
definitions.text: For a set C of vertices, the edge boundary ∂C is the set of edges with exactly one endpoint in C.

source.excerpt: Theorem 1.1 For d ≥ 2, we have that 0 < pc(d) < 1. A self-avoiding path of length n is a sequence of edges e1, …, en with ei ≠ ej for i ≠ j, such that ei and ei+1 share an endpoint for every 1 ≤ i < n.

source.alignment: The source states 0 < p_c(d) < 1 and proves p_c(d) ≥ 1/(2d) with self-avoiding paths and p_c(d) < 1 with open dual circuits that surround the origin. The authored statement adds the explicit bounds 1/(2d − 1) and 5/6. The authored proof follows the same two arguments, but it replaces the topological claim about circuits around the origin by a parity argument on the edge boundary of a finite cluster.

proof.scope: The full statement for every d ≥ 2, with the explicit bounds 1/(2d − 1) and 5/6.

steps.text: Lower bound. Suppose the cluster of 0 is infinite and fix n ≥ 1. Only finitely many vertices lie at graph distance less than n from 0, so the cluster contains a vertex x with |x|₁ ≥ n. A shortest open path from 0 to x visits no vertex twice and has length at least n. Its first n edges form an open self-avoiding walk of length n from 0. There are at most 2d(2d − 1)^(n−1) self-avoiding walks of length n from 0, and each uses n distinct edges, so it is open with probability pⁿ. The union bound gives θ_d(p) ≤ 2d(2d − 1)^(n−1) pⁿ. If p < 1/(2d − 1), the right side tends to 0 as n → ∞, so θ_d(p) = 0. Hence p_c(d) ≥ 1/(2d − 1).

Reduction to the plane. The edges of ℤ^d with both endpoints in the plane ℤ² × {0}^(d−2) carry an independent percolation with parameter p, which is bond percolation on ℤ². If the cluster of 0 in this plane is infinite, then the cluster of 0 in ℤ^d is infinite. So θ_d(p) ≥ θ_2(p), and it suffices to prove θ_2(p) ≥ 3/8 for p ≥ 5/6.

Parity of the boundary. Let d = 2, suppose the cluster C of 0 is finite, and let H be the set of dual edges e* with e ∈ ∂C. Each e ∈ ∂C is closed, because otherwise its outer endpoint would be in C. So every edge of H is open. Every dual vertex has even degree in H. Indeed, it is the centre of a unit square with corners x₁, x₂, x₃, x₄, and the sides in ∂C are the places where membership in C changes along the closed walk x₁x₂x₃x₄x₁. Let f_k be the edge from (k, 0) to (k + 1, 0). Along the walk (0, 0), (1, 0), (2, 0), …, membership in C starts true and is false from some point on. So H contains an odd number of the dual edges f_k* with k ≥ 0.

A short circuit. A finite graph with all degrees even is a union of edge-disjoint cycles. To see this, take a longest path in it. Its last vertex has a second neighbour, which lies on the path, so the graph has a cycle. Remove the cycle and repeat, because the degrees stay even. The counts of edges f_k* with k ≥ 0 add over the cycles of H, so some cycle Γ of H, of length n ≥ 4, contains an odd number of them. Dual vertices have y-coordinates in ℤ + 1/2, and only the edges f_k* (k ∈ ℤ) join y = −1/2 to y = 1/2. A closed walk changes the sign of y an even number of times. So Γ contains an odd number of edges f_k* with k < 0 as well. Thus Γ contains f_k* with k ≥ 0 and f_{−m−1}* with m ≥ 0, whose endpoints have x-coordinates k + 1/2 and −m − 1/2. Each of the two arcs of Γ between them has at least k + m + 1 edges, so n ≥ 2(k + 1) and k < n/2.

Counting. Steps s3 and s4 show that {C finite} is contained in the union, over n ≥ 4, over 0 ≤ k < n/2 and over dual cycles Γ of length n through f_k*, of the events {all edges of Γ are open in the dual}. A dual cycle of length n through a fixed dual edge, minus that edge, is a self-avoiding dual path of length n − 1 from a fixed endpoint. So there are at most 4 · 3^(n−2) ≤ 3ⁿ such cycles. A cycle has n distinct dual edges, so all are open with probability (1 − p)ⁿ. There are at most n values of k. The union bound gives 1 − θ_2(p) ≤ ∑_{n≥4} n (3(1 − p))ⁿ.

Conclusion. For p ≥ 5/6 we have 3(1 − p) ≤ 1/2, and ∑_{n≥4} n 2^(−n) = 2 − (1/2 + 2/4 + 3/8) = 5/8. So θ_2(p) ≥ 3/8, and step s2 gives θ_d(p) ≥ 3/8 > 0. Hence p_c(d) ≤ 5/6. Together with step s1, 1/(2d − 1) ≤ p_c(d) ≤ 5/6.

applications.title: Percolation bounds for the square lattice
applications.inputs: Bond percolation on ℤ² (d = 2). The proof gives a lower bound for p_c(2) and a lower bound for θ_2(p) at the edge density p = 9/10.
applications.hypotheses: The square lattice has d = 2, and the edges are independent with the same parameter p, as the theorem requires.

steps.text: Step s1 with d = 2 gives θ_2(p) = 0 for p < 1/(2 · 2 − 1) = 1/3, so p_c(2) ≥ 1/3.
At p = 9/10 the ratio in step s5 is x = 3(1 − p) = 3/10. The series bound is ∑_{n≥4} n xⁿ = x/(1 − x)² − x − 2x² − 3x³.
Hence θ_2(9/10) ≥ 1 − 2511/49000 = 46489/49000, which is more than 0.948. So at density 0.9 the origin is in an infinite cluster with probability at least about 95%.
The theorem gives 1/3 ≤ p_c(2) ≤ 5/6. The Harris–Kesten theorem nm:statphys-harris-kesten gives the exact value p_c(2) = 1/2, which lies inside these bounds.

applications.conclusion: For bond percolation on the square lattice, 1/3 ≤ p_c(2) ≤ 5/6, and θ_2(9/10) ≥ 46489/49000.

limitations: The bounds are far from the true values. For example, p_c(2) = 1/2 by the Harris–Kesten theorem, and p_c(d) is asymptotic to 1/(2d) as d → ∞.
The theorem does not say what happens at p = p_c. Whether θ_d(p_c) = 0 is known for d = 2 and for large d, and is open in general.
The proof of the upper bound uses the planar dual lattice and works only through the reduction to ℤ².

results.name: Smirnov's theorem on Cardy's formula
aliases: Cardy's formula for critical site percolation
results.statement: Consider critical site percolation on the triangular lattice δT with mesh δ > 0, in which each site (each hexagon of the dual hexagonal lattice) is black with probability 1/2, independently. Let Ω be a Jordan domain with four distinct boundary points a, b, c, d in counterclockwise order, and let (Ω_δ, a_δ, b_δ, c_δ, d_δ) be discrete domains of δT that converge to (Ω, a, b, c, d) in the sense of Carathéodory. Let j = e^(2πi/3), let T be the equilateral triangle with vertices 1, j, j², and let φ be the conformal map from Ω onto T with φ(a) = 1, φ(b) = j and φ(c) = j². Then φ(d) = x + j²(1 − x) for a unique x ∈ (0, 1), and the probability that a black path in Ω_δ joins the boundary arc (a_δ b_δ) to the arc (c_δ d_δ) converges to x as δ → 0.
hypotheses: Sites of the triangular lattice are black independently with probability 1/2.
The domain Ω is a Jordan domain with four distinct boundary points a, b, c, d in counterclockwise order, and the discrete domains converge to it in the sense of Carathéodory.

prerequisites.reason: Step s4 uses Russo–Seymour–Welsh crossing bounds, which the source states also hold for site percolation on the triangular lattice, to get a Hölder bound.
Step s4 extracts uniformly convergent subsequences of the observables with the Arzelà–Ascoli theorem.
Step s5 shows that every subsequential limit of the observable is holomorphic with Morera's theorem.
The statement and step s5 use the conformal map from Ω onto the triangle T that the Riemann mapping theorem provides.
Step s5 identifies the limit with the conformal map through the boundary correspondence of Carathéodory's theorem.

concepts: site percolation on the triangular lattice

definitions.name: topological rectangle
definitions.text: A Jordan domain Ω with four distinct boundary points a, b, c, d in counterclockwise order. The arc (ab) is the counterclockwise boundary arc from a to b.

definitions.name: parafermionic observable
definitions.text: For a mid-edge z of Ω_δ, F(z) = F_a(z) + j F_b(z) + j² F_c(z), where F_a(z) is 2^(−N) times the number of configurations of loops with a path from a to z and a path from b to c. N is the number of faces of Ω_δ.

source.citation: Hugo Duminil-Copin, Introduction to Bernoulli percolation, lecture notes, Institut des Hautes Études Scientifiques, 2018.
source.revision: Author's online version dated October 7, 2018, 30 pages.
source.module: Chapter 4, Section 4.3 Conformal invariance of two-dimensional percolation
source.excerpt: Theorem 4.8 (Smirnov) Consider a family of topological rectangles (Ωδ, aδ, bδ, cδ, dδ)δ>0 converging to (Ω, a, b, c, d) in the Caratheodory sense. Then, lim_{δ→0} P1/2[(aδbδ) ↔ (cδdδ) in Ωδ] = x, where d is mapped to x + j²(1 − x) by the conformal map from Ω to T mapping a to 1, b to j and c to j².
source.attribution: © Hugo Duminil-Copin. Quoted from the author's lecture notes Introduction to Bernoulli percolation for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The authored statement is the theorem of the source, with the lattice model and the triangle T written out. The outline follows the version of Smirnov's proof due to Khristoforov that the source presents on pp. 25-28: the parafermionic observable, Remark 4.9, Lemma 4.10 and Lemma 4.13. Smirnov's original proof appeared in C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris 333 (2001).

results.proof_status: outline of the cited published proof. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of Theorem 4.8 in Duminil-Copin, Introduction to Bernoulli percolation (2018), Section 4.3, pp. 25-28, which presents Khristoforov's version of Smirnov's proof. Steps s3 and s4 cite Lemma 4.10 and Lemma 4.13 of the source.

steps.text: Loop representation. Colour the hexagons of δH (the sites of δT) black or white, and colour the hexagons outside Ω_δ white. The edges of δH between hexagons of different colours form a loop configuration, an even subgraph. This is a bijection, so there are 2^N loop configurations, where N is the number of faces of Ω_δ. For mid-edges u, v, r, s let E^{uv,rs} be the set of configurations of loops with one self-avoiding path from u to v and one from r to s.

Observable and its range. For a mid-edge z set F_a(z) = 2^(−N) |E^{az,bc}|, define F_b and F_c by cyclic permutation of a, b, c, and set F = F_a + j F_b + j² F_c. Remark 4.9 of the source shows F_a + F_b + F_c = 1: for a fixed η₀ in the union of the three sets, η ↦ η Δ η₀ is a bijection onto the 2^N loop configurations. So F(z) is a convex combination of 1, j and j², and F maps Ω_δ into the triangle T. On the arc (c_δ a_δ), F_b = 0, so F takes values on the side [j², 1], and similarly on the other two arcs. The source also shows that F_a(z) for z on (c_δ a_δ) equals the probability of a black crossing from (a_δ b_δ) to the arc from c_δ to z.

Discrete holomorphicity. Lemma 4.10 of the source: for every vertex v of Ω_δ with surrounding mid-edges p, q, r in counterclockwise order, (p − v)F(p) + (q − v)F(q) + (r − v)F(r) = 0. Its second proof groups configurations in triples that add or remove the edges at v. The contributions in each triple differ by the factors j and j², and 1 + j + j² = 0. By Remark 4.11, this relation says that the discrete contour integral of F around each elementary triangle of δT vanishes. Summing over triangles, the discrete integral along every closed lattice contour inside Ω_δ vanishes.

Precompactness. Lemma 4.13 of the source: F_a(z) equals the probability that the interface γ from b_δ to c_δ does not disconnect z from a_δ. Two points z and z′ are separated by γ only if no black circuit or black boundary-to-boundary path surrounds or separates both. The Russo–Seymour–Welsh bounds on crossings of annuli give |F_a(z) − F_a(z′)| ≤ C|z − z′|^α away from the boundary, uniformly in δ. So the family (F^δ) is equicontinuous and bounded, and the Arzelà–Ascoli theorem gives subsequences that converge uniformly on compact subsets of Ω.

Identification of the limit. Let F be a subsequential limit. Step s3 passes to the limit as the vanishing of ∮F(z)dz along every triangle, so F is holomorphic by Morera's theorem. By step s2, F maps the arcs (ab), (bc), (ca) of ∂Ω onto the sides [1, j], [j, j²], [j², 1] of T, injectively, with F(a) = 1, F(b) = j, F(c) = j². The principle of corresponding boundaries then shows that F is the conformal map φ from Ω onto T. The limit is the same for every subsequence, so F^δ → φ.

Evaluation at d. Since d_δ lies on (c_δ a_δ), step s2 gives F^δ(d_δ) = F_a(d_δ) + j²(1 − F_a(d_δ)), where F_a(d_δ) is the crossing probability from (a_δ b_δ) to (c_δ d_δ). The source then passes to the limit at the boundary point d_δ with step s5 and obtains the limit φ(d) = x + j²(1 − x). The numbers 1 and j² are affinely independent, so the coefficient F_a(d_δ) converges to x.

source.ref: H. Duminil-Copin, Introduction to Bernoulli percolation, lecture notes (IHES, version of October 7, 2018), Theorem 4.8, Lemmas 4.10 and 4.13 and the proof of Theorem 4.8, pp. 25-28.

applications.title: Crossing probability in an equilateral triangle (Carleson's form)
applications.inputs: The domain Ω = T, the triangle with vertices a = 1, b = j, c = j², and the boundary point d = 2/3 + (1/3) j² on the side from c to a, two thirds of the way from c.
applications.hypotheses: T is a Jordan domain, the four points are distinct and in counterclockwise order, and critical site percolation is taken on fine triangular lattice approximations of T.

steps.text: The identity map is the conformal map from T onto T with a ↦ 1, b ↦ j and c ↦ j². So φ(d) = d = 2/3 + (1/3) j².
Matching φ(d) = x + j²(1 − x) gives x = 2/3. The two barycentric weights add up to one.

The theorem gives the limit 2/3 for the probability of a black path from the side (ab) to the part (cd) of the third side. In general the limit equals |d − c|/|a − c|, so it grows linearly as d moves from c to a.
On the triangular lattice, either a black path joins (ab) to (cd) or a white path joins (bc) to (da), and not both. So the white crossing has limit probability 1 − 2/3 = 1/3.

applications.conclusion: In the equilateral triangle, the scaling limit of the crossing probability is the relative position of d on the side from c to a, here 2/3, and the dual white crossing has limit 1/3.

limitations: The proof uses the triangular lattice in an essential way, through the cube roots of unity and the colour symmetry of site percolation. Cardy's formula for bond percolation on ℤ² is still open.
The theorem gives the limit but no rate of convergence. Later work gives polynomial rates for some domains.

results.name: Connective constant of the hexagonal lattice
aliases: Nienhuis conjecture for the honeycomb lattice
results.statement: Let ℍ be the hexagonal (honeycomb) lattice, and let c_n be the number of n-step self-avoiding walks on ℍ that start at a fixed vertex. Then the connective constant μ = lim_{n→∞} c_n^(1/n) exists and μ = √(2 + √2) = 2 cos(π/8) ≈ 1.84776.
hypotheses: ℍ is the hexagonal lattice: the planar graph of the regular tiling of the plane by hexagons, in which every vertex has exactly three neighbours.
c_n counts the n-step self-avoiding walks on ℍ that start at one fixed vertex.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 uses the Hammersley–Welsh decomposition of a walk into bridges, which the source adapts to the hexagonal lattice to show that bridges and all walks have the same growth rate μ.

definitions.name: self-avoiding walk
definitions.text: An n-step self-avoiding walk is a sequence of n + 1 distinct vertices in which consecutive vertices are neighbours.

definitions.name: connective constant
definitions.text: μ = lim_{n→∞} c_n^(1/n), the exponential growth rate of the number c_n of n-step self-avoiding walks. The limit exists because c_{n+m} ≤ c_n c_m.

definitions.name: bridge
definitions.text: On ℍ, a bridge is a self-avoiding walk that starts and ends at midpoints of horizontal edges, never returns to the vertical line through its start, and never goes to the right of the vertical line through its end.

definitions.name: holomorphic observable
definitions.text: For a domain Ω of mid-edges, a boundary mid-edge a, σ ∈ ℝ and z ≥ 0, F_z(x) = Σ e^(−iσ W_ω(a,x)) z^(ℓ(ω)), summed over the self-avoiding walks ω in Ω from a to the mid-edge x. Here W_ω(a,x) is the total rotation of ω in radians and ℓ(ω) is its number of vertices.

source.citation: Roland Bauerschmidt, Hugo Duminil-Copin, Jesse Goodman and Gordon Slade, Lectures on self-avoiding walks, in Probability and Statistical Physics in Two and More Dimensions, Clay Mathematics Proceedings 15, American Mathematical Society, 2012. arXiv:1206.2092.
source.revision: arXiv 1206.2092v1, 11 June 2012, as downloaded in October 2026.
source.module: Section 1.3 Subadditivity and the connective constant (Theorem 1.2), with the proof in Section 3 The connective constant on the hexagonal lattice
source.excerpt: Theorem 1.2. The connective constant for the hexagonal lattice is µ = √(2 + √2). The proof of Theorem 1.2 is presented in Section 3 below.
source.attribution: © Roland Bauerschmidt, Hugo Duminil-Copin, Jesse Goodman and Gordon Slade. Quoted from the authors' Lectures on self-avoiding walks for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The authored statement is the statement of the source, with the definition of μ made explicit. The theorem is due to Duminil-Copin and Smirnov (Annals of Mathematics 175, 2012), and Nienhuis predicted the value in 1982. The source states it as Theorem 1.2 and proves it as Theorem 3.1 in Section 3. The outline follows that proof.

results.proof_status: outline of the cited published proof. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of Theorem 1.2 (stated again as Theorem 3.1) in Bauerschmidt, Duminil-Copin, Goodman and Slade, Lectures on self-avoiding walks (2012), Section 3, pp. 17-22, which presents the proof of Duminil-Copin and Smirnov. Step s1 takes from the source the equality of the bridge growth rate and μ on ℍ. Steps s2 and s4 take from Lemmas 3.4 and 3.5 of the source the pairing of walks and the values of the boundary windings.

steps.text: Reduction to generating functions. Extend each walk by two half-edges so that it starts and ends at mid-edges, start it at the mid-edge a = 0 of a horizontal edge, and let ℓ(ω) be its number of vertices. This changes c_n by at most a bounded factor and a shift of the length by one, so μ does not change. Let b_n count the bridges of length n from a, and let χ(z) = Σ c_n z^n and B(z) = Σ b_n z^n. Let z_c = 1/√(2 + √2). The source states that the proof of its Corollary 2.7 (the Hammersley–Welsh argument) adapts to ℍ, so μ_Bridge = lim b_n^(1/n) = μ. The radius of convergence of χ is 1/μ, and that of B is 1/μ_Bridge = 1/μ. So two facts are sufficient: B(z) < ∞ for every z < z_c, which gives μ ≤ 1/z_c, and B(z_c) = ∞ or χ(z_c) = ∞, which gives μ ≥ 1/z_c.

The holomorphic observable (Lemma 3.4 of the source). Let Ω be a finite simply connected domain of mid-edges, a a mid-edge of its boundary, and F(x) = Σ_{ω⊂Ω: a→x} e^(−iσ W_ω(a,x)) z^(ℓ(ω)). Lemma 3.4 states that, for z = z_c and σ = 5/8, every vertex v of Ω with adjacent mid-edges p, q, r satisfies (p − v)F(p) + (q − v)F(q) + (r − v)F(r) = 0. Here mid-edges and vertices are points of ℂ. The proof writes the left side as a sum of contributions (x − v)e^(−iσ W_ω(a,x)) z^(ℓ(ω)) of the walks ω that end at x ∈ {p, q, r}. It partitions these walks into pairs and triplets. A pair is two walks that visit all three mid-edges and differ only in the direction of the loop from v back to v. A triplet is a walk that visits one mid-edge together with its two extensions by one step through v.

Cancellation in pairs and triplets. Orient p, q, r counter-clockwise around v, and let j = e^(2πi/3) and λ = e^(−iσπ/3). Then q − v = j(p − v) and r − v = j̄(p − v). For a pair that ends at q and r, the source uses that Ω is simply connected and a ∈ ∂Ω to get the windings W(a,p) − 4π/3 and W(a,p) + 4π/3, with equal lengths. So the pair contributes (p − v)e^(−iσ W(a,p)) z^ℓ (jλ̄⁴ + j̄λ⁴). With σ = 5/8 this factor is 2 cos(3π/2) = 0. In a triplet the two extensions have windings W(a,p) − π/3 and W(a,p) + π/3 and one more vertex. So the triplet has the factor 1 + z(jλ̄ + j̄λ) = 1 + 2z cos(7π/8) = 1 − 2z cos(π/8), because λ = e^(−5πi/24). This factor is zero exactly when z = 1/(2 cos(π/8)) = 1/√(2 + √2) = z_c, since cos²(π/8) = (2 + √2)/4. This is the only place where the value of z_c enters the proof.

The strip identity (Lemma 3.5 of the source). Let S_{T,L} be the domain of T columns of hexagons, cut at height L at the angle π/3. Let α and β be its left and right sides, ε and ε̄ its top and bottom, and a ∈ α. Let A_{T,L}, B_{T,L} and E_{T,L} be the sums of z^(ℓ(ω)) over walks in S_{T,L} from a to α∖{a}, to β, and to ε ∪ ε̄. Add the relation of s2 over all vertices of S_{T,L}. An interior mid-edge x is the midpoint of its two end vertices, so its two terms cancel. Only boundary mid-edges remain: −Σ_α F + Σ_β F + j Σ_ε F + j̄ Σ_ε̄ F = 0. A walk from a to α winds by π or −π, a walk to β winds by 0, and a walk to ε or ε̄ winds by 2π/3 or −2π/3. The reflection in the horizontal line through a pairs the walks to the top and to the bottom, and F(a) = 1 comes from the walk of length 0. So Σ_α F = 1 + cos(5π/8) A_{T,L} = 1 − c_α A_{T,L} and j Σ_ε F + j̄ Σ_ε̄ F = c_ε E_{T,L}. This gives 1 = c_α A_{T,L}(z_c) + B_{T,L}(z_c) + c_ε E_{T,L}(z_c), with c_α = cos(3π/8) and c_ε = cos(π/4).

Limits in L and the bound below z_c. The sums A_{T,L}(z) and B_{T,L}(z) increase in L. By s4 and monotonicity in z they are bounded for z ≤ z_c, so they converge to A_T(z) and B_T(z), the sums over walks in the infinite strip S_T. At z_c the identity of s4 then makes E_{T,L}(z_c) decrease in L to a limit E_T(z_c), and 1 = c_α A_T(z_c) + B_T(z_c) + c_ε E_T(z_c). So B_T(z_c) ≤ 1. A walk counted by B_T is a bridge of span T, and it has at least T vertices. So for z < z_c, B_T(z) ≤ (z/z_c)^T B_T(z_c) ≤ (z/z_c)^T. Each bridge from a has exactly one span T, so B(z) = Σ_T B_T(z) ≤ Σ_T (z/z_c)^T < ∞.

First case: E_T(z_c) > 0 for some T. By s5, E_{T,L}(z_c) ≥ E_T(z_c) for every L. Walks that end on the top or bottom of S_{T,L} for different L end at different heights, so they are different walks from a. So χ(z_c) ≥ Σ_{L≥1} E_{T,L}(z_c) ≥ Σ_{L≥1} E_T(z_c) = ∞.

Second case: E_T(z_c) = 0 for every T. Then 1 = c_α A_T(z_c) + B_T(z_c) for every T. The source observes that a walk counted by A_{T+1} but not by A_T visits a vertex next to the right side of S_{T+1}. Cut it at the first such vertex and add half-edges. After a vertical translation, the two parts are two bridges of span T + 1, and the walk is recovered from them. So A_{T+1}(z_c) − A_T(z_c) ≤ K B_{T+1}(z_c)² for a constant K > 0 that comes from the cut vertex, which both parts contain. The source writes K = z_c. A direct count of the shared vertex gives K = 1/z_c, and the argument below works for every K > 0. Subtract the identities for T and T + 1. This gives c_α K B_{T+1}² + B_{T+1} ≥ B_T, all at z_c. Let m = min(B_1(z_c), 1/(c_α K)) > 0, where B_1(z_c) > 0 because the straight crossing of S_1 is a bridge. Induction on T gives B_T(z_c) ≥ m/T. Indeed, if B_{T+1} < m/(T+1), then, since x ↦ c_α K x² + x increases for x ≥ 0, c_α K B_{T+1}² + B_{T+1} < c_α K (m/(T+1))² + m/(T+1) ≤ (m/(T+1))(1/(T+1) + 1), because c_α K m ≤ 1, and (m/(T+1))(1/(T+1) + 1) = m(T+2)/(T+1)² ≤ m/T ≤ B_T, a contradiction. So B(z_c) ≥ Σ_T m/T = ∞. With s1 and s5, μ = 1/z_c = √(2 + √2).

source.ref: R. Bauerschmidt, H. Duminil-Copin, J. Goodman and G. Slade, Lectures on self-avoiding walks (Clay Math. Proc. 15, 2012), Theorem 1.2 (p. 4) with its proof as Theorem 3.1, Lemmas 3.4 and 3.5 in Section 3, pp. 17-22.

applications.title: Critical monomer fugacity of a polymer on a honeycomb surface
applications.inputs: A flexible polymer adsorbed on a honeycomb surface such as a graphene sheet. Each monomer occupies a lattice site, and no two monomers share a site. In a grand canonical ensemble a chain of n steps has the weight z^n. Two fugacities: z = 0.54 and z = 0.55.
applications.hypotheses: The chain conformations are the self-avoiding walks on the hexagonal lattice from a fixed vertex, so c_n counts them. The weight depends only on the length. The theorem needs no other hypothesis.

steps.text: The partition function is χ(z) = Σ c_n z^n. Its radius of convergence is 1/μ. Submultiplicativity c_{n+m} ≤ c_n c_m and the subadditivity lemma (Lemma 1.1 of the source) give c_n ≥ μ^n for every n, so χ(1/μ) = ∞. So the ensemble has a finite partition function exactly when z < z_c = 1/μ.
The theorem gives μ = √(2 + √2). Then μ² − 2 = √2, so μ is a root of f(x) = x⁴ − 4x² + 2. For x > √2, f′(x) = 4x(x² − 2) > 0, so μ is the only root of f above √2. The value f(1.8477) is negative.
The value f(1.8478) is positive. So 1.8477 < μ < 1.8478, and the critical fugacity z_c = 1/μ lies between 1/1.8478 and 1/1.8477, so 0.54118 < z_c < 0.54122.
At z = 0.54 the product with the upper bound of μ is 0.54 × 1.8478 = 0.997812 < 1, so z < z_c. The partition function is finite, and the weight c_n z^n of length n decays exponentially.

At z = 0.55 the product with the lower bound of μ is 0.55 × 1.8477 = 1.016235 > 1, so z > z_c and χ(0.55) = ∞. Elementary counts give only (1 + √5)/2 ≤ μ ≤ 2. The lower bound counts the self-avoiding walks that never step left in the brick-wall picture of ℍ, whose number grows like the Fibonacci numbers. The upper bound counts the walks that never reverse a step. These bounds place z_c only between 0.5 and 0.6181.

applications.conclusion: The critical monomer fugacity of the honeycomb polymer ensemble is z_c = 1/√(2 + √2) ≈ 0.5412. The ensemble is finite at z = 0.54 and infinite at z = 0.55, and the entropy per monomer of long chains is ln μ ≈ 0.6140.

limitations: The theorem gives only the exponential growth rate. The predicted correction c_n ∼ A μ^n n^(γ−1) with γ = 43/32 in two dimensions is not proved.

The proof uses the special geometry of ℍ: three mid-edges at angles 2π/3 around each vertex and the value σ = 5/8. It does not give the connective constant of ℤ², which is known only numerically, μ ≈ 2.63816.
The relation of Lemma 3.4 is a weak form of discrete holomorphicity. It does not by itself prove the conjectured convergence of the walk at z_c to SLE(8/3).

results.name: Hammersley–Welsh bound for self-avoiding walks
results.statement: Let d ≥ 1. Let c_n be the number of n-step self-avoiding walks ω on ℤ^d with ω(0) = 0, and let µ = lim_{n→∞} c_n^(1/n) be the connective constant. For n ≥ 1 let b_n be the number of n-step bridges, that is, self-avoiding walks with ω(0) = 0 and ω₁(0) < ω₁(i) ≤ ω₁(n) for 1 ≤ i ≤ n, where ω₁ is the first coordinate, and let b_0 = 1. Then b_n ≤ µ^n for every n, and for every n ≥ 0, c_n ≤ b_(n+1) exp(π √(2(n + 1)/3)) ≤ µ^(n+1) exp(π √(2(n + 1)/3)). Consequently b_n^(1/n) → µ, and for every B > π √(2/3) there is n₀ such that c_n ≤ µ^(n+1) e^(B√n) for all n ≥ n₀.
hypotheses: The walks are nearest-neighbour self-avoiding walks on the hypercubic lattice ℤ^d, d ≥ 1, started at the origin.
µ is the limit of c_n^(1/n), which exists because c_(n+m) ≤ c_n c_m.

prerequisites.reason: Step s5 uses Euler's partition identity ∏_k (1 + x^k) = ∏_(k odd) (1 − x^k)⁻¹ to write the generating function of partitions into distinct parts.
Step s5 applies the AM-GM inequality to 1, x², …, x^(2j−2), which gives 1 − x^(2j) ≥ j x^(j−1)(1 − x²).
Step s5 uses the Basel sum Σ_j 1/j² = π²/6, which produces the constant π √(2/3) in the bound.

definitions.name: bridge
definitions.text: An n-step self-avoiding walk with ω₁(0) < ω₁(i) ≤ ω₁(n) for 1 ≤ i ≤ n. Its first coordinate stays strictly above the start and never exceeds the end.

definitions.name: half-space walk
definitions.text: An n-step self-avoiding walk with ω₁(0) < ω₁(i) for 1 ≤ i ≤ n. The number of such walks from 0 is h_n, with h_0 = 1.

definitions.name: partitions into distinct parts
definitions.text: P_D(A) is the number of ways to write A = A₁ + … + A_k with A₁ > … > A_k ≥ 1, and P_D(0) = 1.

definitions.name: connective constant
definitions.text: µ = lim c_n^(1/n) = inf c_n^(1/n). The limit exists by Fekete's lemma because log c_n is subadditive.

source.alignment: The source bounds c_n by b_(n+1) e^(B√n) for every B > π √(2/3) and all large n, using the Hardy–Ramanujan asymptotics of P_D (Theorem 2.4). The authored statement gives the explicit factor exp(π √(2(n + 1)/3)) for every n ≥ 0, which implies the source bound. The authored proof follows the source proof (Proposition 2.5, (2.14) and (2.16)) and replaces the Hardy–Ramanujan asymptotics by an elementary generating-function bound.

proof.scope: The full statement for every d ≥ 1 and every n ≥ 0, including b_n^(1/n) → µ and the form with a constant B > π √(2/3).

steps.text: Bridges are supermultiplicative: b_(n+m) ≥ b_n b_m. Attach an m-step bridge, translated to start at the end ω(n) of an n-step bridge. The first part has ω₁ ≤ ω₁(n) and the second has ω₁ > ω₁(n) after its start, so the result is self-avoiding and is a bridge, and the map is injective. Hence b_n^k ≤ b_(kn) ≤ c_(kn), so b_n ≤ (c_(kn)^(1/(kn)))^n → µ^n as k → ∞.

c_n ≤ Σ_(m=0)^n h_(n−m) h_(m+1). Given an n-step walk ω, let x₁ be the minimum of ω₁ and m the last time with ω₁(m) = x₁. Then (ω(m), …, ω(n)) has ω₁ > x₁ after time m, so it is an (n − m)-step half-space walk. The walk (ω(m) − e₁, ω(m), ω(m − 1), …, ω(0)) starts at first coordinate x₁ − 1 and then stays at ω₁ ≥ x₁, so it is an (m + 1)-step half-space walk. For fixed m the pair determines ω.

Decompose a half-space walk with n ≥ 1. Set n₀ = 0. Let n₁ be the last time at which ω₁ is maximal, n₂ the last time after n₁ at which ω₁ is minimal over times after n₁, n₃ the last time after n₂ at which ω₁ is maximal over times after n₂, and so on, until n_K = n. Let A_i = |ω₁(n_i) − ω₁(n_(i−1))|. Because n_(i−1) is the last time of its extreme value, all later values are strictly less extreme. For n₀ = 0 this is the half-space condition. This gives A₁ > A₂ > … > A_K > 0, and A₁ + … + A_K ≤ n. The walk is a bridge exactly when K = 1, and then A₁ is its span.

Let h_n[a₁, …, a_k] count half-space walks with K = k and A_i = a_i. Reflect the part after n₁ in the hyperplane ω₁ = ω₁(n₁). The part before n₁ has ω₁ ≤ ω₁(n₁) and the reflected part has ω₁ > ω₁(n₁) after n₁, so the new walk is self-avoiding. Its decomposition is [a₁ + a₂, a₃, …, a_k], and n₁ is the last time with ω₁ ≤ ω₁(0) + a₁, so the map is injective. Iteration gives h_n[a₁, …, a_k] ≤ b_(n, a₁+…+a_k), the number of bridges with span a₁ + … + a_k. Summing over the decreasing sequences gives h_n ≤ Σ_A P_D(A) b_(n,A) ≤ P_D(n) b_n. Here P_D is nondecreasing, because adding 1 to the largest part maps partitions of A into distinct parts injectively to those of A + 1.

Let S_N = Σ_(a+b=N) P_D(a) P_D(b), the coefficient of x^N in Q(x)², where Q(x) = ∏_k (1 + x^k) = ∏_(k odd) (1 − x^k)⁻¹. For 0 < x < 1, all coefficients are nonnegative, so S_N ≤ x^(−N) Q(x)². Also log Q(x) = Σ_(k odd) Σ_j x^(jk)/j = Σ_j x^j/(j(1 − x^(2j))). By AM-GM, 1 − x^(2j) = (1 − x²)(1 + x² + … + x^(2j−2)) ≥ (1 − x²) j x^(j−1). So log Q(x) ≤ (π²/6) x/(1 − x²). With x = e^(−s), x/(1 − x²) = 1/(2 sinh s) ≤ 1/(2s). Hence S_N ≤ exp(Ns + π²/(6s)), and s = π/√(6N) gives S_N ≤ exp(π √(2N/3)).

Steps s2 and s4, with h_0 = P_D(0) b_0 = 1, give c_n ≤ Σ_m P_D(n − m) P_D(m + 1) b_(n−m) b_(m+1). Step s1 gives b_(n−m) b_(m+1) ≤ b_(n+1), and the remaining sum is at most S_(n+1). By step s5, c_n ≤ b_(n+1) exp(π √(2(n + 1)/3)), and b_(n+1) ≤ µ^(n+1) by step s1. Then b_(n+1)^(1/(n+1)) ≥ c_n^(1/(n+1)) e^(−o(1)) → µ, so b_n^(1/n) → µ. Finally π √(2(n + 1)/3) ≤ B √n for large n when B > π √(2/3).

applications.title: Bridges and the connective constant of the square lattice
applications.inputs: Self-avoiding walks on ℤ². Exact enumeration gives b_4 = 17, b_8 = 631, c_7 = 2172 and c_8 = 5916.
applications.hypotheses: The walks are nearest-neighbour self-avoiding walks on ℤ² started at the origin, so d = 2 and every claim of the theorem applies.

steps.text: Supermultiplicativity predicts b_8 ≥ b_4² = 17². The enumeration value b_8 = 631 satisfies this, since 17² = 289.
Since b_n ≤ µ^n, every bridge count gives a lower bound: µ ≥ 631^(1/8) ≈ 2.239. Since µ = inf c_n^(1/n), µ ≤ 5916^(1/8) ≈ 2.961. Numerical work gives µ ≈ 2.638.
For n + 1 = 150 the exponent in the bound is π √(2 · 150/3) = π √100 = 10π. So b_150 ≥ c_149 e^(−10π).

Each walk of 150 steps is a walk of 149 steps followed by one of at most 3 non-reversing steps, so c_150 ≤ 3 c_149. Hence at least a fraction e^(−10π)/3 ≈ 7.6 · 10^(−15) of all 150-step walks are bridges.

applications.conclusion: Bridges are rarer than self-avoiding walks only by a factor e^(O(√n)). So their growth constant equals µ, and finite bridge counts give rigorous lower bounds such as µ ≥ 631^(1/8) on ℤ².

limitations: The bound c_n ≤ µ^n e^(O(√n)) is far from the predicted growth c_n ~ A µ^n n^(γ−1). In dimensions 2, 3 and 4 only small improvements of the exponent are known.
The constant π √(2/3) comes from partitions into distinct parts. It is not believed to be sharp for walks.

results.name: Hara–Slade theorem on self-avoiding walk in dimensions d ≥ 5
aliases: mean-field behaviour of self-avoiding walk above four dimensions
γ = 1 and ν = 1/2 for self-avoiding walk in d ≥ 5
results.statement: Let d ≥ 5. Let c_n be the number of n-step nearest-neighbour self-avoiding walks on ℤ^d that start at 0, let µ = lim_n c_n^(1/n) be the connective constant, and let E_n be the uniform distribution on these walks. There are constants A > 0, D > 0 and ε > 0, which depend on d, such that c_n = Aµ^n[1 + O(n^(−ε))] and E_n|ω(n)|² = Dn[1 + O(n^(−ε))] as n → ∞. Moreover, under E_n the process t ↦ ω(⌊nt⌋)/√(Dn), t ≥ 0, converges in distribution to a Brownian motion B on ℝ^d with E[B(t)B(t)ᵀ] = (t/d)I.
hypotheses: The walks are nearest-neighbour strictly self-avoiding walks on ℤ^d.
The dimension satisfies d ≥ 5.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 derives the lace expansion by repeated inclusion-exclusion on the self-intersections of a walk.
Step s2 uses the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality in ‖H_z ∗ G_z‖_∞ ≤ ‖H_z‖_∞ + ‖H_z‖₂², which feeds the diagrammatic estimates.
Steps s2 and s3 use Parseval's identity to write the bubble diagram ‖H_z‖₂² = B(z) − 1 as an integral of |Ĝ_z(k) − 1|².
Step s3 uses the bootstrap Lemma 5.9 of the source, which rests on the intermediate value theorem for the continuous function f.
Step s3 passes from z < z_c to z = z_c in the bound ‖H_z‖₂² ≤ c β with the monotone convergence theorem.
Step s6 turns the convergence of the Fourier transforms ĉ_n(k/√(Dn))/c_n to e^(−|k|²/(2d)) into convergence in distribution.

definitions.name: two-point function and susceptibility
definitions.text: G_z(x) = Σ_n c_n(x) z^n, where c_n(x) counts the n-step self-avoiding walks from 0 to x, and χ(z) = Σ_x G_z(x) = Σ_n c_n z^n. Both converge for 0 ≤ z < z_c = 1/µ.

definitions.name: bubble diagram
definitions.text: B(z) = Σ_x G_z(x)². The bubble condition is B(z_c) < ∞.

definitions.name: lace expansion
definitions.text: An identity Ĝ_z(k) = 1/(1 − 2dz D̂(k) − Π̂_z(k)) with D̂(k) = d⁻¹ Σ_j cos k_j. The function Π_z(x) is an alternating sum of diagrams with N = 1, 2, … loops that record self-intersections.

source.alignment: The authored statement is Theorem 4.1 of the source, which attributes it to Hara and Slade (1992), with the normalization of the Brownian limit written out. Theorem 6.2 of Slade's Saint-Flour notes The Lace Expansion and its Applications (p. 52) states the same result with ε < min{(d − 4)/2, 1} for c_n and ε < min{(d − 4)/4, 1} for the mean-square displacement, and with 1 ≤ A ≤ 1.493 and 1.098 ≤ D ≤ 1.803 for d = 5. The outline follows the lace-expansion proof of Sections 3-5 of those notes and cites the computer-assisted Hara-Slade papers for d = 5 and for the coefficient asymptotics.

results.proof_status: outline of the cited published proof. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the lace-expansion proof in Slade, The Lace Expansion and its Applications (Lecture Notes in Mathematics 1879), Sections 3-5 and Exercise 5.19, which Section 6.1 of those notes and Section 4 of the source use for the theorem of Hara and Slade (1992). Steps s2 and s3 cite Theorem 4.1, Lemma 5.9 and Theorem 5.8 of the notes. Steps s4 and s6 cite the Hara-Slade papers, which neither the notes nor the source reproduce.

steps.text: Lace expansion (Section 3 of the notes). Repeated inclusion-exclusion on the self-intersections gives the convolution equation ĉ_n(k) = 2d D̂(k) ĉ_(n−1)(k) + Σ_(m=1)^n π̂_m(k) ĉ_(n−m)(k) (3.26), where π_m = Σ_N (−1)^N π_m^(N) and π_m^(N) ≥ 0 is a sum over m-step walks whose laces have N edges, drawn as diagrams with N loops. For 0 ≤ z < z_c = 1/µ the generating functions satisfy Ĝ_z(k) = 1/(1 − 2dz D̂(k) − Π̂_z(k)) (3.30).

Diagrammatic estimates (Theorem 4.1 of the notes). With H_z = G_z − δ_0, Σ_x Π_z^(1)(x) ≤ 2dz‖H_z‖_∞ and Σ_x Π_z^(N)(x) ≤ ‖H_z‖_∞ ‖H_z ∗ G_z‖_∞^(N−1) for N ≥ 2, with similar bounds for Σ_x [1 − cos(k·x)] Π_z^(N)(x). Since ‖H_z ∗ G_z‖_∞ ≤ ‖H_z‖_∞ + ‖H_z‖₂² and ‖H_z‖₂² = B(z) − 1, a small bubble diagram makes the series over N converge and makes Π̂_z small.

Bootstrap (Lemma 5.9 and Theorem 5.8 of the notes). Define p(z) by χ(z) = 1/(1 − 2d p(z)) and let Ĉ_p(k) = 1/(1 − 2dp D̂(k)) be the random-walk two-point function. Let f(z) = max{2dz, sup_k |Ĝ_z(k)|/Ĉ_(p(z))(k), f₃(z)}, where f₃ compares second differences in k. f is continuous on [0, z_c) with f(0) = 1. Lemmas 5.12, 5.14 and 5.16 of the notes show that f(z) ≤ 4 implies f(z) ≤ 1 + Cβ, where β bounds the random-walk integral ∫ D̂(k)²/[1 − D̂(k)]² dk/(2π)^d of (5.2). Hence f ≤ 1 + Cβ on [0, z_c). This gives the infrared bound Ĝ_z(k) ≤ (1 + Cβ) Ĉ_(p(z))(k) and, by monotone convergence, B(z_c) − 1 ≤ cβ.

Every dimension d ≥ 5 (Hara and Slade, as reported in Section 6.1 of the notes). For the nearest-neighbour model, β in (5.2) is small only for large d, so step s3 alone covers d ≥ d₀. Hara and Slade close the same bootstrap for every d ≥ 5 with sharper diagrammatic bounds and computer-assisted numerical bounds on random-walk integrals. The notes state that d = 5 is large enough only barely. The result is the bubble condition and the infrared bound for every d ≥ 5.

Generating-function asymptotics (Exercise 5.19 of the notes). At k = 0, χ(z) = 1/(1 − 2dz − Π̂_z(0)). The bounds hold up to z_c, χ(z) ↑ ∞ as z ↑ z_c, so 1 − 2dz_c − Π̂_(z_c)(0) = 0 and χ(z) ∼ A(1 − z/z_c)^(−1) with A = z_c^(−1)[2d + ∂_zΠ̂_(z_c)(0)]^(−1). Differentiating (3.30) twice in k at k = 0, where the gradient of the denominator vanishes by symmetry, gives Σ_x |x|² G_z(x) = χ(z)² [2dz + Σ_x |x|² Π_z(x)] for z < z_c.

Coefficients and scaling limit (Hara and Slade, cited by the notes). Hara and Slade bound the lace-expansion coefficients at z_c well enough to transfer the singularities of step s5 to the coefficients. This gives c_n z_c^n → A and Σ_x |x|² c_n(x) z_c^n = ADn[1 + O(n^(−ε))], which are (4.1) and (4.2) of the source. The same analysis of ĉ_n(k) gives ĉ_n(k/√(Dn))/c_n → e^(−|k|²/(2d)), as in (6.1) of the notes. By Lévy's continuity theorem the finite-dimensional laws converge to those of B, and tightness gives convergence in distribution of the rescaled walk.

source.ref: G. Slade, The Lace Expansion and its Applications, Lecture Notes in Mathematics 1879, Theorem 6.2 (p. 52), Theorem 4.1 (p. 28), Theorem 5.8 and Lemma 5.9 (p. 41), Exercise 5.19 (p. 50).

applications.title: End-to-end distance and mutual avoidance of long polymers in five dimensions
applications.inputs: A linear polymer modelled by an n-step self-avoiding walk on ℤ⁵ with n = 10000 monomers, and the bounds 1 ≤ A ≤ 1.493 and 1.098 ≤ D ≤ 1.803 for d = 5 from Theorem 6.2 of Slade's Saint-Flour notes (p. 52).
applications.hypotheses: The walk is a nearest-neighbour self-avoiding walk and d = 5 ≥ 5, so the theorem applies. The error terms O(n^(−ε)) are ignored, so the numbers are leading-order values.

steps.text: To leading order E_n|ω(n)|² = Dn. With n = 10000 the lower bound is 1.098 · 10000 = 10980.

The upper bound is 1.803 · 10000 = 18030. So the root-mean-square end-to-end distance lies between √10980 ≈ 104.8 and √18030 ≈ 134.3 lattice spacings. Simple random walk gives √10000 = 100. Self-avoidance only changes the constant, not the exponent ν = 1/2.

Cutting a 2n-step self-avoiding walk at its midpoint gives a bijection with pairs of n-step self-avoiding walks from 0 that avoid each other except at 0. So c_(2n)/c_n² is the probability that two independent uniform n-step self-avoiding walks avoid each other. The theorem gives c_(2n)/c_n² → Aµ^(2n)/(A²µ^(2n)) = 1/A.
With 1 ≤ A ≤ 1.493 the limit 1/A lies between 1000/1493 ≈ 0.670 and 1. So two long polymers that start at the same point avoid each other with probability at least about 0.67.

applications.conclusion: In five dimensions a self-avoiding polymer of 10000 monomers has a root-mean-square size between about 105 and 134 lattice spacings, of the same order as a random walk. Two such polymers from a common point avoid each other with probability at least about 0.67 in the limit.

limitations: The proof for d = 5 and d = 6 is computer assisted. The constants A, D and ε are not explicit beyond the numerical bounds for d = 5 in Slade's notes.
The theorem says nothing about d = 2, 3, 4. There the critical exponents are expected to differ from the random-walk values, with logarithmic corrections in d = 4.
This outline cites the transfer from generating functions to coefficients and the tightness argument without detail.

results.name: Switching lemma for random currents
results.statement: Let G = (V, E) be a finite graph and let β_e ≥ 0 for each edge e. A current is a map n: E → {0, 1, 2, …}. Its sources ∂n are the vertices x for which Σ_{e∋x} n_e is odd, its weight is w(n) = ∏_e β_e^(n_e)/n_e!, and its trace n̂ is the set of edges e with n_e > 0. For B ⊂ V let F_B be the set of edge sets ω ⊂ E such that every connected component of (V, ω) contains an even number of points of B. Then for all A, B ⊂ V and every bounded or nonnegative F on currents, Σ_{∂n₁=A, ∂n₂=B} F(n₁ + n₂) w(n₁) w(n₂) = Σ_{∂n₁=AΔB, ∂n₂=∅} F(n₁ + n₂) w(n₁) w(n₂) 1[(n₁ + n₂)^ ∈ F_B], where AΔB is the symmetric difference of A and B.
hypotheses: G = (V, E) is a finite graph without loops, and every edge weight β_e is a nonnegative real number.
F is a real function on currents that is bounded, or nonnegative with values in [0, ∞].

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 regroups the absolutely convergent double series over pairs (n₁, n₂) by the value of m = n₁ + n₂, which Fubini's theorem for counting measure allows.
Step s3 applies the degree-sum formula to a sub-multigraph inside one connected component, which shows that the component contains an even number of odd-degree vertices.

definitions.name: current
definitions.text: A map n: E → {0, 1, 2, …} that puts a number of copies on each edge. Its sources ∂n are the vertices of odd total degree.

definitions.name: weight of a current
definitions.text: w(n) = ∏_e β_e^(n_e)/n_e!. Summed over all currents it gives ∏_e e^(β_e), which is finite.

definitions.name: trace of a current
definitions.text: The edge set n̂ = {e : n_e > 0}. It turns a current into a bond percolation configuration.

definitions.name: event F_B
definitions.text: The set of edge sets ω such that each connected component of the graph (V, ω) contains an even number of points of B. For B = {x, y} it says that x and y are connected in ω.

source.alignment: The source states the lemma for a constant inverse temperature β and an arbitrary F. The authored statement allows a weight β_e on each edge and requires F to be bounded or nonnegative, so that both sums are defined. The authored proof follows the source proof: the change of variables m = n₁ + n₂, the multigraph with m_e copies of each edge, and the bijection N ↦ N Δ K for a set K with sources B.

proof.scope: The full statement for every finite graph, all nonnegative edge weights, all A, B ⊂ V, and every bounded or nonnegative F.

steps.text: Σ_n w(n) = ∏_e Σ_k β_e^k/k! = ∏_e e^(β_e) < ∞, so for bounded F both sides converge absolutely, and for nonnegative F all terms are nonnegative. Hence the sums may be regrouped by m = n₁ + n₂. For fixed m the pairs are n₁ = n and n₂ = m − n with 0 ≤ n ≤ m on each edge, and w(n) w(m − n) = w(m) ∏_e C(m_e, n_e). The parity of a degree sum is additive, so ∂(n₁ + n₂) = ∂n₁ Δ ∂n₂. On both sides ∂m = AΔB, and given ∂m = AΔB the condition ∂n = A forces ∂(m − n) = B, while ∂n = AΔB forces ∂(m − n) = ∅. So it suffices to prove, for every m with ∂m = AΔB, that Σ_{n≤m, ∂n=A} ∏_e C(m_e, n_e) = 1[m̂ ∈ F_B] Σ_{n≤m, ∂n=AΔB} ∏_e C(m_e, n_e).

Let M be the multigraph on V with m_e distinct copies of each edge e. A subset N of the copies with n_e copies of e can be chosen in ∏_e C(m_e, n_e) ways, and its odd-degree vertices form exactly the set ∂n. So for every D ⊂ V the sum Σ_{n≤m, ∂n=D} ∏_e C(m_e, n_e) equals the number of subsets N ⊂ M with ∂N = D. The identity of step s1 becomes #{N ⊂ M : ∂N = A} = 1[m̂ ∈ F_B] · #{N ⊂ M : ∂N = AΔB}.

Let C be a connected component of (V, m̂). Every copy in M with an endpoint in C has both endpoints in C. For N ⊂ M, the degree-sum formula applied to the copies of N inside C shows that |∂N ∩ C| is even. Suppose m̂ ∉ F_B, and take C with |B ∩ C| odd. Since ∂M = AΔB and |∂M ∩ C| is even, |A ∩ C| ≡ |∂M ∩ C| + |B ∩ C| ≡ 1 mod 2. So no N ⊂ M has ∂N = A, and both sides of the identity are 0.

Suppose m̂ ∈ F_B. In each component C of (V, m̂), split the even set B ∩ C into pairs {x_i, y_i}. Since C is connected in m̂, there is a simple path γ_i in m̂ from x_i to y_i. In a simple path the two ends have degree 1 and the inner vertices have degree 2, so the odd-degree vertices of γ_i are x_i and y_i. Fix one copy in M of each edge of m̂ and let K be the symmetric difference of the sets of fixed copies along the paths γ_i. Degree parities add under symmetric difference, so ∂K = Δ_i {x_i, y_i} = B, because the pairs are disjoint.

The map N ↦ N Δ K is an involution of the subsets of M, so it is a bijection. It satisfies ∂(N Δ K) = ∂N Δ ∂K = ∂N Δ B. So it maps {N : ∂N = A} onto {N : ∂N = AΔB}, and the two counts are equal. Together with step s3, the identity of step s2 holds for every m with ∂m = AΔB. Multiplying by F(m) w(m) and summing over m gives the switching lemma.

applications.title: Squared spin correlation on a path of two edges
applications.inputs: The Ising model with free boundary condition on the path x – z – y, with inverse temperature β = ln 2 on both edges, so cosh β = 5/4 and tanh β = 3/5.
applications.hypotheses: The graph is finite, the edge weights β = ln 2 are positive, and F ≡ 1 is bounded. Expanding each factor exp(βσ_uσ_v) = Σ_k (βσ_uσ_v)^k/k! and summing over spins gives ⟨σ_xσ_y⟩ = Σ_{∂n={x,y}} w(n) / Σ_{∂n=∅} w(n), the random current expansion.

steps.text: Apply the switching lemma with A = B = {x, y} and F ≡ 1. Then AΔB = ∅, and dividing by (Σ_{∂n=∅} w(n))² gives ⟨σ_xσ_y⟩² = P(x and y are connected in (n₁ + n₂)^), where n₁ and n₂ are independent sourceless currents with law proportional to w.

A sourceless current on this path has an even value on each edge, because x and y are leaves. The weight factorizes over the two edges, so the edges are independent. On one edge P(n_e = 0) = 1/cosh β = 4/5 for each current.
An edge is open in (n₁ + n₂)^ unless both currents vanish on it. So P(edge open) = 1 − (4/5)² = 9/25, which equals tanh²β = (3/5)².

The points x and y are connected exactly when both edges are open. By independence this probability is (9/25)² = 81/625. So ⟨σ_xσ_y⟩² = 81/625 and ⟨σ_xσ_y⟩ = 9/25 = tanh²β, the known value for a path.

applications.conclusion: On the path x – z – y at β = ln 2, the switching lemma gives ⟨σ_xσ_y⟩² = 81/625. This agrees with the direct value ⟨σ_xσ_y⟩ = tanh²β = 9/25.

limitations: The lemma is an exact identity for finite graphs. Infinite-volume statements need a separate limit argument.
The lemma is special to the Ising model and its currents with Poisson-type weights. It has no direct analogue for the Potts model with q ≥ 3.

results.name: Aizenman–Higuchi theorem on the Gibbs states of the two-dimensional Ising model
aliases: translation invariance of all two-dimensional Ising Gibbs states
results.statement: Consider the nearest-neighbour ferromagnetic Ising model on ℤ² with zero field, Hamiltonian H_Λ(σ) = −Σ σ_iσ_j over the nearest-neighbour pairs {i, j} with {i, j} ∩ Λ ≠ ∅, at inverse temperature β > β_c = ½ ln(1 + √2). Let µ^+_β and µ^−_β be the plus and minus states and m*_β = µ^+_β(σ_0) > 0. Then every infinite-volume Gibbs measure µ, that is, every probability measure on {−1, 1}^(ℤ²) that satisfies the DLR equations, equals αµ^+_β + (1 − α)µ^−_β with α = (m*_β + µ(σ_0))/(2m*_β) ∈ [0, 1]. In particular every Gibbs measure is translation invariant, and µ^+_β and µ^−_β are the only extremal Gibbs measures.
hypotheses: The model is the nearest-neighbour ferromagnetic Ising model on ℤ² with zero field.
The inverse temperature satisfies β > β_c.
µ is an infinite-volume Gibbs measure: it satisfies the DLR equations for every finite Λ ⊂ ℤ².

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 uses Kramers–Wannier self-duality, which writes the ratio Z^ω/Z^+ of partition functions as a dual correlation function and gives the random-line weights.
Step s2 uses the FKG inequality, a consequence of the Holley inequality, to compare a decreasing event under two boundary conditions.
Steps s2 and s3 sum the bounds over the at most 64n² pairs of contour endpoints with a union bound.

definitions.name: open contour
definitions.text: In a box with boundary condition ω, the dual edges between disagreeing spins split into lines. The open lines have both endpoints on the boundary, and the set b(ω) of these endpoints depends only on ω.

definitions.name: surface tension τ_β
definitions.text: The free energy per unit length of an interface between the + and − phases, as a function of its direction, extended to ℝ² by homogeneity. For β > β_c it is a norm on ℝ².

definitions.name: plus and minus states
definitions.text: µ^+_β and µ^−_β are the weak limits of the finite-volume Gibbs measures with all-plus and all-minus boundary conditions as the box grows to ℤ².

source.citation: Loren Coquille and Yvan Velenik, A finite-volume version of Aizenman-Higuchi theorem for the 2d Ising model, arXiv:1003.6034, 2010. Published in Probability Theory and Related Fields 153 (2012).
source.revision: arXiv 1003.6034v3, December 22, 2010.
source.module: Section 1 Introduction and results, and Section 3 Proof of the main result
source.excerpt: Corollary 1.1. For any β > βc, Gβ = {αµ+ + (1 − α)µ− : 0 ≤ α ≤ 1}. It is easy to check that the estimate we have on the error term in Theorem 1.1 is essentially optimal
source.attribution: © Loren Coquille and Yvan Velenik. Quoted from the authors' arXiv paper A finite-volume version of Aizenman-Higuchi theorem for the 2d Ising model for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: Corollary 1.1 of the source is the Aizenman–Higuchi theorem for β > β_c, which Aizenman and Higuchi proved independently in 1980-1981. The authored statement adds the formula for α from the proof of the corollary on p. 10. The outline follows the new proof of the source, through its finite-volume Theorem 1.1 (p. 3) and Lemmas 3.1-3.3.

results.proof_status: outline of the cited published proof. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.1 in Coquille and Velenik (2012), Section 3, pp. 4-10, with the tools of Appendix A. Steps s1 to s4 cite the source for the contour estimates and the Ornstein-Zernike prefactors.

steps.text: Contours and tools (Appendix A of the source). Fix a box Λ_n = {−n, …, n}² and any boundary condition ω. The open contours of σ have endpoints in the set b(ω). By self-duality there are weights q_(Λ;β) on families of open contours with Z^ω/Z^+ = Σ q_(Λ;β)(Γ) (A.2). The source cites the bounds Σ_(Γ:i→j) q ≤ e^(−τ_β(j−i)) (A.3), a BK-type inequality (A.5), and (A.6) for contours through a point z. For β > β_c the surface tension τ_β is a norm with the sharp triangle inequality τ_β(x) + τ_β(y) − τ_β(x + y) ≥ κ_β(‖x‖ + ‖y‖ − ‖x + y‖) (A.1).

Far contours stay away (Lemma 3.1). Fix max{2ξ, 3/4} < a < 1. If the segment bb′ misses the box of radius 2n^a, the contour Γ_(b,b′) reaches Λ*_(n^a) with probability at most e^(−C₁n^(2a−1)). DLR conditioning and FKG reduce this to the boundary condition ±(b, b′), where the contour must cross the line L at distance n^a from bb′. Lemma A.2 gives Z^±/Z^+ ≥ e^(−C₂n^ρ) e^(−τ_β(b′−b)) for some ρ < 2a − 1. A triangle with base at most 3n and height at least n^a has ‖z − b‖ + ‖z − b′‖ − ‖b′ − b‖ ≥ c n^(2a−1), so (A.1) gives an excess cost C₃n^(2a−1). A union bound over at most 64n² pairs ends the proof.

At most one crossing contour (Lemma 3.2). Let N_cr count the open contours that meet Λ*_(n^a). On the event of step s2, two neighbouring crossing contours have endpoints b₁, b₂ and b′₁, b′₂ within distance C₆n^a on opposite sides. After conditioning on the outer contours, (A.5) and (A.3) bound the weight of the two crossings by e^(−τ_β(b′₁−b₁)−τ_β(b′₂−b₂)) ≤ e^(−C₇n), while Z^ω′ ≥ e^(−C₈n^a) Z^+. Polynomially many choices give µ^ω_(Λn)(N_cr ≥ 2) ≤ e^(−C₅n^(2a−1)).

The unique interface misses the centre (Lemma 3.3). On the event I₁ of a unique crossing contour Γ, condition on its parts outside Λ_(n^a) and on all other contours. This leaves a domain with boundary condition ±(d, d′) for two points d, d′ on ∂*Λ_(n^a). If the segment dd′ misses the box of radius n^a/2, the argument of step s2 gives e^(−C₁₃n^a). Otherwise Lemma A.1 gives Z^±/Z^+ ≥ C₁₄n^(−a/2) e^(−τ_β(d′−d)), and (A.6) gives at most C₁₅n^(−a) e^(−τ_β(d′−d)) for the contours through each z ∈ ∂*Λ_(2n^ξ). Summing over the O(n^ξ) points z gives µ^ω(Γ ∩ Λ*_(2n^ξ) ≠ ∅, I₁) ≤ C₁₂n^(ξ−a/2).

Finite-volume theorem (Theorem 1.1). On I₀ (no crossing contour) a circuit of constant spin surrounds Λ_(n^a). On I₁, outside the event of step s4, a circuit of constant spin surrounds Λ_(2n^ξ). Condition on the largest such circuit γ and its sign. The DLR equation gives ⟨f⟩^±_(Λ(γ)), and exponential relaxation (A.8) replaces it by ⟨f⟩^±_β with error ‖f‖|S(f)|e^(−C n^ξ) for F_(Λ_(n^ξ))-measurable f. With steps s3 and s4 this gives ⟨f⟩^ω_(Λn) = α_(n,ω)⟨f⟩^+_β + (1 − α_(n,ω))⟨f⟩^−_β + O(‖f‖_∞ n^(ξ−a/2)). With a close to 1 the error is O(‖f‖_∞ n^(−δ)) for some δ > 0.

Infinite volume (Corollary 1.1). Let µ be a Gibbs measure and f local. The DLR equation gives µ(g) = ∫⟨g⟩^ω_(Λn) dµ(ω), so step s5 gives µ(g) = A_n⟨g⟩^+_β + (1 − A_n)⟨g⟩^−_β + O(‖g‖_∞ n^(−δ)) with A_n = ∫α_(n,ω) dµ(ω) ∈ [0, 1]. For g = σ_0 this reads µ(σ_0) = (2A_n − 1)m*_β + O(n^(−δ)). Since m*_β > 0, A_n → α = (m*_β + µ(σ_0))/(2m*_β). For g = f and n → ∞, µ(f) = α⟨f⟩^+_β + (1 − α)⟨f⟩^−_β. Local functions determine µ, so µ = αµ^+_β + (1 − α)µ^−_β.

source.ref: L. Coquille and Y. Velenik, A finite-volume version of Aizenman-Higuchi theorem for the 2d Ising model, arXiv:1003.6034, Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.1 (p. 3), Lemmas 3.1-3.3 and Section 3.3 (pp. 4-10).

applications.title: The two-dimensional Dobrushin state is the symmetric mixture of the two phases
applications.inputs: The Ising model on ℤ² at some β > β_c, in boxes Λ_n = {i : −n ≤ i₁ ≤ n, −n ≤ i₂ ≤ n − 1} with the Dobrushin boundary condition: + where i₂ ≥ 0 and − where i₂ < 0.
applications.hypotheses: β > β_c holds by choice. Every subsequential weak limit µ of the finite-volume Dobrushin states satisfies the DLR equations, because the interaction has finite range. So the theorem applies to µ.

steps.text: The map σ_i ↦ −σ_ī with ī = (i₁, −1 − i₂) maps Λ_n onto itself and preserves the Dobrushin boundary condition and the energy. So every limit µ satisfies µ(σ_0) = −µ(σ_0̄) with 0̄ = (0, −1).
The theorem gives µ = αµ^+_β + (1 − α)µ^−_β, so µ is translation invariant. Hence µ(σ_0̄) = µ(σ_0), and step a1 gives µ(σ_0) = 0.
The formula for α gives α = (m*_β + µ(σ_0))/(2m*_β) = (m*_β + 0)/(2m*_β). In units of m*_β this is (1 + 0)/2 = 1/2.
So every subsequential limit equals ½µ^+_β + ½µ^−_β. Since all subsequential limits agree and the space of states is compact, the full sequence of Dobrushin states converges to this mixture.

applications.conclusion: In two dimensions the interface of the Dobrushin boundary condition does not stay near the origin. In the limit the origin sees the + phase or the − phase with probability 1/2 each. In dimension d ≥ 3 at low temperature the Dobrushin state is not translation invariant.

limitations: The proof of the source needs β > β_c. For β ≤ β_c the Gibbs measure is unique, but that fact needs other arguments, in particular at β = β_c.
The statement is special to dimension 2. In dimension d ≥ 3 Dobrushin states exist at low temperature, and they are not translation invariant.
The theorem does not describe the interface. Its diffusive fluctuations enter the proof only through the bound n^(ξ−a/2) of Lemma 3.3.

results.name: Existence of non-translation-invariant Dobrushin states in the Ising model in dimension d ≥ 3
aliases: van Beijeren's proof of Dobrushin's theorem
results.statement: Let d ≥ 3 and β > β_c(d − 1), where β_c(d − 1) is the critical inverse temperature of the Ising model on ℤ^(d−1) with zero field and m*_(d−1)(β) is its spontaneous magnetization. Let Λ_n = {i ∈ ℤ^d : −n ≤ i_j ≤ n for 1 ≤ j < d, −n ≤ i_d ≤ n − 1}, and let ⟨·⟩^Dob_n be the Ising Gibbs state in Λ_n at inverse temperature β and zero field with the Dobrushin boundary condition η_i = +1 if i_d ≥ 0 and η_i = −1 if i_d < 0. Then there is a sequence n_k ↑ ∞ such that ⟨f⟩^Dob = lim_k ⟨f⟩^Dob_(n_k) exists for every local function f, ⟨·⟩^Dob is an infinite-volume Gibbs state, and ⟨σ_0⟩^Dob ≥ m*_(d−1)(β) > 0 > −m*_(d−1)(β) ≥ ⟨σ_0̄⟩^Dob, where 0̄ = (0, …, 0, −1). In particular ⟨·⟩^Dob is not invariant under the vertical translation by e_d.
hypotheses: The dimension satisfies d ≥ 3.
The inverse temperature satisfies β > β_c(d − 1), and the magnetic field is zero.
The finite-volume states use the boxes Λ_n and the Dobrushin boundary condition, + on {i_d ≥ 0} and − on {i_d < 0}.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 uses compactness of the space of states and the DLR property of limits of finite-volume Gibbs states to get the Gibbs state ⟨·⟩^Dob.
Step s3 uses the Holley (FKG) inequality to show that ⟨σ_0⟩ does not decrease when a field on the top layer increases.
Step s4 applies the first GKS inequality to the duplicated system, and step s5 uses GKS monotonicity of the plus states in the volume and in β.
Step s5 uses the Peierls argument to know that β_c(d − 1) < ∞ when d − 1 ≥ 2, so the range of β is not empty.

definitions.name: Dobrushin boundary condition
definitions.text: The boundary configuration η with η_i = +1 when i_d ≥ 0 and η_i = −1 when i_d < 0. It forces a + phase above and a − phase below, so every configuration has an interface between them.

definitions.name: reflected site
definitions.text: For i = (i_1, …, i_d) the site ī = (i_1, …, i_(d−1), −1 − i_d) is the mirror image of i in the plane x_d = −1/2. The box Λ_n is symmetric under i ↦ ī.

definitions.name: critical inverse temperature β_c(d − 1)
definitions.text: The number inf{β ≥ 0 : m*_(d−1)(β) > 0} for the Ising model on ℤ^(d−1), where m*_(d−1)(β) is the limit of the magnetization at the origin in boxes with + boundary condition.

source.citation: Sacha Friedli and Yvan Velenik, Statistical Mechanics of Lattice Systems: A Concrete Mathematical Introduction, Cambridge University Press, 2017.
source.revision: Authors' online version, revised version of August 22, 2017.
source.module: Chapter 3, Section 3.10.7 Non-translation-invariant Gibbs states and interfaces
source.excerpt: Theorem 3.58. Assume d ≥ 3. Then, for all β > βc(d − 1), there exists a sequence of integers n_k ↑ ∞ along which ⟨·⟩^Dob_{β,0} … is a well-defined Gibbs state that satisfies ⟨σ0⟩^Dob_{β,0} > 0 > ⟨σ0̄⟩^Dob_{β,0}. In particular, ⟨·⟩^Dob_{β,0} is not invariant under vertical translations.
source.attribution: © Sacha Friedli and Yvan Velenik. Quoted from the authors' book Statistical Mechanics of Lattice Systems for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The authored statement is Theorem 3.58 of the source with the boxes and the boundary condition of the source written out. It adds the explicit bound ⟨σ_0⟩^Dob ≥ m*_(d−1)(β), which the source proof gives on p. 149. The outline follows the source proof on pp. 148-149, which uses Proposition 3.59 (van Beijeren's inequality) and Exercise 3.39.

results.proof_status: outline of the cited published proof. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of Theorem 3.58 in Friedli and Velenik (2017), pp. 148-149, with the proof of Proposition 3.59 (van Beijeren's argument) on p. 148. Step s4 states the GKS argument that the source leaves as Exercise 3.39.

steps.text: Limit state. The space of probability measures on {−1, 1}^(ℤ^d) is compact for convergence of local functions. A diagonal argument over a countable dense set of local functions gives n_k ↑ ∞ along which ⟨f⟩^Dob_(n_k) converges for every local f (Exercise 3.8 of the source). The interaction has finite range, so every such limit satisfies the DLR equations and is a Gibbs state.

Antisymmetry (3.88)-(3.89). The map T(σ)_i = −σ_ī maps Λ_n onto itself and sends edges to edges, so it preserves Σ σ_iσ_j. Since i_d ≥ 0 exactly when ī_d ≤ −1, the Dobrushin condition satisfies η_ī = −η_i, so T also preserves the boundary terms. Hence ⟨σ_0⟩^Dob_n = −⟨σ_0̄⟩^Dob_n for every n, and the limit gives ⟨σ_0⟩^Dob = −⟨σ_0̄⟩^Dob.

Comparison with a symmetric box. Let B_n = [−n, n]^d. Then B_n ∖ Λ_n is the layer {i_d = n}, where η = +1. Add a field h ≥ 0 on this layer to the Dobrushin state in B_n. The Holley (FKG) inequality shows that ⟨σ_0⟩ does not decrease in h. As h → ∞ the layer spins become +1, and the state tends to ⟨·⟩^Dob_n. So ⟨σ_0⟩^Dob_n ≥ ⟨σ_0⟩^Dob_(B_n).

Van Beijeren's inequality (Proposition 3.59): ⟨σ_0⟩^Dob_(B_n) ≥ ⟨τ_0⟩^+, the magnetization of an independent (d − 1)-dimensional + state in [−n, n]^(d−1). Reflect in x_d = 0 by i ↦ i′. For i_d > 0 put s_i = (σ_i + σ_i′)/2, t_i = (σ_i − σ_i′)/2. On the layer i_d = 0 put s_i = (σ_i + τ_i)/2, t_i = (σ_i − τ_i)/2. Then s_i = 0 exactly when t_i ≠ 0. Mirror edge pairs give 2(s_is_j + t_it_j), layer-0 vertical pairs give 2s_i(s_k + t_k), and the boundary gives fields 2t_i above the layer and 2s_k on it. All coefficients are nonnegative. Fix A = {s_i = 0}. One ±1 variable remains per site, so the first GKS inequality gives ⟨t_0⟩ ≥ 0, which is the claim.

Conclusion. Steps s3 and s4 give ⟨σ_0⟩^Dob_(n_k) ≥ ⟨τ_0⟩^+_([−n_k, n_k]^(d−1)). By GKS the right side decreases to m*_(d−1)(β) as k → ∞, and m*_(d−1) does not decrease in β. So m*_(d−1)(β) > 0 for β > β_c(d − 1), and the Peierls argument gives β_c(d − 1) < ∞ since d − 1 ≥ 2. Hence ⟨σ_0⟩^Dob ≥ m*_(d−1)(β) > 0, and step s2 gives ⟨σ_0̄⟩^Dob ≤ −m*_(d−1)(β) < 0. A state invariant under the translation by e_d would give ⟨σ_0̄⟩ = ⟨σ_0⟩.

source.ref: S. Friedli and Y. Velenik, Statistical Mechanics of Lattice Systems, Cambridge University Press 2017, Theorem 3.58 (p. 147), Proposition 3.59 and the proofs on pp. 148-149.

applications.title: A pinned interface in the three-dimensional Ising model
applications.inputs: The Ising model on ℤ³ with the Dobrushin boundary condition at β = ½ ln(2 + √5) ≈ 0.722, so sinh(2β) = 2.
applications.hypotheses: Here d = 3. The critical value of the two-dimensional model is β_c(2) = ½ ln(1 + √2) ≈ 0.441, with sinh(2β_c(2)) = 1. Since sinh is increasing and sinh(2β) = 2 > 1, β > β_c(2).

steps.text: The theorem gives ⟨σ_0⟩^Dob ≥ m*_2(β), the spontaneous magnetization of the two-dimensional model. Yang's formula gives m*_2(β) = (1 − sinh(2β)^(−4))^(1/8).
With sinh(2β) = 2 the term under the eighth root is 1 − 1/2⁴ = 15/16.
So ⟨σ_0⟩^Dob ≥ (15/16)^(1/8) ≈ 0.9920 and ⟨σ_0̄⟩^Dob ≤ −0.9920, where 0̄ = (0, 0, −1) is the site just below the origin.

For a ±1 spin, P(σ = +1) = (1 + ⟨σ⟩)/2. So σ_0 = +1 with probability at least 0.996 and σ_0̄ = −1 with probability at least 0.996. The interface passes between the two layers with probability at least 0.992.

applications.conclusion: At β ≈ 0.722 the Dobrushin state of the three-dimensional model keeps the interface between the layers x_3 = 0 and x_3 = −1 near the origin with probability at least 0.992. This state is not translation invariant.

limitations: The argument gives nothing for β_c(d) < β ≤ β_c(d − 1). In d = 3 a roughening transition is expected in this range, and above the roughening temperature the interface is expected to delocalize.
The theorem gives the limit only along a subsequence and does not describe the interface. Dobrushin's original cluster-expansion proof shows that the interface is rigid at very low temperature.
The result does not hold in d = 2: there every Gibbs state of the Ising model is translation invariant (Aizenman and Higuchi).

results.name: Critical point of the Ising model on the Bethe lattice
aliases: Ising critical temperature on the regular tree
Bethe lattice critical point β_c = atanh(1/k)
results.statement: Let k ≥ 2 and let T be the (k + 1)-regular tree with root o. For n ≥ 1 let B_n be the set of vertices at distance at most n from o and S_n the set at distance exactly n. For β ≥ 0 and η ∈ {−1, 1}^(S_n), let μ^η_{n,β} be the probability measure on σ ∈ {−1, 1}^(B_n) with σ = η on S_n and weight proportional to exp(β Σ σ_x σ_y), where the sum runs over the edges xy of T inside B_n. Let m_n(β) be the mean of σ_o under μ^+_{n,β}, the measure with η ≡ +1. Then m_n(β) is nonincreasing in n and converges to a limit m(β) ≥ 0. For every η, |μ^η_{n,β}(σ_o)| ≤ m_n(β), and μ^−_{n,β}(σ_o) = −m_n(β). Moreover m(β) > 0 if and only if k tanh β > 1. So the critical inverse temperature is β_c = atanh(1/k) = coth⁻¹ k = (1/2) ln((k + 1)/(k − 1)). For β ≤ β_c the root magnetization tends to 0 uniformly in η. For β > β_c the plus and minus boundary conditions give the different limits ±m(β).
hypotheses: T is the (k + 1)-regular tree with k ≥ 2, so every vertex other than the root has k children and the root has k + 1 children.
The interaction is the nearest-neighbour ferromagnetic Ising interaction with coupling 1, at inverse temperature β ≥ 0 and zero magnetic field.

prerequisites.reason: Step s3 uses the monotone convergence of the bounded, nonincreasing sequence of plus-boundary fields a_j to its limit a*.
Step s4 applies the intermediate value theorem to ψ = φ − id on [h₀, kβ] to find a positive fixed point of φ when k tanh β > 1.

definitions.name: Bethe lattice
definitions.text: The infinite tree in which every vertex has the same degree k + 1. It is also called the Cayley tree or the (k + 1)-regular tree.

definitions.name: cavity field
definitions.text: For a vertex x below the root, the number h_x such that the subtree of x, with its boundary spins fixed and the edge to the parent removed, gives σ_x the law proportional to e^(h_x σ_x).

definitions.name: root magnetization
definitions.text: The mean μ^η_{n,β}(σ_o) of the root spin under the finite-volume measure with boundary condition η on S_n.

source.citation: Russell Lyons, Phase transitions on nonamenable graphs, Journal of Mathematical Physics 41 (2000), 1099-1126.

source.module: Section 7 The Ising Model on Trees
source.excerpt: Theorem 7.1. If T is any tree, then its critical β equals coth−1 br(T).
source.attribution: © Russell Lyons. Quoted from the author's survey Phase transitions on nonamenable graphs for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states the result for every tree with branching number br(T). For the (k + 1)-regular tree br(T) = k, which gives β_c = coth⁻¹ k, the result of Kurata, Kikuchi and Watari that the source recalls just before Theorem 7.1. That sentence lists the unique and non-unique regimes in the opposite order. The authored statement uses the standard direction, with order for β > β_c, and the authored proof is the standard cavity recursion on the regular tree, because the survey gives no proof.
