proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement for every k ≥ 2 and β ≥ 0. The proof treats the root magnetization in finite volume and its limit, not the full set of infinite-volume Gibbs measures.

steps.text: For x in B_n with x ≠ o, let Z_x(s) be the partition function of the subtree of x inside B_n with σ_x = s and the boundary spins fixed. Summing over the children y gives Z_x(s) = ∏_y Σ_t e^(βst) Z_y(t). For x ∉ S_n write Z_x(s) = c_x e^(h_x s), and for y ∈ S_n set h_y = η_y · ∞. Then Σ_t e^(βst) Z_y(t) is proportional to cosh(βs + h_y), or equals e^(βsη_y) for y ∈ S_n. Hence h_x = Σ_y f(h_y) with f(h) = (1/2) ln(cosh(h + β)/cosh(h − β)) = atanh(tanh β · tanh h) and f(±∞) = ±β. The same computation at the root, with its k + 1 children, gives μ^η_{n,β}(σ_o) = tanh(H_o) with H_o = Σ_{y child of o} f(h_y).

Let θ = tanh β ∈ [0, 1). The function f is odd and nondecreasing, f(0) = 0, |f(h)| ≤ β, and f(h) < β for finite h when β > 0. With t = tanh h, f′(h) = θ(1 − t²)/(1 − θ²t²). The derivative of (1 − t²)/(1 − θ²t²) in t is 2t(θ² − 1)/(1 − θ²t²)², which is negative for t > 0 and θ < 1. So f′ is strictly decreasing on [0, ∞) when β > 0, f is strictly concave there, and f′(0) = θ. Set φ = k f.

Under the plus boundary condition all vertices at height j above S_n have the same field a_j, with a_0 = ∞, a_1 = kβ and a_(j+1) = φ(a_j). Since φ is nondecreasing and a_1 ≤ a_0, induction gives a_(j+1) ≤ a_j, and all a_j ≥ 0. So a_j decreases to a limit a* ≥ 0, and continuity of φ gives φ(a*) = a*. If b ≥ 0 and φ(b) = b, then b ≤ a_j for all j by induction, so a* is the largest fixed point of φ in [0, ∞). The root sees k + 1 children at height n − 1, so m_n(β) = tanh((k + 1) f(a_(n−1))). This is nonincreasing in n and tends to m(β) = tanh((k + 1) f(a*)), which is positive exactly when a* > 0 and β > 0.

For β = 0 all fields vanish and m(β) = 0. Let β > 0 and ψ(h) = φ(h) − h on [0, ∞). Then ψ(0) = 0, ψ is strictly concave, and ψ′(0) = kθ − 1. If kθ ≤ 1, strict concavity gives ψ(h) < ψ(0) + ψ′(0)h ≤ 0 for h > 0, so 0 is the only fixed point, a* = 0 and m(β) = 0. If kθ > 1, then ψ(h₀) > 0 for some small h₀ > 0, and ψ(kβ) = k f(kβ) − kβ < 0 by step s2. The intermediate value theorem gives a fixed point b in (h₀, kβ), so a* ≥ b > 0 and m(β) > 0. The condition kθ > 1 is β > atanh(1/k) = (1/2) ln((k + 1)/(k − 1)).

For any η, a vertex x at height j satisfies |h_x| ≤ a_j. This holds at height 0 because a_0 = ∞. If it holds at height j, then |h_x| ≤ Σ_y |f(h_y)| = Σ_y f(|h_y|) ≤ k f(a_j) = a_(j+1), because f is odd and nondecreasing. At the root |H_o| ≤ (k + 1) f(a_(n−1)), so |μ^η_{n,β}(σ_o)| ≤ m_n(β). The spin flip σ ↦ −σ maps μ^+_{n,β} to μ^−_{n,β}, so the minus boundary condition gives −m_n(β). With steps s3 and s4 this proves all claims.

applications.title: The Bethe lattice with coordination number 3
applications.inputs: The 3-regular tree, so k = 2. Inverse temperatures β_c = atanh(1/2) and β = ln 2, where tanh(ln 2) = 3/5.
applications.hypotheses: Every vertex has degree 3, so T is the (k + 1)-regular tree with k = 2. The coupling is ferromagnetic and the field is zero.

steps.text: The critical point solves 2 tanh β_c = 1. Then e^(2β_c) = (1 + 1/2)/(1 − 1/2) = 3, so β_c = (1/2) ln 3 ≈ 0.549. The mean-field (Curie–Weiss) approximation with 3 neighbours predicts 1/3 instead.
At β = ln 2 we have tanh β = (4 − 1)/(4 + 1) = 3/5, so k tanh β = 6/5 > 1. By the theorem m(ln 2) > 0, and the plus and minus boundary conditions give different limits.
The plus recursion starts at a_1 = kβ = 2 ln 2 with tanh(2 ln 2) = 15/17. Then θ tanh a_1 = (3/5)(15/17) = 9/17, and f(a_1) = (1/2) ln((17 + 9)/(17 − 9)) = (1/2) ln(13/4).
So a_2 = 2 f(a_1) = ln(13/4) ≈ 1.179, which is smaller than a_1 = 2 ln 2 ≈ 1.386, as step s3 predicts. The fields decrease to the largest fixed point a* > 0 of φ = 2f.

applications.conclusion: On the Bethe lattice with coordination number 3 the critical inverse temperature is β_c = (1/2) ln 3 ≈ 0.549. At β = ln 2 the root keeps a positive magnetization under the plus boundary condition in the limit.

limitations: The theorem controls the root magnetization. Uniqueness of the infinite-volume Gibbs measure for β ≤ β_c needs a further argument for all local observables, which the source covers for all trees.
The free boundary condition has a different threshold on trees: the free measure stays extremal up to atanh(1/√k), the result of Bleher, Ruiz and Zagrebnov.

results.name: Continuity of the phase transition of the Ising model in dimension d ≥ 3
aliases: vanishing of the spontaneous magnetization at criticality
results.statement: Consider the nearest-neighbour Ising model on ℤ^d with zero field. Let µ^+_β and µ^f_β be the infinite-volume limits at inverse temperature β of the Gibbs states in boxes with + and with free boundary conditions. Let m*(β) = µ^+_β[σ_0] and β_c = inf{β > 0 : m*(β) > 0}. (a) Let d ≥ 2 and β > 0. If µ^f_β[σ_0σ_x] → 0 as ‖x‖ → ∞, then m*(β) = 0. (b) If d ≥ 3, then m*(β_c) = 0. So the spontaneous magnetization vanishes at the critical point, and the phase transition is continuous.
hypotheses: The model is the nearest-neighbour Ising model on ℤ^d with zero field and the plus and free infinite-volume states.
For part (a), d ≥ 2 and the free two-point function tends to 0 at infinity.
For part (b), d ≥ 3.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 uses the infrared bound µ^f_β[σ_xσ_y] ≤ (C/β) G(x, y) for β < β_c to show that the free two-point function at β_c tends to 0.
Step s1 uses the transience of simple random walk in d ≥ 3, which makes the Green function G(x, y) finite and lets it tend to 0.
Step s1 uses GKS monotonicity of finite-volume free correlations in β and in the volume, and step s6 uses the second GKS inequality µ^+[σ_0σ_x] ≥ m*(β)².
Step s2 derives the percolation formulas (4.12) and (4.13) of the source from the switching lemma for random currents.

Step s4 adapts the Burton–Keane argument to show that the current percolation P^+_β has at most one infinite cluster, and step s6 uses uniqueness of the infinite cluster of the wired random-cluster measure.
Step s5 uses the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality E[N_n²] ≥ (E N_n)² for the number N_n of sites of a box that connect to infinity.
Step s6 writes edge densities and connection probabilities of the random-cluster measures with the Ising correlations through the Edwards–Sokal coupling.

definitions.name: continuous phase transition
definitions.text: The phase transition at β_c is continuous when m*(β_c) = 0, so the spontaneous magnetization does not jump at the critical point.

definitions.name: current percolation P^+_(G,β)
definitions.text: The law of the set of edges with n₁(e) + n₂(e) > 0, where n₁ is a random current whose sources lie on the boundary of G and n₂ is an independent sourceless current, with weights w_β(n₁) w_β(n₂).

definitions.name: Green function
definitions.text: G(x, y) is the expected number of visits to y of simple random walk on ℤ^d that starts at x. It is finite when d ≥ 3.

source.citation: Hugo Duminil-Copin, Lectures on the Ising and Potts models on the hypercubic lattice, arXiv:1707.00520, 2017. Published in PIMS-CRM Summer School in Probability, Springer Proceedings in Mathematics and Statistics 299, 2019.

source.module: Section 4.3 Continuity of the phase transition for Ising models on Zd for d ≥ 3
source.excerpt: Theorem 4.4 (Aizenman, DC, Sidoravicius [5]) For the Ising model at inverse temperature β on Zd, (MAGβ) implies (LROβ). As a consequence, the spontaneous magnetization is equal to 0 at criticality.
source.attribution: © Hugo Duminil-Copin. Quoted from the author's lecture notes on the Ising and Potts models for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: Part (a) of the authored statement is the contrapositive form of (MAGβ) ⇒ (LROβ) that the source proof gives: absence of long-range order implies m*(β) = 0. Part (b) is the consequence at criticality, which the source derives from (4.9) for d ≥ 3. The result is due to Aizenman, Duminil-Copin and Sidoravicius, Comm. Math. Phys. 334 (2015). The outline follows the proof in Section 4.3 of the lecture notes.

results.proof_status: outline of the cited published proof. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of Theorem 4.4 in Duminil-Copin, Lectures on the Ising and Potts models on the hypercubic lattice (arXiv:1707.00520), Section 4.3, pp. 43-48. Steps s3 and s4 cite Lemmas 4.6 and 4.7 of the source. Step s5 writes out the second-moment argument that the source states in one sentence.

steps.text: Part (b) from part (a). For β < β_c the infrared bound gives µ^f_β[σ_xσ_y] ≤ (C/β) G(x, y). The finite-volume free correlations increase in the volume and in β (GKS) and are continuous in β, so µ^f_(β_c)[σ_xσ_y] = sup_n sup_(β<β_c) µ^f_(Λ_n,β)[σ_xσ_y] ≤ (C/β_c) G(x, y). This is (4.9) of the source. For d ≥ 3 simple random walk is transient, and G(0, x) → 0 as ‖x‖ → ∞. So the hypothesis of part (a) holds at β_c.

Percolation formulas (Lemma 4.5 of the source). Expand the + state in a finite graph G with random currents whose sources may lie on ∂G. The switching lemma gives (4.12): µ^+_G[σ_xσ_y] µ^f_G[σ_xσ_y] = P^+_(G,β)[x ↔ y] for interior x, y. It also gives (4.13): 0 ≤ µ^+_G[σ_xσ_y] − µ^f_G[σ_xσ_y] ≤ sinh(β)^(−1) P^+_(G,β)[A(xy)] for each edge xy, where A(xy) asks that xy is open and that, without xy, x and y connect to ∂G but not to each other.

Infinite volume (Lemma 4.6 of the source). Given the parities of the currents, each edge is open independently, and the parity law of the sourceless current satisfies P^f[C_F] = µ^f[e^(−βK_F)] cosh(β)^|F| with K_F = Σ_(xy∈F) σ_xσ_y. This formula and the convergence of the Ising states give a limit P^+_β of P^+_(Λ_n,β). The source proves that P^+_β is translation invariant and ergodic.

Uniqueness (Lemma 4.7 of the source). P^+_β has at most one infinite cluster almost surely. The proof is the Burton–Keane argument. P^+_β has no finite-energy property, so the source uses the insertion tolerance P^+_β[ω_xy = 1 | A] ≥ c_IT and coarse trifurcations in place of trifurcations.

No infinite cluster. Assume µ^f_β[σ_0σ_x] → 0. Letting G ↑ ℤ^d in (4.12) gives f(x) := P^+_β[0 ↔ ∞, x ↔ ∞] ≤ P^+_β[0 ↔ x] ≤ µ^f_β[σ_0σ_x] → 0, where the first inequality uses step s4. Let θ = P^+_β[0 ↔ ∞] and let N_n count the sites of Λ_n that connect to infinity. Cauchy–Schwarz gives θ²|Λ_n|² ≤ E[N_n²] = Σ_(x,y∈Λ_n) f(y − x) = o(|Λ_n|²). So θ = 0, and there is no infinite cluster almost surely.

Conclusion. In (4.13), A(xy) forces x ↔ ∂Λ_m for every m < n, so in the limit µ^+_β[σ_xσ_y] − µ^f_β[σ_xσ_y] ≤ sinh(β)^(−1) P^+_β[x ↔ ∞] = 0 for every edge. The Edwards–Sokal coupling with p = 1 − e^(−2β) gives φ^ξ[ω_xy] = (p/2)(1 + µ^ξ[σ_xσ_y]), so the free and wired random-cluster measures φ^0 ≤ φ^1 have equal edge densities and coincide. The wired measure φ^1 has at most one infinite cluster (Burton–Keane), so µ^+_β[σ_0σ_x] = φ^1[0 ↔ x] = φ^0[0 ↔ x] = µ^f_β[σ_0σ_x] → 0. The second GKS inequality gives m*(β)² ≤ µ^+_β[σ_0σ_x], so m*(β) = 0.

source.ref: H. Duminil-Copin, Lectures on the Ising and Potts models on the hypercubic lattice, arXiv:1707.00520, Theorem 4.4 (p. 45), Lemmas 4.5-4.7 and the proof on pp. 45-48.

applications.title: A unique Gibbs state and finite Swendsen–Wang clusters at the critical point of the three-dimensional Ising model
applications.inputs: The nearest-neighbour Ising model on ℤ³ at its critical inverse temperature β_c, and the coupled random-cluster model with q = 2 and p_c = 1 − e^(−2β_c), whose clusters are the Swendsen–Wang clusters.
applications.hypotheses: The dimension is d = 3 ≥ 3, so part (b) of the theorem applies at β_c.

steps.text: Part (b) gives m*(β_c) = µ^+_(β_c)[σ_0] = 0. By spin-flip symmetry µ^−_(β_c)[σ_0] = −m*(β_c) = 0 as well.
The minus state is stochastically dominated by the plus state. Under a monotone coupling σ^− ≤ σ^+, P(σ^−_x ≠ σ^+_x) = µ^+[σ_x = 1] − µ^−[σ_x = 1] = m*(β_c) = 0 for each x. So µ^+_(β_c) = µ^−_(β_c).
Every Gibbs state at β_c lies between µ^− and µ^+ in the stochastic order. So the Ising model on ℤ³ has exactly one Gibbs state at β_c, as it has for β < β_c.
The Edwards–Sokal coupling gives φ^1_(p_c,2)[0 ↔ ∞] = m*(β_c) = 0. By translation invariance and a countable union, the wired random-cluster measure at p_c has no infinite cluster almost surely.

applications.conclusion: At the critical point of the three-dimensional Ising model the plus and minus states coincide, the Gibbs state is unique, and the critical random-cluster (Swendsen–Wang) clusters are all finite.

limitations: The theorem gives no rate for m*(β) as β ↓ β_c. Mean-field bounds in high dimensions need other methods, and the exponent in d = 3 is not known rigorously.
Part (b) uses the infrared bound, which needs d ≥ 3 and reflection positivity. In d = 2 the same conclusion follows from the exact solution of Onsager and Yang.
The proof is special to the Ising model. For the planar q-state Potts model with q ≥ 5 the transition is discontinuous.

results.name: Phase transition of the Curie–Weiss model
results.statement: Let N ≥ 1 and β ≥ 0. On {−1, 1}^N let μ_{N,β}(σ) = Z_{N,β}⁻¹ exp(β M_N²/(2N)), where M_N = σ₁ + … + σ_N, and let m_N = M_N/N. (a) If β ≤ 1, then for every ε > 0 there is c > 0 such that μ_{N,β}(|m_N| ≥ ε) ≤ e^(−cN) for all large N. (b) If β > 1, then the equation tanh(βm) = m has exactly one solution m* = m*(β) in (0, 1). For every ε > 0 there is c > 0 such that μ_{N,β}(||m_N| − m*| ≥ ε) ≤ e^(−cN) for all large N. For 0 < ε < m*, the probabilities μ_{N,β}(|m_N − m*| < ε) and μ_{N,β}(|m_N + m*| < ε) both tend to 1/2. So the critical inverse temperature is β_c = 1.
hypotheses: The spins σ₁, …, σ_N take values in {−1, 1}, and their joint law is the Curie–Weiss Gibbs measure μ_{N,β} with zero magnetic field.
The inverse temperature β ≥ 0 is fixed while N → ∞.

prerequisites.reason: Step s3 uses the Heine–Cantor theorem: the function φ is uniformly continuous on [−1, 1], so its maximum over the grid A_N converges to its maximum over [−1, 1].
Step s4 uses the intermediate value theorem to find a point m* in (0, 1) where atanh(m)/m equals β.
Step s5 uses the extreme value theorem: φ attains its maximum on the compact set F_ε, so this maximum is strictly smaller than the global maximum.

definitions.name: Curie–Weiss model
definitions.text: The Ising model on the complete graph with N vertices. Every pair of spins interacts with strength β/N, so the weight of σ is exp(β M_N²/(2N)).

definitions.name: magnetization density
definitions.text: m_N = (σ₁ + … + σ_N)/N, the mean spin. It takes values in the grid A_N = {−1 + 2k/N : k = 0, …, N}.

definitions.name: spontaneous magnetization
definitions.text: For β > 1, the positive solution m*(β) of the mean-field equation tanh(βm) = m. It is the typical absolute value of m_N.

source.alignment: The source uses the Hamiltonian −(dβ/N) Σ_{i,j} ω_i ω_j, so its β_c = 1/(2d). The authored statement uses the weight exp(β M_N²/(2N)), which is the source model with β replaced by 2dβ, so β_c = 1. The authored statement adds the uniqueness of m* and the limit 1/2 for each sign. The authored proof follows the source proof through Proposition 2.5 and the mean-field equation (2.12), pp. 61-64, with explicit binomial bounds in place of Stirling's formula.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement, parts (a) and (b), for every β ≥ 0.

steps.text: Exactly C(N, k) configurations have k plus spins, and each of them has m_N = (2k − N)/N. So for m = −1 + 2k/N in the grid A_N, μ_{N,β}(m_N = m) = Z_{N,β}⁻¹ C(N, k) exp(βN m²/2), and Z_{N,β} is the sum of these N + 1 weights.

Let p = k/N and H(p) = −p log p − (1 − p) log(1 − p), so H(p) = s(m). The binomial(N, p) terms t_j = C(N, j) p^j (1 − p)^(N−j) sum to 1. Hence C(N, k) e^(−N H(p)) = t_k ≤ 1. For 0 < p < 1, the ratio t_{j+1}/t_j = (N − j)p/((j + 1)(1 − p)) is at least 1 exactly when j ≤ (N + 1)p − 1 = k − 1 + k/N. So t_j increases up to j = k and decreases after k, and t_k is the largest of N + 1 terms with sum 1. For p = 0 or 1, t_k = 1. In all cases (N + 1)⁻¹ e^(N s(m)) ≤ C(N, k) ≤ e^(N s(m)).

Let φ(m) = βm²/2 + s(m), a continuous function on [−1, 1]. For a set F ⊂ [−1, 1], steps s1 and s2 give μ_{N,β}(m_N ∈ F) ≤ (N + 1) e^(N sup_F φ) / ((N + 1)⁻¹ e^(N max_{A_N} φ)). Every point of [−1, 1] lies within 1/N of A_N. By the Heine–Cantor theorem φ is uniformly continuous, so max_{A_N} φ ≥ max φ − δ_N with δ_N → 0. If η = max φ − sup_F φ > 0, then μ_{N,β}(m_N ∈ F) ≤ (N + 1)² e^(−N(η − δ_N)) ≤ e^(−Nη/2) for all large N.

The function φ is even. On (−1, 1) it is smooth with φ′(m) = βm − atanh(m), because s′(m) = −(1/2) log((1 + m)/(1 − m)). For 0 < m < 1 write φ′(m) = m(β − g(m)) with g(m) = atanh(m)/m = Σ_{k≥0} m^(2k)/(2k + 1). The function g is continuous and strictly increasing, g(0+) = 1, and g(m) → ∞ as m → 1. If β ≤ 1, then φ′ < 0 on (0, 1), so 0 is the only maximizer of φ on [−1, 1]. If β > 1, the intermediate value theorem and monotonicity give one m* in (0, 1) with g(m*) = β. Then φ′ > 0 on (0, m*) and φ′ < 0 on (m*, 1), so the maximizers of φ are exactly ±m*. The condition g(m) = β is equivalent to tanh(βm) = m, so m* is the only solution of this equation in (0, 1).

Let M be the set of maximizers from step s4 and F_ε = {m ∈ [−1, 1] : dist(m, M) ≥ ε}. If F_ε is empty there is nothing to prove. Otherwise F_ε is compact and contains no maximizer, so by the extreme value theorem sup_{F_ε} φ < max φ. Step s3 gives μ_{N,β}(m_N ∈ F_ε) ≤ e^(−cN) for large N. For β ≤ 1 this is part (a). For β > 1 it is the first claim of part (b).

The map σ ↦ −σ preserves μ_{N,β} and sends m_N to −m_N. So the events {|m_N − m*| < ε} and {|m_N + m*| < ε} have the same probability. For ε < m* they are disjoint, and by step s5 their union has probability at least 1 − e^(−cN). Hence each probability lies between (1 − e^(−cN))/2 and 1/2, and it tends to 1/2.

applications.title: An exact value of the spontaneous magnetization
applications.inputs: The Curie–Weiss model at inverse temperature β = (5/3) ln 2 ≈ 1.155, with a large number N of spins.
applications.hypotheses: The spins have the Curie–Weiss law μ_{N,β} with zero field. The value β = (5/3) ln 2 is fixed and larger than 1, because ln 2 ≈ 0.693 > 3/5.

steps.text: Try m = 3/5 in the mean-field equation. Then βm = (5/3)(3/5) ln 2 = ln 2, and tanh(ln 2) = (e^(2 ln 2) − 1)/(e^(2 ln 2) + 1) = (4 − 1)/(4 + 1).
So tanh(βm) = m holds at m = 3/5. By part (b) the equation has exactly one solution in (0, 1), so m*(β) = 3/5.
A configuration with m_N = 3/5 has a fraction (1 + 3/5)/2 of plus spins. This fraction is 4/5.
By part (b), for each ε in (0, 3/5) the magnetization m_N lies within ε of 3/5 or of −3/5 with probability at least 1 − e^(−cN). Each of the two signs has a probability that tends to 1/2.

applications.conclusion: At β = (5/3) ln 2, a typical configuration of a large Curie–Weiss system has about 80% of its spins equal. The common sign is plus or minus with probability close to 1/2 each.

limitations: The theorem treats zero magnetic field only. With a field h ≠ 0 the magnetization concentrates at one solution of tanh(βm + h) = m for every β.
The bounds e^(−cN) are not explicit in c. The fluctuations of m_N on smaller scales are the subject of the Ellis–Newman limit theorems.

results.name: Ellis–Newman limit theorems for the Curie–Weiss magnetization
aliases: critical fluctuations of the Curie–Weiss model
results.statement: For N ≥ 1 and β ≥ 0 let σ₁, …, σ_N have the Curie–Weiss law μ_{N,β}(σ) = Z_{N,β}⁻¹ exp(β S_N²/(2N)) on {−1, 1}^N, where S_N = σ₁ + … + σ_N. (a) If 0 ≤ β < 1, then S_N/√N converges in distribution to the normal law N(0, 1/(1 − β)). (b) If β = 1, then S_N/N^(3/4) converges in distribution to the law with density exp(−x⁴/12) / ∫_ℝ exp(−t⁴/12) dt. (c) If β > 1, then S_N/N converges in distribution to (δ_(m*) + δ_(−m*))/2, where m* is the unique solution in (0, 1) of tanh(βm) = m.
hypotheses: For each N the spins σ₁, …, σ_N have the Curie–Weiss law μ_{N,β} with zero magnetic field.
The inverse temperature β ≥ 0 does not depend on N.

prerequisites.reason: Step s2 passes to the limit in the integrals of g(y) e^(−F_N(y)) with the dominated convergence theorem.
Steps s3 and s4 use Taylor's theorem for log cosh near 0 and the integral form of the remainder for G(u) = u²/2 − log cosh u.
Step s3 removes the Gaussian convolution with characteristic functions and concludes with Lévy's continuity theorem.
Step s3 treats β = 0, where the spins are independent fair signs, with the classical central limit theorem.
Step s4 removes the vanishing term W/N^(1/4) with Slutsky's theorem.
Step s5 takes part (c) from the phase transition theorem of the Curie–Weiss model, which gives concentration of S_N/N near ±m* with limit probability 1/2 for each sign.

definitions.name: Curie–Weiss law
definitions.text: The probability measure on {−1, 1}^N proportional to exp(β S_N²/(2N)). Every pair of spins interacts with strength β/N.

definitions.name: Hubbard–Stratonovich transform
definitions.text: Adding an independent Gaussian variable to a rescaled S_N turns the quadratic weight exp(β S_N²/(2N)) into a product of independent factors cosh(βu).

definitions.name: limit law at the critical point
definitions.text: The probability law on ℝ with density proportional to exp(−x⁴/12). Its tails decay faster than Gaussian tails, and it is not a normal law.

If β < 1 then (1/√N) SN ⇒ N(0, 1/(1−β)), where N(µ, σ²) denotes the normal distribution with mean µ and variance σ². … Theorem 5. Suppose X1, X2, . . . , XN are CW(1, N)-distributed random variables. Then (1/N^{3/4}) SN ⇒ µ where µ is a measure with Lebesgue density ρ(x) = C e^{−x⁴/12}.

source.alignment: Theorems 3, 4 and 5 of the source (pp. 5-6) together state the limit theorems of Ellis and Newman (1978) for the same normalization of the Curie–Weiss model. The authored statement collects the three regimes and adds β = 0 to part (a). The source proves the theorems by the method of moments. The authored proof uses instead the Gaussian (Hubbard–Stratonovich) transform of Ellis and Newman, and it takes part (c) from the record on the Curie–Weiss phase transition.

proof.scope: The full statement, parts (a), (b) and (c), for every fixed β ≥ 0.

steps.text: Let β > 0, 0 ≤ γ < 1, and let W have law N(0, 1/β), independent of the spins. Then Y_N = W/N^(1/2−γ) + S_N/N^(1−γ) has a density proportional to exp(−N G(y/N^γ)), with G(u) = βu²/2 − log cosh(βu). Indeed, given S_N = s the density of Y_N at y is proportional to exp(−βN^(1−2γ)(y − sN^(γ−1))²/2). Expanding the square gives the factor exp(−βs²/(2N)), which cancels the Curie–Weiss weight. The remaining sum over σ is exp(−βN^(1−2γ)y²/2) Σ_σ exp(βyN^(−γ) Σ_i σ_i) = exp(−βN^(1−2γ)y²/2) (2 cosh(βyN^(−γ)))^N. With u = y/N^γ this is a constant times exp(−N G(u)).

Suppose Y_N has density proportional to e^(−F_N), F_N(y) → F(y) for every y, and e^(−F_N) ≤ h for an integrable h that does not depend on N. Then for every bounded continuous g, dominated convergence gives ∫ g e^(−F_N) → ∫ g e^(−F) and ∫ e^(−F_N) → ∫ e^(−F) > 0. So E g(Y_N) converges to ∫ g e^(−F) / ∫ e^(−F), and Y_N converges in distribution to the law with density proportional to e^(−F).

Part (a). For β = 0 the spins are independent fair signs with variance 1, and the central limit theorem gives S_N/√N ⇒ N(0, 1). Let 0 < β < 1 and γ = 1/2. Since cosh x ≤ e^(x²/2), G(u) ≥ β(1 − β)u²/2, so N G(y/√N) ≥ β(1 − β)y²/2, which gives an integrable bound. Taylor's theorem gives log cosh x = x²/2 + O(x⁴), so N G(y/√N) → β(1 − β)y²/2. By step s2, Y_N = W + S_N/√N converges to N(0, 1/(β(1 − β))). By independence the characteristic function of S_N/√N is φ_(Y_N)(t) e^(t²/(2β)), which tends to exp(−t²/(2β(1 − β)) + t²/(2β)) = exp(−t²/(2(1 − β))). Lévy's continuity theorem gives S_N/√N ⇒ N(0, 1/(1 − β)).

Part (b). Let β = 1 and γ = 1/4, so W has law N(0, 1) and G(u) = u²/2 − log cosh u, with G(0) = G′(0) = 0 and G″(u) = tanh²u. Since tanh(u)/u decreases on (0, ∞), tanh²u ≥ tanh²(1) u² for |u| ≤ 1, and the integral form of Taylor's remainder gives G(u) ≥ tanh²(1) u⁴/12 there. G is even and convex with G(1) > 0, so G(u) ≥ G(1)|u| for |u| ≥ 1. Hence N G(y/N^(1/4)) ≥ min(tanh²(1) y⁴/12, G(1)|y|), an integrable bound for e^(−N G). Taylor's theorem gives log cosh u = u²/2 − u⁴/12 + O(u⁶), so N G(y/N^(1/4)) → y⁴/12. By step s2, Y_N = W/N^(1/4) + S_N/N^(3/4) converges to the law with density proportional to e^(−y⁴/12). Since W/N^(1/4) → 0 in probability, Slutsky's theorem gives the same limit for S_N/N^(3/4).

Part (c). Let β > 1 and 0 < ε < m*. The Curie–Weiss phase transition theorem gives P(|S_N/N − m*| < ε) → 1/2 and P(|S_N/N + m*| < ε) → 1/2. So for every bounded continuous g, E g(S_N/N) differs from (g(m*) + g(−m*))/2 by at most the oscillation of g on the two ε-intervals plus a term that tends to 0. Letting ε → 0 gives S_N/N ⇒ (δ_(m*) + δ_(−m*))/2.

applications.title: Size of magnetization fluctuations below and at the critical point
applications.inputs: A Curie–Weiss magnet with N = 4096 spins, at β = 1/2 and at the critical value β = 1.
applications.hypotheses: The spins have the Curie–Weiss law with zero field. The values β = 1/2 < 1 and β = 1 fall under parts (a) and (b).

steps.text: At β = 1/2 part (a) gives S_N/√N ⇒ N(0, 1/(1 − β)). The limit variance is 1/(1 − 1/2) = 2, twice the value for independent spins.
For N = 4096, √N = 64, so S_N is approximately normal with standard deviation 64√2 ≈ 90.5. For example, |S_N| ≤ 181 has probability close to P(|Z| ≤ 2) ≈ 0.954 for a standard normal Z.
At β = 1 part (b) puts the fluctuations on the scale N^(3/4). Since 4096 = 8⁴, N^(1/4) = 8 and N^(3/4) = 8³ = 512.

So at the critical point S_N is of order 512, which is N^(1/4) = 8 times the scale √N = 64 of the high-temperature phase. The limit law of S_N/512 has density proportional to exp(−x⁴/12), which is flatter at 0 than a normal density.

applications.conclusion: At β = 1/2 the total magnetization of 4096 spins fluctuates on the scale 64√2 with a normal shape. At β = 1 it fluctuates on the larger scale 512 with the non-normal shape exp(−x⁴/12).

limitations: The theorem gives convergence in distribution only. Convergence of moments and rates of convergence need further arguments, such as the method of moments or Stein's method.
The theorem fixes β. If β depends on N and tends to 1, the scaling and the limit law depend on the speed of convergence.

results.name: Lyons' theorem on the critical probability of percolation on trees
results.statement: Let T be a locally finite, infinite tree with root o. For a vertex x let |x| be its distance from o, and identify each edge with its endpoint farther from o. A flow on T is a function θ ≥ 0 on the vertices x ≠ o with θ(x) = Σ_{y child of x} θ(y) for every x ≠ o. Its strength is Σ_{|x|=1} θ(x). The branching number is br T = sup{λ > 0 : some flow of positive strength satisfies θ(x) ≤ λ^(−|x|) for every x ≠ o}. Then 1 ≤ br T ≤ ∞. In Bernoulli bond percolation on T with parameter p, P_p(o ↔ ∞) = 0 for every p < 1/br T, and P_p(o ↔ ∞) > 0 for every p > 1/br T. Hence the critical probability p_c(T) = sup{p ∈ [0, 1] : P_p(o ↔ ∞) = 0} equals 1/br T, with 1/∞ = 0. Quantitatively, if a flow of strength s > 0 satisfies θ(x) ≤ λ^(−|x|) for all x ≠ o and pλ > 1, then P_p(o ↔ ∞) ≥ s(pλ − 1)/(s(pλ − 1) + 1 − p).
hypotheses: T is an infinite tree in which every vertex has finite degree, with a fixed root o.
Each edge of T is open with probability p ∈ [0, 1], independently of all other edges.

prerequisites.reason: Steps s1 and s3 use Kőnig's infinity lemma: an infinite, connected, locally finite subtree that contains o contains an infinite ray from o.
Step s2 applies the max-flow min-cut theorem to the finite network of vertices within distance n of o, with capacity p^|x| on the edge into x.
Step s2 extracts, with the Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem and a diagonal argument, a subsequence of finite flows that converges at every vertex.
Step s3 bounds the probability of an infinite open ray by the sum, over the edges of a cutset, of the probabilities of open paths from o to these edges.
Step s6 applies the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality to X_n · 1[X_n > 0], which gives the second-moment bound P(X_n > 0) ≥ (E X_n)²/E X_n².

definitions.name: flow on a rooted tree
definitions.text: A function θ ≥ 0 on the non-root vertices with θ(x) equal to the sum of θ over the children of x. The value θ(x) is the amount that passes through the edge into x.

definitions.name: branching number
definitions.text: br T is the supremum of the λ > 0 for which a flow of positive strength satisfies θ(x) ≤ λ^(−|x|) at every vertex. For the b-ary tree br T = b.

definitions.name: cutset
definitions.text: A set Π of non-root vertices (edges) such that every infinite ray from o passes through a vertex of Π.

definitions.name: critical probability
definitions.text: p_c(T) = sup{p : P_p(o ↔ ∞) = 0}, where o ↔ ∞ is the event that the open cluster of o is infinite.

source.citation: Russell Lyons and Yuval Peres, Probability on Trees and Networks, Cambridge Series in Statistical and Probabilistic Mathematics 42, Cambridge University Press, 2016.

source.excerpt: Theorem 5.15. (Lyons, 1990) For every locally finite, infinite tree T, pc(T) = 1/br T.
source.attribution: © Russell Lyons and Yuval Peres. Quoted from the authors' book Probability on Trees and Networks for identification of the cited result.

source.alignment: The source defines br T by flows on p. 81 and gets the theorem from the first-moment bound (5.6), p. 140, and Theorem 5.14, p. 144, which uses electrical networks. The authored statement adds the definitions and an explicit lower bound for P_p(o ↔ ∞). The authored proof keeps the first-moment half of the source and replaces the electrical-network half by a direct second-moment computation with a flow, which is the weighted second-moment method of Section 5.3.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement, including br T ≥ 1, both halves of p_c(T) = 1/br T, and the explicit lower bound.

steps.text: Let θ be a flow of strength s. By induction on n, conservation gives Σ_{|x|=n, x≥u} θ(x) = θ(u) for every u ≠ o with |u| ≤ n, and Σ_{|x|=n} θ(x) = s. By Kőnig's lemma T contains an infinite ray from o, and the flow equal to 1 on this ray and 0 elsewhere satisfies θ(x) ≤ λ^(−|x|) for λ = 1. So br T ≥ 1. If λ′ < λ, every flow admissible for λ is admissible for λ′, so all λ < br T are admissible.

Let 0 < p ≤ 1 and suppose δ = inf_Π Σ_{x∈Π} p^|x| > 0, where Π runs over cutsets. Fix n and direct each edge away from o, with capacity p^|x| on the edge into x. Merge the vertices at level n into one sink. Every o–sink cut contains a set of edges that meets each path from o to level n, and such a set is a cutset of T. By the max-flow min-cut theorem there is a flow θ_n from o to level n with 0 ≤ θ_n(x) ≤ p^|x|, conservation at each x with 1 ≤ |x| < n, and strength δ after scaling down. T has countably many vertices, so the Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem and a diagonal argument give a subsequence with θ_n(x) → θ(x) at every x. Conservation involves finitely many children, so θ is a flow of strength δ with θ(x) ≤ (1/p)^(−|x|). Hence br T ≥ 1/p.

Let p < 1/br T. For p = 0 the claim is trivial. For p > 0 step s2 gives inf_Π Σ_{x∈Π} p^|x| = 0. If the cluster of o is infinite, Kőnig's lemma gives an infinite open ray from o, which passes through some x in a given cutset Π. Then all |x| edges from o to x are open, an event of probability p^|x|. The union bound gives P_p(o ↔ ∞) ≤ Σ_{x∈Π} p^|x| for every cutset Π, so P_p(o ↔ ∞) = 0.

Let p > 1/br T. Choose λ with 1/p < λ < br T. By step s1 there is a flow θ of strength s > 0 with θ(x) ≤ λ^(−|x|). For n ≥ 1 set X_n = Σ_{|x|=n} θ(x) p^(−n) 1[o ↔ x]. Since P_p(o ↔ x) = p^n, E X_n = s. The paths from o to x and to y share exactly |x ∧ y| edges, where x ∧ y is their last common vertex, so P_p(o ↔ x, o ↔ y) = p^(2n − |x∧y|) and E X_n² = Σ_{|x|=|y|=n} θ(x)θ(y) p^(−|x∧y|).

Write p^(−|x∧y|) = 1 + Σ_u (1 − p) p^(−|u|), where u runs over the vertices with u ≠ o and u ≤ x ∧ y, that is, the common ancestors of x and y other than o. Exchanging the finite sums and using step s1 gives E X_n² = s² + (1 − p) Σ_{1≤|u|≤n} p^(−|u|) θ(u)². Since θ(u)² ≤ θ(u) λ^(−|u|) and Σ_{|u|=k} θ(u) = s, the level k contributes at most s (pλ)^(−k). As pλ > 1, E X_n² ≤ s² + (1 − p) s/(pλ − 1) for every n.

By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, s = E[X_n 1[X_n > 0]] ≤ (E X_n²)^(1/2) P(X_n > 0)^(1/2), so P(X_n > 0) ≥ s²/E X_n² ≥ s(pλ − 1)/(s(pλ − 1) + 1 − p). The event {X_n > 0} is contained in the event A_n that o is joined to level n by an open path. The events A_n decrease, and their intersection is {o ↔ ∞}, because a cluster that meets every level is infinite and an infinite cluster meets every level. So P_p(o ↔ ∞) = lim P_p(A_n) > 0. With step s3 this gives p_c(T) = 1/br T.

applications.title: Percolation on a tree with alternating 2 and 3 children
applications.inputs: The spherically symmetric tree T in which each vertex at even depth has 2 children and each vertex at odd depth has 3 children. Level sizes |T_(2k)| = 6^k and |T_(2k+1)| = 2 · 6^k. Percolation parameter p = 1/2.
applications.hypotheses: T is infinite and every vertex has degree at most 4, so T is locally finite. The edges are open independently with probability 1/2.

steps.text: Any flow of strength s with θ(x) ≤ λ^(−|x|) has s = Σ_{|x|=n} θ(x) ≤ |T_n| λ^(−n) for every n, so λ ≤ liminf |T_n|^(1/n) = √6. Conversely, for λ < √6 the numbers |T_n| λ^(−n) have a positive lower bound c, and the uniform flow θ(x) = c/|T_(|x|)| is then admissible. So br T = √6 and p_c(T) = 1/√6 ≈ 0.408, which is less than 1/2.
Take λ = 9/4. Then λ² = 81/16 < 6, so λ < √6. The margin 6 − λ² equals 15/16.
The uniform flow with c = 8/9 satisfies θ(x) ≤ λ^(−|x|), because |T_(2k)| λ^(−2k) = (96/81)^k ≥ 1 and |T_(2k+1)| λ^(−2k−1) = (8/9)(96/81)^k ≥ 8/9. Its strength is s = 8/9, and pλ − 1 = 9/8 − 1 = 1/8.
The quantitative bound gives P_(1/2)(o ↔ ∞) ≥ s(pλ − 1)/(s(pλ − 1) + 1 − p) = (1/9)/(1/9 + 1/2) = 2/11.

applications.conclusion: On the alternating tree, p_c(T) = 1/√6. At p = 1/2 the root belongs to an infinite open cluster with probability at least 2/11.

limitations: The theorem does not say what happens at p = 1/br T. Both P_p(o ↔ ∞) = 0 and P_p(o ↔ ∞) > 0 occur at criticality, depending on the tree.
The branching number can be smaller than the growth rate liminf |T_n|^(1/n). So the critical probability is not determined by the level sizes alone.

results.name: Existence of infinite-volume Gibbs measures
results.statement: Let Ω₀ be a finite nonempty set, d ≥ 1, and Ω = Ω₀^(ℤ^d) with the product topology and the σ-algebra F generated by the cylinder sets. Let π = {π_Λ}, Λ ⋐ ℤ^d, be a specification: each π_Λ is a proper probability kernel from F_(Λᶜ) to F, and π_Λ π_Δ = π_Λ whenever Δ ⊂ Λ. Assume that π is quasilocal: for each finite Λ and each cylinder set C, the map ω ↦ π_Λ(C | ω) is continuous. Then the set G(π) of probability measures µ on (Ω, F) with µπ_Λ = µ for every finite Λ is not empty. More precisely, for each ω ∈ Ω, the sequence µ_n = π_(B(n))(· | ω) has a weakly convergent subsequence, and every weak limit of a subsequence lies in G(π). If Φ = {Φ_B} is a potential with Σ_(B ∋ i) ‖Φ_B‖_∞ < ∞ for every i ∈ ℤ^d (in particular, if Φ has finite range), then the Gibbsian specification π^Φ is quasilocal, so the set G(Φ) of Gibbs measures for Φ is not empty.
hypotheses: The single-spin space Ω₀ is finite, and Ω = Ω₀^(ℤ^d) carries the product topology and the σ-algebra generated by the cylinder sets.
π = {π_Λ} is a specification: a family of proper probability kernels with π_Λ π_Δ = π_Λ for all finite Δ ⊂ Λ.
π is quasilocal: ω ↦ π_Λ(C | ω) is continuous for every finite Λ and every cylinder set C.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 uses Tychonoff's theorem to show that the product Ω = Ω₀^(ℤ^d) of finite discrete spaces is compact.
Step s2 uses Prokhorov's theorem on the compact metric space Ω to extract a weakly convergent subsequence of the finite-volume measures.
Step s4 uses Dynkin's π-λ theorem to show that two probability measures that agree on all cylinder sets are equal.
Step s5 uses dominated convergence for the counting measure to show that the tail sums of an absolutely summable potential tend to 0.

definitions.name: proper probability kernel
definitions.text: A map π_Λ: F × Ω → [0, 1] such that π_Λ(· | ω) is a probability measure for each ω, ω ↦ π_Λ(A | ω) is F_(Λᶜ)-measurable for each A, and π_Λ(B | ω) = 1_B(ω) for every B ∈ F_(Λᶜ). The configuration ω outside Λ is the boundary condition.

definitions.name: specification and compatible measure
definitions.text: A specification is a family π = {π_Λ} of proper probability kernels with π_Λ π_Δ = π_Λ for Δ ⊂ Λ, where (π_Λ π_Δ)(A | ω) = ∫ π_Δ(A | η) π_Λ(dη | ω). A probability measure µ is compatible with π if µπ_Λ = µ for all finite Λ, where µπ_Λ(A) = ∫ π_Λ(A | ω) µ(dω). The set of such µ is G(π).

definitions.name: Gibbsian specification
definitions.text: For a potential Φ = {Φ_B}, with Φ_B an F_B-measurable function for each finite B, set H_Λ(ω) = Σ_(B ∩ Λ ≠ ∅) Φ_B(ω) and π^Φ_Λ(η_Λ | ω) = exp(−H_Λ(η_Λ ω_(Λᶜ)))/Z_Λ^ω, where Z_Λ^ω normalizes the sum over η_Λ ∈ Ω₀^Λ to 1. A measure in G(π^Φ) is a Gibbs measure for Φ.

source.alignment: The source works with Ω₀ = {−1, +1} and remarks that the results hold for any finite single-spin space. The authored statement uses a general finite Ω₀ and adds the claim on Gibbsian specifications, which is Lemma 6.28 of the source (p. 266). The authored proof follows the proof of Theorem 6.26, but it tests the limit only on cylinder events and uses Prokhorov's theorem in place of the diagonal argument of Theorem 6.24.

proof.scope: The full statement: existence for every quasilocal specification on a finite single-spin space, the claim on limit points of π_(B(n))(· | ω), and quasilocality of π^Φ for absolutely summable Φ.

steps.text: Ω₀ with the discrete topology is compact, so Ω is compact by Tychonoff's theorem. The metric ρ(ω, η) = Σ_i 2^(−‖i‖_∞) 1{ω_i ≠ η_i} is finite and generates the product topology, so Ω is a compact metric space. A cylinder set C = {ω : ω_S ∈ E}, with S finite and E ⊂ Ω₀^S, is open and closed, so its indicator 1_C is continuous. The cylinders are countably many and form a base of the topology. So the Borel σ-algebra of Ω equals F, and the cylinders form a π-system that generates F.

Every family of probability measures on the compact metric space Ω is tight, with the compact set Ω itself. Prokhorov's theorem therefore gives, for every sequence (µ_n) of probability measures on Ω, a subsequence (µ_(n_k)) and a probability measure µ such that ∫ g dµ_(n_k) → ∫ g dµ for every continuous g: Ω → ℝ.

Fix ω ∈ Ω and set µ_n = π_(B(n))(· | ω). Fix a finite Λ and take n so large that Λ ⊂ B(n). For A ∈ F, the definition of the composed kernel and the consistency of π give µ_n π_Λ(A) = ∫ π_Λ(A | η) π_(B(n))(dη | ω) = (π_(B(n)) π_Λ)(A | ω) = π_(B(n))(A | ω) = µ_n(A). So µ_n π_Λ = µ_n for all large n.

Let µ be the weak limit of a subsequence (µ_(n_k)), which exists by step s2. Fix a finite Λ and a cylinder C. The function g = π_Λ(C | ·) is continuous by quasilocality, and 1_C is continuous by step s1. Hence µπ_Λ(C) = ∫ g dµ = lim_k ∫ g dµ_(n_k) = lim_k µ_(n_k)π_Λ(C) = lim_k µ_(n_k)(C) = µ(C), where the fourth equality is step s3. The probability measures µπ_Λ and µ agree on the π-system of cylinders, which generates F. Dynkin's π-λ theorem gives µπ_Λ = µ. This holds for every finite Λ, so µ ∈ G(π), and G(π) ≠ ∅.

Let Φ be absolutely summable. The sum defining H_Λ converges, because Σ_(B ∩ Λ ≠ ∅) ‖Φ_B‖_∞ ≤ Σ_(i ∈ Λ) Σ_(B ∋ i) ‖Φ_B‖_∞ < ∞. Lemma 6.15 of the source shows that π^Φ is a specification. Fix Λ, and let ω and ω′ agree on a finite Δ ⊃ Λ, with D the distance from Λ to Δᶜ. A term Φ_B with B ∩ Λ ≠ ∅ can change only if B meets Δᶜ, because Φ_B depends only on the spins in B. Such a B has diameter at least D. So |H_Λ(η_Λ ω_(Λᶜ)) − H_Λ(η_Λ ω′_(Λᶜ))| ≤ 2ε_D, with ε_D = Σ_(i ∈ Λ) Σ_(B ∋ i, diam B ≥ D) ‖Φ_B‖_∞. Each inner sum tends to 0 as D → ∞ by dominated convergence for the counting measure on {B ∋ i}.

By step s5, each Boltzmann weight exp(−H_Λ) and the normalization Z_Λ change by a factor in [e^(−2ε_D), e^(2ε_D)]. So π^Φ_Λ(η_Λ | ω)/π^Φ_Λ(η_Λ | ω′) lies in [e^(−4ε_D), e^(4ε_D)], and both numbers lie in [0, 1], so |π^Φ_Λ(η_Λ | ω) − π^Φ_Λ(η_Λ | ω′)| ≤ e^(4ε_D) − 1. For a cylinder C with base S, π^Φ_Λ(C | ω) = Σ_(η_Λ) π^Φ_Λ(η_Λ | ω) 1_C(η_Λ ω_(Λᶜ)), and the indicator does not change when Δ ⊃ Λ ∪ S. Hence |π^Φ_Λ(C | ω) − π^Φ_Λ(C | ω′)| ≤ |Ω₀|^|Λ| (e^(4ε_D) − 1) for all ω′ in the open set {ω′ : ω′_Δ = ω_Δ}. This bound tends to 0 as Δ grows, so π^Φ is quasilocal, and step s4 gives G(Φ) ≠ ∅.

applications.title: Gibbs measures of an Ising chain with exponentially decaying couplings
applications.inputs: d = 1, Ω₀ = {−1, +1}, β > 0, h ∈ ℝ, and the potential Φ_({i,j})(ω) = −β 2^(−|i−j|) ω_i ω_j for i ≠ j, Φ_({i})(ω) = −h ω_i, and Φ_B = 0 for all other B. Every pair of sites interacts, so the range is infinite.
applications.hypotheses: Ω₀ is finite. Φ_B depends only on the spins in B. The bound in step a1 shows that Φ is absolutely summable, so the theorem applies to π^Φ.

steps.text: Absolute summability: Σ_(B ∋ i) ‖Φ_B‖_∞ = |h| + β Σ_(j ≠ i) 2^(−|i−j|) = |h| + 2β Σ_(m ≥ 1) 2^(−m) = |h| + 2β < ∞ for every i.
The theorem gives a Gibbs measure µ⁺ as a weak limit of π_(B(n))(· | +), where + is the configuration with all spins +1. The same holds for every other boundary condition.
Quasilocality at Λ = {0}: the only sets B ∋ 0 with diam B ≥ D are the pairs {0, j} with |j| ≥ D. So ε_D = β Σ_(|j| ≥ D) 2^(−|j|) = 2β · 2^(1−D) = β 2^(2−D).
For β = 1 and boundary conditions that agree on Δ = {−9, …, 9}, the distance is D = 10 and ε_10 = 2 · (1/2)^9 = 1/256.

Step s6 then bounds the change of the single-site law π_({0})(η_0 | ω) by e^(4/256) − 1 = e^(1/64) − 1 < 0.016. Spins at distance 10 or more change the conditional law at the origin by less than 0.016.

applications.conclusion: For every β > 0 and h ∈ ℝ, the Ising chain with couplings 2^(−|i−j|) has at least one infinite-volume Gibbs measure, and a weak limit of the finite-volume measures with any boundary condition is one of them.

limitations: The theorem gives existence only. It says nothing about uniqueness, and different boundary conditions can give different limits.
Quasilocality is essential. The source gives in Exercise 6.15 a specification that is not quasilocal and has no compatible measure.
The proof uses compactness of Ω. For an unbounded single-spin space, such as ℝ, existence needs extra conditions, for example a confining single-site potential.

results.name: Dobrushin uniqueness theorem
results.statement: Let Ω₀ be a finite set, d ≥ 1, and let π = {π_Λ} be a quasilocal specification on Ω = Ω₀^(ℤ^d). For i ∈ ℤ^d and ω ∈ Ω, let π_i(· | ω) be the law of the spin ω_i under π_({i})(· | ω). For i ≠ j, let C_ij be the supremum of d_TV(π_i(· | ω), π_i(· | ω′)) over all pairs ω, ω′ with ω_k = ω′_k for every k ≠ j, where d_TV(p, q) = ½ Σ_(a ∈ Ω₀) |p(a) − q(a)|. Set C_ii = 0 and c = sup_i Σ_j C_ij. If c < 1 (Dobrushin's condition), then the set G(π) of probability measures compatible with π has exactly one element.
hypotheses: The single-spin space Ω₀ is finite.
π is a quasilocal specification on Ω = Ω₀^(ℤ^d).
Dobrushin's condition holds: c = sup_i Σ_j C_ij < 1.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 uses the existence theorem for quasilocal specifications to show that G(π) is not empty.
Step s2 uses the extreme value theorem on the compact space Ω to find configurations where a continuous f attains its maximum and minimum.
Step s3 uses the Heine–Cantor theorem to approximate a continuous function on Ω uniformly by local functions.
Step s5 uses Dynkin's π-λ theorem to show that two measures that agree on all cylinder sets are equal.

definitions.name: oscillation
definitions.text: For f: Ω → ℝ and i ∈ ℤ^d, δ_i(f) = sup{|f(ω) − f(η)| : ω_k = η_k for all k ≠ i}. The total oscillation is Δ(f) = Σ_i δ_i(f).

definitions.name: Dobrushin interdependence matrix
definitions.text: C_ij measures how much the conditional law of the spin at i can change when only the spin at j changes. Dobrushin's condition says that the total influence on each site, Σ_j C_ij, is at most some c < 1.

definitions.name: quasilocal specification
definitions.text: A consistent family of proper probability kernels π_Λ(· | ω), Λ ⋐ ℤ^d, such that ω ↦ π_Λ(C | ω) is continuous for every cylinder set C. G(π) is the set of probability measures µ with µπ_Λ = µ for all finite Λ.

source.module: Chapter 6, Section 6.5.2 Dobrushin's Uniqueness Theorem
source.excerpt: Theorem 6.31. Let π be a quasilocal specification satisfying Dobrushin's Condition of Weak Dependence: c(π) < 1. (6.37) Then the probability measure specified by π is unique: |G(π)| = 1.

source.alignment: The source defines c_ij with the full ℓ¹ distance Σ|p − q| and states the theorem for Ising spins, with a remark that it holds for any finite single-spin space. The authored statement uses d_TV = ½ Σ|p − q|, which is Dobrushin's usual convention and gives a weaker hypothesis. The authored proof follows the source (Lemma 6.32, Proposition 6.33 and the dusting Lemma 6.34, pp. 269-271) and centers the function at the midpoint of its range in the dusting lemma, which accounts for the factor ½.

proof.scope: The full statement for every finite single-spin space and every quasilocal specification that satisfies Dobrushin's condition.

steps.text: The existence theorem for quasilocal specifications gives G(π) ≠ ∅. Fix µ, ν ∈ G(π). Let CO be the set of continuous f: Ω → ℝ with Δ(f) < ∞. A local function f depends on the spins in a finite set S only. So δ_i(f) = 0 for i ∉ S, δ_i(f) ≤ 2‖f‖_∞ for i ∈ S, and f ∈ CO. Note that C_ii = 0 is automatic: π_i(· | ω) does not depend on ω_i, because π_({i})(A | ·) is F_({i}ᶜ)-measurable.

For f ∈ CO, |µ(f) − ν(f)| ≤ sup f − inf f ≤ Δ(f). The space Ω is compact, so f attains its maximum at some ω¹ and its minimum at some ω². Fix ε > 0. By continuity at ω², there is a box Λ such that |f(η) − f(ω²)| < ε whenever η_Λ = ω²_Λ. Let η = ω²_Λ ω¹_(Λᶜ). Then η and ω¹ differ only at sites of Λ. Change these sites one at a time: each change moves f by at most δ_i(f). So f(ω¹) − f(ω²) ≤ f(ω¹) − f(η) + ε ≤ Σ_(i ∈ Λ) δ_i(f) + ε ≤ Δ(f) + ε, and ε is arbitrary.

Dusting lemma: for f ∈ CO and j ∈ ℤ^d, π_j f ∈ CO, δ_j(π_j f) = 0, and δ_i(π_j f) ≤ δ_i(f) + C_ji δ_j(f) for i ≠ j. Here π_j f(ω) = Σ_a π_j(a | ω) f(a ω_({j}ᶜ)) does not depend on ω_j, so δ_j(π_j f) = 0. Let ω, ω′ differ only at i, and let p = π_j(· | ω), q = π_j(· | ω′), g(a) = f(a ω′_({j}ᶜ)). Then π_j f(ω) − π_j f(ω′) = Σ_a p(a)(f(a ω_({j}ᶜ)) − g(a)) + Σ_a (p(a) − q(a))(g(a) − m), for every constant m, because Σ_a (p(a) − q(a)) = 0. The first sum is at most δ_i(f). With m the midpoint of the range of g, |g − m| ≤ δ_j(f)/2, so the second sum is at most d_TV(p, q) δ_j(f) ≤ C_ji δ_j(f). Summing over i gives Δ(π_j f) ≤ Δ(f) + c δ_j(f) < ∞. Finally π_j f is continuous: f is uniformly continuous by the Heine–Cantor theorem, so local functions g_N with ‖f − g_N‖_∞ → 0 exist, each π_j g_N is a finite combination of the continuous maps π_j(C | ·), and ‖π_j f − π_j g_N‖_∞ ≤ ‖f − g_N‖_∞.

Contraction: if |µ(f) − ν(f)| ≤ αΔ(f) for all f ∈ CO, with 0 < α ≤ 1, then |µ(f) − ν(f)| ≤ cαΔ(f) for all f ∈ CO. Enumerate ℤ^d as k_0, k_1, …. Let P(n) be the claim |µ(f) − ν(f)| ≤ cα Σ_(m<n) δ_(k_m)(f) + α Σ_(m≥n) δ_(k_m)(f) for all f ∈ CO. P(0) is the assumption. Assume P(n) and let i = k_n. Since µπ_({i}) = µ and νπ_({i}) = ν, µ(f) − ν(f) = µ(π_i f) − ν(π_i f). Apply P(n) to π_i f ∈ CO, use δ_i(π_i f) = 0 and step s3: |µ(f) − ν(f)| ≤ cα Σ_(m<n) δ_(k_m)(f) + α Σ_(m>n) δ_(k_m)(f) + αδ_i(f) Σ_k C_ik. The last factor is at most c, which gives P(n + 1). As n → ∞, Σ_(m≥n) δ_(k_m)(f) → 0 because Δ(f) < ∞, and the claim follows.

Step s2 gives the assumption of step s4 with α = 1. Applying step s4 n times gives |µ(f) − ν(f)| ≤ cⁿ Δ(f) for every n and every f ∈ CO. Since c < 1 and Δ(f) < ∞, µ(f) = ν(f). The indicator of a cylinder set is local, so it lies in CO by step s1. So µ and ν agree on the π-system of cylinders, which generates the σ-algebra, and Dynkin's π-λ theorem gives µ = ν. Hence G(π) has exactly one element.

applications.title: Uniqueness of the Gibbs measure of the two-dimensional Ising model at high temperature
applications.inputs: The nearest-neighbor Ising model on ℤ² with Ω₀ = {−1, +1}, inverse temperature β > 0 and any magnetic field h ∈ ℝ. The single-site law is π_i(+1 | ω) = e^u/(e^u + e^(−u)) = (1 + tanh u)/2, with local field u = β(h + Σ_(j∼i) ω_j).
applications.hypotheses: Ω₀ is finite. The potential has finite range, so the Gibbsian specification is quasilocal by the existence theorem. Step a3 checks Dobrushin's condition for β < ½ log(5/3).

steps.text: If ω and ω′ differ only at a neighbor j of i, the local fields differ by 2β. With v the mean of the two fields, d_TV = |tanh(v + β) − tanh(v − β)|/2 = sinh(2β)/(2 cosh(v + β) cosh(v − β)).
Since cosh(v + β) cosh(v − β) = (cosh 2v + cosh 2β)/2 ≥ (1 + cosh 2β)/2 = cosh²β, we get C_ij ≤ sinh(2β)/(2cosh²β) = tanh β for i ∼ j. Also C_ij = 0 if j is not a neighbor of i.
Each site has 4 neighbors, so c ≤ 4 tanh β. Dobrushin's condition holds when tanh β < 1/4, that is, when e^(2β) < (1 + 1/4)/(1 − 1/4) = 5/3.

So the Ising model on ℤ² has exactly one Gibbs measure for all β < ½ log(5/3) ≈ 0.2554 and all h ∈ ℝ. The critical value is β_c = ½ log(1 + √2) ≈ 0.4407, so the criterion covers about 58% of the high-temperature interval.

applications.conclusion: For β < ½ log(5/3) the two-dimensional Ising model has a unique Gibbs measure for every magnetic field h. In ℤ^d the same computation gives uniqueness for tanh β < 1/(2d).

limitations: The condition is sufficient but not necessary. For the Ising model on ℤ² it fails for ½ log(5/3) ≤ β < β_c, where the Gibbs measure is still unique.
At low temperature the criterion gives uniqueness only for a large field |h|. The Ising model has a unique Gibbs measure for every h ≠ 0 at every β, but the proof of that fact uses other methods.
The same contraction argument also gives exponential decay of correlations and stability under perturbations of π. The theorem as stated gives only uniqueness.

results.name: Lanford–Ruelle variational principle for translation-invariant Gibbs measures
results.statement: Let Ω = {−1, 1}^(ℤ^d) with the product σ-algebra, β > 0, and let Φ = {Φ_B}_(B⋐ℤ^d) be a translation-invariant potential (each Φ_B is F_B-measurable and Φ_(B+j)(ω) = Φ_B(θ_(−j)ω)) that is absolutely summable: Σ_(B∋0) ‖Φ_B‖_∞ < ∞. Let H^Φ_Λ = Σ_(B∩Λ≠∅) Φ_B, let π^(βΦ) be the Gibbsian specification π^(βΦ)_Λ(τ_Λ | ω) = e^(−βH^Φ_Λ(τ_Λ ω_(Λᶜ)))/Z^ω_(Λ,βΦ), and let G_θ(βΦ) be the set of translation-invariant probability measures µ with µπ^(βΦ)_Λ = µ for every finite Λ. For a translation-invariant probability measure µ on Ω, let S_Λ(µ) = −Σ_(ω_Λ) µ(ω_Λ) log µ(ω_Λ), B(n) = {−n, …, n}^d, and u_Φ = Σ_(B∋0) Φ_B/|B|. Then the specific entropy s(µ) = lim_n S_(B(n))(µ)/|B(n)| exists, the pressure ψ(Φ) = lim_n log Z^η_(B(n),βΦ)/(β|B(n)|) exists and does not depend on η, and the functional W(µ) = s(µ) − β⟨u_Φ⟩_µ is affine and satisfies W(µ) ≤ βψ(Φ) for every translation-invariant µ, with equality if and only if µ ∈ G_θ(βΦ). The set G_θ(βΦ) is nonempty, so the maximizers of W are exactly the translation-invariant Gibbs measures.
hypotheses: Φ is a translation-invariant potential with Σ_(B∋0) ‖Φ_B‖_∞ < ∞.
W is considered on the set of translation-invariant probability measures on Ω.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 uses the finite-volume variational principle: the relative entropy of a law with respect to a finite Gibbs distribution is nonnegative and vanishes only at that distribution.
Step s1 proves the monotonicity of the relative entropy in the volume with Jensen's inequality for x log x on the conditional laws.
Step s3 needs one Gibbs measure for π^(βΦ) to build a translation-invariant Gibbs measure by averaging translates.
Step s6 writes µ on F_Λ as the density ρ_Λ = dµ_Λ/dν_Λ with respect to a translation-invariant Gibbs measure ν.

definitions.name: specific entropy
definitions.text: s(µ) = lim_n S_(B(n))(µ)/|B(n)| for a translation-invariant µ, where S_Λ(µ) is the Shannon entropy of the marginal of µ on Ω_Λ.

definitions.name: energy density
definitions.text: ⟨u_Φ⟩_µ with u_Φ = Σ_(B∋0) Φ_B/|B|. It is the limit of ⟨H^Φ_(B(n))⟩_µ/|B(n)| for translation-invariant µ.

definitions.name: Gibbs free energy (relative entropy density)
definitions.text: h(µ | Φ) = lim_n H_(B(n))(µ | ν)/|B(n)| for any ν ∈ G_θ(βΦ), where H_Λ(µ | ν) is the relative entropy of the marginals on Ω_Λ.

source.module: Chapter 6, Section 6.9 The variational principle
source.excerpt: Theorem 6.84. Let Φ be an absolutely summable, translation-invariant potential. Define the affine functional W : M1,θ(Ω) → ℝ by µ ↦ W(µ) = s(µ) − β⟨uΦ⟩µ. Then the maximizers of W(·) are the translation-invariant Gibbs measures compatible with π^(βΦ).

source.alignment: The source states the result for the Ising spin space {−1, 1} as Theorem 6.84 and collects it from Proposition 6.75, Proposition 6.78, Theorem 6.79, Proposition 6.81 and Theorem 6.82 (pp. 299-304). The authored statement makes explicit the maximal value βψ(Φ) and the nonemptiness of G_θ(βΦ) (Exercise 6.22, p. 280). The outline follows the proofs of these results in the source.

results.proof_status: outline of the cited published proof. No local formal verification.

proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proofs of Proposition 6.75, Proposition 6.78, Theorem 6.79, Proposition 6.81, Lemma 6.83 and Theorem 6.82 in Friedli and Velenik (2017), Section 6.9, pp. 297-305. Steps s2, s3 and s6 take from the source the subadditive lemma (Lemma B.6), the estimate r_(B(n)) = o(|B(n)|) (Exercise 6.30), the existence of translation-invariant Gibbs measures (Exercise 6.22) and the elementary inequality (6.108).

steps.text: Finite volume. For a finite Λ and laws µ_Λ, ν_Λ on Ω_Λ, the relative entropy H_Λ(µ | ν) = Σ µ_Λ log(µ_Λ/ν_Λ) is nonnegative and vanishes only if µ_Λ = ν_Λ. This is the finite variational principle (Lemma 6.74 and (6.91) of the source). Lemma 6.76 of the source proves H_Δ(µ | ν) ≤ H_Λ(µ | ν) for Δ ⊂ Λ with Jensen's inequality for φ(x) = x log x on the conditional laws of ν given the spins in Δ.

Entropy and energy densities. With the uniform reference measure, step s1 gives S_(Λ∪Λ′)(µ) ≤ S_Λ(µ) + S_(Λ′)(µ) for disjoint Λ, Λ′ (Corollary 6.77). So Λ ↦ S_Λ(µ) is subadditive and translation invariant, and the subadditive lemma (Lemma B.6 of the source) gives the limit s(µ) (Proposition 6.75). S_Λ is concave and S_Λ(αµ + (1 − α)ν) ≤ αS_Λ(µ) + (1 − α)S_Λ(ν) + log 2, so s is affine. For the energy, |H^Φ_(B(n)) − Σ_(j∈B(n)) u_Φ ∘ θ_j| ≤ r_(B(n)) = Σ_(j∈B(n)) Σ_(B∋j, B⊄B(n)) ‖Φ_B‖_∞, which is o(|B(n)|) by Exercise 6.30 of the source. Translation invariance of µ then gives ⟨H^Φ_(B(n))⟩_µ/|B(n)| → ⟨u_Φ⟩_µ (Proposition 6.78).

Pressure. A change of boundary condition changes H^Φ_(B(n)) by at most 2r_(B(n)) (6.100). So for any ν, ν̃ the laws νπ^(βΦ)_(B(n)) and ν̃π^(βΦ)_(B(n)) on Ω_(B(n)) have a density ratio in [e^(−4βr_(B(n))), e^(4βr_(B(n)))], and H_(B(n))(µ | νπ_(B(n)))/|B(n)| and H_(B(n))(µ | ν̃π_(B(n)))/|B(n)| have the same limit if one of them converges (Lemma 6.80). G(βΦ) is nonempty by the existence theorem, and Exercise 6.22 of the source averages translates of a Gibbs measure to get some µ ∈ G_θ(βΦ). Take ν = µ, for which µπ_(B(n)) = µ, and ν̃ = δ_ω. Then (1/|B(n)|)(log Z^ω_(B(n),βΦ) − S_(B(n))(µ) + β⟨H^Φ_(B(n))(· ω_(B(n)ᶜ))⟩_µ) → 0. With step s2 this gives the pressure, its independence of ω, and βψ(Φ) = W(µ) for every µ ∈ G_θ(βΦ) (Theorem 6.79 and (6.98)).

Upper bound. Let ν ∈ G_θ(βΦ) and let µ be translation invariant. Since νπ_(B(n)) = ν, Lemma 6.80 with ν̃ = δ_ω and the computation of step s3 give the Gibbs free energy h(µ | Φ) = lim_n H_(B(n))(µ | ν)/|B(n)| = βψ(Φ) − W(µ) (Proposition 6.81). Relative entropy is nonnegative, so W(µ) ≤ βψ(Φ). By step s3, equality holds for every µ ∈ G_θ(βΦ).

Localization (Lemma 6.83). Assume H_(B(n))(µ | ν)/|B(n)| → 0, fix Δ ⊂ B(k) and δ > 0, and choose n with H_(B(n))(µ | ν) ≤ δ|B(n)|/(2|B(k)|). Put m^d ≥ |B(n)|/(2|B(k)|) disjoint translates B_1(k), …, B_(m^d)(k) of B(k) into B(n), let Λ(ℓ) = B_1(k) ∪ ⋯ ∪ B_ℓ(k) and Δ(ℓ) the copy of Δ in B_ℓ(k). Monotonicity gives H_(Λ(ℓ)) − H_(Λ(ℓ)∖Δ(ℓ)) ≤ H_(Λ(ℓ)) − H_(Λ(ℓ−1)), and these terms telescope to at most H_(B(n))(µ | ν) ≤ δ m^d. So some ℓ has 0 ≤ H_(Λ(ℓ))(µ | ν) − H_(Λ(ℓ)∖Δ(ℓ))(µ | ν) ≤ δ, and a translation gives a finite Λ ⊃ B(k) with 0 ≤ H_Λ(µ | ν) − H_(Λ∖Δ)(µ | ν) ≤ δ.

Equality implies Gibbs (Theorem 6.82). Let W(µ) = βψ(Φ), fix ν ∈ G_θ(βΦ), so H_(B(n))(µ | ν)/|B(n)| → 0 by step s4. Fix finite Δ, a local f and ε > 0, and let ρ_Λ = dµ_Λ/dν_Λ. Choose a local F_(Δᶜ)-measurable g* with ‖π_Δ f − g*‖_∞ ≤ ε, which exists by quasilocality, and k with B(k) ⊃ Δ ∪ supp f ∪ supp g*. The source's (6.108) gives r > 0 with 1 − x + x log x ≥ r(|x − 1| − ε/2) for x ≥ 0. Apply step s5 with δ = rε/2. Then µπ_Δ(f) − µ(f) splits into six terms. Two are at most ε by the choice of g*. Three vanish, by µ(g*) = ν(ρ_(Λ∖Δ) g*), by µ(f) = ν(ρ_Λ f), and by the DLR property ν(ρ_(Λ∖Δ) π_Δ f) = ν(ρ_(Λ∖Δ) f), since ρ_(Λ∖Δ) is F_(Δᶜ)-measurable. The last term is ν((ρ_(Λ∖Δ) − ρ_Λ) f), and H_Λ − H_(Λ∖Δ) = ν(ρ_(Λ∖Δ) φ(ρ_Λ/ρ_(Λ∖Δ))) ≥ r ν|ρ_Λ − ρ_(Λ∖Δ)| − rε/2 bounds it by ε‖f‖_∞. So |µπ_Δ(f) − µ(f)| ≤ (2 + ‖f‖_∞)ε for every ε, and µ ∈ G_θ(βΦ). With steps s3 and s4, the maximizers of W are exactly the elements of the nonempty set G_θ(βΦ).

source.ref: S. Friedli and Y. Velenik, Statistical Mechanics of Lattice Systems (CUP 2017, revised version of August 22, 2017), Theorem 6.84, p. 305, with Proposition 6.75, Proposition 6.78, Theorem 6.79, Proposition 6.81, Theorem 6.82 and Lemma 6.83, pp. 299-304.

applications.title: Independent spins in a magnetic field
applications.inputs: Dimension d ≥ 1, field h with e^(2βh) = 3, and the potential Φ_({i})(ω) = −hω_i, Φ_B = 0 if |B| ≠ 1.
applications.hypotheses: Φ is translation invariant and Σ_(B∋0) ‖Φ_B‖_∞ = |h| < ∞. Here H^Φ_Λ = −h Σ_(i∈Λ) ω_i, so π^(βΦ)_Λ(· | ω) is the product of the one-site laws p(±1) = e^(±βh)/(2 cosh βh) and does not depend on ω. Hence G(βΦ) = G_θ(βΦ) = {ν}, with ν the product of these laws.

steps.text: The partition function is Z_Λ = (2 cosh βh)^(|Λ|), so βψ(Φ) = log(2 cosh βh). Also u_Φ = −hω_0, so W(µ) = s(µ) + βh⟨ω_0⟩_µ.
For the Gibbs measure ν, p(+1) = e^(2βh)/(e^(2βh) + 1) = 3/(3 + 1) = 3/4.
The magnetization of ν is ⟨ω_0⟩_ν = 2 · (3/4) − 1 = 1/2 = tanh βh.

Under ν the spins are independent, so s(ν) = −(3/4) log(3/4) − (1/4) log(1/4) = log 4 − (3/4) log 3. With βh = (1/2) log 3, W(ν) = log 4 − (3/4) log 3 + (1/4) log 3 = log 4 − (1/2) log 3 ≈ 0.837. This equals log(2 cosh βh) = log(√3 + 1/√3) = log(4/√3), as the theorem requires.

Other translation-invariant measures give smaller values. The fair product measure has W = log 2 ≈ 0.693. The measure (δ_(+) + δ_(−))/2 on the two constant configurations has S_(B(n)) = log 2, so s = 0 and ⟨ω_0⟩ = 0, and W = 0.

applications.conclusion: For independent spins with e^(2βh) = 3, the functional W has the maximum log 4 − (1/2) log 3 = βψ(Φ), and it attains this value only at the product measure with p(+1) = 3/4, which is the unique Gibbs measure.

limitations: The principle characterizes only the translation-invariant Gibbs measures. Non-invariant Gibbs measures, such as the Dobrushin interface states in d ≥ 3, are not maximizers of W in this sense.
The source proves the result for the spin space {−1, 1}. The same proof works for other finite spin spaces, and extensions to compact spin spaces need the general relative entropy.
W is affine, so a first-order phase transition gives a convex set of maximizers with several extreme points, and the principle alone does not select one of them.

results.name: Thermodynamic limit of the Ising pressure
aliases: existence of the Ising free energy density
existence and convexity of the Ising pressure in infinite volume
results.statement: Consider the nearest-neighbor Ising model on ℤ^d, d ≥ 1, with inverse temperature β ≥ 0 and magnetic field h ∈ ℝ. For finite Λ ⊂ ℤ^d let ψ^#_Λ(β, h) = |Λ|⁻¹ log Z^#_Λ(β, h), where # is the free boundary condition, a fixed boundary condition η ∈ {−1, 1}^(ℤ^d) (which may change with Λ), or the periodic boundary condition on a cube. Let Λ_n be a sequence of finite sets that converges to ℤ^d in the sense of van Hove: Λ_n ⊂ Λ_(n+1), ⋃_n Λ_n = ℤ^d, and |∂^in Λ_n|/|Λ_n| → 0, where ∂^in Λ is the set of points of Λ with a neighbor outside Λ. Then ψ(β, h) = lim_n ψ^#_(Λ_n)(β, h) exists and does not depend on the sequence or on the boundary condition. The function ψ is convex on [0, ∞) × ℝ and even in h.
hypotheses: The model is the nearest-neighbor Ising model on ℤ^d with Hamiltonian H_Λ = −β Σ_(i∼j) ω_i ω_j − h Σ_(i ∈ Λ) ω_i, the first sum over the edges counted by the boundary condition #.
Λ_n ⇑ ℤ^d in the sense of van Hove: |∂^in Λ_n|/|Λ_n| → 0. For the periodic boundary condition, Λ_n is a cube of side n.

prerequisites.reason: Step s5 applies Hölder's inequality with exponents 1/α and 1/(1 − α) to the partition function, which proves convexity of the finite-volume pressure.

definitions.name: Ising partition functions
definitions.text: Z^∅_Λ = Σ_(ω ∈ {−1,1}^Λ) exp(β Σ_({i,j} ⊂ Λ, i∼j) ω_i ω_j + h Σ_(i ∈ Λ) ω_i). For a fixed boundary condition η, the sum over edges also includes the edges {i, j} with i ∈ Λ and j ∉ Λ, with ω_j = η_j. For the periodic boundary condition, Λ = {0, …, n − 1}^d is a discrete torus.

definitions.name: pressure
definitions.text: ψ^#_Λ(β, h) = |Λ|⁻¹ log Z^#_Λ(β, h). Up to the factor −1/β it is the free energy per site.

definitions.name: van Hove sequence
definitions.text: A sequence of finite sets Λ_n ↑ ℤ^d with |∂^in Λ_n|/|Λ_n| → 0, so that the boundary is negligible compared with the volume. The boxes B(n) = {−n, …, n}^d form such a sequence.

source.excerpt: Theorem 3.6. In the thermodynamic limit, the pressure ψ(β, h) = lim_(Λ⇑ℤ^d) ψ^#_Λ(β, h) is well defined … Moreover, ψ is convex (as a function on ℝ≥0 × ℝ) and is even as a function of h.

source.alignment: The authored statement makes the three types of boundary condition and the van Hove condition explicit. The authored proof follows the proof on pp. 84-87 of the source: dyadic boxes, coverings by boxes, comparison of boundary conditions, Hölder's inequality (Lemma 3.5) and the spin flip. It adds the counting argument that bounds the covered set [Λ] \ Λ by |∂^in Λ| times the box volume.

proof.scope: The full statement. The proof uses only |∂^in Λ_n|/|Λ_n| → 0, so the limit is the same along every sequence with this property.

steps.text: Dyadic boxes. Write ψ_Λ for the free pressure. Let D_n = {1, …, 2^n}^d. D_(n+1) is the disjoint union of 2^d translates of D_n, and H^∅_(D_(n+1)) is the sum of their free Hamiltonians plus a term R_n from the edges between different translates. These edges cross d middle hyperplanes, each crossed by 2^((n+1)(d−1)) edges, so |R_n| ≤ βd 2^((n+1)(d−1)). Without R_n the sum over configurations factorizes, and each factor is Z^∅_(D_n) because the free Hamiltonian is translation invariant. So e^(−βd 2^((n+1)(d−1))) (Z^∅_(D_n))^(2^d) ≤ Z^∅_(D_(n+1)) ≤ e^(βd 2^((n+1)(d−1))) (Z^∅_(D_n))^(2^d). Division of the logarithm by |D_(n+1)| = 2^(d(n+1)) gives |ψ_(D_(n+1)) − ψ_(D_n)| ≤ βd 2^(−(n+1)). Summing, |ψ_(D_m) − ψ_(D_k)| ≤ βd 2^(−k) for m ≥ k, so ψ = lim_k ψ_(D_k) exists and |ψ_(D_k) − ψ| ≤ βd 2^(−k).

Unions of boxes. Fix k and tile ℤ^d by disjoint translates of D_k. For finite Λ let [Λ] be the union of the N tiles that meet Λ. Each edge between two tiles leaves exactly one tile through one of its d upper faces, which have 2^(k(d−1)) points each. So the interaction W between the tiles of [Λ] satisfies |W| ≤ βdN 2^(k(d−1)) = βd 2^(−k)|[Λ]|. As in step s1, the partition function factorizes up to e^(±|W|), so |ψ_([Λ]) − ψ_(D_k)| ≤ βd 2^(−k).

From [Λ] to Λ. Let Δ = [Λ] \ Λ. A tile that meets Λ and is not inside Λ contains a nearest-neighbor path from a point of Λ to a point outside Λ, so it contains a point of ∂^in Λ. The tiles are disjoint, so there are at most |∂^in Λ| such tiles, and |Δ| ≤ |∂^in Λ| |D_k|. The terms of H^∅_([Λ]) that involve a site of Δ are at most 2d|Δ| edge terms and |Δ| field terms. So |H^∅_([Λ])(ω) − H^∅_Λ(ω_Λ)| ≤ (2dβ + |h|)|Δ|, and the sum over the 2^|Δ| values of ω_Δ gives |log Z^∅_([Λ]) − log Z^∅_Λ| ≤ (2dβ + |h| + log 2)|Δ|. Also |H^∅_Λ| ≤ (dβ + |h|)|Λ| gives |ψ_Λ| ≤ dβ + |h| + log 2 for every Λ. Hence |ψ_Λ − ψ_([Λ])| ≤ |log Z^∅_Λ − log Z^∅_([Λ])|/|Λ| + |ψ_([Λ])| |Δ|/|Λ| ≤ (3dβ + 2|h| + 2 log 2) |D_k| |∂^in Λ|/|Λ|.

Limit and boundary conditions. Steps s1 to s3 give |ψ_(Λ_n) − ψ| ≤ (3dβ + 2|h| + 2 log 2)|D_k| |∂^in Λ_n|/|Λ_n| + 2βd 2^(−k). For fixed k the first term tends to 0, so limsup_n |ψ_(Λ_n) − ψ| ≤ 2βd 2^(−k) for every k, and ψ_(Λ_n) → ψ. For a fixed boundary condition η, the extra edges join a point of ∂^in Λ to a point outside Λ, at most 2d per point, so |H^η_Λ(ω) − H^∅_Λ(ω_Λ)| ≤ 2dβ|∂^in Λ| and |ψ^η_Λ − ψ_Λ| ≤ 2dβ|∂^in Λ|/|Λ| → 0, uniformly in η. For the periodic cube of side n ≥ 3, the d n^(d−1) extra edges give |ψ^per − ψ| ≤ βd/n on that cube, and cubes satisfy |∂^in Λ|/|Λ| ≤ 2d/n → 0.

Convexity and symmetry. The Hamiltonian is affine in (β, h). For α ∈ (0, 1) and (β, h) = α(β₁, h₁) + (1 − α)(β₂, h₂), Z^#_Λ(β, h) = Σ_ω (e^(−H₁(ω)))^α (e^(−H₂(ω)))^(1−α), and Hölder's inequality with exponents 1/α and 1/(1 − α) bounds it by Z^#_Λ(β₁, h₁)^α Z^#_Λ(β₂, h₂)^(1−α). So each ψ^#_Λ is convex, and the pointwise limit ψ is convex, because the convexity inequality passes to the limit. The global flip ω ↦ −ω is a bijection of {−1, 1}^Λ with H^∅_(β,h)(−ω) = H^∅_(β,−h)(ω), so ψ^∅_Λ(β, h) = ψ^∅_Λ(β, −h), and the limit ψ is even in h.

applications.title: Pressure and nearest-neighbor correlation of the Ising chain
applications.inputs: The Ising chain, d = 1, h = 0, with e^β = 2, so 2 cosh β = 5/2 and 2 sinh β = 3/2. Volumes Λ_n = {1, …, n} with free, plus and periodic boundary conditions.
applications.hypotheses: Λ_n has |∂^in Λ_n| = 2, so |∂^in Λ_n|/|Λ_n| = 2/n → 0 and the theorem applies to all three boundary conditions.

steps.text: With the transfer matrix T = [[e^β, e^(−β)], [e^(−β), e^β]], whose eigenvalues are 2 cosh β and 2 sinh β: Z^per_n = (2 cosh β)^n + (2 sinh β)^n, Z^+_n = ((2 cosh β)^(n+1) + (2 sinh β)^(n+1))/2, and Z^∅_n = 2(2 cosh β)^(n−1), because the bond variables ω_k ω_(k+1) are independent under the free sum.
For n = 4 the periodic partition function is (5/2)^4 + (3/2)^4 = 353/8, and the free one is 2(5/2)^3 = 125/4.

Since (3/5)^n → 0, all three pressures tend to ψ(β, 0) = log(2 cosh β) = log(5/2), as the theorem predicts. At n = 4, ψ^per − ψ^∅ = ¼ log(353/250) ≈ 0.086, below the bound β/n = (log 2)/4 ≈ 0.173 of step s4.

Convexity gives the correlation. The ψ^per_n are convex in β and converge to the differentiable ψ, so (ψ_n(β) − ψ_n(β − δ))/δ ≤ ∂_β ψ_n(β) ≤ (ψ_n(β + δ) − ψ_n(β))/δ and n → ∞, then δ → 0, give ∂_β ψ_n → ∂_β ψ. By translation invariance ∂_β ψ^per_n = ⟨ω₁ω₂⟩^per_n.

applications.conclusion: For the Ising chain at e^β = 2, the pressure is log(5/2) for every boundary condition, and the infinite-volume nearest-neighbor correlation is 3/5. The convexity part of the theorem justifies the exchange of the limit and the β-derivative.

limitations: The theorem gives no formula for ψ. Closed forms are known only in special cases, such as d = 1 or d = 2 with h = 0 (Onsager).
Convexity gives one-sided derivatives everywhere, but not differentiability. Points where ψ is not differentiable in h correspond to first-order phase transitions.
The same argument extends to translation-invariant absolutely summable interactions, with the van Hove condition and a tail term of the interaction in place of the edge counts.

results.name: Tail-triviality characterization of extremal Gibbs measures
aliases: extremal Gibbs measures are tail trivial
short-range correlations of extremal Gibbs measures
results.statement: Let Ω₀ be a finite set, Ω = Ω₀^(ℤ^d) with the product σ-algebra F, and for Λ ⊂ ℤ^d let F_(Λᶜ) be the σ-algebra generated by the spins outside Λ. Let π = {π_Λ} be a specification, and let T∞ = ⋂_(Λ finite) F_(Λᶜ) be the tail σ-algebra. For µ ∈ G(π) the following four conditions are equivalent. (1) µ is extremal in the convex set G(π): µ = αµ₁ + (1 − α)µ₂ with α ∈ (0, 1) and µ₁, µ₂ ∈ G(π) implies µ₁ = µ₂ = µ. (2) µ is trivial on T∞: µ(A) ∈ {0, 1} for every A ∈ T∞. (3) Every T∞-measurable function f: Ω → ℝ is µ-almost surely constant. (4) µ has short-range correlations: for every A ∈ F, lim_(n→∞) sup_(B ∈ F_(B(n)ᶜ)) |µ(A ∩ B) − µ(A)µ(B)| = 0, where B(n) = {−n, …, n}^d.
hypotheses: π = {π_Λ} is a specification on Ω = Ω₀^(ℤ^d) with finite Ω₀: a consistent family of proper probability kernels.
µ is a probability measure compatible with π, that is, µ ∈ G(π).

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 uses the monotone convergence theorem to extend the identity π_Λ(1_A h) = h π_Λ(A | ·) from simple to nonnegative F_(Λᶜ)-measurable h.
Step s5 uses the Radon–Nikodym theorem to write a component µ₁ ≤ µ/α of a convex decomposition as a density times µ.
Step s6 uses the tower property to show that X_m = µ(X_n | F_(B(m)ᶜ)) for m > n, which gives the Pythagorean identity for the backward sequence.

definitions.name: specification and G(π)
definitions.text: A specification is a family of proper probability kernels π_Λ(· | ω), Λ ⋐ ℤ^d, with π_Λ π_Δ = π_Λ for Δ ⊂ Λ. Proper means π_Λ(B | ω) = 1_B(ω) for B ∈ F_(Λᶜ), and π_Λ(A | ·) is F_(Λᶜ)-measurable. G(π) is the convex set of probability measures µ with µπ_Λ = µ for all finite Λ.

definitions.name: tail σ-algebra
definitions.text: T∞ = ⋂_(Λ finite) F_(Λᶜ). An event is in T∞ when its occurrence does not change if finitely many spins change, for example the event that the mean magnetization in B(n) has a positive limit.

definitions.name: density measure
definitions.text: For µ ∈ G(π) and a measurable f ≥ 0 with µ(f) = 1, fµ is the probability measure fµ(A) = ∫_A f dµ.

source.citation: Sacha Friedli and Yvan Velenik, Statistical Mechanics of Lattice Systems: A Concrete Mathematical Introduction, Cambridge University Press, 2017.
source.revision: Authors' online version, revised version of August 22, 2017.
source.module: Chapter 6, Section 6.8.1 Properties of extremal Gibbs measures
source.excerpt: Theorem 6.58. Let π be a specification. Let µ ∈ G(π). The following conditions are equivalent characterizations of extremality. 1. µ is extremal. 2. µ is trivial on T∞: if A ∈ T∞, then µ(A) is either 1 or 0. 3. All T∞-measurable functions are µ-almost surely constant. 4. µ has short-range correlations: for all A ∈ F (or, equivalently, for all A ∈ C), lim_(Λ↑ℤ^d) sup_(B∈F_(Λᶜ)) |µ(A ∩ B) − µ(A)µ(B)| = 0.
source.attribution: © Sacha Friedli and Yvan Velenik. Quoted from the authors' online version of the book for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The authored statement is the source statement, with the limit over Λ ↑ ℤ^d written along the boxes B(n). The authored proof follows the proof on pp. 283-285 (Propositions 6.59 and 6.61, Lemma 6.60). It proves (2) ⇒ (1) with the a.s. constant density instead of Proposition 6.61(2), and it replaces the backward martingale convergence theorem by an L² argument along the decreasing σ-algebras.

proof.scope: All four equivalences for every specification and every µ ∈ G(π). The proof does not use the finiteness of Ω₀.

steps.text: A key identity. Let µ ∈ G(π), Λ finite, A ∈ F and h ≥ 0 an F_(Λᶜ)-measurable function. Then µ(1_A h) = ∫ h(ω) π_Λ(A | ω) µ(dω). Proof: for B ∈ F_(Λᶜ), properness gives π_Λ(A ∩ B | ω) = 1_B(ω) π_Λ(A | ω). Indeed, if ω ∈ B then π_Λ(Bᶜ | ω) = 0, and if ω ∉ B then π_Λ(B | ω) = 0. By linearity, π_Λ(1_A h)(ω) = h(ω) π_Λ(A | ω) for simple h ≥ 0, and monotone convergence extends it to all h ≥ 0. Then µ(1_A h) = µπ_Λ(1_A h) = ∫ π_Λ(1_A h) dµ = ∫ h π_Λ(A | ·) dµ, where the first equality is µ = µπ_Λ.

Tail densities preserve G(π). Let µ ∈ G(π) and let h ≥ 0 be T∞-measurable with µ(h) = 1. For every finite Λ, h is F_(Λᶜ)-measurable, so step s1 gives (hµ)π_Λ(A) = ∫ π_Λ(A | ω) h(ω) µ(dω) = µ(1_A h) = hµ(A) for all A ∈ F. Hence hµ ∈ G(π).

Densities in G(π) are tail functions. Let µ ∈ G(π), f ≥ 0 with µ(f) = 1 and fµ ∈ G(π). Set f_n = µ(f | F_(B(n)ᶜ)). For A ∈ F, fµ(A) = ∫ π_(B(n))(A | ·) f dµ = ∫ π_(B(n))(A | ·) f_n dµ = µ(1_A f_n). The middle equality is the defining property of conditional expectation, since π_(B(n))(A | ·) is bounded and F_(B(n)ᶜ)-measurable, and the last one is step s1. With A = {f > f_n} and A = {f < f_n} this gives f = f_n µ-a.s. Let f̃ = limsup_n f_n where it is finite, and 0 elsewhere. Then f̃ = f µ-a.s. For each m, f̃ is a function of (f_n)_(n ≥ m), which are F_(B(m)ᶜ)-measurable. Every finite Λ lies in some B(m), so f̃ is T∞-measurable.

(2) ⇔ (3). Assume (2) and let f be T∞-measurable. For rational q, {f ≤ q} ∈ T∞, so µ(f ≤ q) ∈ {0, 1}. This is nondecreasing in q, with limit 0 as q → −∞ and 1 as q → +∞, because f is real-valued. Let c = inf{q ∈ ℚ : µ(f ≤ q) = 1}, a real number. Continuity of µ along rationals q ↓ c and q ↑ c gives µ(f > c) = 0 and µ(f < c) = 0, so f = c µ-a.s. Conversely, (3) applied to 1_A for A ∈ T∞ gives (2).

(1) ⇔ (2). If (2) fails, take A ∈ T∞ with α = µ(A) ∈ (0, 1). The functions 1_A/α and 1_(Aᶜ)/(1 − α) are T∞-measurable with mean 1, so step s2 puts µ₁ = α⁻¹1_A µ and µ₂ = (1 − α)⁻¹1_(Aᶜ) µ in G(π). Then µ = αµ₁ + (1 − α)µ₂ and µ₁(A) = 1 ≠ µ(A), so µ is not extremal. Conversely, assume (2) and µ = αµ₁ + (1 − α)µ₂ with µ₁, µ₂ ∈ G(π). Then µ₁ ≤ µ/α, so µ₁ ≪ µ, and the Radon–Nikodym theorem gives µ₁ = fµ with f ≥ 0 and µ(f) = 1. By step s3, f = f̃ a.s. with f̃ T∞-measurable, and by step s4, f̃ is a.s. a constant, which must be µ(f) = 1. So µ₁ = µ, and in the same way µ₂ = µ.

(2) ⇔ (4). Fix A ∈ F, let G_n = F_(B(n)ᶜ) and X_n = µ(1_A | G_n). For B ∈ G_n, µ(A ∩ B) − µ(A)µ(B) = ∫_B (X_n − µ(A)) dµ, so the supremum in (4) is at most ‖X_n − µ(A)‖_(L²(µ)). The σ-algebras G_n decrease. For m > n, the tower property gives X_m = µ(X_n | G_m), so X_n − X_m is orthogonal to X_m in L²(µ) and ‖X_n − X_m‖² = ‖X_n‖² − ‖X_m‖². The sequence ‖X_n‖² is nonincreasing and bounded below, so (X_n) is Cauchy in L² and converges to some Y. A subsequence X_(n_k) converges to Y µ-a.s. Let Ỹ = limsup_k X_(n_k) where it is finite, and 0 elsewhere. For each m, Ỹ is a function of the G_m-measurable X_(n_k) with n_k ≥ m, so Ỹ is T∞-measurable and Ỹ = Y a.s. Under (2), step s4 makes Y a.s. constant, and the constant is lim µ(X_n) = µ(A). So ‖X_n − µ(A)‖_(L²) → 0, which is (4). Conversely, if (4) holds and B ∈ T∞, then B ∈ G_n for every n, and A = B in (4) gives |µ(B) − µ(B)²| = 0, so µ(B) ∈ {0, 1}.

applications.title: A mixture of the two Ising phases has long-range correlations
applications.inputs: The two-dimensional Ising model with h = 0 at an inverse temperature β with spontaneous magnetization m = ⟨σ₀⟩_(µ⁺) > 0. The plus and minus states µ⁺ and µ⁻ are translation invariant and extremal (Lemma 6.65 of the source), and µ⁻ is the image of µ⁺ under the global spin flip. Take the mixture µ_λ = λµ⁺ + (1 − λ)µ⁻ with λ = 1/4.
applications.hypotheses: µ⁺, µ⁻ and µ_λ are in G(β, 0), because G(π) is convex. The theorem applies to the extremal measure µ⁺ in the direction (1) ⇒ (4), and to µ_λ in the direction (4) ⇒ (1).

steps.text: Apply (4) to µ⁺ with A = {σ₀ = 1} and B = {σ_i = 1}. B lies in F_(B(n)ᶜ) when i ∉ B(n). Since σ = 2·1{σ = 1} − 1, the covariance of σ₀ and σ_i is 4(µ⁺(A ∩ B) − µ⁺(A)µ⁺(B)), so ⟨σ₀σ_i⟩⁺ − ⟨σ₀⟩⁺⟨σ_i⟩⁺ → 0 as ‖i‖ → ∞. Translation invariance gives ⟨σ_i⟩⁺ = m, so ⟨σ₀σ_i⟩⁺ → m².
The spin flip gives ⟨σ₀σ_i⟩⁻ = ⟨σ₀σ_i⟩⁺ and ⟨σ₀⟩⁻ = −m. So under µ_λ, the covariance is ⟨σ₀σ_i⟩⁺ − ((2λ − 1)m)², and it tends to m²(1 − (2λ − 1)²) = 4λ(1 − λ)m².
For λ = 1/4 the limit is 4 · (1/4) · (3/4) · m² = (3/4)m², which is positive.

With A = {σ₀ = 1} and B = {σ_i = 1}, µ_λ(A ∩ B) − µ_λ(A)µ_λ(B) is one quarter of the covariance, so it tends to (3/16)m² ≠ 0. So µ_λ violates (4). By the theorem, µ_λ is not extremal, and some tail event has a µ_λ-probability strictly between 0 and 1.

applications.conclusion: In the phase-coexistence region, the mixture (1/4)µ⁺ + (3/4)µ⁻ has spin correlations that do not decay: the covariance of σ₀ and σ_i tends to (3/4)m². Only the extremal phases µ⁺ and µ⁻ have short-range correlations.

limitations: The theorem characterizes extremal measures but does not show that they exist. A separate result, the extremal decomposition, writes every Gibbs measure as a mixture of extremal ones.
Condition (4) gives no rate of decay. A rate needs quantitative methods, such as Dobrushin's condition or a cluster expansion.
The theorem concerns extremality in the full set G(π). The symmetric mixture of the two Néel states of the Ising antiferromagnet is translation invariant and ergodic, but it is not extremal in G(π).

results.name: Kotecký–Preiss criterion
aliases: Kotecký–Preiss condition for the convergence of the cluster expansion
results.statement: Let Γ be a finite set of polymers, w: Γ → ℂ a weight, and δ: Γ × Γ → ℝ a symmetric function with δ(γ, γ) = 0 and |δ(γ, γ′)| ≤ 1 for all γ, γ′. Let Ξ = Σ_(Γ′ ⊂ Γ) Π_(γ ∈ Γ′) w(γ) Π_({γ,γ′} ⊂ Γ′) δ(γ, γ′) and ζ = δ − 1. Define the Ursell functions by ϕ(γ₁) = 1 and, for m ≥ 2, ϕ(γ₁, …, γ_m) = (1/m!) Σ_G Π_({i,j} ∈ G) ζ(γ_i, γ_j), where G runs over the connected spanning subgraphs of the complete graph on {1, …, m}. Assume that there is a: Γ → (0, ∞) such that Σ_γ |w(γ)| e^(a(γ)) |ζ(γ, γ*)| ≤ a(γ*) for every γ* ∈ Γ. Then, for every γ₁ ∈ Γ, 1 + Σ_(k≥2) k Σ_(γ₂, …, γ_k) |ϕ(γ₁, …, γ_k)| Π_(j=2)^k |w(γ_j)| ≤ e^(a(γ₁)). Consequently, the cluster expansion L = Σ_(m≥1) Σ_(γ₁, …, γ_m) ϕ(γ₁, …, γ_m) Π_(i=1)^m w(γ_i) converges absolutely, and Ξ = e^L. In particular Ξ ≠ 0 and L is a logarithm of Ξ.
hypotheses: Γ is finite, w: Γ → ℂ, and δ: Γ × Γ → ℝ is symmetric with δ(γ, γ) = 0 and |δ| ≤ 1.
There is a: Γ → (0, ∞) with Σ_γ |w(γ)| e^(a(γ)) |ζ(γ, γ*)| ≤ a(γ*) for every γ* ∈ Γ, where ζ = δ − 1.

prerequisites.reason: Step s5 uses Fubini's theorem for counting measures to regroup an absolutely summable family of terms, once by the number of clusters and once by the total number of polymers.

definitions.name: polymer model
definitions.text: A finite set Γ of polymers with complex weights w(γ) and a symmetric pair interaction δ with δ(γ, γ) = 0 and |δ| ≤ 1. Hard-core models have δ(γ, γ′) = 0 if γ and γ′ are incompatible and δ(γ, γ′) = 1 otherwise.

definitions.name: Ursell function
definitions.text: ϕ(γ₁) = 1 and ϕ(γ₁, …, γ_m) = (1/m!) Σ_G Π_({i,j} ∈ G) ζ(γ_i, γ_j) for m ≥ 2, with G over the connected spanning subgraphs of the complete graph K_m. The function ϕ is symmetric in its arguments, and it is 0 unless the graph of incompatibilities of γ₁, …, γ_m is connected.

definitions.name: cluster expansion
definitions.text: The series Σ_m Σ_(γ₁, …, γ_m) ϕ(γ₁, …, γ_m) Π w(γ_i). As a formal series it is log Ξ.

(5.10) Then, for all γ1 ∈ Γ, 1 + Σ_(k≥2) k Σ_(γ2) ··· Σ_(γk) |ϕ(γ1, γ2, …, γk)| Π_(j=2)^k |w(γj)| ≤ e^(a(γ1)). (5.11) In particular, (5.9) holds.

The authored statement adds the identity Ξ = e^L and proves it from the finite form of Proposition 5.3 and absolute convergence.
