steps.text: Finite expansion. Write Π δ(γ_i, γ_j) = Π (1 + ζ(γ_i, γ_j)) = Σ_G Π_(e ∈ G) ζ over all spanning subgraphs G of K_n. Since δ(γ, γ) = 0, an n-tuple with a repeated polymer contributes 0, so Ξ = 1 + Σ_(n=1)^(|Γ|) (1/n!) Σ_(G ⊂ K_n) Q[G], where Q[G] = Σ_(γ₁, …, γ_n) Π w(γ_i) Π_({i,j} ∈ G) ζ(γ_i, γ_j). Q[G] factorizes over the connected components of G, and the sum of Q over the connected graphs on a set of m vertices equals m! L_m, where L_m = Σ_(γ₁, …, γ_m) ϕ(γ₁, …, γ_m) Π w(γ_i). There are n!/(m₁! ⋯ m_k!) ordered partitions (B₁, …, B_k) of {1, …, n} with |B_r| = m_r, and each set partition into k blocks gives k! ordered partitions. Hence, for each n, (1/n!) Σ_(G ⊂ K_n) Q[G] = Σ_k (1/k!) Σ_(m₁+⋯+m_k = n) Π_r L_(m_r).

Removal of vertex 1. A connected graph G on {1, …, k}, k ≥ 2, is described by the components V′₁, …, V′_l of G minus the vertex 1, a connected graph on each V′_i, and a nonempty set K_i ⊂ V′_i of neighbors of 1 in each V′_i. This gives ϕ(γ₁, …, γ_k) = (1/k!) Σ_l (1/l!) Σ_(V′₁, …, V′_l) Π_i [m_i! ϕ((γ_j)_(j ∈ V′_i)) (Π_(j ∈ V′_i)(1 + ζ(γ₁, γ_j)) − 1)], with m_i = |V′_i| and ordered partitions of {2, …, k}. Since |1 + ζ| = |δ| ≤ 1, the identity Π(1 + α_j) − 1 = (1 + α_n)(Π_(j<n)(1 + α_j) − 1) + α_n and induction give |Π_(j ∈ V′)(1 + ζ(γ₁, γ_j)) − 1| ≤ Σ_(j ∈ V′) |ζ(γ₁, γ_j)|.

Set S_N(γ₁) = 1 + Σ_(k=2)^N k Σ_(γ₂, …, γ_k) |ϕ(γ₁, …, γ_k)| Π_(j≥2) |w(γ_j)| and B_m(γ*) = Σ_(γ₁, …, γ_m) |ϕ(γ₁, …, γ_m)| Π|w(γ_j)| Σ_(j=1)^m |ζ(γ*, γ_j)|. Claim: if S_N(γ) ≤ e^(a(γ)) for all γ, then Σ_(m=1)^N B_m(γ*) ≤ a(γ*) for all γ*. Multiply S_N(γ₁) ≤ e^(a(γ₁)) by |ζ(γ*, γ₁)||w(γ₁)| and sum over γ₁. The hypothesis bounds the right side by a(γ*). The left side is Σ_(m=1)^N m Σ |ζ(γ*, γ₁)||ϕ(γ₁, …, γ_m)| Π|w(γ_j)|. Since ϕ is symmetric in its arguments, m times the term with ζ(γ*, γ₁) equals the sum over j of the terms with ζ(γ*, γ_j). So the left side is Σ_(m≤N) B_m(γ*).

Induction on N. S_1(γ) = 1 ≤ e^(a(γ)). Assume S_N ≤ e^a everywhere. By step s2, for 2 ≤ k ≤ N + 1, k Σ_(γ₂, …, γ_k) |ϕ(γ₁, …, γ_k)| Π|w(γ_j)| is at most (1/(k−1)!) Σ_l (1/l!) Σ_(V′) Π_i m_i! B′_i, where the sum over (γ_j)_(j ∈ V′_i) gives a factor B_(m_i)(γ₁). There are (k−1)!/(m₁! ⋯ m_l!) ordered partitions with sizes m₁, …, m_l, so the bound is Σ_l (1/l!) Σ_(m₁+⋯+m_l = k−1) Π_i B_(m_i)(γ₁). Each m_i ≤ k − 1 ≤ N. Summing over k and dropping the constraint on Σ m_i gives S_(N+1)(γ₁) − 1 ≤ Σ_(l≥1) (1/l!) (Σ_(m=1)^N B_m(γ₁))^l ≤ e^(a(γ₁)) − 1 by step s3. Letting N → ∞ gives the bound of the statement.

Absolute convergence and Ξ = e^L. Multiply the bound by |w(γ₁)| and sum over the finite set Γ: Σ_(m≥1) Σ_(γ₁, …, γ_m) |ϕ| Π|w(γ_i)| ≤ Σ_γ |w(γ)| e^(a(γ)) < ∞, because the factor k ≥ 1 only enlarges the terms. So M = Σ_m |L_m| < ∞ and L = Σ_m L_m converges absolutely. The family of terms (1/k!) Π_(r=1)^k L_(m_r), indexed by k ≥ 1 and (m₁, …, m_k), has absolute sum at most Σ_k M^k/k! < ∞. By Fubini's theorem for counting measures, its sum grouped by k is Σ_k L^k/k! = e^L − 1, and grouped by n = m₁ + ⋯ + m_k it is Σ_n (1/n!) Σ_(G ⊂ K_n) Q[G] = Ξ − 1 by step s1. Hence Ξ = e^L.

applications.title: Low-activity expansion of the hard-core lattice gas on a torus
applications.inputs: The torus Λ = (ℤ/Lℤ)², L ≥ 3, with N = L² sites. Polymers are sites, w(x) = z ∈ ℂ, and δ(x, y) = 0 if x = y or x and y are neighbors, δ(x, y) = 1 otherwise. Then Ξ is the grand partition function of particles with nearest-neighbor exclusion at activity z.
applications.hypotheses: δ is symmetric, δ(x, x) = 0 and |δ| ≤ 1. Take a ≡ 1. For each x*, ζ(x, x*) = −1 for the 5 sites x = x* or x ∼ x*, and 0 otherwise, so the condition reads 5|z|e ≤ 1, that is, |z| ≤ 1/(5e) ≈ 0.0736.

steps.text: For |z| ≤ 1/(5e) the criterion gives Ξ ≠ 0 and log Ξ = L₁ + L₂ + Σ_(m≥3) L_m, with each L_m a homogeneous polynomial of degree m in z. The bound of the theorem holds uniformly in L, so N⁻¹ log Ξ is a power series in z with radius at least 1/(5e), uniformly in the size of the torus.
First terms: L₁ = Σ_x z = Nz. For m = 2, ϕ(x, y) = ζ(x, y)/2 = −1/2 for the 5N ordered pairs with x = y or x ∼ y, so L₂ = −(5/2)Nz². Hence N⁻¹ log Ξ = z − (5/2)z² + O(z³).
Direct check: Ξ = 1 + Nz + (N(N − 1)/2 − 2N)z² + O(z³), because the torus has 2N edges. Then log Ξ = Nz + (N(N − 1)/2 − 2N − N²/2)z² + O(z³) = Nz − (5/2)Nz² + O(z³), as in step a2.
At z = 1/20, which satisfies |z| ≤ 1/(5e), the two-term approximation of the pressure per site is 1/20 − (5/2)(1/20)² = 7/160 = 0.04375.

applications.conclusion: The hard-core lattice gas on ℤ² has a pressure that is an analytic function of the activity for |z| < 1/(5e), with expansion z − (5/2)z² + O(z³), and its partition functions have no zeros in this disk, uniformly in the volume.

limitations: The criterion is sufficient, not sharp. For a single polymer with w = z it gives convergence of log(1 + z) only for |z| ≤ 1/e, while the true radius is 1.
The proof needs |δ| ≤ 1, which covers hard-core and repulsive interactions but not attractive pair interactions.
For infinitely many polymers the same bound holds under the extra condition Σ_γ |w(γ)| e^(a(γ)) < ∞, as the source notes in Remark 5.5.

results.name: Penrose tree-graph bound and convergence of the Mayer expansion
aliases: tree-graph inequality for stable pair potentials
Procacci–Yuhjtman bound on the Mayer coefficients
results.statement: Let V: ℝ^d → ℝ ∪ {+∞} be a measurable even pair potential and β > 0. Assume that V is stable: there is B ≥ 0 such that Σ_(1≤i<j≤n) V(x_i − x_j) ≥ −Bn for all n ≥ 2 and all x_1, …, x_n ∈ ℝ^d. Let G_n and T_n be the sets of connected graphs and of trees on the vertex set {1, …, n}. (a) For all n ≥ 2 and all x_1, …, x_n, |Σ_(g∈G_n) Π_({i,j}∈g) (e^(−βV(x_i − x_j)) − 1)| ≤ e^(βBn) Σ_(τ∈T_n) Π_({i,j}∈τ) (1 − e^(−β|V(x_i − x_j)|)). (b) Assume also that V is tempered: ∫_(|x|≥r_0) |V(x)| dx < ∞ for some r_0 ≥ 0. Then Ĉ(β) = ∫_(ℝ^d) (1 − e^(−β|V(x)|)) dx is finite. For every bounded measurable Λ ⊂ ℝ^d with |Λ| > 0 and every n ≥ 2, the Mayer coefficient C_n(β, Λ) = (1/(|Λ| n!)) ∫_(Λ^n) Σ_(g∈G_n) Π_({i,j}∈g) (e^(−βV(x_i − x_j)) − 1) dx satisfies |C_n(β, Λ)| ≤ e^(βBn) n^(n−2) Ĉ(β)^(n−1)/n!. Hence the Mayer series λ + Σ_(n≥2) C_n(β, Λ) λ^n converges absolutely, uniformly in Λ, for every complex λ with |λ| < R* = 1/(e^(βB+1) Ĉ(β)) (R* = +∞ if Ĉ(β) = 0). For these λ the grand canonical partition function Ξ_Λ(λ) = Σ_(n≥0) (λ^n/n!) ∫_(Λ^n) e^(−β Σ_(i<j) V(x_i − x_j)) dx satisfies Ξ_Λ(λ) = exp(|Λ| (λ + Σ_(n≥2) C_n(β, Λ) λ^n)). In particular Ξ_Λ(λ) ≠ 0.
hypotheses: V: ℝ^d → ℝ ∪ {+∞} is measurable and even, and β > 0.
V is stable with a constant B ≥ 0: Σ_(1≤i<j≤n) V(x_i − x_j) ≥ −Bn for all n ≥ 2 and all x_1, …, x_n.
For part (b): V is tempered, and Λ ⊂ ℝ^d is bounded and measurable with |Λ| > 0.

definitions.name: stable pair potential
definitions.text: An even measurable V: ℝ^d → ℝ ∪ {+∞} with a constant B ≥ 0 such that the energy Σ_(i<j) V(x_i − x_j) of every n-particle configuration is at least −Bn.

definitions.name: tempered pair potential
definitions.text: A pair potential with ∫_(|x|≥r_0) |V(x)| dx < ∞ for some r_0 ≥ 0.

definitions.name: Mayer coefficient
definitions.text: C_n(β, Λ) = (1/(|Λ| n!)) ∫_(Λ^n) Σ_(g∈G_n) Π_({i,j}∈g) (e^(−βV(x_i − x_j)) − 1) dx, the coefficient of λ^n in the Mayer series of |Λ|⁻¹ log Ξ_Λ.

source.module: Section 2.2 Results
source.excerpt: Proposition 1 Let V be a stable pair potential with stability constant B. Then, for any n ≥ 2 and any (x1, …, xn) ∈ ℝ^(dn), the following inequality holds |Σ_(g∈Gn) Π_({i,j}∈Eg) (e^(−βV(xi−xj)) − 1)| ≤ e^(βBn) Σ_(τ∈Tn) Π_({i,j}∈Eτ) (1 − e^(−β|V(xi−xj)|)) (2.18) where Tn denotes the set of all trees with vertex set [n] (a.k.a. labeled trees with n vertices).

source.alignment: Part (a) is Proposition 1 (p. 6), and part (b) is Theorem 1 (p. 5) with the identity Ξ_Λ = exp(|Λ| × Mayer series) added, which the source takes from the formal theory of the Mayer series. The authored statement requires B ≥ 0, because the supremum that defines B in the source can be negative for a potential that is not tempered, and then (2.18) fails at n = 2, for example for V ≡ 1. The authored proof follows Sections 3 and 4 of the source. It orders the edges by (V, label) with the real weights 2^rank in place of the monoid of Definition 7, whose sums are not translation invariant when V takes the value +∞.

proof.scope: The full statement: the tree-graph inequality for stable potentials with B ≥ 0, the bound on the Mayer coefficients, absolute convergence uniformly in Λ, and the identity Ξ_Λ = exp(|Λ| × Mayer series) in the disk.

steps.text: Edge order. Fix n ≥ 2 and x_1, …, x_n. Write V_ij = βV(x_i − x_j) ∈ ℝ ∪ {+∞}, f_ij = e^(−V_ij) − 1 and h_ij = 1 − e^(−|V_ij|) ∈ [0, 1]. Order the edges of the complete graph K_n strictly: e ≺ e′ if V_e < V_e′, or if V_e = V_e′ and e comes before e′ in lexicographic order. Let r(e) be the rank of e and give e the weight 2^(r(e)). Distinct edge sets have distinct total weights, by uniqueness of binary expansions. So each connected graph g has a unique spanning tree T(g) of minimum weight. For a tree τ, let M(τ) be the graph of the edges {i, j} with e ⪯ {i, j} for every edge e of the path from i to j in τ. Then τ ⊂ M(τ).

Partition scheme. Claim: T(g) = τ if and only if τ ⊂ g ⊂ M(τ). First let T(g) = τ and {i, j} ∈ g ∖ τ. For an edge e of the τ-path from i to j, the graph τ − e + {i, j} is a spanning tree of g. Minimality gives 2^(r(e)) < 2^(r({i,j})), so e ≺ {i, j} and {i, j} ∈ M(τ). Next let τ ⊂ g ⊂ M(τ) and suppose that T(g) = τ′ ≠ τ. Both trees have n − 1 edges, so some {i, j} ∈ τ′ is not in τ. Removing {i, j} splits τ′ into two parts. The τ-path from i to j has an edge e ≠ {i, j} that joins the two parts, and τ′ − {i, j} + e is a spanning tree of g. As {i, j} ∈ M(τ), e ≺ {i, j}, so this tree has less weight than τ′. This contradiction gives T(g) = τ. Hence G_n is the disjoint union of the intervals {g: τ ⊂ g ⊂ M(τ)}, τ ∈ T_n.

Penrose identity. Every graph that contains a tree τ is connected. By step s2, Σ_(g∈G_n) Π_(e∈g) f_e = Σ_(τ∈T_n) Π_(e∈τ) f_e Σ_(E ⊂ M(τ)∖τ) Π_(e∈E) f_e = Σ_τ Π_(e∈τ) f_e Π_(e∈M(τ)∖τ) e^(−V_e), because 1 + f_e = e^(−V_e). Let τ⁺ be the set of edges e of τ with V_e ≥ 0. If V_e ≥ 0 then |f_e| = h_e, and if V_e < 0 then |f_e| = e^(−V_e) h_e. Hence |Σ_(g∈G_n) Π_(e∈g) f_e| ≤ Σ_τ Π_(e∈τ) h_e exp(−Σ_(e∈M(τ)∖τ⁺) V_e).

Energy bound. Claim: Σ_(e∈M(τ)∖τ⁺) V_e ≥ −βBn. The edges of τ ∖ τ⁺ form a forest. Let S_1, …, S_k be the vertex sets of its components, singletons included. If {i, j} ∈ M(τ) with i ∈ S_a, j ∈ S_b and a ≠ b, the τ-path from i to j contains an edge e ∈ τ⁺, and e ⪯ {i, j} gives V_ij ≥ V_e ≥ 0. If i, j ∈ S_a and {i, j} ∉ M(τ), then {i, j} ≺ e for an edge e of the τ-path, which lies in τ ∖ τ⁺, so V_ij ≤ V_e < 0. No edge of τ⁺ joins two vertices of one S_a, because τ has no cycle. Drop the terms between different sets (each at least 0) and add the pairs inside each S_a that are not in M(τ) (each negative). This gives Σ_(e∈M(τ)∖τ⁺) V_e ≥ Σ_a Σ_({i,j}⊂S_a) V_ij ≥ −βB Σ_a |S_a| = −βBn, by stability when |S_a| ≥ 2 and by B ≥ 0 when |S_a| = 1. With step s3 this proves part (a).

Integration over trees. Let h(y) = 1 − e^(−β|V(y)|) ∈ [0, 1]. As h ≤ min(1, β|V|), Ĉ(β) ≤ |{|x| < r_0}| + β ∫_(|x|≥r_0) |V| dx < ∞. For a tree τ, take a leaf ℓ with neighbor p. Tonelli's theorem and ∫_Λ h(x_ℓ − x_p) dx_ℓ ≤ Ĉ(β) reduce τ to a tree on n − 1 vertices, so induction gives ∫_(Λ^n) Π_({i,j}∈τ) h(x_i − x_j) dx ≤ |Λ| Ĉ(β)^(n−1). Stability with n = 2 gives V ≥ −2B, so each f_ij is bounded and the integrand of C_n is integrable. By Kirchhoff's theorem, |T_n| is the determinant of nI − J of size n − 1, whose eigenvalues are n (n − 2 times) and 1. So |T_n| = n^(n−2). Integration of part (a) gives |C_n(β, Λ)| ≤ e^(βBn) n^(n−2) Ĉ(β)^(n−1)/n!.

Radius. The series e^n = Σ_k n^k/k! gives n! ≥ n^n e^(−n), so n^(n−2)/n! ≤ e^n/n². If Ĉ(β) > 0, then |C_n(β, Λ)| |λ|^n ≤ Ĉ(β)⁻¹ (e^(βB+1) Ĉ(β) |λ|)^n / n². This bound does not depend on Λ and is summable for |λ| ≤ R*. So the Mayer series converges absolutely, uniformly in Λ, for |λ| < R*. If Ĉ(β) = 0, then C_n(β, Λ) = 0 for every n ≥ 2.

Exponential identity. Stability gives 0 ≤ e^(−βU) ≤ e^(βBn), so the series of Ξ_Λ converges for every λ. Let Z_n = ∫_(Λ^n) Π_(i<j) (1 + f_ij) dx and a_m = m! |Λ| C_m, with C_1 = 1. Expand the product over all subgraphs G of K_n. The integrand of G is a product over the connected components of G in disjoint variables, so Fubini's theorem gives Z_n = Σ_π Π_(P∈π) a_(|P|) over the set partitions π of {1, …, n}. There are n!/(m_1! ⋯ m_k!) ordered set partitions (P_1, …, P_k) with |P_r| = m_r, and each set partition gives k! of them. So Z_n/n! = Σ_k (1/k!) Σ_(m_1+⋯+m_k=n) Π_r a_(m_r)/m_r!. For |λ| < R*, the family (1/k!) Π_r |Λ| C_(m_r) λ^(m_r), indexed by k ≥ 1 and (m_1, …, m_k), is absolutely summable with sum at most exp(|Λ| Σ_m |C_m| |λ|^m) − 1. Grouped by k, its sum is e^(F(λ)) − 1 with F(λ) = |Λ| Σ_(n≥1) C_n λ^n. Grouped by n = m_1 + ⋯ + m_k, its sum is Σ_(n≥1) Z_n λ^n/n! = Ξ_Λ(λ) − 1. Hence Ξ_Λ(λ) = e^(F(λ)) ≠ 0.

applications.title: Mayer coefficients of hard rods on a line
applications.inputs: Dimension d = 1 and the hard-core potential V(x) = +∞ for |x| < 1 and V(x) = 0 for |x| ≥ 1. The volume is the interval Λ = [0, L] with L ≥ 1, and β > 0 is arbitrary.
applications.hypotheses: V is measurable and even. The energy Σ_(i<j) V(x_i − x_j) is never negative, so V is stable with B = 0. V vanishes for |x| ≥ 1, so V is tempered with r_0 = 1. Here 1 − e^(−β|V(x)|) is the indicator of |x| < 1, so Ĉ(β) = 2 for every β.

steps.text: Part (b) with B = 0 and Ĉ(β) = 2 gives |C_n(β, Λ)| ≤ n^(n−2) 2^(n−1)/n! for every interval Λ. The Mayer series converges for |λ| < R* = 1/(2e) ≈ 0.184, and Ξ_Λ has no zero in this disk, for every L.

For n = 2 the only connected graph is the single edge, and e^(−βV(x−y)) − 1 = −1 exactly when |x − y| < 1. So C_2 = −(1/(2L)) |{(x, y) ∈ [0, L]²: |x − y| < 1}|. The complement in the square is two triangles of total area (L − 1)², so C_2 = −(L² − (L − 1)²)/(2L) = −(2L − 1)/(2L).

The bound of part (b) for n = 2 is e^0 · 2^0 · 2/2! = 1. So the bound holds with |C_2| = (2L − 1)/(2L) < 1, and C_2 tends to −1 as L → ∞. For n = 2 the tree-graph inequality (a) is an equality here, because V ≥ 0.
For L = 10 the exact coefficient is C_2 = −(2 · 10 − 1)/(2 · 10) = −19/20.

applications.conclusion: For hard rods of length 1 in any interval [0, L], the pressure (1/L) log Ξ_Λ(λ) is given by a convergent power series in the activity for |λ| < 1/(2e), uniformly in L. The second coefficient is −(2L − 1)/(2L), within the bound 1.

limitations: The radius bound is not sharp. For hard rods on the line the exact infinite-volume pressure (the Tonks gas) has an activity series with radius 1/e, while the theorem gives 1/(2e).
The theorem needs a stability constant B ≥ 0. Every tempered stable potential has one, but the supremum in the source's definition of B can be negative for a potential that is not tempered.
The bounds are uniform in the volume, but the existence of the infinite-volume pressure is a separate thermodynamic-limit argument.
For an attractive potential with B > 0, the factor e^(βB) makes the radius small at low temperature.

results.name: Pirogov–Sinai theory of low-temperature phase diagrams
aliases: low-temperature phase diagram of the Blume–Capel model
results.statement: Let d ≥ 2 and consider the Blume–Capel model on ℤ^d: spins ω_i ∈ {−1, 0, +1}, the nearest-neighbor potential Φ⁰_({i,j})(ω) = (ω_i − ω_j)² for i ∼ j and the single-site potential W_({i})(ω) = −hω_i − λω_i², with (λ, h) in U = {(λ, h) ∈ ℝ²: |λ| ≤ ρ/8, |h| ≤ ρ/8}, where ρ = 5^(−d). Let η⁺, η⁰, η⁻ be the constant configurations +1, 0, −1, with the energy densities e⁺ = −h − λ, e⁰ = 0 and e⁻ = h − λ. Let ψ(λ, h) = lim_n log Z^η_(B(n))/(β|B(n)|) be the pressure, which exists and is the same for every boundary condition η. Then there are β0 < ∞ and numbers ε(β) → 0 and κ(β) → 0 as β → ∞ such that for every β > β0 the following holds. (1) There are C¹ functions ψ̂⁺, ψ̂⁰, ψ̂⁻ on U (the truncated pressures) of the form ψ̂^# = −e^# + ĝ^# with |ĝ^#|, |∂ĝ^#/∂λ|, |∂ĝ^#/∂h| ≤ ε, such that ψ = max_# ψ̂^# on U. Let U^#_β = {(λ, h) ∈ U: ψ̂^#(λ, h) = ψ(λ, h)}. (2) ψ is C¹ in the interior of each U^#_β. (3) Fix δ with 2ε < δ < ρ/16 and let Ǔ = {(λ, h): |λ| < ρ/8 − δ, |h| < ρ/8}. There is a C¹ function h(λ) on (−ρ/8 + δ, ρ/8 − δ) with |h(λ) + λ| < δ and |h′(λ) + 1| ≤ 4ε/(1 − 2ε) such that U⁺_β ∩ Ǔ = {(λ, h) ∈ Ǔ: h ≥ max(h(λ), 0)}, U⁻_β ∩ Ǔ is the image of U⁺_β ∩ Ǔ under (λ, h) ↦ (λ, −h), and U⁰_β ∩ Ǔ is the closure of the rest of Ǔ. (4) At each point of Ǔ on a coexistence line L^(##′)_β = U^#_β ∩ U^(#′)_β with # ≠ #′, the one-sided derivatives satisfy ∂ψ/∂h⁺ > ∂ψ/∂h⁻, and on L^(+0)_β and L^(−0)_β also ∂ψ/∂λ⁺ > ∂ψ/∂λ⁻, so the transitions across these lines are of first order. (5) Let (λ, h) ∈ Ǔ and let # be such that (λ, h) ∈ U^#_β. For every local function f and every sequence of c-connected sets Λ_n ↑ ℤ^d, the limit µ^#(f) = lim_n µ^#_(Λ_n)(f) of the finite-volume Gibbs distributions with boundary condition η^# exists and does not depend on the sequence. It defines a translation-invariant, extremal and ergodic Gibbs measure µ^# with µ^#(σ_0 = #) ≥ 1 − κ(β).
hypotheses: d ≥ 2, and the Blume–Capel model on ℤ^d with Φ⁰_({i,j}) = (ω_i − ω_j)² on nearest-neighbor pairs and W_({i}) = −hω_i − λω_i².
(λ, h) ∈ U = {|λ| ≤ ρ/8, |h| ≤ ρ/8} with the Peierls constant ρ = 5^(−d), and (λ, h) ∈ Ǔ for the coexistence lines and the Gibbs measures.
β > β0, a large constant that depends on d and on the C¹ cutoff function of the construction.

prerequisites.reason: Step s3 uses Theorem 7.29 of the source, whose convergence proof for τ-stable contour weights rests on the Kotecký–Preiss criterion for the cluster expansion.
Step s6 gets the C¹ coexistence curve h(λ) from the implicit function theorem applied to G(λ, h) = ψ̂⁺ − ψ̂⁰.
Step s7 shows that the limit of the finite-volume measures with boundary condition η^# is a Gibbs measure, as in the proof of the existence theorem.
Step s7 proves that µ^# is extremal with the short-range-correlation criterion of the theorem on extremal Gibbs measures.

definitions.name: contour
definitions.text: Let ω equal η^# outside a finite set. A site i is #-correct if ω_j = η^#_j for every j with d∞(i, j) ≤ 1. A contour of ω is a pair γ = (γ̄, ω_γ̄), where γ̄ is a maximal d∞-connected component of the set of sites that are not correct for any #. The label of a component A of ℤ^d ∖ γ̄ is the ground state that ω shows on ∂ex A. The contour is of type # if its unbounded component has label #, int_#′γ is the union of its bounded components with label #′, and intγ = ∪_#′ int_#′γ.

definitions.name: truncated pressure
definitions.text: ψ̂^# is the pressure of the contour model of type # in which each contour weight carries smooth cutoff factors. The cutoff removes a contour when its interior is so large that the phase # is not stable at (λ, h). On U^#_β no contour of type # is removed, and ψ̂^# is the true pressure.

definitions.name: coexistence line
definitions.text: L^(##′)_β = U^#_β ∩ U^(#′)_β for # ≠ #′, the set of parameters at which the two truncated pressures ψ̂^# and ψ̂^(#′) are both maximal.

source.citation: Sacha Friedli and Yvan Velenik, Statistical Mechanics of Lattice Systems: A Concrete Mathematical Introduction, Cambridge University Press, 2017.
source.revision: Authors' online version, revised version of August 22, 2017.
source.module: Chapter 7, Section 7.4 Phase diagram of the Blume–Capel model
source.excerpt: Theorem 7.36 (The pressure of the Blume–Capel model at low temperature). Let β0 be as in Proposition 7.34. For all β > β0, ψ(λ, h) = max_# ψ̂^#(λ, h). As a consequence, 1. The pressure ψ(λ, h) is C¹ in λ and h, everywhere in the interior of each region U^#_β, # ∈ {+, 0, −}. 2. First-order phase transitions occur across each of the coexistence lines
source.attribution: © Sacha Friedli and Yvan Velenik. Quoted from the authors' online version of the book for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states the pressure part as Theorem 7.36 (p. 366) and the Gibbs measures as Theorem 7.41 (p. 368), and the authored statement joins them with the description of the regions U^#_β on p. 365. The authored statement bounds the slope by 4ε/(1 − 2ε), where the source writes 2ε, because |∂G/∂h − ∂G/∂λ| can be as large as 4ε. The outline replaces |int_#′γ| by |intγ| in the cutoff of Definition 7.33, which the source's estimate (7.79) needs. The authored statement writes κ(β) for the function that the source calls δ(β) in (7.99).

results.proof_status: outline of the cited published proof. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proofs of Proposition 7.34, Theorem 7.35, Theorem 7.36 and Theorem 7.41 in Friedli and Velenik (2017), Sections 7.3 and 7.4. Steps s3 and s4 take from the source the cluster expansion of τ-stable weights (Theorem 7.29 and Lemma 7.31), the lattice isoperimetric inequality (Lemma 7.28) and the control of unstable contours in the proof of (7.68). Step s7 takes Lemma 7.42 from the source. Two changes are made. The cutoff in step s3 uses |intγ|^(1/d) where Definition 7.33 of the source uses |int_#′γ|^(1/d), because the source's bound (7.79) needs a^#_n|int_#′γ|^(1/d) ≤ ρ0/2 and the source's cutoff controls only ψ̂^#′_n − ψ̂^#_n. Step s4 calls a contour stable when a^#_n|intγ|^(1/d) ≤ ρ0/8, the threshold of (7.66), and then uses (7.73) with ρ0/(8a) in place of ρ0/(4a).

steps.text: Peierls condition. Since (ω_i − ω_j)² ≥ 1 when ω_i ≠ ω_j, the relative energy H_(Φ⁰)(ω | η^#) is at least the number of edges with ω_i ≠ ω_j, and every incorrect site lies in i + B(2) for an endpoint i of such an edge (Example 7.12 of the source). This gives the Peierls constant ρ = |B(2)|^(−1) = 5^(−d). For a contour γ of type #, the surface energy ‖γ‖ = Σ_(B⊂γ̄) {Φ_B(ω_γ̄) − Φ_B(η^#)} therefore satisfies ‖γ‖ ≥ (ρ − 2‖W‖)|γ̄|. On U, ‖W‖ ≤ |h| + |λ| ≤ ρ/4, so ‖γ‖ ≥ ρ0|γ̄| with ρ0 = ρ/2 (7.40).

Contour representation. Fix the external contours of a configuration in Ω^#_Λ and sum over the configurations in their interiors (7.29). Multiply and divide each Z^#′(int_#′γ) by Z^#(int_#′γ) (7.31) and iterate inside the interiors. With Z^#(Λ) = e^(−βe^#|Λ|) Ξ^#(Λ), this gives the polymer model Ξ^#(Λ) = Σ_Γ Π_(γ∈Γ) w^#(γ) over families of contours of type # in Λ that are pairwise compatible, d∞(γ̄, γ̄′) > 1, with the weights w^#(γ) = e^(−β‖γ‖) Π_#′ Z^#′(int_#′γ)/Z^#(int_#′γ) (7.33)-(7.34). The same resummation gives Lemma 7.26 of the source: the probability under µ^#_Λ that given compatible contours γ′_1, …, γ′_k are external is at most Π_i w^#(γ′_i). The ratios can contain volume terms e^(β(e^# − e^#′)|int_#′γ|), so w^#(γ) need not be small.

Truncated weights. A contour is of class n if |intγ| = n. Fix a C¹ function χ: ℝ → [0, 1] with χ = 1 on (−∞, ρ0/4] and χ = 0 on [ρ0/2, ∞). For class 0 put ŵ^#(γ) = e^(−β‖γ‖). When ŵ^# is defined up to class n, let Ξ̂^#_n be the polymer model with the weights ŵ^# on contours of class ≤ n, Ẑ^#_n(Λ) = e^(−βe^#|Λ|) Ξ̂^#_n(Λ), ψ̂^#_n = −e^# + lim_k log Ξ̂^#_n(B(k))/(β|B(k)|), ψ̂_n = max_# ψ̂^#_n and a^#_n = ψ̂_n − ψ̂^#_n ≥ 0. For γ of class n + 1 put ŵ^#(γ) = e^(−β‖γ‖) Π_#′ χ((ψ̂^#′_n − ψ̂^#_n)|intγ|^(1/d)) Z^#′(int_#′γ)/Z^#(int_#′γ). Then ŵ^# ≤ w^#, and a^#_n|intγ|^(1/d) ≤ ρ0/4 implies ŵ^#(γ) = w^#(γ) (7.63). Each truncated model is controlled by Theorem 7.29 of the source: if translation-invariant weights satisfy w(γ) ≤ e^(−τ|γ̄|) and |dw/ds| ≤ D|γ̄|^(d/(d−1)) e^(−τ|γ̄|) with τ > τ1(D, d), then g = lim_k log Ξ(B(k))/|B(k)| is an absolutely convergent cluster series with |g| ≤ η(τ, ℓ0) = 2e^(−τℓ0/3), Ξ(Λ) = exp(g|Λ| + Δ) with |Δ| ≤ η(τ, ℓ0)|∂in Λ|, and g is C¹ with |dg/ds| ≤ Dη(τ, ℓ0).

Induction on the class (Proposition 7.34). Let τ = ½βρ0 − 6. For β > β0 the source proves by induction on n that (i) ŵ^#(γ) ≤ e^(−τ|γ̄|) on U for all classes k ≤ n, with |∂ŵ^#/∂λ|, |∂ŵ^#/∂h| ≤ D|γ̄|^(d/(d−1)) e^(−τ|γ̄|) and D = 4(β + 2‖χ′‖) for the cutoff of step s3, (ii) a^#_n|intγ|^(1/d) ≤ ρ0/8 implies ŵ^#(γ) = w^#(γ), and (iii) Z^#(Λ) ≤ e^(βψ̂_n|Λ| + c_n|∂ex Λ|) for c-connected Λ with |Λ| ≤ n, where c_n ↑ c_∞ ≤ 3. For (i) at class n + 1: if ŵ^#(γ) ≠ 0, then (ψ̂^#′_n − ψ̂^#_n)|intγ|^(1/d) ≤ ρ0/2 for every #′, so a^#_n|int_#′γ|^(1/d) ≤ ρ0/2. The bound (iii) for Z^#′(int_#′γ), the lower bound Z^#(int_#′γ) ≥ Ẑ^#_n(int_#′γ) ≥ e^(βψ̂^#_n|int_#′γ| − |∂ex int_#′γ|) from Theorem 7.29, and the isoperimetric inequality |∂ex S| ≥ |S|^((d−1)/d) give Z^#′(int_#′γ)/Z^#(int_#′γ) ≤ e^((½βρ0 + 4)|∂ex int_#′γ|) (7.79). The sets ∂ex int_#′γ are disjoint subsets of γ̄, so ŵ^#(γ) ≤ e^(−βρ0|γ̄| + (½βρ0 + 4)|γ̄|) < e^(−τ|γ̄|) (7.80). For (iii) the source fixes the external unstable contours, expands the rest with Theorem 7.29 and sums over the unstable ones with the auxiliary weights e^(−(βρ0 − 6)|γ̄|). Lemma 7.31 gives |ψ̂^#_(n+1) − ψ̂^#_k| ≤ β^(−1) e^(−τk^((d−1)/d)/2) (7.85), which moves n to n + 1 in (ii) and (iii).

Pressure (Theorem 7.35). By (7.85), ĝ^#_n = ψ̂^#_n + e^# is a Cauchy sequence, and its limit ĝ^# is the convergent cluster series of the weights ŵ^# of all classes, with |ĝ^# − ĝ^#_n| ≤ β^(−1) e^(−τn^((d−1)/d)/2) (7.92). Theorem 7.29 and (i) give that ψ̂^# = −e^# + ĝ^# is C¹ on U with |ĝ^#|, |∂ĝ^#/∂λ|, |∂ĝ^#/∂h| ≤ ε = D3^d η(τ, ℓ0) (7.95). Let a^# = max_#′ ψ̂^#′ − ψ̂^#. The limit n → ∞ in (ii) shows that a^#|intγ|^(1/d) ≤ ρ0/8 implies ŵ^#(γ) = w^#(γ) (7.93). Where a^# = 0, every contour of type # has ŵ^# = w^#, so Z^#(B(n)) = Ẑ^#(B(n)) and ψ = ψ̂^#. At each point of U some a^# vanishes, so ψ = max_# ψ̂^# on U, and ψ = ψ̂^# is C¹ in the interior of U^#_β.

Phase diagram (Theorem 7.36). The + ↔ − symmetry gives ψ̂⁺(λ, −h) = ψ̂⁻(λ, h) (Exercise 7.14), so ψ̂⁺ = ψ̂⁻ on h = 0, and ∂ψ̂⁺/∂h ≥ 1 − ε > −1 + ε ≥ ∂ψ̂⁻/∂h gives {ψ̂⁺ ≥ ψ̂⁻} = {h ≥ 0}. Let G(λ, h) = ψ̂⁺ − ψ̂⁰ = h + λ + ĝ⁺ − ĝ⁰. Since |ĝ⁺ − ĝ⁰| ≤ 2ε < δ, G(λ, −λ − δ) < 0 < G(λ, −λ + δ), and ∂G/∂h ≥ 1 − 2ε > 0. So each λ ∈ (−ρ/8 + δ, ρ/8 − δ) has a unique h(λ) with G(λ, h(λ)) = 0 and |h(λ) + λ| < δ. The implicit function theorem makes h(λ) C¹, and h′ + 1 = (∂G/∂h − ∂G/∂λ)/(∂G/∂h) with |∂G/∂h − ∂G/∂λ| ≤ 4ε gives |h′ + 1| ≤ 4ε/(1 − 2ε). This gives U⁺_β ∩ Ǔ = {h ≥ max(h(λ), 0)} and the other regions by symmetry. On a line L^(##′)_β, ψ is locally the maximum of C¹ functions, and its right and left derivatives are the largest and the smallest derivatives of the maximal ones. The h-derivatives of ψ̂⁺, ψ̂⁰, ψ̂⁻ are within ε of 1, 0, −1, and on L^(±0)_β the λ-derivatives satisfy ∂ψ̂^±/∂λ ≥ 1 − ε > ε ≥ ∂ψ̂⁰/∂λ, so the one-sided derivatives differ.

Gibbs measures (Theorem 7.41). Let (λ, h) ∈ U^#_β, so every contour of type # has w^#(γ) = ŵ^#(γ) ≤ e^(−τ|γ̄|). For c-connected Λ, Δ ⊃ B(2n) and f local in B(n), let P = µ^#_Λ ⊗ µ^#_Δ. A connected D with B(n) ⊂ D ⊂ B(2n) is #-surrounding if both configurations equal # on ∂ex D. The largest such set D^# is determined by the spins outside it, and given D^# both configurations inside have the law µ^#_(D^#), so E_P[(f(ω) − f(ω′)) 1_(D^# exists)] = 0. Lemma 7.42 of the source bounds P(no #-surrounding set) by 2|B(n)| e^(−τ′n) with τ′ = τ/2: a path from B(n) to ∂in B(2n) of sites that are not #-correct in both configurations gives a chain of external contours of type # with total support at least n, and Lemma 7.26 sums such chains. Hence |µ^#_Λ(f) − µ^#_Δ(f)| ≤ c‖f‖_∞ n^d e^(−τ′n) (7.100), and the limit exists and does not depend on the sequence. It is a Gibbs measure as in the existence theorem. (7.100) with θ_iΛ_n gives translation invariance. The same surrounding sets give |µ^#(A ∩ B) − µ^#(A)µ^#(B)| = O(n^d e^(−τ′n)) for a cylinder A in F_(B(n)) and B ∈ F_(Λᶜ), so µ^# is extremal by the short-range-correlation criterion, and ergodic since it is also translation invariant. The Peierls bound µ^#_Λ(σ_0 ≠ #) ≤ Σ_(γ: γ̄ ∪ intγ ∋ 0) e^(−τ|γ̄|) gives µ^#(σ_0 = #) ≥ 1 − κ(β).

source.ref: S. Friedli and Y. Velenik, Statistical Mechanics of Lattice Systems (CUP 2017, revised version of August 22, 2017), Theorem 7.36, p. 366, with Proposition 7.34 (p. 357), Theorem 7.35 (p. 364) and Theorem 7.41 (p. 368).

applications.title: Phase diagram of the two-dimensional Blume–Capel model near its triple point
applications.inputs: Dimension d = 2, so ρ = 5^(−2) = 1/25 and ρ0 = 1/50. β is so large that β > β0 and ε(β) < 1/2000, and δ = 1/1000. Two parameter points: P = (λ, h) = (−1/400, 1/1000) and Q = (λ, h) = (1/400, 0).
applications.hypotheses: d = 2 ≥ 2. The choice of δ is admissible because 2ε < 1/1000 < ρ/16 = 1/400. Both points have |λ| = 1/400 < ρ/8 − δ = 1/200 − 1/1000 = 1/250 and |h| ≤ 1/1000 < ρ/8 = 1/200, so they lie in Ǔ ⊂ U.

steps.text: Ground-state energies at P: e⁺ = −h − λ = −1/1000 + 1/400 = 3/2000, e⁰ = 0 and e⁻ = h − λ = 1/1000 + 1/400 = 7/2000. So η⁰ is the unique ground state at P.

Low temperature at P: by part (3), h(λ) > −λ − δ = 1/400 − 1/1000 = 3/2000 > 1/1000 = h, so P is not in the closed set U⁺_β. Since h = 1/1000 > 0, P is not in U⁻_β = {h ≤ min(−h(λ), 0)} either. A neighborhood of P therefore lies in U⁰_β, so ψ = ψ̂⁰ is C¹ near P, and part (5) gives the Gibbs measure µ⁰ with µ⁰(σ_0 = 0) ≥ 1 − κ(β).

At Q, e^± = −λ = −1/400 < 0 = e⁰, so η⁺ and η⁻ are the ground states. By part (3), h(λ) < −λ + δ = −1/400 + 1/1000 = −3/2000 < 0, so max(h(λ), 0) = 0 and Q = (1/400, 0) lies in U⁺_β. By the symmetry it also lies in U⁻_β, so Q is on the line L^(+−)_β, and part (5) gives two Gibbs measures µ⁺ and µ⁻.

Near Q, G = ψ̂⁺ − ψ̂⁰ > 0 because G increases in h and vanishes at h(λ) < 0, so ψ = max(ψ̂⁺, ψ̂⁻). The magnetization ∂ψ/∂h has the right limit ∂ψ̂⁺/∂h ≥ 1 − ε and the left limit ∂ψ̂⁻/∂h ≤ −1 + ε. The jump is at least 2 − 2ε > 2 − 2/2000 = 1999/1000.

applications.conclusion: At P, inside the 0 region of the zero-temperature diagram, the pressure is C¹ and the 0 phase gives a Gibbs measure with most spins equal to 0. At Q, on the line h = 0 with λ > 0, the + and − phases coexist and the magnetization jumps by more than 1999/1000, a first-order transition.

limitations: The theorem does not show that µ⁺, µ⁰ and µ⁻ give all translation-invariant Gibbs measures. The source states this completeness as Theorem 7.46 and refers to Zahradník (1984) for the proof.
The result is perturbative. It needs β > β0 and fields in the square |λ|, |h| ≤ 5^(−d)/8 around the triple point, and it gives no information at moderate temperatures.

The truncated pressures are C¹ continuations of the pressure through the coexistence lines, and they depend on the cutoff. A smoother cutoff gives more regularity, but analytic continuation through the lines fails in general (Remark 7.38 of the source).

results.name: McBryan–Spencer bound on the correlations of the two-dimensional plane rotator
aliases: power-law decay of correlations in the two-dimensional XY model
results.statement: Let µ be an infinite-volume Gibbs measure of the two-dimensional XY model (plane rotator) at inverse temperature β > 0: the spins are S_i = (cos ϑ_i, sin ϑ_i), i ∈ ℤ², with the uniform a priori measure on the angles and the formal Hamiltonian −Σ_(i∼j) S_i · S_j over nearest-neighbor pairs. Let q(t) = 2(cosh t − 1)/t² for t > 0 and t_β = 1/(2πβ). (a) For all i, j ∈ ℤ² with ‖j − i‖₂ ≥ 3, with R = (‖j − i‖₂ − 1)/2, |⟨S_i · S_j⟩_µ| ≤ exp(q(t_β)(4 + 2π)/(4π²β)) R^(−(2 − q(t_β))/(2πβ)). (b) For ε ∈ (0, 1), let β_0(ε) be the unique β_0 > 0 with q(1/(2πβ_0)) = 1 + ε. Then, for all β ≥ β_0(ε) and all i ≠ j ∈ ℤ², |⟨S_i · S_j⟩_µ| ≤ e^(1/β) ‖j − i‖₂^(−(1−ε)/(2πβ)).
hypotheses: µ is an infinite-volume Gibbs measure of the two-dimensional XY model at inverse temperature β > 0.
For part (b): ε ∈ (0, 1) and β ≥ β_0(ε), where q(1/(2πβ_0(ε))) = 1 + ε.

prerequisites.reason: Step s2 moves the integration path of each angle from [−π, π] to [−π, π] + i r_j with Cauchy's integral theorem on a rectangle.

concepts: complex translation of the integration contour

definitions.name: XY model
definitions.text: The spin system on ℤ² with spins S_i = (cos ϑ_i, sin ϑ_i), uniform a priori measure on the angles, and finite-volume Gibbs weights exp(β Σ_({i,j}) cos(ϑ_i − ϑ_j)) over the nearest-neighbor edges that touch the volume.

definitions.name: q(t)
definitions.text: q(t) = 2(cosh t − 1)/t² = Σ_(m≥1) 2t^(2m−2)/(2m)!. It is continuous and strictly increasing on (0, ∞), with limit 1 as t → 0.

source.citation: Sacha Friedli and Yvan Velenik, Statistical Mechanics of Lattice Systems: A Concrete Mathematical Introduction, Cambridge University Press, 2017.
source.revision: Authors' online version, revised version of August 22, 2017.
source.module: Chapter 9, Section 9.4.2 Two-dimensional models
source.excerpt: Theorem 9.12. Let µ be an infinite-volume Gibbs measure associated to the two-dimensional XY model at inverse temperature β. For all ϵ > 0, there exists β0(ϵ) < ∞ such that, for all β > β0(ϵ) and all i ≠ j ∈ ℤ², |⟨Si · Sj⟩µ| ≤ ‖j − i‖₂^(−(1−ϵ)/(2πβ)).
source.attribution: © Sacha Friedli and Yvan Velenik. Quoted from the authors' online version of the book for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states the bound in (b) without the factor e^(1/β), and it proves it with the optimal shift given by the Green function and the asymptotics of the potential kernel (Theorems B.76 and B.77). The authored statement has the same exponent and an extra factor e^(1/β), which tends to 1 as β → ∞, and it adds the explicit bound (a) for every β > 0. The authored proof follows the complex translation (9.22)-(9.26) of the source and replaces the Green function by an explicit dipole of logarithmic profiles, so it needs no random walk asymptotics.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the complex translation in the proof of Theorem 9.12 in Friedli and Velenik, with an explicit test function. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Parts (a) and (b) for every infinite-volume Gibbs measure. The source's form without the factor e^(1/β) is not proved here.

steps.text: Reduction. The argument is the same for every pair, so take i = 0 and j = k with ‖k‖₂ ≥ 3. Let B(n) = {−n, …, n}² and let ⟨·⟩^η_n be the finite-volume Gibbs measure in B(n) with boundary condition η. By the DLR equations, ⟨S_0 · S_k⟩_µ = ∫ ⟨S_0 · S_k⟩^η_n µ(dη) for every n with k ∈ B(n). So it is enough to prove the bound for ⟨S_0 · S_k⟩^η_n, uniformly in η, for one large n. Also |⟨S_0 · S_k⟩^η_n| = |Re ⟨e^(i(ϑ_k − ϑ_0))⟩^η_n| ≤ |⟨e^(i(ϑ_k − ϑ_0))⟩^η_n|.

Complex translation. Write ⟨e^(i(ϑ_k − ϑ_0))⟩^η_n = Z⁻¹ ∫ dθ exp(i(θ_k − θ_0) + β Σ_({a,b}) cos(θ_a − θ_b)), where θ ∈ [−π, π]^(B(n)), the sum runs over the edges with an endpoint in B(n), θ_a = ϑ_a(η) outside B(n), and Z > 0 is the same integral without the factor e^(i(θ_k − θ_0)). Let r: ℤ² → ℝ vanish outside B(n). As a function of one variable θ_a, the integrand is entire and 2π-periodic. Cauchy's integral theorem on the rectangle with corners ±π and ±π + i r_a, whose vertical sides cancel by periodicity, lets us replace θ_a by θ_a + i r_a. Do this for each a ∈ B(n) in turn.

Cosh bound. After the shift, |e^(i(θ_k + i r_k − θ_0 − i r_0))| = e^(−(r_k − r_0)) and |exp(β cos(θ_a − θ_b + i(r_a − r_b)))| = exp(β cosh(r_a − r_b) cos(θ_a − θ_b)). Hence |⟨e^(i(ϑ_k − ϑ_0))⟩^η_n| ≤ e^(−(r_k − r_0)) ⟨exp(β Σ (cosh(r_a − r_b) − 1) cos(ϑ_a − ϑ_b))⟩^η_n ≤ exp(−(r_k − r_0) + β Σ_(all edges of ℤ²) (cosh(r_a − r_b) − 1)), because cosh − 1 ≥ 0 and cos ≤ 1.

Dipole test function. Let g(x) = max(0, log R − log max(|x|, 1)) for x ∈ ℝ², with R = (‖k‖₂ − 1)/2 ≥ 1. g is 1-Lipschitz, g(0) = log R, and g = 0 for |x| ≥ R. Let h_c(x) = g(x − c) for x ∈ ℤ², and r = t(h_k − h_0) with t > 0 and n large. Then h_0(k) = h_k(0) = 0, so r_k − r_0 = 2t log R. If an edge changes both h_0 and h_k, then it has an endpoint a with |a| < R and an endpoint b with |b − k| < R, where a = b is allowed. Then ‖k‖₂ ≤ |a| + |a − b| + |b − k| < 2R + 1 = ‖k‖₂, which is false. So on each edge at most one of t∇h_0, t∇h_k is nonzero, and it has absolute value at most t. For |u| ≤ 1, cosh(tu) − 1 = Σ_(m≥1) (tu)^(2m)/(2m)! ≤ u²(cosh t − 1). Hence Σ_(edges) (cosh(r_a − r_b) − 1) ≤ 2(cosh t − 1) S, where S = Σ_(edges {a,b}) (h_0(a) − h_0(b))².

Dirichlet energy. For a horizontal edge, (h_0(a + e_1) − h_0(a))² = (∫_0^1 ∂_1 g(a + s e_1) ds)² ≤ ∫_0^1 (∂_1 g(a + s e_1))² ds. Summing over the horizontal edges on the line at height y gives ∫_ℝ (∂_1 g(x, y))² dx. Here (∂_1 g)² = x²/(x² + y²)² for 1 < |(x, y)| < R and 0 elsewhere. For y = 0 the integral is 2(1 − 1/R) ≤ 2. For 1 ≤ |y| < R it is at most ∫_ℝ x²/(x² + y²)² dx = π/(2|y|). For |y| ≥ R it is 0. With Σ_(1≤y<R) 1/y ≤ 1 + log R, the horizontal edges give at most 2 + π + π log R. The vertical edges give the same bound, so S ≤ 2π log R + 4 + 2π.

Choice of t and conclusion. With t = t_β = 1/(2πβ), 2β(cosh t − 1) = βq(t)t² = q(t)/(4π²β). Steps s3-s5 give |⟨S_0 · S_k⟩^η_n| ≤ exp(−2t log R + q(t)(2π log R + 4 + 2π)/(4π²β)) = exp(q(t)(4 + 2π)/(4π²β)) R^(−(2 − q(t))/(2πβ)), uniformly in η. Step s1 gives part (a). For part (b), q is strictly increasing, so β ≥ β_0(ε) gives q(t_β) ≤ 1 + ε < 2. If ‖k‖₂ ≥ 3, then R ≥ ‖k‖₂/3 ≥ 1 and (a) gives |⟨S_0 · S_k⟩_µ| ≤ exp((2 + π)/(π²β) + log 3/(2πβ)) ‖k‖₂^(−(1−ε)/(2πβ)), and (2 + π)/π² + log 3/(2π) < 0.7 < 1. If 0 < ‖k‖₂ < 3, then |⟨S_0 · S_k⟩_µ| ≤ 1 ≤ e^(1/β) ‖k‖₂^(−(1−ε)/(2πβ)), because ‖k‖₂^(1/(2πβ)) ≤ 3^(1/(2πβ)) ≤ e^(1/β).

applications.title: Explicit power-law bound at 2πβ = 10
applications.inputs: Inverse temperature β = 5/π ≈ 1.59, so t_β = 1/(2πβ) = 1/10. Any infinite-volume Gibbs measure µ of the two-dimensional XY model at this β, and k ∈ ℤ² with ‖k‖₂ ≥ 3.
applications.hypotheses: Part (a) holds for every β > 0 and every Gibbs measure, so it applies directly. The spin-wave heuristic (9.21) of the source predicts the decay ‖k‖₂^(−1/(2πβ)) = ‖k‖₂^(−1/10).

steps.text: At distance ‖k‖₂ = 10^6 the bound gives |⟨S_0 · S_k⟩_µ| ≤ 1.32 × 10^(−0.5994) ≈ 0.33. The exponent 0.0999 is within 0.1 percent of the spin-wave exponent 1/10.

applications.conclusion: At 2πβ = 10, every Gibbs measure of the two-dimensional XY model satisfies |⟨S_0 · S_k⟩_µ| ≤ 1.32 ‖k‖₂^(−0.0999) for ‖k‖₂ ≥ 3. This is the spin-wave rate ‖k‖₂^(−1/10) up to a factor and a 0.1 percent loss in the exponent.

limitations: The theorem gives an upper bound only. A matching power-law lower bound at low temperature is part of the Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless transition, which the source discusses in Section 9.6.1 but does not prove.
The authored form (b) has the factor e^(1/β). The source states the bound without it, with a proof that uses the asymptotics of the potential kernel of the random walk.
The complex translation uses that each spin is given by one real angle. The source mentions extensions to a larger class of two-dimensional models in Section 9.6.2.

results.name: Fröhlich–Simon–Spencer infrared bound
results.statement: Let d ≥ 1 and ν ≥ 1, and let L ≥ 4 be even. Let T_L = (ℤ/Lℤ)^d with its set E_L of nearest-neighbour edges, and let T*_L = {2πn/L : n ∈ {0, …, L − 1}^d}. Let ρ be a nonzero finite Borel measure on ℝ^ν with compact support. For β > 0 let μ_{L,β} be the probability measure on (ℝ^ν)^{T_L} with density proportional to exp(−β Σ_{{i,j}∈E_L} ‖S_i − S_j‖²) with respect to the product measure ρ^{⊗T_L}, and write ⟨·⟩ for its expectation. Put ε(p) = Σ_{k=1}^d (1 − cos p_k). Then for every p ∈ T*_L \ {0}, Σ_{j∈T_L} e^{ip·j} ⟨S_0 · S_j⟩ ≤ ν/(4β ε(p)). Since ε(p) = d(1 − (1/2d) Σ_{j∼0} cos(p·j)), the right side is also (ν/4βd)(1 − (1/2d) Σ_{j∼0} cos(p·j))⁻¹.
hypotheses: The torus side L is even and at least 4, and the coupling is the nearest-neighbour Gaussian term β‖S_i − S_j‖² with β > 0.
The single-spin measure ρ is a nonzero finite Borel measure on ℝ^ν with compact support.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 takes the maximum of the continuous function Z on a compact set of shift fields.
Step s1 proves that Z is continuous by dominated convergence, with the bound 1 on the integrand.
Step s2 exchanges the integrals over the spins and over the Gaussian variables of the crossing edges.
Step s3 applies the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality in L² of the Gaussian variables of the crossing edges.
Step s5 uses the second-order Taylor expansion of a smooth function at an interior maximum.

definitions.name: Gaussian domination
definitions.text: The inequality Z(h) ≤ Z(0) for every h ∈ (ℝ^ν)^{T_L}, where Z(h) = ∫ exp(−β Σ_{{i,j}∈E_L} ‖S_i − S_j + h_i − h_j‖²) ρ^{⊗T_L}(dS). For the Gaussian free field, where ρ is Lebesgue measure, Z(h) = Z(0) for every h.

definitions.name: reflection through edges
definitions.text: For a direction k and an integer a, Θ changes the k-th coordinate x_k into 2a + 1 − x_k mod L and keeps the other coordinates. It exchanges the halves T⁺ = {x : x_k − a ∈ {1, …, L/2} mod L} and T⁻ = T_L \ T⁺. Every edge that joins the two halves has the form {i, Θi}.

definitions.name: structure factor
definitions.text: ĉ(p) = Σ_j e^{ip·j} ⟨S_0 · S_j⟩ = |T_L|⁻¹ ⟨‖Σ_j e^{ip·j} S_j‖²⟩ ≥ 0. It is the mean squared amplitude of the spin wave with wave vector p.

source.citation: Sacha Friedli and Yvan Velenik, Statistical Mechanics of Lattice Systems: A Concrete Mathematical Introduction, Cambridge University Press, 2017.
source.revision: Authors' online version, revised version of August 22, 2017.
source.module: Chapter 10, Section 10.5 The infrared bound
source.excerpt: Theorem 10.24 (Infrared bound). Let µL;β be the Gibbs distribution associated to a Hamiltonian of the form (10.38). Then, for any p ∈ T⋆L \ {0}, Σ_{j∈TL} e^{ip·j}〈S0 · Sj〉L;β ≤ (ν/4βd){1 − (1/2d)Σ_{j∼0} cos(p · j)}^{−1}.
source.attribution: © Sacha Friedli and Yvan Velenik. Quoted from the authors' online version of Statistical Mechanics of Lattice Systems for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states the bound for the Hamiltonian (10.38) with a compactly supported reference measure on the torus with L even (Remark 10.4), and its right side equals ν/(4βε(p)). The authored statement adds L ≥ 4, because for L = 2 each vertex has only d neighbours and the plane-wave identity −Δα = 2ε(p)α fails. The authored proof follows the source proof through Gaussian domination (Proposition 10.27) and the second variation (10.46)-(10.47). It replaces the series argument of Lemma 10.28 by a Gaussian integral representation of the crossing edges.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the proof of Theorem 10.24 in Section 10.5.3 of the source, with the reflection step done through the Gaussian integral representation of Peled and Spinka, Section 2.7.2. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement, for every even L ≥ 4, every compactly supported ρ, every β > 0 and every p ∈ T*_L \ {0}.

steps.text: The shifted partition function. For h ∈ (ℝ^ν)^{T_L} put Z(h) = ∫ exp(−β Σ_{{i,j}∈E_L} ‖S_i − S_j + h_i − h_j‖²) ρ^{⊗T_L}(dS). The integrand is at most 1 and ρ is finite, so Z is continuous by dominated convergence. Z(h + c) = Z(h) for every constant c ∈ ℝ^ν. Let the support of ρ lie in the ball of radius R. Then Z(0) ≥ e^(−4βR²|E_L|) ρ(ℝ^ν)^{|T_L|} > 0. If ‖h_i − h_j‖ ≥ 2R + s on one edge, then Z(h) ≤ e^(−βs²) ρ(ℝ^ν)^{|T_L|}. Fix s so that this bound is less than Z(0). The set K of h with h_0 = 0 and ‖h_i − h_j‖ ≤ 2R + s on every edge is compact, because the torus is connected. So Z attains its maximum on K, and this maximum is the supremum of Z over all h.

Split at a reflection plane. Let Θ be a reflection through edges with halves T⁺ and T⁻. Since L ≥ 4 is even, Θ is a graph automorphism. It maps the edges inside T⁺ onto the edges inside T⁻, and the crossing edges are the pairs {a, Θa} with a ∈ T⁺. For each crossing edge c, write e^(−β‖x − y‖²) = ∫ e^(i t_c·x) e^(−i t_c·y) γ(dt_c), where γ = N(0, 2βI_ν), x = S_a + h_a and y = S_{Θa} + h_{Θa}. This is the characteristic function of a Gaussian vector. All integrands have modulus at most 1 and all measures are finite, so Fubini's theorem gives Z(h) = ∫ F_h(t) G_h(t) γ^{⊗C}(dt). Here F_h integrates over the spins in T⁺ and depends on h only through h on T⁺. G_h does the same for T⁻.

The reflection inequality. Relabel the spins of T⁻ with Θ. Then G_h is the complex conjugate of F_{h′} for every field h′ with h′_a = h_{Θa} on T⁺. Let h⁺ equal h on T⁺ and h∘Θ on T⁻, and let h⁻ equal h on T⁻ and h∘Θ on T⁺. Then F_{h⁺} = F_h and G_{h⁺} is the conjugate of F_h, so ∫|F_h|² dγ^{⊗C} = Z(h⁺). In the same way ∫|G_h|² dγ^{⊗C} = Z(h⁻). The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality in L²(γ^{⊗C}) gives Z(h)² ≤ Z(h⁺) Z(h⁻).

Gaussian domination. Let N(h) be the number of edges {i, j} with h_i ≠ h_j. Among the maximizers of Z with h_0 = 0, choose h* with the least N(h*). Suppose that N(h*) > 0, take an edge with h*_i ≠ h*_j, and let Θ be the reflection through the midpoint of this edge. By s3, Z(h*)² ≤ Z(h*⁺) Z(h*⁻). Each factor is at most Z(h*), and Z(h*) ≥ Z(0) > 0, so h*⁺ and h*⁻ are maximizers. They agree across every crossing edge, and each of their inner edges copies an inner edge of one half of h*. So N(h*⁺) + N(h*⁻) ≤ 2N(h*) − 2. After a constant shift that sets the value at 0 to zero, one of them contradicts the choice of h*. Hence N(h*) = 0, h* is constant, and Z(h) ≤ Z(0) for every h.

The second variation. For real h put X = Σ_{{i,j}∈E_L} (S_i − S_j)·(h_i − h_j) and Q = Σ_{{i,j}∈E_L} ‖h_i − h_j‖². Expansion of the square gives φ(λ) = Z(λh)/Z(0) = ⟨exp(−2βλX − βλ²Q)⟩. X is bounded, so φ is smooth, and s4 gives φ(λ) ≤ 1 = φ(0). By Taylor's theorem at this interior maximum, φ′(0) = −2β⟨X⟩ = 0 and φ″(0) = 4β²⟨X²⟩ − 2βQ ≤ 0. So ⟨X²⟩ ≤ Q/(2β). For complex h, X(h) = X(Re h) + iX(Im h). Add the bounds for the real and imaginary parts: ⟨|X(h)|²⟩ ≤ (1/2β) Σ_{{i,j}∈E_L} ‖h_i − h_j‖², with the Hermitian norm.

A plane wave. Fix p ∈ T*_L \ {0} and ℓ ∈ {1, …, ν}, and put α_j = e^{ip·j} and h_j = α_j e_ℓ. Each vertex has 2d distinct neighbours because L ≥ 3, so (−Δα)_i = Σ_{j∼i} (α_i − α_j) = 2ε(p) α_i. Summation by parts on the torus gives Σ_{{i,j}} (f_i − f_j)(g_i − g_j) = Σ_i f_i (−Δg)_i. Hence Σ_{{i,j}} |α_i − α_j|² = 2ε(p)|T_L| and X(h) = 2ε(p) Σ_i S_i^ℓ e^{ip·i}. Now s5 gives 4ε(p)² ⟨|Σ_i S_i^ℓ e^{ip·i}|²⟩ ≤ ε(p)|T_L|/β. Since ε(p) > 0 for p ≠ 0, ⟨|Σ_i S_i^ℓ e^{ip·i}|²⟩ ≤ |T_L|/(4βε(p)).

Translation invariance. The measure μ_{L,β} is invariant under the translations of the torus, so ⟨S_i^ℓ S_j^ℓ⟩ depends only on j − i and is even in j − i. Hence ⟨|Σ_i S_i^ℓ e^{ip·i}|²⟩ = Σ_{i,j} e^{ip·(i−j)} ⟨S_i^ℓ S_j^ℓ⟩ = |T_L| Σ_j e^{ip·j} ⟨S_0^ℓ S_j^ℓ⟩. Sum over ℓ = 1, …, ν and divide by |T_L|. This gives Σ_j e^{ip·j} ⟨S_0 · S_j⟩ ≤ ν/(4βε(p)). Finally Σ_{j∼0} cos(p·j) = 2Σ_k cos p_k, so ε(p) = d(1 − (1/2d) Σ_{j∼0} cos(p·j)), which gives the second form.

applications.title: A spin wave of the classical Heisenberg model on a small torus
applications.inputs: The classical Heisenberg model on the torus T_4 in dimension d = 3. The spins are unit vectors in ℝ³, so ν = 3 and ρ is the uniform probability measure on the sphere S². The energy is β Σ_{{i,j}} ‖S_i − S_j‖² with β = 1. The wave vector is p = (π/2, π/2, 0).
applications.hypotheses: L = 4 is even and at least 4. The measure ρ is a probability measure on the unit sphere, which is compact. The vector p = (2π/4)(1, 1, 0) lies in T*_4 \ {0}.

steps.text: On the sphere ‖S_i − S_j‖² = 2 − 2S_i·S_j. So this Gibbs measure is the Heisenberg ferromagnet with coupling 2β = 2 on each edge, and the infrared bound applies with ν = 3.
The dispersion is ε(p) = (1 − cos(π/2)) + (1 − cos(π/2)) + (1 − cos 0) = 1 + 1 + 0 = 2.
The bound gives Σ_j e^{ip·j} ⟨S_0 · S_j⟩ ≤ ν/(4βε(p)) = 3/(4 · 1 · 2) = 3/8.

At β = 0 the spins are independent and the same sum equals ⟨S_0 · S_0⟩ = 1. So at β = 1 the mean squared amplitude of this spin wave is at most 3/8 of its value for independent spins. In absolute terms ⟨‖Σ_j e^{ip·j} S_j‖²⟩ ≤ 64 · 3/8 = 24.

applications.conclusion: For the classical Heisenberg model on the torus of side 4 in three dimensions at β = 1, the structure factor at p = (π/2, π/2, 0) is at most 3/8.

limitations: The bound says nothing at p = 0, where ε(0) = 0. The zero mode carries the magnetization, and the Fröhlich–Simon–Spencer theorem controls it through the sum rule for the other modes.

The proof needs reflection positivity. So it uses the torus, the nearest-neighbour Gaussian coupling and a product single-spin measure. Other boundary conditions, frustrated couplings and most quantum models need different arguments.

results.name: Fröhlich–Simon–Spencer theorem
aliases: Fröhlich–Simon–Spencer theorem on continuous symmetry breaking
results.statement: Let d ≥ 3 and ν ≥ 1, and let ρ be a probability measure on the unit sphere S^{ν−1} ⊂ ℝ^ν. Let T_L = (ℤ/Lℤ)^d with its set E_L of nearest-neighbour edges. For even L ≥ 4 and β > 0, let μ_{L,β} be the probability measure on (S^{ν−1})^{T_L} with density proportional to exp(−β Σ_{{i,j}∈E_L} ‖S_i − S_j‖²) with respect to ρ^{⊗T_L}. Write ⟨·⟩_{L,β} for its expectation and m_L = |T_L|⁻¹ Σ_{j∈T_L} S_j for the magnetization. Put ε(p) = Σ_{k=1}^d (1 − cos p_k) and β₀ = (ν/4)(2π)^{−d} ∫_{[−π,π]^d} dp/ε(p). Then β₀ < ∞, and for every β > 0, liminf_{L→∞, L even} ⟨‖m_L‖²⟩_{L,β} ≥ 1 − β₀/β. Moreover there is a constant K_d < ∞ that depends only on d such that ⟨‖m_L‖²⟩_{L,β} ≥ 1 − νK_d/(4β) for every even L ≥ 4 and every β > 0.
hypotheses: The dimension is d ≥ 3.
The spins are unit vectors: ρ is a probability measure on the unit sphere of ℝ^ν.
The Gibbs measure on the even torus of side L ≥ 4 has the nearest-neighbour weight exp(−β Σ ‖S_i − S_j‖²) with β > 0.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 applies Parseval's identity for the orthonormal Fourier basis of functions on the torus.
Step s2 bounds every nonzero Fourier mode of the spins with the infrared bound.
Step s5 passes to the limit in the Riemann sums with the dominated convergence theorem.

definitions.name: magnetization
definitions.text: m_L = |T_L|⁻¹ Σ_j S_j. Its mean square ⟨‖m_L‖²⟩ = |T_L|⁻² Σ_{i,j} ⟨S_i · S_j⟩ is the average spin-spin correlation over all pairs of sites.

definitions.name: Fourier modes
definitions.text: Ŝ_p = Σ_j e^{ip·j} S_j for p in the dual torus T*_L = {2πn/L : n ∈ {0, …, L − 1}^d}. The zero mode is Ŝ_0 = |T_L| m_L.

definitions.name: critical constant
definitions.text: β₀ = (ν/4)(2π)^{−d} ∫ dp/ε(p). The integral (2π)^{−d} ∫ dp/ε(p) equals G/d, where G is the expected number of visits to the origin of simple random walk on ℤ^d that starts there. So β₀ is finite exactly when the walk is transient, that is, when d ≥ 3.

source.citation: Sacha Friedli and Yvan Velenik, Statistical Mechanics of Lattice Systems: A Concrete Mathematical Introduction, Cambridge University Press, 2017.
source.revision: Authors' online version, revised version of August 22, 2017.
source.module: Chapter 10, Section 10.5.2 Application: Orientational long-range order in the O(N) model
source.excerpt: Theorem 10.25. Assume that d ≥ 3. Let µL,β be defined with respect to a reference measure µ0 under which ‖Si‖2 = 1, almost surely, for all i ∈ TL. Let β0 = (ν/(4d(2π)^d)) ∫_{[−π,π]^d} {1 − (1/2d)Σ_{j∼0} cos(p · j)}^{−1} dp. Then β0 < ∞ and, for any β > β0, lim inf_{L→∞} 〈‖mL‖²₂〉L,β ≥ 1 − β0/β.
source.attribution: © Sacha Friedli and Yvan Velenik. Quoted from the authors' online version of Statistical Mechanics of Lattice Systems for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source constant β₀ equals the authored one, because 1 − (1/2d)Σ_{j∼0} cos(p·j) = ε(p)/d. The authored statement adds L ≥ 4, which the infrared bound needs, and the uniform finite-volume bound, which is the first part of Theorem 2.13 of Peled and Spinka. The authored proof follows the source: the sum rule (10.40), the infrared bound (Theorem 10.24) and the Riemann sum (10.41). The source passes from the Riemann sum to the improper integral without details, and the authored proof does this step by dominated convergence.

source_references.module: Section 2.7 Reflection positivity and long-range order
source_references.excerpt: Theorem 2.13. For any d ≥ 3 and any n ≥ 1 there exists a constant β1(d, n) such that the following holds. Suppose σ : V(T^d_L) → S^{n−1} is randomly sampled from the d-dimensional spin O(n) model at inverse temperature β ≥ β1(d, n). Then (1/|V(T^d_L)|²) Σ_{x,y∈V(T^d_L)} E(⟨σx, σy⟩) ≥ c_{d,n,β}. Moreover, for any d ≥ 1, n ≥ 1 and β > 0, we have the limiting inequality …

source_references.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source_references.alignment: Peled and Spinka use the weight exp(β Σ ⟨σ_u, σ_v⟩) with uniform ρ on the torus of side 2L. This is the authored model with β replaced by β/2. After this change their limiting inequality 1 − (n/2β)∫_{[0,1]^d} dt/Σ_j(1 − cos πt_j) is the authored bound 1 − β₀/β, and their first part is the authored uniform bound. Their proof of (53) is the same sum-rule argument.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the proof of Theorem 10.25 in Section 10.5.2 of the source, with the limit of the Riemann sums done by dominated convergence. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement: finiteness of β₀, the limiting bound for every β > 0 and the uniform finite-volume bound.

steps.text: The sum rule. For p ∈ T*_L put Ŝ_p = Σ_j e^{ip·j} S_j. The functions |T_L|^{−1/2} e^{ip·j}, p ∈ T*_L, form an orthonormal basis of ℂ^{T_L}. Parseval's identity, applied to each coordinate of the spins, gives Σ_{p∈T*_L} ‖Ŝ_p‖² = |T_L| Σ_j ‖S_j‖² = |T_L|², because ‖S_j‖ = 1 almost surely. Since Ŝ_0 = |T_L| m_L, this gives ‖m_L‖² = 1 − |T_L|⁻² Σ_{p≠0} ‖Ŝ_p‖².

The infrared bound. The measure ρ lives on the unit sphere, which is compact, so the infrared bound applies. By translation invariance ⟨‖Ŝ_p‖²⟩ = |T_L| Σ_j e^{ip·j} ⟨S_0 · S_j⟩ ≤ ν|T_L|/(4βε(p)) for p ≠ 0. Take expectations in s1. This gives ⟨‖m_L‖²⟩_{L,β} ≥ 1 − (ν/4β) R_L, where R_L = |T_L|⁻¹ Σ_{p≠0} 1/ε(p).

R_L as an integral. The function ε is 2π-periodic in each coordinate, so we may take the representatives p = 2πn/L with n ∈ {−L/2 + 1, …, L/2}^d. Let C_p = p + [−π/L, π/L)^d. These cubes are disjoint, have volume (2π/L)^d = (2π)^d/|T_L|, and cover D_L = [−π + π/L, π + π/L)^d. Put f_L(q) = 1/ε(p) for q ∈ C_p with p ≠ 0, and f_L(q) = 0 on C_0 and outside D_L. Then R_L = (2π)^{−d} ∫_{ℝ^d} f_L(q) dq.

A bound that does not depend on L. Since 1 − cos t = 2 sin²(t/2) and |sin x| ≥ 2|x|/π for |x| ≤ π/2, we have 1 − cos t ≥ 2t²/π² for |t| ≤ π. So ε(p) ≥ 2|p|²/π² for p ∈ [−π, π]^d. Let p ≠ 0 and q ∈ C_p. Then |p|_∞ ≥ 2π/L, so |q|_∞ ≤ |p|_∞ + π/L ≤ (3/2)|p|_∞ and |q|² ≤ d|q|_∞² ≤ (9d/4)|p|². Hence f_L(q) ≤ π²/(2|p|²) ≤ 9dπ²/(8|q|²). Also D_L ⊂ [−2π, 2π]^d. So 0 ≤ f_L ≤ g with g(q) = (9dπ²/8)|q|⁻² for |q|_∞ ≤ 2π and g = 0 elsewhere. In polar coordinates ∫_{|q|≤r} |q|⁻² dq is a constant times r^{d−2}/(d − 2), which is finite because d ≥ 3. So K_d = (2π)^{−d} ∫ g dq is finite and R_L ≤ K_d for every even L ≥ 4. With s2 this gives the uniform bound ⟨‖m_L‖²⟩_{L,β} ≥ 1 − νK_d/(4β).

The limit. Let q ≠ 0 with |q_k| < π for every k. For large L, q lies in D_L, and the centre p_L(q) of its cube satisfies |p_L(q) − q|_∞ ≤ π/L. So p_L(q) ≠ 0 for large L, and f_L(q) = 1/ε(p_L(q)) → 1/ε(q) because ε is continuous and ε(q) > 0. If |q_k| > π for some k, then q lies outside D_L for large L and f_L(q) = 0. So f_L converges almost everywhere to 1/ε on [−π, π]^d and to 0 outside. Dominated convergence with the bound g of s4 gives R_L → (2π)^{−d} ∫_{[−π,π]^d} dp/ε(p) = 4β₀/ν. In particular β₀ ≤ νK_d/4 < ∞. Now s2 gives liminf ⟨‖m_L‖²⟩_{L,β} ≥ 1 − (ν/4β)(4β₀/ν) = 1 − β₀/β.

applications.title: Long-range order of the classical Heisenberg model on a torus of side 4
applications.inputs: The classical Heisenberg model in dimension d = 3: ν = 3 and ρ is the uniform probability measure on the sphere S². The torus has side L = 4, so |T_4| = 64. The weight is exp(−β Σ ‖S_i − S_j‖²) with β = 1, that is, coupling 2 for S_i · S_j on each edge.
applications.hypotheses: d = 3 ≥ 3. The spins are unit vectors. L = 4 is even and at least 4, and β = 1 > 0. So steps s1 and s2 of the proof apply, and they give ⟨‖m_4‖²⟩ ≥ 1 − (ν/4β) R_4.

steps.text: For L = 4 each coordinate p_k lies in {0, π/2, π, 3π/2}, and 1 − cos p_k takes the values 0, 1, 2, 1. So the numbers of wave vectors with ε(p) = s are the coefficients of x^s in ((1 + x)²)³ = (1 + x)⁶, that is, the binomial coefficients C(6, s).

For large tori the theorem gives the threshold β₀ = (3/4)W, where W = (2π)⁻³ ∫ dp/ε(p) ≈ 0.5055 is Watson's integral for the simple cubic lattice. So β₀ ≈ 0.379, and at β = 1 the limit of ⟨‖m_L‖²⟩ is at least about 0.62.

applications.conclusion: At β = 1 the mean square magnetization of the classical Heisenberg model on the torus of side 4 is at least 3603/5120 ≈ 0.704, and in large tori it stays at least about 0.62.

limitations: The theorem bounds ⟨‖m_L‖²⟩ on the torus. To get infinite-volume Gibbs states with a nonzero magnetization in each direction, one needs a further argument, for example the non-differentiability of the free energy in a field (Theorem 10.1 of the source).
The threshold β₀ is only an upper bound for the critical inverse temperature. For d ≤ 2 the integral diverges and the bound is empty, in line with the Mermin–Wagner theorem.
The proof needs reflection positivity through the infrared bound. It does not cover general finite-range couplings or the quantum Heisenberg ferromagnet.

results.name: Chessboard estimate
results.statement: Let d ≥ 1 and L ≥ 1. Let Λ = {−L + 1, …, L}^d be the vertex set of the discrete torus of side 2L, with its set E of nearest-neighbour edges. Let (S, 𝒮, λ) be a finite measure space and let h: S × S → [0, ∞) be bounded, measurable and symmetric. Assume that Z = ∫ Π_{{u,v}∈E} h(σ_u, σ_v) λ^{⊗Λ}(dσ) is positive, and let σ be a random configuration in S^Λ with density Z⁻¹ Π_{{u,v}∈E} h(σ_u, σ_v) with respect to λ^{⊗Λ}. Let R(v_1, v_2, …, v_d) = (1 − v_1, v_2, …, v_d), with the first coordinate taken modulo 2L, let (Rσ)_v = σ_{Rv}, and let V_0 = {v ∈ Λ : v_1 ≤ 0}. Assume reflection positivity: E[f(σ) f(Rσ)] ≥ 0 for every bounded measurable f: S^Λ → ℝ that depends only on the spins in V_0. Then for all bounded measurable functions f_v: S → ℝ, v ∈ Λ, (E Π_{v∈Λ} f_v(σ_v))^{|Λ|} ≤ Π_{w∈Λ} E Π_{v∈Λ} f_w(σ_v).
hypotheses: The law of σ is the nearest-neighbour model on the torus of side 2L with a bounded symmetric interaction h ≥ 0, a finite single-site measure λ and Z > 0.
Reflection positivity through edges: E[f(σ)f(Rσ)] ≥ 0 for every bounded real f of the spins in V_0.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 applies the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality to the symmetric positive semidefinite bilinear form E[F(σ)G(Rσ)].

definitions.name: reflection through edges
definitions.text: R(v_1, …, v_d) = (1 − v_1, v_2, …, v_d) mod 2L. It exchanges the halves V_0 = {v_1 ≤ 0} and V_1 = {v_1 ≥ 1}. The edges between the halves join the layers v_1 = 0, 1 and v_1 = L, −L + 1, and each of them has the form {v, Rv}.

definitions.name: assignment
definitions.text: A map τ: Λ → Λ that puts the function f_{τ(v)} at the site v. Its value is P(τ) = E Π_v f_{τ(v)}(σ_v). The identity map gives the left side of the estimate, and the constant map τ ≡ w gives a_w = E Π_v f_w(σ_v).

definitions.name: disagreement count
definitions.text: N(τ) is the number of edges {u, v} ∈ E with τ(u) ≠ τ(v). Since the torus is connected, N(τ) = 0 exactly when τ is constant.

source.citation: Ron Peled and Yinon Spinka, Lectures on the spin and loop O(n) models, arXiv:1708.00058, 2019. Published in Sojourns in Probability Theory and Statistical Physics I, Springer, 2019.
source.revision: arXiv v3, dated July 4, 2019, 71 pages.
source.module: Section 2.7.1 Introduction to reflection positivity
source.excerpt: Proposition 2.16 (Chessboard estimate). Let σ be sampled from the density (38) and suppose that the bilinear form defined in (40) is positive semidefinite. Then for any collection of real-valued bounded measurable functions (fv)v∈Λ on (S, S), we have (E ∏_{v∈Λ} fv(σv))^{|Λ|} ≤ ∏_{w∈Λ} E(∏_{v∈Λ} fw(σv)).
source.attribution: © Ron Peled and Yinon Spinka. Quoted from the arXiv version of Lectures on the spin and loop O(n) models for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The authored statement is the source statement with the density (38) and the bilinear form (40) written out. It asks for positivity only for real-valued functions, which is all that the proof uses, and it assumes Z > 0, which the source derives from h not being essentially zero. The authored proof follows the source proof: the weak estimate (42) through an extremal assignment, then a normalization. It writes out the sign change that the source notes at the start of its proof, which covers the case E Π f_v(σ_v) < 0.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the proof of Proposition 2.16 in the source, pp. 30-31. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement, for every family of bounded measurable real functions, including the case where E Π f_v(σ_v) is negative.

steps.text: The reflection form. R is an automorphism of the torus graph and h is symmetric, so Rσ has the same law as σ. For bounded real F, G that depend only on the spins in V_0 put (F, G) = E[F(σ)G(Rσ)]. This form is bilinear. It is symmetric because E[F(σ)G(Rσ)] = E[F(Rσ)G(σ)], and it is positive semidefinite by hypothesis. So the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives (F, G)² ≤ (F, F)(G, G). Translations and coordinate permutations of the torus preserve the law of σ. So the same holds for the reflection R′ through the plane that cuts any given edge, with the halves V_0′ and V_1′ = R′V_0′.

Reflected assignments. Let τ: Λ → Λ and P(τ) = E Π_v f_{τ(v)}(σ_v). For a reflection R′ with halves V_0′ and V_1′, let τ⁰ equal τ on V_0′ and τ∘R′ on V_1′, and let τ¹ equal τ on V_1′ and τ∘R′ on V_0′. Put F(σ) = Π_{v∈V_0′} f_{τ(v)}(σ_v) and G(σ) = Π_{v∈V_0′} f_{τ(R′v)}(σ_v). Both depend only on the spins in V_0′. Since R′ maps V_0′ onto V_1′, P(τ) = (F, G), P(τ⁰) = (F, F) ≥ 0 and P(τ¹) = (G, G) ≥ 0. So P(τ)² ≤ P(τ⁰)P(τ¹) by s1. Every crossing edge has the form {v, R′v}, so τ⁰ and τ¹ agree across all crossing edges. R′ maps the inner edges of V_0′ onto those of V_1′. Hence N(τ⁰) + N(τ¹) = 2N(τ) − 2N_c(τ), where N_c(τ) counts the crossing edges on which τ disagrees.

The weak estimate E Π_v f_v(σ_v) ≤ max_w a_w. By s2 with a constant τ, a_w = P(w) ≥ 0. Let P* be the maximum of P over the finite set of assignments, so P* ≥ 0. If P* = 0, then P(id) ≤ 0 ≤ a_w for every w. If P* > 0, choose a maximizer τ* with the least N(τ*). Suppose that N(τ*) > 0. Take an edge on which τ* disagrees and the reflection R′ through it, so N_c(τ*) ≥ 1. By s2, P*² ≤ P(τ*⁰)P(τ*¹), and both factors lie in [0, P*]. So both equal P*, and both are maximizers. But N(τ*⁰) + N(τ*¹) ≤ 2N(τ*) − 2, so one of them has fewer disagreements than τ*, a contradiction. Hence τ* is constant, equal to some w, and P(id) ≤ P* = a_w.

Normalization. Let δ > 0 and g_v = f_v/(a_v + δ)^{1/|Λ|}. These functions are bounded and measurable, and E Π_v g_w(σ_v) = a_w/(a_w + δ) < 1 for every w. So s3 for the family (g_v) gives E Π_v f_v(σ_v) / Π_v (a_v + δ)^{1/|Λ|} ≤ 1. Let δ → 0. This gives E Π_v f_v(σ_v) ≤ Π_v a_v^{1/|Λ|}.

The sign. Fix v_0 and replace f_{v_0} by −f_{v_0}. The left side E Π_v f_v(σ_v) changes sign. The number a_{v_0} = E Π_v f_{v_0}(σ_v) does not change, because |Λ| = (2L)^d is even, and the other a_w do not involve f_{v_0}. So s4 also gives −E Π_v f_v(σ_v) ≤ Π_v a_v^{1/|Λ|}. Hence |E Π_v f_v(σ_v)| ≤ Π_v a_v^{1/|Λ|}. Raise both sides to the even power |Λ|. This gives (E Π_v f_v(σ_v))^{|Λ|} ≤ Π_w a_w.

applications.title: A down spin in the Ising ring with a magnetic field
applications.inputs: The torus of side 4 in dimension d = 1 (L = 2), which is the ring Λ = {−1, 0, 1, 2}. The spin space is S = {−1, +1} with λ({+1}) = 3 and λ({−1}) = 1, which puts a magnetic field into the single-site measure. The interaction is h(a, b) = 2^{ab}, the Ising coupling e^{Jab} with e^J = 2.
applications.hypotheses: h is bounded, symmetric and positive, λ is finite and Z > 0. Reflection positivity holds by step a1. The number of sites |Λ| = 4 is even.

steps.text: Reflection positivity. h(a, b) = 5/4 + (3/4)ab, which gives 2 for a = b and 1/2 for a ≠ b. So h is a sum of products α(a)α(b) with the nonnegative weights 5/4 and 3/4, for α = 1 and α(a) = a. Expand the two crossing edges {0, 1} and {−1, 2} of R with this formula. Then E[f(σ)f(Rσ)] is a sum of nonnegative weights times squares of real numbers, so it is nonnegative.
Take f_0 = 1_{{−1}} and f_v = 1 for v ≠ 0. Then a_0 = P(σ ≡ −1) and a_w = 1 for w ≠ 0. The estimate gives P(σ_0 = −1)⁴ ≤ P(σ ≡ −1).

With the transfer matrix M = diag(3, 1)·(h(a, b)) = [[6, 3/2], [1/2, 2]] one has M² = [[147/4, 12], [4, 19/4]] and Z = tr M⁴ = 11753/8. The all-minus configuration has weight 1⁴ · 2⁴ = 16, so P(σ ≡ −1) = 16/Z = 128/11753.

So P(σ_0 = −1) ≤ (128/11753)^{1/4} ≈ 0.323. Since Z is at least the weight 3⁴ · 2⁴ = 1296 of the all-plus configuration, also P(σ ≡ −1) ≤ (1/3)⁴. This gives P(σ_0 = −1) ≤ 1/3 for every value of the coupling.
The exact value is (M⁴)_{−−}/Z = (1129/16)/(11753/8) = 1129/23506 ≈ 0.048. It satisfies both bounds.

applications.conclusion: In the Ising ring of four sites with field weights 3 : 1 and e^J = 2, the chessboard estimate gives P(σ_0 = −1) ≤ (128/11753)^{1/4} ≈ 0.323, and the exact value is about 0.048.

limitations: The estimate needs reflection positivity. It holds when the interaction is a positive semidefinite kernel, but it must be checked for each model.
This version uses functions of single sites and reflections through edges. Block functions and reflections through vertices need the general form, for example Theorem 10.11 of Friedli and Velenik.
The bound compares the system with periodic repetitions of one local pattern. It is useful only when these repeated patterns are rare, as at low temperature or in a strong field.

results.name: Dyson–Lieb–Simon theorem on long-range order in quantum antiferromagnets
aliases: Néel order in the quantum Heisenberg antiferromagnet
results.statement: Let d ≥ 1, let S ∈ {1/2, 1, 3/2, …}, let ℓ ≥ 4 be even, and let Λ_ℓ = (ℤ/ℓℤ)^d with unit vectors e₁, …, e_d. On ⊗_{x∈Λ_ℓ} ℂ^{2S+1} let S_x = (S_x^(1), S_x^(2), S_x^(3)) be the spin-S operators at x, with [S_x^(1), S_x^(2)] = iS_x^(3) and its cyclic permutations, S_x · S_x = S(S + 1), and commuting operators at different sites. The Heisenberg antiferromagnet is H_ℓ = 2 Σ_{x∈Λ_ℓ} Σ_{i=1}^d S_x · S_{x+e_i}, and its Gibbs state at β > 0 is ⟨A⟩ = Tr(A e^(−βH_ℓ))/Tr e^(−βH_ℓ). Let Λ*_ℓ = (2π/ℓ){−ℓ/2 + 1, …, ℓ/2}^d, ε(k) = 2 Σ_{i=1}^d (1 − cos k_i), π = (π, …, π), I_ℓ = ℓ^(−d) Σ_{k∈Λ*_ℓ∖{0}} √(ε(k + π)/ε(k)) and α_ℓ(β) = −⟨S_0^(1) S_{e₁}^(1)⟩ − ⟨S_0^(2) S_{e₁}^(2)⟩. Then α_ℓ(β) ≥ 0, and the Néel order parameter satisfies ℓ^(−d) Σ_{x∈Λ_ℓ} (−1)^(x₁+⋯+x_d) ⟨S_0^(3) S_x^(3)⟩ ≥ (1/3)S(S + 1) − (1/2)√(α_ℓ(β)) I_ℓ − (2βℓ^d)^(−1) Σ_{k∈Λ*_ℓ∖{0}} 1/ε(k), where x₁, …, x_d ∈ {0, …, ℓ − 1} are the coordinates of x. If d ≥ 3, then K_d = sup_ℓ ℓ^(−d) Σ_{k∈Λ*_ℓ∖{0}} 1/ε(k) is finite, and for every S with S + 1 > 3√(dK_d) there are β₀ < ∞ and c > 0 such that the Néel order parameter is at least c for every even ℓ ≥ 4 and every β ≥ β₀.
hypotheses: The torus side ℓ is even and at least 4, so the torus is bipartite and the reflections through planes that cut edges are symmetries.
The Hamiltonian is the nearest-neighbour spin-S Heisenberg antiferromagnet H_ℓ = 2 Σ_x Σ_i S_x · S_{x+e_i} without magnetic field, in its Gibbs state at inverse temperature β > 0.
For the long-range order part: d ≥ 3, S + 1 > 3√(dK_d) and β ≥ β₀.

prerequisites.reason: Step s2 uses the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality in the Duhamel expansion to prove the reflection inequality, and step s7 uses it to bound I_ℓ.
Step s2 takes a maximizer of the continuous function Z̃, which exists because Z̃(λv) tends to 0 as |λ| → ∞.
Step s3 compares the second-order Taylor expansions at s = 0 of Z(sv)/Z(0) and of the Gaussian bound.
Step s4 proves the Falk–Bruch inequality with Jensen's inequality for the concave function Φ.
Step s6 uses Parseval's identity on the torus as the sum rule ⟨(T_0^(3))²⟩ = ℓ^(−d) Σ_k ĝ(k).

definitions.name: Néel order parameter
definitions.text: The staggered correlation ℓ^(−d) Σ_x (−1)^(x₁+⋯+x_d) ⟨S_0^(3) S_x^(3)⟩. It equals ℓ^(−2d) ⟨(Σ_x (−1)^(x₁+⋯+x_d) S_x^(3))²⟩ by translation invariance. Néel long-range order means that it stays above a positive constant as ℓ → ∞.

definitions.name: Duhamel inner product
definitions.text: For a hermitian matrix H with Z = Tr e^(−H), (A, B) = Z^(−1) ∫_0^1 Tr e^(−(1−s)H) A* e^(−sH) B ds. The Duhamel two-point function is η(x) = (βZ)^(−1) ∫_0^β Tr T_0^(3) e^(−sH_ℓ) T_x^(3) e^(−(β−s)H_ℓ) ds.

definitions.name: Falk–Bruch inequality
definitions.text: 2⟨A*A + AA*⟩/⟨[A*, [H, A]]⟩ ≤ Φ(4(A, A)/⟨[A*, [H, A]]⟩) with Φ(s) = √s coth(1/√s). It bounds an ordinary expectation by a Duhamel inner product and a double commutator.

source.excerpt: Theorem 3.2. Assume that ℓ is even and that the nearest-neighbour coupling constants satisfy J(3) = 1 ≥ J(1) ≥ −J(2) ≥ 0. Then we have the two lower bounds: (1/ℓ^d) Σ_{x∈Λℓ} ⟨S0(3) Sx(3)⟩per_{Λℓ,β,0} ≥ (1/3)S(S + 1) − (1/2)(Iℓ(d) + √2/ℓ^d) √αℓ(β) − (1/(2βℓ^d)) Σ_{k∈Λ*ℓ\{0}} 1/ε(k), …

source.alignment: The source states Theorem 3.2 for nearest-neighbour couplings with J(3) = 1 ≥ J(1) ≥ −J(2) ≥ 0, and it notes on p. 11 that a sublattice rotation makes it apply to the Heisenberg antiferromagnet. The authored statement is the first bound in antiferromagnet variables. For these couplings r = 1 in (4.33) of the source, so the correction √2/ℓ^d of the source is not needed. The added consequence for d ≥ 3 uses the crude bounds α_ℓ(β) ≤ 2S² and I_ℓ ≤ √(2dK_d) in place of the numerical constants of the source.

proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of the first bound of Theorem 3.2 in Björnberg and Ueltschi (arXiv:2204.12896v2), Sections 4 and 5, applied to the antiferromagnet after the sublattice rotation of p. 11. The source reviews the method of Dyson, Lieb and Simon (1978). Steps s2 to s5 cite Lemmas 4.1, 4.2, 4.4, 5.1 and 5.2 and Corollaries 4.3 and 5.3 of the source. Step s7 replaces the numerical constants of the source by explicit crude bounds.

steps.text: Sublattice rotation (the source, p. 11). Put T_x = S_x when x₁ + ⋯ + x_d is even and T_x = (−S_x^(1), S_x^(2), −S_x^(3)) when it is odd. This is a rotation by π about the second spin axis, so the T_x satisfy the same spin relations. Since ℓ is even, nearest neighbours have opposite parity, and H_ℓ = −Σ_{x∈Λ_ℓ} Σ_{y∼x} (T_x^(1) T_y^(1) − T_x^(2) T_y^(2) + T_x^(3) T_y^(3)). This is the Hamiltonian (2.4) of the source with nearest-neighbour couplings J^(1) = J^(3) = 1 and J^(2) = −1, which satisfy J^(3) = 1 ≥ J^(1) ≥ −J^(2) ≥ 0. The new Hamiltonian is invariant under all translations of the torus. In the new variables the Néel order parameter is ℓ^(−d) Σ_x ⟨T_0^(3) T_x^(3)⟩, and α_ℓ(β) = ⟨T_0^(1) T_{e₁}^(1)⟩ − ⟨T_0^(2) T_{e₁}^(2)⟩ is the quantity (3.8) of the source.

Gaussian domination (Lemmas 5.1 and 5.2 and Corollary 5.3 of the source, pp. 19-23). For a real field v on Λ_ℓ let (Δv)_x = Σ_{y∼x} (v_y − v_x), Z(v) = Tr exp(−β(H_ℓ − Σ_x (Δv)_x T_x^(3))) and Z̃(v) = e^(β(v, Δv)/4) Z(v). Lemma 5.1 of the source expands Tr e^(A + B + ∫C_i D_i dμ(i)) by the Duhamel series and applies the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, with reflected and complex-conjugated operators. In the basis where T^(3) is diagonal, T^(1) and iT^(2) have real matrices, and the source checks that the crossing terms then have the required form with a positive measure because J^(1), J^(3) ≥ 0 ≥ J^(2). Lemma 5.2 of the source gives Z̃(v₁, v₂)² ≤ Z̃(v₁, Rv₁) Z̃(Rv₂, v₂) for every reflection R through a plane that cuts edges. Z̃(λv) → 0 as |λ| → ∞, so Z̃ attains its maximum, and repeated reflections of a maximizer give maximizers with more and more equal values. This is Corollary 5.3 of the source: Z̃(v) ≤ Z̃(0) for every v.

Duhamel infrared bound (Lemma 4.1 of the source, proved on p. 24). Let η(x) = (βZ(0))^(−1) ∫_0^β Tr T_0^(3) e^(−sH_ℓ) T_x^(3) e^(−(β−s)H_ℓ) ds and η̂(k) = Σ_x e^(−ik·x) η(x). By s2, Z(sv)/Z(0) ≤ e^(s²β(v, −Δv)/4) for real s. The first derivative of Z(sv) at s = 0 vanishes by the rotation by π about the third spin axis. The Duhamel formula gives Z(0)^(−1) d²Z(sv)/ds² at s = 0 equal to β² Σ_{x,y} h_x h_y η(x − y) with h = Δv. Both sides of the bound equal 1 with zero derivative at s = 0, so the second derivatives satisfy β² Σ_{x,y} h_x h_y η(x − y) ≤ (1/2)β(v, −Δv). Take v_x = cos(k·x) with k ∈ Λ*_ℓ∖{0}. Then −Δv = ε(k)v and Σ_{x,y} v_x v_y η(x − y) = η̂(k) Σ_x cos²(k·x), so η̂(k) ≤ 1/(2βε(k)).

Falk–Bruch inequality (Lemma 4.2 and Corollary 4.3 of the source, pp. 14-15). Let H be a hermitian matrix, ⟨·⟩ = Z^(−1) Tr(· e^(−H)) and (A, B) the Duhamel inner product. In an eigenbasis of H, F(s) = Tr e^(−(1−s)H) A* e^(−sH) A equals ∫ e^(st) dμ(t) for a positive measure μ. Jensen's inequality for the concave function Φ(s) = √s coth(1/√s) gives Lemma 4.2 of the source: 2⟨A*A + AA*⟩/⟨[A*, [H, A]]⟩ ≤ Φ(4(A, A)/⟨[A*, [H, A]]⟩). The double commutator is nonnegative, because it equals ([A*, H], [A*, H]). Since Φ(s) ≤ s + √s, this gives Corollary 4.3 of the source: (1/2)⟨A*A + AA*⟩ ≤ (1/2)√((A, A)⟨[A*, [H, A]]⟩) + (A, A).

Infrared bound for the ordinary correlation (Lemma 4.4 and (4.33) of the source, pp. 16-18). Take H = βH_ℓ and A = T̂_k^(3) = Σ_x e^(−ik·x) T_x^(3). Then (A, A) = ℓ^d η̂(k), which is at most ℓ^d/(2βε(k)) for k ≠ 0 by s3. With ĝ(k) = Σ_x e^(−ik·x) ⟨T_0^(3) T_x^(3)⟩ ≥ 0, translation and reflection invariance give (1/2)⟨A*A + AA*⟩ = ℓ^d ĝ(k). The source computes ⟨[A*, [βH_ℓ, A]]⟩ = 4βℓ^d e(k), and for these couplings e(k) = α_ℓ(β) Σ_{i=1}^d (1 + cos k_i) = α_ℓ(β) ε(k + π)/2, which is (4.33) of the source with r = 1. At k = 0 the nonnegative double commutator gives 2dα_ℓ(β) ≥ 0, so α_ℓ(β) ≥ 0. For k ≠ 0, s4 gives ĝ(k) ≤ √(e(k)/(2ε(k))) + 1/(2βε(k)) = (1/2)√(α_ℓ(β)) √(ε(k + π)/ε(k)) + 1/(2βε(k)).

Sum rule (proof of Theorem 3.1, (4.30)-(4.32), and of Theorem 3.2 of the source, p. 17). Parseval's identity for the field T^(3) and translation invariance give ⟨(T_0^(3))²⟩ = ℓ^(−d) Σ_{k∈Λ*_ℓ} ĝ(k). The term k = 0 is ℓ^(−d) ĝ(0) = ℓ^(−d) Σ_x ⟨T_0^(3) T_x^(3)⟩, the Néel order parameter. Also (T_0^(3))² = (S_0^(3))². H_ℓ commutes with the total spin, so the Gibbs state is invariant under global spin rotations and ⟨(S_0^(3))²⟩ = (1/3)⟨S_0 · S_0⟩ = (1/3)S(S + 1). The source gets the inequality ≥ from Lemma A.1 for its more general couplings. Insert the bound of s5 for every k ≠ 0. The result is ℓ^(−d) Σ_x ⟨T_0^(3) T_x^(3)⟩ ≥ (1/3)S(S + 1) − (1/2)√(α_ℓ(β)) I_ℓ − (2βℓ^d)^(−1) Σ_{k≠0} 1/ε(k), which is the stated bound.

Long-range order for large spin (the remark on p. 10 of the source, with explicit constants). Let d ≥ 3. The source notes that ℓ^(−d) Σ_{k≠0} 1/ε(k) converges as ℓ → ∞, so the sequence is bounded and K_d is finite. The average of ε(k + π) over Λ*_ℓ is 2d, so the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives I_ℓ ≤ √(ℓ^(−d) Σ_{k≠0} ε(k + π)) √(ℓ^(−d) Σ_{k≠0} 1/ε(k)) ≤ √(2dK_d). Each |⟨T_0^(i) T_{e₁}^(i)⟩| is at most ‖T_0^(i)‖ ‖T_{e₁}^(i)‖ = S², so α_ℓ(β) ≤ 2S². Hence the Néel order parameter is at least (1/3)S(S + 1) − S√(dK_d) − K_d/(2β). If S + 1 > 3√(dK_d), then c₀ = S((S + 1)/3 − √(dK_d)) > 0. For β ≥ β₀ = K_d/c₀ the parameter is at least c = c₀/2, for every even ℓ ≥ 4.

source.ref: J. E. Björnberg and D. Ueltschi, Reflection positivity and infrared bounds for quantum spin systems, arXiv:2204.12896v2, Theorem 3.2 (p. 10), proved with Lemmas 4.1, 4.2, 4.4, 5.1 and 5.2 on pp. 12-24.

applications.title: Néel order bound for spin 3/2 on the 4 × 4 × 4 torus
applications.inputs: The spin-3/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet H_4 = 2 Σ_x Σ_{i=1}^3 S_x · S_{x+e_i} on the torus Λ_4 = (ℤ/4ℤ)³, so d = 3, ℓ = 4 and S = 3/2, at the inverse temperature β = 4.
applications.hypotheses: ℓ = 4 is even and at least 4, and the Hamiltonian is the nearest-neighbour antiferromagnet without field. The bound of the theorem holds for every β > 0.

steps.text: The mode sum. On Λ*_4 each coordinate k_i ∈ {−π/2, 0, π/2, π} gives 1 − cos k_i ∈ {1, 0, 1, 2}, the number of chosen elements of a 2-element set. So ε(k) = 2s, where s is the number of chosen elements among 6, and Σ_{k≠0} 1/ε(k) = (1/2) Σ_{s=1}^6 C(6, s)/s = (1/2)(1517/60). Hence ℓ^(−3) Σ_{k≠0} 1/ε(k) = 1517/7680.

The middle term. The average of ε(k + π) over the 64 wave vectors is 2d = 6, and the term k = 0 is ε(π) = 12. So ℓ^(−3) Σ_{k≠0} ε(k + π) = 6 − 12/64 = 93/16, and Cauchy–Schwarz gives I_4² ≤ (93/16)(1517/7680). With α_4(β) ≤ 2S², the middle term is at most (1/2)√(2S²) I_4 = S√(I_4²/2), and I_4²/2 ≤ 47027/81920 < 16/25. So the middle term is at most (4/5)S.
The first two terms at S = 3/2. The sum rule gives (1/3)S(S + 1) = (1/3)(3/2)(5/2) = 5/4, and the middle term is at most (4/5)(3/2) = 6/5. Their difference is 1/20.

The temperature term at β = 4 is (2βℓ³)^(−1) Σ_{k≠0} 1/ε(k) = 1517/(2 · 4 · 7680) = 1517/61440. So the Néel order parameter is at least 1/20 − 1517/61440 = 311/12288 ≈ 0.0253. The same estimate is positive for every β > 1517/768 ≈ 1.98.

Limits of the crude estimate. For S = 1 the first two terms give 2/3 − 4/5 < 0, so this estimate proves nothing for spin 1 on this torus. The source uses a second bound and numerical values of the mode integrals to reach smaller spins.

applications.conclusion: For the spin-3/2 antiferromagnet on the 4 × 4 × 4 torus at β = 4, ℓ^(−3) Σ_x (−1)^(x₁+x₂+x₃) ⟨S_0^(3) S_x^(3)⟩ ≥ 311/12288 ≈ 0.025.

limitations: The explicit consequence needs a large spin because it uses α_ℓ(β) ≤ 2S². The source combines a second lower bound, the numerical values of I^(d) and Ĩ^(d) and the bound (3.10) of Kubo and Kishi, and it states Néel order at low temperature for every S ≥ 1/2 when d ≥ 3.

In d = 2 the sum ℓ^(−d) Σ_{k≠0} 1/ε(k) grows like log ℓ, so the bound gives no order at positive temperature, in agreement with the Mermin–Wagner theorem. It is useful in the ground state, when β → ∞ before ℓ → ∞.
The method needs reflection positivity. It does not apply to models whose couplings are all positive, such as the quantum Heisenberg ferromagnet.
