results.name: Fröhlich–Spencer theorem on the Kosterlitz–Thouless transition
aliases: Fröhlich–Spencer theorem on the Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless transition
power-law lower bound for the two-dimensional Villain model
results.statement: Let L > 1. Let Λ^free_L be the graph with vertex set {0, …, L − 1}² whose edges join the pairs of points at Euclidean distance 1. Let Λ^zero_L be the multigraph obtained from Λ^free_L by adding one vertex z and, for each vertex j of Λ^free_L, 4 − deg(j) parallel edges between j and z, so that every vertex other than z has degree 4. For β > 0 the Villain model on Λ^zero_L is the probability measure on angles θ = (θ_j) with θ_z = 0 and θ_j ∈ [−π, π) for j ≠ z, with density proportional to Π_{{j,ℓ}} Σ_{m∈ℤ} exp(−(β/2)(θ_j − θ_ℓ + 2πm)²) with respect to Lebesgue measure. The product runs over the edges of Λ^zero_L, and each parallel edge has its own factor. Write E^Vil_{β,L} for the expectation and dist for the graph distance in Λ^zero_L. Then there exist constants β₀ > 0 and C > 0 such that E^Vil_{β,L}[cos θ_j] ≥ (dist(j, z) + 1)^(−C/β) for every L > 1, every β > β₀ and every vertex j of Λ^zero_L.
hypotheses: The graph is the multigraph Λ^zero_L for some L > 1: the square {0, …, L − 1}² with nearest-neighbour edges and a wired boundary vertex z with angle θ_z = 0.
The angles carry the Villain weight Σ_{m∈ℤ} exp(−(β/2)(θ_j − θ_ℓ + 2πm)²) on every edge.
The inverse temperature satisfies β > β₀, where β₀ is an absolute constant.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 expands the periodized Gaussian weight of each edge into its Fourier series by Poisson summation.
Step s2 takes the limit of the Fejér-kernel weights to the integer-valued field by dominated convergence.
Step s5 shifts the Gaussian integration contour by an imaginary spin wave, which is the complex translation identity.
Step s6 removes the odd sine terms with Jensen's inequality for the exponential function.

definitions.name: Villain weight
definitions.text: The 2π-periodic function V_β(t) = Σ_{m∈ℤ} exp(−(β/2)(t + 2πm)²), a periodized Gaussian. Its Fourier series is V_β(t) = (2πβ)^(−1/2) Σ_{n∈ℤ} e^(−n²/(2β)) e^(int).

definitions.name: integer-valued discrete Gaussian free field
definitions.text: On a finite connected graph Λ with a marked vertex v, the probability measure on m : Λ → ℤ with m_v = 0 and weight proportional to exp(−(β/2) Σ_{j∼ℓ} (m_j − m_ℓ)²). Small β is high temperature for this height model.

definitions.name: Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless transition
definitions.text: A phase transition of a two-dimensional model with a continuous symmetry. The spin correlations decay exponentially at high temperature and like a power of the distance at low temperature, and there is no spontaneous magnetization.

proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of Theorem 1.3 in Kharash and Peled (arXiv:1711.04720v1), Section 6 (pp. 32-38), with the renormalization step Theorem 1.6 (Sections 2 and 4) and the Jensen argument of Section 3. Steps s4, s5 and s7 cite Theorem 1.6, Proposition 2.4 and Claims 6.3 and 6.4 of the source for the long estimates. The source presents the proof of Fröhlich and Spencer (1981) in finite volume.

steps.text: Duality (Proposition 6.1 of the source, pp. 32-34). Let x = (x₀, x₁) be a vertex with dist(x, z) = L − x₀. Let χ = 1 on the L − x₀ oriented edges of the horizontal path from x to the right side and then to z, and χ = 0 on the other edges. The symmetry θ ↦ −θ gives E^Vil_β[cos θ_x] = E^Vil_β[e^(i(θ_x − θ_z))], and e^(i(θ_x − θ_z)) = Π_e e^(−iχ_e(θ_k − θ_ℓ)) over the oriented edges e = (k, ℓ). Poisson summation gives Σ_{m∈ℤ} e^(−(β/2)(t + 2πm)² − iχt) = (2πβ)^(−1/2) Σ_{n∈ℤ} e^(−(n + χ)²/(2β)) e^(int). The integral over each angle θ_j, j ≠ z, keeps only the integer edge variables n with zero divergence at j. On the planar multigraph these flows are exactly n_e = m_{k′} − m_{ℓ′} for an integer height function m on the dual graph Λ*_L ≅ Λ^free_{L+1}, unique when m_v = 0. The same computation with χ = 0 gives the partition function, and the constants cancel. Since (n + 1)²/(2β) = n²/(2β) + (n + 1/2)/β, this gives E^Vil_β[cos θ_x] = E^IV_{1/β}[exp(−β^(−1) Σ_e (m_{e,−} − m_{e,+} + 1/2))], where the sum runs over the L − x₀ dual edges that cross the path and E^IV_{1/β} is the integer-valued discrete Gaussian free field at inverse temperature 1/β.

Periodic weights (Section 5.1 and p. 34 of the source). Put β̃ = 1/β and L′ = L + 1. Identify Λ*_L with Λ^free_{L′} by the shift (1/2, 1/2), and put y = (y₀, y₁) = (x₀ + 1, x₁). Let f_y = +1 on {(t, y₁) : y₀ ≤ t < L′}, f_y = −1 on {(t, y₁ + 1) : y₀ ≤ t < L′} and f_y = 0 elsewhere. The dual observable is then exp(−β̃⟨m, f_y⟩ − β̃(L′ − y₀)/2) with L′ − y₀ = L − x₀. Let F_N(t) = 1 + 2 Σ_{q=1}^N (1 − q/N) cos(qt) be the Fejér kernel. Give the field φ the weight Π_j F_N(φ_j) dμ^GFF_{β′} with β′ = β̃/(2π)². As N → ∞, the expectation of e^(⟨φ, g⟩) converges to the expectation of e^(⟨2πm, g⟩) under E^IV_{β̃} for every g with Σ_j g_j = 0, by the summability-kernel property of F_N and dominated convergence ((5.1) of the source). With φ = 2πm the observable becomes exp(−2πβ′⟨φ, f_y⟩ − (2π)²β′(L′ − y₀)/2). Each F_N is (1, 0, 0)-sub-Gaussian in the sense of Definition 1.4 of the source, because |F̂_N(q)| ≤ 1. So a lower bound that is uniform over sub-Gaussian weights passes to the limit N → ∞.

Shift by the dipole potential ((6.4) of the source). Let Δ be the graph Laplacian of Λ^free_{L′} and let σ solve Δσ = 2πf_y with σ_v = 0. The change of variables φ ↦ φ + σ in the Gaussian density exp(−(β′/2)⟨φ, −Δφ⟩) removes the term linear in φ. It gives E_{β′,λ}[exp(−2πβ′⟨φ, f_y⟩ − (2π)²β′(L′ − y₀)/2)] = exp((2π)²β′(⟨f_y, (−Δ)^(−1) f_y⟩ − (L′ − y₀))/2) · Z(σ)/Z(0), where Z(σ) = ∫ Π_j λ_j(φ_j + σ_j) dμ^GFF_{β′}(φ). For the Gaussian free field itself, with all λ_j = 1, the ratio Z(σ)/Z(0) equals 1. The proof must show that the periodic weights lower this ratio by at most a power of L′ − y₀ + 1.

Multiscale expansion (Theorem 1.6 of the source, p. 6, proved in Sections 2 and 4). Theorem 1.6 of the source proves that for Γ > 0, η ∈ ℝ and 0 ≤ θ < 1/16 there are β₀′, c₁ > 0 such that, for β′ < β₀′ and every σ, Z(σ) = Σ_{N∈F} c_N Z_N(σ) with c_N > 0, Σ_N c_N = 1 and Z_N(σ) = ∫ Π_{ρ∈N} [1 + z(β′, ρ, N) cos(⟨φ, ρ̄⟩ + ⟨σ, ρ⟩)] dμ^GFF_{β′}(φ). Each ensemble N is a finite family of integer charge densities ρ with disjoint supports. Every ρ in it is neutral, Σ_j ρ(j) = 0, and |z(β′, ρ, N)| ≤ exp(−(c₁/β′)(‖ρ‖₂² + log₂(d(ρ) + 1))), where d(ρ) is the diameter of the support of ρ. The first part of the proof (Theorem 2.2 of the source) writes Π_j λ_j(ψ_j) as a convex combination of products Π_{ρ∈N} [1 + K(ρ) cos⟨ψ, ρ⟩] over ensembles whose densities have distance at least M min(d(ρ₁), d(ρ₂))^α, with 3/2 < α < 2 and M = 2^16. Each ensemble has at most one non-neutral density ρ_c. It drops out (Step 1 of Section 2.3): the zero mode φ_v is uniform on [−π, π), and ∫_{−π}^{π} cos(Qφ_v + h) dφ_v = 0 for every integer Q = Σ_j ρ_c(j) ≠ 0.

Spin waves and complex translation (Proposition 2.4, (2.19) and Step 4 of Section 2.3 of the source). For each neutral ρ, Proposition 2.4 of the source constructs a real spin wave a_ρ, supported in the ball D(ρ) of radius 2d(ρ) and constant near the other densities of comparable or smaller diameter, with E_{β′}(a_ρ, ρ) = ⟨a_ρ, ρ⟩ − (β′/2)⟨a_ρ, −Δa_ρ⟩ ≥ (1/β′)(‖ρ‖₂²/16 + D₃ Σ_{k≥1} |S_k^sep(ρ)|). Expand the product Π_ρ [1 + K(ρ) cos(⟨φ, ρ⟩ + ⟨σ, ρ⟩)] into exponentials e^(i⟨φ, τ⟩) with neutral τ. The shift φ ↦ φ + ia of the integration contour (Lemma 4.8 of the source, by Cauchy's theorem) gives ∫ e^(i⟨φ, τ⟩) dμ^GFF_{β′} = e^(−E_{β′}(a, τ)) ∫ e^(i⟨φ, τ + β′Δa⟩) dμ^GFF_{β′}. The spin waves of different densities do not interact, so E_{β′}(Σ n(ρ)a_ρ, Σ n(ρ)ρ) = Σ |n(ρ)| E_{β′}(a_ρ, ρ) for n(ρ) ∈ {−1, 0, 1}. This gives the form of step s4 with z = K(ρ) e^(−E_{β′}(a_ρ, ρ)) and ρ̄ = ρ + β′Δa_ρ. The bound |K(ρ)| ≤ e^(D₂A(ρ)) Π_j e^(ρ(j)²) |λ̂_j(|ρ(j)|)| of Theorem 2.2, the sub-Gaussian bound with θ < 1/16 and the cover estimate A(ρ) of Proposition 2.1 then give the bound on |z| in step s4.

Lower bound for each ensemble (Claim 3.1 and (6.6) of the source). Take β′ so small that |z(β′, ρ, N)| < 1/8 for all ρ and N. Claim 3.1 of the source proves 1 + z cos(x + y) ≥ exp(−z sin x sin y/(1 + z cos x) − D₄|z|y²)(1 + z cos x) for 0 < |z| < 1/8. The left side is 2π-periodic in y, so y can be replaced by its representative [y]_{2π} in [−π, π). Apply this with x = ⟨φ, ρ̄⟩ and y = ⟨σ, ρ⟩ for every ρ ∈ N. The measure Z_N(0)^(−1) Π_ρ [1 + z cos⟨φ, ρ̄⟩] dμ^GFF_{β′} is a probability measure that is invariant under φ ↦ −φ. The sum S(N, φ) of the terms −z sin⟨φ, ρ̄⟩ sin⟨σ, ρ⟩/(1 + z cos⟨φ, ρ̄⟩) is odd in φ, so Jensen's inequality gives ∫ e^S ≥ e^(∫S) = 1. Hence Z_N(σ)/Z_N(0) ≥ exp(−D₄ Σ_{ρ∈N} |z(β′, ρ, N)| [⟨σ, ρ⟩]²_{2π}).

Green function estimates (Claims 6.3 and 6.4 of the source, p. 35, proved in Section 6.3 by comparison with the Green function of the torus Λ^per_{2L′}). Claim 6.3 of the source proves that for each D > 0 there is β₁ > 0 with Σ_{ρ∈N} |z(β′, ρ, N)| [⟨σ, ρ⟩]²_{2π} ≤ (β′/D) ln(L′ − y₀ + 1) for β′ < β₁ and every N ∈ F. Claim 6.4 of the source proves ⟨f_y, (−Δ)^(−1) f_y⟩ ≥ (L′ − y₀) − D₅ ln(L′ − y₀ + 1). Take D = D₄. Since Z(0) = Σ_N c_N Z_N(0) with Z_N(0) > 0, steps s4 and s6 give Z(σ)/Z(0) ≥ (L′ − y₀ + 1)^(−β′). With step s3 the expectation of step s3 is at least (L′ − y₀ + 1)^(−cβ′) with c = 1 + (2π)²D₅/2. This is Theorem 6.2 of the source, and its threshold for β′ depends only on (Γ, η, θ).

Return to the Villain model (p. 34 of the source). Apply step s7 with (Γ, η, θ) = (1, 0, 0), so that the bound holds for every F_N with one threshold β₀″. Let N → ∞ as in step s2. For β̃ < (2π)²β₀″ this gives E^IV_{β̃}[exp(−β̃⟨m, f_y⟩ − β̃(L − x₀)/2)] ≥ (L − x₀ + 1)^(−cβ̃/(2π)²). By step s1 with β̃ = 1/β, every β > β₀ = 1/((2π)²β₀″) gives E^Vil_β[cos θ_x] ≥ (dist(x, z) + 1)^(−C/β) with C = c/(2π)², for every x with dist(x, z) = L − x₀. The rotations and reflections of the square preserve Λ^zero_L, the Villain measure and z, and they move every vertex to a vertex whose nearest side is the right side. For x = z both sides equal 1.

source.ref: V. Kharash and R. Peled, The Fröhlich-Spencer proof of the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless transition, arXiv:1711.04720v1, Theorem 1.3 (p. 4), proved in Section 6 (pp. 32-38) with Theorem 1.6 (p. 6) and Section 3 (p. 14).

applications.title: The centre spin of the 3 × 3 Villain box
applications.inputs: The Villain model on Λ^zero_3, a 3 × 3 square of angles with the wired vertex z, at an inverse temperature β > β₀. The observed vertex is the centre c = (1, 1).
applications.hypotheses: L = 3 > 1, the measure is the Villain measure of the theorem with θ_z = 0, and β > β₀. The Gaussian comparison in step a3 holds for every β > 0.

steps.text: Distance. The centre has no edge to z, and each of its neighbours (1, 0), (0, 1), (2, 1) and (1, 2) has one edge to z. So dist(c, z) = 2, and the theorem gives E^Vil_β[cos θ_c] ≥ (2 + 1)^(−C/β) = 3^(−C/β) for β > β₀. The same bound holds for every vertex at distance 2 in every box Λ^zero_L.

Duality. The path c → (2, 1) → z crosses n = L − x₀ = 2 dual edges. Proposition 6.1 of the source gives E^Vil_β[cos θ_c] = E^IV_{1/β}[exp(−β^(−1)⟨m, f⟩ − n/(2β))] on Λ*_3 ≅ Λ^free_4, where f = +1 at (2, 1) and (3, 1), f = −1 at (2, 2) and (3, 2), and f = 0 elsewhere.

Gaussian comparison. Proposition 1.2 of the source, applied to the test function −β^(−1)f, bounds the integer-valued field by the real-valued Gaussian free field: E^Vil_β[cos θ_c] ≤ exp(−(n − ⟨f, (−Δ)^(−1) f⟩)/(2β)). The exact solution of −Δu = f on the 4 × 4 grid gives ⟨f, (−Δ)^(−1) f⟩ = 13/8. So n − ⟨f, (−Δ)^(−1) f⟩ = 2 − 13/8 = 3/8.

Check by effective resistance. The number 3/8 is also the effective resistance R between c and z in Λ^zero_3 with unit conductances. Put potential 1 at c and 0 at z. By symmetry the four side vertices have one potential s and the four corners have one potential k. Kirchhoff's law gives 1 + 2k − 4s = 0 at a side vertex and 2s − 4k = 0 at a corner, so s = 1/3 and k = 1/6. The current out of c is 4(1 − 1/3) = 8/3, so R = 3/8. Thus the upper bound is the spin-wave value exp(−R/(2β)) of the Gaussian approximation.

Conclusion. For β > β₀, 3^(−C/β) ≤ E^Vil_β[cos θ_c] ≤ e^(−3/(16β)). Both bounds have the form e^(−const/β). The two bounds are compatible only if C ln 3 ≥ 3/16, so every constant C for which the theorem holds satisfies C ≥ 3/(16 ln 3) ≈ 0.171.

applications.conclusion: At the centre of the 3 × 3 Villain box, the theorem and the Gaussian comparison give 3^(−C/β) ≤ E[cos θ_c] ≤ e^(−3/(16β)) for β > β₀. So the constant of the theorem satisfies C ≥ 3/(16 ln 3).

limitations: The constants β₀ and C are not explicit. The proof needs β large, and it does not reach the conjectured transition point.

With the McBryan–Spencer upper bound C′(dist + 1)^(−c/β) at every β and the exponential decay at small β, the theorem proves a Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless transition. It does not identify the critical inverse temperature or the exponent at the transition.
The source treats the Villain model only. Fröhlich and Spencer (1981) also treat the XY model, the Z_n clock models and the Coulomb gas, with complex translations for non-Gaussian measures.

results.name: Brascamp–Lieb variance inequality
results.statement: Let V: ℝⁿ → ℝ be twice continuously differentiable, with Hessian H(x) = ∇²V(x) positive definite at every x and Z = ∫e^(−V(x)) dx < ∞. Let μ(dx) = Z⁻¹e^(−V(x)) dx. (a) For every continuously differentiable f: ℝⁿ → ℝ with compact support, Var_μ(f) ≤ ∫⟨H(x)⁻¹∇f(x), ∇f(x)⟩ μ(dx). (b) If moreover H(x) ≥ ρI for all x, with a constant ρ > 0, the same inequality holds for every continuously differentiable f with ∫f² dμ < ∞ and ∫‖∇f‖² dμ < ∞.
hypotheses: V is of class C² on ℝⁿ, its Hessian is positive definite at every point, and e^(−V) is integrable.
In part (a), f is C¹ with compact support. In part (b), ∇²V ≥ ρI for some ρ > 0, and f is C¹ with f and ‖∇f‖ square integrable under μ.

prerequisites.reason: Step s2 applies the Prékopa–Leindler inequality with weights ½ and ½ to e^(2δf − V), e^(−V) and e^(F_δ − V).
Step s1 takes the least eigenvalue m > 0 of the Hessian on a closed ball, a continuous positive function on a compact set.
Step s1 uses the uniform continuity of the Hessian on a closed ball, which gives the modulus ω used in step s4.
Steps s3 and s4 write V(z ± h) and f(z + h) with Taylor's formula, and step s5 expands the exponentials to second order in δ.
Step s6 splits the weighted gradient norm of the cutoff function with Minkowski's inequality.
Step s6 passes to the limit R → ∞ in both sides with the dominated convergence theorem.

definitions.name: log-concave probability measure
definitions.text: A measure with density proportional to e^(−V) for a convex function V. Here V is C² with a positive definite Hessian.

definitions.name: variance under μ
definitions.text: Var_μ(f) = ∫f² dμ − (∫f dμ)², the mean square distance of f from its mean under μ.

definitions.name: midpoint defect
definitions.text: D(z, h) = ½V(z + h) + ½V(z − h) − V(z). It is nonnegative for convex V and equals ½⟨H(z)h, h⟩ to second order in h.

source.citation: Sergey G. Bobkov and Michel Ledoux, From Brunn–Minkowski to Brascamp–Lieb and to logarithmic Sobolev inequalities, Geometric and Functional Analysis 10 (2000), 1028–1052.
source.revision: Journal version (GAFA, Vol. 10, 2000) as posted on the first author's home page.
source.module: Section 2 From Prékopa–Leindler to Brascamp–Lieb
source.excerpt: Proposition 2.1. Assume that V is twice continuously differentiable and strictly convex on Ω. Then, for every smooth enough function f on Ω, Var_µ(f) ≤ ∫⟨V''⁻¹∇f, ∇f⟩ dµ where V''⁻¹ denotes the inverse of the Hessian of V.
source.attribution: © Sergey G. Bobkov and Michel Ledoux. Quoted from the authors' article for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source works on an open convex set Ω and says 'smooth enough function'. The authored statement takes Ω = ℝⁿ, asks for a positive definite Hessian, and names the classes of functions in parts (a) and (b). The authored proof follows the Prékopa–Leindler proof of the source with t = s = ½ (pp. 1031-1032). It replaces the perturbation to V'' ≥ ρ Id in the source by a direct local argument on a ball.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the Prékopa–Leindler proof of Proposition 2.1 in Bobkov and Ledoux (2000). No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Parts (a) and (b) of the statement. Steps s1 to s5 prove part (a), and step s6 proves part (b).

steps.text: Reduction and constants. For f in C_c¹, the mollifications f_k = f * ρ_(1/k) lie in C_c^∞ with supports in one ball, and f_k → f and ∇f_k → ∇f uniformly. H⁻¹ is continuous, hence bounded on that ball, so both sides for f_k converge to those for f. So let f be in C_c^∞ with support in the ball B(0, r). Put M₀ = sup|f| and M₂ = sup‖∇²f‖. Let m > 0 be the least eigenvalue of H(x) over |x| ≤ r + 2, which exists by the extreme value theorem. Let ω be a modulus of continuity of H on that ball, which exists by the Heine–Cantor theorem.

Prékopa–Leindler step. Put D(z, h) = ½V(z + h) + ½V(z − h) − V(z) ≥ 0 and F_δ(z) = sup_h [δf(z + h) − D(z, h)] for δ > 0. Then δf ≤ F_δ ≤ δM₀, and F_δ is lower semicontinuous, hence measurable. For z = (x + y)/2 and h = x − z one has y = z − h, so (e^(2δf(x) − V(x)))^(1/2)(e^(−V(y)))^(1/2) = e^(δf(z + h) − D(z, h) − V(z)) ≤ e^(F_δ(z) − V(z)). The Prékopa–Leindler inequality with weights ½ and division by Z give ∫e^(F_δ) dμ ≥ (∫e^(2δf) dμ)^(1/2).

Far displacements do not compete. Taylor's formula gives D(z, h) = ½∫₀¹(1 − τ)⟨[H(z + τh) + H(z − τh)]h, h⟩ dτ with a nonnegative integrand. Case |z| ≥ r + 1: then f(z) = 0 and ∇f(z) = 0. If z + h is in the support, then |h| ≥ 1, and for τ ≥ 1 − 1/‖h‖ the point z + τh lies in B(0, r + 1), so D ≥ ½m‖h‖² ∫ over [1 − 1/‖h‖, 1] of (1 − τ) dτ = m/4. Otherwise the term is −D ≤ 0. For δ < m/(4M₀) this gives F_δ(z) = 0. Case |z| < r + 1 and ‖h‖ ≥ η with η ≤ 1: the points z ± τh with τ‖h‖ ≤ 1 lie in B(0, r + 2), so D ≥ m‖h‖² ∫₀^(min(1, 1/‖h‖)) (1 − τ) dτ ≥ mη²/2. With η = δ^(1/3) and δ small, mη²/2 ≥ 2δM₀, so δf(z + h) − D ≤ −δM₀ ≤ δf(z).

Near displacements. For |z| < r + 1 and ‖h‖ < η, the bound ‖H(z ± τh) − H(z)‖ ≤ ω(η) gives D(z, h) ≥ ½⟨H(z)h, h⟩ − ½ω(η)‖h‖². Taylor's formula gives δf(z + h) ≤ δf(z) + δ∇f(z)·h + ½δM₂‖h‖². So δf(z + h) − D ≤ δf(z) + δ∇f(z)·h − ½⟨(H(z) − θI)h, h⟩ with θ = δM₂ + ω(δ^(1/3)), which tends to 0. When θ < m, H(z) − θI ≥ (1 − θ/m)H(z), and the maximum over h of the quadratic is at most (δ²/2)(1 − θ/m)⁻¹ q(z) with q = ⟨H⁻¹∇f, ∇f⟩. With s3, for all small δ and all z, F_δ ≤ δf + κ_δ δ² q/2 with κ_δ = (1 − θ/m)⁻¹ → 1.

Second-order expansion. Put a = ∫f dμ, b = ∫f² dμ and Q = ∫q dμ. Since f and q are bounded, e^x = 1 + x + x²/2 + O(x³) gives ∫e^(F_δ) dμ ≤ 1 + δa + δ²b/2 + κ_δδ²Q/2 + O(δ³). Also (∫e^(2δf) dμ)^(1/2) = (1 + 2δa + 2δ²b + O(δ³))^(1/2) = 1 + δa + δ²b − δ²a²/2 + O(δ³). The inequality of s2 then gives δ²(b − a²)/2 ≤ κ_δδ²Q/2 + O(δ³). Divide by δ²/2 and let δ → 0. The result is Var_μ(f) = b − a² ≤ Q, which is part (a).

Part (b). Let H ≥ ρI and let χ be smooth with χ = 1 on the unit ball, χ = 0 outside the ball of radius 2 and ‖∇χ‖ ≤ 2. Put f_R = χ(x/R)f, so part (a) applies to f_R. Write ∇f_R = A_R + B_R with A_R = χ(x/R)∇f and B_R = R⁻¹f∇χ(x/R). Minkowski's inequality for the norm (∫⟨H⁻¹v, v⟩ dμ)^(1/2) splits the right side. Since H⁻¹ ≤ ρ⁻¹I, the B_R part is at most (4ρ⁻¹R⁻²∫f² dμ)^(1/2) → 0. The A_R part tends to (∫⟨H⁻¹∇f, ∇f⟩ dμ)^(1/2) by dominated convergence with the bound ρ⁻¹‖∇f‖². Also f_R → f in L²(μ) by dominated convergence, so Var_μ(f_R) → Var_μ(f).

applications.title: Relative displacement of two coupled anharmonic oscillators
applications.inputs: Two particles on the line with energy V(x₁, x₂) = Σ_i (x_i²/2 + x_i⁴/4) + (J/2)(x₁ − x₂)² at temperature 1, with coupling J = 2. The observable is the relative displacement f(x) = x₁ − x₂.
applications.hypotheses: V is C², and its Hessian H(x) = diag(1 + 3x₁², 1 + 3x₂²) + J·[[1, −1], [−1, 1]] satisfies H(x) ≥ I. So e^(−V) is integrable and part (b) applies with ρ = 1. The observable f is C¹, and f and ∇f = (1, −1) are square integrable because μ has Gaussian tails.

steps.text: Put B = I + J·[[1, −1], [−1, 1]]. Then H(x) − B = diag(3x₁², 3x₂²) ≥ 0, so H(x) ≥ B > 0. The inverse is order reversing: B^(−1/2)HB^(−1/2) ≥ I implies B^(1/2)H⁻¹B^(1/2) ≤ I, that is H(x)⁻¹ ≤ B⁻¹.
The vector v = ∇f = (1, −1) satisfies Bv = (1 + 2J)v. So ⟨H(x)⁻¹v, v⟩ ≤ ⟨B⁻¹v, v⟩ = ‖v‖²/(1 + 2J) = 2/(1 + 2J) at every x.
The Brascamp–Lieb inequality gives Var_μ(x₁ − x₂) ≤ 2/(1 + 2J). For J = 2 the bound is 2/(1 + 2 · 2) = 2/5.

For comparison, the Poincaré bound from H ≥ I alone gives Var_μ(x₁ − x₂) ≤ ‖v‖² = 2, five times larger. Without the quartic terms the measure is Gaussian and the variance is exactly 2/(1 + 2J), so the bound is sharp in that limit.

applications.conclusion: For the coupled anharmonic oscillators with J = 2, the relative displacement has variance at most 2/5. The stiff coupling direction is seen through H⁻¹, which a bound from the smallest eigenvalue cannot see.

limitations: Equality holds for a Gaussian measure (V quadratic) and a linear f, so the inequality is sharp. It bounds only the variance, not the entropy.
Without a uniform lower bound on the Hessian, the authored statement covers only compactly supported f. The original paper of Brascamp and Lieb treats a wider class of functions.

results.name: Bakry–Émery criterion
aliases: Bakry–Émery curvature criterion for logarithmic Sobolev inequalities
results.statement: Let ρ > 0 and let V: ℝⁿ → ℝ be a function such that x ↦ V(x) − ρ‖x‖²/2 is convex. For V of class C² this means ∇²V(x) ≥ ρI for every x. Then Z = ∫e^(−V(x)) dx is finite, and μ(dx) = Z⁻¹e^(−V(x)) dx is a probability measure. For every continuously differentiable f: ℝⁿ → ℝ with ∫f² dμ < ∞ and ∫‖∇f‖² dμ < ∞, Ent_μ(f²) ≤ (2/ρ) ∫‖∇f‖² dμ, where Ent_μ(h) = ∫h log h dμ − ∫h dμ · log ∫h dμ.
hypotheses: The function V − ρ‖x‖²/2 is convex on ℝⁿ for a constant ρ > 0.
The function f is continuously differentiable, and f and ‖∇f‖ are square integrable under μ.

prerequisites.reason: Step s2 applies the Prékopa–Leindler inequality with weights λ and 1 − λ to the functions e^(g/λ − V), e^(−V) and e^(R_λ g − V).
Step s3 bounds g(z + h) by the second-order Taylor expansion of g with a uniform bound on the Hessian, and step s4 expands both sides to first order in 1 − λ.
Steps s5 and s6 pass to the limits δ → 0 and in the mollification with the dominated convergence theorem.
Step s6 uses Fatou's lemma to show that the entropy cannot jump up in the limit of the cutoff functions.

definitions.name: entropy functional
definitions.text: For h ≥ 0 with ∫h dμ < ∞, Ent_μ(h) = ∫h log h dμ − ∫h dμ · log ∫h dμ, with 0 log 0 = 0. Its value lies in [0, ∞].

definitions.name: ρ-uniformly convex function
definitions.text: V is ρ-uniformly convex if V − ρ‖x‖²/2 is convex. Equivalently λV(x) + (1 − λ)V(y) − V(λx + (1 − λ)y) ≥ (ρλ(1 − λ)/2)‖x − y‖² for all x, y and λ ∈ [0, 1].

definitions.name: inf-convolution bound
definitions.text: For λ ∈ (0, 1), R_λ g(z) = sup_h [g(z + h) − (ρλ/(2(1 − λ)))‖h‖²]. It is at least g(z) and tends to g(z) as λ → 1.

source.citation: Roland Bauerschmidt, Thierry Bodineau and Benoit Dagallier, Stochastic dynamics and the Polchinski equation: an introduction, arXiv:2307.07619, 2024.
source.revision: arXiv v2, dated April 23, 2024, 70 pages.
source.module: Section 2.4 Bakry–Émery theorem
source.excerpt: Theorem 2.8 (Bakry–Émery [8]). Consider a probability measure on X = R^N (or a linear subspace) of the form (2.1) and assume that there is λ > 0 such that as quadratic forms: (2.42) ∀φ ∈ X: Hess H(φ) ⩾ λ id. Then the log-Sobolev constant of ν satisfies γ ⩾ λ.
source.attribution: © Roland Bauerschmidt, Thierry Bodineau and Benoit Dagallier. Quoted from the arXiv preprint for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source treats ν ∝ e^(−H) with Hess H ≥ λ id and writes the inequality as Ent_ν(F) ≤ (2/γ)D_ν(√F), so γ ≥ λ is the authored bound with ρ = λ and f = √F. The authored statement assumes only that V − ρ‖x‖²/2 is convex and makes the class of functions explicit. The source proves the result with the Langevin semigroup and the Bakry–Émery computation (2.49). The authored proof follows instead the Prékopa–Leindler proof of Bobkov and Ledoux, which the source reference states in the same convex form.

source_references.excerpt: Lemma 2.3.2 Let V : R^M → R ∪ ∞ satisfy that for some positive constant C, V(x) − ‖x‖₂²/2C is convex. Then, the probability measure ν(dx) = Z⁻¹e^(−V(x))dx, where Z = ∫e^(−V(x))dx, satisfies the logarithmic Sobolev inequality with constant C.

source_references.alignment: This is the convex form of the criterion with C = 1/ρ, quoted by the source from Bobkov and Ledoux (2000). It allows V to take the value +∞, which the authored statement excludes. The source gives no proof at this place.

proof.scope: The full statement under the listed hypotheses.

steps.text: Preliminaries. The convex function V − ρ‖x‖²/2 lies above an affine function a·x + b, so e^(−V(x)) ≤ e^(−ρ‖x‖²/2 − a·x − b) and Z < ∞. For the quadratic q(x) = ρ‖x‖²/2 one has λq(x) + (1 − λ)q(y) − q(λx + (1 − λ)y) = (ρλ(1 − λ)/2)‖x − y‖². Convexity of V − q then gives λV(x) + (1 − λ)V(y) − V(z) ≥ (ρλ(1 − λ)/2)‖x − y‖² for z = λx + (1 − λ)y. Since x − z = (1 − λ)(x − y), the right side equals c_λ‖x − z‖² with c_λ = ρλ/(2(1 − λ)).

Prékopa–Leindler step. Let g be bounded and C² with ‖∇g‖ and ‖∇²g‖ bounded, say ‖∇²g‖ ≤ K. For λ ∈ (0, 1) set R_λ g(z) = sup_h [g(z + h) − c_λ‖h‖²]. It is a supremum of continuous functions, hence lower semicontinuous and measurable. Put u = e^(g/λ − V), v = e^(−V) and w = e^(R_λ g − V). For z = λx + (1 − λ)y, s1 gives g(x) − λV(x) − (1 − λ)V(y) ≤ g(x) − c_λ‖x − z‖² − V(z) ≤ R_λ g(z) − V(z). So w(z) ≥ u(x)^λ v(y)^(1 − λ). The Prékopa–Leindler inequality gives ∫w ≥ (∫u)^λ(∫v)^(1 − λ). After division by Z this reads ∫e^(R_λ g) dμ ≥ (∫e^(g/λ) dμ)^λ.

Bound the supremum. Taylor's theorem with ‖∇²g‖ ≤ K gives g(z + h) ≤ g(z) + ∇g(z)·h + (K/2)‖h‖² for all h. For λ close to 1, c_λ > K/2, and the maximum of ∇g(z)·h − (c_λ − K/2)‖h‖² over h is ‖∇g(z)‖²/(4c_λ − 2K). With ε = 1 − λ this gives R_λ g ≤ g + ε‖∇g‖²/(2ρλ − 2Kε), and the last fraction equals ε/(2ρ) + O(ε²) uniformly in z.

First-order expansion. Since g and ∇g are bounded, the left side of s2 is at most ∫e^g dμ + (ε/(2ρ))∫‖∇g‖²e^g dμ + O(ε²). For the right side put A(s) = ∫e^(sg) dμ, a smooth positive function of s, and Φ(λ) = exp(λ log A(1/λ)). Then Φ(1) = A(1) and Φ'(1) = A(1)[log A(1) − A'(1)/A(1)]. With λ − 1 = −ε, Φ(λ) = A(1) + ε[A'(1) − A(1) log A(1)] + O(ε²). Here A'(1) − A(1) log A(1) = ∫g e^g dμ − ∫e^g dμ · log ∫e^g dμ = Ent_μ(e^g). Comparing the two expansions, dividing by ε and letting ε → 0 gives Ent_μ(e^g) ≤ (1/(2ρ))∫‖∇g‖² e^g dμ.

Square functions. Let f be in C_c^∞ and δ > 0. The function g = log(f² + δ) is smooth, bounded, and has bounded first and second derivatives, so s4 applies. Here e^g = f² + δ and ‖∇g‖²e^g = 4f²‖∇f‖²/(f² + δ) ≤ 4‖∇f‖². So Ent_μ(f² + δ) ≤ (2/ρ)∫‖∇f‖² dμ. As δ → 0, (f² + δ) log(f² + δ) → f² log f² with a uniform bound, and dominated convergence gives Ent_μ(f²) ≤ (2/ρ)∫‖∇f‖² dμ.

General f. Let χ be smooth, χ = 1 on the unit ball, χ = 0 outside the ball of radius 2, ‖∇χ‖ ≤ 2, and f_R = χ(x/R)f. Mollifications of f_R lie in C_c^∞ in a fixed ball and converge to f_R uniformly with their gradients, so s5 holds for f_R. As R → ∞, ∇f_R = χ(x/R)∇f + R⁻¹f∇χ(x/R) → ∇f in L²(μ) and ∫f_R² dμ → ∫f² dμ by dominated convergence. Fatou's lemma applied to f_R² log f_R² + 1/e ≥ 0 gives ∫f² log f² dμ ≤ liminf ∫f_R² log f_R² dμ. Hence Ent_μ(f²) ≤ liminf Ent_μ(f_R²) ≤ (2/ρ)∫‖∇f‖² dμ.

applications.title: Uniform log-Sobolev bound for a lattice anharmonic crystal
applications.inputs: N = 100 sites of a finite graph with edge set E, a coupling J ≥ 0, and the Hamiltonian H(x) = Σ_i (x_i²/2 + x_i⁴/4) + (J/2) Σ_(ij∈E) (x_i − x_j)² on ℝ^N at temperature 1. The observable is the magnetization M = N⁻¹ Σ_i x_i, and the deviation is t = 1/2.
applications.hypotheses: H − ‖x‖²/2 = Σ_i x_i⁴/4 + (J/2)Σ (x_i − x_j)² is a sum of convex functions, so the criterion applies with ρ = 1. Its conclusion holds in particular for bounded C¹ functions with bounded gradient.

steps.text: The Hessian of H is ∇²H = diag(1 + 3x_i²) + J·L_E, where L_E is the graph Laplacian. Both diag(3x_i²) and J·L_E are positive semidefinite, so ∇²H ≥ I at every point. The criterion gives Ent(f²) ≤ 2∫‖∇f‖² dμ with C = 1, for every N and every J ≥ 0.
The magnetization M is Lipschitz with constant 1/√N, because ‖∇M‖ = (N · N⁻²)^(1/2) = N^(−1/2). The Herbst argument with C = 1 and L = N^(−1/2) gives P(|M − E M| ≥ t) ≤ 2exp(−Nt²/2).
For N = 100 and t = 1/2 the exponent is N t²/2 = 100 · (1/2)²/2 = 25/2. So the probability is at most 2e^(−12.5), about 7.5 · 10⁻⁶.
The bound does not depend on J or on the graph. A strong ferromagnetic coupling cannot create a phase transition in this model, because the uniform convexity holds at every J.

applications.conclusion: The Gibbs measure of the anharmonic crystal satisfies a logarithmic Sobolev inequality with constant 1 for every size and coupling. Its magnetization obeys P(|M − E M| ≥ t) ≤ 2exp(−Nt²/2), which is 2e^(−25/2) for N = 100 and t = 1/2.

limitations: The constant is sharp. For V = ρ‖x‖²/2 and f(x) = e^(a·x), equality holds, as in the Gaussian logarithmic Sobolev inequality.
The criterion needs uniform convexity everywhere. A double-well potential such as x⁴/4 − x²/2 is not covered, and there one uses the Holley–Stroock perturbation lemma or a multiscale method.

results.name: Holley–Stroock perturbation lemma
aliases: bounded perturbation lemma for logarithmic Sobolev inequalities
results.statement: Let μ be a probability measure on ℝⁿ and let C > 0. For a probability measure ρ and h ≥ 0 with ∫h dρ < ∞, set Ent_ρ(h) = ∫h log h dρ − ∫h dρ · log ∫h dρ. Let 𝒜 be a class of continuously differentiable functions f: ℝⁿ → ℝ with ∫f² dμ < ∞, and assume Ent_μ(f²) ≤ 2C ∫‖∇f‖² dμ for every f ∈ 𝒜. Let U: ℝⁿ → ℝ be bounded and measurable, with oscillation osc U = sup U − inf U. Define the probability measure ν by dν = Z⁻¹e^(−U) dμ with Z = ∫e^(−U) dμ. Then Ent_ν(f²) ≤ 2C e^(osc U) ∫‖∇f‖² dν for every f ∈ 𝒜.
hypotheses: The probability measure μ satisfies Ent_μ(f²) ≤ 2C∫‖∇f‖² dμ for every f in the class 𝒜.
The function U is bounded and measurable, and ν has density Z⁻¹e^(−U) with respect to μ.
results.empty_prerequisites_reason: The proof uses only the definition of the entropy, the convexity of x log x checked by calculus, and the two bounds on the density e^(−U)/Z.

definitions.name: oscillation

source.excerpt: Exercise 2.11 (Holley–Stroock criterion). Assume a measure ν satisfies the log-Sobolev inequality with constant γ. Then the measure ν^F with dν^F/dν = F satisfies a log-Sobolev inequality with constant γ^F ⩾ (inf F/sup F)γ.
source.attribution: © Roland Bauerschmidt, Thierry Bodineau and Benoit Dagallier. Quoted from the arXiv preprint for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source writes the inequality as Ent_ν(F) ≤ (2/γ)D_ν(√F) (Definition 2.3, p. 7), so its constant γ is 1/C in the authored notation. With density F = Z⁻¹e^(−U), the ratio sup F/inf F is e^(osc U), and the source bound γ^F ≥ (inf F/sup F)γ becomes the authored factor e^(osc U). The source states the result as an exercise and says that it follows from the variational formula (2.61) of Proposition 2.10. The authored proof is that argument written out.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the variational argument that the source names, from the entropy formula (2.61) of Proposition 2.10. No local formal verification.

proof.scope: The full statement, for every function of the class 𝒜 and every bounded measurable U.

steps.text: A nonnegative integrand. For t > 0 and x ≥ 0 put ψ_t(x) = x log x − x log t − x + t, with 0 log 0 = 0. On (0, ∞), ψ_t'(x) = log(x/t) and ψ_t''(x) = 1/x > 0, so ψ_t is convex with its minimum at x = t, where ψ_t(t) = 0. Also ψ_t(0) = t > 0. Hence ψ_t(x) ≥ 0 for all x ≥ 0.

Variational formula. Let ρ be a probability measure and h ≥ 0 with a = ∫h dρ < ∞. Then ∫h log h dρ is well defined in (−∞, ∞], because h log h ≥ −1/e. Integration of ψ_t(h) gives ∫ψ_t(h) dρ − Ent_ρ(h) = a log a − a log t − a + t = ψ_t(a) ≥ 0. So Ent_ρ(h) ≤ ∫ψ_t(h) dρ for every t > 0, with equality when t = a > 0.

Density bounds. Since U is bounded, Z = ∫e^(−U) dμ lies in [e^(−sup U), e^(−inf U)], so 0 < Z < ∞. The density of ν with respect to μ satisfies dν/dμ = Z⁻¹e^(−U) ≤ Z⁻¹e^(−inf U). The density of μ with respect to ν is Z e^(U) ≤ Z e^(sup U). In particular ∫f² dν ≤ Z⁻¹e^(−inf U)∫f² dμ < ∞ for f ∈ 𝒜.

Compare the entropies. Let f ∈ 𝒜 and t = ∫f² dμ. If t = 0, then f = 0 μ-almost everywhere, hence ν-almost everywhere, and Ent_ν(f²) = 0. If t > 0, s2 for ν, the bound ψ_t ≥ 0 and the first density bound of s3 give Ent_ν(f²) ≤ ∫ψ_t(f²) dν ≤ Z⁻¹e^(−inf U) ∫ψ_t(f²) dμ. By the equality case of s2 for μ, the last integral equals Ent_μ(f²).

Conclude. The hypothesis on μ and the second density bound of s3 give Ent_μ(f²) ≤ 2C∫‖∇f‖² dμ ≤ 2C Z e^(sup U) ∫‖∇f‖² dν. Combine this with s4. The factors Z cancel, and Ent_ν(f²) ≤ 2C e^(sup U − inf U) ∫‖∇f‖² dν = 2C e^(osc U) ∫‖∇f‖² dν.

applications.title: A particle in a harmonic trap with a periodic substrate potential
applications.inputs: A classical particle on the line with energy x²/2 + κ cos x at temperature 1, where κ = (log 2)/2. Its Boltzmann law is ν(dx) ∝ exp(−x²/2 − κ cos x) dx. The observable is the position X, and the deviation is r = 4.
applications.hypotheses: Take μ = N(0, 1). By Gross's inequality, μ satisfies the hypothesis with C = 1 for the class 𝒜 of C¹ functions f with f and f' in L²(μ). The perturbation U(x) = κ cos x is bounded and continuous, and ν = Z⁻¹e^(−U)μ.

steps.text: The perturbation has sup U = κ and inf U = −κ, so osc U = 2κ = log 2 and e^(osc U) = 2.
The lemma gives Ent_ν(f²) ≤ 2 · 2 ∫f'² dν for every f ∈ 𝒜. So ν satisfies the logarithmic Sobolev inequality with constant C_ν = 2.
U is even, so ν is symmetric and E_ν X = 0. The function F(x) = x is 1-Lipschitz. The Herbst argument with C_ν = 2 and L = 1 gives ν(|X| ≥ r) ≤ 2exp(−r²/(2 · 2)) = 2exp(−r²/4).
For r = 4 the exponent is 4²/(2 · 2) = 4. So ν(|X| ≥ 4) ≤ 2e^(−4), which is about 0.037.

applications.conclusion: The Boltzmann law of the trapped particle with substrate potential κ cos x, κ = (log 2)/2, satisfies a logarithmic Sobolev inequality with constant 2, and ν(|X| ≥ 4) ≤ 2e^(−4).

limitations: The factor e^(osc U) grows exponentially with the oscillation. For a sum U = Σ_i u(x_i) over N sites, osc U grows linearly in N, so the lemma is applied site by site and combined with tensorization.
The lemma moves a known inequality from μ to ν. It does not prove an inequality for μ itself, and it needs U to be bounded.

results.name: Herbst argument
results.statement: Let μ be a probability measure on ℝⁿ and let C > 0. For h ≥ 0 with ∫h dμ < ∞, set Ent_μ(h) = ∫h log h dμ − ∫h dμ · log ∫h dμ. Assume that Ent_μ(g²) ≤ 2C ∫‖∇g‖² dμ for every bounded continuously differentiable g: ℝⁿ → ℝ with bounded gradient. Let F: ℝⁿ → ℝ satisfy |F(x) − F(y)| ≤ L‖x − y‖ for all x, y, with a constant L > 0. Then F is μ-integrable, and ∫exp(λ(F − ∫F dμ)) dμ ≤ exp(Cλ²L²/2) for every λ ∈ ℝ. Consequently μ(F − ∫F dμ ≥ r) ≤ exp(−r²/(2CL²)) and μ(|F − ∫F dμ| ≥ r) ≤ 2 exp(−r²/(2CL²)) for every r ≥ 0.
hypotheses: The probability measure μ on ℝⁿ satisfies the logarithmic Sobolev inequality Ent_μ(g²) ≤ 2C∫‖∇g‖² dμ for every bounded continuously differentiable g with bounded gradient.
The function F is Lipschitz with constant L > 0 for the Euclidean norm.

source.excerpt: Lemma 2.3.3 (Herbst) Assume that P satisfies the LSI on R^M with constant c. Let G be a Lipschitz function on R^M, with Lipschitz constant |G|_L. Then for all λ ∈ R, E_P[e^(λ(G−E_P(G)))] ≤ e^(cλ²|G|_L²/2), and so for all δ > 0 P(|G − E_P(G)| ≥ δ) ≤ 2e^(−δ²/2c|G|_L²).
source.attribution: © Greg W. Anderson, Alice Guionnet and Ofer Zeitouni. Quoted from the authors' preprint of An Introduction to Random Matrices for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source assumes the inequality for every differentiable function in L²(P). The authored statement needs it only for bounded C¹ functions with bounded gradient, and it adds the one-sided tail bound. The authored proof follows the proof of the source (pp. 40-42): the differential inequality for (1/λ) log E e^(λG) in the bounded smooth case, then truncation and Gaussian mollification. For the passage to unbounded F, it uses a direct second-moment bound and Fatou's lemma in place of the uniform integrability argument of the source.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the proof of Lemma 2.3.3 in Anderson, Guionnet and Zeitouni. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement, for every Lipschitz F and every real λ and r ≥ 0.

steps.text: Bounded smooth case. Let G be bounded and continuously differentiable with ‖∇G‖ ≤ L everywhere. For λ > 0 put Z(λ) = E e^(λG). Since G is bounded, Z is smooth and Z'(λ) = E[G e^(λG)]. Apply the hypothesis to g = e^(λG/2), which is bounded with bounded gradient (λ/2)e^(λG/2)∇G. This gives Ent(e^(λG)) ≤ 2C(λ²/4)E[‖∇G‖² e^(λG)] ≤ (Cλ²L²/2) Z(λ). The left side equals λZ'(λ) − Z(λ) log Z(λ). Set K(λ) = λ⁻¹ log Z(λ). Then K'(λ) = (λZ' − Z log Z)/(λ² Z) ≤ CL²/2. As λ → 0+, K(λ) → (log Z)'(0) = E G, because log Z(0) = 0. Integration gives log E e^(λG) ≤ λ E G + Cλ²L²/2 for λ > 0. The function −G gives the case λ < 0, and λ = 0 is trivial.

Bounded Lipschitz case. Let H be bounded and L-Lipschitz. Let p_ε be the centered Gaussian density with covariance εI and set H_ε = H * p_ε. Then H_ε is smooth, bounded by sup|H|, and L-Lipschitz, since it is an average of translates of H. A differentiable L-Lipschitz function has ⟨∇H_ε(x), u⟩ = lim_(t→0) (H_ε(x + tu) − H_ε(x))/t ≤ L‖u‖ for every u, so ‖∇H_ε‖ ≤ L. Also |H_ε(x) − H(x)| ≤ L∫‖y‖p_ε(y)dy ≤ L√(nε). So s1 gives E e^(λH_ε) ≤ exp(λE H_ε + Cλ²L²/2). As ε → 0, H_ε → H uniformly with a common bound, and dominated convergence gives E e^(λH) ≤ exp(λE H + Cλ²L²/2) for every λ ∈ ℝ.

Unbounded F. Let F_k = max(−k, min(F, k)). Each F_k is bounded and L-Lipschitz, |F_k| ≤ |F|, and F_k → F pointwise. By s2 and Markov's inequality, μ(|F_k − E F_k| ≥ r) ≤ 2e^(−r²/(2CL²)) (the argument of s4). Fubini's theorem gives E(F_k − E F_k)² = ∫₀^∞ 2r μ(|F_k − E F_k| > r) dr ≤ ∫₀^∞ 4r e^(−r²/(2CL²)) dr = 4CL². Choose m with μ(|F| ≤ m) ≥ 3/4 and r₀ with 2e^(−r₀²/(2CL²)) < 1/4. For k ≥ m the events {|F_k| ≤ m} and {|F_k − E F_k| < r₀} have total probability above 1, so they meet, and |E F_k| < m + r₀. Hence sup_k E F_k² < ∞. Fatou's lemma gives E|F| ≤ liminf E|F_k| < ∞, so F is integrable, and dominated convergence with |F_k| ≤ |F| gives E F_k → E F. Fatou's lemma applied to e^(λF_k) then gives E e^(λF) ≤ liminf exp(λE F_k + Cλ²L²/2) = exp(λE F + Cλ²L²/2).

Tail bounds. For r ≥ 0 and λ > 0, Markov's inequality applied to e^(λ(F − E F)) gives μ(F − E F ≥ r) ≤ e^(−λr) E e^(λ(F − E F)) ≤ exp(−λr + Cλ²L²/2). The choice λ = r/(CL²) minimizes the exponent and gives exp(−r²/(2CL²)). The same bound for −F, which is also L-Lipschitz, controls μ(F − E F ≤ −r). The sum of the two bounds gives μ(|F − E F| ≥ r) ≤ 2exp(−r²/(2CL²)).

applications.title: Concentration of the free energy of a random field Ising model
applications.inputs: A finite graph with N = 400 vertices and edge set E, a coupling β ≥ 0, and independent standard normal fields h = (h_1, …, h_N). The free energy is F(h) = log Σ_σ exp(β Σ_(ij∈E) σ_iσ_j + Σ_i h_iσ_i), where σ runs over {−1, 1}^N. The deviation is t = 1/4 per spin.
applications.hypotheses: The law of h is the standard Gaussian measure on ℝ^N, which satisfies the logarithmic Sobolev inequality with C = 1 (Gross's inequality). Step 1 shows that F is Lipschitz with L = √N.

steps.text: F is smooth with ∂F/∂h_i = ⟨σ_i⟩, the Gibbs average of σ_i, which lies in [−1, 1]. So ‖∇F(h)‖ ≤ √N for every h. The mean value theorem along the segment from h to h' gives |F(h) − F(h')| ≤ √N ‖h − h'‖.
The Herbst argument with C = 1 and L = √N gives P(|F − E F| ≥ r) ≤ 2exp(−r²/(2N)) for every r ≥ 0. Put r = Nt to get P(|F/N − E F/N| ≥ t) ≤ 2exp(−Nt²/2).
For N = 400 and t = 1/4 the exponent is N t²/2 = 400 · (1/4)² / 2 = 25/2. So the probability is at most 2e^(−12.5), which is about 7.5 · 10⁻⁶.
The bound holds for every graph, every β and every N. It does not need any information about the phase of the model, because only the bound ‖∇F‖ ≤ √N enters.

applications.conclusion: The free energy per spin of the random field Ising model satisfies P(|F/N − E F/N| ≥ t) ≤ 2exp(−Nt²/2). For N = 400 and t = 1/4 this is at most 2e^(−25/2).

limitations: The constant in the exponent is sharp for the Gaussian measure and linear F, but the bound uses only the Lipschitz constant. It does not see a small typical gradient.
The hypothesis is a logarithmic Sobolev inequality. A Poincaré inequality alone gives only exponential, not Gaussian, tails for Lipschitz functions.

results.name: Stroock–Zegarlinski equivalence of strong mixing and the logarithmic Sobolev inequality
aliases: Equivalence of the logarithmic Sobolev inequality and the Dobrushin–Shlosman mixing condition
results.statement: Let d ≥ 1, let M be a finite set with at least two elements, let ν be the uniform probability measure on M, and let Ω = M^(ℤ^d). Use the distance d(x, y) = max_k |x_k − y_k| on ℤ^d. Let Φ = (φ_X) be a potential of finite range R: for each finite X ⊂ ℤ^d, φ_X is a function on Ω that depends only on the spins in X, φ_X = 0 when diam X > R, and ‖Φ‖ = sup_i Σ_{X∋i} ‖φ_X‖_∞ < ∞. For a finite Λ ⊂ ℤ^d and ω ∈ Ω, the local Gibbs measure is E^ω_Λ(f) = ν_Λ(e^(−U_Λ) f)/ν_Λ(e^(−U_Λ)), where U_Λ = Σ_{X∩Λ≠∅} φ_X, ν_Λ = ν^(⊗Λ) integrates the spins in Λ, and the spins outside Λ are those of ω. For a function f on Ω let Λ(f) be the smallest set of sites on which f depends, let ∇_j f(σ) = ∫ f(σ with σ_j replaced by s) dν(s) − f(σ), |∇f|² = Σ_j |∇_j f|² and |||f||| = Σ_j ‖∇_j f‖_∞, and let E^ω_Λ(f, g) = E^ω_Λ(fg) − E^ω_Λ(f)E^ω_Λ(g). Then the following three conditions are equivalent. (SM) Strong mixing: there are A, κ ∈ (0, ∞) such that |E^ω_Λ(f, g)| ≤ A e^(−κ d(Λ(f), Λ(g))) |||f||| |||g||| for every finite Λ ⊂ ℤ^d, every ω ∈ Ω and all non-constant functions f, g on Ω that depend only on the spins in Λ. (SG) Uniform spectral gap: there is m ∈ (0, ∞) such that m E^ω_Λ((f − E^ω_Λ f)²) ≤ E^ω_Λ(|∇f|²) for every finite Λ, every ω and every function f that depends on finitely many spins. (LS) Uniform logarithmic Sobolev inequality: there is c ∈ (0, ∞) such that E^ω_Λ(f log(f/E^ω_Λ f)) ≤ c E^ω_Λ(|∇f^(1/2)|²) for every finite Λ, every ω and every function f ≥ 0 that depends on finitely many spins and has E^ω_Λ f > 0, with 0 log 0 = 0.
hypotheses: The single-spin space M is a finite set with at least two elements, and ν is the uniform probability measure on M.
Φ = (φ_X) is a potential on ℤ^d of finite range R with ‖Φ‖ = sup_i Σ_{X∋i} ‖φ_X‖_∞ < ∞.

prerequisites.reason: Step s2 bounds the covariance of P_t f and P_t g by the product of their standard deviations, which the spectral gap makes small.
Step s5 gets the logarithmic Sobolev inequality of each cube measure E^ω_(X_k) from that of the product measure by the Holley-Stroock perturbation lemma.
Step s6 uses that the powers of the positive stochastic matrix Π converge to the projection onto its invariant law E^ω_Λ.

definitions.name: local Gibbs measure E^ω_Λ
definitions.text: The probability measure on the configurations that equal ω outside Λ, with density proportional to e^(−U_Λ) with respect to ν^(⊗Λ) on the spins in Λ.

definitions.name: discrete gradient ∇_j
definitions.text: ∇_j f = ν_j f − f, where ν_j f averages f over the spin at j with the measure ν and keeps the other spins fixed.

definitions.name: |||f|||
definitions.text: The semi-norm Σ_j ‖∇_j f‖_∞. The oscillation of f is at most 2|||f|||.

definitions.name: range of a potential
definitions.text: The potential Φ has range R when φ_X = 0 for every set X of diameter larger than R.

definitions.name: logarithmic Sobolev inequality
definitions.text: An inequality Ent(f) ≤ c E(|∇f^(1/2)|²) between the entropy of a function f ≥ 0 and the Dirichlet form of its square root.

source.citation: Alice Guionnet and Boguslaw Zegarlinski, Lectures on logarithmic Sobolev inequalities, Séminaire de Probabilités XXXVI, Lecture Notes in Mathematics 1801, Springer, 2002, pp. 1-134.
source.revision: Numdam digitization of Séminaire de probabilités (Strasbourg), tome 36 (2002), pp. 1-134.
source.module: Chapter 8, Section 8.3 Equivalence Theorem
source.excerpt: Theorem 8.8 The following conditions are equivalent (i) Strong mixing conditions There exists M ∈ (0, ∞) such that for any Λ ⊂⊂ ℤ^d, any ω ∈ Ω, and any local functions f and g localized in Λ, |E^ω_Λ(f, g)| ≤ e^(−M d(Λ(f), Λ(g))) |||f||| |||g||| … (iii) Uniform spectral gap inequality … (iv) Uniform logarithmic Sobolev inequality: There exists a constant c ∈ (0, ∞) such that for any Λ ⊂⊂ ℤ^d and all ω ∈ Ω, E^ω_Λ(f log(f/E^ω_Λ f)) ≤ c E^ω_Λ(|∇f^(1/2)|²) for any non negative function f …
source.attribution: © Alice Guionnet and Boguslaw Zegarlinski (Springer-Verlag, 2002). Quoted from the Numdam copy of the lecture notes for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The authored statement keeps conditions (i), (iii) and (iv) of Theorem 8.8 in the discrete setting of the notes (finite M, uniform ν, finite range), and it leaves out condition (ii), complete analyticity. Condition (SM) has a constant A in front of the exponential, as condition (SDC) (5.4.68) of the same notes, and it uses the semi-norm |||f||| = Σ_j ‖∇_j f‖_∞ of Section 5.4 and Exercise 8.1. The proof outline follows Remarks 3-5 after the theorem and the proof of the logarithmic Sobolev inequality from strong mixing in Section 5.4.

results.proof_status: outline of the cited published proof. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of Theorem 8.8 in Guionnet and Zegarlinski (2002), that is Remarks 3-5 on p. 103, Section 5.2 (pp. 54-55), Section 5.4 (pp. 64-79) and Section 8.1 (pp. 96-99). Steps s2-s6 take the exponential approximation property, Theorem 5.9, Lemmas 5.10-5.12, Theorem 5.13 and Lemma 5.5 from the source. The source proves the implication (i) ⇒ (iv) for the chain on ℤ^d and for unions of translated cubes, and it states the finite-volume form. The original proofs are in Stroock and Zegarlinski, Comm. Math. Phys. 144 (1992) 303-323 and 149 (1992) 175-193.

steps.text: (LS) implies (SG). This is Remark 3 on p. 103 of the source. Fix Λ, ω and a function g that depends on finitely many spins, and put f = (1 + εg)² for small ε > 0. The discrete gradient is linear and vanishes on constants, so ∇_j f^(1/2) = ε∇_j g. A second-order expansion of x log x gives E^ω_Λ(f log(f/E^ω_Λ f)) = 2ε² E^ω_Λ((g − E^ω_Λ g)²) + O(ε³). Divide (LS) by ε² and let ε → 0. This gives (SG) with m = 2/c.

(SG) implies (SM). This is Remark 5 on p. 103 of the source. Let P_t = e^(tL) with L = Σ_{i∈Λ}(E_i − 1), where E_i is the conditional expectation of the spin at i given the other spins under E^ω_Λ. P_t is reversible for E^ω_Λ, and E^ω_Λ(f, g) = E^ω_Λ(P_t(fg) − P_t f · P_t g) + E^ω_Λ(P_t f, P_t g). The conditional law of one spin has a density between e^(−2‖Φ‖) and e^(2‖Φ‖) with respect to ν. So E^ω_Λ|∇_i f|² ≤ e^(4‖Φ‖) E^ω_Λ((f − E_i f)²), and the spectral gap of −L is at least m' = m e^(−4‖Φ‖) (compare Exercise 5.1 of the source). The variance of f is at most (osc f)²/4 ≤ |||f|||². With the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality this gives |E^ω_Λ(P_t f, P_t g)| ≤ e^(−2m't) |||f||| |||g|||. Remark 5 bounds the first term with the exponential approximation property (Theorem 8.2 of the source, proved in (8.1.4)-(8.1.12) on pp. 96-99). For each a > 0 there is B such that ‖P_t(fg) − P_t f · P_t g‖_∞ ≤ e^(−at) |||f||| |||g||| when d(Λ(f), Λ(g)) ≥ Bt. The choice t = d(Λ(f), Λ(g))/B gives (SM).

(SM) gives control of boundary changes. Condition (SM) contains condition (SDC) (5.4.68) of the source for every finite X and every ω. Theorem 5.9 of the source (pp. 72-73) turns it into the strong mixing condition (SMC) (5.4.67): Var_Y(E_X f) ≤ C(Y) e^(−ε d(Y, Λ(f) ∩ X)) |||f||| for every cube Y ⊂ X^c, where Var_Y(F) is the largest change of F when only the spins in Y change and C(Y) depends only on the size of Y. The proof writes E^ω_X(f) − E^ω̃_X(f) = E^ω̃_X(ξ, f) with the density ξ = dE^ω_X/dE^ω̃_X. When ω and ω̃ differ only on Y, ξ depends only on the spins of X within distance R of Y, so (SDC) bounds this covariance.

(SMC) gives sweeping-out relations. For i ∉ Λ with d(i, Λ) ≤ R these are the bounds (5.4.94): (ν_i|∇_i(E_Λ f)^(1/2)|²)^(1/2) ≤ α_ii (E_Λ ν_i|∇_i f^(1/2)|²)^(1/2) + Σ_{j∈Λ∪{i}} α_ij (E_i E_Λ ν_j|∇_j f^(1/2)|²)^(1/2). Theorem 5.13 of the source (pp. 77-79) proves them for every Λ that is a union of translates of one cube, with α_ij ≤ D e^(−ε|i−j|) under (SMC). Its proof applies Lemma 5.11 (pp. 75-77) cube by cube. That lemma bounds the gradient at i of (E_Λ F)^(1/2) by the gradient of F^(1/2) at i, plus gradients at sites j ∈ Λ weighted by the influence coefficients η^(Λ)_(i,X) = Var_{Λ∩X}(E_{Λ∖X}(ξ_(i,Λ))). Here ξ_(i,Λ) is the density that removes the interaction of the spin at i. Lemma 5.12 gives the uniform spectral gap bound m_(Λ,Y) ≥ m_0 e^(−4‖Φ‖|Y|) that the lemma needs, and (SMC) gives η^(Λ)_(i,X) ≤ C e^(−ε d(i, X)). Lemma 5.10 (pp. 73-74) treats the sites at distance larger than R from the remaining volume.

Block chain. Fix L, let X_k = k + [0, 2(L + R)]^d, and split the cubes into 2^d families Γ_s whose cubes are at mutual distance larger than 2R (Section 5.4.2 of the source, pp. 65-66). Let 𝔼_s be the product of the E_(X_k) with X_k ⊂ Γ_s, and let Π = 𝔼_(2^d−1) ⋯ 𝔼_0. Each E^ω_(X_k) satisfies a logarithmic Sobolev inequality with constant c̃ ≤ c_0 e^(4‖Φ‖(2(L+R))^d), by the Holley-Stroock perturbation of the product measure ν^(⊗X_k) (Property 4.6 of the source). The product property (Theorem 4.4 of the source) passes this inequality to each 𝔼_s. Lemma 5.5 of the source (pp. 66-70) then proves with the sweeping-out relations that |∇(Πf)^(1/2)|² ≤ λ Π|∇f^(1/2)|² (5.4.46) and Π(f log f) − (Πf) log(Πf) ≤ 2c̄ Π|∇f^(1/2)|² (5.4.47), with a finite constant c̄ from Remark 5.6. By (5.4.63) the exponential decay of α_ij makes λ < 1 when L is large.

Iteration and conclusion. Put f_n = Π^n f. A telescoping sum as in (5.2.5)-(5.2.9), with (5.4.46) applied k times to the k-th term, gives (5.4.49): Π^n(f log f) − f_n log f_n ≤ (2c̄/(1 − λ)) Π^n|∇f^(1/2)|² for every n. For a finite volume Λ with boundary condition ω, the same construction uses the sets X_k ∩ Λ. Then Π is a stochastic matrix on M^Λ with positive entries and invariant law E^ω_Λ. By the Perron-Frobenius theorem Π^n F → E^ω_Λ F for every F, and n → ∞ gives (LS) with c = 2c̄/(1 − λ). This constant depends only on d, R, |M|, ‖Φ‖ and the constants of (SM). The source carries out these steps for the chain on ℤ^d (proof of (Civ), pp. 70-71). It states on p. 70 that (5.4.49) follows without the limiting Gibbs measure, and Remark 4 on p. 103 refers to these chapters for (i) ⇒ (iv). With steps s1-s5 this closes the cycle (LS) ⇒ (SG) ⇒ (SM) ⇒ (LS).

source.ref: A. Guionnet and B. Zegarlinski, Lectures on logarithmic Sobolev inequalities, Séminaire de Probabilités XXXVI (2002), Theorem 8.8 on p. 102, Remarks 3-5 on p. 103, Sections 5.2 and 5.4, pp. 54-79.

applications.title: No uniform logarithmic Sobolev inequality for the low-temperature two-dimensional Ising model
applications.inputs: The lattice ℤ² with the distance max_k |x_k − y_k|, the spin space M = {−1, 1} with uniform ν, and the nearest-neighbour Ising potential φ_{x,y}(σ) = −βσ_xσ_y for |x − y|₁ = 1, all other φ_X = 0, at β = (1/2) log 6. The boxes B(n) = {−n, …, n}², the boundary conditions + (all spins +1) and − (all spins −1), and the observable σ₀.
applications.hypotheses: M is finite and ν is uniform. Each bond {x, y} has diameter 1 in the distance max_k |x_k − y_k|, so R = 1, and ‖Φ‖ = 4β < ∞ because each site lies in 4 bonds. The Peierls argument (nm:statphys-peierls-argument) applies because x = 3e^(−2β) = 3/6 = 1/2 < 1.

steps.text: The Peierls bound gives µ⁺_{B(n)}(σ₀ = −1) ≤ δ with δ = (2/3) x⁴(4 − 3x)/(1 − x)² and x = 3e^(−2β). Here x = 3/6 = 1/2, so δ = 5/12.
So ⟨σ₀⟩⁺_{B(n)} ≥ 1 − 2δ = 1/6, and spin-flip symmetry gives ⟨σ₀⟩⁻_{B(n)} = −⟨σ₀⟩⁺_{B(n)}. Hence ⟨σ₀⟩⁺_{B(n)} − ⟨σ₀⟩⁻_{B(n)} ≥ 2(1 − 2δ) = 1/3 for every n.

One boundary flip. A site y outside B(n) with a neighbour in B(n) has exactly one such neighbour x, and there are 4(2n + 1) such sites y. Let ω and ω̃ agree except at y, with ω_y = +1 and ω̃_y = −1. Then ξ = dE^ω_{B(n)}/dE^ω̃_{B(n)} = e^(2βσ_x)/E^ω̃_{B(n)}(e^(2βσ_x)) depends only on σ_x, and E^ω(σ₀) − E^ω̃(σ₀) = E^ω̃(ξ, σ₀). Here |||σ₀||| = 1 and |||ξ||| = (e^(2β) − e^(−2β))/(2E^ω̃(e^(2βσ_x))) ≤ (e^(4β) − 1)/2 = (36 − 1)/2 = 35/2.

Suppose that (LS) holds. The theorem then gives (SM) with some A and κ. The site x lies on the boundary of B(n), so d(x, 0) = n, and one flip changes ⟨σ₀⟩ by at most A e^(−κn) · (35/2) · 1. Flip the 4(2n + 1) boundary spins from − to + one at a time. Then ⟨σ₀⟩⁺ − ⟨σ₀⟩⁻ ≤ 4(2n + 1)(35/2) A e^(−κn) = 70(2n + 1) A e^(−κn), which tends to 0 as n → ∞.
This contradicts the lower bound 1/3 of step a2 for large n. So (SM) fails, and by the theorem (SG) and (LS) fail too. No constants m and c work for all finite volumes and all boundary conditions.

applications.conclusion: For the two-dimensional Ising model at β = (1/2) log 6 there is no logarithmic Sobolev inequality and no spectral gap inequality with constants that are uniform in the finite volume and the boundary condition. The obstruction is the long-range effect of the boundary condition that the Peierls argument shows.

limitations: The conditions quantify over all finite volumes, including irregular ones. Remark 2 of the source notes that versions for van Hove sequences of regular volumes (Lu and Yau, Martinelli and Olivieri) cover a larger class of potentials.
The constants are poor: the block argument gives a log-Sobolev constant that grows like e^(4‖Φ‖(2(L+R))^d) in the block size L.
At low temperature, for example in the two-dimensional Ising model above the critical inverse temperature, strong mixing fails, so the theorem gives no uniform inequality there.

results.name: Lieb–Robinson bound
results.statement: Let Γ be a finite set with a metric d. For each x ∈ Γ let ℋ_x be a finite-dimensional Hilbert space. For Z ⊂ Γ let 𝒜_Z be the algebra of operators on ⊗_{x∈Z} ℋ_x, embedded in 𝒜_Γ. Let each H_x ∈ 𝒜_{x} be self-adjoint, and let Φ assign to each Z ⊂ Γ a self-adjoint Φ(Z) ∈ 𝒜_Z. Set H = Σ_x H_x + Σ_Z Φ(Z) and τ_t(A) = e^(itH) A e^(−itH). Let F: [0, ∞) → (0, ∞) and C > 0 satisfy Σ_{z∈Γ} F(d(x, z)) F(d(z, y)) ≤ C F(d(x, y)) for all x, y ∈ Γ, and set ‖Φ‖ = max_{x,y∈Γ} Σ_{Z∋x,y} ‖Φ(Z)‖ / F(d(x, y)). Let S(X) be the set of Z ⊂ Γ that meet both X and Γ∖X, and let ∂_Φ X be the set of x ∈ X that lie in some Z ∈ S(X) with Φ(Z) ≠ 0. Let X, Y ⊂ Γ be disjoint and nonempty, A ∈ 𝒜_X and B ∈ 𝒜_Y. Then for all t ∈ ℝ, ‖[τ_t(A), B]‖ ≤ (2‖A‖‖B‖/C)(e^(2C‖Φ‖|t|) − 1) D(X, Y), where D(X, Y) = min(Σ_{x∈∂_Φ X} Σ_{y∈Y} F(d(x, y)), Σ_{x∈X} Σ_{y∈∂_Φ Y} F(d(x, y))).
hypotheses: Γ is a finite set with a metric d, and each site x carries a finite-dimensional Hilbert space ℋ_x.
Each on-site term H_x is self-adjoint in 𝒜_{x}, and each interaction term Φ(Z) is self-adjoint in 𝒜_Z.
F: [0, ∞) → (0, ∞) and C > 0 satisfy Σ_z F(d(x, z)) F(d(z, y)) ≤ C F(d(x, y)) for all x, y ∈ Γ.
X and Y are disjoint nonempty subsets of Γ, A ∈ 𝒜_X and B ∈ 𝒜_Y.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 rewrites the time derivative of the commutator [W(t), B] with the Jacobi identity for commutators.

definitions.name: interaction
definitions.text: A map Φ that assigns to each subset Z of Γ a self-adjoint operator Φ(Z) that acts only on the sites of Z.

definitions.name: Heisenberg dynamics
definitions.text: The family of maps τ_t(A) = e^(itH) A e^(−itH), t ∈ ℝ, generated by the Hamiltonian H.

definitions.name: Φ-boundary
definitions.text: ∂_Φ X is the set of points x ∈ X that lie in some Z with Φ(Z) ≠ 0 that meets both X and its complement.

definitions.name: Lieb–Robinson velocity
definitions.text: A speed v such that ‖[τ_t(A), B]‖ is exponentially small in d(X, Y) − v|t|. The theorem with F_μ(r) = e^(−μr)F(r) gives v ≤ 2C_μ‖Φ‖_μ/μ.

source.citation: Bruno Nachtergaele and Robert Sims, Lieb-Robinson bounds in quantum many-body physics, in: Entropy and the Quantum, Contemporary Mathematics 529, American Mathematical Society, 2010, pp. 141-176.
source.module: Section 2, Section 2.1 Bounded Interactions
source.excerpt: Theorem 2.3. Let Γ be a finite set and fix a collection of local Hamiltonians {Hx}x∈Γ and an interaction Φ over Γ. Let X and Y be subsets of Γ with d(X, Y) > 0 and take any set Λ ⊃ X ∪ Y. For any pair of local observables A ∈ AX and B ∈ AY, the estimate ‖[τtΛ(A), B]‖ ≤ (2‖A‖‖B‖/C)(e^(2C‖Φ‖|t|) − 1) D(X, Y), holds for all t ∈ ℝ.
source.attribution: © Bruno Nachtergaele and Robert Sims. Quoted from the authors' lecture notes on arXiv for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source allows unbounded on-site Hamiltonians and a finite volume Λ inside Γ. The authored statement takes finite-dimensional sites and Λ = Γ, which is the same theorem for the restricted system. It writes out the sets S(X), ∂_Φ X and D(X, Y) that the source defines in (2.9), (2.10) and (2.12). The authored proof follows the proof of the source on pp. 5-7, with the interaction picture, the norm-preserving Lemma 2.4 and the iteration (2.30)-(2.35).

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the iteration proof of Theorem 2.3 in Nachtergaele and Sims. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement for all real t, with both terms of the minimum in D(X, Y).

steps.text: Fix A ∈ 𝒜_X. Let G = Σ_{x∈Γ} H_x + Σ_{Z⊂X} Φ(Z) and σ_t(A) = e^(itG) A e^(−itG). The part of G in 𝒜_X commutes with Σ_{x∉X} H_x, which lies in 𝒜_{Γ∖X}. So σ_t maps 𝒜_X onto 𝒜_X and keeps the norm. The difference H − G equals Σ_{Z∈S(X)} Φ(Z) + Σ_{Z⊂Γ∖X} Φ(Z), and the last sum commutes with 𝒜_X. Set W(t) = τ_t(σ_{−t}(A)), K(t) = Σ_{Z∈S(X)} τ_t(Φ(Z)) and f(t) = [W(t), B]. Differentiation gives W′(t) = i τ_t([H − G, σ_{−t}(A)]) = i[K(t), W(t)]. The Jacobi identity in the form [[P, W], B] = [P, [W, B]] − [W, [P, B]] gives f′(t) = i[K(t), f(t)] − i Σ_{Z∈S(X)} [W(t), [τ_t(Φ(Z)), B]].

K(t) is self-adjoint and continuous in t. Let U(t) solve U′ = iK(t)U with U(0) = 1. Then (U*U)′ = −iU*KU + iU*KU = 0, so U(t) is unitary. Put g(t) = U(t)* f(t) U(t). Then g′ = U*(f′ − i[K, f])U = −i Σ_{Z∈S(X)} U*[W, [τ_t(Φ(Z)), B]]U. Here ‖g(t)‖ = ‖f(t)‖, g(0) = [A, B] and ‖W(s)‖ = ‖A‖. Integration from 0 to t ≥ 0 gives ‖f(t)‖ ≤ ‖[A, B]‖ + 2‖A‖ Σ_{Z∈S(X)} ∫_0^t ‖[τ_s(Φ(Z)), B]‖ ds.

For Z ⊂ Γ and t ≥ 0 let C_B(Z, t) be the supremum of ‖[τ_t(A′), B]‖/‖A′‖ over nonzero A′ ∈ 𝒜_Z. Then C_B(Z, t) ≤ 2‖B‖. Also C_B(Z, 0) ≤ 2‖B‖δ_Y(Z), where δ_Y(Z) = 1 if Z meets Y and 0 otherwise, because 𝒜_Z commutes with 𝒜_Y when Z ∩ Y = ∅. Since σ_{−t} is a norm-preserving bijection of 𝒜_X, the supremum of ‖f(t)‖/‖A‖ over A equals C_B(X, t). With ‖[τ_s(Φ(Z)), B]‖ ≤ ‖Φ(Z)‖ C_B(Z, s), step s2 gives C_B(X, t) ≤ C_B(X, 0) + 2 Σ_{Z∈S(X)} ‖Φ(Z)‖ ∫_0^t C_B(Z, s) ds. The derivation holds for every nonempty X ⊂ Γ, not only for the set of the theorem.

Insert the inequality of step s3 into itself n times, for sets Z₁ ∈ S(X), Z₂ ∈ S(Z₁), and so on. The integrals over 0 ≤ s_k ≤ … ≤ s₁ ≤ t give the factors t^k/k!. Use C_B(Z, 0) ≤ 2‖B‖δ_Y(Z) for the initial terms and C_B ≤ 2‖B‖ in the remainder. With N = Σ_{Z⊂Γ} ‖Φ(Z)‖ < ∞ this gives C_B(X, t) ≤ 2‖B‖ Σ_{k=0}^{n} (2t)^k a_k/k! + 2‖B‖(2Nt)^(n+1)/(n+1)!, where a_0 = δ_Y(X) = 0 and a_k = Σ_{Z₁∈S(X)} Σ_{Z₂∈S(Z₁)} … Σ_{Z_k∈S(Z_{k−1})} δ_Y(Z_k) ∏_{i=1}^k ‖Φ(Z_i)‖. The remainder tends to 0 as n → ∞. So C_B(X, t) ≤ 2‖B‖ Σ_{k≥1} (2t)^k a_k/k!.

Bound a_k. A term of a_k is nonzero only if every Φ(Z_i) ≠ 0 and Z_k meets Y. Then Z₁ contains a point x ∈ ∂_Φ X, because every point of Z₁ ∩ X has the defining property. Consecutive sets meet, so there are points z_i ∈ Z_i ∩ Z_{i+1} for i < k, and Z_k contains a point y ∈ Y. Put z_0 = x and z_k = y. All terms are nonnegative. So if we drop the constraints Z_{i+1} ∈ S(Z_i) and sum over all such points, we get a_k ≤ Σ_{x∈∂_Φ X} Σ_{y∈Y} Σ_{z₁,…,z_{k−1}∈Γ} ∏_{i=1}^k Σ_{Z∋z_{i−1},z_i} ‖Φ(Z)‖. Each inner sum is at most ‖Φ‖F(d(z_{i−1}, z_i)) by the definition of ‖Φ‖. Sum over z₁, then z₂, up to z_{k−1}, with the convolution bound each time. This gives a_k ≤ ‖Φ‖^k C^(k−1) Σ_{x∈∂_Φ X} Σ_{y∈Y} F(d(x, y)).

Insert step s5 into step s4: C_B(X, t) ≤ (2‖B‖/C) Σ_{k≥1} (2C‖Φ‖t)^k/k! · Σ_{x∈∂_Φ X} Σ_{y∈Y} F(d(x, y)), and the series equals e^(2C‖Φ‖t) − 1. Multiply by ‖A‖. For t < 0, apply the result to −H. Its interaction −Φ has the same norm and the same boundary sets, and its dynamics at time −t is τ_t. For the second sum in D(X, Y), note that ‖[τ_t(A), B]‖ = ‖τ_{−t}([τ_t(A), B])‖ = ‖[τ_{−t}(B), A]‖. Apply the bound with the roles of (X, A) and (Y, B) exchanged and with time −t. Since d is symmetric, this gives the second sum. So the smaller of the two bounds holds.

applications.title: Light cone of the spin-1/2 Heisenberg chain
applications.inputs: A chain Γ = {1, …, L} ⊂ ℤ with d(x, y) = |x − y|, sites ℂ², H_x = 0 and Φ({x, x+1}) = J S_x·S_{x+1} with J > 0. The decay function is F_μ(r) = e^(−μr)(1 + r)^(−2) with μ = 1. A ∈ 𝒜_{x} and B ∈ 𝒜_{y} with |x − y| = r ≥ 1.
applications.hypotheses: The sites are finite-dimensional and every bond term is self-adjoint. Step a2 shows that C = 24 is a valid convolution constant for F_μ. The supports {x} and {y} are disjoint.

steps.text: Each bond term has norm (3/4)J, because S_x·S_{x+1} has eigenvalue 1/4 on the triplet and −3/4 on the singlet. A pair at distance 1 lies in one bond, and one site lies in at most two bonds. So ‖Φ‖_μ = max(3J/2, (3J/4)/F_μ(1)) = max(3J/2, 3Je^μ) = 3Je^μ.

Here ∂_Φ{x} ⊂ {x}, so D({x}, {y}) ≤ e^(−r)(1 + r)^(−2). With μ = 1 the exponent is 2C‖Φ‖_1|t| = 2 · 24 · 3eJ|t| = 144eJ|t|. The theorem gives ‖[τ_t(A), B]‖ ≤ (‖A‖‖B‖/12)(e^(144eJ|t|) − 1) e^(−r)(1 + r)^(−2).
Take A = S^z_x and B = S^z_y, both of norm 1/2, at distance r = 10. The prefactor is (1/2)(1/2)/12 · (1 + 10)^(−2) = 1/5808. So ‖[τ_t(S^z_x), S^z_y]‖ ≤ (1/5808)(e^(144eJ|t|) − 1)e^(−10).
The bound is less than (‖A‖‖B‖/12) e^(−(r − v|t|)) with v = 144eJ. So a signal from x reaches y only after a time of order r/v, for every chain length L.

applications.conclusion: For one-site observables at distance r in the spin-1/2 Heisenberg chain, ‖[τ_t(A), B]‖ ≤ (‖A‖‖B‖/12)(e^(144eJ|t|) − 1)e^(−r)(1 + r)^(−2), uniformly in L. The Lieb–Robinson velocity is at most 144eJ.

limitations: The constants are far from sharp. For the Heisenberg chain the true speed of propagation is of order J, not 144eJ.
The theorem needs bounded interaction terms. Lattices of coupled oscillators have unbounded terms and need separate arguments.
The bound says nothing inside the light cone, where the commutator can be of order ‖A‖‖B‖.

results.name: Exponential clustering theorem
aliases: Exponential clustering theorem for gapped ground states
Gap implies exponential decay of correlations
results.statement: Let V be a finite set with a metric d. At each x ∈ V let ℋ_x be a Hilbert space of dimension at most N, and for X ⊂ V let ℋ_X = ⊗_{x∈X} ℋ_x and 𝒜_X = B(ℋ_X). Let Φ assign to each X ⊂ V a self-adjoint Φ(X) ∈ 𝒜_X, let H = Σ_{X⊂V} Φ(X), and let τ_z(B) = e^(izH) B e^(−izH) for z ∈ ℂ. For λ > 0 put D(X) = max_{x,y∈X} d(x, y) and ‖Φ‖_λ = max_{x∈V} Σ_{X∋x} |X| ‖Φ(X)‖ N^(2|X|) e^(λD(X)). Suppose that H has at least two eigenvalues. Let E₀ be the lowest eigenvalue, P₀ the projection onto its eigenspace, γ > 0 the distance from E₀ to the rest of the spectrum, and Ω a unit vector with HΩ = E₀Ω. Let x ∈ V and Y ⊂ V with x ∉ Y, let d(x, Y) = min_{y∈Y} d(x, y), and put μ = γλ/(4‖Φ‖_λ + γ). Then for all A ∈ 𝒜_{x} and B ∈ 𝒜_Y with P₀BΩ = P₀B*Ω = 0, and for all b with 0 ≤ γb ≤ 2μd(x, Y), |⟨Ω, A τ_(ib)(B) Ω⟩| ≤ ‖A‖ ‖B‖ (1 + 2|Y|/π + 1/√(πμd(x, Y))) e^(−μd(x, Y)(1 + γ²b²/(4μ²d(x, Y)²))). In particular, if E₀ is a simple eigenvalue, then |⟨Ω, ABΩ⟩ − ⟨Ω, AΩ⟩⟨Ω, BΩ⟩| ≤ ‖A‖ ‖B − ⟨Ω, BΩ⟩1‖ (1 + 2|Y|/π + 1/√(πμd(x, Y))) e^(−μd(x, Y)) for all A ∈ 𝒜_{x} and B ∈ 𝒜_Y.
hypotheses: V is a finite metric space with local Hilbert spaces of dimension at most N, and H = Σ_X Φ(X) with self-adjoint Φ(X) ∈ 𝒜_X.
The lowest eigenvalue E₀ of H is separated from the rest of the spectrum by a gap γ > 0, and Ω is a ground state vector.
A acts at the site x, B acts on Y with x ∉ Y, and P₀BΩ = P₀B*Ω = 0.

prerequisites.reason: Steps s1 and s4 write the correlation as an integral against the spectral measure of H, which lives on [γ, ∞).
Step s2 writes f(ib) as a contour integral over the boundary of the upper half disc with Cauchy's integral formula.
Step s2 removes the semicircle and step s4 removes the remainders of Lemma 1 with the dominated convergence theorem.
Step s5 bounds the commutator ‖[A, τ_t(B)]‖ for |t| ≤ s with a Lieb-Robinson bound of the form (7) of the source.

definitions.name: spectral gap
definitions.text: The distance γ between the lowest eigenvalue E₀ of H and the next point of the spectrum of H.

definitions.name: ‖Φ‖_λ
definitions.text: The interaction norm max_x Σ_{X∋x} |X| ‖Φ(X)‖ N^(2|X|) e^(λD(X)), which weights each term by its size and its diameter.

definitions.name: τ_(ib)(B)
definitions.text: The imaginary-time evolution e^(−bH) B e^(bH) of B. For b = 0 it is B itself.

source.citation: Bruno Nachtergaele and Robert Sims, Lieb-Robinson bounds and the exponential clustering theorem, Communications in Mathematical Physics 265 (2006), 119-130.
source.revision: arXiv:math-ph/0506030v3, 2 September 2005.
source.module: Section 2 Main Results
source.excerpt: Theorem 2 (Exponential Clustering) There exists µ > 0 such that for all A ∈ Ax , B ∈ AY , x ∉ Y , for which P0 BΩ = P0 B∗ Ω = 0, and b sufficiently small, there is a constant c(A, B) such that
source.attribution: © 2005 Bruno Nachtergaele and Robert Sims. Quoted from the authors' arXiv version of the paper for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source proves Theorem 2 in a representation with H ≥ 0, HΩ = 0 and a gap γ, with the constants (11) and (12) and the range 0 ≤ γb ≤ 2μd(x, Y). The authored statement is the case of a finite system, where the representation is the defining one and H is shifted by E₀. The connected correlation bound is the source's remark (13), with the norm of B − ⟨Ω, BΩ⟩1 written explicitly.

results.proof_status: outline of the cited published proof. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of Theorem 2 in Nachtergaele and Sims (2006), Section 3.2, pp. 7-10. Step s4 takes the Gaussian contour limit from Lemma 1 of the source, and step s5 takes the Lieb-Robinson estimate (7) from Theorem 1 of the source. The parameter choice in step s6 is the one of eq. (47).

steps.text: Spectral form of the correlation. Replace H by H − E₀. This does not change τ_z, and now H ≥ 0 and HΩ = 0. Then f(z) = ⟨Ω, Aτ_z(B)Ω⟩ = ⟨A*Ω, e^(izH)BΩ⟩ = ∫ e^(izE) dμ_(A,B)(E), with the complex spectral measure μ_(A,B)(·) = ⟨A*Ω, P(·)BΩ⟩ of total variation at most ‖A‖ ‖B‖. Because P₀BΩ = 0, this measure lives on [γ, ∞). So f is entire, and |f(z)| ≤ ‖A‖ ‖B‖ e^(−γ Im z) for Im z ≥ 0. The value of interest is f(ib).

Contour integral. For 0 < b < T, Cauchy's formula on the boundary of the upper half disc of radius T gives f(ib) = (1/2πi)∮ f(z)/(z − ib) dz (eq. (29) of the source). On the semicircle z = Te^(iθ) the bound of step s1 gives |f(z)| ≤ ‖A‖ ‖B‖ e^(−Tγ sin θ) (eq. (30)), so that part is at most (T/(T − b))(‖A‖ ‖B‖/2π)∫_0^π e^(−Tγ sin θ) dθ, which tends to 0 by dominated convergence. So f(ib) = lim_(T→∞) (1/2πi)∫_(−T)^T f(t)/(t − ib) dt (eq. (32)). The case b = 0 follows at the end by continuity of f.

Gaussian cut-off. Fix α > 0 and write f(t)e^(αb²) = f(t)e^(−αt²) + f(t)(e^(αb²) − e^(−αt²)) and f(t)e^(−αt²) = ⟨Ω, τ_t(B)AΩ⟩e^(−αt²) + ⟨Ω, [A, τ_t(B)]Ω⟩e^(−αt²) (eqs. (33)-(34)). So e^(αb²)|f(ib)| ≤ lim sup (I + II + III), where I contains ⟨Ω, τ_t(B)AΩ⟩, II contains the commutator, and III contains the factor e^(αb²) − e^(−αt²).

The two spectral terms. Lemma 1 of the source (p. 9) proves lim_(T→∞)(1/2πi)∫_(−T)^T e^(iEt)e^(−αt²)/(t − z) dt = (1/(2√(πα)))∫_0^∞ e^(iwz) e^(−(w−E)²/(4α)) dw, uniformly in Im z > 0. For I the spectral variable enters as e^(−iEt) with E ≥ γ, because P₀B*Ω = 0. The Gaussian tail then gives lim sup I ≤ (1/2)‖A‖ ‖B‖ e^(−γ²/(4α)) (eq. (39)). For III the Fourier identity e^(iEt)e^(−αt²) = (1/(2√(πα)))∫ e^(iwt)e^(−(w−E)²/(4α)) dw at t = ib leaves only the part w < 0. Completing the square shows that this part is at most (1/2)e^(−E²/(4α)) when 2αb ≤ γ ≤ E. So lim sup III ≤ (1/2)‖A‖ ‖B‖ e^(−γ²/(4α)) (eqs. (45)-(46)).

The commutator term. Since b ≥ 0, |t − ib| ≥ |t|, so II ≤ (1/2π)∫ ‖[A, τ_t(B)]‖ e^(−αt²)/|t| dt (eq. (40)). Split at |t| = s. For |t| ≤ s use the Lieb-Robinson bound ‖[A, τ_t(B)]‖ ≤ 2|Y| ‖A‖ ‖B‖ (e^(2|t|‖Φ‖_λ) − 1) e^(−λd(x, Y)), which Theorem 1 of the source proves as eq. (7), together with ∫_0^s (e^(ct) − 1)/t dt ≤ e^(cs). For |t| ≥ s use ‖[A, τ_t(B)]‖ ≤ 2‖A‖ ‖B‖ and the Gaussian tail. This gives II ≤ (2|Y|/π)‖A‖ ‖B‖ e^(2s‖Φ‖_λ − λd(x, Y)) + ‖A‖ ‖B‖ e^(−αs²)/(s√(πα)) (eq. (41)).

Choice of the parameters. Take α = γ/(2s) and choose s with s(2‖Φ‖_λ + γ/2) = λd(x, Y) (eq. (47)), so s = 2μd(x, Y)/γ. Then γ²/(4α) = αs² = λd(x, Y) − 2s‖Φ‖_λ = γs/2 = μd(x, Y), and s√(πα) = √(πμd(x, Y)). The condition 2αb ≤ γ becomes γb ≤ 2μd(x, Y), and αb² = γ²b²/(4μd(x, Y)). Adding the bounds of steps s4 and s5 and dividing by e^(αb²) gives the stated estimate. For a simple E₀ the condition P₀BΩ = P₀B*Ω = 0 holds for B − ⟨Ω, BΩ⟩1, and b = 0 gives the connected correlation bound.

source.ref: B. Nachtergaele and R. Sims, Lieb-Robinson bounds and the exponential clustering theorem, Comm. Math. Phys. 265 (2006), arXiv:math-ph/0506030v3, Theorem 2 on p. 4 and its proof in Section 3.2, pp. 7-10.

applications.title: Correlation decay in the transverse-field Ising chain
applications.inputs: The open chain V = {1, …, 2000} with d(x, y) = |x − y| and spin 1/2 at each site, so N = 2. H = −h Σ_x σ^z_x − J Σ_x σ^x_x σ^x_(x+1) with h = 1 and J = 1/16. Take λ = ln 2, A = σ^z_100 and B = σ^z_1430 − ⟨Ω, σ^z_1430 Ω⟩1, so d(x, Y) = 1330.
applications.hypotheses: The Jordan-Wigner transformation maps H to free fermions whose mode energies are the singular values of 2(hI − JS), with S the shift matrix. They are at least 2(h − J) > 0, so the ground state is unique and the gap is γ ≥ 2(h − J). The bound holds with any smaller positive value in place of γ. A acts at x = 100, B acts on Y = {1430}, and ⟨Ω, BΩ⟩ = 0, so P₀BΩ = P₀B*Ω = 0.

steps.text: The sets that contain an inner site x are {x} with |X| = 1, ‖Φ‖ = h, D = 0 and two bonds with |X| = 2, ‖Φ‖ = J, D = 1. So ‖Φ‖_λ = 4h + 2 · 2 · 16 · J e^λ = 4 + 64 · (1/16) · 2 = 12.
The gap satisfies γ ≥ 2(h − J) = 2(1 − 1/16) = 15/8. Use γ = 15/8 in the theorem.
At distance 1330 the exponent is μ · 1330 = 50 ln 2, so e^(−μd(x, Y)) = 2^(−50).
The prefactor is ‖A‖ ‖B‖ (1 + 2/π + 1/√(50π ln 2)) ≤ 1 · 2 · 2 = 4, because ‖B‖ ≤ 2, 2/π < 0.64 and √(50π ln 2) > 10. So the connected correlation is at most 4 · 2^(−50) = 2^(−48).

applications.conclusion: In the ground state of the chain, |⟨σ^z_100 σ^z_1430⟩ − ⟨σ^z_100⟩⟨σ^z_1430⟩| ≤ 2^(−48). The theorem gives the correlation length bound 1/μ = 133/(5 ln 2), about 38 sites, from the gap and the interaction norm only.

limitations: The rate μ = γλ/(4‖Φ‖_λ + γ) is far from optimal in many models, and the bound gives nothing when the gap closes in the limit of large systems.
The converse is false: there are models with a unique ground state and exponential decay of correlations but no spectral gap.
With a degenerate ground state the condition P₀BΩ = 0 is a real restriction, and the theorem then controls ⟨Ω, ABΩ⟩ only for such B.
