results.name: Ben Arous–Guionnet large deviation principle for the empirical spectral measure
aliases: large deviations for the empirical measure of β-ensembles
results.statement: Let β > 0 and let V: ℝ → ℝ be continuous with lim inf_(|x|→∞) V(x)/(β′ log|x|) > 1 for some β′ > 1 with β′ ≥ β. Let (λ_1, …, λ_N) have the law P^N(dλ) = (Z^N)⁻¹ ∏_(i<j) |λ_i − λ_j|^β e^(−N Σ_i V(λ_i)) ∏_i dλ_i, and let L_N = N⁻¹ Σ_i δ_(λ_i). For a probability measure μ on ℝ let Σ(μ) = ∫∫ log|x − y| μ(dx) μ(dy) if ∫ log(|x| + 1) μ(dx) < ∞ and Σ(μ) = −∞ otherwise. Let c = inf_ν (∫ V dν − (β/2) Σ(ν)), and let I(μ) = ∫ V dμ − (β/2) Σ(μ) − c if ∫ V dμ < ∞ and I(μ) = ∞ otherwise. Then c is finite and I is a good rate function with values in [0, ∞]. The laws of L_N on the space of probability measures with the weak topology satisfy a large deviation principle with speed N² and rate function I: lim inf N⁻² log P^N(L_N ∈ O) ≥ −inf_O I for every open set O, and lim sup N⁻² log P^N(L_N ∈ F) ≤ −inf_F I for every closed set F.
hypotheses: V is continuous and lim inf_(|x|→∞) V(x)/(β′ log|x|) > 1 for some β′ > 1 with β′ ≥ β.
The points λ_1, …, λ_N have the joint density proportional to ∏_(i<j) |λ_i − λ_j|^β e^(−N Σ_i V(λ_i)).

prerequisites.reason: Step s2 shows that the level sets of I are tight, and Prokhorov's theorem makes the closed tight level sets compact.
Step s3 bounds log Z^N from below by −CN² with Jensen's inequality for a product reference measure.
Steps s4 and s5 remove the truncation f ∧ M and the truncation of μ to [−M, M] with the monotone convergence theorem.
Step s1 explains that Varadhan's lemma would give the result if the energy functional were bounded and continuous, which the proof replaces by direct estimates.

definitions.name: β-ensemble
definitions.text: The law P^N of N real points with density proportional to ∏_(i<j) |λ_i − λ_j|^β e^(−N Σ V(λ_i)). For V(x) = x²/4 and β = 1 or β = 2 it is the law of the rescaled eigenvalues of the GOE or the GUE.

definitions.name: logarithmic energy
definitions.text: Σ(μ) = ∫∫ log|x − y| μ(dx) μ(dy), the noncommutative entropy of μ in the source. The rate function is the energy ∫ V dμ − (β/2) Σ(μ) of a continuous charge distribution, minus its minimum c.

definitions.name: good rate function
definitions.text: A function I with values in [0, ∞] whose level sets {I ≤ M} are compact for every M.

source.citation: Greg W. Anderson, Alice Guionnet and Ofer Zeitouni, An Introduction to Random Matrices, Cambridge Studies in Advanced Mathematics 118, Cambridge University Press, 2010.
source.revision: Authors' preprint of the Cambridge University Press book (PDF created 2009-08-27), 506 pages.
source.module: Chapter 2, Section 2.6.1 Large deviations for the empirical measure
source.excerpt: Theorem 2.6.1 Let L_N = N⁻¹ ∑ δ_(λ_i^N) where the random variables {λ_i^N} are distributed according to the law P^N_(V,β) of (2.6.1) … Then, the family of random measures L_N satisfies, in M_1(ℝ) equipped with the weak topology, a large deviation principle with speed N² and good rate function I^V_β.
source.attribution: © Greg W. Anderson, Alice Guionnet and Ofer Zeitouni. Quoted from the authors' preprint of An Introduction to Random Matrices for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The authored statement writes out the law (2.6.1), the growth condition (2.6.2), the entropy (2.6.4), the rate function (2.6.5) and the constant (2.6.6) of the source. The excerpt omits the reference to the growth condition (2.6.2), which the authored statement states. The source attributes the result to Ben Arous and Guionnet (1997). The outline follows the proof of Theorem 2.6.1 in the source and cites Lemma 2.6.2 of the source for the properties of the rate function.

results.proof_status: outline of the cited published proof. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of Theorem 2.6.1 in Anderson, Guionnet and Zeitouni (2010), Section 2.6.1, which presents the proof of Ben Arous and Guionnet (1997). Step s2 cites Lemma 2.6.2 of the source for the properties of I. Step s6 cites Appendix D of the source for the passage from a weak large deviation principle and exponential tightness to the full principle.

steps.text: Energy form of the density. Put f(x, y) = V(x)/2 + V(y)/2 − (β/2) log|x − y|. Then Σ_(i≠j) f(λ_i, λ_j) = (N − 1) Σ_i V(λ_i) − β Σ_(i<j) log|λ_i − λ_j|. So P^N(dλ) = (Z^N)⁻¹ exp(−N² ∫∫_(x≠y) f dL_N dL_N) ∏_i e^(−V(λ_i)) dλ_i. If μ ↦ ∫∫ f dμ dμ were bounded and continuous, Varadhan's lemma would give the result at once. The proof must handle the singularity of f on the diagonal and its growth at infinity.

The rate function. Lemma 2.6.2 of the source proves these facts. From log|x − y| ≤ log(|x| + 1) + log(|y| + 1) and the growth condition, f is bounded below by a constant b_f and f → ∞ at infinity and near the diagonal, so c is finite and I ≥ 0. I(μ) + c = sup_M ∫∫ (f ∧ M) dμ dμ is a supremum of continuous functions, so I is lower semicontinuous. The bound μ(|x| > L)² ≤ (I(μ) + c − b_f)/(K′(L) − b_f), with K′(L) → ∞, makes each level set tight, hence compact by Prokhorov's theorem. A Fourier formula for Σ(μ − ν) shows that Σ is strictly concave, so I has a unique minimizer σ_V.

Exponential tightness. Jensen's inequality with respect to the product of the probability densities e^(−V)/∫ e^(−V) gives log Z^N ≥ −CN². The growth condition gives constants a > 0 and c′ with f(x, y) ≥ a|V(x)| + a|V(y)| + c′. Together these give the source bound (2.6.21): P^N(∫ |V| dL_N ≥ M) ≤ e^(−2aN²M + (C − c′)N²) (∫ e^(−V(x)) dx)^N. The set {μ : ∫ |V| dμ ≤ M} is compact because V → ∞ at infinity, so the laws of L_N are exponentially tight at speed N².

Upper bound on small balls. Let P̄^N = Z^N P^N and d the bounded Lipschitz metric. The points are almost surely distinct, so ∫∫ (f ∧ M) dL_N dL_N = ∫∫_(x≠y) (f ∧ M) dL_N dL_N + M/N. Hence P̄^N(d(L_N, μ) ≤ ε) ≤ e^(MN) ∫_(d(L_N, μ) ≤ ε) exp(−N² ∫∫ (f ∧ M) dL_N dL_N) ∏ e^(−V(λ_i)) dλ_i. Since f ∧ M is bounded and continuous, this gives lim_(ε→0) lim sup N⁻² log P̄^N(d(L_N, μ) ≤ ε) ≤ −∫∫ (f ∧ M) dμ dμ. The limit M → ∞ and monotone convergence give the bound −∫∫ f dμ dμ, which is (2.6.22). The same argument gives lim sup N⁻² log Z^N ≤ −c, which is (2.6.23).

Lower bound on small balls. It is enough to treat μ with I(μ) < ∞, so μ has no atoms. Truncation to [−M, M] and monotone convergence reduce the bound to compactly supported μ. Let x_(1,N) < ⋯ < x_(N,N) be the quantiles of μ at spacing 1/(N + 1). For large N the event {|λ_i − x_(i,N)| < δ/2 for all i} lies in {d(L_N, μ) < δ}. On this event, for ordered points, |x_(i,N) − x_(j,N) + λ_i − λ_j| ≥ max(|x_(i,N) − x_(j,N)|, |λ_i − λ_j|). This splits the integral into P_(N,1) × P_(N,2) as in (2.6.25). The source bounds the volume factor P_(N,2) below by (δ/((β + 2)N))^(N(β/2 + 1)) times e^(−N² η(δ)), where η(δ) → 0 by the continuity of V, so (2.6.26) gives lim_(δ→0) lim inf N⁻² log P_(N,2) ≥ 0. Riemann sums give N⁻¹ Σ V(x_(i,N)) → ∫ V dμ, and the monotonicity of log gives lim inf N⁻² log P_(N,1) ≥ β ∫∫_(x<y) log(y − x) dμ dμ − ∫ V dμ = −∫∫ f dμ dμ. This is (2.6.24).

Conclusion. The lower bound of step s5 for every μ and the upper bound (2.6.23) give lim N⁻² log Z^N = −inf_μ ∫∫ f dμ dμ = −c. Division by Z^N turns (2.6.22) and (2.6.24) into the weak principle (2.6.28): lim_(ε→0) lim N⁻² log P^N(d(L_N, μ) ≤ ε) = −∫∫ f dμ dμ + c = −I(μ). Appendix D of the source (Corollary D.6) shows that a weak large deviation principle together with exponential tightness from step s3 gives the full principle with a good rate function.

source.ref: G. W. Anderson, A. Guionnet and O. Zeitouni, An Introduction to Random Matrices (Cambridge University Press 2010), Theorem 2.6.1 with Lemma 2.6.2, Section 2.6.1, pp. 71-80.

applications.title: Cost of a stretched spectrum for the Gaussian orthogonal ensemble
applications.inputs: β = 1 and V(x) = x²/4, so that P^N is the law of the eigenvalues of the GOE matrix scaled by 1/√N. The semicircle law σ on [−2, 2]. For s > 0 the dilated law μ_s, the image of σ under x ↦ sx. The value s = √2.
applications.hypotheses: V is continuous and V(x)/log|x| → ∞, so the growth condition holds for every β′ > 1. The source (Lemma 2.6.2(e) and Exercise 2.6.4) identifies σ as the unique minimizer, through the identity ∫ log|x − y| σ(dy) = x²/4 − 1/2 for |x| ≤ 2.

steps.text: Integrate the identity ∫ log|x − y| σ(dy) = x²/4 − 1/2 against σ. Since ∫ x² dσ = 1, Σ(σ) = 1/4 − 1/2 = −1/4.
The minimum is c = ∫ V dσ − (1/2) Σ(σ) = 1/4 + 1/8.
Dilation gives ∫ V dμ_s = s²/4 and Σ(μ_s) = log s + Σ(σ) = log s − 1/4. So I(μ_s) = s²/4 + 1/8 − (1/2) log s − 3/8 = s²/4 − 1/4 − (1/2) log s, which is 0 at s = 1 and positive for s ≠ 1.
For s = √2 the polynomial part is 2/4 − 1/4 = 1/4, so I(μ_√2) = (1 − log 2)/4 ≈ 0.0767.
The open ball lower bound, the closed ball upper bound and the lower semicontinuity of I give lim_(ε→0) lim N⁻² log P^N(d(L_N, μ_√2) < ε) = −(1 − log 2)/4.

applications.conclusion: The probability that the GOE spectrum looks like a semicircle stretched by the factor √2 decays like exp(−N²(1 − log 2)/4 + o(N²)), which is about e^(−0.0767 N²). The speed N² makes such a global deformation much less likely than a shift of one eigenvalue, which costs only e^(−O(N)).

limitations: The theorem needs the explicit joint density of a β-ensemble. It does not apply to Wigner matrices with independent non-Gaussian entries, as the source notes.
The principle concerns the empirical measure at speed N². The deviations of a single extreme eigenvalue occur at speed N and need a separate principle, which the source treats in Section 2.6.2.
The rate function is explicit, but its minimizer σ_V is explicit only for special potentials such as V(x) = βx²/4.

results.name: Johansson's theorem on the fluctuations of last-passage percolation
aliases: Tracy–Widom limit for exponential last-passage percolation
results.statement: Let u(i, j), i, j ≥ 1, be independent exponential random variables with mean 1. For M, N ≥ 1 let H(M, N) = max_π Σ_{(i,j)∈π} u(i, j), where π runs over the up/right lattice paths from (1, 1) to (M, N). In the continuous-time totally asymmetric simple exclusion process that starts with one particle at each site k ≤ 0, H(M, N) has the law of the time at which the particle that starts at −(N − 1) completes its M-th jump. Let F(s) = det(I − A)_{L²[s,∞)} be the Tracy–Widom distribution function, where A(x, y) = (Ai(x)Ai′(y) − Ai′(x)Ai(y))/(x − y) is the Airy kernel. Then for every γ ≥ 1 and s ∈ ℝ, P[(H([γN], N) − (1 + √γ)² N)/(γ^(−1/6)(1 + √γ)^(4/3) N^(1/3)) ≤ s] → F(s) as N → ∞.
hypotheses: The weights u(i, j) are independent and exponentially distributed with mean 1.
The ratio of the two sides is fixed: M = [γN] with a constant γ ≥ 1.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 uses the Knuth (RSK) correspondence: the last-passage time of a nonnegative integer matrix is the first row of the common shape of the two tableaux.

definitions.name: last-passage time
definitions.text: H(M, N) = max_π Σ_{(i,j)∈π} u(i, j) over up/right paths π from (1, 1) to (M, N) in the grid of random weights u(i, j).

definitions.name: totally asymmetric simple exclusion process
definitions.text: Particles on ℤ, at most one per site. Each particle jumps one step to the right at rate 1 if the target site is empty. The step initial condition puts one particle at each site k ≤ 0.

definitions.name: Tracy–Widom distribution
definitions.text: The law with distribution function F(s) = det(I − A)_{L²[s,∞)} for the Airy kernel A. It is the limit law of the rescaled largest eigenvalue of a GUE matrix.

source.citation: Kurt Johansson, Shape fluctuations and random matrices, Communications in Mathematical Physics 209 (2000), 437–476.
source.revision: arXiv v2 (math/9903134), revised version of 19 August 1999.
source.module: Section 1 Introduction and results (Theorem 1.6 with its proof), Sections 2, 3 and 5
source.excerpt: Theorem 1.6. For each γ ≥ 1, lim (1/N) E[H([γN], N)] = (1 + √γ)², … Furthermore, assume that a_N = O(N^(1/3)) as N → ∞ and pick d_N so that d_N − (1 + 1/√γ)a_N = o(N^(1/3)) as N → ∞. Then, for each γ ≥ 1, lim P[(H(γN + a_N, N) − (1 + √γ)²N − d_N)/(γ^(−1/6)(1 + √γ)^(4/3)N^(1/3)) ≤ s] = F(s).
source.attribution: © Kurt Johansson. Quoted from the author's arXiv version for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The authored statement is (1.22) of Theorem 1.6 with a_N = [γN] − γN and d_N = 0, which satisfy the conditions of the source, and the exclusion process description comes from Section 1 of the source. The outline follows the proof of (1.22): Proposition 1.4, the Laguerre Fredholm determinant (1.23), the kernel limit (1.24) and the convergence argument of Lemma 3.1. The source gives full details for geometric weights (Theorem 1.2) and states that the exponential case is similar.

results.proof_status: outline of the cited published proof. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of Theorem 1.6, equation (1.22), in Johansson (2000), Section 1, with Propositions 1.3 and 1.4, Lemmas 2.1 to 2.3 and Lemma 3.1. Step s4 takes the kernel limit (1.24) from the source, which states it without the details, and step s5 takes the Fredholm series limit of Lemma 3.1 and the identity (1.9) of Tracy and Widom.

steps.text: Geometric weights and the Meixner ensemble (Section 2 and Proposition 1.3 of the source). Let w(i, j) be independent with P(w = k) = (1 − q)q^k, k ≥ 0, and let G(M, N) be the last-passage time (1.1) for these weights, with M ≥ N. Lemma 2.1 states that G(M, N) is the length of the longest weakly increasing subsequence of the generalized permutation that encodes the matrix W = (w(i, j)). Since P(W = A) = (1 − q)^(MN) q^k for every matrix A with entry sum k, Lemma 2.2 states that W is uniform given its entry sum. The Knuth correspondence maps these matrices bijectively to pairs of semistandard Young tableaux of a common shape λ ⊢ k with entries in [N] and [M], and G(M, N) = λ₁. Lemma 2.3 counts the semistandard tableaux of shape λ with entries in [N] as Π_{i<j}(λ_i − λ_j + j − i)/(j − i). With h_j = λ_j + N − j this gives Proposition 1.3: P[G(M, N) ≤ t] = Z_{M,N}^(−1) Σ Π_{i<j}(h_i − h_j)² Π_i C(h_i + M − N, h_i) q^(h_i), summed over h ∈ ℕ^N with max h_i ≤ t + N − 1.

Exponential limit and the Laguerre ensemble (Proposition 1.4 of the source). If X_L is geometric with parameter 1 − 1/L, then X_L/L converges in law to an exponential variable with mean 1. The last-passage time is a continuous function of the weights, so P[H(M, N) ≤ t] is the limit of formula (1.13) with q = 1 − 1/L and t replaced by [Lt]. The sum over h becomes a Riemann sum with x_i = h_i/L, and the source obtains (1.18): P[H(M, N) ≤ t] = (Z′_{M,N})^(−1) ∫_{[0,t]^N} Π_{i<j}(x_i − x_j)² Π_j x_j^(M−N) e^(−x_j) d^N x. By Remark 1.5 this is the distribution function of the largest eigenvalue of AA*, where A is an N × M matrix with independent complex Gaussian entries of mean 0 whose real and imaginary parts have variance 1/2 (the Laguerre ensemble).

Fredholm determinant (proof of Theorem 1.6 in the source). Put c = (1 + √γ)², ρ = γ^(−1/6)(1 + √γ)^(4/3), a_N = [γN] − γN and α_N = (γ − 1)N + a_N = [γN] − N. Let ℓ_n^α be the orthonormal polynomials for the weight x^α e^(−x) on [0, ∞), with leading coefficients κ_n, and let K_N^α(x, y) = (κ_{N−1}/κ_N)(ℓ_N^α(x)ℓ_{N−1}^α(y) − ℓ_N^α(y)ℓ_{N−1}^α(x))/(x − y) · (x^α e^(−x) y^α e^(−y))^(1/2) be the Laguerre kernel in Christoffel–Darboux form. The standard random matrix computation (Mehta, Chapter 5, as in Section 3 of the source) turns (1.18) into the Fredholm expansion (1.23): P[H([γN], N) ≤ cN + ρN^(1/3)s] = Σ_{k≥0} ((−1)^k/k!) ∫_{[s,∞)^k} det(ρN^(1/3) K_N^(α_N)(cN + ρN^(1/3)ξ_i, cN + ρN^(1/3)ξ_j))_{i,j≤k} d^kξ.

Edge asymptotics of the kernel (equation (1.24) of the source). The rescaled kernel converges to the Airy kernel (1.7): ρN^(1/3) K_N^(α_N)(cN + ρN^(1/3)ξ, cN + ρN^(1/3)η) → A(ξ, η) = (Ai(ξ)Ai′(η) − Ai′(ξ)Ai(η))/(ξ − η), uniformly for ξ and η in compact sets. The method is a saddle point analysis of the contour integral L_n^α(x) = (e^x/2πi) ∮_C e^(−xz) z^(n+α)/(z − 1)^(n+1) dz, with C a circle around z = 1. At the spectral edge x = cN two critical points of the exponent merge, and the local cubic term produces the Airy function. The source does not write out this analysis. It states that the proof is the same as for the Meixner kernel, which Section 5 of the source (Lemma 5.1) carries out with a contour integral for the Meixner polynomials.

Limit of the Fredholm series (Lemma 3.1 of the source). Lemma 3.1 proves, for kernels on the integers, that the Fredholm series converge to F(s) = det(I − A)_{L²[s,∞)} under four conditions: (3.6) a uniform bound on the sum of the diagonal values K_N(x, x) to the right of each rescaled point τ ≥ −M₁, (3.7) a sum smaller than ε to the right of a large rescaled point L, (3.8) uniform convergence of the rescaled kernel to the Airy kernel on compact sets, and (iv) positive definiteness of the matrices (K_N(x_i, x_j)). Positive definiteness gives |det(K_N(x_i, x_j))| ≤ Π_j K_N(x_j, x_j) (3.10). With (3.6) and (3.7), this bound lets the proof cut the series after finitely many terms and restrict the sums to a bounded window, where (3.8) applies. Lemma 3.2 checks the conditions for the Meixner kernel. For the Laguerre kernel, which is also positive definite because it is the kernel of an orthogonal projection, the source states that (1.23), (1.24) and estimates as in Lemma 3.1 give the limit, and it does not write out the details. Hence P[H([γN], N) ≤ cN + ρN^(1/3)s] → Σ_k ((−1)^k/k!) ∫_{[s,∞)^k} det(A(ξ_i, ξ_j)) d^kξ = F(s) for every s ∈ ℝ. Tracy and Widom proved that F(s) also equals exp(−∫_s^∞ (x − s)u(x)² dx) (1.9).

source.ref: K. Johansson, Shape fluctuations and random matrices, Comm. Math. Phys. 209 (2000), 437-476, Theorem 1.6, pp. 8-10 of arXiv math/9903134, with Propositions 1.3 and 1.4, Section 2 and Lemma 3.1.

applications.title: Jump time of a particle in the exclusion process
applications.inputs: Rost's totally asymmetric simple exclusion process starts with one particle at each site k ≤ 0. Each particle jumps one step to the right at rate 1 when the target site is empty. Consider the particle that starts at −999 and the time T at which it completes its 1000-th jump.
applications.hypotheses: By the theorem, T has the law of H(M, N) with N = 1000 and M = 1000, so γ = 1 ≥ 1. The weights u(i, j) are independent exponential variables with mean 1.

steps.text: The centring is (1 + √γ)² N = (1 + 1)² · 1000 = 4000.
The scale is γ^(−1/6)(1 + √γ)^(4/3) N^(1/3) = 2^(4/3) · 10, because 10³ = N. Its cube is 2⁴ · 10³ = 16000, so the scale is about 25.2.
The theorem gives P(T ≤ 4000 + 25.2 s) ≈ F(s). So T is close in law to 4000 + 25.2χ, where χ has the Tracy–Widom law.
With the mean −1.7711 of the Tracy–Widom law, the approximating law has mean about 4000 + 25.2 · (−1.7711) ≈ 3955.4, and its fluctuations are of order N^(1/3) = 10 times a constant, not of order √N.

applications.conclusion: The particle that starts at −999 makes its 1000-th jump at a time near 4000, with random fluctuations of size about 25 that follow the Tracy–Widom law.

limitations: The proof uses the exact determinantal formulas for geometric and exponential weights. The source states the extension to other weight laws as Conjecture 1.9.
The theorem gives convergence in distribution only. The source does not prove convergence of moments.

Corollary 1.7 of the source deduces from (1.22) Tracy–Widom fluctuations for the number Y([ut], t) of particles to the right of [ut] in the exclusion process. The source states that this deduction is straightforward and does not write it out.

results.name: Baik–Deift–Johansson theorem
aliases: Tracy–Widom limit for the longest increasing subsequence
results.statement: For N ≥ 1 let π be a uniformly random permutation of {1, …, N}, and let l_N be the length of its longest increasing subsequence, that is the largest k for which some i_1 < … < i_k satisfy π(i_1) < … < π(i_k). Let u be the solution of the Painlevé II equation u″ = 2u³ + xu with u(x) ∼ −Ai(x) as x → +∞, where Ai is the Airy function. Let F(t) = exp(−∫_t^∞ (x − t) u(x)² dx), the Tracy–Widom distribution function of the largest eigenvalue of the Gaussian Unitary Ensemble. Then for every t ∈ ℝ, P((l_N − 2√N)/N^(1/6) ≤ t) → F(t) as N → ∞.
hypotheses: The permutation π is uniformly distributed on the symmetric group S_N.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 uses the Schensted case of the Robinson–Schensted–Knuth correspondence: l_N is the first row of the common shape of the two tableaux.
Step s2 uses Szegő's strong limit theorem D_k(λ) → e^λ to write log φ_n(λ) as the sum of log κ_k² over k ≥ n.

definitions.name: longest increasing subsequence
definitions.text: For a permutation π of {1, …, N}, the largest k such that π(i_1) < … < π(i_k) for some i_1 < … < i_k.

definitions.name: Tracy–Widom distribution
definitions.text: The law with distribution function F(t) = exp(−∫_t^∞ (x − t)u(x)² dx), where u is the Hastings–McLeod solution of Painlevé II. It is the limit law of the rescaled largest eigenvalue of a GUE matrix.

definitions.name: Poissonization
definitions.text: Replacing the fixed size N by a Poisson(λ) random size: φ_n(λ) = e^(−λ) Σ_N λ^N P(l_N ≤ n)/N!.

source.citation: Jinho Baik, Percy Deift and Kurt Johansson, On the distribution of the length of the longest increasing subsequence of random permutations, Journal of the American Mathematical Society 12 (1999), 1119–1178.
source.revision: arXiv v2 (math/9810105), revised version of 25 March 1999.
source.module: Section 1 Introduction (statement), Sections 2 to 9 and Appendix A (proof)
source.excerpt: Theorem 1.1. Let S_N be the group of all permutations of N numbers with uniform distribution and let l_N(π) be the length of the longest increasing subsequence of π ∈ S_N. Let χ be a random variable whose distribution function is F. Then, as N → ∞, χ_N ≡ (l_N − 2√N)/N^(1/6) → χ in distribution.
source.attribution: © Jinho Baik, Percy Deift and Kurt Johansson. Quoted from the authors' arXiv version for identification of the cited result.

source.alignment: The authored statement is Theorem 1.1 of the source, with the definition (1.4) to (1.6) of F written into the statement. The outline follows the proof in the source: Gessel's Toeplitz determinant, orthogonal polynomials on the circle, the Riemann–Hilbert problem with Deift–Zhou steepest descent, the summation of Lemma 7.1 and the de-Poissonization of Section 8. The convergence of moments (Theorem 1.2 of the source) is not part of this record.

proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of Theorem 1.1 in Baik, Deift and Johansson (1999), Sections 1 to 9 and Appendix A. Steps s3 to s6 take Lemmas 4.1, 4.3, 5.1, 6.3, 7.1, 8.1 and 8.2 and the properties (2.14) to (2.18) of the Painlevé II problem from the source without their proofs.

steps.text: Poissonization and Gessel's identity (Section 1 and Appendix A of the source). Let F_N(n) = P(l_N ≤ n) and φ_n(λ) = e^(−λ) Σ_{N≥0} λ^N F_N(n)/N!, which is P(L(λ) ≤ n) for a Poisson(λ) number of points. The Schensted correspondence maps S_N bijectively to pairs of standard Young tableaux of a common shape μ ⊢ N, and the longest increasing subsequence of π is the length of the first row of μ. So F_N(n) = (1/N!) Σ f(μ)², summed over shapes μ ⊢ N with first row at most n, where f(μ) is the number of standard tableaux of shape μ. Appendix A of the source combines this with the Frobenius–Young formula for f(μ) and turns a Hankel determinant into a Toeplitz determinant. This proves Gessel's identity (1.12): φ_n(λ) = e^(−λ) D_{n−1}(λ), with D_{n−1}(λ) = det(d_{j−k})_{0≤j,k≤n−1} and d_j = (2π)^(−1) ∫_0^{2π} exp(2√λ cos θ − ijθ) dθ.

Orthogonal polynomials on the circle (equations (1.23) to (1.25) of the source). Let p_k(z) = κ_k z^k + … be the orthonormal polynomials for the weight exp(2√λ cos θ) dθ/(2π) on the unit circle. Then κ_k² = D_{k−1}(λ)/D_k(λ) (1.24). For fixed λ, Szegő's strong limit theorem gives D_k(λ) → e^λ as k → ∞. The product of κ_k² over n ≤ k ≤ K telescopes to D_{n−1}/D_K, so log φ_n(λ) = Σ_{k≥n} log κ_k²(λ) (1.25). The asymptotics of φ_n(λ) thus reduce to asymptotics of κ_k²(λ) that are uniform in k ≥ n.

Riemann–Hilbert problem and equilibrium measure (Sections 1 and 4 of the source). Let Y(z; k+1, λ) be the 2 × 2 matrix function that is analytic off the unit circle Σ, has the jump Y₊ = Y₋ [[1, z^(−(k+1)) e^(√λ(z + 1/z))], [0, 1]] on Σ, and satisfies Y z^(−(k+1)σ₃) = I + O(1/z) at infinity. Lemma 4.1 of the source (after Fokas, Its and Kitaev) states that Y exists and is unique, and κ_k²(λ) = −Y₂₁(0; k+1, λ) (1.27). With γ = 2√λ/(k+1), Lemma 4.3 computes the equilibrium measure of the field V(z) = −(γ/2)(z + 1/z) on Σ: dμ_V = (1 + γ cos θ)dθ/(2π) if γ ≤ 1, and for γ > 1 a measure on the arc |θ| ≤ θ_c with sin²(θ_c/2) = 1/γ. The g-function g(z) = ∫ log(z − s) dμ_V(s) (1.28) replaces the exponentially growing jump entries by oscillating or decaying ones.

Steepest descent and the Painlevé II parametrix (Sections 2, 5 and 6 of the source). The Deift–Zhou steepest descent method deforms the transformed Riemann–Hilbert problem, opens lenses, and compares its solution with explicit model solutions. Near the critical value γ = 1 the local model is the Riemann–Hilbert problem of Section 2 with p = −q = 1 and r = 0 (2.15). Its solution m^PII gives the solution u(x) = 2i m^PII_{1,12}(x) of u″ = 2u³ + xu (2.14), with d/dx(2i m^PII_{1,22}(x)) = u(x)² (2.18) and m^PII_{1,22}(x) → 0 as x → +∞ (2.17). The source takes the existence of this solution from Deift and Zhou. Lemma 5.1 (γ ≤ 1) and Lemma 6.3 (γ > 1) of the source prove the resulting estimates, with q = k + 1. If γ ≤ 1 − δ, then |κ²_{q−1} − 1| ≤ Ce^(−cq). If γ is within a distance of order q^(−2/3) of 1, then κ²_{q−1} − 1 equals i2^(4/3) q^(−1/3) m^PII_{1,22}(t) up to an error C(M)q^(−2/3), where t is the rescaled distance of γ from 1.

Summation over k (Section 7 of the source). The sum Σ_{k≥n} log κ_k² of the window estimates is a Riemann sum for an integral of 2i m^PII_{1,22}. Lemma 7.1 of the source states the result. Put t = 2^(1/3)(n+1)^(2/3)(1 − 2√λ/(n+1)) (7.10). In the window −M ≤ t ≤ M, |log φ_n(λ) − ∫_t^∞ 2i m^PII_{1,22}(y) dy| ≤ C(M)/n^(1/3) + Ce^(−M^(3/2)/4), with C independent of M. Parts (i), (ii), (iv) and (v) of Lemma 7.1 bound log φ_n(λ) outside this window, and part (v) comes from Johansson's earlier paper.

De-Poissonization and conclusion (Sections 8 and 9 of the source). Write q_{n,N} = F_N(n). Lemma 8.1, from Johansson's earlier paper, states q_{n,N+1} ≤ q_{n,N}. With this monotonicity, Lemma 8.2 gives, for fixed m > 0 and for explicit μ_N > N > ν_N with |μ_N − N| and |ν_N − N| of order at most √N log N, the bounds φ_n(μ_N) − C/N^m ≤ q_{n,N} ≤ φ_n(ν_N) + C/N^m for 0 ≤ n ≤ N. Put n = [2√N + tN^(1/6)], so that P((l_N − 2√N)/N^(1/6) ≤ t) = q_{n,N}. The quantity t_N = 2^(1/3)(n+1)^(2/3)(1 − 2√μ_N/(n+1)) tends to t, and the same holds for ν_N. Lemma 7.1 with N → ∞ and then M → ∞ gives φ_n(μ_N) → exp(∫_t^∞ 2i m^PII_{1,22}(y) dy), and the same limit for ν_N. Since 2i m^PII_{1,22}(y) = −∫_y^∞ u(x)² dx by (2.17) and (2.18), integration by parts gives ∫_t^∞ 2i m^PII_{1,22}(y) dy = −∫_t^∞ (x − t)u(x)² dx. Hence P((l_N − 2√N)/N^(1/6) ≤ t) → F(t).

source.ref: J. Baik, P. Deift and K. Johansson, On the distribution of the length of the longest increasing subsequence of random permutations, J. Amer. Math. Soc. 12 (1999), 1119-1178, Theorem 1.1, p. 2 of arXiv math/9810105, proof in Sections 4 to 9 and Appendix A.

applications.title: Number of piles in patience sorting
applications.inputs: A deck of N = 10⁶ cards in uniformly random order is dealt by patience sorting: each card goes on the leftmost pile whose top card is larger, or starts a new pile on the right.
applications.hypotheses: The order of the deck is a uniform random permutation of 10⁶ cards. By a result of Aldous and Diaconis, the greedy patience sorting algorithm makes exactly l_N piles, where l_N is the length of the longest increasing subsequence.

steps.text: The centring is 2√N = 2 · 1000 = 2000, because 1000² = 10⁶.
The scale is N^(1/6) = 10, because 10⁶ = N.
The theorem gives P(number of piles ≤ 2000 + 10t) → F(t). So the law of the number of piles is close to the law of 2000 + 10χ, where χ has the Tracy–Widom law F.
The source reports the mean −1.7711 of F from numerical solutions of Painlevé II. The approximating law 2000 + 10χ then has mean 2000 + 10 · (−1.7711) = 1982.289.

applications.conclusion: Patience sorting of a shuffled deck of a million cards makes about 2000 piles, and the random correction is about 10χ with χ from the Tracy–Widom law, centred near −17.7 piles.

limitations: The theorem gives convergence in distribution only. The convergence of the moments of (l_N − 2√N)/N^(1/6) is Theorem 1.2 of the source and needs the tail bounds (1.7) and (1.8).
The proof uses the exact determinantal structure of uniform permutations. It does not apply to other laws on permutations without new integrable structure.

results.name: Marchenko–Pastur theorem
results.statement: Let ξ be a real random variable with E ξ = 0 and E ξ² = 1, and let y ∈ (0, ∞). For each n ≥ 1 let p = p(n) ≥ 1 be an integer, with p/n → y as n → ∞. Let X_n be a p × n random matrix whose entries are independent copies of ξ, with all X_n defined on one probability space. Let S_n = (1/n) X_n X_nᵀ, and let μ_n = (1/p) Σ_{i=1}^p δ_{λ_i} be the empirical distribution of the eigenvalues λ_1, …, λ_p of S_n. Let a = (1 − √y)², b = (1 + √y)², and let μ_y = (1 − 1/y)⁺ δ_0 + √((x − a)(b − x))/(2π y x) 1_{[a,b]}(x) dx be the Marchenko–Pastur law. Then, almost surely, μ_n converges weakly to μ_y as n → ∞.
hypotheses: The entries of each matrix X_n are independent real random variables with the law of ξ, where E ξ = 0 and E ξ² = 1.
The dimensions satisfy p(n)/n → y for a constant y ∈ (0, ∞).

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 diagonalizes the positive semidefinite matrix C with the spectral theorem to bound the resolvent and the quadratic forms.
Steps s1, s3 and s4 use the Sherman–Morrison case of the Woodbury identity for the rank-one update C + wwᵀ.
Step s2 bounds first absolute moments of the quadratic form by second moments, and step s4 does the same for s_n − E s_n.
Step s2 shows ε_p → 0, step s6 shows continuity of s_ν, and step s7 takes the limit v ↓ 0 in the inversion formula.
Step s3 applies the Azuma–Hoeffding inequality to the martingale differences d_k with |d_k| ≤ 2/(pv).
Step s3 turns the summable tail bounds for s_n − E s_n into almost sure convergence with the Borel–Cantelli lemma.
Step s4 integrates the bound of step s2 over the independent matrix G_1, and step s7 exchanges the integrals in the inversion formula.
Step s6 extracts weakly convergent subsequences from the tight sequence (μ_n) with Prokhorov's theorem.
Step s7 uses the uniqueness part: a finite measure on ℝ is determined by the integrals of continuous functions with compact support.

definitions.name: empirical spectral distribution
definitions.text: For a p × p real symmetric matrix with eigenvalues λ_1, …, λ_p, the probability measure (1/p) Σ_i δ_{λ_i}.

definitions.name: Stieltjes transform
definitions.text: For a probability measure μ on ℝ, the function s_μ(z) = ∫ μ(dλ)/(λ − z) on the upper half-plane Im z > 0. For μ_n it equals (1/p) tr(S_n − z)^(−1).

definitions.name: Marchenko–Pastur law
definitions.text: The probability measure μ_y with an atom of mass (1 − 1/y)⁺ at 0 and density √((x − a)(b − x))/(2π y x) on [a, b], where a = (1 − √y)² and b = (1 + √y)².

source.citation: Pavel Yaskov, A short proof of the Marchenko–Pastur theorem, Comptes Rendus Mathématique 354 (2016), 319–322.
source.module: Section 2 Main results, Section 3 Proofs
source.excerpt: Theorem 2.1. If (A) holds, then (1) holds. … Proposition 2.1. Let {X_pk} be independent random variables with EX_pk = 0, EX²_pk = 1 for each p ⩾ 1. Then (2) holds if and only if (A) holds for x_p = (X_p1, …, X_pp), p ⩾ 1.
source.attribution: © Pavel Yaskov. Quoted from the author's arXiv version for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: Yaskov's Theorem 2.1 proves the almost sure convergence (1) to the Marchenko–Pastur law for matrices with i.i.d. columns under his assumption (A) on quadratic forms. With Proposition 2.1 and the Lindeberg condition (2), which holds for i.i.d. entries with variance 1, it gives the authored statement. The authored proof follows his resolvent method, but proves the quadratic-form bound directly by truncation, writes out the martingale concentration step, and identifies the limit by Stieltjes inversion instead of a citation of Bai and Zhou.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the resolvent proof of Theorem 2.1 in Yaskov (2016). No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement, for i.i.d. real entries with mean 0 and variance 1 and every ratio y ∈ (0, ∞), including y = 1 and y > 1.

steps.text: Notation and resolvent bounds. Write ℂ⁺ = {z : Im z > 0} and z = u + iv with v > 0. For a probability measure μ on ℝ let s_μ(z) = ∫ μ(dλ)/(λ − z), the Stieltjes transform. Let x_1, …, x_n ∈ ℝ^p be the columns of X_n, so S_n = (1/n) Σ_k x_k x_kᵀ. Let G = (S_n − z)^(−1) and s_n(z) = s_{μ_n}(z) = (1/p) tr G. Now let C be a real symmetric positive semidefinite p × p matrix and w ∈ ℝ^p. The spectral theorem gives C = Σ_j λ_j u_j u_jᵀ with λ_j ≥ 0 and an orthonormal basis (u_j) of ℝ^p. Put c_j = (u_jᵀw)² ≥ 0, so wᵀ(C − z)^(−1)w = Σ_j c_j/(λ_j − z). (a) ‖(C − z)^(−1)‖ = max_j 1/|λ_j − z| ≤ 1/v. (b) Im(z/(λ − z)) = λv/|λ − z|² ≥ 0 for λ ≥ 0. Hence Im(z tr(C − z)^(−1)) ≥ 0 and Im(z(1 + wᵀ(C − z)^(−1)w)) ≥ v, so |1 + wᵀ(C − z)^(−1)w| ≥ v/|z|. (c) If w ≠ 0, the Sherman–Morrison formula gives tr(C − z)^(−1) − tr(C + wwᵀ − z)^(−1) = wᵀ(C − z)^(−2)w/(1 + wᵀ(C − z)^(−1)w) = Σ_j c_j(λ_j − z)^(−2)/(1 + Σ_j c_j(λ_j − z)^(−1)). The numerator has modulus at most Σ_j c_j/|λ_j − z|², and the imaginary part of the denominator equals v Σ_j c_j/|λ_j − z|². So the two traces differ by at most 1/v in modulus.

Quadratic forms. Let x ∈ ℝ^p have independent entries X_1, …, X_p with the law of ξ, and let B be a complex p × p matrix. Then E[xᵀBx] = tr B and E|xᵀBx − tr B| ≤ ‖B‖ p ε_p, where ε_p = (p^(1/4) + √2)/√p + 2E[|ξ² − 1|; |ξ² − 1| > p^(1/4)]. Proof. Write xᵀBx − tr B = Σ_k b_kk Y_k + Σ_{j≠k} b_jk X_j X_k with Y_k = X_k² − 1. For j ≠ k and j′ ≠ k′, E[X_j X_k X_j′ X_k′] is 1 if {j, k} = {j′, k′} and 0 otherwise. So E|Σ_{j≠k} b_jk X_j X_k|² = Σ_{j≠k} b_jk(b̄_jk + b̄_kj) ≤ 2 Σ_{j,k} |b_jk|² = 2 tr(BB*) ≤ 2p‖B‖², and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives E|Σ_{j≠k} b_jk X_j X_k| ≤ ‖B‖√(2p). For M > 0 let U_k = Y_k 1{|Y_k| ≤ M} − E[Y_k 1{|Y_k| ≤ M}] and V_k = Y_k − U_k. Since E Y_k = 0, V_k = Y_k 1{|Y_k| > M} − E[Y_k 1{|Y_k| > M}], so E|V_k| ≤ 2E[|Y_1|; |Y_1| > M]. The U_k are independent and centred with variance at most M², and |b_kk| ≤ ‖B‖, so the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives E|Σ_k b_kk U_k| ≤ ‖B‖M√p. Take M = p^(1/4). Since E|Y_1| ≤ 2, the dominated convergence theorem gives ε_p → 0 as p → ∞.

Concentration. Fix z ∈ ℂ⁺. Let F_k be the σ-field generated by x_1, …, x_k, and E_k = E[· | F_k]. Let G_k = (S_n − (1/n)x_k x_kᵀ − z)^(−1) and s_n^(k) = (1/p) tr G_k. The variable s_n^(k) does not depend on x_k, and the columns are independent, so (E_k − E_{k−1}) s_n^(k) = 0. Step s1(c) with C = S_n − (1/n)x_k x_kᵀ and w = x_k/√n gives |s_n − s_n^(k)| ≤ 1/(pv). So s_n − E s_n = Σ_{k=1}^n d_k with martingale differences d_k = (E_k − E_{k−1})(s_n − s_n^(k)) and |d_k| ≤ 2/(pv). The Azuma–Hoeffding inequality, applied to the real part and to the imaginary part, gives P(|s_n − E s_n| > 2ε) ≤ 4 exp(−ε²p²v²/(8n)). For large n, p ≥ yn/2, so the bound is at most 4 exp(−ε²y²v²n/32), which is summable in n. The Borel–Cantelli lemma for ε = 1/j, j = 1, 2, …, gives s_n(z) − E s_n(z) → 0 almost surely. The d_k are orthogonal, so also E|s_n − E s_n|² ≤ 4n/(p²v²).

Self-consistent equation. Let y_n = p/n and t_n = E s_n(z). From G(S_n − z) = I, p = tr(G S_n) − z tr G = (1/n) Σ_k x_kᵀ G x_k − zp s_n. Let q_k = (1/n) x_kᵀ G_k x_k. The Sherman–Morrison formula gives (1/n) x_kᵀ G x_k = q_k/(1 + q_k) = 1 − 1/(1 + q_k). Division by n gives y_n(1 + z s_n) = 1 − (1/n) Σ_k 1/(1 + q_k). The columns are exchangeable, so y_n(1 + z t_n) = 1 − E[1/(1 + q_1)]. Step s1(b) gives |1 + q_1| ≥ v/|z| and, since (1/n) tr G = y_n s_n, also |1 + y_n t_n| ≥ v/|z|. Hence |E[1/(1 + q_1)] − 1/(1 + y_n t_n)| ≤ (|z|/v)² E|q_1 − y_n t_n|. Now E|q_1 − y_n t_n| ≤ E|q_1 − (1/n) tr G_1| + (1/n) E|tr G_1 − tr G| + y_n E|s_n − t_n|. The matrix G_1 is independent of x_1 and ‖G_1‖ ≤ 1/v. So step s2, applied for fixed G_1 and integrated with Fubini's theorem, bounds the first term by y_n ε_p/v. Step s1(c) bounds the second term by 1/(nv). Step s3 and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality bound the third term by 2/(v√n). Since p → ∞, all three terms tend to 0. So y_n(1 + z t_n) − 1 + 1/(1 + y_n t_n) → 0.

The limit of s_n(z). Let a = (1 − √y)², b = (1 + √y)², let √ be the principal square root, R(z) = √(z − a)√(z − b) and r(z) = (1 − y − z + R(z))/(2yz) for z ∈ ℂ⁺. Then R(z)² = (z − a)(z − b) = (z + y − 1)² − 4yz. Write z − a = ρ₁e^(iθ₁) and z − b = ρ₂e^(iθ₂) with θ₁, θ₂ ∈ (0, π). Then R(z) = √(ρ₁ρ₂) e^(i(θ₁+θ₂)/2) and v² = ρ₁ρ₂ sin θ₁ sin θ₂ ≤ ρ₁ρ₂ sin²((θ₁ + θ₂)/2) = (Im R(z))², because sin θ₁ sin θ₂ = (cos(θ₁ − θ₂) − cos(θ₁ + θ₂))/2. So Im R(z) ≥ v. The numbers t_n satisfy |t_n| ≤ 1/v. Let t be the limit of a convergent subsequence. Step s4 and |1 + y_n t_n| ≥ v/|z| give y(1 + zt) = 1 − 1/(1 + yt). Multiplication by (1 + yt)/y gives yz t² + (y + z − 1)t + 1 = 0. The roots of this equation are r_± = (1 − y − z ± R(z))/(2yz). Step s1(b) gives Im(z s_n) ≥ 0, so Im(zt) ≥ 0. But Im(z r_−) = (−v − Im R(z))/(2y) < 0, so t = r_+ = r(z). All convergent subsequences have the same limit, so t_n → r(z). With step s3, s_n(z) → r(z) almost surely, for each fixed z ∈ ℂ⁺.

Tightness and limit points. Put c = 1 + y = (a + b)/2. Then R(z)² − (z − c)² = ab − c² = −4y, so R(z) − (z − c) = −4y/(R(z) + z − c), and |R(z) + z − c| ≥ Im(R(z) + z) ≥ 2v. Since 2y(z r(z) + 1) = R(z) − (z − c), this gives |z r(z) + 1| ≤ 1/v. Let Q = {u + iv : u, v rational, v > 0}, a countable dense subset of ℂ⁺. By step s5 the event E on which s_n(z) → r(z) for all z ∈ Q has probability 1. Fix an outcome in E. For a probability measure μ on ℝ and w > 0, 1 − w Im s_μ(iw) = ∫ λ²/(λ² + w²) μ(dλ) ≥ μ(|λ| ≥ w)/2. For each integer w ≥ 1, iw ∈ Q, so limsup_n μ_n(|λ| ≥ w) ≤ 2(1 − w Im r(iw)) ≤ 2|1 + iw r(iw)| ≤ 2/w. Each μ_n is a probability measure, so the sequence (μ_n) is tight. By Prokhorov's theorem every subsequence has a further subsequence that converges weakly to a probability measure ν. For z ∈ ℂ⁺ the real and imaginary parts of λ ↦ 1/(λ − z) are bounded and continuous, so s_ν(z) = r(z) for z ∈ Q. Both functions are continuous on ℂ⁺ (s_ν by dominated convergence), and Q is dense, so s_ν = r on ℂ⁺.

Identification of ν. Let A = (1 − 1/y)⁺. Then 1 − y + 2yA = |1 − y|. Extend √ to the closed upper half-plane H̄ by √(−s) = i√s for s > 0. Then R is continuous on H̄, R(0) = −|1 − y|, and h(z) = r(z) + A/z = (R(z) − R(0))/(2yz) − 1/(2y). For w₁, w₂ ∈ H̄ the roots √w₁ and √w₂ lie in the closed first quadrant, so |√w₁ − √w₂| ≤ |√w₁ + √w₂| and |√w₁ − √w₂|² ≤ |w₁ − w₂|. Hence |R(z) − R(0)| ≤ (√(|z| + a) + √b)|z|^(1/2), and |h(z)| ≤ C_K(1 + |z|^(−1/2)) for z ∈ H̄ with 0 < |z| ≤ K. Let g be continuous with compact support. Fubini's theorem gives (1/π)∫ g(x) Im s_ν(x + iv) dx = ∫ E[g(λ + vΓ)] ν(dλ), where Γ has the standard Cauchy law. As v ↓ 0, dominated convergence gives the limit ∫ g dν. The same computation for the point mass at 0 gives (1/π)∫ g(x) Im(−A/(x + iv)) dx → A g(0). For h, dominated convergence with the bound C_K(1 + |x|^(−1/2)) gives (1/π)∫ g(x) Im h(x + iv) dx → (1/π)∫ g(x) Im h(x) dx. For real x ≠ 0, Im h(x) = Im R(x)/(2yx). Here R(x) is real for x ∉ (a, b), and R(x) = i√((x − a)(b − x)) for a < x < b. So ∫ g dν = A g(0) + ∫_a^b g(x)√((x − a)(b − x))/(2πyx) dx = ∫ g dμ_y. Such integrals determine a finite measure on ℝ, so ν = μ_y. Thus on E every subsequence of (μ_n) has a further subsequence that converges weakly to μ_y, and so μ_n → μ_y weakly.

applications.title: Noise eigenvalues of a sample covariance matrix
applications.inputs: A data set has n = 1000 observations of p = 250 variables. All variables are independent, standardized noise with mean 0 and variance 1, so the true covariance matrix is the identity. The sample covariance matrix is S = (1/n) X Xᵀ with the 250 × 1000 data matrix X.
applications.hypotheses: The entries of X are independent with mean 0 and variance 1. The ratio p/n = 1/4 stays fixed as both dimensions grow, so y = 1/4. The theorem then describes the eigenvalues of S for large n.

steps.text: The lower edge of the Marchenko–Pastur law for y = 1/4 is a = (1 − √y)² = (1 − 1/2)² = 1/4.
The upper edge is b = (1 + √y)² = (1 + 1/2)² = 9/4.
Since y < 1, the law has no atom at 0. The eigenvalue spread b − a = 4√y = 2, although every true eigenvalue equals 1.
The density at the true value x = 1 is √((1 − 1/4)(9/4 − 1))/(2π · (1/4) · 1) = √15/(2π), about 0.62. The eigenvalues of S are spread over [1/4, 9/4] with this density, not concentrated at 1.

applications.conclusion: For 250 variables and 1000 observations of pure noise, the sample covariance eigenvalues fill the interval [1/4, 9/4] in the limit. Sample eigenvalues far from 1 inside this interval come from the dimension ratio alone, not from structure in the data.

limitations: Weak convergence of μ_n does not control single eigenvalues. The convergence of the largest eigenvalue of S_n to b needs more, for example a finite fourth moment of ξ.
The theorem gives no rate of convergence and no fluctuation law for the eigenvalues near the edges a and b.
Yaskov's Theorem 2.1 also covers i.i.d. columns with dependent entries, under his assumption (A) on quadratic forms.

results.name: Extinction criterion for Galton–Watson branching processes
results.statement: Let (Z_n)_{n≥0} be a Galton–Watson process with Z₀ = 1: each individual of generation n has k children with probability p_k (k = 0, 1, 2, …), independently of all other individuals, and Z_{n+1} is the total number of these children. Let f(s) = Σ_k p_k s^k for s ∈ [0, 1], let m = Σ_k k p_k ∈ [0, ∞], and let q = P(Z_n = 0 for some n) be the extinction probability. Assume p₁ ≠ 1. Then q is the smallest root of f(s) = s in [0, 1]. Moreover q = 1 if and only if m ≤ 1. If m > 1, then q < 1 and q is the only root of f(s) = s in [0, 1).
hypotheses: The process starts from one individual, and the numbers of children of all individuals are independent with the common law (p_k)_{k≥0} on {0, 1, 2, …}.
The offspring law is not the point mass at 1, that is p₁ ≠ 1.

prerequisites.reason: Step s4 lets s increase to 1 in the series Σ p_k(1 + s + … + s^(k−1)) with the monotone convergence theorem, which gives the limit m.
Step s4 applies the intermediate value theorem to f(s) − s on [0, s₀], where the function is nonnegative at 0 and negative at s₀.

definitions.name: Galton–Watson process
definitions.text: The generation sizes Z₀ = 1, Z₁, Z₂, … of a population in which each individual independently has a random number of children with a fixed law (p_k).

definitions.name: offspring generating function
definitions.text: f(s) = E[s^L] = Σ_k p_k s^k for s ∈ [0, 1], where L has the offspring law. Its left derivative at 1 is the mean m = Σ_k k p_k.

definitions.name: extinction probability
definitions.text: q = P(Z_n = 0 for some n ≥ 1), the probability that the population dies out.

source.citation: Russell Lyons and Yuval Peres, Probability on Trees and Networks, Cambridge Series in Statistical and Probabilistic Mathematics 42, Cambridge University Press, 2016.
source.revision: Authors' online version of the book, as downloaded in October 2026.
source.module: Chapter 5, Section 5.1 Galton–Watson Branching Processes
source.excerpt: Proposition 5.4. (Extinction Criterion) Provided p₁ ≠ 1, we have (i) q = 1 ⇔ f′(1) ≤ 1; (ii) q is the smallest root of f(s) = s in [0, 1] – the only other possible root being 1.
source.attribution: © Russell Lyons and Yuval Peres. Quoted from the authors' book Probability on Trees and Networks for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states the criterion with f′(1) in place of m and reads it from the graph of f, with no written proof. The authored statement uses the mean m, allows m = ∞, and adds that q < 1 is the only root in [0, 1) when m > 1. The authored proof follows the generating-function argument of Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorems 4.3.10 to 4.3.12, pp. 231-233, and replaces the martingale step for m ≤ 1 by the inequality 1 − f(s) ≤ m(1 − s).

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the generating-function argument of the cited sources. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement, for every offspring law with p₁ ≠ 1, including the case m = ∞.

steps.text: Let f_n(s) = E[s^(Z_n)] with the convention 0⁰ = 1. Given Z_{n−1} = j, Z_n is the sum of j independent copies of the offspring number L, so E[s^(Z_n) | Z_{n−1} = j] = f(s)^j. Hence f_n(s) = E[f(s)^(Z_{n−1})] = f_{n−1}(f(s)). Induction from f₀(s) = s gives f_n = f ∘ … ∘ f (n times). In particular q_n := P(Z_n = 0) = f_n(0) satisfies q₀ = 0 and q_{n+1} = f(q_n).

If Z_n = 0, then Z_{n+1} = 0. So the events {Z_n = 0} increase in n, and their union is the extinction event. Continuity of probability along an increasing sequence of events gives q = lim q_n. The series f has nonnegative coefficients with Σ p_k = 1, so it converges uniformly on [0, 1], and f is continuous and nondecreasing there. Thus q = lim f(q_n) = f(q). If r ∈ [0, 1] and f(r) = r, then q₀ = 0 ≤ r, and q_n ≤ r implies q_{n+1} = f(q_n) ≤ f(r) = r. By induction q_n ≤ r for all n, so q ≤ r. Hence q is the smallest root of f(s) = s in [0, 1].

Case m ≤ 1. For s ∈ [0, 1) and k ≥ 1, 1 − s^k = (1 − s)(1 + s + … + s^(k−1)) ≤ k(1 − s), with strict inequality when k ≥ 2. Summation gives 1 − f(s) = Σ_k p_k(1 − s^k) ≤ m(1 − s), with strict inequality if p_k > 0 for some k ≥ 2. If m < 1, then 1 − f(s) < 1 − s. If m = 1, then Σ_k (k − 1)p_k = 0, that is Σ_{k≥2} (k − 1)p_k = p₀. If p_k = 0 for every k ≥ 2, this forces p₀ = 0 and p₁ = 1, which the hypothesis excludes. So some p_k with k ≥ 2 is positive and again 1 − f(s) < 1 − s. In both cases f(s) > s on [0, 1), so the smallest root is 1 and q = 1.

Case m > 1 (m = ∞ is allowed). For s ∈ [0, 1), (1 − f(s))/(1 − s) = Σ_k p_k(1 + s + … + s^(k−1)). Each term increases to k p_k as s increases to 1, so the monotone convergence theorem gives the limit m > 1. Choose s₀ < 1 with (1 − f(s₀))/(1 − s₀) > 1, that is f(s₀) < s₀. The function g(s) = f(s) − s is continuous, g(0) = p₀ ≥ 0 and g(s₀) < 0. The intermediate value theorem gives a root in [0, s₀], so q ≤ s₀ < 1 by step s2.

Uniqueness for m > 1. Since Σ_k (k − 1)p_k = m − 1 > 0, some p_k with k ≥ 2 is positive. Then f′(s) = Σ_k k p_k s^(k−1) is strictly increasing on [0, 1), so f and g are strictly convex on [0, 1] (f is continuous at 1). If g had three roots r₁ < r₂ < r₃ in [0, 1], strict convexity would give g(r₂) < 0, which is false. Because g(1) = 0, g has at most one root in [0, 1). With step s4, q is the only root of f(s) = s in [0, 1). Steps s3 and s4 together show that q = 1 if and only if m ≤ 1.

applications.title: Percolation probability of bond percolation on the binary tree
applications.inputs: The rooted binary tree, in which every vertex has 2 children. Each edge is open with probability p = 3/4, independently. The open cluster of the root is studied.
applications.hypotheses: The open children of distinct vertices are independent, and each vertex has a Binomial(2, 3/4) number of open children. So the sizes of the generations of the open cluster form a Galton–Watson process with p₀ = 1/16, p₁ = 6/16, p₂ = 9/16. Then p₁ ≠ 1.

steps.text: The offspring generating function is f(s) = (1 − p + ps)² = (1/4 + 3s/4)², and the mean is m = 2p = 3/2 > 1. The criterion gives q < 1, so the root percolates with positive probability.
Solve f(s) = s. The equation (1 − p + ps)² = s has the roots s = 1 and s = ((1 − p)/p)². For p = 3/4 the root in [0, 1) is (1/3)² = 1/9.
The percolation probability is θ(p) = 1 − q = 1 − ((1 − p)/p)² for p > 1/2, and θ(p) = 0 for p ≤ 1/2 because then m = 2p ≤ 1. At p = 3/4, θ = 1 − 1/9 = 8/9.

applications.conclusion: Bond percolation on the binary tree has critical probability 1/2. At p = 3/4 the root lies in an infinite open cluster with probability 8/9.

limitations: The criterion gives the probability of extinction but not its speed. For m < 1, P(Z_n > 0) ≤ m^n, and the exact rate needs the L log L condition.
For m > 1 the result does not describe the growth of Z_n on survival. The Kesten–Stigum theorem gives that Z_n/m^n has a nonzero limit if and only if E[L log⁺ L] < ∞.

results.name: Kesten–Stigum theorem
aliases: L log L criterion for supercritical branching processes
results.statement: Let (Z_n)_{n≥0} be a Galton–Watson process with Z₀ = 1 and offspring law (p_k)_{k≥0}, let L have this law, let f(s) = Σ_k p_k s^k, and let q be the extinction probability. Assume that the mean m = E L satisfies 1 < m < ∞. Then W_n = Z_n/m^n is a nonnegative martingale, and it converges almost surely to a finite limit W. The following three conditions are equivalent: (i) P(W = 0) = q, (ii) E W = 1, (iii) E[L log⁺ L] < ∞. If E[L log⁺ L] = ∞, then W = 0 almost surely.
hypotheses: The process starts from one individual, and the numbers of children of all individuals are independent with the common law (p_k)_{k≥0} on {0, 1, 2, …}.
The mean number of children m = Σ_k k p_k satisfies 1 < m < ∞.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 gets the almost sure limit W of the martingale Z_n/m^n, and step s4 gets the limit of a submartingale bounded in L¹, from Doob's martingale convergence theorem.
Step s1 uses Fatou's lemma for E W ≤ 1, and step s3(b) uses it to show E[W; sup_j W_j ≤ K] = 0 under the Galton–Watson law.
Step s3(a) applies the Vitali convergence theorem to the uniformly integrable martingale W_n to get E W = 1.
Step s4 fixes the immigration sequence (Y_k) and integrates over it with Fubini's theorem, since the tree is built from independent ingredients.
Step s5 applies the Borel–Cantelli lemma to the events {log⁺ Y_k > εk} to show that the immigration grows slower than m^(k/2).
Step s6 applies the second Borel–Cantelli lemma to the independent events {Y_k > m^a m^k} to show that W = ∞ under the size-biased law.
Step s7 uses the extinction criterion: for m > 1 the only roots of f(s) = s in [0, 1] are q < 1 and 1.

definitions.name: Galton–Watson process
definitions.text: The generation sizes Z₀ = 1, Z₁, Z₂, … of a population in which each individual independently has a random number of children with a fixed law (p_k).

definitions.name: L log⁺ L condition
definitions.text: E[L log⁺ L] = Σ_k p_k k log⁺ k < ∞, where log⁺ x = max(log x, 0). It is slightly stronger than a finite mean and weaker than a finite moment of order 1 + δ for any δ > 0.

definitions.name: size-biased law
definitions.text: For a variable L ≥ 0 with finite positive mean m, the law of L̂ with P(L̂ = k) = k P(L = k)/m.

source.citation: Russell Lyons, Robin Pemantle and Yuval Peres, Conceptual proofs of L log L criteria for mean behavior of branching processes, Annals of Probability 23 (1995), 1125–1138.
source.revision: arXiv v1 (math/0404083), author version of 19 September 1994.
source.module: Section 1 Introduction (statement), Sections 2 and 3 (proof)
source.excerpt: Theorem A: Supercritical Processes (Kesten and Stigum (1966)). Suppose that 1 < m < ∞ and let W be the limit of the martingale Zn/mn. The following are equivalent: (i) P[W = 0] = q; (ii) E[W] = 1; (iii) E[L log+ L] < ∞.
source.attribution: © Russell Lyons, Robin Pemantle and Yuval Peres. Quoted from the authors' arXiv version for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The authored statement is Theorem A of the source, with the added claim that W = 0 almost surely when E[L log⁺ L] = ∞, which the source proof also gives. The authored proof follows Sections 2 and 3 of the source: size-biased trees, the density W_n on the first n levels, and Seneta's dichotomy for immigration (Theorem 3.1). It proves the two parts of the measure-change dichotomy (3.2) and (3.3) that the source cites from Durrett, and it proves Proposition 3.2 with the extinction criterion.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the size-biased tree proof of Lyons, Pemantle and Peres (1995), Sections 2 and 3. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement, for every offspring law with mean 1 < m < ∞. Steps s3 and s4 prove the measure-change facts and the immigration dichotomy that the source cites.

steps.text: Martingale limit. Given Z_n, the next generation is a sum of Z_n independent offspring numbers with mean m, so E[Z_{n+1} | Z_0, …, Z_n] = m Z_n and W_n = Z_n/m^n is a nonnegative martingale with E W_n = 1. Doob's martingale convergence theorem gives W_n → W almost surely with W finite, and Fatou's lemma gives E W ≤ 1. Work on the space of rooted ordered trees with the Galton–Watson law GW. Let F_n be the σ-field of the first n levels, Z_n(t) the size of level n of a tree t, W_n(t) = Z_n(t)/m^n, and W(t) = limsup_n W_n(t) ∈ [0, ∞] for every tree t. Then W = lim W_n GW-almost surely.

Size-biased tree. Let L̂ have P(L̂ = k) = k p_k/m, a probability law because Σ k p_k = m < ∞. Build a tree with a spine v₀, v₁, …: the spine vertex v_{j−1} gets L̂_j children, with L̂_1, L̂_2, … independent copies of L̂. One of these children, chosen uniformly, is v_j, and every other child gets an independent Galton–Watson descendant tree. Let ĜW* be the joint law of the tree and the spine, and ĜW the law of the tree. For a tree t and a vertex v at level n, let [t]_n be the event that the first n levels agree with t and [t; v]_n the event that also v_n = v. Induction on n proves ĜW*([t; v]_n) = GW([t]_n)/m^n. The case n = 0 is trivial. If the root of t has k children with descendant trees t⁽¹⁾, …, t⁽ᵏ⁾ and v lies in t⁽ⁱ⁾, then ĜW*([t; v]_{n+1}) = (k p_k/m)(1/k) ĜW*([t⁽ⁱ⁾; v]_n) Π_{j≠i} GW([t⁽ʲ⁾]_n) = GW([t]_{n+1})/m^{n+1}, because GW([t]_{n+1}) = p_k Π_j GW([t⁽ʲ⁾]_n). The size-biased tree has a spine, so it never dies out. Summation over the Z_n(t) vertices v at level n gives ĜW([t]_n) = W_n(t) GW([t]_n). The events [t]_n form a countable partition that generates F_n, so W_n is the density of ĜW with respect to GW on F_n.

Change of measure. For A ∈ F_n, step s2 gives E_GW[W_n; A] = ĜW(A). (a) Assume W < ∞ ĜW-almost surely. Then sup_j W_j < ∞ ĜW-almost surely, so δ(K) = ĜW(sup_j W_j > K) → 0 as K → ∞. Hence sup_n E_GW[W_n; W_n > K] = sup_n ĜW(W_n > K) ≤ δ(K) → 0, and (W_n) is uniformly integrable under GW. With W_n → W GW-almost surely, the Vitali convergence theorem gives E_GW W = lim E_GW W_n = 1. (b) Assume W = ∞ ĜW-almost surely. Fix K > 0 and let A_n = {max_{j≤n} W_j ≤ K} ∈ F_n. These events decrease to A = {sup_j W_j ≤ K}, and ĜW(A) = 0. On A, W_n 1_{A_n} = W_n → W GW-almost surely, so Fatou's lemma gives E_GW[W; A] ≤ liminf_n E_GW[W_n; A_n] = lim_n ĜW(A_n) = ĜW(A) = 0. So W = 0 GW-almost surely on {sup_j W_j ≤ K}. Under GW the sequence W_n converges to a finite limit, so sup_j W_j < ∞ almost surely. The union over K = 1, 2, … gives W = 0 GW-almost surely.

Spine decomposition. Let Y_k = L̂_k − 1 be the number of children of v_{k−1} other than v_k. These Y_k children are at level k, and they start independent Galton–Watson trees. So under ĜW*, Z_n − 1 is the size of generation n of a branching process with immigration Y_k at generation k, and Z_n ≥ Y_n. The random tree is a measurable function of independent ingredients: the sequence (L̂_k), the uniform choices of the spine and the attached trees. By Fubini's theorem it suffices to fix a sequence y = (y_k) of values of (Y_k) and to study the attached trees. With y fixed, let Z'_n = Z_n − 1 and M_n = Z'_n/m^n. Each of the Z'_n vertices off the spine has an independent offspring number with mean m, and y_{n+1} new vertices join. So E[M_{n+1} | first n levels] = M_n + y_{n+1}/m^{n+1} ≥ M_n, and E M_n = Σ_{k≤n} y_k m^(−k). If Σ_k y_k m^(−k) < ∞, then (M_n) is a nonnegative submartingale bounded in L¹, and Doob's martingale convergence theorem gives a finite limit almost surely. Since 1/m^n → 0, W_n = 1/m^n + M_n then converges to a finite limit.

Moment condition. E[log⁺ Y_1] = Σ_k (k p_k/m) log⁺(k − 1) = m^(−1) E[L log⁺(L − 1)], with log⁺ 0 = 0. For k ≥ 2, 0 ≤ k log k − k log(k − 1) = k log(k/(k − 1)) ≤ k log 2, and E[L log 2] = m log 2 < ∞. So E[log⁺ Y_1] < ∞ if and only if E[L log⁺ L] < ∞. Assume E[L log⁺ L] < ∞ and let X_k = log⁺ Y_k and ε = (log m)/2 > 0. Then Σ_k P(X_k > εk) ≤ Σ_k P(X_1/ε > k) ≤ E[X_1]/ε < ∞. The Borel–Cantelli lemma gives X_k ≤ εk for all large k, that is Y_k ≤ m^(k/2). Hence Σ_k Y_k m^(−k) < ∞ almost surely. Step s4, applied for almost every fixed y, shows that W_n converges to a finite limit ĜW*-almost surely. So W < ∞ ĜW-almost surely, and step s3(a) gives E W = 1.

Infinite moment. Assume E[L log⁺ L] = ∞. By step s5, X = log⁺ Y_1/log m has E X = ∞. For a nonnegative variable, E X ≤ Σ_{j≥0} P(X > j), so for each integer a ≥ 0 the sum Σ_{k≥1} P(X_k > k + a) is infinite, with X_k = log⁺ Y_k/log m. These events are independent, so the second Borel–Cantelli lemma gives X_k > k + a for infinitely many k, that is Y_k > m^a m^k infinitely often. Since Z_k ≥ Y_k, W_k > m^a infinitely often. As a is arbitrary, W = limsup_k W_k = ∞ ĜW-almost surely. Step s3(b) gives W = 0 GW-almost surely, so P(W = 0) = 1.

Conclusion. Let W⁽ⁱ⁾ be the martingale limit of the descendant tree of the i-th child of the root. Given Z_1, the W⁽ⁱ⁾ for i ≤ Z_1 are independent copies of W, and W_{n+1} = m^(−1) Σ_{i≤Z_1} W⁽ⁱ⁾_n gives W = m^(−1) Σ_{i≤Z_1} W⁽ⁱ⁾ almost surely. So W = 0 exactly when every W⁽ⁱ⁾ = 0, and conditioning on Z_1 gives P(W = 0) = Σ_k p_k P(W = 0)^k = f(P(W = 0)). Because m > 1, the extinction criterion says that the roots of f(s) = s in [0, 1] are q < 1 and 1. Hence P(W = 0) ∈ {q, 1}. (iii) ⇒ (ii) is step s5. (ii) ⇒ (i): E W = 1 excludes P(W = 0) = 1, so P(W = 0) = q. (i) ⇒ (iii): if E[L log⁺ L] = ∞, step s6 gives P(W = 0) = 1 ≠ q. The last claim of the statement is step s6.

applications.title: Growth of a dividing cell population
applications.inputs: A cell population starts from one cell. In each generation, every cell dies with probability 1/4 or divides into two cells with probability 3/4, independently of the other cells.
applications.hypotheses: The cell counts form a Galton–Watson process with p₀ = 1/4 and p₂ = 3/4. The mean is m = 3/2, so 1 < m < ∞. The offspring number is bounded, so E[L log⁺ L] = (3/4)·2 log 2 < ∞ and condition (iii) holds.

steps.text: Compute the mean number of daughter cells: m = 0·(1/4) + 2·(3/4) = 3/2.
The extinction probability solves f(s) = 1/4 + (3/4)s² = s, that is 3s² − 4s + 1 = 0, with roots 1/3 and 1. So q = 1/3. Check f(1/3) = 1/3.
By the theorem, Z_n/(3/2)^n → W with E W = 1 and P(W = 0) = q = 1/3. So W > 0 exactly when the population survives, and E[W | W > 0] = 1/(1 − 1/3) = 3/2.

On survival the population grows like W·(3/2)^n with a random factor W of mean 3/2. At generation n = 10 the mean of the leading term W·(3/2)^10 on survival is (3/2)·(3/2)^10 = 177147/2048, about 86.5 cells.

applications.conclusion: A surviving population of dividing cells grows at the exact rate (3/2)^n up to a random factor W > 0, and this factor has mean 3/2 given survival.

limitations: The theorem gives the rate m^n only up to the random factor W. It does not give the law of W, which solves the distributional equation W = m^(−1) Σ_{i≤Z_1} W⁽ⁱ⁾.
If E[L log⁺ L] = ∞, the theorem says only that Z_n/m^n → 0. The Seneta–Heyde theorem gives constants c_n with c_{n+1}/c_n → m such that Z_n/c_n has a nonzero finite limit on survival.

results.name: Pólya's recurrence theorem
aliases: Pólya's theorem on simple random walk
recurrence of simple random walk in dimensions one and two
results.statement: Let d ≥ 1 and let S_n = X₁ + … + X_n be simple random walk on ℤ^d: S₀ = 0, and the steps X₁, X₂, … are independent and uniform on the 2d vectors ±e₁, …, ±e_d. Let ρ = P(S_n = 0 for some n ≥ 1) and φ(t) = (1/d) Σ_{j=1}^{d} cos t_j. Then Σ_{n≥0} P(S_n = 0) = 1/(1 − ρ) = (2π)^(−d) ∫_{[−π,π]^d} dt/(1 − φ(t)), where all three expressions equal +∞ when ρ = 1. If d = 1 or d = 2, then ρ = 1 and S_n = 0 for infinitely many n almost surely: the walk is recurrent. If d ≥ 3, then ρ < 1 and S_n = 0 for only finitely many n almost surely: the walk is transient.
hypotheses: The walk starts at the origin, S₀ = 0.
The steps X₁, X₂, … are independent, and each is uniform on the 2d nearest-neighbour vectors ±e₁, …, ±e_d of ℤ^d.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 exchanges expectation and an infinite sum of indicators with the Tonelli form of Fubini's theorem to get E V = Σ P(S_n = 0).
Step s3 lets r increase to 1 in Σ r^n P(S_n = 0) and on the set {φ ≥ 0} with the monotone convergence theorem.
Step s3 passes to the limit r → 1 on the set {φ < 0}, where 1/(1 − rφ) lies in [1/2, 1], with the dominated convergence theorem.
Step s4 uses Jordan's inequality sin u ≥ 2u/π on [0, π/2] to get the lower bound 1 − cos u ≥ 2u²/π² for |u| ≤ π.

definitions.name: simple random walk on ℤ^d
definitions.text: The random walk S_n = X₁ + … + X_n whose independent steps are uniform on the 2d unit vectors ±e₁, …, ±e_d.

definitions.name: recurrent and transient
definitions.text: The walk is recurrent if it returns to its starting point with probability 1, and transient otherwise.

definitions.name: Green function at the origin
definitions.text: G = Σ_{n≥0} P(S_n = 0), the expected number of visits to the origin, including the visit at time 0.

source.alignment: The source states only the dichotomy and gets it from the Fourier criterion of Theorem B.72, p. 514. The authored statement adds the identity between the Green function, the return probability and the Fourier integral, and the almost sure finiteness or infiniteness of the number of returns. The authored proof follows Theorem B.72 and Corollary B.73. It replaces the local Taylor bounds of the source by global bounds on the whole torus from Jordan's inequality.

proof.scope: The full statement in every dimension d ≥ 1, with the identity for the Green function.

steps.text: Let τ₀ = 0 and τ_k = inf{m > τ_{k−1}: S_m = 0} be the successive return times. For every j, the event {τ_k = j} depends only on X₁, …, X_j, and the walk (S_{j+i} − S_j)_{i≥0} is independent of X₁, …, X_j with the law of S. So P(τ_{k+1} < ∞) = Σ_j P(τ_k = j) ρ = ρ P(τ_k < ∞), and P(τ_k < ∞) = ρ^k. The number of visits V = Σ_{n≥0} 1{S_n = 0} equals Σ_{k≥0} 1{τ_k < ∞}. Tonelli's theorem gives G := Σ_n P(S_n = 0) = E V = Σ_k ρ^k = 1/(1 − ρ), with value +∞ when ρ = 1. If ρ = 1, every τ_k is finite almost surely, so the walk returns infinitely often. If ρ < 1, then E V < ∞, so V < ∞ almost surely.

The characteristic function of one step is E e^(i t·X₁) = (1/2d) Σ_j (e^(i t_j) + e^(−i t_j)) = φ(t), and independence gives E e^(i t·S_n) = φ(t)^n. For x ∈ ℤ^d, (2π)^(−d) ∫_{[−π,π]^d} e^(i t·x) dt = 1 if x = 0 and 0 otherwise. Since S_n takes finitely many values, the expectation and the integral commute, and P(S_n = 0) = (2π)^(−d) ∫_{[−π,π]^d} φ(t)^n dt.

Fix r ∈ [0, 1). Since |rφ| ≤ r < 1, the geometric series Σ_n (rφ(t))^n converges uniformly to 1/(1 − rφ(t)), so Σ_n r^n P(S_n = 0) = (2π)^(−d) ∫ dt/(1 − rφ(t)). As r increases to 1, the left side increases to G by monotone convergence. On {φ ≥ 0} the integrand increases to 1/(1 − φ) (which is +∞ only at t = 0), so monotone convergence applies. On {φ < 0} the integrand lies in [1/2, 1] and converges to 1/(1 − φ), so dominated convergence applies. Hence G = (2π)^(−d) ∫_{[−π,π]^d} dt/(1 − φ(t)) in [1, ∞].

For |u| ≤ π, write 1 − cos u = 2 sin²(u/2). Jordan's inequality |sin(u/2)| ≥ |u|/π gives 1 − cos u ≥ 2u²/π², and the elementary bound cos u ≥ 1 − u²/2 gives 1 − cos u ≤ u²/2. Averaging over the d coordinates gives 2|t|²/(π² d) ≤ 1 − φ(t) ≤ |t|²/(2d) on [−π, π]^d. Hence 2d/|t|² ≤ 1/(1 − φ(t)) ≤ π² d/(2|t|²).

By step s4, G is finite if and only if ∫_{[−π,π]^d} |t|^(−2) dt is finite. The cube contains the ball of radius π and lies in the ball of radius π√d. In polar coordinates ∫_{|t|≤R} |t|^(−2) dt = σ_{d−1} ∫₀^R r^(d−3) dr, where σ_{d−1} is the area of the unit sphere. For d = 1 the integral ∫_{−π}^{π} t^(−2) dt is infinite, and for d = 2 the integral ∫₀^π r^(−1) dr is infinite. For d ≥ 3 the value is σ_{d−1}(π√d)^(d−2)/(d − 2) < ∞. So G = ∞ and ρ = 1 for d ≤ 2, and G < ∞ and ρ = 1 − 1/G < 1 for d ≥ 3. Step s1 converts this into the almost sure statements on the number of returns.

applications.title: A vacancy that hops in a simple cubic crystal escapes with positive probability
applications.inputs: A vacancy in a simple cubic crystal ℤ³ jumps at each step to one of its 6 nearest neighbours with probability 1/6 each, independently of the past. The quantity of interest is ρ, the probability that it ever comes back to its initial site.
applications.hypotheses: The positions of the vacancy form simple random walk on ℤ³ started at its initial site, so the theorem applies with d = 3.

steps.text: By step s4 with d = 3, 1/(1 − φ(t)) ≤ 3π²/(2|t|²) on [−π, π]³. The cube lies in the ball of radius π√3, and in ℝ³ the integral ∫_{|t|≤R} |t|^(−2) dt equals 4πR.
Use the rational bounds √3 ≤ 7/4 and π ≤ 22/7: G ≤ (3/4)(7/4)(22/7) = 33/8.
The identity 1 − ρ = 1/G gives the escape probability 1 − ρ ≥ 8/33, so the return probability satisfies ρ ≤ 1 − 8/33 = 25/33.

The expected number of returns is G − 1 = ρ/(1 − ρ) ≤ 33/8 − 1 = 25/8. In contrast, on a square lattice ℤ² (a crystal surface) the same vacancy returns with probability 1 and returns infinitely often.

applications.conclusion: A vacancy in a simple cubic crystal never returns to its initial site with probability at least 8/33, and it makes at most 25/8 returns on average. The crude bound uses only step s4. The exact value from Watson's integral is ρ ≈ 0.34.

limitations: The theorem concerns the nearest-neighbour walk with equal step probabilities. The dichotomy between d ≤ 2 and d ≥ 3 also holds for random walks on ℤ^d with centred steps of finite variance that generate ℤ^d, by the Chung–Fuchs criterion, but the value of G changes.
The theorem does not give the speed of escape in d ≥ 3 or the growth of the number of visits in d ≤ 2. For example, the expected number of visits to 0 up to time 2n grows like (1/π) log n in d = 2.

results.name: Nash-Williams criterion for recurrence
aliases: Nash-Williams inequality for effective resistance to infinity
results.statement: Let G = (V, E) be an infinite, connected, locally finite graph with conductances c(e) ∈ (0, ∞) on its edges. Let π(x) = Σ_{y∼x} c(x, y), and let the network random walk jump from x to a neighbour y with probability c(x, y)/π(x). Fix a ∈ V and let τ_a⁺ = inf{n ≥ 1: X_n = a}. A set Π ⊂ E separates a from ∞ if every infinite simple path that starts at a uses an edge of Π. Let Π₁, Π₂, … be pairwise disjoint edge sets that each separate a from ∞, and let s_k = Σ_{e∈Π_k} c(e) ∈ (0, ∞]. Then the effective resistance R(a ↔ ∞) := 1/(π(a) P_a(τ_a⁺ = ∞)) satisfies R(a ↔ ∞) ≥ Σ_k 1/s_k, with 1/∞ = 0. In particular, if Σ_k 1/s_k = ∞, then P_a(τ_a⁺ < ∞) = 1: the network is recurrent.
hypotheses: The graph G is infinite, connected and locally finite, and every edge has a conductance c(e) ∈ (0, ∞).
The edge sets Π₁, Π₂, … are pairwise disjoint, and each of them meets every infinite simple path that starts at a.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 conditions on the first step of the walk with the Markov property to show that the hitting probability v is harmonic off {a} ∪ Z_m.
Step s4 applies the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality to Σ_{e∈Π} |θ(e)| = Σ_{e∈Π} √c(e) · √r(e) |θ(e)| to bound the energy of the flow on one cutset.
Step s5 uses Kőnig's infinity lemma: an infinite, connected, locally finite graph contains an infinite simple path from each vertex, so the component of a off Π_k is finite.

definitions.name: network random walk
definitions.text: The Markov chain on V with transition probabilities P(x, y) = c(x, y)/π(x), where π(x) = Σ_{y∼x} c(x, y).

definitions.name: cutset separating a from ∞
definitions.text: A set Π of edges such that every infinite simple path that starts at a uses at least one edge of Π.

definitions.name: effective resistance to infinity
definitions.text: R(a ↔ ∞) = 1/(π(a) P_a(τ_a⁺ = ∞)), with value +∞ when the walk returns to a almost surely. It is the limit of the effective resistances from a to the complements of large finite sets.

definitions.name: unit flow
definitions.text: An antisymmetric function θ on oriented edges with Σ_y θ(a, y) = 1 at the source a and Σ_y θ(x, y) = 0 at every other vertex x outside the sink set. Its energy is Σ_e r(e) θ(e)², where r = 1/c.

source.alignment: The source states the recurrence conclusion and proves it from the Nash-Williams inequality for finite networks (Proposition 9.16 and Lemma 9.15, pp. 123-124) and the formula (21.2) for the escape probability. The authored statement adds local finiteness, defines separation from ∞ by infinite simple paths, and gives the quantitative bound R(a ↔ ∞) ≥ Σ_k 1/s_k. The authored proof follows the same route. It proves the energy identity for the unit current directly, so Thomson's principle is not needed, and it uses Kőnig's lemma so that the cutsets may be infinite.

proof.scope: The full statement, for finite or infinite cutsets in a locally finite network.

steps.text: Let d be the graph distance, V_m = {x: d(a, x) ≤ m} and Z_m = {x: d(a, x) = m}. Let G_m be the finite network of all edges of G with both ends in V_m. A vertex x with d(a, x) < m has all its neighbours in V_m. For x ∈ V_m let v(x) = P_x(τ_a < τ_{Z_m}), where τ_A is the first time n ≥ 0 with X_n ∈ A. Then v(a) = 1, v = 0 on Z_m, and the Markov property at time 1 gives v(x) = Σ_y P(x, y) v(y) for x ∈ V_m ∖ (Z_m ∪ {a}). Set i(x, y) = c(x, y)(v(x) − v(y)) and div i(x) = Σ_{y∼x} i(x, y) = π(x)(v(x) − Σ_y P(x, y)v(y)). So div i = 0 off {a} ∪ Z_m, and I_m := div i(a) = π(a)(1 − P_a(τ_a⁺ < τ_{Z_m})). A shortest path from a to Z_m shows I_m > 0.

Energy identity. Sum over ordered pairs of neighbours in G_m and exchange the names x and y in half of the sum: Σ_{e∈G_m} c(e)(v(x) − v(y))² = Σ_{x∈V_m} v(x) Σ_{y∼x} c(x, y)(v(x) − v(y)). The terms with x ∈ Z_m vanish because v(x) = 0, and the other x have all their neighbours in G_m. So the sum equals Σ_x v(x) div i(x) = v(a) I_m = I_m. Hence θ = i/I_m is a unit flow from a to Z_m, and its energy is Σ_e r(e)θ(e)² = I_m/I_m² = 1/I_m, where r = 1/c.

Cutset bound. Let Π be a set of edges of G_m such that every path in G_m from a to Z_m uses an edge of Π. Let A be the set of vertices that a path from a with no edge of Π reaches. Then A ∩ Z_m = ∅, so Σ_{x∈A} div θ(x) = div θ(a) = 1. By antisymmetry the terms θ(x, y) with both x and y in A cancel, so 1 = Σ_{x∈A, y∉A, y∼x} θ(x, y). Each such edge lies in Π, because otherwise y would be in A. Hence Σ_{e∈Π} |θ(e)| ≥ 1.

The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives 1 ≤ (Σ_{e∈Π} |θ(e)|)² ≤ (Σ_{e∈Π} c(e)) (Σ_{e∈Π} r(e)θ(e)²). Suppose that the disjoint sets Π₁ ∩ E(G_m), …, Π_N ∩ E(G_m) each separate a from Z_m in G_m. Their conductance sums are at most s₁, …, s_N. Summing the energy over these disjoint sets gives 1/I_m = Σ_e r(e)θ(e)² ≥ Σ_{k≤N} 1/s_k.

Let C_k be the set of vertices that a path in G from a with no edge of Π_k reaches. The graph on C_k with the edges of G ∖ Π_k is connected and locally finite. If it were infinite, Kőnig's lemma would give an infinite simple path from a that avoids Π_k, which contradicts the hypothesis. So C_k is finite. Choose m_N larger than d(a, x) for every x ∈ C₁ ∪ … ∪ C_N. For m ≥ m_N, a path in G_m from a to Z_m leaves C_k, and its first edge out of C_k lies in Π_k. So the hypothesis of step s4 holds for every m ≥ m_N.

The event {τ_a⁺ = ∞} is contained in the complement of {τ_a⁺ < τ_{Z_m}}. Steps s1, s4 and s5 give, for m ≥ m_N, π(a) P_a(τ_a⁺ = ∞) ≤ I_m ≤ (Σ_{k≤N} 1/s_k)^(−1). Let N → ∞. Then π(a) P_a(τ_a⁺ = ∞) ≤ (Σ_k 1/s_k)^(−1), that is R(a ↔ ∞) ≥ Σ_k 1/s_k. If the series diverges, P_a(τ_a⁺ = ∞) = 0 and the walk returns to a almost surely.

applications.title: Recurrence of diffusion in a disordered planar resistor network
applications.inputs: The square lattice ℤ² with arbitrary edge conductances c(e) ∈ [1, 2], for example a random resistor network in a thin conducting film. The base point is a = 0. Let Λ_n = [−n, n]² and let Π_n be the set of edges from Λ_{n−1} to ℤ² ∖ Λ_{n−1}, for n ≥ 1.
applications.hypotheses: The graph ℤ² is infinite, connected and locally finite, and all conductances are in (0, ∞). Every infinite simple path from 0 leaves the finite box Λ_{n−1}, and the edge that it uses to leave lies in Π_n. The sets Π_n are disjoint because their inner ends lie on the disjoint boundaries of the boxes.

steps.text: Count the edges: the boundary of Λ_{n−1} has 8(n − 1) vertices for n ≥ 2. Each of them has one outward edge, and each of the 4 corners has one more. So |Π_n| = 8n − 4 = 4(2n − 1), which also holds for n = 1.
Since c(e) ≤ 2, s_n ≤ 8(2n − 1), so 1/s_n ≥ 1/(8(2n − 1)). For the first three cutsets this gives the partial lower bound (1/8)(1 + 1/3 + 1/5) = 23/120 for R(0 ↔ ∞).
In general Σ_{n=1}^{N} 1/(2n − 1) ≥ ∫_1^{N+1} dx/(2x − 1) = (1/2) log(2N + 1), so R(0 ↔ ∞) ≥ (1/16) log(2N + 1) for every N. Hence Σ_n 1/s_n = ∞.
The criterion gives R(0 ↔ ∞) = ∞ and P_0(τ_0⁺ < ∞) = 1 for every choice of the conductances in [1, 2].

applications.conclusion: A particle that diffuses in a planar network with conductances between 1 and 2 returns to its start with probability 1, whatever the disorder. The first N cutsets alone give R(0 ↔ ∞) ≥ (1/16) log(2N + 1), and this bound has no upper limit as N grows.

limitations: The criterion is sufficient but not necessary: there are recurrent networks for which Σ_k 1/s_k < ∞ for every choice of disjoint cutsets.
The criterion only proves recurrence. A proof of transience needs an upper bound on the effective resistance, for example a unit flow of finite energy and Thomson's principle.

results.name: Rayleigh monotonicity principle
results.statement: Let G = (V, E) be a finite connected graph and let a ≠ z be vertices. For an assignment r of resistances r(e) ∈ (0, ∞) to the edges, let R(a ↔ z; r) be the effective resistance between a and z in the network (G, 1/r). (i) If r and r′ are two such assignments with r(e) ≤ r′(e) for every edge e, then R(a ↔ z; r) ≤ R(a ↔ z; r′). Equivalently, the effective conductance 1/R(a ↔ z) is a nondecreasing function of each edge conductance. (ii) If G⁺ is obtained from G by adding one edge, with any resistance in (0, ∞), between two vertices of G, then the effective resistance between a and z in G⁺ is at most that in G, for the same resistances on the edges of G.
hypotheses: G = (V, E) is a finite connected graph, and a and z are distinct vertices.
In part (i), r and r′ are assignments of resistances in (0, ∞) to the edges with r(e) ≤ r′(e) for every edge e.

prerequisites.reason: Steps s1 and s2 use Thomson's principle: the effective resistance is the minimum energy of a unit flow and equals the energy of the unit current flow.

definitions.name: unit flow from a to z
definitions.text: An antisymmetric function θ on oriented edges with Σ_y θ(x, y) = 0 at every vertex x ∉ {a, z} and Σ_y θ(a, y) = 1.

definitions.name: energy of a flow
definitions.text: E_r(θ) = Σ_{e∈E} r(e) θ(e)², with one term for each unoriented edge.

definitions.name: effective resistance
definitions.text: R(a ↔ z; r) = 1/‖I‖, where W is the voltage (W(a) = 1, W(z) = 0, harmonic at the other vertices) and ‖I‖ = Σ_y c(a, y)(W(a) − W(y)) is the strength of its current.

source.excerpt: Theorem 9.12 (Rayleigh's Monotonicity Law). If {r(e)} and {r′(e)} are two assignments of resistances to the edges of the same graph G that satisfy r(e) ≤ r′(e) for all e, then R(a ↔ z; r) ≤ R(a ↔ z; r′).
