source.alignment: Part (i) is the source theorem, with the finite connected graph and the positive resistances made explicit. Part (ii) is Corollary 9.13 of the source (adding an edge does not increase the effective resistance). The authored proof of part (i) follows the source proof through Thomson's principle (Theorem 9.10), with the current flow of r′ as the explicit test flow. The proof of part (ii) extends the current flow of G by zero on the new edge.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the proof of Theorem 9.12 and Corollary 9.13 in Levin and Peres through Thomson's principle. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Both parts of the statement for finite connected graphs with resistances in (0, ∞).

steps.text: Part (i). The definition of a unit flow from a to z involves only the graph, not the resistances. Let i′ be the unit current flow of the network with resistances r′. It is a unit flow from a to z for both assignments. Thomson's principle for r gives R(a ↔ z; r) ≤ E_r(i′) = Σ_e r(e) i′(e)². Since r(e) ≤ r′(e) and i′(e)² ≥ 0 for every edge, Σ_e r(e) i′(e)² ≤ Σ_e r′(e) i′(e)² = E_{r′}(i′). Thomson's principle for r′ says that the current flow attains the minimum, so E_{r′}(i′) = R(a ↔ z; r′). Together, R(a ↔ z; r) ≤ R(a ↔ z; r′).

Part (ii). The graph G⁺ is finite and connected, because it contains the connected graph G on the same vertex set. Let i be the unit current flow of G from a to z, and let θ be equal to i on the oriented edges of G and equal to 0 on both orientations of the new edge e₀. Then θ is antisymmetric, and its divergence at each vertex is the same as that of i, because the new edge adds 0. So θ is a unit flow from a to z in G⁺. Its energy in G⁺ is E(i) + r(e₀) · 0² = E(i), which is the effective resistance in G by Thomson's principle. Thomson's principle in G⁺ then gives R_{G⁺}(a ↔ z) ≤ E_{G⁺}(θ) = R_G(a ↔ z).

Conductance form. The effective conductance is C(a ↔ z) = 1/R(a ↔ z) and the edge conductances are c(e) = 1/r(e). Raising one conductance c(e) lowers r(e) and leaves the other resistances fixed. By part (i) this does not increase R(a ↔ z), so it does not decrease C(a ↔ z). Hence C(a ↔ z) is nondecreasing in each edge conductance.

applications.title: Bracketing a Wheatstone bridge with one degraded resistor
applications.inputs: Vertices a, b, c, z and edges ab, ac, bc, bz, cz (a Wheatstone bridge with bridge edge bc). The resistor ab has resistance 2 Ω, and the other four resistors have 1 Ω.
applications.hypotheses: The bridge graph is finite and connected, and a ≠ z. All resistances lie in (0, ∞). The all-1 Ω assignment is pointwise at most the given one. The bridge without the edge bc is still connected, and the full bridge is obtained from it by adding bc.

steps.text: Lower bound. With all five resistors equal to 1 Ω, the exchange of b and c is a symmetry that fixes a and z, so W(b) = W(c). Harmonicity at b gives W(b) = (1 + W(c) + 0)/3, so W(b) = W(c) = 1/2. The current out of a is (1 − 1/2) + (1 − 1/2) = 1, so R = 1 Ω. Part (i) gives R(a ↔ z) ≥ 1 Ω for the degraded bridge.

Upper bound. Delete the bridge edge bc. The branch a–b–z has resistance 2 + 1 = 3 Ω and the branch a–c–z has 1 + 1 = 2 Ω, in parallel, so the resistance is 3 · 2/(3 + 2) = 6/5 Ω. Adding bc back cannot increase it by part (ii), so R(a ↔ z) ≤ 6/5 Ω.

Exact value. With W(a) = 1 and W(z) = 0, harmonicity at b (conductances 1/2, 1, 1) and at c (conductances 1, 1, 1) gives 5W(b) = 1 + 2W(c) and 3W(c) = 1 + W(b). The solution is W(b) = 5/13 and W(c) = 6/13. The current out of a is (1/2)(1 − 5/13) + (1 − 6/13) = 11/13, so R(a ↔ z) = 13/11 Ω.
Check of the bracket: 1 ≤ 13/11 ≤ 6/5, because 13/11 − 1 = 2/11 ≥ 0 and 6/5 − 13/11 = 1/55 ≥ 0. The two monotonicity bounds already fix R(a ↔ z) to within 0.2 Ω without solving the network.

applications.conclusion: Rayleigh's principle brackets the effective resistance of the degraded bridge between 1 Ω and 6/5 Ω. The exact value 13/11 Ω lies in this interval, close to the upper bound.

limitations: The principle gives only an order between two networks. A quantitative estimate needs a test flow (Thomson's principle) or a cutset bound (Nash-Williams inequality).

The statement is for finite networks. The same argument gives monotonicity of the effective resistance to infinity, so a subnetwork of a recurrent network is recurrent. Shorting two vertices (gluing them) also does not increase the effective resistance.

results.name: Thomson's principle
results.statement: Let G = (V, E) be a finite connected graph with a conductance c(x, y) = c(y, x) > 0 on each edge and resistance r = 1/c. Let a ≠ z be vertices. A flow from a to z is an antisymmetric function θ on oriented edges with div θ(x) = Σ_y θ(x, y) = 0 for every x ∉ {a, z}. It is a unit flow if div θ(a) = 1. Its energy is E(θ) = Σ_{e∈E} r(e) θ(e)², with one term for each unoriented edge. There is a unique function W with W(a) = 1, W(z) = 0 and c(x)W(x) = Σ_y c(x, y)W(y) for every x ∉ {a, z}, where c(x) = Σ_y c(x, y). Let I(x, y) = c(x, y)(W(x) − W(y)) and ‖I‖ = div I(a). Then ‖I‖ > 0. Put R(a ↔ z) = 1/‖I‖ and i = I/‖I‖ (the unit current flow). Then i is a unit flow from a to z, and every unit flow θ from a to z satisfies E(θ) = R(a ↔ z) + E(θ − i). In particular R(a ↔ z) = min{E(θ) : θ a unit flow from a to z}, and i is the unique minimizer.
hypotheses: G = (V, E) is a finite connected graph, and each edge {x, y} carries a conductance c(x, y) = c(y, x) > 0.
The vertices a and z are distinct.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 uses the rank–nullity theorem: the square linear system for the voltage has only the zero solution for zero data, so it is solvable for every boundary data.

definitions.name: electrical network
definitions.text: A finite connected graph with a conductance c(x, y) = c(y, x) > 0 on each edge. The resistance of an edge is r = 1/c, and c(x) = Σ_y c(x, y).

definitions.name: flow from a to z
definitions.text: An antisymmetric function θ on oriented edges, θ(x, y) = −θ(y, x), with div θ(x) = Σ_y θ(x, y) = 0 at every x ∉ {a, z}. Its strength is div θ(a). A unit flow has strength 1.

definitions.name: energy of a flow
definitions.text: E(θ) = Σ_{e∈E} r(e) θ(e)², with one term for each unoriented edge. The term is well defined because θ(e)² does not depend on the orientation.

definitions.name: voltage and unit current flow
definitions.text: The voltage W has W(a) = 1, W(z) = 0 and c(x)W(x) = Σ_y c(x, y)W(y) at every x ∉ {a, z}. Its current is I(x, y) = c(x, y)(W(x) − W(y)) (Ohm's law), and the unit current flow is i = I/‖I‖ with ‖I‖ = div I(a).

definitions.name: effective resistance
definitions.text: R(a ↔ z) = (W(a) − W(z))/‖I‖ = 1/‖I‖: the voltage drop between a and z per unit of current.

source.citation: David A. Levin and Yuval Peres, with contributions by Elizabeth L. Wilmer, Markov Chains and Mixing Times, second edition, American Mathematical Society, 2017.

source.module: Chapter 9, Section 9.4 Effective Resistance
source.excerpt: Theorem 9.10 (Thomson's Principle). For any finite connected graph, R(a ↔ z) = inf{E(θ) : θ a unit flow from a to z}. The unique minimizer in the inf above is the unit current flow.
source.attribution: © David A. Levin and Yuval Peres. Quoted from Markov Chains and Mixing Times, second edition, for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states the principle with an infimum and the uniqueness of the minimizer, and it defines R(a ↔ z) through a voltage. The authored statement includes the existence of the voltage and adds the exact energy identity E(θ) = R(a ↔ z) + E(θ − i). The source proves the theorem by compactness and the cycle law (Proposition 9.4). The authored proof uses the orthogonal decomposition of a flow into the current and a sourceless flow, as in Lyons and Peres, Probability on Trees and Networks, Section 2.4, equation (2.10).

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the orthogonal decomposition argument of Lyons and Peres (Section 2.4) for the result cited from Levin and Peres. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement: existence and uniqueness of the voltage, positivity of the strength, the energy identity and the unique minimizer.

steps.text: Voltage. The conditions W(a) = 1, W(z) = 0 and c(x)W(x) = Σ_y c(x, y)W(y) for x ∉ {a, z} form a square linear system in the |V| − 2 unknowns W(x), x ∉ {a, z}. Suppose that g satisfies the homogeneous system: g is harmonic off {a, z} and g(a) = g(z) = 0. Let x be a vertex where g is maximal. If x ∉ {a, z}, then g(x) is an average of the values of g at the neighbours of x with positive weights, so every neighbour is also a maximum point. Follow a shortest path from x to the set {a, z}. All its vertices before the last one lie outside {a, z}, so the maximum spreads along the path to a or z. Hence max g = 0. The same argument for −g gives min g = 0, so g = 0. By the rank–nullity theorem the square system is solvable for every boundary data, and its solution W is unique. The same maximum argument, applied to W − 1 and to −W, gives 0 ≤ W ≤ 1.

Current. The function I(x, y) = c(x, y)(W(x) − W(y)) is antisymmetric, and div I(x) = c(x)W(x) − Σ_y c(x, y)W(y) = 0 for x ∉ {a, z}. Each oriented edge and its reverse cancel in Σ_x div I(x), so this sum is 0 and div I(z) = −div I(a). Since W ≤ 1, ‖I‖ = Σ_y c(a, y)(1 − W(y)) ≥ 0. If ‖I‖ = 0, every neighbour of a has W = 1. Take a path a = x₀, x₁, …, x_m = z without repeated vertices. Then W(x₁) = 1 is maximal. If x₁ ≠ z, then x₁ is harmonic, so W(x₂) = 1, and so on up to W(z) = 1. This contradicts W(z) = 0. So ‖I‖ > 0 and i = I/‖I‖ is a unit flow from a to z. With U = W/‖I‖ we have r(x, y) i(x, y) = U(x) − U(y) and U(a) − U(z) = 1/‖I‖ = R(a ↔ z).

Summation by parts. Let θ be any antisymmetric function on oriented edges. The product r i θ has the same value on both orientations of an edge, so Σ_{e∈E} r(e) i(e) θ(e) = ½ Σ_{x,y} (U(x) − U(y)) θ(x, y), where the double sum runs over ordered pairs of neighbours. The part with U(x) equals ½ Σ_x U(x) div θ(x). In the part −½ Σ U(y) θ(x, y), exchange the names x and y and use θ(y, x) = −θ(x, y). It also equals ½ Σ_x U(x) div θ(x). Hence Σ_{e∈E} r(e) i(e) θ(e) = Σ_x U(x) div θ(x).

Energy identity. Let θ be a unit flow from a to z. As in step s2, the divergences of θ sum to 0, so div θ equals 1 at a, −1 at z and 0 elsewhere. Step s3 gives Σ_e r(e) i(e) θ(e) = U(a) − U(z) = R(a ↔ z). With θ = i this gives E(i) = R(a ↔ z). Put φ = θ − i. Then div φ = 0 at every vertex, so step s3 gives Σ_e r(e) i(e) φ(e) = 0. Expansion of the square gives E(θ) = E(i) + 2 Σ_e r(e) i(e) φ(e) + E(φ) = R(a ↔ z) + E(θ − i).

Minimum. Every r(e) is positive, so E(θ − i) ≥ 0, with equality only if θ(e) = i(e) on every edge. Hence E(θ) ≥ R(a ↔ z) for every unit flow θ from a to z, with equality only for θ = i. Since i is itself a unit flow with E(i) = R(a ↔ z), the minimum exists, equals R(a ↔ z), and the unit current flow is the unique minimizer.

applications.title: Effective resistance between opposite corners of a cube of unit resistors
applications.inputs: The cube graph with vertex set {0, 1}³ and 12 edges between vertices that differ in one coordinate. Every edge is a 1 Ω resistor. The terminals are a = 000 and z = 111.
applications.hypotheses: The cube graph is finite and connected, and every conductance equals 1 > 0. The terminals 000 and 111 are distinct.

steps.text: Test flow θ₁: send 1/3 along each of the three paths 000 → 100 → 110 → 111, 000 → 010 → 011 → 111 and 000 → 001 → 101 → 111. The six inner vertices are distinct, and each receives 1/3 and sends 1/3, so θ₁ is a unit flow. It uses 9 edges with value 1/3, so E(θ₁) = 9 · (1/3)² = 1 and Thomson's principle gives R(a ↔ z) ≤ 1.

Symmetric flow θ₂: 1/3 on each of the 3 edges at 000, 1/6 on each of the 6 edges between level 1 and level 2, and 1/3 on each of the 3 edges at 111. A level-1 vertex receives 1/3 and sends 2 · 1/6, and a level-2 vertex receives 2 · 1/6 and sends 1/3, so θ₂ is a unit flow. Its energy is 3 · (1/3)² + 6 · (1/6)² + 3 · (1/3)² = 5/6, so R(a ↔ z) ≤ 5/6.

The flow θ₂ is the unit current flow. Put U = 0 at level 3, U = 1/3 at level 2, U = 1/2 at level 1 and U = 5/6 at level 0. Then θ₂(x, y) = U(x) − U(y) on every edge. The node law for θ₂ says that U is harmonic at the inner vertices, so W = U/U(a) is the voltage and θ₂ = i. Hence R(a ↔ z) = E(i) = 5/6.

The energy identity gives E(θ₁) − R(a ↔ z) = E(θ₁ − i). Here θ₁ − i is 0 on the edges at the terminals, 1/6 on the three used middle edges and −1/6 on the three unused middle edges, so E(θ₁ − i) = 6 · (1/6)² = 1/6 = 1 − 5/6.

applications.conclusion: The effective resistance between opposite corners of the unit cube of 1 Ω resistors is 5/6 Ω. The crude test flow along three disjoint paths gives the bound 1 Ω, and its excess energy 1/6 is exactly the energy of its difference from the current flow.

limitations: The principle gives upper bounds on R(a ↔ z) from test flows. Lower bounds need a dual tool, such as Dirichlet's principle for the effective conductance or the Nash-Williams inequality.

The statement is for a finite network. On an infinite network the effective resistance to infinity is the infimum of the energies of unit flows to infinity, and it is finite exactly when the random walk is transient (T. Lyons' criterion).

results.name: Commute time identity
results.statement: Let G = (V, E) be a finite connected graph with a conductance c(x, y) = c(y, x) > 0 on each edge. Put c(x) = Σ_y c(x, y) and c_G = Σ_x c(x) = 2 Σ_{e∈E} c(e). Let (X_t)_{t≥0} be the random walk on the network, with transition probabilities P(x, y) = c(x, y)/c(x), and let τ_y = min{t ≥ 0 : X_t = y}. For distinct vertices a and b, let W be the unique function with W(a) = 1, W(b) = 0 and W(x) = Σ_y P(x, y)W(y) at every other vertex x, and let R(a ↔ b) = 1/Σ_y c(a, y)(1 − W(y)) be the effective resistance. Then the commute time between a and b satisfies E_a τ_b + E_b τ_a = c_G R(a ↔ b).
hypotheses: G = (V, E) is a finite connected graph, and each edge carries a conductance c(x, y) = c(y, x) > 0.
The vertices a and b are distinct, and (X_t) is the random walk with P(x, y) = c(x, y)/c(x).

prerequisites.reason: Step s2 uses the existence and uniqueness of the voltage W and the positivity of its current strength, which the cited record proves with the maximum principle.
Step s4 exchanges the sum over times with the sum over states in Σ_x ρ(x)P(x, y), which Tonelli's theorem allows for nonnegative terms.
Step s5 uses the rank–nullity theorem for P − I and its transpose to show that the invariant row vectors form a one-dimensional space.
Step s3 sums the geometric series Σ_{k≥1} (1 − p)^(k−1) = 1/p for the mean number of visits to a before τ_b.

definitions.name: random walk on a network
definitions.text: The Markov chain on V with P(x, y) = c(x, y)/c(x), where c(x) = Σ_y c(x, y). It is reversible, and π(x) = c(x)/c_G is a stationary distribution.

definitions.name: commute time
definitions.text: E_a τ_b + E_b τ_a, the mean time for the walk started at a to reach b and then return to a.

definitions.name: effective resistance
definitions.text: R(a ↔ b) = 1/‖I‖, where ‖I‖ = Σ_y c(a, y)(W(a) − W(y)) is the current that leaves a under the voltage W with W(a) = 1 and W(b) = 0.

definitions.name: escape probability
definitions.text: P_a(τ_b < τ_a⁺), where τ_a⁺ = min{t ≥ 1 : X_t = a} is the first return time to a.

source.module: Chapter 10, Section 10.3 Commute Time
source.excerpt: Proposition 10.7 (Commute Time Identity). Let (G, {c(e)}) be a network, and let (X_t) be the random walk on this network. For any nodes a and b in V, t_{a↔b} = c_G R(a ↔ b).
source.attribution: © David A. Levin and Yuval Peres. Quoted from Markov Chains and Mixing Times, second edition, for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states the identity for a network with t_{a↔b} = E_a τ_b + E_b τ_a and a finite connected graph from its Chapter 9 conventions. The authored statement writes out the network, the walk and the effective resistance. The authored proof follows the source proof: the cycle trick (Lemma 10.5 and Remark 10.6), the Green function at a (Lemma 9.6) and the escape probability (Proposition 9.5). It also proves the finiteness of the hitting times and the uniqueness of the stationary distribution that the source takes from earlier chapters.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the proof of Proposition 10.7 in Levin and Peres. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full identity for every finite connected network and every pair of distinct vertices.

steps.text: Finite hitting times. Let n = |V|. Since G is connected, from every vertex x there is a path to b of length at most n, and the walk follows it with positive probability. Let δ > 0 be the smallest of these probabilities over x. By the Markov property at the times n, 2n, …, P_x(τ_b > kn) ≤ (1 − δ)^k, so E_x τ_b = Σ_{t≥0} P_x(τ_b > t) ≤ n/δ < ∞ for every x and b. The proof below also uses the strong Markov property at hitting times: given X_T = y at a finite hitting time T, the walk after T is a walk started at y, independent of the walk before T. For a discrete-time chain this follows from the Markov property by splitting on the events {T = m}.

Escape probability. Let h(x) = P_x(τ_b < τ_a). Then h(a) = 0 and h(b) = 1. For x ∉ {a, b} both hitting times are at least 1, and conditioning on the first step gives h(x) = Σ_y P(x, y)h(y). So 1 − h has the defining properties of the voltage W, and by uniqueness of the voltage 1 − h = W. Conditioning on the first step from a gives the escape probability p = P_a(τ_b < τ_a⁺) = Σ_y P(a, y)h(y) = Σ_y (c(a, y)/c(a))(1 − W(y)) = 1/(c(a)R(a ↔ b)). In particular p > 0.

Green function at a. Under P_a let N be the number of times t < τ_b with X_t = a, the visit at time 0 included. If the walk has made k visits to a before τ_b, the strong Markov property at the k-th visit says that it makes another one before τ_b with probability P_a(τ_a⁺ < τ_b) = 1 − p. Hence P_a(N ≥ k) = (1 − p)^(k−1) for k ≥ 1, and E_a N = Σ_{k≥1} (1 − p)^(k−1) = 1/p = c(a)R(a ↔ b).

Cycle trick. Under P_a let τ = min{t ≥ τ_b : X_t = a}. The strong Markov property at τ_b and step s1 give E_a τ = E_a τ_b + E_b τ_a < ∞. Put ρ(x) = E_a Σ_{t=0}^{τ−1} 1{X_t = x} = Σ_{t≥0} P_a(X_t = x, t < τ). The event {t < τ} depends only on X_0, …, X_t, so the Markov property and Tonelli's theorem give Σ_x ρ(x)P(x, y) = Σ_{t≥0} P_a(X_{t+1} = y, t < τ) = Σ_{s≥1} P_a(X_s = y, s ≤ τ). This equals ρ(y) − P_a(X_0 = y) + P_a(X_τ = y), because τ ≥ 1. Both correction terms equal 1{y = a}, since X_0 = X_τ = a. So ρP = ρ, and Σ_x ρ(x) = E_a τ.

Uniqueness of the invariant vector. The vector π(x) = c(x)/c_G satisfies πP = π, because Σ_x c(x)P(x, y) = Σ_x c(x, y) = c(y). If Pf = f, let x be a maximum point of f. Then f(x) is an average of its neighbours' values with positive weights, so every neighbour is a maximum point too, and connectivity makes f constant. So the kernel of P − I has dimension 1. By the rank–nullity theorem, P − I has rank |V| − 1, and so does its transpose. Hence the row vectors ν with νP = ν form a one-dimensional space, and ρ = (E_a τ) π.

Conclusion. The visits to a before τ are the N visits before τ_b, because τ is the first visit to a at or after τ_b. So ρ(a) = E_a N = c(a)R(a ↔ b) by step s3. Step s5 gives ρ(a) = (E_a τ) c(a)/c_G. Since c(a) > 0, E_a τ = c_G R(a ↔ b), and step s4 gives E_a τ_b + E_b τ_a = c_G R(a ↔ b).

applications.title: Commute time across a disordered one-dimensional chain
applications.inputs: The path with vertices 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and bond conductances c(0,1) = 1, c(1,2) = 2, c(2,3) = 1, c(3,4) = 2 (a random conductance model on a chain of length 4). The walk jumps to a neighbour with probability proportional to the bond conductance. The terminals are a = 0 and b = 4.
applications.hypotheses: The path is finite and connected, all conductances are positive, and 0 ≠ 4. The walk is the network random walk of these conductances.

steps.text: Effective resistance. On a path the node law forces the same current I through every bond, and Ohm's law gives a voltage drop I/c(e) across each bond. So W(0) − W(4) = I Σ_e 1/c(e), and R(0 ↔ 4) = 1 + 1/2 + 1 + 1/2 = 3 (resistances in series add).
Total conductance. c_G = 2 Σ_e c(e) = 2(1 + 2 + 1 + 2) = 12. The commute time identity gives E_0 τ_4 + E_4 τ_0 = 12 · 3 = 36.

Direct check. With vertex weights c(0), …, c(4) = 1, 3, 3, 3, 2, the first-step equations give E_0 τ_4 = Σ_{k=1}^4 (1/c(k−1,k)) Σ_{j<k} c(j) = 1 + 2 + 7 + 5 = 15 and E_4 τ_0 = 1 + 5 + 4 + 11 = 21. The two one-way times differ, but their sum is 15 + 21 = 36, as the identity predicts.

Effect of disorder. For a chain of n bonds, the identity gives commute time 2(Σ_e c(e))(Σ_e 1/c(e)) ≥ 2n² by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, with equality only for equal conductances. Here 36 > 2 · 4² = 32, so the disorder slows the commute by the factor 36/32 = 9/8.

applications.conclusion: The mean commute time between the ends of the disordered chain is 36 steps (15 out and 21 back). The identity reduces it to one series resistance and one total conductance, and it shows that any disorder in the bond conductances increases the commute time above the value 2n² of the uniform chain.

limitations: The identity gives only the sum E_a τ_b + E_b τ_a. The two one-way hitting times can be very different, unless a symmetry of the network exchanges a and b.
The identity needs a reversible chain, that is a random walk on a network. For a nonreversible chain the commute time is not given by an effective resistance of this form.
The identity is for finite networks. On an infinite recurrent network, such as the simple random walk on ℤ², the effective resistance between two vertices is finite but the commute time is infinite.

results.name: Wilson's algorithm
aliases: Wilson's algorithm for uniform spanning trees
results.statement: Let p be the transition matrix of an irreducible Markov chain on a finite state space V, and fix a state r ∈ V. A spanning tree rooted at r is a set t of directed edges (x, y) with p(x, y) > 0 that has exactly one edge out of each x ≠ r, no edge out of r and no directed cycle. Its weight is Ψ(t) = ∏_{(x,y)∈t} p(x, y). Wilson's method fixes any order of V ∖ {r} and sets T(0) = {r}. While T(i) does not contain every state, it runs the chain from the first state in the order that is not in T(i), independently of all earlier runs, until the run hits a state of T(i). It adds the loop erasure of this path to T(i) to get T(i + 1). Then the method stops with probability 1, and its final tree T satisfies P(T = t) = Ψ(t)/∑_{t′} Ψ(t′) for every spanning tree t rooted at r, where t′ runs over all spanning trees rooted at r. In particular, the law of T does not depend on the order. Now let G = (V, E) be a finite connected simple graph with conductances c(e) > 0 on its edges, and let p(x, y) = c(x, y)/π(x) with π(x) = ∑_y c(x, y). Then T without orientation is a spanning tree of G with P(T = t) = Ξ(t)/∑_{t′} Ξ(t′), where Ξ(t) = ∏_{e∈t} c(e) and t′ runs over all spanning trees of G. If c(e) = 1 for every edge, T is a uniform spanning tree of G.
hypotheses: p is the transition matrix of an irreducible Markov chain on a finite state space V, and r ∈ V is any state.
The order of the starting states in V ∖ {r} is arbitrary but fixed, and each run of the chain is independent of the earlier runs.
For the second part, G is a finite connected simple graph with conductances c(e) > 0, and p is the network random walk p(x, y) = c(x, y)/π(x).

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 uses the Ionescu-Tulcea theorem to build a probability space that carries the countable family of independent stack entries S_i^x.

definitions.name: loop erasure
definitions.text: For a finite path ⟨x₀, …, x_l⟩, set u₀ = x₀. If u_k ≠ x_l, let u_{k+1} = x_{i+1} with i the last time j at which x_j = u_k. Stop at the first m with u_m = x_l. The loop erasure is the path ⟨u₀, …, u_m⟩, which has no repeated state.

definitions.name: spanning tree rooted at r
definitions.text: A set of directed edges with p(x, y) > 0, one out of each state x ≠ r and none out of r, with no directed cycle. Its edges point toward r.

definitions.name: weighted uniform spanning tree
definitions.text: The random spanning tree T of a network with P(T = t) proportional to Ξ(t) = ∏_{e∈t} c(e). For c ≡ 1 it is the uniform spanning tree.

source.module: Chapter 4, Section 4.1 Generating Uniform Spanning Trees
source.excerpt: Theorem 4.1. Given any finite-state, irreducible Markov chain and any state r, Wilson's method yields a random spanning tree rooted at r with distribution proportional to Ψ( • ). Therefore, for any finite, connected, undirected graph, Wilson's method yields a random spanning tree that, when the orientation and root are forgotten, has distribution proportional to Ξ( • ).

source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The authored statement defines Wilson's method, the loop erasure and the weights Ψ and Ξ, which the source gives in the text before Theorem 4.1. It adds that the method stops with probability 1 and restricts the network part to simple graphs. The authored proof follows the cycle-popping proof of the source with Lemma 4.2 on p. 100. It adds the arguments that the source leaves short: why loop erasure pops visible cycles, why the stack version has the law of independent runs, and why each run stops.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the cycle-popping proof of Theorem 4.1 and Lemma 4.2 in Lyons and Peres. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement for every finite irreducible chain, every root and every order, and the network part for finite connected simple graphs with positive conductances.

steps.text: Stacks. Let S_i^x, for x ∈ V ∖ {r} and i ≥ 1, be independent states with P(S_i^x = y) = p(x, y). The Ionescu-Tulcea theorem gives a probability space for this countable family. The state r has an empty stack. Call (x, S_i^x) the edge of color i at x. The top under x is its first entry that is not yet removed. The visible graph has one edge from each x ≠ r to its top. To pop a visible cycle means to remove the tops under all its states. If the visible graph has no cycle, the out-edges from any x pass through distinct states and must end at r, the only state with no out-edge. So the visible graph is then a spanning tree rooted at r.

Order lemma (Lemma 4.2 of the source). Fix the stacks. A colored cycle C is poppable if some colored cycles C₁, …, C_n = C can be popped in this order, each one visible at its turn. Claim: if a visible cycle C′ ≠ C is popped first, C stays poppable. If C′ has no state in common with C₁, …, C_n, the pop of C′ does not change their tops. Otherwise let C_k be the first that meets C′, at a state x. No earlier C_j contains x, so the edge of C_k out of x is the present top edge at x, which is also the edge of C′. Its head is again in C′ and C_k, and the same argument continues around C′ until it returns to x. So C_k = C′ and k < n. Pops of disjoint cycles commute, so C′, C₁, …, C_{k−1}, C_{k+1}, …, C_n is a valid order.

Consequence. Let 𝒞 be the set of poppable colored cycles. Take any procedure that pops visible cycles until none is visible. By step s2 applied after each pop, each C ∈ 𝒞 stays poppable until the procedure pops it. When no cycle is visible, no C is poppable, because the first cycle of its order must be visible. A procedure pops only poppable cycles, and each colored cycle at most once. So a procedure that stops pops exactly 𝒞. Thus either 𝒞 is infinite and no procedure stops, or every procedure stops after it pops 𝒞. In the second case the final top under x is S^x_{n_x+1}, where n_x is the number of cycles of 𝒞 through x. So the final tree is a function of the stacks only.

Wilson's method pops cycles. Run it on the stacks. The walk reads the top under its present state without removal. It keeps a path ⟨u₀, …, u_m⟩ outside T(i) with top(u_j) = u_{j+1} for j < m. Let y = top(u_m). If y is in T(i), add the path and y to the tree. If y = u_j, then u_j, …, u_m with their tops form a visible cycle: pop it, cut the path to ⟨u₀, …, u_j⟩ and continue from u_j. Otherwise append y. A new point x_{t+1} changes only the last visit to x_{t+1}, so the last-visit definition shows that the kept path is the loop erasure of the walk. A state departs again only after its top is popped. So its k-th departure reads S_k^x, and the walk moves like the chain.

Law of the stack version. Each history h of the procedure up to a move is the event that finitely many fixed entries take fixed values. The next entry that the move reads is a fixed entry S_k^u that is not among them. So P(h and next state y) = P(h) p(u, y). The moves are therefore successive independent runs of the chain, and the stack version has the law of Wilson's method. For a nonempty set A, irreducibility gives each x a path into A of length at most |V| with positive probability, and ε > 0 is the least of these. By the Markov property, a run misses A up to time k|V| with probability at most (1 − ε)^k → 0. So each of the at most |V| − 1 runs ends, and the method stops with probability 1. Then every top is a tree edge and no cycle is visible. By step s3, 𝒞 is finite with probability 1, and the output is the tree T of step s3.

Law of the tree. Let X be the set of pairs (O, t) that occur as (𝒞, T) for some stacks. For (O, t) ∈ X, take an order C₁, …, C_n of O that is valid for such stacks. Its validity depends only on the entries S_i^x = y for the edges (x, y) of color i in O. If also S^x_{n_x+1} = t(x) for x ≠ r, the visible graph after these pops is t, so step s3 gives (𝒞, T) = (O, t). These places are distinct, so P(𝒞 = O, T = t) = Ψ(O)Ψ(t), with Ψ(O) the product of p over the edges of O. The same argument with any spanning tree t′ rooted at r shows (O, t′) ∈ X. So X = X₁ × X₂, with X₂ the set of all spanning trees rooted at r. Countable additivity over X₁ gives P(T = t) = Ψ(t) ∑_{O∈X₁} Ψ(O). These probabilities add to 1, so P(T = t) = Ψ(t)/∑_{t′} Ψ(t′).

Network case. The network walk is irreducible because G is connected, and p(x, y) > 0 exactly when xy ∈ E. Then Ψ(t) = ∏_{e∈t} c(e)/∏_{x≠r} π(x) = Ξ(t) π(r)/∏_{x∈V} π(x), and the last factor does not depend on t. Each spanning tree of G has exactly one orientation toward r: orient the first edge of the tree path from each x ≠ r to r out of x. This is a bijection between spanning trees of G and spanning trees rooted at r. So the unoriented tree has P(T = t) = Ξ(t)/∑_{t′} Ξ(t′). For c ≡ 1, Ξ ≡ 1 and T is uniform.

applications.title: Exact law of Wilson's method on a weighted triangle network
applications.inputs: The triangle network on states 0, 1, 2 with conductances c(01) = 1, c(12) = 2, c(02) = 3. Then π(0) = 4, π(1) = 3, π(2) = 5. The root is r = 0, and the order of the other states is 1, 2.
applications.hypotheses: The triangle is a finite connected simple graph, and every conductance is positive. So the network walk is an irreducible chain on three states, and both parts of the theorem apply.

steps.text: First run from 1 to {0}. From 1 the walk goes to 0 with probability 1/3 and to 2 with probability 2/3. From 2 it goes to 0 with probability 3/5 and back to 1 with probability 2/5, which erases the loop. With a = P(loop erasure is ⟨1, 0⟩), a = 1/3 + (2/3)(2/5)a, so a = 5/11.
Second run. If the first path is ⟨1, 0⟩, the walk from 2 hits {0, 1} at 0 with probability 3/5 and at 1 with probability 2/5. This gives the tree {01, 02} with probability (5/11)(3/5) = 3/11.

The tree {01, 12} has probability (5/11)(2/5) = 2/11. The first path is ⟨1, 2, 0⟩ with probability 6/11, and it gives the tree {12, 02}. The weights Ξ of the three trees are 1 · 3 = 3, 1 · 2 = 2 and 2 · 3 = 6, with sum 11. So the method gives exactly Ξ(t)/11, as the theorem states.

Kirchhoff check. P(01 ∈ T) = 3/11 + 2/11 = 5/11. The effective resistance between 0 and 1 is the parallel sum of 1 and 1/2 + 1/3 = 5/6, which is (5/6)/(1 + 5/6) = 5/11. So P(01 ∈ T) = c(01) R_eff(0 ↔ 1), which is Kirchhoff's formula for the weighted spanning tree.

applications.conclusion: On the weighted triangle with conductances 1, 2, 3, Wilson's method from root 0 returns the trees {01, 02}, {01, 12}, {12, 02} with probabilities 3/11, 2/11, 6/11. These are the conductance products divided by 11, and the edge probability 5/11 agrees with Kirchhoff's effective resistance formula.

limitations: The theorem gives the law of the output but not the running time. By Exercise 4.25 of the source, the expected number of steps is ∑_x π(x)(E_x[τ_r] + E_r[τ_x]), with π the stationary distribution.
The statement is for finite chains. On an infinite transient network, Wilson's method rooted at infinity gives the wired uniform spanning forest (Proposition 10.1 of the source).

For a chain that is not reversible, the unoriented tree has a law proportional to Ψ of its orientation toward r, and this law depends on r in general. Only the reversible case gives the law Ξ, which does not depend on the root.

results.name: Varopoulos–Carne bound
results.statement: Let G = (V, E) be a countable connected graph with at least two vertices and graph distance d, and let c(x, y) = c(y, x) > 0 be conductances on its edges with π(x) = Σ_y c(x, y) < ∞ for every x. Let P(x, y) = c(x, y)/π(x) be the transition probabilities of the network random walk, let p_n(x, y) be its n-step transition probabilities, and let ‖P‖_π be the norm of P as an operator on ℓ²(V, π), with inner product (f, g)_π = Σ_x π(x) f(x) g(x). Then for all x, y ∈ V and every n ≥ 1, p_n(x, y) ≤ 2 √(π(y)/π(x)) ‖P‖_π^n exp(−d(x, y)²/(2n)).
hypotheses: G = (V, E) is a countable connected graph with at least two vertices and graph distance d.
The conductances satisfy c(x, y) = c(y, x) > 0 on edges, and π(x) = Σ_y c(x, y) is finite for every x. The walk has P(x, y) = c(x, y)/π(x), so it is reversible with respect to π.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 uses the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality to show that P is a contraction of ℓ²(V, π), and step s5 bounds (f_x, T_k(S) f_y)_π by ‖T_k(S)‖.
Step s1 exchanges the sums over x and y of nonnegative terms when it computes ‖Pf‖²_π, which Tonelli's theorem allows.
Step s3 expands ((w + w⁻¹)/2)^n by the binomial theorem to get the law q_n of simple random walk on ℤ.
Step s3 uses de Moivre's formula (e^(iθ))^k = cos kθ + i sin kθ to take the real part of the binomial expansion.
Step s4 diagonalizes the truncated operator S in an orthonormal eigenbasis of the finite-dimensional space H_B to bound ‖T_k(S)‖ by 1.
Step s6 applies Markov's inequality to e^(λS_n) to get the Chernoff bound for simple random walk on ℤ.
Step s7 lets the finite sets B increase to V and passes to the limit in the path sums by monotone convergence.

definitions.name: network random walk
definitions.text: The Markov chain on V with P(x, y) = c(x, y)/π(x), π(x) = Σ_y c(x, y). It is reversible: π(x)P(x, y) = c(x, y) = π(y)P(y, x).

definitions.name: ℓ²(V, π) and ‖P‖_π
definitions.text: The Hilbert space of functions f on V with Σ_x π(x) f(x)² < ∞. The number ‖P‖_π = sup{‖Pf‖_π : ‖f‖_π ≤ 1} is the operator norm of P on it.

definitions.name: Chebyshev polynomials
definitions.text: The polynomials T_k, k ∈ ℤ, with T_k(cos θ) = cos kθ and T_(−k) = T_k. T_k has degree |k| and |T_k(s)| ≤ 1 for s ∈ [−1, 1].

definitions.name: law of simple random walk on ℤ
definitions.text: q_n(k) = P(S_n = k) = 2^(−n) C(n, (n + k)/2) if |k| ≤ n and n + k is even, and q_n(k) = 0 otherwise.

source.citation: Russell Lyons and Yuval Peres, Probability on Trees and Networks, Cambridge Series in Statistical and Probabilistic Mathematics 42, Cambridge University Press, 2016.
source.revision: Corrected and updated paperback edition, authors' online version of 19 August 2026, 716 pages.
source.module: Chapter 13, Section 13.2 The Varopoulos–Carne Bound
source.excerpt: Theorem 13.4. (Varopoulos–Carne Bound) For any reversible random walk, we have p_n(x, y) ≤ 2 √(π(y)/π(x)) ‖P‖_π^n e^{−d(x,y)²/(2n)}.
source.attribution: © Russell Lyons and Yuval Peres. Quoted from Probability on Trees and Networks for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states the bound for any reversible (network) random walk in the setting of its Chapters 2 and 6. The authored statement makes the countable connected graph, the conductances and the space ℓ²(V, π) explicit. The authored proof follows the source proof (Lemma 13.5 with Chebyshev polynomials and the tail bound (13.11) for simple random walk on ℤ). The source gets the operator inequality (13.12) in infinite dimensions from Exercise 13.30 or from the spectral theorem in Section 13.9. The authored proof truncates P to finite vertex sets and uses only the finite-dimensional spectral theorem.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the Chebyshev polynomial proof of Theorem 13.4 in Lyons and Peres, with a truncation to finite vertex sets. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement for every countable connected network with finite vertex weights, every pair of vertices and every n ≥ 1.

steps.text: The operator P. For f, g in ℓ²(V, π), (f, Pg)_π = Σ_{x,y} c(x, y) f(x) g(y), which is symmetric in f and g, so P is self-adjoint. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality for the weights P(x, ·), (Pf(x))² ≤ Σ_y P(x, y) f(y)². Tonelli's theorem then gives ‖Pf‖²_π ≤ Σ_y f(y)² Σ_x c(x, y) = ‖f‖²_π, so ‖P‖_π ≤ 1. For neighbours u and v, (1_u, P1_v)_π = c(u, v) > 0, so ‖P‖_π > 0.

Truncation. Fix x, y and a finite set B ⊂ V that contains x and y. Let H_B be the finite-dimensional space of functions supported in B, and let P_B = 1_B P 1_B, which maps H_B to H_B. For g, h in H_B, (g, P_B h)_π = (g, Ph)_π, so P_B is self-adjoint on H_B, and ‖P_B‖ ≤ ‖P‖_π. Put f_x = 1_x/√π(x) and f_y = 1_y/√π(y), two unit vectors. Expanding the matrix product gives (P_B^n 1_y)(x) = p_n^B(x, y), the sum of P(z₀, z₁)⋯P(z_{n−1}, z_n) over paths x = z₀, …, z_n = y with all z_j ∈ B. Hence p_n^B(x, y) = √(π(y)/π(x)) (f_x, P_B^n f_y)_π. A path from x to y has at least d = d(x, y) steps, so (f_x, P_B^i f_y)_π = 0 for 0 ≤ i < d.

Chebyshev expansion. For s = cos θ and w = e^(iθ), the binomial theorem gives s^n = ((w + w⁻¹)/2)^n = Σ_{k∈ℤ} q_n(k) w^k, where q_n is the law of simple random walk on ℤ after n steps. By de Moivre's formula the real part of w^k is cos kθ = T_k(s), so s^n = Σ_k q_n(k) T_k(s) for every s ∈ [−1, 1]. Two polynomials that agree on infinitely many points are equal, so the identity holds as polynomials. Substituting the operator S = P_B/‖P‖_π gives S^n = Σ_k q_n(k) T_k(S), that is P_B^n = ‖P‖_π^n Σ_k q_n(k) T_k(S).

Spectral bound. The operator S is self-adjoint on the finite-dimensional inner product space H_B, so it has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues λ_j. Since ‖S‖ ≤ ‖P‖_π/‖P‖_π = 1, every |λ_j| ≤ 1. In the same basis T_k(S) is diagonal with entries T_k(λ_j) ∈ [−1, 1], so ‖T_k(S)‖ ≤ 1 for every k.

Combination. By steps s2 and s3, p_n^B(x, y) = √(π(y)/π(x)) ‖P‖_π^n Σ_k q_n(k) (f_x, T_k(S) f_y)_π. If |k| < d, T_k(S) is a linear combination of S⁰, …, S^|k|, so (f_x, T_k(S) f_y)_π = 0 by step s2. If |k| ≥ d, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and step s4 give |(f_x, T_k(S) f_y)_π| ≤ ‖T_k(S)‖ ‖f_x‖_π ‖f_y‖_π ≤ 1. Hence p_n^B(x, y) ≤ √(π(y)/π(x)) ‖P‖_π^n Σ_{|k|≥d} q_n(k).

Tail of simple random walk. Σ_{|k|≥d} q_n(k) = P(|S_n| ≥ d) for simple random walk S_n on ℤ. If d = 0 this is 1 ≤ 2. If d ≥ 1, for λ > 0 Markov's inequality gives P(S_n ≥ d) ≤ e^(−λd) E e^(λS_n) = e^(−λd)(cosh λ)^n. Term by term, λ^(2m)/(2m)! ≤ λ^(2m)/(2^m m!), so cosh λ ≤ e^(λ²/2) and P(S_n ≥ d) ≤ e^(−λd + nλ²/2). The choice λ = d/n gives e^(−d²/(2n)). By symmetry P(S_n ≤ −d) is the same, so Σ_{|k|≥d} q_n(k) ≤ 2e^(−d²/(2n)).

Removal of the truncation. Steps s5 and s6 give p_n^B(x, y) ≤ 2√(π(y)/π(x)) ‖P‖_π^n e^(−d²/(2n)) for every finite B that contains x and y, and the bound does not depend on B. Let B_m be finite sets that contain x and y and increase to the countable set V. Each path of length n from x to y lies in B_m for all large m, so the path sums p_n^(B_m)(x, y) increase to p_n(x, y) by monotone convergence. The bound therefore holds for p_n(x, y).

applications.title: Uniform Gaussian bound for the random conductance model on ℤ²
applications.inputs: The square lattice ℤ² with nearest-neighbour edges and conductances c(e) ∈ [1, 2], chosen arbitrarily or at random (an environment of the random conductance model). The walk is the network random walk. Time n = 100 and two sites x, y at lattice distance ‖x − y‖₁ = 40.
applications.hypotheses: ℤ² is a countable connected graph, and its graph distance is the ℓ¹ distance. Every conductance is positive, and π(x) is a sum of four conductances, so 4 ≤ π(x) ≤ 8 is finite. The bound holds in every environment, with no averaging over the disorder.

steps.text: Prefactor. Since 4 ≤ π ≤ 8, the ratio π(y)/π(x) is at most 8/4 = 2, so √(π(y)/π(x)) ≤ √2. Step s1 of the proof gives ‖P‖_π ≤ 1. The theorem gives p_n(x, y) ≤ 2√2 exp(−‖x − y‖₁²/(2n)) for every environment.
Exponent for n = 100 and ‖x − y‖₁ = 40: 40²/(2 · 100) = 8. So p_100(x, y) ≤ 2√2 e^(−8), which is about 9.5 × 10⁻⁴.

Displacement tail. There are 4j sites at ℓ¹ distance j ≥ 1 from x, and p_n(x, y) = 0 if ‖x − y‖₁ > n. Summing the bound gives P_x(‖X_n − x‖₁ ≥ r) ≤ 8√2 Σ_{j=r}^{n} j e^(−j²/(2n)). For n = 100 and r = 60 the sum gives a bound of about 2.3 × 10⁻⁵.

Diffusive scale. The bound is small once r is a large multiple of √n. So in every environment with conductances in [1, 2], the walk moves at most a distance of order √(n log n) in n steps with high probability, the same scale as for the homogeneous lattice.

applications.conclusion: For the random conductance model on ℤ² with conductances in [1, 2], p_n(x, y) ≤ 2√2 exp(−‖x − y‖₁²/(2n)) in every environment. For n = 100 the walk is farther than 60 lattice steps from its start with probability at most about 2.3 × 10⁻⁵.

limitations: The bound is an upper bound only. It has the Gaussian exponent with constant 1/2 for every graph and gives no matching lower bound.
The bound needs reversibility. For a nonreversible walk the operator P is not self-adjoint and the Chebyshev expansion argument fails.
When ‖P‖_π < 1, as on nonamenable graphs, the factor ‖P‖_π^n adds exponential decay in n. On ℤ^d, ‖P‖_π = 1 and only the Gaussian factor remains.

results.name: Gaussian correlation inequality
results.statement: Let μ be a centered Gaussian measure on ℝ^d, possibly degenerate, and let K, L ⊂ ℝ^d be closed convex sets that are symmetric (K = −K and L = −L). Then μ(K ∩ L) ≥ μ(K) μ(L). Equivalently, for every centered Gaussian vector X = (X₁, …, X_n) with n = n₁ + n₂ and all t₁, …, t_n > 0, P(|X₁| ≤ t₁, …, |X_n| ≤ t_n) ≥ P(|X₁| ≤ t₁, …, |X_{n₁}| ≤ t_{n₁}) · P(|X_{n₁+1}| ≤ t_{n₁+1}, …, |X_n| ≤ t_n).
hypotheses: μ is a centered Gaussian measure on ℝ^d. Its covariance matrix may be singular.
K and L are closed, convex and symmetric about the origin.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 writes each closed symmetric convex set as a countable intersection of symmetric strips with the Hahn-Banach separation theorem.
Step s1 removes the nondegeneracy assumption by a limit, and step s2 uses Lemma 6 of the source, which is a dominated convergence argument, to differentiate under the integral.
Step s3 uses the principal axis theorem in Lemma 4 of the source to compute the Gaussian integral of exp(−⟨Ax, x⟩).
Step s3 uses the Weinstein–Aronszajn identity |I + A₁A₂| = |I + A₂A₁| in Lemma 4 of the source to get |I + ΛC|.
Step s3 uses the expansion |I + A| = 1 + ∑_J |A_J| of Lemma 5 i) of the source, which follows from the Laplace expansion by induction on n.
Step s5 uses Fubini's theorem in Lemmas 7 and 8 of the source to compute the total mass and the Laplace transform of the density h_{3,C}.
Step s6 integrates the mixed derivative of h_τ over the box K one variable at a time with the fundamental theorem of calculus.

definitions.name: centered Gaussian measure
definitions.text: The law N(0, C) on ℝ^d of a random vector X such that ⟨v, X⟩ is a centered normal variable for every v ∈ ℝ^d. Its covariance matrix C is positive semidefinite.

definitions.name: symmetric set
definitions.text: A set K ⊂ ℝ^d with K = −K, that is, x ∈ K exactly when −x ∈ K.

definitions.name: symmetric strip
definitions.text: A set {x ∈ ℝ^d : |⟨x, v⟩| ≤ t} with v ∈ ℝ^d and t ≥ 0. It is closed, convex and symmetric.

source.citation: Rafał Latała and Dariusz Matlak, Royen's proof of the Gaussian correlation inequality, in: Geometric Aspects of Functional Analysis, Israel Seminar (GAFA) 2014–2016, Lecture Notes in Mathematics 2169, Springer, 2017, pp. 265–275.
source.revision: arXiv:1512.08776v1 of 29 December 2015, 9 pages.
source.module: Section 1 Introduction (Theorem 2), Section 2 Proof of Theorem 2, Section 3 Auxiliary Lemmas
source.excerpt: Theorem 2. Let n = n₁ + n₂ and X be an n-dimensional centered Gaussian vector. Then for any t₁, …, t_n > 0, P(|X₁| ≤ t₁, …, |X_n| ≤ t_n) ≥ P(|X₁| ≤ t₁, …, |X_{n₁}| ≤ t_{n₁}) P(|X_{n₁+1}| ≤ t_{n₁+1}, …, |X_n| ≤ t_n).
source.attribution: © Rafał Latała and Dariusz Matlak. Quoted from Royen's proof of the Gaussian correlation inequality for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source states the set form as Theorem 1 on p. 1 and the equivalent strip form as Theorem 2 on p. 2. In arXiv v1, Theorem 1 omits the word convex, which the abstract and the reduction to strips need, so the declaration cites Theorem 2. The authored statement gives both forms and allows a degenerate covariance. The outline follows the proof of Theorem 2 in Section 2 of the source, which presents Royen's 2014 proof, with Lemmas 4 to 8 of Section 3.

results.proof_status: outline of the cited published proof. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: Outline: the steps follow the proof of Theorem 2 in Latała and Matlak (arXiv 1512.08776), Section 2, pp. 2-4, which presents Royen's proof. Steps s2, s3 and s5 cite Lemmas 4 to 8 of the source (pp. 4-9) for the differentiation under the integral, the Laplace transform of Gaussian squares, the determinant identities and the gamma-type densities.

steps.text: Reduction to strips. A closed symmetric convex set is an intersection of countably many symmetric strips {|⟨x, v⟩| ≤ t}: separate it from small rational balls outside it with the Hahn-Banach separation theorem, and symmetrize each half-space. By continuity of μ along decreasing intersections, it is enough to take K and L as finite intersections of strips. With X_i = ⟨v_i, G⟩ for G ∼ μ, this is Theorem 2. Strips with t_i = 0 follow from t_i + ε as ε ↓ 0. For t_i > 0 the events {|X_i| = t_i} are null, so replacing C by C + εI and letting ε → 0 lets us assume that the covariance matrix C of X is positive definite.

Interpolation. Write C in blocks C_{ij} of size n_i × n_j and set C(τ) = [[C₁₁, τC₁₂], [τC₂₁, C₂₂]] = τC(1) + (1 − τ)C(0) for τ ∈ [0, 1], a positive definite matrix. Let X(τ) ∼ N(0, C(τ)), Z_i(τ) = X_i(τ)²/2 and s_i = t_i²/2. Under C(0) the two blocks are independent, so Theorem 2 says F(1) ≥ F(0) for F(τ) = P(Z(τ) ∈ K), K = [0, s₁] × ⋯ × [0, s_n]. Let f(x, τ) be the density of Z(τ). Lemma 6 of the source gives an integrable bound on sup_τ |∂f/∂τ| and so F′(τ) = ∫_K ∂f/∂τ(x, τ) dx. It remains to show that this integral is nonnegative.

Laplace transform. Lemma 4 of the source computes E exp(−½∑ λ_i X_i²) = |I + ΛC|^(−1/2) for Λ = diag(λ₁, …, λ_n) ≥ 0, by the principal axis theorem and |I + A₁A₂| = |I + A₂A₁|. So ∫ e^(−⟨λ, x⟩) f(x, τ) dx = |I + ΛC(τ)|^(−1/2), and by Lemma 6 the τ-derivative passes under this integral. Lemma 5 i) gives |I + ΛC(τ)| = 1 + ∑_{∅≠J⊂[n]} |C(τ)_J| ∏_{j∈J} λ_j, where C(τ)_J is the principal submatrix on J.

Monotone minors. Split J = J₁ ∪ J₂ with J₁ = J ∩ [n₁]. If J₁ or J₂ is empty, C(τ)_J = C_J does not depend on τ. Otherwise the Schur complement formula (3) of Lemma 5 gives |C(τ)_J| = |C_{J₁}| |C_{J₂}| ∏_{i=1}^{|J₁|} (1 − τ² ν_i), where ν_i are the eigenvalues of C_{J₁}^(−1/2) C_{J₁J₂} C_{J₂}^(−1) C_{J₂J₁} C_{J₁}^(−1/2). By (4) of Lemma 5 they lie in [0, 1], so each factor is nonnegative and nonincreasing in τ. Hence a_J(τ) = −∂|C(τ)_J|/∂τ ≥ 0, and ∂/∂τ |I + ΛC(τ)|^(−1/2) = ½ |I + ΛC(τ)|^(−3/2) ∑_J a_J(τ) ∏_{j∈J} λ_j.

Gamma-type densities. Lemmas 7 and 8 of the source build, for a positive definite C, a probability density h_{3,C} on (0, ∞)^n with ∫ e^(−⟨λ, x⟩) h_{3,C}(x) dx = |I + ΛC|^(−3/2). It is a mixture of products of gamma densities with shapes 3/2 + k, k ≥ 0. It is built from C = ηI + AAᵀ with η > 0 and three independent copies of N(0, AAᵀ/(2η)). Since the parameter 3/2 is above 1, Lemma 7 iii) shows that ∂^{|J|} h/∂x_J is integrable and has the Laplace transform ∏_{j∈J} λ_j times that of h. With h_τ = h_{3,C(τ)}, the two sides of ∂f/∂τ = ∑_{∅≠J} ½ a_J(τ) ∂^{|J|} h_τ/∂x_J have the same Laplace transform for all λ ≥ 0, so they are equal almost everywhere.

Integration over the box. Lemma 7 ii) of the source gives lim_{x_i→0+} ∂^{|I|} h_τ/∂x_I = 0 for i ∉ I. Integrate ∂^{|J|} h_τ/∂x_J over K in the variables x_j, j ∈ J, one at a time with the fundamental theorem of calculus. The lower limits give 0, so ∫_K ∂^{|J|} h_τ/∂x_J dx = ∫_{∏_{j∉J}[0, s_j]} h_τ(s_J, x_{J^c}) dx_{J^c} ≥ 0, because h_τ ≥ 0. With a_J(τ) ≥ 0 this gives F′(τ) ≥ 0. So F is nondecreasing on [0, 1], F(1) ≥ F(0), and Theorem 2 follows.

source.ref: R. Latała and D. Matlak, Royen's proof of the Gaussian correlation inequality, arXiv:1512.08776v1 (GAFA Seminar 2014-2016, LNM 2169, 2017), Theorem 2, Section 2, pp. 2-4, and Lemmas 4-8, pp. 4-9.

applications.title: Joint coverage of confidence regions for two groups of parameters
applications.inputs: An estimator θ̂ ∈ ℝ⁵ with θ̂ − θ ∼ N(0, Σ) and a known positive definite Σ. Group A is (θ₁, θ₂), with the ellipse region R_A = {θ : (θ̂_A − θ_A)ᵀ Σ_AA^(−1) (θ̂_A − θ_A) ≤ q}, q = 2 ln 20 ≈ 5.99. Group B is (θ₃, θ₄, θ₅), with the box region R_B = {θ : max_{i∈B} |θ̂_i − θ_i| ≤ c}, where c is chosen from Σ_BB alone so that P(θ ∈ R_B) = 0.95. The cross-covariance Σ_AB is unknown.
applications.hypotheses: The law μ = N(0, Σ) of θ̂ − θ is a centered Gaussian measure on ℝ⁵. The set K = {x : x_Aᵀ Σ_AA^(−1) x_A ≤ q} is a sublevel set of a positive semidefinite quadratic form, so it is closed, convex and symmetric. The set L = {x : max_{i∈B} |x_i| ≤ c} is an intersection of three symmetric strips.

steps.text: Coverage of R_A. For x ∼ N(0, Σ), x_Aᵀ Σ_AA^(−1) x_A has the chi-squared law with 2 degrees of freedom, so P(K) = 1 − e^(−q/2). With q = 2 ln 20 this is 1 − 1/20 = 19/20.
Joint coverage. The event {θ ∈ R_A and θ ∈ R_B} is {θ̂ − θ ∈ K ∩ L}. The theorem gives μ(K ∩ L) ≥ μ(K) μ(L) = (19/20)² = 361/400 = 0.9025, for every cross-covariance Σ_AB.
Comparison with the Bonferroni bound. The union bound gives only 1 − 1/20 − 1/20 = 9/10 = 0.90. The correlation inequality gains (1/20)² = 0.0025, and it needs no model for Σ_AB.
Sharpness. If Σ_AB = 0, the two groups are independent and μ(K ∩ L) = μ(K) μ(L) = 0.9025 exactly. So 0.9025 is the best bound that holds for all cross-covariances.

applications.conclusion: Two 95% confidence regions with symmetric convex shapes, one for each group, have joint coverage at least 0.9025 for every correlation between the groups. This is better than the Bonferroni bound 0.90 and is attained when the groups are independent.

limitations: The inequality needs both sets to be symmetric. For a Gaussian measure and nonsymmetric convex sets the inequality can fail.
The theorem gives no rate or stability: it does not say how much μ(K ∩ L) exceeds μ(K) μ(L) when the sets are correlated.
Remark 3 of the source notes the extension to centered Gaussian measures on separable Banach spaces by approximation, and Royen's original proof covers some multivariate gamma laws.

results.name: Kac's lemma
results.statement: Let (X_n)_{n≥0} be a stationary sequence of random variables with values in a measurable space (S, 𝒮): for every k ≥ 0 the shifted sequence (X_{k+n})_{n≥0} has the same law as (X_n)_{n≥0}. Let A ∈ 𝒮 with P(X_0 ∈ A) > 0, and let T_A = inf{n ≥ 1 : X_n ∈ A}, with inf ∅ = ∞, be the first return time to A. Then E[T_A 1{X_0 ∈ A}] = P(X_n ∈ A for some n ≥ 0). In particular T_A < ∞ almost surely on {X_0 ∈ A}. If moreover P(X_n ∈ A for some n ≥ 0) = 1, then E[T_A | X_0 ∈ A] = 1/P(X_0 ∈ A).
hypotheses: The sequence (X_n)_{n≥0} is stationary: each shifted sequence (X_{k+n})_{n≥0} has the same law as (X_n)_{n≥0}.
The measurable set A satisfies P(X_0 ∈ A) > 0. For the last formula, A is visited at some time n ≥ 0 almost surely.

prerequisites.reason: Step s1 writes E[T_A 1{X_0 ∈ A}] as a series of tail probabilities, and step s4 passes to the limit in K, both by the monotone convergence theorem.

definitions.name: stationary sequence
definitions.text: A sequence (X_n)_{n≥0} such that for every k ≥ 0 and m ≥ 0 the vectors (X_k, …, X_{k+m}) and (X_0, …, X_m) have the same law.

definitions.name: first return time
definitions.text: T_A = inf{n ≥ 1 : X_n ∈ A}, the first time after 0 at which the sequence is in A. It equals ∞ if the sequence never returns.

definitions.name: measure-preserving form
definitions.text: If T preserves a probability μ and X_n(ω) = T^n ω, then (X_n) is stationary under μ, and the lemma reads ∫_A T_A dμ = μ(⋃_{n≥0} T^(−n)A).

source.citation: Rick Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, fifth edition, Cambridge University Press, 2019.
source.revision: Author's online version 5 of January 11, 2019 (PDF created 2019-03-29), 490 pages.
source.module: Chapter 6, Section 6.3 Recurrence
source.excerpt: Theorem 6.3.3. If P(X_n ∈ A at least once) = 1, then under P(·|X_0 ∈ A), t_n = T_n − T_{n−1} is a stationary sequence with E(T_1|X_0 ∈ A) = 1/P(X_0 ∈ A).
source.attribution: © Rick Durrett. Quoted from Probability: Theory and Examples, fifth edition, for identification of the cited result.
source.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
source.alignment: The source assumes that A is visited almost surely, proves that the gaps between returns are stationary under P(·|X_0 ∈ A), and gives the mean return time 1/P(X_0 ∈ A). The authored statement keeps only the mean return time, and it adds the identity E[T_A 1{X_0 ∈ A}] = P(X_n ∈ A for some n ≥ 0) without the visiting hypothesis. The source extends the sequence to negative times (Theorem 6.1.4) and decomposes by the last visit before time 0. The authored proof uses the same last-visit decomposition inside the window {0, …, K − 1}, so it needs no two-sided extension.

results.proof_status: authored proof that follows the last-visit decomposition in the proof of Theorem 6.3.3 in Durrett, inside a finite time window. No local formal verification.

proof.verification: No local formal verification. No accepted judgment exists yet.
proof.scope: The full statement: the identity without extra hypotheses, the almost sure finiteness of T_A on {X_0 ∈ A}, and the mean return time under the visiting hypothesis.

steps.text: Tail sum. The variable T_A takes values in {1, 2, …} ∪ {∞}, and T_A = Σ_{k≥1} 1{T_A ≥ k}, also when T_A = ∞. For k ≥ 1, {T_A ≥ k} = {X_1 ∉ A, …, X_{k−1} ∉ A} (for k = 1 this is the whole space). Put E_k = {X_0 ∈ A, X_1 ∉ A, …, X_{k−1} ∉ A}. The monotone convergence theorem applied to the partial sums gives E[T_A 1{X_0 ∈ A}] = Σ_{k≥1} P(E_k), where both sides may be infinite at this point.

Shift by stationarity. Fix K ≥ 1 and 1 ≤ k ≤ K. The vector (X_{K−k}, …, X_{K−1}) has the same law as (X_0, …, X_{k−1}), because the sequence is stationary and K − k ≥ 0. Hence P(E_k) = P(F_k), where F_k = {X_{K−k} ∈ A and X_j ∉ A for every j with K − k < j ≤ K − 1}.

Last-visit decomposition. The event F_k says that K − k is the last time j in the window {0, 1, …, K − 1} with X_j ∈ A. Different values of k give different last times, so F_1, …, F_K are pairwise disjoint. Their union is the event G_K that X_j ∈ A for some 0 ≤ j ≤ K − 1, because on G_K the last such time j exists and equals K − k for exactly one k between 1 and K. Hence Σ_{k=1}^K P(E_k) = Σ_{k=1}^K P(F_k) = P(G_K).

Limit. As K → ∞, the left side of step s3 increases to Σ_{k≥1} P(E_k), and G_K increases to G = {X_n ∈ A for some n ≥ 0}, so P(G_K) → P(G) by monotone convergence of indicators. With step s1, E[T_A 1{X_0 ∈ A}] = P(G) ≤ 1. A nonnegative variable with finite mean is finite almost surely, so T_A < ∞ almost surely on {X_0 ∈ A}. If P(G) = 1, division by P(X_0 ∈ A) > 0 gives E[T_A | X_0 ∈ A] = E[T_A 1{X_0 ∈ A}]/P(X_0 ∈ A) = 1/P(X_0 ∈ A).

applications.title: Mean recurrence time in the Ehrenfest urn model
applications.inputs: The Ehrenfest model with N = 10 molecules in two halves of a box. At each step one molecule, chosen uniformly, moves to the other half. X_n is the number of molecules in the left half, a Markov chain on {0, 1, …, 10} with P(k, k − 1) = k/10 and P(k, k + 1) = (10 − k)/10.
applications.hypotheses: Start the chain from π(k) = C(10, k)/2^10. Then every shifted chain has the same law, so (X_n) is stationary. The chain is finite and irreducible, so it visits each state almost surely. Given X_0 = j, the chain is the chain started at j by the Markov property, so E[T_{{j}} | X_0 = j] = E_j T_j.

steps.text: Stationarity of π. Detailed balance π(k)(10 − k)/10 = π(k + 1)(k + 1)/10 holds because C(10, k)(10 − k) = C(10, k + 1)(k + 1). Summation of detailed balance π(x)P(x, y) = π(y)P(y, x) over x gives πP = π, so the chain started from π is a stationary sequence.
Ordered state. For A = {0} (all molecules in the right half), π(0) = 2^(−10). Kac's lemma gives E_0 T_0 = 1/π(0) = 2^10 = 1024 steps.
Balanced state. For A = {5}, π(5) = C(10, 5)/2^10 = 252/1024. Kac's lemma gives E_5 T_5 = 1024/252 = 256/63, about 4.06 steps.

Macroscopic box. The same argument with N molecules gives E_0 T_0 = 2^N. For N = 100 this is 2^100, about 1.27 × 10^30 steps. A return to the ordered state is certain by step s4 of the proof, but its mean waiting time is astronomically long.

applications.conclusion: In the Ehrenfest model with 10 molecules, the mean time to return to the state with all molecules on one side is 1024 steps, while the balanced state recurs about every 4.06 steps. The ratio π(5)/π(0) = 252 explains why recurrence (Poincaré, Zermelo) does not contradict the observed approach to equilibrium.

limitations: The lemma gives only the mean return time. The law of T_A can be far from geometric, and its variance can be infinite.

For an irreducible Markov chain on a countable set with a stationary distribution π, the lemma gives E_x T_x = 1/π(x) once one knows that the stationary chain visits x almost surely, which holds because such a chain is recurrent.

Without the visiting hypothesis the mean return time is P(X_n ∈ A for some n ≥ 0)/P(X_0 ∈ A). It is smaller than 1/P(X_0 ∈ A) when A is missed with positive probability, which can happen only for a nonergodic sequence.
